Following this, we had a discussion with the junior doctors in the department, who do this documentation, to make them aware of the BT guidelines, and to improve adherence. The 2nd-cycle included retrospective data collection from 01.09.2023 to 15.102023. Results BT-documentation during the 2nd-cycle showed significant improvement to adherence above 80% in most of the criteria where it needed improvement in the 1st-cycle. Conclusions This clinical audit successfully improved the BT-documentation adherence to the guidelines, showing that through simple educational methods, the documentation practices could be improved significantly. Our plan for subsequent improvement includes posters in the departmental resource room to increase the awareness, and to re-audit in December 2023.
affiliations: East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust , Ashford , United Kingdom
University of Plymouth , Plymouth , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.217.title: 310 Documentation and Consent Audit in HPB Patients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.217.abstract: Abstract Aim Investigating documented information relating to the care of the hepatobiliary patients to ensure record-keeping standards are being met and written consent for procedures are recorded in accordance to trust and national guidance. Method 17 patient files, selected at random, were included in this audit. Microsoft Forms application was utilised to complete the data collection. The files were audited against trust guidelines regarding documentation and consent. Results Although all entries were legible and signed oftentimes GMC number and designation was omitted (81%). Allergy status and drug history had also been omitted from most records (62 and 63% respectively). Regarding consent, all forms were present in the notes, and all properly described the name/ benefits/ risks of the procedure. In 77% of consent forms, it was not documented whether an information leaflet has been provided to the patient. Only the minority of patients received a carbon copy of their consent form (23%). When the carbon copy remained in the patient’s file, the consenter had failed to circle “no” indicating patient did not accept the copy in every case. Abbreviations were used in over half of the consent forms audited (54%). Conclusions Key areas for improvement in documentation and consent were underlined by this audit. Proper and clear highlighting of patient’s allergies and drug histories is an important area for improvement regarding documentation. Consenters should make more efforts to offer patient information leaflets and carbon copies of consent forms to patients and to document this appropriately.
affiliations: University Hospital Coventry & Warwickshire , Coventry , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.219.title: 322 Correlation Between Quantitative Faecal Immunochemical Test (qFIT) and Colorectal Operation - Clinical Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.219.abstract: Abstract Aim To uncover any potential link between quantitative faecal immunochemical test (qFIT) result, and the colorectal operation performed; and to give insight that could assist future work in creating a tool clinicians could use to earlier predict tumour site or guide the treatment and management of colorectal cancer. Preliminary search does not show this has been studied before. Method Data was collected through a clinical audit with the Centre for Colorectal Surgery in Belfast City Hospital. This retrospective study into 208 patients who had an operation with the centre during 2022, manually checked the available 161 case notes of which 63 had a qFIT result. Then explored for any correlations between qFIT result to operation, tumour location, stage, and age. Results Patients that got a positive qFIT<100, 47.1% had a R Hemi or Extended R Hemi. 41.2% of positive qFIT<100 had an R hemi. 40% of positive qFIT<200 had a R hemi. 47.6% of qFIT results were 400+. 27.0% of the patient population got a qFIT<100. qFIT correlated with tumour stage and of the patients studied, 0 had died at the time of audit. Conclusions A link between positive qFIT<100 and Right Hemicolectomy was observed. A finding that could impact care of patients with colorectal cancer.
affiliations: Queen's University Belfast School of Medicine, Dentistry and Biomedical Sciences , Belfast , United Kingdom
Centre of Colorectal Surgery Belfast City Hospital - Belfast Health & Social Care Trust , Belfast , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.221.title: 329 An Audit into the Prescription of Maintenance IV Fluids for General Surgery Patients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.221.abstract: Abstract Introduction Intravenous (IV) fluids are vital for maintaining surgical patients in a "nil by mouth" (NBM) state. They prevent dehydration, maintain electrolyte balance, support perfusion, provide nutrition, administer medications, stabilize blood pressure, monitor fluid balance, and address emergencies. The central objective of this audit is to assess the level of adherence to NICE guidelines in the surgical department concerning the prescription of IV fluids. Method During the pre-intervention phase, a two-week audit was conducted across three surgical wards where patients were in a nil by mouth (NBM) state. Each day, the audit involved a comprehensive review of patient records and drug charts. Additionally, inquiries were made with the respective nurses in charge to gather information on the IV fluids administered to the patients. The Intervention phase was also two weeks, across the same surgical wards. Intervention included a proforma and teaching to foundation doctors on the ward, to comply with NICE guidelines. Results The first cycle showed that no patients were given IV fluids according to NICE guidelines. The NICE guidelines state the following: According to the NICE guidelines, the recommended daily maintenance fluid requirements consist of:25-30 ml/kg/day of water,Approximately 1 mmol/kg/day of potassium, sodium, and chloride, andApproximately 50-100 g/day of glucose, primarily to prevent starvation ketosis (although it's important to note that this alone does not address the patient's nutritional needs). Second cycle is currently in progress, but early signs show a positive improvement Conclusions IV fluids are vital for maintaining "nil by mouth" patients.
affiliations: East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust, Hastings, United Kingdom. Gradscape , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.223.title: 341 Improving Plastic Surgery Inpatient Referrals at a Major Trauma Centre: A Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.223.abstract: Abstract Aim Online plastic surgery referrals at the Royal Sussex County Hospital are often incomplete or inappropriate. Establishing reasons for rejection and streamlining referrals will reduce inappropriate referrals and time to assessment and management. Method Referrals between July 2020 and February 2023 were audited, and data used to create a new referral form. Changes included a prerequisite referral checklist, wound assessment section and required clinical photography. Prospective audit was performed over 3 months. Results 1038 referrals were reviewed including 147 rejected referrals (14.2%). The most common reason for rejection was inappropriate referrals (63%), including 31% not requiring surgical intervention and 32% having been referred to the wrong specialty. 41.5% were submitted without clinical photography. Other rejection reasons included patients declining intervention (8.8%), incomplete referrals (7.5%) or duplicates (7.5%). Commonly omitted sections included results (70%), allergies (65%) and medication (16%). Prospective audit after referral form amendments involved 168 new referrals, with 37 rejected (22.0%). The most common reason for rejection remained inappropriate referrals (70.3%, p=0.64). 19% of forms were submitted without clinical photography (p=0.37), despite required confirmation of available photographs. Other rejection reasons included patient declining intervention (10.8%, p=0.09), incomplete referrals (5.4% p=0.07) and duplicates (5.4%, p=0.07). Conclusions Streamlining the referral form reduced incomplete referrals and the number submitted without clinical photography. A prerequisite checklist reduced inappropriate referrals. The new wound assessment section facilitated advice to be given to referrers, diverting patients for local management. The modified referral form will ensure continued improvement in efficiency of the inpatient plastic surgery service.
affiliations: Imperial College , London , United Kingdom
University Hospitals Sussex , Brighton , United Kingdom
Swansea Bay University Health Board , Swansea , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.225.title: 343 Distal Radius Fracture Emergency Analgaesia and Management Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.225.abstract: Abstract Aim To audit analgesia used in the initial management of patients with Distal Radius Fractures (DRFs) that require manipulation against the current standards. Method Standards used were 2018 British Society for Surgery to the Hand (BSSH) guidelines, which recommend intravenous regional anaesthesia and haematoma blocks when manipulating DRFs. Data collection using survey dissemination at 2 tertiary centres included adult patients presenting between 13/08/2022 and 26/11/2022 with DRFs. Exclusion criteria were open fractures, multiple fractures and major trauma. Patient factors and management, with corresponding pain Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) before, during and post manipulation were recorded. Imaging was reviewed to determine radiographic measurements on presentation and in clinic. Data was recorded using REDCap database. Results There were 33 mostly female (F:M 29:4) patients included. Only 24.24% had no co-morbidities. Comorbidities included Hypertension (42.42%), Ischaemic Heart Disease (24.24%) and Asthma (21.21%). Most patients (87.88%) received Methoxyflurane (Penthrox), the remainder had Lidocaine haematoma block. Manipulations were mostly performed by staff from A+E (63.64%). Increased pain scores during manipulation were reported in 64.29% of patients, with a median increase of 7 points. Decreased post manipulation scores were reported in 87.10% with a median decrease of 16 points. Further manipulation was required in 27.27%. Operative fixation was required in 21.21%. Conclusions In conclusion the current guidelines are not being followed in the centres we audited. Methoxyflurane was used for the majority of patients, with good outcomes. Further data is required from multiple centres across the UK to assess whether guidelines need to be updated.
affiliations: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston , Bristol , United Kingdom
Warrington Hospital , Warrington , United Kingdom
Liverpool University Hospitals NHS Trust , Liverpool , United Kingdom
Alder Hey Hospital , Liverpool , United Kingdom
Arrowe Park Hospital , Liverpool , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.226.title: 357 An Audit of Quality of Discharge Summaries in Cardiac Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.226.abstract: Abstract Aim We performed a single-centre closed loop audit assessing the completeness and quality of e-discharge summaries following cardiac surgery against local standards. Method The e-discharge summaries of patients who underwent cardiac surgery form 1/08/2023 to 10/08/2023 were audited against the standards set by the local hospital’s e-discharge summary template. Results and recommendations were shared at a team meeting of the hospital, and on a poster displayed in the MDT office. The same data was then collected for patients who underwent cardiac surgery from 25/10/2023 to 6/11/2023. Results 110 patients were included across 2 cycles. Of 16 domains of interest, 5 were complete in 100% of e-discharge summaries in the first cycle, increasing to 7 in the second. The proportion of summaries with the ‘reason for admission’ misplaced in the clinical summary instead of the allocated field decreased from 43% to 40%, while proportion of GP requests with the reasoning in the allocated box rose from 55% to 57%.For those with no requests to the GP, this was initially specified in the mandatory field as N/A or equivalent in 23% rising to 48% in cycle two, whereas for those who had no ECHOs during the admission, this was specified in 20% initially, rising to 27%. The proportion avoiding acronym use decreased from 17% to 15%. Conclusions Even though compliance improved between the two cycles, the standard of 100% was not met for most criteria. Further team education and revision of the template itself is required to allow information reporting in a succinct, user-friendly format.
affiliations: University of Cambridge, School of Clinical Medicine , Cambridge , United Kingdom
Royal Papworth Hospital, Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery , Cambridge , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.229.title: 372 Imaging in Gynaecomastia: Audit of Imaging Practice at BHRUT to Establish Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.229.abstract: Abstract Aim Our study aim was to audit our imaging practice against national standards to formulate guidelines and standardise practice. Method The authors performed a retrospective data collection of imaging and pathology for clinically suspected gynaecomastia in our breast unit between January and December 2023, using hospital radiology and pathology computer information systems. Data included clinical history, clinical, ultrasound and mammographic scores. Patients with clinical suspicion of malignancy (written on imaging request or P4/P5) were excluded. Descriptive statistics were performed. Results A total of 148 male patients had been referred for imaging with P1 (19), P2 (113), P3 (11) or no P value (34), clinical history stating or querying gynaecomastia. Ultrasound was performed in all patients. All P1 and P2 patients were U1 or U2, and M1 or M2 if mammogram was performed (0/19 P1 patients, 20/113 P2 patients, 4/11 P3 patients). In P1, P2 and no P value patients, 6/166 patients underwent ultrasound-guided biopsy (5/6 B2 gynaecomastia, 1/6 B1 benign angiolipoma). In P3 patients, two biopsies were performed: B2 gynaecomastia in one patient, but one biopsy (M4U4) revealed B5b invasive carcinoma. Conclusions The findings support guideline formulation where imaging is not indicated for typical (P1, P2) gynaecomastia. Imaging should, however, be performed where there is any doubt at all about the clinical diagnosis. The probability of finding cancer when performing imaging of clinically benign findings in the male breast is negligible. Routine imaging of gynecomastia should be discouraged.
affiliations: Department of General Surgery, Barking Havering and Redbridge University Trust , London , United Kingdom
Barts Health NHS Trust , London , United Kingdom
Endocrine Surgery Unit, Department of Surgery and Cancer, Hammersmith hospital, Imperial College Healthcare NHS trust , London , United Kingdom
General Surgery, Barking Havering & Redbridge University Trust, NHS Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.231.title: 380 Audit of the Management of Suspected Ureteric Colic in Barnet Hospital Emergency Department
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.231.abstract: Abstract Aim Ureteric colic is a common presentation to the Emergency Department (ED) causing significant morbidity and socio-economic burden for both the patient and healthcare provider. Prompt diagnosis and symptom control aims to improve the patient experience and facilitate treatment. Our aim was to audit management within our department based on BAUS/NICE guidelines. Method We performed a retrospective review of 100 consecutive patients presenting to our ED with suspected ureteric colic who had a CT-KUB. Data was collected based on BAUS/NICE guidelines for management of suspected ureteric colic. Results 98% of patients had a CT-KUB performed within 14 hours of arrival in the ED with average time to CT-KUB of 4hrs 50mins. 22% of patients had an obstructive ureteric stone identified. Of these, 45% had a stone <4.9mm, and 55% had a stone >5mm. 75% of patients with a stone identified were referred to the renal stone MDT and 45% had a repeat CT-KUB requested. 52% of patients received analgesia in the ED, with most patients receiving oral paracetamol with an average time to administration of any analgesia from triage of 3hrs 26mins. 51% of patients had their calcium measured and 4% urate measured. Conclusions This audit demonstrates excellence in performance in terms of diagnostic imaging for suspected ureteric colic within our department. However, we identify a need to improve appropriate analgesia administration and diagnostic work up in terms of biochemistry relevant to stone pathology through education and pathway review. A second cycle of audit is currently being completed to review these interventions.
affiliations: Royal Free London NHS Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.232.title: 401 Cardiovascular Risk Factor Optimisation Amongst Inpatients with Peripheral Artery Disease – a Single-Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.232.abstract: Abstract Aim Patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD) are highly co-morbid and thus may benefit from cardiovascular disease risk factors optimisation at the time of admission. This audit aimed at reviewing adherence to NICE guidelines for secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease amongst hospital in patients with critical limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) or intermittent claudication (IC). Method A retrospective review of all CLTI or IC inpatient admissions to a tertiary referral vascular surgery centre, over 9 months, was performed. We assessed adherence to five NICE recommendations for cardiovascular risk factor optimisation: 1) smoking cessation 2) lipid modification 3) antiplatelet therapy 4) blood pressure control 5) diabetes risk assessment, with target adherence of 100%. Results 97 admissions for PAD were recorded (CLTI n=87, 89.7%; IC n=10, 10.3%). The average age was 70.8±11.7 years, and 68.4% were male. Smoking cessation service was provided to 40.5% of eligible patients, lipid modification to 18.8%, blood pressure control to 29.5%, diabetes risk assessment to 21.1%, and antiplatelet therapy to 38.9%. Admissions longer than 10 days had a significantly higher rate of adherence (>10 days 35.5% vs ≤10 days 19.8%, p=0.017). Conclusions There are gaps in risk factor optimisation amongst PAD inpatients, with risk factors either not documented, or addressed appropriately. Shorter, elective hospital admissions were associated with worse risk factor optimisation. A dedicated review of risk factors should be offered to all PAD inpatients early during their admission. To achieve the best long-term adherence, multidisciplinary engagement of geriatrics, smoking cessation, diabetes, and primary care is essential.
affiliations: St George’s Vascular Institute, St George's University Hospital , London , United Kingdom
Department of Geriatric Medicine, St George's University Hospital , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.237.title: 432 Perioperative Antithrombotic Agent Use in Cutaneous Surgery: A Complete Audit Cycle
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.237.abstract: Abstract Aim Management of antithrombotic therapy prior to cutaneous surgery is a contentious topic with mixed opinions. The primary of this audit was to analyse the incidence of post-operative bleeding following cutaneous surgery in our minor operations theatre over two audit cycles. Secondary aims included measuring the standards outlined by BSDS and BSH peri-operative antithrombotic guidelines and assessing bleeding by risk. Method A single centre retrospective review of all patients undergoing cutaneous surgery on established antithrombotic therapy between 8/9/22 - 31/10/22 (cycle 1) and 10/7/2023 to 15/09/2023 (cycle 2) was conducted. A poster 'cheat sheet' containing antithrombotic agent advice was displayed in the department, forming the intervention. Results A total of 165 patients underwent cutaneous surgery with continuation of their antithrombotic agent. A reduction in post-operative bleeding from 8.6% to 7.4% in the second cycle was observed. The most common agent associated with bleeding in both cohorts was a DOAC, 33.3% and 42.9%, respectively. Overall, high risk operations had a proportionally higher incidence of post-op bleed compared with lower risk; 26.7% versus 4.6%, respectively. We recommended aspirin monthotherapy was not ceased before surgery, this improved from 80% to 71.4%. Equally we saw an increase in pre-op INR from 75% to 100% for warfarin users. Conclusions Patient factors, indication for antithrombotic agent and risk of the procedure should be all considered when listing for surgery, to help determine how the antithrombotic agent should be managed. Postoperative bleeding increases the risk of delayed wound healing, graft/flap failure and wound infection, and therefore should be considered.
affiliations: Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust , Birmingham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.238.title: 458 Post-COVID-19 Regularisation of Emergency Laparoscopic Cholecystectomies: A Single-Centred Multi-Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.238.abstract: Abstract Aim The COVID-19 pandemic has increased the number of emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomies due to elective surgery cancellations. However, the impact of COVID-19 on the timing of surgery remains unclear. The Association of Upper Gastrointestinal Surgery (AUGIS) advised to perform an emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours of diagnosing acute cholecystitis. This audit aims to evaluate the impact of the post-COVID-19 period on the timing of emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomies. Method A retrospective analysis of patients who underwent an emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy, in the post-pandemic period, between January and December 2022 was conducted. Primary outcomes include admission to imaging time, admission to theatre time, length of hospital stay, intra- and post-operative complications. Outcomes were audited against AUGIS guidelines and compared with previous audit cycles during the pre-pandemic (2019) and pandemic (2021) periods. Results In 2022, 411 patients underwent an emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Median admission to imaging time was 11 hours (IQR 4.6-21.9). Median admission to theatre time was 70.7 hours (IQR 48.4-107.7), compared to 106.5 hours in 2019 and 76.7 hours in 2021. Median length of hospital stay was 5.6 days (IQR 4.0-8.1), compared to 7.5 days in 2019 and 5.3 days in 2021. There were 38 (9.2%) subtotal cholecystectomies, 112 (27.3%) on-table cholangiograms, and 57 (13.9%) CBD explorations performed. 61(14.8%) patients had post-op complications including 9 (2.2%) bile leaks, 5 (1.2%) retained stones, and 7(1.7%) collections. Conclusions Timings to emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomies continue to improve in the post-COVID-19 period and is consistent with AUGIS recommendations.
affiliations: Royal Stoke Hospital , Stoke-on-Trent , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.239.title: 469 Operation Notes Audit: Excellent Bridge in Continuity of Care
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.239.abstract: Abstract Background Operation notes are vital as part of patient care in-line with Good Medical Practice to provide excellent continuity of care and for medicolegal purposes. This also to raise awareness on existing guidelines and accuracy of operation note documentation. Aim To assess compliance of op-notes documentation against Royal College of Surgeons (England) Good Surgical Practice Guidelines “1.3 Record your work clearly, accurately and legibly” in ENT Department Imperial College NHS. Method This is a retrospective 2-cycles audit (n=27) analysing October 2023 theatre list for first cycle and November 2023 theatre list for second cycle. Inclusion and exclusion criteria applied to ensure uniformity of data collected based on type of operations. Data documentation analysed against domains in RCS guidelines. Results Results are compared for both cycles, for which the results of first cycle were presented in a regional meeting. Almost all domains achieved 100% compliance of documentation except deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis (10%), blood loss (5%), antibiotic prophylaxis (85%) and anaesthetists name (50%). Part of the discussion is that blood loss should be documented even in minor cases with minor bleeding risk. DVT prophylaxis might be overlooked in some cases (e.g., hemithyroidectomy which require only overnight inpatient). Conclusions Surgical teams are responsible in documenting clear plans and instructions peri-operatively to provide optimum level of patient care, reduce perioperative complications, improve patient satisfaction and ensuring patient safety.
affiliations: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.240.title: 489 Management of ACL Injuries and the Impact of the Coronavirus Pandemic: A Regional Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.240.abstract: Abstract Aim 15,000 anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstructions are performed annually in the United Kingdom. The aim of this audit was to compare local management of ACL injury at the University Hospitals of Morecambe Bay NHS Foundation Trust (UHMBT) to current British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma (BOAST) guidelines. A secondary aim was to understand the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on the management of ACL reconstruction. Method The audit was registered with the local audit department. Lists of patients with ACL reconstructions were obtained across two time periods and data was extracted from the electronic patient record software and PACS. The pre-covid period, was defined between 1st of July 2018 and the 1st of July 2019. The post-covid period was defined between 1st of July 2021 and 1st of July 2022. Microsoft Excel software was used for analysis. Results Sixty cases were identified, with a mean age of 28. 37 patients were from the pre-covid period, and 23 patients from the post-covid period. 82% of patients underwent a timely clinic assessment following initial presentation, in accordance with guidelines. 37% of cases had an MRI scan completed within 14 days. 38% of cases were referred for prehabilitation. The average time to surgery was 230.5 days in the pre-covid period, increasing to 353.9 days in the post-covid period. 84% of patients had post-operative physiotherapy. Conclusions The results demonstrate poor compliance with current guidance. The COVID-19 pandemic had a significant impact on average time to surgery. An improved multidisciplinary approach is required to improve functional outcomes.
affiliations: University Hospitals of Morecambe Bay NHS Foundation Trust , Barrow-in-Furness , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.242.title: 513 A Clinical Audit on the Use of Red Cell Transfusions in a DGH’s Trauma and Orthopaedics Ward
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.242.abstract: Abstract Aim To compare the practice of prescribing, administering, and monitoring transfusions, with the current local Trust guidelines in order to determine the proportion of inappropriate blood transfusions especially in times of regional and national shortage of blood products Method For a six-week period in 2022, numerous endpoints were measured, reflecting the specifications of the Trust guideline. Based on the results from this initial data, a teaching session was conducted to create awareness of the Trust guideline amongst all rotational doctors. A subsequent re-audit was conducted to determine the effectiveness of the intervention. Following data analysis, further suggestions were discussed and implemented. Results Prior to intervention, 34 units were transfused across 16 patients with the mean age being 81.88 years. Post-teaching session, 11 units were transfused with the mean age being 79.58 years. 26.4% units were transfused for active haemorrhage, none were due to major haemorrhage, compared to 18.2% for active haemorrhage post-teaching session. 73.5% transfusions were inappropriate, defined as transfusions conducted in those who did not meet the haemoglobin level (Hb) threshold stated in the guideline. This significantly reduced post-teaching session to 45.5%. Transfusion-associated circulatory overload assessment was completed in 58.8%, improving to 90.9% post-intervention. Conclusions Simple measures such as an induction booklet highlighting the Trust’s blood transfusion guideline ensured rotational doctors were aware of the local protocol, preventing a significant proportion of inappropriate red cell transfusions.
affiliations: Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust , Aylesbury , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.243.title: 530 Repatriation of Care for Ambulatory Orthopaedic Trauma Patients Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.243.abstract: Abstract Aim The safe repatriation of care for non-local ambulatory orthopaedic trauma patients to their local trust is vital. Poor documentation and communication between trusts leads to delayed treatment and poor outcomes. Thorough documentation is required to prove that a satisfactory referral has been made. This audit, with two-closed loop cycles, aimed to improve the repatriation process. Method At a London MTC, electronic patient records were reviewed over a one-month period, examining 6 areas to assess referral quality to local trusts (initial data collection, n=17). Interventions were implemented, followed by a re-audit over a further one-month period (n=25), which was then repeated (n=18) after secondary interventions. Initial interventions consisted of the development of new departmental guidelines (referral pathway, electronic repatriation letter template, patient information e-leaflet). Secondary interventions consisted of educational posters and a doctor tutorial. Audit standards: BOAST Fracture Clinic Services and trust recommendations. Results Documentation of: Named local trust in clerking, 65% to 96% to 89%; Evidence of phone referral, 94% to 96% to 100%; SHO/registrar’s name taking referral, 24% to 88% to 94%; Local trust Consultant on-call’s name, 6% to 48% to 83%; Repatriation letter sent to local trust, 0%* to 92% to 94%. Uploading of the repatriation letter to electronic record, 0%* to 40% to 89% (*letter only introduced during initial interventions). Conclusions Improvements have been made in all areas, increasing the quality and accountability in referrals to local trusts. We recommend the introduction of formal referral pathways for non-local ambulatory orthopaedic trauma patients to prevent miscommunication and treatment delays.
affiliations: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.255.title: 656 Is Routine Group and Save Required for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy? An Audit of a High Volume NHS Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.255.abstract: Abstract Aim Bleeding is a recognised complication of laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC). Yet very few patients require blood transfusion in the perioperative phase. However, it is routine practice for patients undergoing LC to have a group and save (G&S) prior to surgery. This audit aims to assess number of LC patients at Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust who required transfusions, and the number who had “valid” group and save (G&S) samples obtained within 72 hours pre-operatively. Method Records of patients who had either elective or emergency LC at Northumbria Healthcare NHS Trust between 1st January 2021 to 31st December 2022 were reviewed retrospectively using theatre and transfusion records. Results A total of 836 patients were included (557 female and 279 male, age ranges 19 to 90 years old). Out of 571 elective LC, none required transfusion. 383 had a “valid” G&S, despite 360 having at least one historical sample. Of 265 emergency LC, 245 patients had a “valid” G&S, despite 207 having at least one historical sample. No patients needed intra-operative transfusion. 2 emergency LC patients required non-urgent post-operative transfusion where G&S sampling could have been taken once transfusion decision was made. One patient had cirrhosis and anaemia secondary to liver metastases, and the other developed a post-operative liver haematoma. Conclusions This audit suggested that no patients required intra-operative transfusion, and very few patients required peri-operative transfusion for LC. Eradication of routine G&S sampling is likely to provide financial and environmental benefits without increasing the risk profile of this procedure.
affiliations: Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust , Newcastle upon Tyne , United Kingdom
Newcastle University , Newcastle upon Tyne , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.256.title: 686 National Audit Assessing the Imaging of Acute Pancreatitis at Mater Dei Hospital, Malta
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.256.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this audit is to assess the imaging of acute pancreatitis (AP) in patients admitted to Mater Dei Hospital, Malta using the Royal College of Radiologists (RCR) recommendations as standard. Method Retrospective data of patients admitted with AP between 1/1/22 and 31/12/22 was collected. Timing of initial CT (at least 72 hours after symptom onset), CT report inclusion of prognostic factors, and timing of ultrasonography (US) of the gallbladder (within 24 hours of diagnosis) were analysed. Results 187 patients were included in this study. 99 patients were investigated with a CT scan during their admission, with only 25.3% of these patients being scanned at least 72 hours after developing symptoms. 74.7% of CTs were done within 72 hours of symptom onset. 47.3% of patients who had an early CT received a further CT or MRCP scan in the same admission. 24.2% of CTs mentioned all 3 key prognostic factors outlined in the RCR recommendations: pancreatic necrosis, free intraperitoneal fluid, and peripancreatic fat stranding. Only 20.2% of patients had an US examining the gallbladder within 24 hours of diagnosis. Conclusions Results show that CT scans are being performed too early in the clinical course of AP, with little reliance on US as a quick, non-invasive, and inexpensive first-line scan. Early CTs in AP generally do not alter management and risk missing complications. Our aim is to improve local practices through multiple educational sessions addressed towards emergency doctors, general surgeons, and radiologists.
affiliations: Mater Dei Hospital , Msida , Malta

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.258.title: 709 An Audit of the Impact of the Introduction of Faecal Immunochemical Testing on Colorectal Two Week Wait Referral Practices and Colorectal Cancer Diagnoses
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.258.abstract: Abstract Aim Waiting lists on the colorectal 2 week wait (2WW) pathway have grown more than any other tumour group since the pandemic. Faecal Immunochemical Testing (FIT) has a high sensitivity for the detection of colorectal cancer (CRC). A change in the southwest clinical network 2WW referral criteria was made from 2023, with greater emphasis on FIT. This audit examined the impact of this guideline change on referral practices to the colorectal 2WW service and resultant cancer diagnoses. Method A single centre retrospective review of electronic medical records and referral documentation for patients referred to a colorectal 2WW service in 2022 (September-December) prior to guidelines changing, and 2023 (January-April) following guidelines changing, was performed. Referral numbers, use of FIT, endoscopy numbers, and pathologies found were examined and compared between cohorts. Result: Referrals to the 2WW service reduced by more than 50% (837 in 2022 vs. 399 in 2023). A FIT was performed in 374 (44.8%) patients in 2022 and 297 (75.0%) in 2023. There were 560 colonoscopies performed in the first cohort compared to 270 in the 2023 cohort. A CRC was detected in 24 patients in the 2022 cohort compared to 20 patients in the 2023 cohort (p=0.06). Conclusions The introduction of FIT to the 2WW colorectal service has resulted in fewer referrals. This has reduced the requirement for endoscopy with no reduction in diagnosis of colorectal cancer.
affiliations: Bristol Royal Infirmary , Bristol , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.259.title: 718 An Audit of Chaperone Documentation in the Breast Clinic
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.259.abstract: Abstract Aim The General Medical Council and the governing trust (NHS Lothian) for our local hospital provide clear guidance on the role of chaperones within the breast clinic; specifically for all intimate examinations, a chaperone should be offered regardless of the genders of practitioner and patient, and the patient’s response to this should be documented. This entitlement to a chaperone is important in protecting staff and patients. This two-cycle audit reviews the documentation of chaperones in the breast clinic at a single centre, and whether consent to intimate examination is documented. Method Documentation was assessed for all adults attending low-risk or new patient clinic in both cycles (from 04-10/07/23, then 13-16/11/23), reviewing the staff grade assessing the patient, whether consent was recorded, and whether a chaperone had been accepted, refused, or not documented. The second cycle was conducted after putting up posters to remind medics to document and remind nursing staff to check this data. Results Junior doctor documentation of offering a chaperone increased by 43.7%, although consultant and ANP documentation decreased, by 20% and 34% respectively. When accepted, the chaperone’s name is recorded in all cases, and their grade in 3% more cases following our intervention. Conclusions Following intervention to target the lack of documentation in clinic notes, a significant positive change has been affected in junior doctors’ records. This change has however not been seen among consultants and ANPs, highlighting the ongoing need to improve documentation standards, to keep in line with national and local guidelines, and to protect our staff and patients.
affiliations: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh , Edinburgh , United Kingdom
Western General Hospital , Edinburgh , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.261.title: 752 VTE Prophylaxis and VTE Assessment Form in Plastic Surgery: A Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.261.abstract: Abstract Aim Failure to conduct a risk assessment and administer suitable venous thromboprophylaxis in surgical patients is deemed as negligence. It was estimated that 25,000 deaths in the UK was due to VTE in 2004-2005. Seventy percentage of hospital acquired VTE is potentially preventable with appropriate VTE prophylaxis. The Trust published a form for risk assessment for VTE for surgical patient. Our aim was to examine the departments adherence to the trust guidelines. Method All plastic surgery inpatients with a stay longer than 24 h were reviewed for VTE prophylaxis prescription for a period of two weeks. This was followed by presenting the audit results in a departmental meeting and introducing a checkbox to the handover list with posters placed in the doctors’ office. VTE assessment forms were placed in a clear divider and attached to the poster to remind doctors. Two weeks later, a re-audit was undertaken. Results In first audit, 22 patients were eligible for VTE prophylaxis compared to 24 in the re-audit. VTE chemoprophylaxis prescribing improved after intervention from 69.5% to 95%. Mechanical prophylaxis increased by 15.8%. Most importantly, the use of the VTE risk assessment form improved from 0 to 70%. Inappropriate chemoprophylaxis prescription reduced from 18.8% to 8%. Conclusions Despite the improvement in results after educating doctors and introducing the checkbox, our goal to be 100% compliant has not yet been met. Given the nature of the rapid turnover of junior doctors, a more robust system incorporating VTE assessment in the electronic system and replacing the paper form is required.
affiliations: Sheffield Teaching Hospital , Sheffield , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.262.title: 759 Lost in Translation: Breast Surgery Pathology Reporting Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.262.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate and consistent reporting of surgical specimens is essential to guide appropriate clinical decisions in management of patients with breast cancer. In 2017 NHS England consolidated pathology services with hub and spoke networks which aimed to improve efficiency and reduce variation in service delivery. Following a Serious Incident within our well-performing breast unit, it was clear that strengthening communication by standardised reporting in merged services improves patient safety. An audit was performed to review reporting consistency. Method The Royal College of Pathologists (RCPath) guideline 'Pathology reporting of breast disease in surgical excision specimens' describes a dataset that 90% of reports should include. We reviewed breast cancer operations from October to December 2021 at one unit and analysed reports for inclusion of guideline components. Margin and lymph node re-excisions were excluded. Results Of 126 reports 65 were included. Procedures were wide local excision (65%) and mastectomy (35%). Specimen type, histological grade, and presence of invasive disease were well reported but other items were inconsistently documented, including date of surgery (0%), core biopsy site identified (1.5%) and presence of microinvasion (4.3%). Conclusions There was variation in the pathology reporting of breast cancer. Multi-disciplinary team clinical decisions are based upon these results and error could arise if components are omitted or incomplete when reports are published. Investigating incidents drives change that makes services robust and enhances patient safety. Service improvement considerations need not be onerous or impact tight demand and capacity needs. We propose implementation of a streamlined reporting proforma that includes RCPath core dataset components.
affiliations: Ashford and St Peter's Hospital , Chertsey , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.263.title: 760 Intravenous Maintenance Fluid Prescribing in Nil-by-Mouth Patients in General Surgery: A Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.263.abstract: Abstract Aim Inappropriate intravenous fluid prescribing in peri-operative nil-by-mouth patients increases the risk of electrolyte, metabolic imbalances, and starvation ketosis.(1) NICE guidelines offer recommendations for intravenous maintenance fluid prescribing in nil by mouth' patients. (2) This audit assessed the prescribing of maintenance intravenous fluids in nil-by-mouth patients in our General Surgery department. Method We retrospectively audited our practice over two randomized 14-day periods pre and post-intervention to check compliance with guidelines. Inclusion criteria included non-diabetic patients, no pre-existing electrolyte imbalances and nil-by-mouth for ≥24hrs. Interventions: We delivered teaching sessions to FY1/2 on General surgery highlighting NICE guidelines on correct IV fluids prescribing. Posters summarizing this were displayed around the surgical wards. Results Cycle 1 showed significant lack in the prescribing of potassium and glucose in our department. Cycle 2 revealed that 82% of patients met their daily water requirements, while 94% and 96% met their sodium and chloride requirements, respectively. This translates to 40%, 10% and 11% increase in adherence to recommended water, sodium, and chloride intake, respectively. Although a small percentage of patients met their glucose (24%) and potassium (16%) requirements, the department witnessed a 55% and 54% increase in prescribing of glucose-containing and supplemental potassium-containing bags, respectively. Conclusions This audit identified an area of miseducation in our department and created a positive impact in the correct prescribing of maintenance fluids, particularly in the prescribing of potassium and glucose in nil-by-mouth patients.
affiliations: University Hospital of North Durham , Durham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.247.title: 581 A Standard Base Audit Regarding Documentation of Urinary Catheterization of the Patients Who Had a Urinary Catheter Inserted in a General Surgical Ward at Sri Jayewardenepura General Hospital, Sri Lanka
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.247.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the documentation of urinary catheterization of patients who had a urinary catheter inserted in the ward and to achieve good documentation following urinary catheterization Method We performed a standard base audit on documentation of urinary catheterization of the patients who had a urinary catheter inserted in the ward. We collected the initial retrospective data from the patient's notes and observed any documentation of urinary catheterization. The data was analysed and then a printed document was introduced to the ward to be filled following urinary catheterization. After 5 months we have carried out the re-audit to check for the improvement of documentation. Results A total of 50 patients were included. Before the implementation of the printed form for the documentation of catheterization, only 2% of patients had complete documentation following a urinary catheterization. After the implementation of the form, the documentation following urinary catheterization has improved to 88%. Conclusions The documentation of urinary catheterization has been recommended in the guidelines to ensure patients’ safety. The documentation of the indication, pre-insertion examinations and observations, catheter details, the volume of water instilled in the balloon, characteristics of the initial urine drained, and last but not least the removal plan is important for patient management and safety. These domains have been entered in the form and introduced to the ward to be filled and pasted on the patients' notes following a urinary catheterisation.
affiliations: University Hospital Plymouth NHS Trust , Plymouth , United Kingdom
Sri Jayewardenepura General Hospital , Colombo , Sri Lanka

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.248.title: 582 A Re- Audit of the Metabolic Screening for Patients with Urinary Tract Calculi and the Implementation of an Electronic Requesting Bundle
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.248.abstract: Abstract Introduction Renal colic is one of the commonest elective and emergency Urological presentations. As highlighted in NICE and EAU guidelines, serum calcium and uric acid levels should be measured in such patients as part of a metabolic screening. This audit aims to reassess the compliance of this at a local DGH. Method All patients diagnosed with a urinary tract calculus between 1/5/2023 and 31/7/2023 were included and retrospective data was collected which included the serum calcium and uric acid levels. The results were compared with a previous audit in 2022. Results 65 patients were eligible for inclusion. 46% of patients had their serum calcium level measures in the current audit compared to 65% in 2022. 37% of patients had their uric acid level measured in the current audit compared to 46% in 2022. Discussions Despite previous audits and interventions by means of education and posters, there has been a decline in the metabolic screening of patients with urinary tract stones. Via the trust electronic requesting system, we have implemented a “renal colic” bundle which includes the automatic selection of FBC, UEs, CRP, INR, Serum Calcium and Serum Uric acid levels for such patients. This convenient integrated IT feature will aim to improve the metabolic screening of these patients. Key stakeholders have been educated on the importance of metabolic screening and of the newly implemented bundle. We aim to re-audit in 6 months.
affiliations: Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust , Birmingham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.201.title: 60 Audit of Outpatient Management of Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss at St George’s Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.201.abstract: Abstract Introduction Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) is an acute otological problem and early treatment is thought to improve prognosis. ENT UK guidelines advise oral steroids as first-line treatment, followed by intra-tympanic steroids if there is no improvement. The aim of this audit was to assess outpatient management of SSNHL at St George’s Hospital. Method Data was collated from January – March 2023 of ENT emergency outpatient clinics for patients referred for SSNHL. Those without confirmation of SSNHL on pure tone audiometry (PTA) were excluded. Further analysis was made regarding treatment received and response. Results Our results showed that 36 patients were referred for SSNHL. 50% (18) were confirmed to be SSNHL on PTA. 83.3% (15) received a course of oral prednisolone with 20% (3) showing significant improvement in hearing. Of the 87% (13) who did not or had partial response to corticosteroid treatment, 38% (5) subsequently received IT steroid injections. 1 patient had an isolated IT steroid injection as they presented late. Of all those who received IT Injections (6), 67% (4) showed improvement in hearing. Conclusions Despite a poor response rate to oral prednisolone, 62% (8) were not subsequently treated with IT steroid injections. For 6 patients, the time delay from onset of symptoms was too great suggesting IT injection would be futile, 1 patient declined, 1 patient moved out of area. Further analysis into time delay from onset of SSNHL to ENT assessment would be beneficial. Consensus on maximum time limit to benefit from intratympanic steroid injection would also be of benefit.
affiliations: St George's Hospital , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.202.title: 75 Audit of Pain Control in Surgical Inpatients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.202.abstract: Abstract Introduction Pain is a significant feature in surgical patients and is complicated by multiple underlying mechanisms and co-morbidities. Optimal pain control is an important feature of care as prolonged pain can impair quality of life, reduce mobility, healing, delay hospital discharge and cause detrimental pathophysiological changes. The aim of audit is to assess the quality of pain control including side effects of analgesics in surgical inpatients at Lincoln County Hospital NHS Trust. Method Prospective review of patients and their clinical records was undertaken in 50 surgical inpatients and repeated in 54 patients following a departmental educational presentation. Outcomes were measured against the WHO analgesic ladder and NICE 147 guideline. Results Pain was managed adequately in 30% patients in the first cycle and in 46% the second cycle. Prescribing habits were inadequate in 30% of patient’s vs 16% of patients in the first cycle. Prophylactic laxatives were prescribed in 100% of eligible patients in the second cycle, and anti-emetics were offered to 92% in the first cohort vs 82% in the second. Overall, it can be seen that changeover of staff affects the prescribing habits which should be unique for all surgical inpatients. Conclusions Pain management of surgical patients has improved following a departmental intervention. However, measures to address pain and opiate side effects should be continued with involvement of the entire team including nurses, clinicians and pain team practitioners.
affiliations: Nottingham University Hospital , Nottingham , United Kingdom
Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, Queens Medical Centre, Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust , Nottingham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.206.title: 184 Closed-Loop Audit on Upper Limb Bite Injuries at a Major Trauma Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.206.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess compliance of management of upper limb bite injuries with Departmental guidelines, generate an action plan to address areas requiring improvement, and close the loop to review outcomes. Method A total of 38 patients in April 2023 and 27 patients in October 2023 presented to University Hospital Coventry. Trust electronic software was used to identify patients and collect data that reflected the standards set by the Departmental guideline, including treatment given at first presentation and subsequent management. Results The Departmental guideline was updated in accordance with The British Society for Surgery of the Hand. This resulted in an improved 86% of all patients, including 100% with infection, who required an operation to be completed within 24 hours. First contact practitioners provided a thorough washout in 25% of patients in the Emergency Department. An overall 30% required a formal washout in theatre by a surgeon, of which 25% required a second operation. Further, all but one patient initially discharged from the Emergency Department to Hand Trauma Clinic were managed conservatively, and 23% required more than one follow-up appointment. Additional recommendations focused on enabling better care by first contact practitioners, including clinical training for simple wound excision and washout in ED and encouraging improved documentation, as well as providing a dedicated minor ops room with accessible equipment. Conclusions A closed-loop audit on the management of upper limb bite injuries showed a marked improvement in achieving compliance with a revised Departmental guideline, with further recommendations targeted at enabling first contact practitioners.
affiliations: University Hospital Coventry , Coventry , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.265.title: 766 Audit of Stratified Treatment Escalation Plan Completion and DNACPR in Patients with Femoral Fractures – 4th Cycle
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.265.abstract: Abstract Aim Assess how many patients admitted on the fragility fractures ward (including hip, shaft, distal, periprosthetic fractures) had escalation (STEP) forms completed. We audited whether this was done in a timely fashion, which specialties and grades filled in the forms, if was there a weekend effect in form completion, and if the decisions were communicated with patients or relatives. Method In this 4th cycle of the audit, notes of patients admitted on the fragility fracture ward in the period 14/09/23 - 25/10/23 were examined prospectively. Paper and electronic notes were assessed for presence of escalation and DNACPR forms completion, and for evidence of discussion. Standards were set as internally as 100% for all measures: evidence of STEP form completion, completion done within 24 hours, and evidence of escalation plan discussion. Results 30 patients were audited. STEP form completion was 100% however 13% contained minor errors, needing correction; STEP completed within 24 hours of admission to the ward = 77%; documentation of discussion if for less than full escalation 58% (cognitively intact) and 64% (cognitively impaired). Conclusions All patients audited had a STEP form completed. STEP form completion within 24 hours improved from cycle 3. Documentation of discussions did not meet the standard for cognitively intact and cognitively impaired patients for less than full escalation. To improve future care, posters will be displayed, audit mentioned in junior doctors' inductions, and email reminders sent to all grades. Further cycles are being planned, and e-documentation system utilisation for improvement is under consideration.
affiliations: South Tees University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Middlesbrough , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.267.title: 777 Local Audit Based on MAGIC Study to Improve Abscess Management at Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.267.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess efficacy of current management approaches of subcutaneous abscess at the Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust (RD&E). Method Our audit is based on the MAGIC (Management of Acute surGIcal absCesses) national audit which involved anonymous retrospective analysis of patient records at the RD&E during September – December 2022. We collected data on patient demographics, clinical characteristics, and their management. Furthermore, we conducted a literature review to compare our results to the recommended practice. Results 31 patients records were analysed whereby 22 underwent surgical intervention (general anesthetic 17, local anesthetic 5) whereby the most common incision type was transverse (n=7). Nine patients were diabetic, two were immunosuppressed, 29 had hidradenitis suppurativa, while 19 had a past medical history of abscesses (n=31). The most common abscess type was pilonidal sinus (n=10). Eighteen patients received antibiotics prior to hospital admission, 12 of whom underwent surgery. Furthermore, 19 patients received antibiotics upon admission to hospital (n=31). Of the surgically treated cohort, 19 underwent packing and six were discharged with antibiotics. Conclusions Most subcutaneous abscess are approached surgically. However, postoperative care varies widely, with prolonged packing and frequent use of antibiotic postoperatively. Literature reviews have suggested no benefit of postoperative packing and specified certain circumstances of antibiotic use. Furthermore, clear communication with primary care providers detailing clear postoperative instructions is vital for patient safety and cost effectiveness.
affiliations: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust , Exeter , United Kingdom
University of Exeter , Exeter , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.270.title: 802 Assessing the Below Knee Amputation Service in a London Major Trauma Centre: An Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.270.abstract: Abstract Aim For certain complex orthoplastic patients, a below knee amputation (BKA) is the best form of reconstruction. An audit was carried out to assess whether orthoplastic patients undergoing BKAs at a major trauma centre in London were being managed according to best practice guidance set out by NICE and the Vascular Society. Method A retrospective review was carried out to analyse all BKAs that were performed on orthoplastic patients at the Royal London Hospital between 2020-2022. Patients were found by manually searching through the plastic surgery departmental inpatient database, and their electronic medical notes were reviewed for information specifically related to the recommendations set out by NICE guidelines for complex fractures and the Vascular Society’s guidance for major amputations. Results 19 cases were identified. The average age of patients was 45.8 years. 11 amputations were emergencies, 8 were planned. The average time to surgery once a decision was made to amputate was 1.75 days. Compliance was 100% with having an MDT discussion pre-operatively, recording the decision to amputate in the patient’s notes, and making a formal referral to the amputee rehabilitation team for prosthetics. Areas of lower compliance included giving written counselling to families, naming a discharge co-ordinator pre-operatively, and review by the pain team within 24 hours post operation. Conclusions This audit has identified specific areas for improvement and will help to develop a written pathway for lower limb amputations in the trust, ensuring that patients undergoing BKAs receive the best care possible.
affiliations: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Trust , Cambridge , United Kingdom
Royal London Hospital , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.276.title: 893 Addressing the Potential Harms in Vascular Surgery Inpatients with Diabetes: A Double Audit and Intervention Project on HbA1c Monitoring and Diabetes Management
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.276.abstract: Abstract Aim Diabetes mellitus confers crucial prognostic consequences in vascular surgery patients. Derangements in long- and short-term glycaemic control predispose to increased risks of post-revascularisation amputation and overall cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. This project aims to address these potential risks by improving departmental HbA1c monitoring practice and diabetes management knowledge at a tertiary centre through a comprehensive educational intervention. Method A retrospective audit of HbA1c monitoring practice in vascular surgery admissions from August-September 2023 for peripheral arterial disease or diabetic foot infections was performed against a locally agreed guidance-based 3-monthly monitoring frequency. An educational audit on clinical staff’s knowledge of relevant practical and theoretical aspects to diabetes management was performed through a multiple-choice assessment. An educational teaching programme was subsequently designed and delivered. Post-intervention HbA1c monitoring was prospectively reassessed between October-November 2023, and a post-intervention knowledge assessment was performed. Results Mean pre-admission HbA1c values in the pre- and post-intervention admission cohorts were 78.6±18.4 mmol/mol (n=21) and 73.6±35.7 mmol/mol (n=12) respectively. Repeat HbA1cs were required in 38% of pre-intervention and 50% of post-intervention admissions. Appropriate HbA1c re-checks on indicated admissions increased from 25% to 86% post-intervention. Mean knowledge assessment performance increased from 56% to 77% with improved mean scores in all knowledge domains. Conclusions Gaps in departmental understanding of practical diabetes management and monitoring relevant to vascular surgery patients with diabetes were effectively addressed through the educational intervention. Referral practice for multidisciplinary diabetes optimisation and harm reduction should be a further area of focus given the patient cohort's highly elevated HbA1c measurements.
affiliations: Department of Vascular Surgery, Aberdeen Royal Infirmary , Aberdeen , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.275.title: 858 Post Operative Opioid Prescribing in Patients Undergoing Primary Elective Total Hip Replacement (THR): A Closed-Loop Clinical Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.275.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess departmental performance versus NICE NG180 recommendations for post operative analgesia in patients undergoing primary THR. Method Local databases were reviewed, and patients selected based on the following inclusion criteria:Elective patients undergoing Total Primary Hip ReplacementNo contraindications to oral intake.Aged 60+ The extracted data were as follows:Immediate post operative regular opioid prescribed on Day 0 (D0).Regular post operative opioid prescribed on D0?How many hours from end of surgery to receiving 1st oral opioid dose?Pain reported on D0 post operative.Pain reported on Day 1 (D1) post operatively. The initial loop involved data from May 2023-July 2023, with the second cycle reauditing based on data from collected from September 2023-November 2023 following implementation of printed posters of NICE NG180 and face to face education on post operative analgesia. Results In comparison to the first cycle of the audit, there has been a 30% increase in the number of purely regular oral opioid prescriptions on D0. A 10% increase in the number of patients receiving their oral opioid dose within 2 hours post operatively is seen between cycles in those with a regular opioid prescription. Whilst the 2-8 hour and >8-hour prescriptions remained at similar percentages for comparative patient sizes. Conclusions The interventions implemented after the first cycle have shown improvement in departmental performance. To better this further, we propose creating an electronic prescription order set to help clinicians appropriately manage post operative analgesia requirements in this patient group.
affiliations: University College London Hospital , London , United Kingdom
University College London , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.278.title: 929 An Audit of the Perioperative Clinical Assessment and Documentation of Delirium in Older Patients Following Vascular Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.278.abstract: Abstract Aim Guidelines established by the Centre for Perioperative Care recommend daily screening for delirium using a validated tool such as the 4-AT and proactively documenting delirium in patients aged 65 years and over. This audit evaluated the assessment and documentation of delirium in older patients following vascular surgery. Method Patients aged ≥ 65 years who had undergone vascular surgery in August 2023 were identified. Data was collected retrospectively with access to the Trust electronic patient record system on a bespoke Microsoft Excel spreadsheet and analysis was carried out using SPSS®. Results Of the 51 patients identified, delirium was screened using the 4-AT tool in only 39.2% (n=20) of patients and on average 90 hours post-operatively. The highest documented score was 7 (n=1), with 7.8% (n=4) of patients scoring 1, 2 or 3 and the majority scoring 0 (n=15). The 4-AT was never documented in a consultant-led surgical post-operative review (100%, n=51). Additionally, there were concerns of delirium documented in 7 instances in the post-operative period, with the 4-AT documented in 5 of those instances. Conclusions This audit demonstrates poor compliance with perioperative care standards on screening for delirium using the 4-AT and documenting delirium, highlighting the need to increase awareness and improve the perioperative clinical pathway for older people undergoing vascular surgery. Our recommendations include discussion with stakeholders to identify barriers to assessment and documentation of delirium, (2) use of the mantra: 'Post-op bloods and 4AT' during post-operative reviews, and (3) education of various healthcare professionals in completing the 4-AT proforma on the ward.
affiliations: Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust , Leeds , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.282.title: 964 Intra-Operative Tourniquet Use in Lower Limb Orthopedic Surgery: A BOAST Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.282.abstract: Abstract Aim Surgical tourniquets reduce operative time and blood loss and improve visualisation of the surgical field. However, risks include pain, neurovascular and local tissue damage. Operative tourniquet pressure should be baseline systolic pressure plus 70-130mmHg. Ischaemic tourniquet time should be less than 120 minutes. We aim to audit the use and documentation of surgical tourniquets of lower limbs surgery undertaken at a single DGH over a 6-month period against BOAST guidelines. Method Retrospective data collected on torniquet use, torniquet time, pressure and patient demographics recorded collected from operation notes and theatre logbooks. Results 66 patients were included, mean age 55 (7-92) years. 95.4% (62/66) of lower limb procedures had recorded use of tourniquet. 78.5% (51/66) had the total tourniquet time recorded. Mean tourniquet time was 82.4 (15-130) minutes. 58.7% (37/62) had inflation pressure recorded. Mean inflation pressure was 265.7mmHg (150-300). 5 patients (7.6%) exceeded the maximum recommended tourniquet time without deflation. Conclusions Our results indicated that level of documentation of tourniquet use fell below the standards set out in BOAST guidelines. A second cycle will determine whether implemented changes in the theatre documentation system has conferred change.
affiliations: Mid & South Essex NHS Trust , Basildon , United Kingdom
Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital , Stanmore , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.281.title: 943 Audit of Endoscopy Service Safety in District General Hospital Rated ‘Inadequate’ by the CQC
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.281.abstract: Abstract Aim In June 2021 the overall CQC rating of Weston General Hospital (WGH) was ‘inadequate’. A wave of changes including a merger of trusts between Bristol and Weston-Super-Mare has aimed at improving services across the board. The endoscopy service at WGH offers inpatient and outpatient investigations to thousands of patients every year. We aimed to evaluate the safety of the service offered over a 12-month period, using measures set out by the Joint Advisory Group on GI endoscopy and other published statistics. Method A retrospective review of periendoscopic complications in OGD, ERCP, flexible sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy leading to re-admission within eight days of procedure or death within thirty days of procedure. Each case was analysed, using paper and digital case notes, for clinical course, outcomes and learning points. Results There were a total of 3428 cases between June 2021 and May 2022. There was an overall readmission rate within eight days of 0.002% (1 ERCP, 1 OGD, 4 colonoscopy). There was a mortality rate of 0.0003% (1 case of post-ERCP pancreatitis). A review of cases showed all complications were recognised complications of the given procedure and treated appropriately in a timely manner. Conclusions It was concluded that the endoscopy service at WGH was safe and viable. Numbers of readmissions and deaths related to endoscopy were similar to previous audits and well below the published rates of complications in literature.
affiliations: UHBW , Bristol , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.285.title: 975 A Re-Audit on Bowel Preparation for Colonoscopy in a Surgical Unit of a Tertiary Care Hospital, Sri Lanka
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.285.abstract: Abstract Aim This re-audit assessed changes in colonoscopy preparation practices at a Sri Lankan tertiary care hospital, aligning with ESGE guidelines. The primary goal was to gauge adherence improvements after introducing a protocol and educational initiatives. Method Conducted from May to July 2023, the initial audit identified deficiencies, leading to protocol development based on ESGE guidelines. Educational initiatives for nursing and junior staff were implemented, adjusting split-dose timing, discontinuing enema use, and providing clear instructions. A re-audit from August to October 2023 assessed the impact, analysing records through descriptive statistics. Results The re-audit revealed substantial improvements in colonoscopy preparation adherence to ESGE recommendations. The total number of patients undergoing the procedure was 88 in the initial audit and 96 in the re-audit. Adherence to a low fibre diet rose from 22.72% (n=20) to 90.62% (n=87), and compliance with enhanced instructions improved from 14.7% (n=13) to 70.8% (n=69). Routine enema use was eliminated (0% to 100%). Compliance for split-dose preparation increased from 42.04% (n=37) to 81.25% (n=78), and last dose timing within 5 hours improved similarly. Specific instructions to patients and clinic staff significantly improved from 28.4% (n=25) to 97.9% (n=94). Conclusions In conclusion, the re-audit emphasizes significant improvements in colonoscopy preparation, highlighting the positive impact of introduced changes. These findings underscore the effectiveness of evidence-based guidelines, education, and continuous audits. Implementing a checklist, staff, and patient education has proven essential for transforming and enhancing bowel preparation quality. These simple yet focused measures are essential in transforming and streamlining the quality of bowel preparation.
affiliations: Colombo South Teaching Hospital , Colombo , Sri Lanka

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.287.title: 986 Is the NELA Section on the CEPOD Form Completed for General Surgical Patients Upon Emergency Theatre Booking? - a Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.287.abstract: Abstract Aim The National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) mandates the assessment of all emergencies surgical patients for inclusion in its database based on specific criteria. Fulfilment of these criteria prompts the addition of patient details and pertinent clinical information to the NELA database. Method In an initial audit, 50 CEPOD forms were retrospectively reviewed to assess the completion of the NELA section. A re-audit involving 40 CEPOD forms was conducted prospectively over a span of 10 days, following interventions aimed at improving NELA completion rates. Results The initial audit revealed that only 42.7% of the CEPOD forms completed by the general surgery team included the NELA section, indicating substantial room for improvement. Discussions with junior doctors and nurses highlighted various reasons for non-completion, notably a lack of understanding among newly rotated doctors regarding the significance of NELA. Consequently, interventions were introduced:Formal emails were sent to all surgical junior doctors.Informal discussions were held with surgical junior doctors and nurses.Posters were placed in proximity to where CEPOD forms were collected. Upon re-audit, the completion rate significantly increased to 87.5%, marking a substantial overall improvement of 44.8%. Conclusions Enhancing awareness among doctors and nurses resulted in more than a twofold increase in completion rates. Therefore, it is recommended to discuss about NELA with each new batch of junior doctors at the commencement of their rotations to increase awareness and emphasise the importance of NELA. Moreover, conducting a larger-scale study over an extended period is advised for a more comprehensive evaluation.
affiliations: Portsmouth University Hospitals NHS Trust , Portsmouth , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.286.title: 980 Audit of the Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Pathway in Frimley Park Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.286.abstract: Abstract Aim To confirm the proportion of patients that stayed overnight in the hospital after their cholecystectomy. To determine the major causes of patients staying overnight in the hospital. To ensure Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy is being performed according to Get It Right First time (GIRFT) guideline GIRFT recommendation Anticipated day case rate of 90%. Standard positioning of patient, with slight head up, table rotation towards surgeon. Use intermittent pneumatic compression for DVT prophylaxis. Local anaesthetic to all port sites before insertion of ports (10mls 0.5% bupivacaine*). Use of three 5mm ports and one 10mm port. Low pressure CO2 insufflation (10mmHg). Meticulous washout at end of procedure. Instillation of 30mls 0.25% bupivacaine* around liver and gallbladder. No drains Method All cases of Elective Cholecystectomy done within July 1st, 2023, to October 31st 2023 at Frimley Park Hospital was included in the study. Electronic case notes and Operative notes was used to get required data. A total of 107 Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy was recruited Results Day case Rate was 45% (58 of 107 stayed overnight), Although 85% eventually went home the morning after the Surgery. Interestingly , 34% of those that stayed overnight had no Clinical indication to stay and was mostly Patient personal preference and delay in Recovery time. No surgeon documented the Pneumoperitoneum pressure used Conclusions Use of GIRFT recommended surgical technique. Proper documentation of the reason patient stayed overnight. All patients should be counselled Preoperatively to have someone to pick them once medically fit to go home even if recovery gets delayed to 20.00hrs.
affiliations: Frimley Health NHS foundation Trust, Camberley, United Kingdom. Wirral University teaching Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , Wirral , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.288.title: 995 The Standard of Evening Handover in the Acute Surgical Department of a Single Regional Centre: A Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.288.abstract: Abstract Aim Handover is an important period that represents a potential risk to patient safety. The Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCSEng) have published guidelines on safe handover practice. The aim of this closed-loop two-cycle audit was to ensure general surgery patients at a single regional centre were handed over according to RCSEng guidelines. Method Evening handovers were prospectively audited between May 2023 to July 2023 using a proforma adapted from the RCSEng guidelines. A questionnaire relating to junior doctors’ views on the evening handover was disseminated prior to the first cycle. The intervention was an educational guide for foundation doctors on how to effectively hand over surgical patients, based on the RCSEng guidelines. P-values were calculated using a Mann-Whitney U test. Results 15 evening handovers were audited in the first cycle; of 84 patients handed over, 31% (26/84) met the RCSEng handover ‘minimum’ standard. 13 evening handovers were audited in the second cycle; 84 patients were handed over, the ‘minimum’ standard rate increased to 67% (56/84) (p=0.003). There were 25 responses to the questionnaire, 92% (23/25) were by foundation doctors, 48% (12/25) volunteered wanting more teaching on handovers. Conclusions Introduction of an educational handover guide is a useful method to improve the quality of surgical handovers, particularly in regional centres that may have a more complex case mix. This guide was later introduced as part of the ‘induction pack’ for foundation doctors rotating into surgery.
affiliations: Acute Surgical Unit, University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust , Southampton , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.292.title: 1056 Audit of Compliance with Local Guidelines on Opioid and Laxative Co-Prescribing in General Surgery Patients at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.292.abstract: Abstract Aim Constipation is a well-known side-effect of opioids, which are often prescribed in post-operative patients already at risk of ileus. Opioid associated constipation can further affect postoperative recovery and delay discharge. University Hospitals Birmingham guidelines suggest patients prescribed regular or as-required opioids for >1 day should be co-prescribed both stimulant and softener laxatives. This audit aims to assess compliance with these guidelines in the General Surgery department at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham. Method Inpatients under the upper gastrointestinal, sarcoma, and colorectal teams on a single date were identified and included. Retrospective review of drug charts was undertaken to identify patients prescribed opioids for >1 day and those co-prescribed laxatives. Stool charts were reviewed to assess bowel opening and Bristol stool charting. Results 87% (n=35) out of 40 patients were prescribed opioids. 34% (n=12) of these patients were co-prescribed laxatives; only 17% (n=6) were co-prescribed laxatives with both stimulant and softener action. Bowel motions were charted for 74% (n=26) of patients prescribed opioids. Conclusions Compliance with local guidelines on co-prescribing of laxatives with opioids is below expected. Accurate documentation of bowel motions and Bristol stool charting is important in guiding on laxative indication and prescription to prevent opioid associated constipation. Results of this audit will be shared with the department and education provided. Nursing staff will be encouraged to complete bowel charting in patients prescribed opioids. A re-audit will be undertaken after these measures are implemented.
affiliations: Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham , Birmingham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.293.title: 1065 Beyond the Incision: Optimising Secondary Prevention Prescriptions for Vascular Surgery Admissions Through a Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.293.abstract: Abstract Aim Vascular surgery patients carry some of the highest chronic disease and mortality burden, often driven by atherosclerotic, pro-thrombotic pathophysiology. Cardiovascular mortality risk reduction through secondary prevention by anti-platelets and statins is essential, but studies repeatedly demonstrate deficiencies in initiating such therapies. We aim to improve the identification and initiation of secondary prevention agents for vascular surgery inpatients at a tertiary centre through education and structured handover practice.
