Method A retrospective audit was performed on pre-admission and on-discharge anti-platelet and statin prescribing in vascular surgery admissions from August-October 2023. Education on guidance-based secondary prevention therapies was delivered, and modifications to the daily handover pro-forma were implemented to monitor prescribing. A prospective post-intervention re-audit was subsequently performed on admissions from October-November 2023. Results On admission, 70% of the 89 pre-intervention and 49% of the 47 post-intervention cohorts presented with concurrent anti-platelet or anti-coagulant and statin therapy. Pre-intervention, anti-platelets were initiated by discharge in 36% of patients admitted without anti-platelets or anti-coagulants, and statins were initiated in 20% of patients admitted without lipid-lowering therapy. This increased to 55% and 41% of such patients respectively post-intervention. However, 15% and 13% of the pre- and post-intervention cohorts respectively remain discharged on no secondary prevention therapies. Conclusions Education and modifications to handover documentation improved the identification and prescribing of secondary prevention therapy for vascular surgery patients in relative terms. Patients without secondary prevention therapies accounted for a significant proportion of admissions irrespective of time-period and there remains further scope to improve secondary prevention prescribing in this high-risk patient group.
affiliations: Department of Vascular Surgery, Aberdeen Royal Infirmary , Aberdeen , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.294.title: 1083 Assessment of Antibiotic Prescribing Compliance: Are We Adhering to NICE Guidelines for Recording Stop/Review Dates in Surgical Wards- A Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.294.abstract: Abstract Aim We've noticed instances where general surgical patients received antibiotics without a recorded stop/ review date in electronic prescribing system, potentially exceeding the recommended duration resulting in neutropenic sepsis in one instance . We aim to ensure compliance with NICE antibiotic prescribing guidelines by reviewing our practices and making necessary improvements for better patient care. Method Initial retrospective data analysis involved 50 inpatients receiving antibiotics in the surgical ward. For the subsequent re-audit, we implemented interventions and performed a prospective analysis on data from 40 patients over a two-week period in the same ward. Results Initial Audit Findings: Only 56% of patients had a recorded stop/review date for antibiotics. Discussions with junior doctors highlighted several reasons: Lack of Awareness of the NICE guideline of antibiotics stewardship. Patient Transfers: Patients moving between teams resulted in existing prescriptions without updated reviews. Paper Documentation: Decisions about antibiotics were documented in paper notes, not reflected on electronic prescribing system. Based on these findings, we implemented the following interventions: informal discussions and an email to junior doctors highlighting the findings and relevant NICE guidelines, along with placing physical posters in doctors' stations for easy reference. In the re-audit, 61.1% of patients had recorded stop/review dates, indicating more than 10% improvement. Conclusions Following discussions with prescribers post re-audit, our plan involves engaging with the electronic prescribing system. We propose adding an option to input review dates and making it mandatory to include stop/ review date when prescribing antibiotics to ensure sustained adherence to NICE guideline.
affiliations: Queen Alexandra Hospital , Portsmouth , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.295.title: 1099 Audit of Immediate Discharge Letters in General Surgery in Royal Alexandra Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.295.abstract: Abstract Aim To determine what percentage of immediate discharge letters for general surgical patients meet pre-defined standards. Method All immediate discharge letters (IDLs) for patients discharged over a week-long period from two general surgical wards in a single hospital were analysed. Results were compared to the 16 criteria outlined in current Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN) guidelines, plus 3 further criteria agreed locally. A template for IDLs was then created and distributed amongst junior doctors writing IDLs after presentation at a local research meeting. Data was subsequently recollected recording the same criteria. Categorical data was analysed using a chi squared test. Results n=129 patients were included (n=67 in round 1; n=62 in round 2). Those without an IDL were excluded. On re-auditing, 15/16 (94%) of the SIGN criteria were documented more frequently, however only 5 of these were statistically significant (31.3%, p < 0.05). Results had also improved in all three of the locally agreed criteria, however only 1 of these was statistically significant. Overall, 0% of IDLs prior to the implementation of the template had all SIGN criteria present, rising to 6% after implementation of the template, however this was not statistically significant. Conclusions Implementation of an IDL template has improved the quality of IDLs for general surgery patients in the RAH, however further work is required to improve this further and create substantive change in the long-term.
affiliations: Royal Alexandra Hospital , Paisley , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.296.title: 1110 Thoracic Theatres: Audit of Theatre Efficiency
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.296.abstract: Abstract Aim Turnover time is the cumulative time of processes between procedure finish (final dressing applied) and next procedure start (knife to skin). This audit aims to establish current turnover times and identify individual process times within patient turnover to improve theatre efficiency. Method This audit spanned between 22/5/2023-22/6/2023. Patient turnovers (N=41) from all elective thoracic procedures (N=61), across 19 operating days were examined. Operating days (N=2) with single cases were excluded from analysis. A process map was used to visualise the processes involved in patient turnover. Individual process times were extracted from Bluspier and data analysis performed using Microsoft Excel. All descriptive statistics are reported as mean±standard deviation with 95% confidence intervals. Results Mean procedure and turnover time were 93±16 and 94±14 minutes respectively. The audit revealed 2 main processes contributing to current turnover times, handover from theatre to recovery bay (23±8 minutes) and subsequent patient sign-in and transfer to anaesthetic room (36±6 minutes). Both processes make up 54±13 minutes of current turnover times. Recovery bay availability was influenced by ward/ ITU availability, with patients ready for discharge spent an extra 48±13 minutes in recovery pending ward transfer. This causes time blocks for the anaesthetic team who are unable to complete handover to recovery resulting in delays for subsequent patient sign-in. Conclusions Ideal solutions to improve turnover times would involve parallel processing with concurrent handover and patient sign-in and workforce expansion to improve ward availability. However, with limited resources, a cost-neutral solution would be difficult to achieve.
affiliations: Keele University School of Medicine , Stoke-On-Trent , United Kingdom
Royal Stoke University Hospital , Stoke-On-Trent , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.299.title: 1134 Audit on Timeliness of Imaging in Bicep Tendon Ruptures
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.299.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aimed to assess the time interval between the date of injury and the acquisition of imaging for patients suspected of bicep tendon ruptures. The primary objective was to identify areas for improvement in reducing delays and optimizing the diagnostic timeline. Method A retrospective analysis was conducted on a cohort of 28 patients presenting with suspected bicep tendon ruptures between January 2022 and September 2023 at Basingstoke North Hampshire Hospital. Electronic medical records were systematically reviewed to extract data on the time elapsed from the reported date of injury to the date of imaging, encompassing modalities such as ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Results The audit revealed considerable variability in the time taken to obtain imaging from date of presentation, with an average duration of 7.8 days. The average time from date of presentation to surgery performed was 23.2 days. Notably, delays were mainly due to patient unattendance and scheduling appointments for scans. Conclusions The findings underscore the importance of streamlining the diagnostic pathway for bicep tendon ruptures to reduce the time between injury and imaging/surgical procedure.
affiliations: Basingstoke North Hampshire Hospital , Basingstoke , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.298.title: 1115 The Role of Ultrasound and Computer Tomography Imaging in the Management of Suspected Acute Appendicitis at a District General Hospital: A Clinical Audit Evaluating Our Practice Against International Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.298.abstract: Abstract Aim Definitive diagnosis of acute appendicitis (AA) continues to pose a clinical challenge. Computer tomography (CT) is the gold-standard imaging modality for diagnosis, but ultrasound (USS) remains first-line and recommended for paediatric and young patients given the absence of ionising radiation. We conducted an audit evaluating the use of imaging as a diagnostic adjunct in diagnosing AA and whether it reduced the negative appendicectomy rate in a large UK district general hospital. A high NAR has both a significant patient impact (complications, increased hospital length of stay) and healthcare resource burden. Method We performed a retrospective analysis of electronic health records for a pre-Covid cohort of 344 patients who underwent a coded diagnostic laparoscopy/laparoscopic appendicectomy between 1st January 2019 and 1st January 2020. Histological confirmation of appendicitis was utilised as the gold-standard. Results USS was performed in only 10% of patients, particularly young females (16-35), and had 44% sensitivity, 88% specificity, 57% positive predictive value (PPV) and 84% negative predictive value (NPV). CT was performed in 22% of patients with 99% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% PPV and 88% NVP. Use of imaging (versus DLA) was associated with greater length of stay and readmission rates. Conclusions Despite its widespread use, ultrasound’s low sensitivity and PPV render its clinical utility debatable, particularly in females. Additionally, by counting occasions whereby ultrasound fails to visualise the appendix as negative results, its specificity is inaccurately increased. Therefore, CT remains gold standard given its highest sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing AA and its association with a reduction in NAR.
affiliations: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Cambridge , United Kingdom
Peterborough City Hospital, NWAFT , Peterborough , United Kingdom
North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust , Peterborough , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.300.title: 1142 National Audit of NICE Guidance for Endovascular Repair of Popliteal Aneurysms: The Kings Experience
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.300.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate care for patients undergoing covered stenting for popliteal aneurysms against NICE guidance, and to assess peri-procedural and post-procedural outcomes of patients. Method Retrospective collection of data in patients who had undergone endovascular repair of popliteal aneurysms from 30/5/2010 to 30/5/2023. 11 patients met inclusion criteria. Data collection was based on the NICE guidance clinical audit tool for endovascular repair of popliteal aneurysms. This included presenting symptoms, demographics, pre-procedure imaging findings, procedure details, duration of patency of the stent, peri-procedural complications, post procedure medical management and whether limb salvage was achieved. Results All 11 patients had vascular MDT discussion prior to procedure. Mean age was 71, 9 patients were male and 2 females. 5 stents remained patent to time of data collection or at the time of their death from other causes. There were no significant immediate complications. Of 6 failed stents, only one patient required amputation. Three patients had stents which remained patent for over a year with mean patency of 37 months, and 3 remained patent for less than a year. Stents that failed <1 year had reduced run-off vessels (mean 2). The smallest stent diameter (6mm) failed within 7 months. All patients had appropriate antiplatelet therapy. Conclusions Local experience of 11 endovascular stent for popliteal aneurysms. 6 failed and 3 failed within one year of insertion, with 1 patient requiring amputation. MDT input and full patient consent are mandatory prior to endovascular management of popliteal aneurysms. Technically, reduced run-off and narrower stents may be associated with poorer outcomes.
affiliations: Kings College Hospital , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.302.title: 1167 A Closed Loop Audit to Benchmark Care for Emergency Department Attendances with Renal Colic
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.302.abstract: Abstract Aim Benchmark care against the NICE Standards for assessment and management of Renal Colic patients. Produce patient leaflet highlighting stone diet. Re-audit and assess care for renal colic patient, following he introduced changes in first cycle including patient leaflet & renal order-set. Highlight areas that may need improvement and improve the awareness clinicians. Method Using electronic system and notes, care for the most recent 150 patients attending St Heliers and Epsom A&E, coded on system as “Ureteric Stones”, was benchmarked against NICE guidance during two cycles (2022 & 2023) as bellow:CTKUB request, completion, and report timeTime between arrival, prescription, delivery & choice of analgesiaTime between arrival and Urological intervention.Proportion who had bone profile requested.Proportion that received stone diet advice as per documentation. Results 100% CTKUB was reported within 24HRs (97.9% cycle 1). 71.9% of total patients received NSAIDS as analgesia in cycle 2 (54.5% cycle 1). 100% who required surgical intervention, had it within 48HRs in cycle 2 (70% cycle 1). 94.7% had calcium requested in cycle 2 (77.9% in cycle 1). In cycle 1, only 8.7% received dietary/fluid advice, this is improved to 39.4% in cycle 2. Conclusions Department currently successful in meeting the NICE quality standards for timing of CTKUB and Surgical management of ureteric stones. We have improved by 17.4% in prescribing appropriate analgesia and by16.8% improvement in serum calcium requests. Department improvement by 30.7% in giving patient advice regarding lifestyle and dietary changes for secondary prevention.
affiliations: Epsom & St Helier Hospitals , London , United Kingdom
St George’s University of London , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.304.title: 1187 An Audit Assessing the Diagnostic Yield of Ultrasound Imaging for Suspected Acute Appendicitis in Paediatric Patients Against Royal College of Radiologists Benchmarks
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.304.abstract: Abstract Aim Prompt and accurate diagnosis of appendicitis in children is crucial to avert the risks of delayed treatment and reduce unnecessary appendectomies resulting from false-positive diagnoses. This audit aimed to evaluate the diagnostic sensitivity of ultrasound imaging in paediatric patients presenting with suspected acute appendicitis at a District General Hospital, seeking to meet or exceed the Royal College of Radiologists' (RCR) recommended target sensitivity of over 85% (1). Method In this retrospective study, we analysed the medical records of 102 children aged 2-16 who underwent appendectomies (open, laparoscopic, or diagnostic) over a two-year period. Ultrasound scans and corresponding medical records were reviewed to assess the concordance between pre-operative ultrasound findings and post-operative histopathology results. Results Among the 102 patients evaluated, histopathology confirmed appendicitis in 77 cases. Ultrasound correctly identified 52 of these cases, resulting in a diagnostic sensitivity of 67.5%, below the RCR's advised benchmark of 85%. For the 25 patients without histopathological evidence of appendicitis, ultrasound accurately diagnosed 17. Conclusions The diagnostic sensitivity of ultrasound for suspected appendicitis in our paediatric cohort was below the RCR guideline, highlighting a need for improvement. To enhance diagnostic accuracy, we recommend additional training for sonographers in paediatric appendicitis imaging and consideration of second-opinion protocols for equivocal cases. Further investigation into a dedicated paediatric ultrasound service may also be another way of to improve quality of scans.
affiliations: Basildon University Hospital , Basildon , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.303.title: 1168 Documentation During Upper Gastrointestinal Surgery Admission Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.303.abstract: Abstract Aim Admissions in surgery is one of the most important part of the patient care pathway and sets the trajectory for the rest of their stay. Without good documentation, the decisions made can be missed out and this will eventually lead to deficiency in the patient’s management. In this audit we aim to analyse documentation during admissions and look at ways to improve them. Method A retrospective review of documentation done during the admission for 50 random admissions in upper gastrointestinal surgery was assessed using the principles from Take Ten and the Shine Toolkit. Change implemented before second audit cycle: lecture at induction on how surgical assessment unit works, how admission and post-take ward round work, how to document & clarifications of job roles. The percentage of documentation was determined and going to be presented in a local audit meeting. Results 1st Audit Cycle vs 2nd Audit Cycle as percentage for documentation of History of Presenting Complaint (100%, 100%), NEWS (46%, 54%), Examination findings (96%, 94%), Diagnosis / Impression (94%, 94%), Advise to Patients (0%, 16%), Medication (42%, 54%) and Name of Clinician (60%, 72%). Conclusions The documentation during Surgical Admission improved in most areas and thus help lead to more safe and efficient patient care. However, there is still significant work that needs to be done. Further recommendations include implementing the Surgical Assessment for Emergencies (SAFE) Ward Round Tool, using electronic notes and availability of more computer on wheels.
affiliations: University Hospitals of North Midlands NHS Trust , Stoke-on-Trent , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.308.title: 1263 Audit on the Response to Raised National Early Warning Score (NEWS) in a Small District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.308.abstract: Abstract Aim Primary objective: percentage of patients seen by a clinician within the Trust's NEWS guidelines. Secondary objectives time interval for response, escalation to registrar/critical care outreach team (CCOT) and appropriate changes to NEWS monitoring. Method Retrospective study with a sample of 60 patients who scored 3+ in a single parameter or 5+ in total score. Events were categories to 3+ (in a single parameter), 5-6 and 7+. Timeline of the patient's raised NEWS were identified and documentation surrounding the relevant events were used to identify various information include: time of raised NEWS, time of escalation from nurse to clinician, time for clinician to review, escalation to senior clinician/CCOT, changes to NEWS monitoring. Results A total of 172 events occurred (NEWS 3+; 48, NEWS 5-6; 90, NEWS 7+; 34). Patients reviewed were 43.75%, 62.22% and 91.18% respectively. The median time for review for patients scoring 5-6 and 7+ were 1.03h and 1.00h respectively. Only 38.46% of patients scoring 5-6 and 20% of patients scoring 7+ were escalated to the registrar on call or CCOT. Changes to monitoring NEWS interval were 85.56% and 91.18% for NEWS 5-6 and NEWS 7+ respectively. Conclusions The data was presented at the local meeting to raise awareness. Downfalls of the audit included small sample size and the risk of implementing escalation changes during August handover.
affiliations: Ulster Hospital , Belfast , United Kingdom
Southport Hospital , Southport , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.313.title: 1293 Audit of Initial Management of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding as per the British Society of Gastroenterology Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.313.abstract: Abstract Introduction Lower gastrointestinal (LGI) bleeding is a frequent presentation to acute surgical teams. It can range in severity from mild to life-threatening, and most commonly presents with haematochezia. This data explores the implementation of the British Society of Gastroenterology’s guidelines at a District General Hospital lacking a management pathway for LGI bleeding. Method Data was collected on all patients presenting to the Emergency Department with per rectal (PR) bleeding. This was retrospectively collected from July to August 2023. Data collected included shock index at presentation, details for Oakland Scoring, hospital admission, complications, and follow up. Results All minor LGI bleeds (Oakland score of ≤8) were discharged with no readmission within 28 days. In July, four of 45 major bleeds were unstable, with one undergoing CT angiogram, compared to two of 27 in October with one undergoing CT angiogram. Of the 45 major bleeds in July, 32 were admitted (71.1%) and 13 were discharged (28.9 %), 5 without endoscopy. In October, 15 of 27 major bleeds were admitted (55.6%) and 12 discharged (44.4%), all with endoscopy. In July, three patients (23.1%) were re-admitted within 28 days, compared to one patient (8.3%) in October. Conclusions Despite integration efforts, there was minimal improvement in Oakland Scoring compliance, with many major LGI patients discharged. Nonetheless, all major bleed patients in cycle 2 had follow-up endoscopy organised and fewer patients were readmitted. This study could be improved upon with improved integration efforts for Oakland Scoring and Shock Index, such as providing the algorithm in a portable online format.
affiliations: George Eliot Hospital NHS Trust , Nuneaton , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.312.title: 1286 A Closed Loop Audit of the Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Elective Laparoscopic Cholecystectomies at a DGH
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.312.abstract: Abstract Aim To re-audit the compliance of departmental practice to the antimicrobial guidelines for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies. A Cochrane review found no evidence to support the use of antibiotic prophylaxis in elective cases. Method A retrospective study looking at all the elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies for the period between 1st June 2023 to 30th September 2023 using local Bluespier theatre software. Electronic operation notes were reviewed to identify cases where antibiotics were given. The main indications were bile spillage, conversion to open and cholecystitis amongst others. Total number of cholecystectomies carried out over the period was 92. At present gentamicin and metronidazole as a single dose was the choice. Results Antibiotic use during laparoscopic cholecystectomy is between 39% and 63% due to many cases not documenting the use of antibiotics. Adherence to guidelines reduced from 36% (2019) to 3% in 2023. Patients who received correct antibiotics allergic to penicillin was 75% (2019) and 100% in 2023. Continued lack of antibiotic documentation, use and indication in operation notes. Continued overuse of co-amoxiclav 60% (2019) and 87% in 2023. Conclusions Antibiotic prophylaxis in elective cholecystectomies was only performed correctly in 3% of cases. This can have a major impact on patient safety and also the financial aspect to the trust. Understanding why surgeons have failed to adopt the local guidelines may benefit in changing practice. We suggested an education session from the microbiology team to help better understand the importance of antibiotic stewardship and using laminated guidelines in theatre to ensure this is followed closely.
affiliations: Barnsley District General Hospital , Barnsley , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.314.title: 1296 A Closed Loop Audit to Evaluate the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Protocol in a Tertiary Oncoplastic Breast Reconstruction Unit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.314.abstract: Abstract Aim A closed loop audit to assess the enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocol before and after implementation of an ERAS proforma, in patients who have undergone breast free flap reconstruction. To analyse the impact on patients after implementation. Method Retrospective data collection from March to June 2022 and September to November 2023, in a tertiary oncoplastic breast unit. Inclusion criteria: all patients who had undergone breast free flap reconstruction for breast cancer. Thirty-one patients in total. An ERAS proforma was designed in line with Trust standards and based on input from the oncoplastic breast MDT. The proforma included the following categories: pre-operation, operation day, day one, two and three post operation. The data was collected, analysed, and compared to data collected before implementation. Results The first audit showed poor adherence to the ERAS protocol, this improved after implementation of an ERAS proforma in the following areas: location of the proforma in notes, 0% found in notes before, 92% after. Anti-emetics prescribed 32% before and 100% after. Anti-inflammatory medication plus proton pump inhibitor prescribed 32% before and 100% after. Analgesia, laxatives, and enoxaparin prescribed in 100% of patients before and after implementation. Day 1 TWOC occurred 0% before and 50% after implementation. Day 2 drain documentation/management 26% before and 100% after. The average length of hospital stay was 5.5 days before, 3.75 days after. Therefore, inpatient hospitalisation was reduced by 1.75 days. Conclusions Adherence to an ERAS protocol is beneficial in managing patients during the perioperative period and leads to reduced inpatient hospitalisation.
affiliations: Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust , Sheffield , United Kingdom
Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust , Nottingham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.322.title: 1169 Local Trust Audit Reviewing the Use of NABCOP’s Fitness Assessment Guidance in Patients ≥70 Presenting to New Patient Breast Clinic in Royal Bolton Hospital Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.322.abstract: Abstract Aim The National Audit of Breast Cancer in Older Patients (NABCOP) has developed a fitness assessment form which should be completed for all patients who are ≥70 years when initially attending the breast clinic for suspected cancer. This form aims to standardise frailty assessment within this population and assist with treatment decisions. The form comprises of three sections: Clinical Frailty Scale, Abbreviated Mental Test Score and three further questions regarding co-morbidities. The Royal Bolton NHS Foundation Trust Breast Unit was audited against this national standard. Method This was a prospective audit assessing the compliance and completion of the fitness assessment form in patients ≥70 years attending new patient breast clinics over a two-week period. The results were then presented, and teaching provided to staff on the importance of this national standard. The fitness assessment forms were re-printed on yellow paper and the nursing staff were instructed to highlight patients ≥70 years on each clinic list. Data was then re-collected over another two-week period to close the audit cycle loop. Results During the first cycle, 14 patients who met the inclusion criteria were identified with a 0% compliance rate. After the interventions, as outlined above, the second cycle identified thirty-four patients with an 88.2% (30) compliance rate. Conclusions The compliance rate in using NABCOP’s fitness assessment score at the Royal Bolton NHS Foundation Trust Breast Unit significantly increased following education and the introduction of yellow paper visual prompts in clinics.
affiliations: Bolton Breast Unit, Royal Bolton Hospital , Bolton , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.326.title: 404 A Reflection on a 3-Cycle Audit in the Use of Perioperative ACE-Inhibitors and A2RBs in Cardiac Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.326.abstract: Abstract Aim ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin-2-receptor blockers are stopped 24 hours preoperatively as continued use can cause hemodynamic instability and complications including kidney dysfunction, atrial fibrillation and increased mortality. To reflect on the results across 3 cycles to see if our recommendations have led to any improvements towards meeting the standard of 100% patients having ACEi and A2RBs being stopped at least 24 hours preoperatively with any clinical exceptions documented. Method There were 3 rounds of data collection (corresponding with each cycle) where patient inpatient notes and drug charts were reviewed. Emergencies and those not on ACE/A2RB were excluded. The first round of data was collected from 50 sequential patients admitted from October 2019 to January 2020, second round from 51 patients reviewed in December 2021 and the third round had been collected from 50 sequential patients admitted from January to June 2023. Results In cycle 1, 96% ACEi/A2RBs stopped with reasoning not documented for continuations (n=1). Recommendation was a team meeting to remind of protocol. In cycle 2, 76% ACEi/A2RBs stopped with reasoning not documented for 50% of continuations (n=12). Recommendation was a team meeting to remind of protocol, particularly ward and in-house-unit (IHU) staff. In cycle 3, 92% ACEi/A2RBs stopped with reasoning not documented for continuations (n=2). Conclusions The results suggest our recommendations have been effective along with the trust’s recent implementation of an online prescribing platform which has made it easier to track medications patients are given, reinforcing the positive impact of technology in reducing medical errors and ultimately improving patient outcomes.
affiliations: Newcastle University , Newcastle , United Kingdom
James Cook University Hospital , Middlesbrough , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.327.title: 407 Peri-Operative Usage of Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) in Cardiac Surgery: A 3-Cycle Audit Reflection
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.327.abstract: Abstract Aim PPIs reduce gastric ulceration after cardiac surgery; thus patients should receive it the day prior and of surgery. GI protection should continue until patient is eating and drinking, unless on DAPT and continued until discharge. Discharge letter should clearly state the indication and duration for prescribed PPI where patient is on DAPT. The aim of this 3-cycle audit study was to results to see if our recommendations improved compliance. Method Three cycles of data were collected from sequential patients where patient in-patient notes, drug charts and discharge letters were reviewed – first round (n=50, Oct 2019 - Jan 2020), second round (n=51, Dec 2021), third round (n=50, Jan to Jun 2023). Results Across 3 cycles, patients prescribed PPI preoperatively were 96%, 100% and 86% respectively. The data across 3 cycles showed that once drinking and eating, patients discontinued from PPI were 25%, 6% and 19% with continuations documented in 38%, 12% and 38% cases. 100% patients on DAPT were continued on PPI and after discharge with 87%, 68% and 62% having indication and duration for the PPI prescription documented in the discharge letters over 3 cycles. Conclusions Data over 3 cycles showed non-adherence to the standards persisted across most domains despite recommendations of team reminders of PPI protocols. This can be contributed to action-based errors in recording n drug charts as universal/standard documentation practices were not used. These could be mitigated by including guidelines on tick-box-checklists preoperatively, at ward rounds and discharge letters. This would be more time-effective, ultimately leading to better compliance.
affiliations: Newcastle University , Newcastle , United Kingdom
James Cook University Hospital , Middlesbrough , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.329.title: 590 VTE Prophylaxis Post-Thoracic Cancer Surgery: An Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.329.abstract: Abstract Aim The administration of extended VTE prophylaxis for 28 days has been recommended by NICE for patients following major cancer surgery in the abdomen or pelvis. Manchester Foundation Trust (MFT) has expanded upon this guideline to include patients having thoracic cancer surgery. However, the policy is occasionally not adhered to, owing to prescription errors and more. Our aim was to investigate policy compliance and identify areas for improvement to help optimise patient safety. Method For the first cycle, electronic records were scrutinised for patients who had thoracic surgery between 1st August 2023 to 14th August 2023 to ascertain if the above policy was followed. This included calculating the number of days for which Dalteparin was administered whilst the patient was in hospital, or, if the patient was discharged, (as in most cases), how many doses they were discharged with. Following this, a poster was created describing the MFT protocol and distributed across the thoracic ward, with an electronic version being sent on a secure messaging application to junior members of the team. For the second cycle the same method was adopted over a two-week period starting on 23rd October 2023. Results The first cycle demonstrated compliance as 82%. Following the intervention, compliance had increased to 90%. Conclusions The distribution of the poster highlighting the protocol had increased the number of patients receiving the correct VTE prophylaxis. However, with VTE being a serious post-operative complication, it is essential to aim for 100% compliance. Perhaps this can be achieved through further intervention such as departmental teaching.
affiliations: Manchester Foundation Trust , Manchester , United Kingdom
Wythenshawe Hospital, Manchester Foundation Trust , Manchester , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.330.title: 598 Chest Drain Monitoring Post-Thoracic Surgery: An Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.330.abstract: Abstract Aim Most patients have a chest drain inserted during thoracic surgery to remove fluid (such as blood, pus, or chyle) and air from the thoracic cavity. They are also inserted to create negative pressure within the pleural space to aid re-expansion of the lungs. The monitoring of chest drains is therefore vital to enable monitoring and thus management of surgical complications. Manchester Foundation Trust has a protocol concerning chest drain monitoring through documentation of certain parameters:Tube patencyDrain swingingDrain bubblingDrainage volume and typeDrain clampingDrain site conditionSuction levelBottle change date and time. Our aim was to investigate protocol compliance to ensure optimal patient management. Method For the first cycle, electronic records were scrutinised for patients who had thoracic surgery between 1st August 2023 to 14th August 2023 to ascertain if the aforementioned parameters were recorded. Following this, a poster was created highlighting the protocol and distributed across the department. For the second cycle the same method was adopted over a two-week period starting on 23rd October 2023. Results The first cycle demonstrated compliance for documentation of drain bubbling, fluid volume/type and suction as 90%, 84% and 87% respectively, and 0% for remaining parameters. The second cycle demonstrated compliance for documentation of drain bubbling, fluid volume/type, suction and drain site condition as 100%. Compliance for tubing patency was 14%, drain swinging 36%, drain clamping 21% and bottle change 21%. Conclusions The poster demonstrated improvement in documentation of all parameters, thereby aiding in the management of these patients.
affiliations: Manchester Foundation Trust , Manchester , United Kingdom
Wythenshawe Hospital, Manchester Foundation Trust , Manchester , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.331.title: 615 Audit of Documentation of Operation Name During Hospital Stay
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.331.abstract: Abstract Background Errors in the handover of patients from the cardiothoracic operating room (OR) to the intensive care unit (ICU) can compromise patient safety. We have previously shown that standardising the operation names and educating junior medical staff enhanced the accuracy of operation note titles. Aim This study aimed to assess operation name accuracy and consistency in OR and ICU notes, evaluating the impact of operation name standardisation and staff education. Method A prospective study of cardiac surgery patients at St. Bartholomew's Hospital was undertaken from November 29 to December 10, 2021. Operation notes were the standard and documents collected from the patients’ records were classed as fully accurate, containing acceptable/unacceptable variation, or inaccurate. Operation names were then standardised, and staff education followed. A subsequent data collection occurred from November 13 to November 19, 2023, under the same criteria. Results Pre-intervention, 30% of OR notes and 9% of ICU notes accurately named the operation. Post-intervention, this increased to 84% and 23%, respectively. Pre-intervention, the urgency was either incorrect or not documented in 2% of OR notes and 87% of ICU notes, which decreased to 0% and 29% post-intervention, respectively. Conclusions Improvements in documentation were observed post-intervention in both OR and ICU notes. However, significant discrepancies persisted in ICU notes. This is likely due to frequent staff turnover (every 2 years for surgical training, 3 months for ICU) and inadequate understanding of surgical details. In conclusion, continuous education is essential for sustained improvements in documentation accuracy.
affiliations: University of Aberdeen , Aberdeen , United Kingdom
St Bartholomew's Hospital , London , United Kingdom
Queen Mary University of London , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.334.title: 812 Audit on Chest Drain Clinic: Are We Utilising the Service Effectively?
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.334.abstract: Abstract Aim The chest drain clinic service, under the Department of Thoracic Surgery, designed to provide follow-ups for patients discharged with ambulatory chest drains. This audit assessed the clinic's effectiveness in ensuring safety, regular reviews, and its impact on costs and bed utilization. Method A retrospective analysis of a one-year period identified 97 patients discharged home with ambulatory chest drains. Patients progress and complications assessed throughout their follow-ups. In addition, number of bed days saved along with service costs from the day of discharge to the day of chest drain removal were calculated and analysed. Results The study found that 64% of these patients required only one clinic visit before their drains were removed. This led to 60% reduction in inpatient admissions, resulting in a remarkable total of 1,038 saved bed days. There was substantial cost savings, totalling approximately £361,200 over the study period. These savings allowed the service to care for an additional 173 inpatients, generating potential income of £1,038,000 for the trust. Furthermore, minimal number of 7.2% patients required re-admission due to complications such as pain, infection, or worsening surgical emphysema. These patients could re-enter care directly from the chest drain clinic, bypassing emergency department, thereby saving time and resources. Conclusions In summary, the chest drain follow-up clinic has demonstrated its effectiveness not only in patient safety and regular reviews but also in substantial cost savings, increased bed availability, and efficient re-admission procedures. This study highlights the significance of expanding and optimizing such services within healthcare institutions, benefiting both patients and healthcare providers.
affiliations: City Hospital , Nottingham, Nottingham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.339.title: 1226 Audit of Chest Drain Stitch Removal in Thoracic Surgery Inpatients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.339.abstract: Abstract Aim Most Thoracic Surgery inpatients undergo chest drain insertion during their hospitalisation. Some patients, however, experience extended stays or readmission after drain removal. Our departmental guidelines recommend removing stitches 5-7 days post-drain removal. This audit aims to evaluate and enhance our practice in this regard. Method This retrospective study included patients who remained as inpatients or were readmitted on day-7 following the removal of a chest drain that required stitches. The study was conducted in two cycles, the first cycle involved patients discharged from Thoracic Surgery between August 23rd and September 23rd. The second cycle took place six weeks after implementing an intervention that involved documenting the date of drain removal on the electronic medical records (EMR) with a recommended range for stitch removal. Results In the first cycle, there were 17 patients with 24 drains/stitches, with stitches remaining in place for a range of 6-44 days (median 10.5 days). In the second cycle, involving 14 patients with 22 drains/stitches, the range decreased to 4-18 days (median 7 days) post-intervention. Compliance improved from 20.8% to 54.5%. Importantly, we observed a reduction in incidents of bleeding, difficulty, or abandonment of stitch removal in the second cycle, as opposed to two cases in the first. Conclusions Timely removal of stitches following chest drain removal is essential for postoperative care, reducing the risk of complications associated with delayed removal. Our intervention significantly improved our practice. We recommend the continued implementation of EMR documentation as an effective means of enhancing patient care.
affiliations: Thoracic Surgery Department, Queen Elizabeth Hospital , Birmingham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.416.title: 1084 Clinical Audit of Surgical Site Infection in Emergency General Surgery Unit at London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.416.abstract: Abstract Aim To reduce the rate of wound infection in surgical patients in Emergency General Surgery Unit of Northwick Park Hospital. To access adherence to national guidelines by Emergency General surgery unit. To access the rate of Surgical site infection in Emergency General surgery unit at Northwick Park Hospital. To check if the rate of Surgical site infection in Emergency General surgery unit is in line with the national standard. Method This was an audit of NICE guideline((NG125)) undertaken in a retrospective manner. Data was collected through questionnaires and patient hospital records. Questionnaires where populated by contacting patients for feedback. Results Nice prescribed a target of 100% in the categories audited. The only exception is perioperative showering that NICE recommended should be carried out whenever possible. Pre-op Nose Swab 61% Perioperative showering 44% Theatre Wear 100% Informed to remove all jewelleries 97% Informed about pre-op antibiotics 66.67% Informed about intra-op antibiotics 14.29% Informed about closure method 77.14% Post op wound dressing services 44% Wound dressing education 49.29% Post op surgical site infection 6.76% Conclusions Overall, Northwick Park hospital maintain a commendable adherence to NICE guideline. This is evident from the very low rate of surgical site infection observed. Strict adherence could be seen in areas that are routinely recommended by NICE. Shortcomings recorded are due to failure in certain levels of communication than non-adherence to guidelines. To ameliorate this, it was concluded that checklist with all the shortcomings should be discussed with every patient and given leaflets to cover these before discharge.
affiliations: London North West University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.419.title: 1178 A Study to Audit the Breach of CEPOD Guidelines in Emergency General and Colorectal Surgeries
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.419.abstract: Abstract Aim Is to audit any breach of local CEPOD guidelines by comparing the time of booking to the time of surgery, for emergency general and colorectal operations. Method The audit was done by gathering data about theatre booking time, comparing it to when the surgery took place, and calculating whether time to surgery breached the CEPOD guidelines or not. Study was conducted in the general and colorectal surgery department in Leicester Royal Infirmary, over a span of 2 weeks. All general surgical abscesses, appendicectomies, and emergency bowel operations were included in the study. Results A total of 90 emergency cases were selected for this study. These included 30 abscesses (perianal, perineal, gluteal, etc) of which 27% breached the CEPOD time to surgery. 33 appendicectomies (laparoscopic and open combined) were recorded, and 30% breached CEPOD time to surgery. There were 27 emergency bowel operations divided into 21 colorectal and 6 upper GI surgeries. Out of the colorectal operations, 67% required bowel resection, and 43% needed a stoma. 33% of all colorectal surgeries breached the CEPOD time to surgery guidelines. As per CEPOD categories, 18% of category 2, 31% of category 3, 26% of category 4, and 37% of category 5 breached the CEPOD guidelines. Overall, 28% of cases breached the CEPOD category. Conclusions This audit reveals there is scope of improvement in adhering to CEPOD guidelines while booking emergency general surgical cases.
affiliations: University of Leicester Medical School , Leicester , United Kingdom
University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust , Leicester , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.433.title: 1138 A Closed Loop Audit of Laparoscopic Appendicectomy Documentation with the Introduction of an Operation Note Template to Improve Adherence to the 2022 GIRFT Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.433.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aimed to assess documentation of laparoscopic appendicectomies and measure the effect of introducing an electronic operation note template. Operation documentation is of great importance to patient care, clinical communication, facilitating research and providing a legal record. In 2022, GIRFT, RCS and ASGBI produced the ‘Best practice for Laparoscopic Appendicectomy Documentation guideline (September 2022) which contained forty-four recommendations. Method Between 1st June 2022 and 30th September 2022, 99 laparoscopic appendicectomies were performed at Broomfield Hospital, Essex whose operation notes were appropriate to be audited against the GIRFT guideline. Subsequently, an operation note template was designed on Microsoft Word using the guideline and refined with feedback from stakeholders including the surgeons who would be using it. The template was rolled out across the general surgery department in November 2022. Laparoscopic appendicectomies carried out between 1st December 2022 and 31st March 2023 were then reaudited. Results Between June and September 2022, prior to the introduction of the template, the average adherence to the guideline was 35%. Between December 2022 and March 2023, the average adherence was 55%, but was 89% in operation notes which used the template. Positive feedback on the template included ease of use and reduced time to complete compared to typing on a blank document. Conclusions This audit has demonstrated the important role templates play in significantly improving documentation and adherence to guidelines which positively affects patient care. The improvement in adherence even when the template was not used is likely due to the heightened awareness of the guideline.
affiliations: Broomfield Hospital , Essex , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.435.title: 79 Neurovascular Status Documentation in Complex Limb Fractures: First Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.435.abstract: Abstract Aim Assessing neurovascular status post-fracture is vital to detect complications and guide medical actions. Fractures can cause neurovascular problems and timely recognition prevents long-term damage. Neurovascular status should be recorded on admission to establish a baseline and identify those that need urgent surgery, and the findings should be well documented. Method Neurovascular documentation for patients with fractures of the tibia or femur was audited over the period of one year at a major trauma centre according to NICE guidelines. 885 patients met the inclusion criteria, giving a total of 959 fractures. Results Poor compliance was defined as <75% of guidelines followed. 911/959 (95%) of all fractures had a basic mention of neurovascular status in patient notes. 492/959 (51%) had gross sensation documented, 143/959 (15%) had a named nerve assessment, 71/959 (7%) had motility assessed using the MRC scale and 367/959 (38%) had a pulse assessment, with the pulses assessed documented. We recommend a pre-written template for clinicians detailing the different aspects of the neurovascular examination and documentation. This template will remind clinicians of examination and documentation, enabling ongoing monitoring, facilitating prompt detection of issues, thus improving outcomes, and reducing long-term complications. Conclusions Inadequate documentation of neurovascular status in patient records poses a risk to those requiring urgent surgery or experiencing neurovascular compromise, potentially leading to long-term complications. Ensuring an error-free documentation process is crucial and a primary goal for the trauma and orthopaedic department.
affiliations: University of Cambridge School of Clinical Medicine , Cambridge , United Kingdom
Department of Trauma and Orthopaedics, Addenbrookes Major Trauma Unit, Cambridge University Hospitals , Cambridge , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.434.title: 1143 Audit of Conversion Rate from Laparoscopic to Open for Patients Undergoing Elective Colorectal Resection 2021-2022
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.434.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aims to compare the conversion rates from laparoscopic to open procedures for elective colorectal surgeries done in our hospital during 2021 and 2022 and to compare the results with the standard conversion rate of 14.3% as mentioned by the journal of society of laparoscopic and robotic surgeons in 2014. Method Data was collected from hospital computerised system. Inclusion criteriaPatients undergoing elective resection for colorectal cancer from January 2021 to December 2022.Patients undergoing elective colorectal surgeries for benign conditions including ulcerative colitis, sigmoid colon resections for recurrent diverticulitis, colectomies for endoscopically unresectable polyps with high grade dysplasia. Total of 41 patients underwent surgery in 2021, and 45 in 2022. Results Over the 24-month period, 86 patients underwent colorectal surgeries. Laparoscopic approach was attempted in 83 (96.5%) patients, and primary open surgery was performed in 03 (3.4%) patients. Of the 83 Laparoscopic procedures, 78 (93.9%) were successfully completed laparoscopically and 05 (6.1%) were converted to the open procedure. The annual conversion rate for colon cancer resections was 10.3% (3 of 29 converted to open surgeries in 2021) and 9.5% (2 of 21 converted to open procedures in 2022). The annual conversion rate for rectal cancer was 0% for both years; all 8 procedures completed laparoscopically in 2021 and all 11 procedures completed successfully laparoscopically in 2022. Conclusions Our audit showed that the conversion rate in our hospital for colorectal surgeries is only 6 % which is better than the international standards.
affiliations: Letterkenny University Hospital , Letterkenny , Ireland

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.466.title: 966 Managing Infection Risk in Flexible Cystoscopy: An Audit and Service evaluation
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.466.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this audit and service evaluation was to investigate the way in which the infection risk associated with diagnostic and therapeutic flexible cystoscopy was managed in one NHS trust, and to consider the impact that positive urinalysis rates prior to flexible cystoscopy had on service delivery. Method All appointments for both diagnostic and therapeutic flexible cystoscopy across the trust were audited prospectively for a two-month period. Results 276 appointments were booked across this time period, of which 237 were attended and documented. Of these appointments, flexible cystoscopies went ahead in 219 patients and were completed in 215 patients, terminated early in 4 patients. Urinalysis was performed and recorded in 227 appointments. 18 asymptomatic patients tested positive for nitrites, indicating bacteriuria. 3 patients were symptomatic for urinary tract infection, including 1 patient who also underwent urinalysis and tested positive for nitrites. None of the patients who were symptomatic for urinary tract infection underwent flexible cystoscopy. Of the 18 asymptomatic patients who tested positive for nitrites, 9 were cancelled due to infection risk. Infection was the most common reason that a flexible cystoscopy did not go ahead. 72 appointments had no safety netting for infection risk documented. Conclusions There was an excellent rate of performing and recording urinalysis in this trust. There is room for improvement for the documentation of infection related safety netting. The decision to cancel appointments on the basis of infection risk in asymptomatic patients was taken on a case-by-case basis, though no symptomatic patients underwent flexible cystoscopy.
affiliations: St George's, University of London , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.458.title: 634 Biodegradable Temporising Dermal Matrix Graft for Open Foot Wounds, an Audit from a Tertiary Vascular Unit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.458.abstract: Abstract Aim Following diabetic foot attacks many patients are left with exposed bone, which can lead to osteomyelitis and failure to heal. These patients are currently treated with simple dressings or vacuum therapy and skin grafts. However, vacuum therapy is expensive, requires intensive follow-up and can be inconvenient to patients. An alternative is to apply a polyurethane-based, biodegradable temporising matrix – currently used in burns practice. The aim of this project was to audit the safety and preliminary efficacy of the matrix in healing open foot wounds in a tertiary vascular unit. Method Consecutive patients receiving matrix cover from January 2021 were retrieved from the theatre database. 10 patients met our inclusion criteria, 5 males and 5 female patients with a mean age of 69 years. Five (50%) were diabetic, 10% were smokers and 40% were ex-smokers. Two patients died prior to wound healing and one patient was lost to follow-up leaving 7 patients. Results Safety: One patient developed surgical site infection, managed with wound washout and dressing changes with no loss of matrix. No patient developed osteomyelitis. Efficacy: Wound healing occured in 5 patients, after a median of 51 days (IQR 12 days). One patient underwent an additional skin graft on top of the matrix and healed. One patient did not heal. Conclusions In this early report we found a low rate of matrix infection or requirement for skin grafting. Two-thirds of wounds healed following matrix application. A comparative study of matrix vs vacuum therapy would be valuable.
affiliations: Anglia Ruskin University , Chelmsford , United Kingdom
Mid and South Essex Vascular Unit , Basildon , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.449.title: 436 Infra-Inguinal Angiogplasty Outcomes Audit Through the Lens of GRIFT and Sustainable Delivery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.449.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate the clinical outcomes in patients with Critical Limb Ischaemia (CLI) six months after lower limb arterial angioplasty. To quantify the risk of index limb loss within our cohort and develop a dataset for further audit and quality improvement. Assess surgical resource usage and reconcile with national Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) strategy and sustainable service delivery. Post-pandemic challenges including increased waiting lists have elevated the risk of angioplasty failure since the 2018 GIRFT Vascular Surgery Report. Method A Health Intelligence dataset was obtained for all lower limb angiograms for a thirteen-month period beginning in January 2022 for a single tertiary centre. Morbidity and mortality data were collected. Results The cohort included 129 patients with a mean age of 71.9 years (range: 39-96 years). Limb salvage was successful in 53% of patients (n=69) with 15% of patients requiring a subsequent amputation (n=19). Of patients who underwent BKA, 50% would receive the BKA within 60 days (n=9). However, the rate of debridement excluding amputation at 6 months post-angioplasty was 18% (n=23). Mortality at 6 months was 25% (n=32). Conclusions Lower limb angioplasty remains crucial for limb salvage and symptom control. Utilisation of pre-angioplasty prognostic scores aid in assessing procedure risk and supporting collaborative decision-making. Review of the CLI patients who required early amputation will allow for development of a stratification/scoring system to predict successful angioplasty, aligning with principles of GIRFT and promoting sustainable medical practice.
affiliations: University of Aberdeen , Aberdeen , United Kingdom
NHS Grampian , Aberdeen , United Kingdom
NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde , Glasgow , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.526.title: 840 Audit Cycle of Surgical Management of Traumatic Open Hand Wounds at BRI – Compliance with BSSH Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.526.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess whether the Plastic Surgery Department at Bradford Royal Infirmary are compliant with BSSH guidelines regarding timing of surgery for open soft tissue hand traumas (target rate 100%). Method Two retrospective data collection sets between 11th October 7th November 2021 and 7th March to 3rd April 2022 using Bradford’s Electronic Patient Records (EPR) and Xero PACS to review Plastic Trauma Clinic (PTC) clerking notes; Operation notes and Clinic letters. Patients included were all adult patients attending PTC with open soft tissue injuries needing definitive surgical treatment in an operating theatre/PTC. Results The initial study found a compliance rate of 74%, with a 62.5% compliance when it was the patient’s dominant hand. The number of individual soft tissues for repair was 14 for Flexor Tendon (FT), 17 for Extensor Tendon (ET) and Digital Nerve (DN) with compliance rates of 83.3% for FT and 76.4% for both ET and DN. The repeat cycle found an overall compliance of 72% with 62.5% for FT and DN and 81.5% for ET. Conclusions The main reason for non-compliance was due to hospital bed capacity and a lack of list space. Recommendations to improve theatre efficiency was made but despite this the same issues presented in the 2nd cycle. There was a total of 69 days of delay from the initial operation date, resulting in 17 overnight stays. Further recommendations to accurately plan allocated theatre time and not rely on the acute list to reduce cancellations have been made with a view to re-assess.
affiliations: Bradford Royal Infirmary , Bradford , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.528.title: 1032 Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy for Malignant Melanoma: An Audit Assessing Departmental Compliance with National Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.528.abstract: Abstract Aim To investigate and improve local departmental compliance with the current NICE Guidelines (2022) on sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) for malignant melanoma (MM). Method Two consecutive audit cycles of all patients undergoing SLNB for MM: Cycle A (1st June-22nd August 2023) and Cycle B (1st September–31st November 2023). Data collected from electronic records (Pathpoint/Cerner), including demographics; T-stage; Breslow Thickness; lymphovascular invasion (LVI); mitotic index; ulceration; intraoperative SNLB assessment and sentinel lymph node positivity. Results of Cycle A were delivered to the department prior to Cycle B. Exclusion criteria: SLNB not for MM (e.g., breast cancer), nodal clearance. Results Cycle A: 35 patients included: 20 Females + 15 Males, aged 33–80 years (Mean 62.26 years). Cycle B: 42 patients included: 15 Females + 27 Males, aged 25–88 years (Mean 60.0 years). Cycle B summary: 3/42 (7.1%) – no clear indication for SLNB (8.6% Cycle A) 0/42 (0%) - no T stage documented (0% Cycle A) 0/42 (0%) - no Breslow Thickness documented (2.9% Cycle A) 4/42 (9.5%) - no LVI documented (14.3% Cycle A) 4/42 (9.5%) - no mitotic index documented (14.3% Cycle A). Conclusions Our department demonstrated successful compliance with NICE guidelines on SLNB for melanoma at 92.6% in Cycle B (91.4% in Cycle A). Documentation of preoperative staging, Breslow Thickness and intraoperative narrative was also satisfactory at 100% for both cycles. Further work is required to ensure histology findings (Ulceration, Mitotic Index & LVI) and node appearance is accurately documented.
affiliations: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.537.title: 113 R-E-S-P-E-C-T: A Closed-Loop Audit Increasing the Quality of ReSPECT Documentation in a Tertiary Surgical Centre in the United Kingdom
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.537.abstract: Abstract Aim Resuscitation Council UK guidelines suggest Recommended Summary Plans for Emergency Care and Treatment (ReSPECT) must be considered for all patients at risk of deterioration or cardiac arrest or who want to have their wishes documented. This quality improvement project aims to evaluate the use of ReSPECT forms in acute general surgical admissions and improve compliance with the ReSPECT process. Method The audit was registered with the local audit department (REF: GENSUR/CA/2023-24/03). Data was collected in the form of random spot-checks, quantitatively and qualitatively evaluating the completion of ReSPECT forms for all patients admitted via the general surgical ‘take’ at a large inner-city hospital. The first intervention was the addition of ReSPECT forms to the surgical admissions proforma. Second-cycle intervention involved educating clinical teams about the importance of ReSPECT completion by delivering a teaching session and producing a novel poster to be displayed in the unit. Results The initial completion rate of accurate ReSPECT forms was 8%, with 30% counter-signed by the responsible consultant. Re-audit following the first intervention showed ReSPECT form completion rate of 27%, with 50% of forms counter-signed by a consultant. Conclusions The addition of ReSPECT forms to the surgical admission proformas is a simple and effective way of increasing compliance. Overall quality of ReSPECT documentation improved with our interventions, however, there remains scope for further improvement and ongoing education of clinical teams is paramount to improving compliance with the ReSPECT process long-term.
affiliations: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust , Bristol , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.549.title: 464 ENT Handover Audit Using ‘RAAAIDSSS’ Method: Initial Step in Excellent Patient Care
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.549.abstract: Abstract Background Patient handover is vital in ensuring patient safety and quality of patient care, in line with Royal College of Surgeons Guidance of Safe Handover (2007). ‘RAAAIDDSSS’ method stands for resection (surgery), airway, anticoagulant, antibiotics, intake, drain, serology, scans, structure (plans). It shows comprehensive clinical updates for planning best management, ensuring smooth flow of activity and reducing morbidity. This method is ideal as otolaryngology patients often have altered airway anatomy and airway plans and consequently variable feeding routes. Aim To audit the compliance of RAAAIDSSS method. Method This is a prospective audit in ENT Department Imperial College Hospital NHS Trust, done in August and October 2023, with sample (n=100) for each cycle. The format was implemented in handover sheet and case presentation was run according to this method. Results First cycle showed good compliance to RAAAIDSSS handover method. The least compliant component is ‘structure’ which showed only 62%. Results were presented in local teaching. Second cycle showed significant improvement. Almost all components showed 100% compliance, except for the ‘intake’, which was 90%. Overall shows positive compliance to this handover method. Conclusions The department has showed improved compliance with the RAAIDSSS method. This audit brings significant positive impacts and changes to clinical practice in terms of patient safety, service efficiency and quality of patient care. This audit also holds valuable clinical value and opens doors for further audits as well as project expansion regionally and nationally.
affiliations: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.562.title: 649 Retrospective Audit into Management of Periprosthetic Joint Infections as per National and International Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.562.abstract: Abstract Aim The main aim of this quality improvement project is to improve care of patients with peri-prosthetic joint infections (PJI), by assuring appropriate diagnostics are sent and antibiotics recommended are as per Pro-Implant and British Orthopaedic association (BOA) guidelines, which are international and national guidelines. Method Retrospective analysis of all tissue samples received for patients with periprosthetic joint infections during August 2022 and August 2023 from patients across Manchester. There were 68 samples (17 patients) in total with peri-prosthetic joint infections out of 197 samples (62 patients). These were all compared to standards set by the Pro-Implant and BOA. Multiple criteria were compared by analysing clinic letters and Labcentre documentation. Results The results show a 100% compliance in discussion of PJI diagnosis with microbiologists, correctly labelling samples, and CRP analysis. However, we struggled with making diagnosis as per guidelines, sending more than 5 samples and discussing discharge antibiotic plans with microbiologists. Furthermore, we didn’t utilise sonification, PCR and histology to aid diagnosis. We also struggled with meeting the appropriate interval time between stages of two stage exchanges. Conclusions In conclusion, there is room for improvement in certain criteria’s’ as per the guidelines:Engagement with orthopaedic stakeholder to explore barriers to compliance.Dedicated MDT compromising of orthopaedic surgeons, infection doctors.Creation of an intraoperative pro-forma for suspected PJIs’ to act as a reminder to surgeons and allow clear documentation.Availability and awareness of guidelines to orthopaedic teamFunding for PCR, sonification and histopathologyJoint follow up clinic with microbiologist to improve patient follow up plans.
affiliations: Royal Oldham Hospital , Oldham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.573.title: 745 Improving Time to ERCP for Acute Gallstone Cholangitis Admissions at a District General Hospital: A Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.573.abstract: Abstract Background NICE guidelines recommend prompt endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) within 72 hours for adults with acute gallstone cholangitis, especially in moderate-to-severe cases. We audited our management of obstructive gallstone disease to enhance timely access to ERCP. Method We conducted a closed loop audit at a UK district general hospital, assessing time to ERCP for patients with acute gallstone cholangitis. Severity was graded using the 2018 Tokyo Guidelines. Data was collected over a 5-month period (01/05/2023 to 01/10/2023), analysed and presented to the surgical multi-disciplinary team. Additional referral pathways to 3 nearby tertiary care centre for ERCP were established. Post-intervention admissions were re-audited over a second 5-month period (01/01/2023 to 01/06/2023) to assess the effect of the new referral pathways. Results Forty-one patients underwent ERCP for acute gallstone cholangitis. Pre-intervention, median time to ERCP overall was 10 days (5–24), 8 days (5–19) for moderate-to-severe cases, and 28 days (9–46) for mild cases. Post-intervention, median time to ERCP overall was 6 days (4–9), 6 days (6–8) for moderate-to-severe cases, and 4 days (4–25) for mild cases. Median length of stay pre- and post-intervention was 8 (6–13) and 7 days (4–10), respectively. Conclusions By establishing referral pathways to tertiary care centres, we successfully reduced time to ERCP for local patients with moderate-to-severe cases. This change contributed to shorter waiting times for ERCP in mild cases and decreased overall length of stay. Collaborative efforts between district general hospitals and tertiary centres improve outcomes in the management of acute gallstone cholangitis.
affiliations: Princess Alexandra Hospital , Harlow , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.577.title: 805 An Audit on Managing Acute Pancreatitis in the Adult Critical Care Unit in a DGH
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.577.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of the audit is to describe current practice in the management of patients with severe acute pancreatitis admitted to ACCU and to improve quality and consistency of care for this group of patients by developing local clinical guidance on the use of antibiotics and nutritional support. Method A retrospective case note study of the 2-year period between 01/09/2020 to 31/09/2022 at a district general hospital. All adult patient admitted to critical care with acute pancreatitis was included in this study. Results A total of 11 patients were included in our study. 10 patients had antibiotics prescribed during their stay in critical care while one did not as advise by microbiologists. Antibiotic was initiated in 7 cases prior to admission to critical care, with 5 completed the courses of antibiotics which 3 of whom did not have a positive culture or any other sources of infection. With regards to nutrition support, 7 patients were fed via nasogastric tube and 1 with nasojejunal tube. 4 patients were not reviewed by a dietitian during their stay under critical care due to short length of stay over weekend. Conclusions This audit suggests the need for a separate management guideline on managing acute pancreatitis patients in critical care settings. Routine prophylactic antibiotics should be avoided. Regular microbiology rounds would be beneficial in improving quality of care. Early initiation of nutrition on patients in hypercatabolic state is a priority in improving care. Daily dietitian review would enhance the quality and consistency of care.
affiliations: King's Mill Hospital , Sutton-in-Ashfield , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.586.title: 972 Improving Surgical Ward Round Documentation: A Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.586.abstract: Abstract Background The surgical ward round (WR) is a critical multidisciplinary process. Adequate documentation of WRs have medicolegal and patient safety implications. Checklists have been known to improve outcomes, but there is no set template recommended for WR documentation. Aim This quality improvement project aimed to firstly, identify areas of poor documentation in WR notes and secondly, to improve these areas with the use of a template. Method Over three months, 20 dates were randomly chosen with an online random data generator. Variables were identified from literature recommendations. WR notes from 54 patients were analysed (cycle 1). Results were discussed in an expert-led meeting, and templates were constructed. To assess any improvement, 20 prospective WR notes were similarly analysed (cycle 2). Results Templates significantly improved documentation of lab findings (p=0.02), investigations (p=0.02) and plan (p=<0.01). For all other variables, no significant change was found. Fluid balance and drug chart reviews were significantly worse after the template introduction. Fluid balance, Estimate Discharge Date (EDD) and nursing presence on the round scored particularly poorly in both cycles. Conclusions The use of a WR template improves some aspects of documentation. Further work and perhaps a more robust intervention is required to improve overall WR documentation.
affiliations: University Hospital Lewisham , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.596.title: 1277 Audit: Patient-Controlled Epidural Analgesia vs. Continuous Infusion
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.596.abstract: Abstract Aim Investigating and quantifying continuous infusions require post-operatively. Determining the agent of choice in epidural top-ups. Investigating Diamorphine dosing in epidural infusions peri-operatively and post-operatively. Method Retrospective cross-sectional study. A comprehensive literature review utilizing PubMed, where exclusion criteria involved including only ‘free full text’ and publications released in the last decade. Data from operations requiring continuous analgesic infusion from the previous year was collected via spreadsheet software, and statistically analysed. Results In a study of 70 surgical patients receiving peri-operative and post-operative epidural analgesia, the average duration of epidural use was 3 days, with an average of 1.77 top-ups per patient. Of these patients, 36 required top-ups, primarily using Levobupivacaine (53.98%) and Diamorphine (46.02%). Levobupivacaine frequency increased with more top-ups, whilst fewer top-ups were required with Diamorphine. In intra-operative continuous epidural infusion, Diamorphine doses of 10mg were most common, with 15mg as the second preferred dose, correlating with lower top-up frequencies. Conclusions Introducing patient-controlled epidural analgesia (PCEA) in our surgical department would allow manual Levobupivacaine dosing to be replaced by patient self-administration, reducing clinician input by 54%. This hybrid approach, termed 'continuous infusion with demand dosing,' involves a background infusion set by the anaesthetist and supplemented by patient demand. PCEAs offer immediate pain relief and a dose-sparing effect of ∼47% of local anaesthetic. Transitioning from continuous epidural infusions to PCEA could significantly reduce healthcare staff intervention in post-operative pain management by at least 50%, simplifying the process and potentially introducing a Diamorphine dosing protocol for enhanced safety and consistency.
affiliations: University of Glasgow , Glasgow , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.602.title: 480 RCS Good Surgical Practice Consent Guidelines: An Audit of Compliance After the Introduction of Digital Consent
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.602.abstract: Abstract Background Informed consent is an ethical and legal obligation of modern-day clinicians. It protects patients from harm and doctors from litigation. Digital consent may enhance patients’ satisfaction and understanding, whilst also facilitating shared decision making. At our institution, digital consent (Concentric®) was introduced to the General Surgery department in May 2022. Aim To evaluate whether electronic consent forms on Concentric® followed RCS Good Surgical Practice Guidelines. Method A retrospective review was conducted on all patients consented using Concentric® by the General Surgery team for the calendar month of August 2023. Endoscopic procedures, blood transfusions and duplicate consent forms were excluded. Data was collected based on current RCS Good Surgical Practice Guidelines. Additional information was extracted from the theatre management software (ORMIS), correlating the time of consent with the date of the procedure. Results Over the month, 398 consent episodes were evaluated. Compliance with RCS standards was as follows: benefits and risks of procedures (100%), clinicians involved (100%), indication for procedure (87%), alternative treatment (62%), and patient information leaflet with follow-up information (37%). Among elective procedures (186 episodes), only 32% of patients were consented prior to the day of surgery. Where there was a significant interval (>24 hours) between the original consent signing and the operation, only 52% had consent reconfirmed. Conclusions This audit identified areas of good practice and areas for improvement in relation to digital consent in general surgery. Making fields on the form mandatory would likely improve compliance with current RCS standards.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.685.title: 1090 A UK-Wide Audit on Peri-Operative Practices During Deceased Donor Kidney Transplantation: Results from a Prospective National Transplant Access to Theatre (NTACT) Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.685.abstract: Abstract Aim The outcomes of deceased donor kidney transplants are mainly affected by donor and recipient factors. There is little data on whether variations in perioperative practices could also affect the outcomes and there is also little data on the standard perioperative practices across the UK. This study aims to identify current perioperative practices from a prospective National Transplant Access to Theatre (NTACT) audit. Method A multicentre, prospective audit of adult deceased donor kidney-only transplants was conducted across 14 UK transplant centres from February to September 2022. Data collected via RedCap focused on pre-operative antibiotic use, surgeon's grade, post-operative destination, crossmatch, and advanced haemodynamic monitoring. Descriptive statistics were used for analysis. Results Among 476 kidney-only transplants, 29 were excluded, leaving 446 transplants for analysis. Pre-operatively, 98.4% received antibiotics, with co-amoxiclav (n=147), ciprofloxacin (n=92), and amikacin (n=69) being most common. Consultant surgeons led 91.7% (n=409) of operations, while consultant anaesthetists led 61.4%. Notably, central lines (67.7% n=302), arterial lines (44.2% n=197), and advanced hemodynamic monitoring (27.6% n=123) were employed. Goal-directed fluid therapy was administered in 71.7% (n=320) of cases, with 71.6% (n=229) using static parameters. Post-operatively, 76.9% (n=343) were sent to a transplant ward, while 9.4% (n=42) and 10.8% (n=48) were directed to the intensive care unit and high dependency unit, respectively. Conclusions This audit highlights significant variations in perioperative practices, prompting further exploration into their potential impact on postoperative outcomes such as graft function and mortality.
