DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.019.title: eP24 Streamlining Diverticulitis Care: An Audit of Hospital Admission Practices
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.019.abstract: Abstract Aim Colonic diverticulosis affects about 25% of the population in developed countries, with 25% of these individuals developing symptoms, creating a significant burden on healthcare resources. This audit aimed to enhance clinicians' confidence in discharging patients with uncomplicated Hinchey 1 diverticulitis, reduce antibiotic use, ensure dietary advice is provided to all patients, and improve adherence to national guidelines for outpatient colonoscopy requests. Methods A prospective analysis was conducted, collating data on patients reviewed by surgical teams in A&E across two centres. Data collected included the date of admission, initial investigations (observations, bloods, imaging) and management (antibiotics, fluids, complications and follow-up colonoscopies). After the first cycle, we reported findings at our M&M session, teaching session and created posters throughout the department to reiterate the learning points. Results Prospective observations captured 20 patients in the first cycle and 15 patients in the second cycle, admitted between March-April 2024 and July-August 2024. Post-intervention, there was a positive correlation between admissions and the presence of significant co-morbidities, consistent with NICE guidelines. Although no reduction in IV antibiotic use was observed for uncomplicated diverticulitis, dietary advice significantly improved, with a 57.8% increase in specific guidance. Additionally, outpatient colonoscopy requests after diverticulitis flares rose by 30.7%, with notable improvements in the timing of these requests. Conclusions The interventions led to better adherence to guidelines, reducing unnecessary hospital admissions, and improving dietary advice and colonoscopy follow-ups. Targeted teaching and department-wide posters effectively enhanced guideline adherence, thereby improving patient outcomes.
affiliations: Department of General Surgery, Queens Hospital, Barking, Havering and Redbridge University Foundation Trust ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.075.title: eP95 Peri-operative Analgesia Use in Emergency Surgery: A Single-Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.075.abstract: Abstract Aims Pain management is widely recognised as a key part of peri-operative care. National guidance recommends routine use of paracetamol peri-operatively and NSAIDs post-operatively. Intravenous (IV) and oral paracetamol have equivalent analgesic efficacy. IV paracetamol has a higher carbon footprint, increased financial and time cost yet remains commonly used. NSAIDs are safe and effective for post-operative pain and have been shown to reduce opioid consumption in this setting. This audit investigated peri-operative analgesia practices for patients undergoing emergency surgery at our centre. Methods Retrospective data was collected for 47 patients undergoing emergency surgery over a one-month period. Prescriptions were reviewed using Electronic Prescribing and Medicines Administration software. Electronic records were used to identify patients with contraindications for NSAIDs, including structural kidney disease, stage 4 or 5 CKD, concomitant anticoagulation, asthma, and allergies. Results 89% of patients received paracetamol peri-operatively, 83% of which were regular prescriptions. Less than half received paracetamol at the maximum frequency. 83% of paracetamol prescriptions were for IV/oral route without preference for the oral. There were 44 (0.94 per patient) and 47 (1 per patient) pre- and post-operative IV administrations of paracetamol respectively. This included 34 avoidable IV administrations where patients were given oral medications concurrently. Only 28% of patients without contraindications were prescribed NSAIDs post-operatively, of which 15% were regular. Conclusions Prescribing and administration practices are crucial in ensuring optimal analgesic use. Further education regarding this topic and investigation into the barriers preventing maximal administration frequency, oral paracetamol & NSAID use is required.
affiliations: Musgrove Park Hospital ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.052.title: eP71 Audit of Emergency Laparotomy Workload in a District General Hospital: Are We Compliant with NELA Data Entry?
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.052.abstract: Abstract Aim The National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) requires all emergency laparotomies to be registered on its database after completion of care. This audit aimed to evaluate our compliance with NELA data entry by comparing the hospital's workload with national NELA data. Method This retrospective audit was conducted over two cycles, covering a total of 30 months. The first cycle focused on NELA Year 8, a 12-month period, which included 61 patients. The second cycle assessed NELA Years 9 and 10, covering an 18-month period, with 75 and 38 patients, respectively. All emergency laparotomies were included, while elective surgeries and procedures not captured by NELA were excluded. Data were extracted from patient records and compared with the NELA database. Analysis was performed using Microsoft Excel. Results In the first cycle (Year 8), 61 procedures were eligible for NELA registration, but only 31 (50%) were entered, with just 4 (13%) meeting the submission deadline. Additionally, 18 (67%) cases were registered more than 6 months after discharge, with an average delay of 206 days. Following the intervention, the second cycle showed marked improvement. In Year 9, 84% of cases were registered, and in Year 10, 95%. The average time to data entry decreased to 100 days, and all cases were submitted before the deadline. Conclusion Timely NELA data entry is essential for accurate representation of departmental activity. Significant improvements in compliance were achieved through targeted interventions, demonstrating the effectiveness of focused efforts in meeting national audit requirements.
affiliations: North Manchester General Hospital ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.101.title: eP127 Assessing quality and completeness of emergency general surgical operative notes: audit from a single institution
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.101.abstract: Abstract Aims To improve the quality and completeness of emergency (CEPOD) operative notes written by surgical trainees in a single institution Methods CEPOD operation notes from August 1st 2024 - August 31st 2024 were retrospectively reviewed and assessed against Royal College of Surgeons Good Surgical Practice recommendations of what to include in an operative note. Results Operation notes for 78 patients were assessed. 20% (N=16) were written by Core Trainees, 60% by Specialist Trainees (N=47) and 20% by Consultants (N=15). The areas that were most complete included: type of incision (N=71; 91%), operative diagnosis (N=74; 95%), operative findings (N=77; 99%) and the post-operative care plan (N=75; 96%). The areas that were least complete included: blood loss (N=5; 6%), DVT prophylaxis (N=20; 25%), details of implanted material where appropriate (N=2; 50%) and antibiotic prophylaxis (N=41; 52%). Conclusions Areas of improvement have been identified and have been addressed in the form of introducing a standard Emergency Surgery operation note template, introduced and accessible to all surgical trainees. A prospective re-audit is being undertaken in October 2024.
affiliations: Musgrove Park Hospital ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.061.title: eP80 Transitioning from trauma: Audit on discharge quality for major trauma patients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.061.abstract: Abstract Introduction Major trauma patients require complex multidisciplinary management with significant physical, medical, psychological, and social community rehabilitation needs. Clear effective communication on discharge is vital to ensure safe transition of care from hospital to community services. This audit aims to assess discharge quality, identify issues, and improve transition of care for major trauma patients. Methods Data was collected on major trauma patient discharge summaries before and after the implementation of a standardised discharge proforma, local training and education. Results were audited against the RCP discharge summary toolkit. The standard was that records would be 100% complete. Results The initial audit (n=20) revealed that discharges were often incomplete, unclear, and of insufficient quality with an average completion rate of 44.1%. Following proforma introduction, staff education and training this improved to 66.57%. Root cause analysis of issues comparing discharge between patients admitted on specialist major trauma ward (n=20,73.14%) vs outlier wards (n=20,60.00%) revealed significant disparity (t(50)=5.42, p=0.000). Following further reinforcement, a third cycle revealed improvement at 78.92% (trauma ward 81.08% vs outliers 76.76%; t(50)=2.12, p=0.037). Conclusion Major trauma patients are a unique cohort requiring comprehensive yet clear discharge to facilitate transition of care into the community. This can involve a multitude of different surgical specialties. Long-term quality improvement and education of rotational trainees on induction is essential for sustained quality. Patients on outlier wards are at higher risk of discharge issues. We present our proforma for multiply injured patients to improve discharge communication and patient care.
affiliations: Barts Health NHS Trust ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.102.title: eP128 New Doctors Cross-Specialty Induction Programme: A Closed Loop Quality Improvement Project at a Tertiary Acute Hospital in UK
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae318.102.abstract: Abstract Introduction Doctors in acute specialities are required to provide effective, timely and safe patient care. Human factors can make cross-speciality working challenging. Siloed departmental junior doctor inductions often do not promote effective multidisciplinary working across the on-call and emergency service provision. This quality improvement project (QIP) trials a joint specialty induction programme to promote collaboration, understanding and teamwork at one of the largest hospitals in the UK. Methods A pre-QIP structured survey was carried out to ascertain the induction experiences of the previous junior doctor rotation. A collaborative approach between surgical, medical and emergency (ED) departments were used to create a joint induction programme which was audited following its pilot. Results The joint induction programme shared the responsibilities for each speciality as well as the clinical, organisational and educational pressures that individuals may face, such as ED patient flow targets, or surgical logbook number targets. New components also detailed holistic support of residents, wellbeing and academic opportunities. The programme was piloted in August 2024. Most respondents (85%) agreed that the joint induction promoted a better understanding and greater teamwork within the hospital. More attendees rated the new induction as more effective than a departmental one. Conclusion This QIP demonstrates a joint induction programme to be an effective and collaborative approach for inducting new doctors in complex tertiary care centres. Together with increasing demands on NHS services and educational pressures on trainees, initiatives promoting better teamwork and hospital cohesion are particularly important within acute specialities.
affiliations: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae323.037.title: BHSeP44 Extraperitoneal approach to Abdominal Wall Reconstruction (AWR): the ‘closed’ posterior component separation
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae323.037.abstract: Abstract The foundation of AWR is posterior component separation by Rives-Stoppa (RS) retro-rectus sublay mesh repair, and transversus abdominis release (TAR). Traditional teaching dictates an initial laparotomy with full adhesiolysis to enable fascial closure and an intraperitoneal approach to component separation. We describe a novel extraperitoneal AWR approach, performing posterior component separation and sublay mesh repair with the peritoneum remaining closed. This maintains an intact visceral sac for faster dissection, reduced bowel handling, and facilitates take-down of the hernial orifice. We present our 3-year follow-up series of extraperitoneal ‘closed’ AWR. Method Retrospective case-note analysis of consecutive patients (n = 231) undergoing AWR 2018-2021 by a single plastic and general surgeon consultant team, with 3-year follow-up period. Results Extraperitoneal component separation was performed in all 231 patients as either RS (n = 186, 80.5%) or TAR (n = 45, 19.5%). Radical skin excision provided surgical access in 225 patients (97.4%), mean excision weight 1297 g (85–18000 g), mean BMI 30.9 (16.9–55.4). Direct fascial closure achieved in 97% (bridged repair n = 7, 3%). Hernia recurrence 1.7% (n = 4) at 3 years. Intraperitoneal procedures (bowel resection/anastomosis) performed in 2 patients (1.5%). Postoperative ileus 0%. Mean inpatient stay 4.6 days (SD 2.5). Post-operative complications; surgical site occurrence (SSO) (n = 26, 11.3%); respiratory (n = 21, 9.1%): VTE (n = 4, 1.7%): seroma (n = 16, 6.9%). Subsequent small bowel obstruction/laparotomy (n = 1, 0.4%). Conclusion The extraperitoneal approach to AWR is a safe, effective and reproducible technique, minimising postoperative ileus and bowel injury risk, promotes shorter duration of surgery and early postoperative discharge. This provides excellent outcomes and low hernia recurrence rate.
affiliations: Whiston Hospital , Prescot ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf036.007.title: IBC Oxford University Oral Abstract 7 - Outcomes of Braun procedure for reflux after OAGB- audit from a single centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf036.007.abstract: Abstract Introduction One anastomosis gastric bypass is an established bariatric procedure that gives good weight loss and resolution of obesity related morbidity. However, some patients suffer with bile reflux, presenting with debilitating symptoms like vomiting, nausea and retro-sternal burning. These symptoms can be difficult to control medically, and some patients require surgical intervention. Conversion to Roux-en-Y bypass is the most common procedure but it is major revisional surgery. Braun procedure, consisting of jejuno-jejunal anastomosis 30 cm distal to GJ anastomosis to bypass bile away from stomach is a less invasive option. Methods In this retrospective study of a prospective database, we analysed the outcomes of all the patients who underwent Braun procedure from October 2016–January 2024 for resolution of symptoms of bile reflux and to compare them with those of RYGB conversion. Patients who present with bile reflux are managed in the MDT setting and offered medical management. Diagnosis is confirmed with OGD and Barium study. Non-respond and those with severe reflux are offered surgical options of Braun Procedure and RYGB. Choice of procedure is based on MDT discussion considering the severity of reflux, quality of life, percentage excess weight loss and patient’s choice.Steps of Braun surgery- Video link. Results Total number of OAGB procedures done were 1024, 35 patients (3.4%) presented with bile reflux needing surgical management. 31/35 (88.6%) underwent Braun procedure. 4/35 (11.4%) underwent conversion to RYGB (3 for poor weight loss/weight regain and 1 patient choice). 27/31 Braun’s patients (88%) had immediate resolution of reflux symptoms, 23 (74%) maintained at 2 years follow up. None of the 4 had conversion to RYGB with 3 well controlled on PPI and one refused further surgery. 4/31 (13%) Braun’s patients did not improve at all. These were converted to RYGB. In total 8 patients had RYGB conversion (4 primary and 4 after failed Braun’s). All these patients had resolution of symptoms at 1 year follow up. There was no significant morbidity in either group. OAGB to RYGB group had 2 days hospital stay versus Braun group treated as day case. Conclusions Conversion to RYGB is the gold standard procedure for managing bile reflux Braun’s procedure is a safe and effective day case procedure with acceptable success rate and should be considered as an alternative.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf036.003.title: IBC Oxford University Oral Abstract 3 - Audit of outcome of SADIS- results from a single bariatric centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf036.003.abstract: Abstract Introduction Obesity is a growing concern globally. Surgical treatment of obesity includes Sleeve gastrectomy and Gastric bypass. These procedures can suffer inadequate weight loss and weight re-gain. SADIS- Single anastomosis Duodeno-ileal switch is a variant of Duodenal switch procedure that it gives good weight loss, weight maintenance and resolutions of obesity related morbidity. There has been concern about the nutritional deficiencies associated with SADIS and it is a technically challenging procedure, so it has limited the uptake. Methods It is a retrospective study with prospective data collection. We analyzed our results of all patients who underwent SADIS procedure from January 2016–December 2022. Primary aim-Weight loss and morbidity resolution at 6 months, 1 year, 2 years and 6–10 yearsNutritional deficiencies. Results 17 patients underwent SADIS procedure from January 2016–December 2022. Of these patients, majority are women. Age range between 27–62. Average BMI 55 kg/m2, BMI range 35 kg/m2–96.2 Kg/m2. Average weight loss was 32% (15%–53%) at 6 months, 69.6% (34%–90%) at 1 year and 86.2%. (Range 43%–109%) at 2 years, 6–10 years follow up is available for 16 out of 17 patients (One patient was lost to follow up). Average weight loss was 76% (62%–96%). None of the patients had protein energy malnutrition. 4 patients had Zinc and 3 had Calcium deficiency, all managed with oral replacement. Conclusions SADIS gives good outcomes in terms of weight loss and resolution of co-morbidities. Long term weight maintenance is better than bypass. Risk of nutritional deficiencies is acceptable and similar to bypass

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf092.047.title: A Paradigm Shift Towards Centralized Colorectal Cancer Surgery – A Nationwide Audit Using Administrative Data on 34’106 Patients Across Ten Years
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf092.047.abstract: Abstract Background Oncologic colorectal surgery has evolved significantly, leading to increasing surgical complexity necessitating subspecialty training. Concepts such as total mesocolic excision, D2/D3 lymphadenectomy or the widespread acceptance of robotics are known factors driving centralization. Aims The aim of the present study is to analyze the distribution of colorectal cancer surgery by level of complexity and size / case numbers of hospitals involved. We sought to test whether a shift towards specialized cancer care with improved access to minimal-invasive techniques has occurred following political initiatives to centralize cancer care. Methods The national BFS (Swiss federal statistic office) database was queried including the years 2012-2022. Parameters of interest included case numbers per center, complexity of resections, patient age, cancer site, type of access and available outcome parameters including in-hospital mortality, morbidity, surgical site infections or reoperations. Results A total of 34’106 colorectal cancer resections (44.2% female) were performed during the study period. The majority of resections were performed in large, non-academic centers. Only three centers performed a median of more than 100 resections per year during the study period. The percentage of patients operated in smaller hospitals declined from 38% to less than 20%, with the greatest increase in oncologic resections noted in large cantonal hospitals (50% to 71%). 6.7% of resections were performed in patients <50 years of age (early-onset colorectal cancer) with a 30% increase in absolute terms over the analyzed period. A late but notable trend towards robotic access occurred on a national level. Conclusion Despite the previous acceptance of general surgery care for colorectal cancer patients, a paradigm shift towards centralized treatment has occurred in the past 10 years in Switzerland. This shift is accompanied by higher rates of robotic access and growing numbers of early-onset colorectal cancer, underscoring the increased complexity and contemporary expectance of specialized care in this frequent disease.
affiliations: Department of Visceral Surgery and Transplantation, University Hospital Zurich , USZ, Zurich
Basel Academy, Institut for Quality and Research in Medicine , Basel

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.452.title: 487 Optimising Non-Operative Management of Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction: A Closed-Loop Audit Driving the Creation of Trust-Wide Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.452.abstract: Abstract Aim Small bowel obstruction (SBO) is a common surgical emergency with diverse management practices, as highlighted by the National Audit on Small Bowel Obstruction (NASBO). This study explores variations in patient characteristics, treatment strategies, and outcomes to identify practice differences that may impact patient outcomes, aiming to streamline management guidelines for SBO. Method This prospective study was conducted at a district general hospital in the UK, focusing on patients presenting with SBO to the emergency general surgery service. The first cycle, from December 2023 to March 2024, included 40 patients, while the second cycle, from May 2024 to July 2024, included 46 patients. Data on the timeline from diagnosis to resolution, with emphasis on non-operative management, were extracted from the hospital database and analysed using descriptive statistics in Excel. No patient identifiers were used, and approval was granted by the information governance team. Results A total of 86 patients were included, with a median age of 75 years. Mechanical causes were identified in 97% of cases, with adhesions affecting 47%. Non-operative management was successful in 60%, while 40% required surgery. Among patients with adhesional SBO, 78% of those who underwent a water-soluble oral contrast challenge were successfully managed non-operatively. Nutritional support was documented for 76% of patients, and 37% experienced recurrent SBO, with 80% requiring emergency surgery. Conclusions The use of water-soluble oral contrast showed a high success rate, emphasizing its potential in non-operative management. Close monitoring of recurrent SBO cases may reduce the need for surgical intervention.
affiliations: Wirral University Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Merseyside ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.357.title: 838 Cutting Through the Chaos: An Audit on Operating Theatre Delays
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.357.abstract: Abstract Aim To identify where theatre delays occur in cardiothoracic theatre and develop simple, low-cost, easily applicable methods for improvement. Method Prospective data was collected over one week. Standards were zero preventable delays, and 100% occurrence of required hair removal as stated in trust guidelines. After the first cycle, education to relevant clinicians alongside educational posters promoting the "Ready4Theatre" initiative, which includes being showered, hair removal and changed, were distributed to improve adherence and reduce theatre delays. Repeat prospective data was collected again. Results The greatest reduction in delays was in arrival in the anaesthetic room from 81% to 51%, and time from arrival in the theatre to the operation starting from 52% to 36%. This suggests that the simple measures to enable patients to be ready were effective. This is supported by the fact that 90% of patients underwent hair removal before arrival in the theatre, compared to 41% before. However, 86% of patients still had delays in some areas of their theatre journey, and hair removal in 50% of patients was inadequate. Conclusions Simple measures such as increased awareness and educational posters can reduce delays over a short period. However, improvements were still required, which could be achieved by developing trust guidelines. Guidance regarding hair removal improved adherence to this standard; however, it was still inappropriate, and therefore, future work will provide easy-to-refer posters that depict detailed hair removal guides. Although focused on cardiac surgery, the basic principles of "Ready4Theatre" could be deployed by other specialities to reduce preventable delays.
affiliations: Queen Elizabeth Hospital , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.274.title: 760 Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS) Following Distal Radius Fractures: An Audit to Improve Service Provision to the Distal Radius Fracture Patient Population
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.274.abstract: Abstract Aim Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), characterized by severe sensitivity to touch, skin changes, and joint stiffness, is a post-traumatic complication affecting the upper and lower extremities. This audit evaluated numerous clinical endpoints in the management of distal radius fracture (DRF) patients who developed CRPS, with the aim of improving service provision. Clinical endpoints were audited against the BSSH guidelines for DRF management. Method DRF patients with CRPS symptoms who underwent hand therapy between January 2023 to October 2024 were included. Clinical endpoints included duration from injury to definitive management and rehabilitation, type and duration of post-injury and post-operative immobilisation, and casting complications. Results Thirteen patients (100% female) were identified. Post-injury, all DRFs were immobilized in a backslab. Six patients (46%) were managed conservatively in a full cast for 6-weeks, on average 4-days from injury. Seven patients (54%), all with an intra-articular DRF, underwent surgery on average 6-days for injury, with six (46%) requiring an open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) and one (8%) managed with closed reduction and percutaneous pinning (CRPP) and full cast. Post-ORIF, Futura splint immobilization was used for five patients (86%) and backslab followed by Futura splint for one patient (14%), with 6-weeks of immobilization on average. Average duration from casting to physiotherapy was 54-days, in comparison to 35-days post-operatively. Conclusions Patients with intra-articular DRFs underwent surgery on average 6-days post-injury, while BSSH recommends surgery within 72hrs. The average duration of casting and post-operative immobilization was 6-weeks, whereas BSSH recommends 4-weeks. These findings aim to improve the management of DRFs.

Department of Occupational Therapy, UL Hospitals Group , Limerick ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.175.title: 1129 A Retrospective Audit Evaluating Post-Operative Outcomes in Patients Undergoing Oesophagectomy for Oesophageal Cancer
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.175.abstract: Abstract Introduction Oesophageal cancer is a prevalent and challenging malignancy requiring complex surgical intervention. Oesophagectomy, while offering curative benefits, is associated with significant postoperative morbidity. A thorough evaluation of post-operative outcomes is essential to refine perioperative protocols and improve recovery following surgery. Aim To evaluate post-operative outcomes in patients undergoing Oesophagectomy, focusing on complications, oncological clearance, nutritional recovery, and length of stay in patients without feeding jejunostomies performed during the index operation. Method A retrospective audit was performed on patients undergoing an Oesophagectomy at the Royal Liverpool University Hospital from January 2019 to June 2021. Using electronic patient records, data were collected on patient demographics, perioperative variables, and postoperative outcomes. Results 82 patients were included, all undergoing open surgery. The overall complication rate was 71.9% (n=59), with an anastomotic leak rate of 13.4% (n=11, 95% CI: 7.66-22.45%) and a chyle leak rate of 6.1% (n=5, 95% CI: 2.6-13.5%). Delayed conduit emptying requiring endoscopic intervention was observed in 28% (n=23). Respiratory complications arose in 40.2% (n=33, 95% CI: 30.3-51.1%) of the cohort. R0 resection was achieved in 85.4% (n=70) of cases. The average post-operative BMI reduction was 2.92 kg/m² (SD=2.31). Parenteral nutrition was used in 25.6% (n=21), and tube enteral feeding was utilised in 18.3% (n=15). Feeding jejunostomy was ultimately required in 7.3% (n=6). Mean length of stay was 23 days (SD=18.6). Conclusions This audit demonstrates the significant post-operative outcomes and challenges faced with patients undergoing an Oesophagectomy, highlighting the incidence of serious complications and the need for advanced nutritional support.
affiliations: Royal Liverpool University Hospital , Liverpool ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.591.title: 307 The Impact of COVID-19 on Timely Reversal of Defunctioning Loop Ileostomy Following Low Anterior Resection: A Cohort Study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.591.abstract: Abstract Aim The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted healthcare systems, causing delays in elective surgeries and potential adverse patient outcomes. A covering loop ileostomy, commonly created during low anterior resection, is ideally reversed within 2–4 months. Delays beyond 6 months are linked to increased patient distress and complication risks. This study assessed the pandemic's impact on ileostomy reversal timing by comparing pre-COVID-19 and COVID-19 era timelines. Method We analysed a prospectively maintained colorectal operative database, identifying patients with covering loop ileostomies after anterior resection in 2017–2018 and 2020–2021. Stoma formation and reversal rates were compared between these cohorts using Chi-square and independent Student t-tests, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results Seventy-eight patients had low anterior resections with ileostomies (45 pre-COVID and 33 during COVID). Of these, 32 patients in 2017–2018 and 19 in 2020–2021 were analysed. Groups were matched for age (65.02 vs. 64.99 years, p = 0.09), gender ratio, and adjuvant chemotherapy rates (5 vs. 2 patients, p = 0.08). All suitable pre-COVID patients underwent reversal, but 7 suitable COVID-era patients remained unreversed by study end. Mean time to reversal was 5.1 months pre-COVID vs. 10.7 months during COVID (p = 0.0001). Conclusions The COVID-19 pandemic significantly delayed timely reversal of loop ileostomies. Patients during the pandemic waited twice as long for stoma reversal compared to the pre-COVID era.
affiliations: Basildon University Hospital , Essex ,
Whipps Cross Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.313.title: 1126 Reporting of Thyroid Cytology Specimens and Their Correlation with Thyroid Histology: The 1st Cycle of an Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.313.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate compliance with RCPath standards for thyroid cytology, including the inclusion of Thy categories in all reports, distribution of cases across categories, correlation of cytology results with histology after thyroidectomy, and adherence to MDTM discussion standards for high-risk categories (Thy4/Thy5). Method A retrospective review of 253 thyroid cytology and histology samples from July 2023 to October 2024 was conducted across two tertiary centres within the same NHS trust. Reports were assessed for Thy category inclusion and prose explanations. Histological correlation from thyroidectomy specimens was analysed where available. Prevalence rates for malignancy and neoplasia were calculated for each Thy category. Compliance was measured against benchmarks: 100% inclusion of Thy categories, a Thy5 PPV of 97–99%, and 100% MDTM discussion for Thy4 and Thy5 cases. Results All reports (100%) included Thy categories and prose explanations, meeting RCPath standards. Case distribution showed Thy3f (32%) and Thy5 (19.2%) as the most prevalent categories. Malignancy prevalence rates were Thy5 (92.3%), Thy4 (85.7%), Thy3f (35%), and Thy3a (25%). MDTM discussion rates were 100% for Thy4 and Thy5, while Thy3f (76.4%) and Thy3a (63.6%) had lower rates. Conclusions While Thy5 PPV remains strong (92.3%), it falls short of the benchmark (97-99%), necessitating improvements in diagnostic accuracy. MDTM discussions met standards for high-risk categories but were lower for indeterminate categories (Thy3a/Thy3f), highlighting opportunities for improvement. Enhanced multidisciplinary collaboration, targeted interventions and a planned re-audit aim to address these gaps and ensure alignment with national standards.
affiliations: University of Leicester , Leicester ,
University Hospitals Derby and Burton , Derby and Burton ,
University Hospitals Derby and Burton , Derby ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.312.title: 1121 Comprehensive Care for Geriatric and Frail Surgical Patients: A Multi-Cycle Audit and Review of Outcomes
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.312.abstract: Abstract Aim A National Confidential Enquiry of Patient Outcome and Death 2010 report highlighted deficiencies in care for elderly surgical patients, recommending routine geriatrician input. This audit, conducted in a district general hospital’s general surgery department, aims for 95% of eligible emergency laparotomy patients to receive geriatric review and compares 30-day mortality and average length of stay (LOS) to national averages. Method A multi-cycle audit with three periods of data collection, analysed patients aged ≥80 or ≥65 and frail undergoing emergency abdominal surgery. Data sources included patient notes, electronic referrals, and the NELA database. Results 2017/18: 13 patients, 15.4% 30-day average mortality, 23% geriatric review. A liaison consultant was employed as a result. 2020/21: 14 patients, 15.8% mortality, 17.7-day average LOS, 64.3% geriatric review. Following this, an eReferral system was introduced, but the liaison role became vacant. 2023/24: 26 patients, 3.8% mortality, 23.2-day average LOS, 4.2% geriatric review. Conclusions Despite initial improvements, the department remains noncompliant with national standards. The department is underperforming compared to national averages for LOS (11 days) and geriatric review (33.2%) but a better 30-day mortality (9.0%). The department remains noncompliant with national standards. Dedicated time in geriatricians’ job plans is needed for consistent reviews, but reliance on a single individual creates vulnerabilities. A multidisciplinary team approach is essential for reliability. Following this audit cycle, the liaison role was re-established. Recommendations include mandatory clinical frailty scoring on admission, appointing a 'geriatric lead' surgeon and integrating geriatric care into resident inductions, with summary posters present in the doctors’ office.
affiliations: Barnsley Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , Barnsley ,
Leeds Teaching Hospitals , Leeds ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.311.title: 1112 An Audit of Trauma Call Attendance and Documentation at a Major Trauma Centre in London: Improving Trauma Care
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.311.abstract: Abstract Aim Adherence to NICE and local guidelines of trauma calls significantly reduces mortality, morbidity, and healthcare costs. Accurate documentation of attendance and roles during trauma calls is crucial for guideline compliance, quality assurance, and medico-legal accountability. This audit aims to assess and enhance adherence to trauma call documentation. Method An audit was conducted over two weeks in November 2024 at St. Mary's Hospital London, a major trauma centre. Data were retrospectively collected via pre-alert forms (Signal App, Microsoft Teams) and electronic patient records. Data points included trauma type (code red/black), specialty attendance, sign-in sheet completion, role documentation, and admission details, comparing in-hours and out-of-hours performance. Results Of 103 trauma calls, 31% lacked completed sign-in sheets, and team roles were recorded in only 22%. 64 patients were admitted, 56 under surgical specialties. The admitting surgical specialty was present from the start of the trauma call in 55% of cases. Attendance for obligatorily attending specialties based on records varied considerably: Major Trauma/Neurosurgery (94%), Anaesthetics (64%), Trauma and Orthopaedics (50%), and General Surgery (40%). Identified barriers to accurate documentation included unfamiliarity with electronic systems, consecutive trauma calls, and resource issues (e.g., faulty computers). Documentation was poorer out-of-hours. Conclusions The audit highlights critical gaps in trauma call documentation, with incomplete records posing risks to care delivery, guideline adherence, and medico-legal safety. Proposed improvements include implementing a tap-in card system for automated sign-in, documentation templates, and identifying attendance barriers through staff surveys. These changes aim to enhance compliance with guidelines and improve multidisciplinary coordination in trauma care.
affiliations: St Mary’s Hospital, Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.264.title: 672 An Audit of Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsies for Malignant Melanoma
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.264.abstract: Abstract Aim Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) has been used as staging tool for Malignant Melanoma for over 20 years. This audit sought to ensure that standards are being met in melanoma patients undergoing SLNB at the Royal Free Hospital. Method A retrospective audit examined electronic notes for patients undergoing SLNBs for melanoma from September-November 2024. NICE guidelines 2022 set our standard to determine eligibility for SLNB. It recommends SLNB in melanoma patients with a Breslow thickness >1mm or to consider SLNB in patients with Breslow thickness 0.8-1mm with at least one of ulceration, lymphovascular invasion or a mitotic rate ≥2/mm2. Results After screening, 61 patients were included. 15/61 (24.6%) of these patients had a Breslow thickness between 0.8 and 1mm. 7/15 (46.7%) patients were appropriately offered SLNB due to having a mitotic index ≥2/mm2. 7/15 (46.7%) did not meet criteria for SLNB. 1/15 (6.7%) did not have documented lymphovascular invasion, ulceration or mitotic index and therefore potentially did not meet criteria. The lymph nodes from all 15 of these patients were negative for melanoma deposits on histopathology. Overall departmental compliance was 53/61 (87%), which was reduced compared to 97.4% at the previous audit cycle. Conclusions SLNB carries risks of increased morbidity and mortality and therefore it is very important that it is carried out on eligible patients only. Despite ongoing audit within the department, sustained change has not yet been achieved. This audit highlights the importance of further intervention to ensure long-lasting compliance with the NICE 2022 standard for SLNB in patients with melanoma.
affiliations: Royal Free Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.211.title: 81 Prescribing of Appropriate Dual Antiplatelet Therapy Following Emergency Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting Procedure Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.211.abstract: Abstract Aim Dual antiplatelet therapy is an integral component of post-operative management following an emergency coronary artery bypass grafting procedure. Our aim was to assess whether patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting at Essex Cardiothoracic Centre were discharged with appropriate 1-year dual antiplatelet therapy according to EACTS guidelines. Method Discharge records were retrospectively reviewed between May-August 2023 to identify patients who underwent emergency coronary artery bypass grafting. Subsequently, eligible patients discharge summaries were reviewed to establish post-operative antiplatelet therapy status. The intervention implemented involved providing departmental education on dual antiplatelet guidelines to resident doctors and placing posters in the doctor’s office to serve as a point of reference. In addition, a registrar would counter-check antiplatelet medication on the day of patient discharge. A re-audit of patients discharged between September-November 2023 was conducted to assess the effects of the aforementioned intervention. Results Our results demonstrated, prior to intervention, 56 patients underwent emergency coronary artery bypass grafting between May–August 2023. Of which, 82.14% of patients had appropriate post-operative dual antiplatelet therapy on discharge, however 100% of patients had one antiplatelet drug prescribed on discharge. Following intervention, 55 patients underwent emergency coronary artery bypass grafting with 100% of patients being discharged with appropriate post-operative dual antiplatelet therapy. Conclusions Dual antiplatelet therapy following coronary artery bypass grafting is vital to prevent short term post-operative complications and improve long term outcomes. This audit demonstrates how departmental education and introduction of a check prior to discharge can help to improve achieving optimal dual antiplatelet prescribing.
affiliations: Essex Cardiothoracic Centre , Basildon ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.210.title: 74 Surgical Precision: A Comprehensive Audit of Operation Notes at Shendi Teaching Hospital and El-Mek Nimer University Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.210.abstract: Abstract Aim Clinical audits are essential for enhancing the quality of clinical practice and patient safety by measuring outcomes and implementing changes based on best practices. Maintaining proper operative notes in surgical practice is crucial for patient safety, continuity of care, and legal compliance. This study explored the critical components of operation notes, the impact of suboptimal documentation on patient care, and the role of clinical audits in driving quality improvement initiatives. Method A retrospective clinical audit was conducted to assess the accuracy, completeness, and overall quality of operation notes for surgical procedures performed at El-mek Nimer University Hospital and Shendi Teaching Hospital. The audit standard criteria were from the Royal College of Surgeons. Results The implementation of the comprehensive audit at Shendi Teaching Hospital led to a notable improvement in the documentation of operative notes, with improvements ranging from 1% to 37%, except for a few items, such as the name of the operative procedure carried out, any extra procedure and the reason it was performed, anticipated blood loss, and antibiotic prophylaxis, which decreased. There was a general increase in compliance with the documentation guidelines for operation notes at both hospitals. Adherence to documentation guidelines could have been more suboptimal for most criteria measured. Conclusions The audits demonstrated a significant improvement in the documentation of postimplementation operation notes. These results underscore the importance of adhering to the guidelines set by the Royal College of Surgeons to ensure comprehensive and accurate medical records.

Shendi Teaching Hospital , Shendi ,
El-mek Nimer University Hospital , Shendi ,
