DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.011.title: 807 A Retrospective Audit of the Royal College of Surgeons Undergraduate Curriculum in Surgery (2023) Among Scottish Medical Students
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.011.abstract: Abstract Aim The Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) advocates for a standardized undergraduate surgical curriculum to prepare medical students for surgical training. In Scotland, the diversity of training hospitals—encompassing tertiary, district general (DGH), and rural general hospitals (RGH)—raises questions about whether students achieve these learning outcomes. This audit examined if Scottish medical students meet RCS surgical learning outcomes and how hospital type influences experiences. Method An electronic questionnaire was distributed to final and penultimate-year medical students across Scotland, assessing confidence in achieving RCS outcomes and perceptions of surgical placement quality. Results Forty-six students responded: 30% trained in tertiary hospitals, 56% in DGHs, and 13% in RGHs. Placements averaged 4–6 weeks, primarily in General Surgery (76%), with exposure to 2–3 additional specialties. While 56% of students felt they met the learning outcomes, only 42% felt adequately prepared for a surgical FY1 role. Most students (94%) had operating theatre exposure, but only 42% had assessed or presented patients in outpatient clinics, indicating a critical gap in clinical training. DGHs were most valued (40%) for hands-on opportunities and mentorship. Tertiary hospitals, while promoting team integration, reported higher bullying incidents. RGHs, though resource-limited, were appreciated by 20% of students for personalized learning and exposure to rural surgery. Conclusions These findings reveal variability in placement quality and gaps in achieving RCS learning outcomes, with implications for surgical education. Enhancing clinical training and optimizing placements could improve surgical preparedness and recruitment to underserved areas.
affiliations: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary , Aberdeen ,
Aberdeen Royal Infirmary , Abderdeen ,
Queen Elizabeth University Hosptial , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.337.title: 862 Blood Product Utilisation in Breast Surgery: An Audit of Clinical and Financial Outcomes
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.337.abstract: Abstract Aim Preoperative blood grouping and saving is routine for elective breast surgery, though transfusion requirements are low (3.8%, higher in reconstruction). Current guidelines at St. Vincent’s Hospital recommend group and screen for mastectomy and reconstruction but lack protocols for wide local excision (WLE) or sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB). This audit assessed adherence to these guidelines and evaluated the cost-effectiveness of preoperative group and screen in breast surgery. Method This retrospective audit reviewed 129 patients who underwent elective breast surgery between 9 September and 28 November 2024. Data collected included demographics, surgical details, haemoglobin levels, and transfusion requirements. Analysis was performed using R 4.1, and findings were presented to relevant stakeholders. Results Of the 129 patients (median age 63.5), 40 (31%) underwent mastectomy/reconstruction, and 85 (66%) underwent WLE/SLNB. Preoperative group and screen were performed in 90% of mastectomy/reconstruction cases and 21% of WLE/SLNB cases. No patients required transfusion. At least 24 unnecessary type and screen orders were identified, incurring additional costs. Conclusions Routine group and screen for elective mastectomy and reconstruction is widely adhered to but resulted in no transfusions, questioning its necessity. For minor procedures, testing is infrequent and variable. These findings highlight the economic inefficiency of unnecessary preoperative blood sampling, suggesting that clinical judgment based on patient-specific risk factors could improve cost-efficiency while maintaining safe care standards.
affiliations: SVUH , Dublin ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.296.title: 1007 Improving Discharge Letter Timeliness in Vascular Services: A Two-Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.296.abstract: Abstract Aim Discharge letters are crucial for ensuring continuity of care between secondary and primary care providers. Delays can lead to disrupted follow-up care, medication errors and patient safety risks. According to Trust guidelines, discharge letters should be available to GPs within 24 hours of discharge. This audit aimed to assess delays in discharge letters within the Vascular service at University Hospitals North Midlands, identify contributing factors, and propose recommendations to improve timeliness. Method This retrospective audit consisted of two cycles. The first cycle, conducted from May to June 2022, identified delays and informed interventions presented to the clinical team. The second cycle, conducted from December 2023 to February 2024, re-evaluated progress. Data included time from discharge to letter authorisation, admission reason, procedures undertaken and patient location. Results In the first cycle, 52 delayed discharge letters were identified, with an average delay of 14.6 days. In the second cycle, delays were reduced to 35, but the average delay time increased to 19.4 days. Significant improvements were seen in Central Treatment Suite Day cases, which demonstrated no delay in 2024. However, 44% of delays in both cycles were angioplasty cases performed in interventional radiology, where no juniors are based. Conclusions Overall, a reduction in the number of delayed discharge letters was shown, paired with an increase in the average delay. Presenting the second cycle findings led to agreed changes, including assigning responsibility for interventional radiology letters and keeping patients on vascular lists until letters are completed. A new audit cycle is underway to assess further improvements.
affiliations: University Hospitals North Midlands , Stoke-on-Trent ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.331.title: 562 Identifying Patients Undergoing Surgery for DCIS Suitable for Sentinel Node Biopsy – a Single Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.331.abstract: Abstract Aim Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast cancer precursor, confined to the ducts, with a very low risk of lymph node metastasis (<1%). The NICE guidelines recommend sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) for patients undergoing mastectomy for DCIS to detect occult invasive disease. For breast-conserving surgery (BCS), SLNB is considered in high-risk patients, such as those with extensive microcalcifications, a palpable mass, or mass-like lesions, due to the added morbidity and resource use of SLNB. Method Data were prospectively collected from patients undergoing BCS or mastectomy for DCIS at a single unit between 2017 and 2022. Parameters included pre-operative tumor size, histological grade, type of surgery, and postoperative tumor size and histology, with SLNB data recorded where applicable. Results Eighty-five patients underwent WLE and 17 mastectomies. Mean age was 62 years in both groups. Four high-risk BCS patients underwent upfront SLNB; one had microinvasion. Of the 81 BCS patients without upfront SLNB, three developed invasive disease and underwent SLNB as a second procedure. The odds ratio for upfront SLNB in high-risk patients was 8.66 (95% CI: 0.68–109.9, p=0.0956), indicating higher likelihood of invasive disease postoperatively, though not statistically significant, due to small sample size. Conclusions This audit supports selective SLNB for high-risk patients undergoing BCS. While the high-risk group was more likely to have invasive disease, the result was not statistically significant due to the small sample size. Further studies are needed to refine SLNB indications in DCIS.
affiliations: Wrightington Wigan and Leigh NHS Trust , Wigan ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.262.title: 643 Audit of Accuracy of Clinical Coding for Complex Abdominal Wall Surgeries
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.262.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate coding is crucial to ensure appropriate remuneration for clinical procedures. The coding process is prone to error as coders, who are non-clinical, rely on clinical documentation to determine what they believe are the appropriate ICD and OPCS-4 codes. This is particularly complex in plastic surgery where operations often have subtle differences. This study audited the accuracy of coding of complex abdominal wall reconstructive operations in the Royal Free Hospital and reviewed its financial implications. Method Patients were included who underwent complex abdominal wall reconstructive surgeries, which we defined as requiring both general surgery and plastic surgery input, between August and November 2024. Their overall HRG codes, and corresponding ICD and OPCS-4 codes, were reviewed for accuracy based on documentation available for each patient. Results were discussed with senior clinicians and the clinical coding team and HRG codes were amended as appropriate. Results Overall, four cases were included. Changes were made to ICD and OPCS-4 codes in all 4 cases. The addition of the clinician-validation process led to more accurate coding for these cases, resulting in significant financial savings of, on average, £6,000 per case. Conclusion This audit emphasised the importance of collaboration between clinicians and coders to ensure accurate clinical coding and minimise potential financial loses for NHS trusts. Increased awareness of clinical coding by the clinical team and clear documentation are essential.
affiliations: Royal Free Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.221.title: 212 An Audit on Single-Centre Compliance with BOAST Standards and Local Infection Control Policy for Safe Intraoperative Tourniquet Use in Plastic Surgery Theatres
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.221.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate tourniquet infection control and tourniquet safety compliance at Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust (MYTT) Plastic Surgery Theatres against trust's six-use-day tourniquet infection control policy and BOAST standards. Method A one-month retrospective audit reviewing electronic and paper records of plastic surgery cases where arm and digital tourniquets were used. The scrub team was surveyed regarding awareness of the six-use-day infection control policy, and if tourniquet cuffs were marked after each use. Data on tourniquet type, skin integrity, isolation, exsanguination, pressure, duration, and six-use-markings were analysed using Excel. Results Of 62 cases, 43 used arm tourniquets and 19 digitals. Tourniquet duration was documented in 90.3%, type in 67.7% and pressure in only 39.5% of operation notes. Electronic peri-operative pathway achieved 100% compliance, while paper care pathways had compliance rates of 90.3%, 97.7%, and 88.7% for type, pressure, and duration, respectively. Skin integrity, isolation, and exsanguination methods were not recorded in any notes. Fixed pressure of 250 mmHg was used in 95.3% of cases, exceeding BOAST standards in 53.5%. All cases met the 120-minute duration limit. Tourniquets were not marked but were disposed after each list. Conclusions Overall, tourniquets were used safely but written documentation was poor, indicating a clear need for improvement. Documentation by the scrub team was significantly better than by the operating team, with digital records providing more comprehensive documentation. 250mmhg was used irrespective of patients' SBP. Tourniquets were not marked as per trust policy. To improve practices, a teaching session and poster reminders have been introduced, with plan to re-audit.
affiliations: Pinderfields Hospital , Wakefield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.220.title: 211 Improving Compliance with GIRFT Guidelines: A Cross-Site Re-Audit of Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Across Frimley Health NHS Trust
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.220.abstract: Abstract Aim This re-audit evaluated the proportion of patients requiring overnight stays following laparoscopic cholecystectomy, investigated causes of delayed discharge, and assessed compliance with the Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) guidelines. It was conducted in Frimley Health NHS Trust as a cross-site comparison between Frimley Park and Wexham Park Hospitals to identify best practices. Updated GIRFT recommendations from September 2022 were adapted into Frimley Health’s local guidelines and evaluated during this audit. The guidelines suggest a 90%-day case rate with standardised surgical techniques, including patient positioning with a slight head-up angle, table rotation towards the surgeon, and intermittent pneumatic compression. Three 5mm ports, one 10mm port, and low-pressure CO₂ insufflation (10mmHg) are recommended. Local anaesthetic (30mls - 0.25% bupivacaine) should be instilled around the liver and gallbladder while avoiding surgical drains. Method This closed-loop audit compared data from the initial cycle (July–October 2023, Frimley Park, n=107) with a second cycle (April–June 2024) across Frimley Park (n=121) and Wexham Park (n=72). Data were retrospectively collected from case notes and operative records. Metrics included day-case rates, guideline compliance, reasons for delayed discharge, and 14-day readmissions. Results Day case rates improved from 45% to 70% at Frimley Park, with pain (30%) and drain monitoring (28%) as common causes of delays. Wexham Park achieved 77.8%, aligning with GIRFT targets. Both sites reported low 14-day readmission rates (9%) and consistent patient safety outcomes. Conclusions This cross-site audit facilitated shared learning and progress. Continued efforts are needed to enhance pain management, patient counselling, and adherence to surgical protocols.
affiliations: Frimley Park Hospital , Frimley ,
Wexham Park Hospital , Slough ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.200.title: 611 PAPAYA Study (Paediatric Appendicitis Pathway and Audit Yield Assessment)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.200.abstract: Abstract Aim Appendicitis is one of the most common causes of acute abdominal pain in children, often requiring surgical intervention. However, despite advances in diagnostic techniques, the negative appendicectomy rate—where the appendix is removed, but histology confirms it was not inflamed — remains higher than desired. This multicentre study aimed to investigate the causes for the high negative appendicectomy rate in paediatric patients across the UK. Method A multicentre study was conducted from August 2020 to August 2024 at 8 UK district general hospitals(DGHs). Patients were identified using clinical coding and radiological text reports. Cases were eligible for inclusion if they were admitted with a suspicion of appendicitis. Results The negative appendicectomy rate was 21% over the study period. Additionally, statistical analysis showed that there was a significant difference in age between operative and conservative management groups (p = 0.0023).The Spearman correlation is close to zero (0.004),with a high p-value(0.951), indicating that there is no association between PAS scores and histology results, similar to the correlation between the ultrasound (US) and the histological findings(p= 0.336). Finally, the use of antibiotics on admission didn't prevent the re-admission of patients treated conservatively(p=0.039). Conclusions There is a discrepancy between the GIRFT reported negative rate of appendicectomy in district general hospitals versus the tertiary centres. A new study looking at the management techniques of a suspected paediatric appendicitis in tertiary centres versus DGHs is planned to start in 2025 to throw light on the main aetiology for the discrepancy.
affiliations: Imperial College London , London ,
Ipswich Hospital , Ipswich ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.644.title: 647 Sustainability in Abdominal Wall Reconstruction: An Eco-Audit of the Abdominal Wall Reconstruction Pathway
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.644.abstract: Abstract Aim Abdominal wall reconstruction is a procedure requiring input from multiple specialities and is often performed on complex multimorbid patients. These patients often require a high level of care, the environmental impact of which has yet to be explored. Method A retrospective study of 23 patients undergoing abdominal wall reconstruction at a single centre was performed. Process mapping and life-cycle analyses were performed for surgical and inpatient stay including facilities, consumables, medical gases, equipment, food and linen and travel. Estimates for carbon dioxide emissions were generated for each stage of the care pathway, with variability considered, as well as potential areas of savings. Results This study estimated the carbon footprint of a patient undergoing abdominal wall reconstruction surgery to be approximately 669.56kgCO2eq. Inpatient stay overwhelmingly had the highest overall contribution to the carbon footprint (558.0kgCO2eq., 83.3% overall pathway emissions). From bottom-up calculations, patient travel was the predominant source of carbon emissions (58.47kgCO2eq, 52.41%) followed by the production and transport of equipment and building electricity, gas, oil and water usage. Conclusions This is the first study to estimate the carbon footprint of a surgical pathway for complex patients, using abdominal wall reconstruction as an example. Strategies to combat the impact of carbon emissions and increase sustainability included increased implementation of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocols to reduce inpatient stay, increased accuracy of waste segregation and continued use of total intravenous anaesthetic.
affiliations: University College London , London ,
Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.302.title: 1048 Evaluating Inpatient Management of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding - A Retrospective Single Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.302.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aims to evaluate inpatient management of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding (LGIB) at a single District General Hospital over a 2-month period using British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidelines as gold standard management. Method Data of patients admitted with LGIB in August and September 2024 was retrospectively collected. Results Patients with LGIB were admitted 44 times across 2 months. 11 patients (25%) had no imaging, treatment or procedure with a combined total of 29 bed days between them. 6 of them (14%) were unnecessary admissions as per met BSG criteria. 9 patients (20%) had no imaging or procedure and were treated with intravenous fluids alone. They also accounted for 29 bed days. 3 of them (7%) were unnecessary admissions as per BSG criteria. 4 patients (9%) were treated with tranexamic acid. 7 patients (16%) had blood transfusions including 3 (7%) who did not meet BSG criteria for transfusion. 2 patients (5%) had a CT angiogram against guidelines as both had a Shock Index <1 although one was anaemic and hypotensive. Meanwhile, 4 patients (9%) had a Shock Index >1 and did not have a CT angiogram as guidelines suggest. 3 patients (7%) had inpatient flexible sigmoidoscopies despite being haemodynamically stable with the reason for inpatient intervention given as ‘ongoing bleeding’. Conclusions A significant proportion of LGIB admissions have minimal or no intervention. Inpatient management does not appear to follow BSG guidelines. Work needs to be done to prevent unnecessary admissions including research into the use of Virtual Wards for this patient group.
affiliations: Mid Yorkshire NHS Teaching Trust , Wakefield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.301.title: 1044 Improving Surgical Handover Quality: A Two-Cycle Audit Using RCS Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.301.abstract: Abstract Aim Effective handovers are essential for patient safety and continuity of care in surgery. The Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) has developed comprehensive guidelines in which a minimum dataset is recommended for inclusion when handing over patients to incoming surgical teams. This audit aims to evaluate and enhance the quality of surgical handovers in a tertiary hospital by measuring current practices against the RCS guidelines. Method A two-stage Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle was conducted. Data on surgical handover sessions in a tertiary hospital over a week was collected and handover sheets were retrospectively reviewed. Following the first cycle, a standardized handover sheet was developed. In the second cycle, posters were placed to reinforce these guidelines. Compliance was re-audited at 1-month intervals after each intervention to assess improvements and monitor progress. Results In the first cycle, 50 handovers were reviewed, revealing deficiencies in key areas such as patient identification (75%), date of admission (30%), location (80%), responsible consultant (40%), diagnosis (60%) and results of significant/ pending investigations (50%). Re-audit data demonstrated significant improvements after implementing interventions, including standardized handover sheets and posters. Patient identification rose to 95%, diagnosis 75%, date of admission 50%, location 88%, responsible consultant 60%, diagnosis 75% and results of significant/ pending investigations 67%. Overall compliance with the RCS minimum dataset improved from 45% to 75%. Conclusions The audit demonstrated that targeted interventions improved compliance with RCS guidelines for surgical handovers. This highlights the effectiveness of structured interventions in enhancing the safety and reliability of surgical handovers.
affiliations: Glasgow Royal Infirmary , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.300.title: 1030 A Completed Audit Cycle on Listed Complications on Consent Forms for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy at a Single Centre, Heartlands Treatment Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.300.abstract: Abstract Introduction GMC Guidelines state that consent forms should make patients aware of all the probable complications of procedures and surgeries. This audit aimed to assess whether all 8 NHS-listed and other relevant complications were mentioned in consent forms. Two complete audit cycles were carried out, with an intervention implemented after the first cycle to improve compliance with the guidelines on documenting potential procedure complications followed by a second cycle. Method A single-center prospective study was conducted on patients undergoing Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy between August 2023 to December 2024. Data was collected on complications recorded, additional procedure requirements, and the consenting person’s grade. After the first cycle, the data were analyzed, and departmental awareness was raised, followed by a second cycle. Results Thirty first cycle records showed compliance for bile-duct injury and bleeding was 100%, infection at 90%, and visceral injury at 83%. Anaesthetic risks, 56.7%, and post-cholecystectomy syndrome, 45%, had the lowest compliance. Audit presentation alongside awareness posters via team messaging platforms, resulted second audit cycle of 13 records where a compliance of 100% was noted for all NHS-listed complications except for visceral injury (84.6%) and venous thromboembolism (61.5%). Compliance improved for all other complications except for pain where compliance was reduced by 48%. Conclusions Listing relevant complications in consent forms is crucial. Awareness through different platforms aside from audit meetings can help raise compliance. On-going audit cycles will help maintain compliance as new residents rotate to the department. Procedure-specific consent forms complementing specific patient information sheets will be the ideal next step.
affiliations: Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham , Birmingham ,
Birmingham Heartlands Hospital , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.209.title: 66 A One Year Retrospective Audit on the Success Rate and Visual Acuity Changes Following a Macular Hole Repair Surgery in Galway University Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.209.abstract: Abstract Aim A macular hole is an anatomical opening in the neurosensory retina which develops at the fovea and causes loss of central vision which is debilitating to patients' quality of life. Macular holes are generally repaired surgically by performing a combination of different techniques such as pars plana vitrectomy, internal limiting membrane (ILM) peel or flap and a type of gas tamponade. This Audit allows the evaluation of surgical outcomes with regards to macular hole closure rates, visual acuity outcomes, patient waiting time and complications. Method This audit reviewed all macular hole repair surgeries performed by the vitreo-retinal consultant Mr. Paul-Eduard Stanciu in the ophthalmology department of Galway University Hospital (GUH) over the past year (July 2023 to July 2024). Variables analyzed include surgical method, visual acuity, closure rates and complications. Results This audit included 32 patients that had undergone an ILM peel (N=21) or ILM peel with ILM patch graft or a flap (N=11). Visual acuity in logMAR was analysed at 2 and 6 weeks postoperatively and an overall improvement was noted at 6 weeks (change at 2 weeks: 0.03 [SD, 0.54], P=.09 and change at 6 weeks: -0.29 [SD,0.29], P=.22). Surgical success and macular hole closure rate was calculated using post-operative OCT scans and was 96.55%. Conclusions MH repair surgery done at GUH had a success rate of 96.55% and a notable visual acuity improvement at 6 weeks. There was no statistically significant difference between the surgical methods used (ILM peel vs ILM peel + graft or flap).
affiliations: Galway University Hospital , Galway ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.481.title: 405 A Single-Centre Retrospective Audit to Determine Utilisation of Parenteral Nutrition in Paediatric Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.481.abstract: Abstract Aim Parenteral Nutrition (PN) is utilised in surgery to support post-operative recovery and meet metabolic demands. However, the use of PN in the paediatric surgical population is not well-characterised, with risks associated with overprescription. We aimed to investigate if current PN use in paediatric surgical patients reflects general paediatric artificial nutrition guidelines. Method A single-centre retrospective audit was conducted to assess PN usage over one year (2023) in paediatric surgery, excluding neonates. Data collected included: patient demographics, duration of PN and complications encountered. Optimal benefit was standardised at receiving ≥5 days PN based on guidelines by European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) in 2005. Results A total of 27 patients (19 M: 8F) were identified (median age: 8 years, range: 2 months–16 years) with a total of 28 PN episodes recorded. Sub-optimal PN was common (n = 15, 54%) with the population receiving 3 days of median full-dose feed. PN was utilised most commonly following: appendicectomy and bowel obstruction (n = 7 per group, 25% respectively). There were nine complications (32%) with central lines, namely: loss of access resulting in abrupt cessation of PN (n = 4) and infection (n = 2). No significant difference in PN duration optimisation was observed with pre-nutritional dietician review. Conclusions This study shows the potential risk of overprescription and adverse events of sub-optimal PN use in paediatric surgical patients. There is a need for targeted national guidelines specific for paediatric surgical populations; with future prospective national studies informing healthcare professionals of optimised feeding regimes.
affiliations: University of Cambridge , Cambridge ,
Paediatric Surgery Unit, Addenbrooke's Hospital , Cambridge ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.008.title: 450 Timeliness of Surgical Stabilisation of Rib Fractures: An Audit Against BOAST-15 Guidelines in a Major Trauma Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.008.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess adherence to BOAST-15 blunt chest wall trauma guidelines on time from injury to surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF) at a major trauma centre and identifying factors influencing delays. A 72-hour benchmark post-injury was used, allowing an additional 24 hours beyond the 48-hour recommendation to account for assessment, conservative management trial, and surgical planning. Method Retrospective electronic note analysis (November 2020 - July 2024) was conducted to determine the date of injury and of SSRF. Patient characteristics such as Injury Severity Score (ISS), mechanisms of injury, ventilation requirements, ITU vs PTU stay, and pain relief methods were recorded. Results Of the 119 patients included, the median time to SSRF was 3 days(range 1-12), with 74 (62.2%) undergoing surgery within 72 hours and 45(37.8%) experiencing delays. Standard deviation of 2.41 days also highlights variability in timing. Longer ITU stays correlated moderately with increased time to surgery (Spearman’s coefficient 0.479, p<0.001), and assisted ventilation patients had a significantly higher mean time to SSRF (4.3 vs. 3.0 days, p=0.028). These findings suggest ITU and ventilation requirements could influence time to SSRF. Conclusions Streamlined pre-operative pathways and expedited multidisciplinary decision-making are needed to address delays in surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF). Given pre-existing evidence linking earlier surgical intervention for rib fractures to better outcomes, balancing timely intervention with patient safety is crucial. As this audit found limited correlation between most clinical variables and surgical timing, further exploration of other clinical, systemic, and logistical factors is needed to reduce delays and improve patient outcomes.
affiliations: Cardiff University , Cardiff ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.277.title: 794 A Prospective Audit of All Refetrrals to the On-Call Orthopaedic Service at Queen Elizabeth University Hospital (Glasgow)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.277.abstract: Abstract Aim To quantify referrals and investigate possible areas for improvement Method A prospective audit was conducted over a 2-week period (10th-23rd June), collecting data on all the referrals that were made to the 1st and 2nd on-call registrars. Data included patient CHI, referral location, diagnosis and management outcomes. A total of 381 referrals were recorded, with 313 being included in the final analysis after excluding incomplete data. All patients were followed up at 2 months via portal. Results Referrals were originated from various locations, including A&E, minor injury units, general practice and in-hospital wards or other hospitals. A significant number of referrals were remote (42%). Although this audit looked into all referrals and their diagnoses, a focus on back-pain referrals was made for this audit. Back pain cases accounted for 22% of all referrals, with 76-77% requiring no orthopaedic intervention beyond conservative approaches such as bracing or onward referrals to other specialties. Overall, 45% of all referrals during this 2-week period required no orthopaedic intervention which highlighted inefficiencies within the current referral system. Conclusions This audit emphasised the heavy workload on the on-call registrar and further demonstrated the need for streamlining referral pathways, particularly for cases like back pain which often do not necessitate orthopaedic input. Implementing referral pathways could help reduce some of the workload on the on-call service which in turn could optimise patient care.
affiliations: Queen Elizabeth Hospital , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.229.title: 269 Ureteric Stent Encrustation: A Retrospective Audit on the Effects of Prolonged Stent Dwell Time
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.229.abstract: Abstract Background With increasing waiting lists across the NHS, ureteric stents are being left in situ for longer periods of time. Delayed stent removal or forgotten stents are associated with increased patient morbidity and complications which are often difficult to manage. Aim The aim of this retrospective study was to evaluate the incidence of encrustation as well as morbidity associated with prolonged dwell time of ureteric stents. Method A retrospective analysis of the emergency theatre database from January 2023 till December 2023 was performed to identify patients who underwent emergency ureteric stent insertion. Data regarding patient demographics, the primary reason for the stent insertion, total indwelling time, number of encrusted stents and type of procedure performed to make patients stent free were recorded. Results A total of 104 patients were included in this study. 82.6% of patients had emergency stenting due to stones, 14.4% from ureteric obstruction secondary to tumours and 3% due to trauma. The average time from emergency stenting to definitive procedure was 140 days. During this period 16% of patients were re-admitted with stent symptoms, 3% with urosepsis and 0.9% with blocked stents. 11.5% of these patients had stent encrustation with 16.7% requiring complex ureteroscopy and laser fragmentation of the encrustation during the definitive ureteroscopy. Conclusions Indwelling ureteric stents following emergency procedures can cause significant morbidity in patients if left in for a prolonged time. This study highlights the complications associated with prolonged stent dwell time. This can be avoided by ensuring timely definitive ureteroscopy and stent removals.
affiliations: The Royal London Hospital , London ,
Queen Mary University , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.219.title: 209 Assessment of Bone Health in Postmenopausal Breast Cancer Patients Starting Adjuvant Aromatase Inhibitors: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.219.abstract: Abstract Background Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are a cornerstone in the adjuvant treatment of hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. However, AIs are associated with accelerated bone loss and an increased risk of fractures, necessitating proactive management of bone health. NICE guidelines recommend bone mineral density (BMD) assessment using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans and appropriate supplementation with calcium and vitamin D for patients at risk. Aim To evaluate the adherence to NICE guidelines regarding bone health assessment and management in postmenopausal breast cancer patients commencing adjuvant AI therapy. Method This retrospective audit included data from 1,137 breast cancer cases treated over three years at Charing Cross Hospital (CXH) and West Middlesex University Hospital (WMUH). Among these, 458 postmenopausal women receiving AIs were identified. Data were collected on the frequency of baseline DEXA scans. Results Of the 458 postmenopausal patients on AIs, only 61% (280/458) underwent a baseline DEXA scan prior to or shortly after starting therapy. Follow-up DEXA scans were conducted in 35% (161/458) of patients at appropriate intervals. Regarding supplementation, 52% (239/458) of patients were prescribed calcium and vitamin D during their treatment. These findings highlight significant gaps in adherence to guideline. In the Second cycle following intervention the results progress. Conclusions The audit underscores the need for improved compliance with national guidelines to enhance bone health care for postmenopausal breast cancer patients on AIs. Recommendations include implementing standardized pathways for DEXA scanning and supplementation, alongside education for oncology and breast clinic teams to ensure patients receive comprehensive follow-up care.
affiliations: West Middlesex University Hospital , london ,
Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.515.title: 481 Improving Practices in Extravasation Injury Management: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.515.abstract: Abstract Aim Extravasation, the leakage of drugs/fluids into surrounding tissues during intravenous administration, can cause severe complications such as necrosis, gangrene, and contractures if not promptly managed. This audit aimed to evaluate current management practices for extravasation injuries at our hospital and develop a standardised protocol to reduce morbidity and improve patient outcomes. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on all cases coded as extravasation injuries in our electronic patient records (EPIC) from 2018 to 2023. Data collected included time of injury recognition, type of extravasated agent, site of injury, initial management strategies, referral to plastic surgery, complications and outcomes. Results A total of 36 cases were identified, with 53% involving irritant agents and 47% vesicants. Initial management was inconsistent: time of recognition was documented in 53%, infusion stopped, and limb elevated in 67%, and injury photographed in 56%. Plastic surgery advice was sought in 81% of cases. Complications, including skin necrosis, blistering, and compartment syndrome, were observed in 22%, and 11% of cases required surgical intervention. Conclusions The incidence of documented extravasation injuries appears lower than in other trusts, highlighting gaps in recognition and coding. This audit revealed significant variability in management practices, highlighting the need for a hospital-specific guideline, emphasising detailed documentation and coding, early identification, prompt intervention, and standardised management protocol. Implementation of these guidelines has the potential to improve patient outcomes and reduce complications. Future steps include staff education and a re-audit to evaluate the impact of the new guideline.
affiliations: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Cambridge ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.238.title: 333 An Audit on New Cancer Diagnosis in Orthopaedic Inpatients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.238.abstract: Abstract Aim New diagnosis of malignancy is a common finding in Orthopaedic departments. Patients present with atraumatic pain, fractures or Cauda Equina syndrome. Over 70% of malignant bone lesions are found to be metastatic and prompt investigation is required to identify the primary site and initiate appropriate management. This study aimed to identify the number of new cancer diagnosis in Orthopaedic inpatients and audit the time taken from diagnosis to investigation. Mortality at one year was used as a marker of outcome. Method A Retrospective study was conducted over a 3-year period from 2020-2023 in the Orthopaedics department at The Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, Glasgow. Keywords “CTTAP” were cross-referenced with consultant orthopaedic surgeon names in the online imaging system. This identified 267 cases. Scan results were reviewed to identify 47 cases of confirmed malignancy. Cases were analysed to compile indications for admission and pathology. Data was compared to The Scottish Cancer National Standards on wait times. 1 year mortality was assessed and compared to Scottish average. Results 47 patients had new malignancy confirmed whilst inpatients. Neck of femur fracture and atraumatic pain were the most common presenting complaints. 36% of patients had a cancer of unknown primary. 68% of patients met current cancer diagnosis standards. At one year, 55% of patients were deceased. Conclusions The number of patients receiving timely investigation was below the national average. Mortality at one year was higher than the Scottish average. A prospective study and further analysis are recommended to investigate how delay in investigation affects 1 year mortality.
affiliations: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.237.title: 328 Assessing Patient Satisfaction and Confidence in Post-Operative Wound Care: A Clinical Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.237.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess patient satisfaction with post-operative wound care and education, focusing on confidence in managing wounds at home and identifying areas for improvement. Method A survey was conducted over one month in a skin dressings clinic, involving 25 patients. Questions addressed satisfaction with post-operative wound care, confidence in home wound management, and the provision of educational materials. Results Of the patients surveyed, 96% were either satisfied or very satisfied with their post-operative wound care. However, only 12% reported feeling somewhat confident in managing their wounds at home, and 12% indicated they would have felt more confident with additional information. Notably, 22% of patients reported not receiving a pre-operative educational leaflet. Conclusions While overall satisfaction with care is high, gaps in patient confidence and education remain. To address these issues, a target of 100% leaflet distribution is proposed, alongside the development of a more detailed leaflet covering wound expectations and post-operative care instructions. Implementing these measures and re-auditing will help evaluate their impact and ensure continuous improvement in patient education and confidence.
affiliations: Musgrove Park Hospital , Taunton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.143.title: 242 Audit of Postoperative Laboratory Tests Following Elective Lower Limb Arthroplasty. Do They Influence Treatment?
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.143.abstract: Abstract Aim Orthopaedic departments are moving towards reducing patient length of stay and day case arthroplasty. We aimed in our departmentTo determine if all elective hip and knee arthroplasty patients have routine postoperative laboratory tests (i.e. full blood count and renal function), andTo determine if the results of these investigations influence post-operative care. Method Retrospective chart review of 104 consecutive arthroplasty patients in one hospital between 3/4/24 and 5/6/24; 54 total knee replacements and 50 total hip replacements. Results Average age was 68.2 years (38 – 82). 60 patients were female. Mean ASA was 2.2. Mean length of stay was 3 days, median was 2 days. Two patients were discharged on the day of surgery (day zero). Four (3.8%) patients had no post-operative blood tests. Mean drop in haemoglobin was 22.5 g/L. Mean post-operative haemoglobin was 113.3 g/L (86 – 157). No patients received a blood transfusion or post-operative iron supplementation. Mean pre-operative and post-operative creatinine were 78.5 and 78.3 µmol/dL, respectively. Mean pre-operative and post-operative eGFR were 76.1 and 75.2 mL/min/1.73m2, respectively. Seven patients were prescribed post-operative intravenous fluids; one for an acute kidney injury and six for hyponatraemia. Conclusions The results raise the question as to whether we need to perform routine postoperative blood tests on this patient population. Postoperative blood tests could potentially be targeted at higher risk populations. A larger sample is needed to determine this. This could allow for potential cost saving for routine postoperative bloods and of clinician and laboratory technicians’ time.
affiliations: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.353.title: 594 An Audit Investigating Patient Outcomes for Open vs Endoscopic Vein Harvesting for Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery (CABG)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.353.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aims to investigate the postoperative trends and complications of endoscopic versus open vein harvesting analysing pain, wound healing, length of stay and AMEXO functional score. Method This was a retrospective audit focusing on 25 patients, 15 underwent endoscopic harvesting and the remaining 10 open. An examination and questionnaire were completed on the day of the procedure as well as day 3 and 10 post operatively. Results Multiple domains were investigated between the endoscopic cohort (EC) and open cohort (OC). Average length of stay was longer for the OC (9 days), compared to the EC (8 days). On day 10 both cohorts scored equal for functionality (AMEXO 8) however at day 3 the EC had superior performance, with an average score of 7.7, compared to 6.8 for the OC. Similarly, the EC experienced a reduced pain score of 7.2 on day 3 while the OC scored 8. Ultimately both cohorts scored similar for pain outcomes on day 10 (EC 2.1, OC 2). SEPSIS criteria were used to analyse wound healing; all patients in the EC experienced ‘satisfactory’ wound healing, whereas only 60% of patients within the OC did. The remaining 40% experiences ‘disturbed’ wound healing. Conclusions There is evidence to suggest endoscopic vein harvesting for CABG is associated with reduced postoperative pain, improved wound healing and reduced length of hospital stay. All the evidence found in this study is in keeping with the previous literature, showing more favourable outcomes for the endoscopic cohort.
affiliations: University of Manchester , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.695.title: 693 A Retrospective Audit for Analysing Prostheses in Peri-Prosthetic Hip Fractures for Adult Patients at East Lancashire Hospitals Trust (ELHT)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.695.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aims to evaluate patients in ELHT with Periprosthetic Hip Fractures and their management from 2020 to 2023. Background Periprosthetic Hip fractures are fractures that occur in the region of a hip implant following a hip arthroplasty. It is an increasingly prevalent complication of hip arthroplasty that can be attributed to the increase in arthroplasty procedures performed, a rise in the ageing population and a desire to improve quality of life. Method This was a retrospective audit was performed at ELHT. Patient data was collected from the Orthopaedic register and parameters were set to include patients having a periprosthetic hip fracture from 2020 to 2023. Exclusion criteria were set to exclude periprosthetic fractures before 2020 or after 2023. We got a sample population consisting of 48 patients. Results 25 patients had cemented hip prostheses and 23 had uncemented prostheses in their primary procedure. Among those with cemented hip prostheses, 10 patients were managed conservatively, 9 patients had an ORIF and 4 patients underwent a revision procedure whereas, among those with uncemented hip prostheses, 9 patients were managed conservatively, 6 patients had an ORIF and 5 patients underwent a revision procedure. Furthermore, 20 cases of Vancouver B fractures were noted in uncemented prostheses as compared to 12 in cemented prostheses. Conclusions The most common prostheses that sustained a periprosthetic hip fracture was the C Stem implant, 12 patients. The most common management in this sample population was conservative management which was in 39.6% of patients.
affiliations: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust , Bristol ,
East Lancashire Hospitals Trust , Blackburn ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.691.title: 511 An Audit on the Use of a Calibration Marker in Neck of Femur Fracture X Rays
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.691.abstract: Abstract Background In the UK, 75,000 hip fractures occur annually. Accurate radiographic and clinical assessment is required to inform timely and appropriate intervention for these patients. A ball calibration marker is used for templating of neck of femur fractures (NOF). As per NICE Guidelines, all patients receiving an X-ray for a possible NOF should have a calibration marker included on X-ray for operative planning. Aim To assess radiological investigations performed for NOFs in an MTC and compare with a previous QIP in the same trust in 2018, which showed an improvement from 64-73% compliance with this standard. Method Patients were identified who had NOF documented in the trauma database. For this repeat loop of the audit, patients with a NOF between 01/05/24 – 31/8/24 were identified. Online records were assessed to see if calibration markers were used at the time of the original radiograph. Basic statistical analysis was completed on an anonymised spreadsheet. Results From May - August 2024, 144 patients were admitted with NOFs. Only 44% of these patients had a ball calibration marker used in original X-ray. Conclusions Following the first loop in 2018, most patients who had a confirmed NOF had a ball calibration marker used. However, there has been a reduction in concordance, with less than half of the patients having an appropriate ball calibration marker on the initial X-Ray. A re-audit will be done to improve this compliance and shows the importance of regular interventions to maintain the efficacy of QIPs in busy departments.
affiliations: Royal Victoria Infirmary , Newcastle Upon Tyne ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.543.title: 329 Audit of Compliance of Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) Risk Assessment and Prescription of Prophylaxis in the General Surgery Directorate at Darlington Memorial Hospital (DMH)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.543.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess compliance of VTE risk assessment and prescription of prophylaxis in General Surgery directorate at DMH according to NICE guidelines and compare it with the compliance of the cohort following implementation of teaching, posters, and verbal reminder interventions. Method A single day for each cohort, 17th July 2024 and 18th October 2024, were randomly selected for analysis. Inpatients under the General Surgery directorate were isolated on the EPR system and data collated from these records. Those awaiting review, those who hadn’t yet had a decision for admission, and patients admitted under different specialties were excluded. VTE assessment and prescription were classified into No/Yes/Yes, Delayed. Results Overall improvement in the completion of VTE Risk assessments between audit cycles (96.4% vs 90.7%), though a higher proportion of the assessments delayed (35.7% vs 16.3%). Overall improvement in the number of patients with VTE Prophylaxis prescribed (96.4% vs 88.4%), with the majority being prescribed on admission. Conclusions VTE is one of the most preventable causes of mortality and morbidity in hospitalised patients. Surgical inpatients are at an increased risk, typically due to the nature of their condition and the effect on Virchow’s Triad, and appropriate risk assessment and prescription of prophylaxis paramount. Frequent teaching and reminders are effective intervention to keep up VTE compliance, therefore repeated reminders should be delivered to the working doctors. Going forward, a qualitative audit to assess reasoning for increased delayed assessments, and introduction of teaching at induction should be considered.
affiliations: Darlington Memorial Hospital , Darlington ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.536.title: 193 Breaking Barriers in Achieving Excellence for National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) Documentation: A Successful Quality Improvement Framework
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.536.abstract: Abstract Aim This QIP conducted at the Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother Hospital (QEQMH) addresses the insufficient documentation of patient data entry on the National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) website. The focus is centred on surgical patients who had emergency general abdominal surgery at QEQMH. Our aim is to reach the target of ≥85% formal mortality risk assessment documented on NELA to achieve the Emergency Laparotomy Best Practice Tariff 2023-2025 for our trust. Method We conducted two Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles over a one-year period across 60 surgical patients at QEQMH who meet the inclusion criteria for NELA, evaluating the completion of their data entries on NELA website. The proposed interventions include presenting at Clinical Governance meetings of Surgical and Anaesthetics departments, conducting surveys, enhancing induction process to provide Surgical trainees with NELA website log-in details and creating a QR code on CEPOD booking form to facilitate documentation. Results The audit highlighted deficiencies in recording surgical patients who had emergency general abdominal surgery on NELA, revealing only 11.7% (n=7) were documented. 3 months after our interventions, we re-audited to assess for improvement and recorded a 76.2% increase in documentation with 86.2% (n=50) using the NELA tool, achieving our compliance target of ≥85%. Conclusions Engaging with Surgical and Anaesthetics team is a key aspect; this involved identifying challenges, providing instructions, and creating feedback channels. We were successful in significantly improving the use of NELA Patient Data Entry tool after implementing interventions and have a multifaceted strategy to involve the Peri-operative (POPS) team and IT department in the future.
affiliations: East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust , Margate ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.314.title: 1132 The Impact of Time-to-Operation for Hand Trauma: A Local Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.314.abstract: Abstract Introduction The British Society for Surgery on the Hand (BSSH) recommends time from injury to operative intervention is 24 hours for open fractures and bites, 7-days for closed fractures and 4-days for other injuries requiring surgery. Method We conducted a retrospective audit of hand trauma requiring operative management over 3-months and the time from injury to surgical intervention. Infection (diagnosed at the time of operation or at any presentation following surgery), surgeon grade, anaesthetic method and injury mechanism were recorded. Fishers exact and chi-squared tests were used to assess for differences in the rate of delay and the impact on outcomes. Results 46 cases were recorded with the primary surgeon recorded as a registrar in 100%. 5 of 46 cases (10.8%) were completed on the CEPOD list, with all other cases on a designated trauma list. 4 of 5 cases met BSSH guidelines. 24 cases (52%) did not meet these criteria. Of open fractures (7) and bites (8), 73% were not operated within 24 hours. 33% of closed fractures (1 of 3) were not operated within 7 days and 46% of other hand trauma (13 of 28) were not operated within 4 days of injury. Injury type did not affect the chance of delay (p=0.22). 6 were diagnosed with injury-related infection (13%) and the effect of delay was not statistically significant (p=0.90). Conclusions Small numbers have limited the ability to reveal this impact on outcomes however the potential impact and prevalence of delay has been highlighted. Future work and continuous audit will be undertaken.
affiliations: Countess of Chester Hospital , Chester ,
University of Manchester , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.273.title: 750 ‘BARI-MED’ AUDIT a Multi-Disciplinary Team Audit Streamlining Medication Prescription on Discharge for Bariatric Patients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.273.abstract: Abstract Introduction Patients undergoing bariatric surgical procedures must go home post operatively with 6 weeks of liquid/crushed medications as well as a liquid diet as per British Obesity & Metabolic Surgery Society (BOMSS) guidelines. There were inconsistencies in the medications, formulations and durations prescribed on discharge for patients undergoing bariatric procedures. This closed loop audit aimed to improve prescription accuracy of discharge medications dispensed for patients having bariatric procedures at a tertiary centre. Method A retrospective first cycle was performed from July 2023- December 2023. A digital prescription tab/checklist was then created by working with the MDT (Specialist pharmacist, bariatric CNS) based on patient feedback and financial factors. A prospective second cycle was performed from April 2024 – May 2024 after educating junior doctors, ACPs, trainee pharmacists about bariatric surgery guidelines and about the digital new prescription tab. Results Accuracy increased in all medications prescribed on discharge from cycle one (n=35 patients) to cycle two (n=12 patients) after . Paracetamol liquid prescription improved from 49% (cycle 1) to 58% (cycle 2), codeine phosphate tablet from 11% (cycle 1) to 42% (cycle 2), senna liquid from 11% (cycle 1) to 58% (cycle 2) and ondansetron liquid from 20% (cycle 1) to 58% (cycle 2) and lansoprazole dispersible tablet from 97% (cycle 1) to 100% (cycle 2). Enoxaparin prescription was consistently 100% across both cycles. Conclusions Successful implementation of the digital prescription checklist with the collaboration of MDT members lead to improved prescription accuracy and better patient outcomes for bariatric surgical procedures on discharge.
