Warrington Hospital , Warrington ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.271.title: 743 Adherence to Prophylactic Antibiotic Guidelines in Elective Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: An Audit of Current Practice
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.271.abstract: Abstract Aim Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) is commonly performed for conditions such as symptomatic cholelithiasis, gallstone pancreatitis, and acute or chronic cholecystitis. This audit assessed prophylactic antibiotic use in elective LC at a district general hospital and evaluated adherence to established guidelines. According to the Surgical Infection Society (SIS), the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), and local NHS trust guidelines, prophylactic pre-operative antibiotics are not recommended for low-risk patients undergoing elective LC, as they do not significantly reduce the risk of surgical site infections (SSIs). Method A retrospective audit was conducted on elective LC cases performed from January 2024 to July 2024. Data from medical records and operation notes were reviewed to assess antibiotic use, guideline adherence, SSI rates, and the cost impact of unnecessary antibiotics. Patients with biliary infections, intraoperative bile spillage, on-table cholangiogram or common bile duct exploration, and gallbladder malignancies/polyps were excluded. Results Seventy-six patients were included in the audit. Guideline adherence was observed in only 5.3% of cases, while 94.7% received prophylactic antibiotics contrary to recommendations. The postoperative complication rate was 3.9%, with three patients affected: one with an SSI, one with an intra-abdominal collection, and one with a surgical site hematoma. The SSI occurred in a patient who did not receive antibiotics, though this finding lacks statistical significance due to the small size of the no-antibiotic subgroup. Conclusions The audit highlights poor adherence to guidelines for prophylactic antibiotic use in elective LC, emphasizing the need for educational interventions to improve guideline compliance and reduce unnecessary antibiotic costs.
affiliations: Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother Hospital , Margate ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.269.title: 711 A Clinical Audit of Adherence to Sepsis Protocol Initiation at Ward Level in a Level 3 (General Hospital)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.269.abstract: Abstract Introduction A 7-week retrospective audit on management of hospital inpatients who meet the criteria for sepsis protocol initiation as per HSE National Clinical Guideline no. 26 Aim To evaluate and identify areas of quality improvement in clinician compliance with HSE national clinical guideline no 26 on initiation of sepsis protocol for inpatients in a level 3 General Hospital. Method A retrospective audit was completed covering 7 weeks. Cases which met the triggers for sepsis protocol initiation were identified from clinical notes of patients transferred and discharged from two inpatient wards in a level 3 hospital. Cases with ED initiation of protocol were excluded. Compliance with sepsis protocols was assessed through completion of the HSE proforma or clinical documentation. Patient demographics, admission diagnosis, adherence to the sepsis 6 bundle, and aspects completed were recorded. Results 295 cases were audited. 36 (12.2%) Positive sepsis triggers were identified. Use of existing HSE proforma was low (13.89% of cases). This form was completed in only 1 case. Average completion of the six aspects of the sepsis bundle documented was 55.5%. Antibiotic administration had the highest compliance rate (31/36). Conclusions Use of the existing HSE proforma was minimal. As a result, compliance with Sepsis protocols varied significantly between clinicians. Revision of the sepsis proforma is required with further education for clinicians on identification and compliance required.
affiliations: Wexford General Hospital , Wexford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.267.title: 698 Rate of Testicular Torsion and Variations in Operative Techniques for Scrotal Exploration - a Single Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.267.abstract: Abstract Aim Establish the rate of testicular torsion and variations in practise of scrotal exploration from a single-centre, general surgical unit. Method Following local approval, data was collected from 1st June to 1st November 2024 and stored securely on an NHS database. The primary outcome was rate of testicular torsion at scrotal exploration. Secondary outcomes were types of incision, rate of orchidopexy and suture material used. Outcomes were compared to recent guidelines submitted by BAUS/BURST consensus (FIX-IT study). Results During this period, 41 scrotal explorations were performed with an average population age of 14-years (range 4 to 28) of whom 4 (9.8%) were confirmed to have testicular torsion. An orchidectomy was performed on one patient with an unviable testicle, while the other 3 had bilateral orchidopexies. Of those with no signs of testicular torsion, 10 (27.0%) had torted cyst of Morgagni and 9 (24.3%) had suspected epidydmo-orchitis. Thirty-three of these patients underwent orchidopexy (89.2%) of whom 3 were bilateral and only a single patient had documented evidence of bell-clapper deformity. A transverse and longitudinal para-median incision were the most common approach (43.9% and 41.5%, respectively) and the majority of orchidopexies were 3-point fixations with polydioxanone (PDS) suture (66.7%). Conclusions The rate of torsion at exploration was comparatively low to other national observational studies. There is variation amongst general surgeons in the decision making and operative technique for scrotal exploration. Following local intervention aiming for consensus, a second cycle will be performed.
affiliations: Grange University Hospital , Newport ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.266.title: 691 Audit on the Outcomes of GreenLight Laser Photovaporization of the Prostate at Freeman Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.266.abstract: Abstract Aim GreenLight laser photovaporization of the prostate (GL PVP) has emerged as a widely accepted, minimally invasive treatment for benign prostatic enlargement (BPE). GL PVP was introduced at the Freeman in 2023, this audit aims to assess patient outcomes, waiting times for the BPH service, following its introduction. Method A retrospective audit of GLPVP patient data from March 2023 - April 2024 reviewed: (a) waiting times & LOS, (b) complications, (c) TWOC success, and (d) symptomatic relief. Results 88 men underwent GLL between March 2023-June 2024, mean age 70yrs, 25/88 were anticoagulated. Mean prostate size for GLPVP = 57cc, (range = 20-114cc). Mean prostate size for TURP = 41cc (range= 30-75cc). Mean time on wait list in days for All patients undergoing GLPVP n=88 was 154 days. 98% patients were discharged on the same day. 17/88 had complications including UTI (requiring oral antibiotics) 8%, Haematuria 3%, Urethral stricture (required surgical intervention) 3%, Failed to improve required salvage HoLEP 1%. 97% had a successful initial TWOC, 1/88 required a long-term catheter, the other passed on second TWOC. 71/88 patient have had their follow up. 80% have reported complete symptomatic benefit. Reason for incomplete resolution of symptoms included Ongoing LUTS, Dribble incontinence and LTC. Conclusions In summary this audit has shown GLPVP is safe, effective method of treatment for BPE that has the ability to deal with larger prostate sizes and convert patients previously booked for TURP. GLPVP has improved overall waiting time for bladder outlet surgery at the Freeman hospital with excellent symptomatic benefit.
affiliations: Freeman Hospital , Newcastle ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.726.title: 953 Improving Documentation of Operation Notes for Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumour: A Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.726.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate documentation of transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) is vital for patient care and outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate and improve TURBT documentation at a general hospital in London by implementing a standardised operation note template. Method In cycle 1, TURBT operation notes from March–August 2023 was reviewed against an 8-point checklist to identify poorly documented domains. A 12-point standardised template was introduced in June 2024. Cycle 2 re-audited notes from July–October 2024 to assess for improvement. Results Cycle 2 (n=9) had higher documentation compared to cycle 1 (n=40) in the following domains: number of tumours (100% vs 86.21%), size of largest tumour (88.89% vs 65.52%), tumour characteristics (100% vs 89.66%), recurrent or primary tumour (66.67% vs 31.03%), carcinoma in situ assessment (55.56% vs 3.45%), clinical tumour stage (55.56% vs 10.34%) and separate base biopsy (66.67% vs 10.34%). Cycle 1 showed higher documentation rate for detrusor muscle visualisation (71.43% vs 55.56%). Additional useful domains which were included in the template showed good completion rate; tumour location (100%), ureteric orifice involvement (77.78%), visually complete resection (66.67%), and perforation assessment (77.78%). Conclusions The introduction of a standardised TURBT operation note greatly improved documentation. This will enhance post-operative follow up care by ensuring all essential information is included for accurate bladder cancer risk group stratification.
affiliations: Homerton University Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.259.title: 598 Audit of Transperineal Prostate Biopsy: An Alternative to the Transrectal Approach
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.259.abstract: Abstract Aim Current NICE guidelines recommend transrectal prostate biopsy (TRPBx) under local anaesthetic for prostate cancer investigation, but this carries infection risks due to rectal needle passage. Transperineal prostate biopsy (TPPBx) offers a safer alternative with lower infection rates. Emerging evidence, including this study, highlights the safety and diagnostic accuracy of TPPBx, supporting its potential as the preferred approach. Method A retrospective study including 163 male patients who underwent LA TPPBx at a South London hospital between February 2022 and March 2024. Data were collected from a Trust surgery database, covering demographics, MRI findings, and histological outcomes. Results A total of 163 patients, with an average age of 64 years (range 40–81), underwent LA TPPBx. Clinically significant prostate cancer (≥ Grade 2) was detected in 59.3% (97/163) of cases, while 72.2% (118/163) demonstrated any prostate cancer (≥ Grade 1). PI-RADS 5 lesions detected clinically significant disease in 90% of cases, compared to 53% for PI-RADS 4. Grade 5 cancers correlated with larger lesion size (mean 23.75 mm). Postoperative complications occurred in four patients (2.47%), all managed conservatively without long-term sequelae. No infection-related or intraoperative complications were reported. Histological outcomes strongly correlated with MRI metrics and PSA levels, confirming their predictive value. Conclusions LA TPPBx is an effective and safe diagnostic tool, achieving high detection rates for clinically significant cancer. MRI parameters, including PI-RADS scores, lesion size, and PSA levels, demonstrated strong predictive value. These findings support TPPBx as a safer, more accurate alternative to TRPBx, reinforcing its clinical utility.
affiliations: St George's University of London , London ,
St George's Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.457.title: 898 Management of Splenic Trauma at Aintree University Hospital: An Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.457.abstract: Abstract Introduction Damage of the spleen can result in haemorrhage and life-threatening haemodynamic instability. This study aimed to evaluate the management of traumatic splenic injury at a major trauma centre against current international guidelines and identify areas of good practice and areas for improvement. Method Data was obtained from an existing data set of trauma patients presenting between 2018-2022. Patients with splenic injury confirmed on CT scan were included. Electronic and scanned notes were reviewed for data collection, and results were analysed. Standards included:80% of patients received CT/FAST scan.100% of patients receiving correct grading of their splenic injury according to American Association for Surgery of Trauma (AAST) guidelines.100% of patients received correct treatment based upon the World Society of Emergency Surgery guidelines. Results All patients underwent CT scan (n=115). 73% received AAST grading, of whom 93% were graded correctly. 64% had non operative management in the form of conservative management and/or interventional radiological embolization. 37% underwent operative management. 5% failed conservative management and required surgery. 37% were managed according to WSES guidelines. Management was undetermined in 27% due to lack of AAST grading. Patients with WSES III and IV had a lower adherence to management (40% and 43% respectively) versus WSES I and II. Conclusions This audit highlights the variability in current guideline adherence and applicability for the management of splenic trauma. Intervention, education, and re-audit are required to improve patient outcomes.
affiliations: Aintree University Hospital , Liverpool ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.225.title: 235 A Retrospective Audit on the Use of Staging Scans in Patients with Gleason 3+4/4+3 Prostate Cancer in a Single Specialist UK Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.225.abstract: Abstract Aim Patients with suspected prostate cancer undergo diagnostic staging and grading with mpMRI and biopsy +/- metastatic staging. Guidelines advocate against the routine use of bone scans in patients with low-risk disease but recommend staging CT and bone scans in patients with unfavourable intermediate risk disease (Gleason 4+3) and/or patients with locally advanced disease (T3). We aimed to audit the use of staging scans in patients with Gleason 3+4/4+3 prostate cancer. Method Patients diagnosed with Gleason 3+4/4+3 prostate cancer in 2022 were identified. Data was retrospectively collected using electronic patient records including the presence/absence of cribriform pattern on biopsy histology, local tumour stage (T stage), and PSA (>20/<20). Results 196 patients with Gleason 3+4/4+3 prostate cancer were included in the analysis, 49/196 (25%) of whom had evidence of cribriform histology. All patients with a PSA>20 (N=22) underwent staging with at least a bone scan. 50/93 (54%) patients with Gleason 4+3 had staging scans performed. 3/79 (4%) of Cambridge Prognostic Group 1 patients (Gleason 3+4, PSA <20, T2) had staging scans. Patients with cribriform were more likely to undergo staging scans (X2 p<0.001). Conclusions The use of staging scans in patients with PSA >20 was excellent. However, there was variation in the use of staging scans in patients with T3 disease and/or Gleason 4+3. In patients with favourable intermediate risk disease, staging scans are occasionally being performed unnecessarily. We recommend the use of a proforma to help prompt decision making as to which patients require staging scans as recommended by international guidelines.
affiliations: Stepping Hill , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.223.title: 221 Follow-Up for Patients with Radiologically Diagnosed Gallbladder Polyps in Primary Care: A 2-Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.223.abstract: Abstract Aim In 2019, local care commissioning group released primary care guidance for interval ultrasound imaging of patients with gallbladder polyps based on size and risk factors. Primary outcome of this audit: number of polyp patients lost to follow-up (LTFU) in one GP practice. Method Search of electronic medical records for diagnoses inclusive of biliary polyp pathology, completed 22/05/2024. Data collected by 2 investigators: demographics, imaging indication, ultrasound findings, comorbidities, identification of LTFU, those indicated for referral for surgical assessment. Intervention: invitation for repeat imaging, or consultation with doctor. Results Search yielded 76 records, 4 removed as diagnoses were not polypoid pathology. Of 72 patients, 58% female. Median age 55.5(IQR:22.25) years. Self-reporting per GovUK ethnicities: 48.6% white, 15.3% other(Arab/other), 13.9% other Asian, 8.3% mixed, 5.6% Indian, 5.6% Black Afro-Caribbean, 2.8% undeclared. 30/72(41.6%) patients were LTFU, 31/72(43.1%) complied with guidance, 11/72(15.3%) were due appointments within guidelines. Indications for abdominal imaging: 30(41.7%) for abdominal pain, 23(31.9%) for incidental deranged liver function tests, 4(5.6%) for change in bowel habit, and 15(20.8%) other abdominal complaints. 4 had no documented polyp size; of 68 patients, mean size at diagnosis was 5.2±2.7mm. 16/68(23.5%) had >1 polyp at diagnosis. Median months overdue: 36(IQR 45.5). Of high-risk factors identified, Indian ethnicity was associated with 46.6% greater average polyp size. Conclusions 41.6% of individuals were LTFU, key factors ensuring adequate follow-up were patient education, and empowered health accountability to self-report for imaging. 100% of individuals were returned to surveillance following intervention.
affiliations: Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust , London ,
University College London , London ,
Pimlico Health at The Marven , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.579.title: 1136 Turning Data into Action: A Regional Audit and Quality Improvement Project to Elevate Core Surgical Training Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.579.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate and improve access to theatre and clinic opportunities, and overall training standards for Core Surgical Trainees (CSTs) in the East of England (EoE). Method A combined quality improvement and audit approach reflecting JCST Quality Indicators was adopted across three data collection cycles (December 2023, April 2024, November 2024), involving 50 CSTs across 14 trusts in EoE. Structured surveys and direct communication were used to collect quantitative and qualitative data, analysed using Excel statistical tools and thematic analysis. Findings were synthesised into actionable recommendations and presented to the Surgical Trainee Committee and trust leadership, facilitating targeted interventions, including rota redesign, resource reallocation, and improved planning processes. Results Response rates were 47%, 69%, and 58%. Initially, 45% (9/21) of trainees reported consistent access to theatre, which increased to 68% (21/31) and 78% (20/26) following interventions. Clinic access remained lower, with 19% (4/21), 39% (12/31), and 50% (13/26) reporting scheduled clinic time. Consistently, >75% report inability to attend mandatory teaching. Barriers included service provision demands, short rotations, prioritisation of other staff (junior SpRs and PAs), workplace culture and insufficient protected time. Improvements were observed in six trusts; however, three showed no measurable progress, highlighting systemic challenges. Conclusions This project demonstrates the value of data-driven decision-making, stakeholder collaboration, and tailored interventions in driving meaningful improvements. While regional progress is encouraging, addressing persistent disparities requires national-level policy changes in addition to strong local leadership. These findings highlight the importance of evidence-based frameworks in transforming complex systems to achieve equitable and sustainable outcomes.
affiliations: Norfolk & Norwich University Hospital , Norwich ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.239.title: 335 Ensuring Informed Decisions: A Single Institution Closed-Loop Audit on Patient Information Leaflet Use for Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumour
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.239.abstract: Abstract Aim Obtaining informed consent is crucial in-patient care, ensuring patients are aware of the risks, benefits, and procedures before surgical treatment. The Royal College of Surgeons advises providing patients with patient information leaflets (PILs) to support their understanding. The British Association of Urological Surgeons (BAUS) provides QR codes linking to its leaflets, which can be easily added to electronic clinic letters. This audit aimed to assess clinicians’ use of the BAUS “Transurethral Telescopic Resection of a Bladder Tumour” leaflet when listing patients for Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumour (TURBT) at an NHS hospital in North- West England. Method Retrospective data was initially collected for 20 patients who underwent TURBT between October and November 2024. The clinic letters corresponding to the appointment listing the patients for TURBT were reviewed to identify whether the aforementioned BAUS leaflet was provided, either in physical form or via a QR code. Following this, an email was sent to all Consultants and Registrars, encouraging the use of PILs. A re-audit was then conducted. Results Initially, just 30% of patients (6 of 20) were provided with the TURBT PIL. However, after a departmental reminder, the provision rate increased to 80%, with 16 of 20 patients receiving the leaflet in the re-audited data. Conclusions While there was notable improvement in providing the PIL, further efforts are needed to ensure all patients receive written materials to support informed decision-making. Standardising the provision of PILs and conducting regular re-audits are essential to ensure full compliance and optimise patient understanding.
affiliations: Manchester Royal Infirmary , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.499.title: 1027 Improving the Management of Gallbladder Disease: A Quality Improvement Audit on Imaging Delays, Surgical Timing, and Length of Stay
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.499.abstract: Abstract Aim To identify inefficiencies in managing gallstone-related conditions at Barnet Hospital—focusing on imaging delays, surgical timing, and length of stay (LOS)—and propose an innovative Hot Gallbladder Pathway (HGB) to improve outcomes and resource utilisation. Method A retrospective audit of 125 consecutive patients admitted with gallstone-related complications was conducted between 26 June and 26 September 2024. Data on demographics, imaging, surgery, and LOS were collected from electronic records and analysed against NICE and AUGIS guidelines. Results Of 125 patients (median age 61 years [IQR 45–76]; 39.2% male), 54.5% presented with acute cholecystitis. Median delays were 5 days [IQR 2–15] for MRCP and 8 days [IQR 6–13] for ERCP. Only 18.4% underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC), with a median time to surgery of 95 days [IQR 43.5–324.5], far exceeding the recommended 7 days. LOS was prolonged (8 days [IQR 5–14]), with imaging delays and readmissions (49.6% of patients were readmitted) compounding inefficiencies. Conclusions This audit highlights substantial deviations from national standards, demonstrating the need for systemic change. The proposed HGB pathway integrates expedited imaging, dedicated theatre lists, and multidisciplinary collaboration to optimise care delivery. Scalable across NHS trusts, this model aligns with national priorities to enhance outcomes, reduce costs, and address regional disparities in gallstone disease management.
affiliations: University College London Medical School , London ,
Barnet Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.108.title: 532 Understanding of the Clinical Audit Among Healthcare Professionals
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.108.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate the knowledge, participation, and barriers to conducting surgical audits among medical students and foundation doctors in Nepal, focusing on identifying actionable solutions to foster audit culture in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Method A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 101 participants, comprising medical students (60%) and foundation doctors (40%) from Nepal’s medical colleges and teaching hospitals. Respondents completed a structured questionnaire assessing familiarity with audit principles, prior participation in audits, and perceived barriers to conducting audits. Results While 72.3% of respondents were familiar with audit principles, only 54.5% had participated in clinical audits, primarily in data collection (63%), with fewer involved in analysis (22%) or implementation (8%). Prior audit training was associated with greater confidence in conducting audits (P < 0.01, OR = 3.2, 95% CI: 1.8–5.6). Barriers included a lack of training (51%), time constraints (47%), and limited resources (43%). Resource limitations were more frequently reported by government institution participants (P = 0.04, OR = 2.5), while time constraints were emphasized by private institution respondents (P = 0.05, OR = 1.8). Importantly, 96% expressed interest in audit workshops, highlighting the need for structured training programs. Conclusions This study reveals significant gaps in audit practice among medical students and foundation doctors in Nepal. Addressing barriers through targeted education, training workshops, and systemic support can strengthen the role of clinical audits in improving surgical outcomes and aligning LMICs with global healthcare standards.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.340.title: 946 Post-Operative Venous Thromboprophylaxis: An Audit on Departmental Compliance with Association of Breast Surgery (ABS UK) Recommendations
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.340.abstract: Abstract Introduction Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) can cause significant post-operative morbidity and mortality. In breast cancer patients, this represents the second most common cause of death and has a combined incidence of <0.4% after all procedures¹,². The Association of Breast Surgery have recommendations on chemoprophylaxis in identified high risk groups². Aim This audit aimed to assess departmental VTE outcomes and guideline compliance. Method Retrospective audit of patients undergoing breast surgery under one consultant between December 2023-November 2024. Data was collected from electronic/paper patient records and included: demographics, operation type, anaesthetic type/duration, hospital stay and VTE on imaging. Results 169 patients underwent surgery, 119 (73.5%) for malignant pathology: 35 mastectomy and 84 conservative surgeries. Three patients had immediate reconstruction. Eleven patients had general anaesthetic duration >3 hours, and 22 patients had predisposing conditions for VTE. Two patients, undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy and mammoplasty, had chemoprophylaxis prescribed. Although 1 patient underwent imaging for suspected pulmonary embolism, all patients were negative for VTE. Conclusions Departmental VTE outcomes were compliant with the national risk (<0.4%), in-line with current guidance. VTE chemoprophylaxis was not commonly prescribed in higher risk groups, however this did not impact outcomes. VTE prophylaxis in breast surgery should be considered differently to other general surgery procedures: further work is required to create a breast-specific, standardised local protocol.
affiliations: Ysbyty Gwynedd, Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board , Bangor ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.310.title: 1108 An Audit of the Completeness of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Documentation and the Development of a Consistent Electronic Documentation Template
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.310.abstract: Abstract Aim The complete documentation of operative procedures is important for its medico-legal implications as well as enabling better post-operative care for patients. The Royal College of Surgeons England (RCSE) has set out guidelines for what should be recorded within all operative documentation. We undertook an audit to determine compliance rates with these guidelines and developed an electronic template document for use within our trust EPR system. Method We examined the operative notes for all Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy cases, both elective and emergency, within a 2-month period at Chelsea and Westminster hospital (N=30) and recorded which of the criteria set out in the RCSE guidance was included. We devised an EPR template document which included all the guidance criteria as well as utilising drop down menu’s with commonly used options to improve ease of use and free text space to allow for more description. This template was advertised through a poster presentation to the specialist registrar’s responsible for writing operative notes. Results Our audit showed poor initial compliance for the following criterion: Operative Indications (33%), Positioning and Skin Preparations (27%, 10%), Number of Clips Applied to Cystic Duct/Artery (53%), Post-Operative Antibiotic requirement (57%), Post-Operative Bloods (20%), VTE Prophylaxis (40%) and post-admission follow up (57%). Conclusions Initial audit shows poor compliance in several areas of key documentation. Our EPR template helps to improve compliance with the national guidance on operative documentation for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy, with our work able to be expanded to include other common General Surgical Procedures such as Appendicectomy.
affiliations: Chelsea and Westminster Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.309.title: 1099 Enhancing Patient Safety in the General Surgery Department Through Timely Treatment Escalation Plans: A Standard Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.309.abstract: Abstract Treatment escalation plans (TEPs) are critical for ensuring patient safety upon admission and during clinical deterioration. It is essential that TEPs are completed promptly after admission to meet established standards. This study aimed to evaluate whether TEP completion times in the general surgery (GS) department of a hospital in central London align with the trust’s standard, which specifies that TEPs should be completed within 36 hours of admission. A standard audit was conducted, comparing the average time to complete TEPs before and after an educational intervention. Two audit cycles were undertaken, including all emergency admissions under GS. The time from admission to TEP completion was measured. After the first cycle, an educational intervention was implemented, consisting of posters distributed to junior doctors encouraging prompt TEP completion. The second cycle assessed the intervention’s impact. In the first cycle, the average time to complete TEPs was 39.6 hours, which decreased to 34.6 hours in the second cycle. Although this reduction did not achieve statistical significance (p > 0.05), the average completion time met the trust’s standard after the intervention. The average age of patients was 61.6 years in the first cycle and 56 years in the second. Additionally, the percentage of patients discharged before TEP completion decreased from 15% to 5%. This study highlights the positive impact of educational interventions on junior doctors, improving adherence to guidelines and enhancing patient safety.
affiliations: Salisbury District Hopsital , Salisbury ,
Guys and St Thomas' Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.249.title: 499 Rib Fracture Pathway Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.249.abstract: Abstract Aim Blunt chest wall trauma accounts for 15% of emergency department presentations worldwide. Multi-disciplinary care pathways and risk stratifying scores are used to identify and treat high risk patients and prevent complications. This closed loop audit aimed to assess and improve compliance to our Trust’s Rib Fracture Pathway. Method The audit was conducted at a single NHS trust. All patients admitted with rib fractures between 01/02/2024 and 31/03/2024 were included in the first cycle. The intervention included presentation of the first cycle results and circulation of the trust Rib Fracture Pathway. The second cycle included all patients with rib fractures admitted between 01/07/2024 to 31/08/2024. Patient electronic notes were analysed and data recorded in Microsoft Excel. Results There were 40 and 41 patients included in the first and second audit cycles respectively. Documentation of Battle score increased from 5% to 15% and prescription of correct analgesia increased from 10% to 35%. The percentage of patients who received lidocaine patches increased from 12.5% to 56%. The percentage of patients, in whom it was indicated, that received a rib block within 24 hours of admission increased from 25% to 38%. There was no improvement in consultations with Major Trauma Centers for patients that fulfilled discussion criteria. Conclusions In summary, our audit has shown improvement in compliance with the current Rib Fracture Pathway, however overall compliance remains low. Development of a rib fracture prescribing ‘careplan’ and update of our trust Rib Fracture Pathway are currently in progress to enhance patient care.
affiliations: East Surrey Hospital , Redhill ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.247.title: 441 Improving Trauma Call Effectiveness and Adherence to Guidelines: A Two-Cycle Audit in a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.247.abstract: Abstract Aim The high volume of trauma calls, leading to resource allocation issues, staff dissatisfaction, and patient safety concerns, prompted this project. The aim was to evaluate trauma call effectiveness, adherence to Major Trauma Network Northwest London Guidelines, patient outcomes, and the impact of interventions on imaging timelines and documentation. Method Trauma calls were reviewed over two audit cycles (1/4/24-10/6/24 and 14/10/24-14/11/24). Interventions between the two periods included educational sessions, the presentation of findings to key stakeholders and relevant departments, and the assigning of an emergency department trauma lead at the start of each shift. In addition, a silver trauma toolkit was introduced for staff to follow. Key metrics included call appropriateness, protocol adherence, documentation rates and patient outcomes. Results In the first cycle, 216 trauma calls (101 adults, 98 silver, 17 paediatric) were recorded, with 58.4% adherence to guidelines. Primary and secondary survey documentation rates were 92.1% and 81.2%, respectively. Average imaging times were 3 hours 10 minutes (general trauma) and 6 hours 29 minutes (silver trauma). Post-intervention, 70 calls (30 adult, 38 silver, 2 paediatric) were logged, with adherence increasing to 71.8% for general trauma and 100% for silver trauma. Primary and secondary survey documentation improved to 96.9% and 90.6%, and imaging times reduced to 2 hours 29 minutes (general) and 3 hours 21 minutes (silver). Conclusions Education, divisional discussion, and assigning a trauma lead reduced inappropriate calls and improved adherence to guidelines and documentation. However, education in a department with high staff turnover or temporary staffing remains a challenge.
affiliations: Hillingdon Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.246.title: 430 A Closed Loop Audit on Legibility of Post-Operative Instruction Documentation in Otolaryngology Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.246.abstract: Abstract Aim National guidelines recommend that medical documentations should be recorded clearly, accurately, and legibly. Illegible post-operative instructions pose risk to patient safety due to misinterpretation. We aimed to assess the compliance to these guidelines within an ENT unit. Method Retrospective analyses of a total of 40 operation notes, each being the last case from each otolaryngology theatre list to prevent selection bias, in Castle Hill Hospital, Hull, were included. The first loop included 20 cases between August 2023 and September 2023 whereas the second loop included 20 cases between March 2024 and April 2024. The responses from three staff members were averaged to decide on the legibility of each note. The data from the first loop was analysed and the results presented to the department to raise awareness, followed by the second loop. Results The first loop showed that only 35% (n=7) of the operation notes were legible and 25% (n=5) were electronic notes. Legibility of electronic notes and handwritten notes were 100% (n=5) and 13% (n=2) respectively. After raising awareness on these findings to the department, the second loop showed improvement of legibility to 65% (n=13) and increased in use of electronic notes to 50% (n=10). Electronic notes remain 100% (n=10) legible whereas handwritten notes legibility improved to 30% (n=3). Conclusions This closed loop audit showed that there is less than 100% compliance with national standards and further improvements required. This audit proved that electronic notes were 100% legible hence should be encouraged.
affiliations: Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust , Hull ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.245.title: 427 Histological Findings in Emergency Appendicectomy and Impact on Patient Management: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.245.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is a leading cause of acute abdominal pain, with faecaliths and lymphoid hyperplasia being common etiologies. However, unusual pathological findings, such as parasitic infections, benign, or malignant neoplasms, although rare, significantly alter patient management. This audit aimed to evaluate the histological findings from appendicectomies in our unit and assess whether appropriate follow-up was undertaken, specifically through colorectal multidisciplinary team (MDT) referrals. Methods We retrospectively reviewed appendicectomy cases from March 2022 to March 2024. Patient records were identified through CEPOD theatre lists, including both laparoscopic and open appendectomies. The audit focused on identifying histological outcomes, patient demographics, and adherence to follow-up protocols, particularly for neoplastic findings. Exclusion criteria included patients without histology or those treated conservatively. Results A total of 305 patients underwent appendicectomy. Histological analysis confirmed acute appendicitis in 279 cases (91.5%). Fifteen cases (4.9%) were negative for acute appendicitis, while seven cases (2.3%) involved neoplastic findings: three neuroendocrine tumors (NET), one florid follicular hyperplasia, and three appendix adenocarcinomas. Other rare findings included pinworm infestation, fatty metaplasia, and mucocele. All cases of NET and adenocarcinomas were referred to the colorectal MDT for further management. The average age of patients with NET was 32 years, with all managed in accordance with current guidelines. Conclusions Routine histopathological examination (HPE) of appendectomy specimens plays a crucial role in identifying uncommon pathologies that alter patient management. Our findings support the continued practice of routine HPE for all appendicectomy specimens, given the significant implications of neoplastic findings.
affiliations: WSH NHS Trust , Bury St Edmunds ,
WVT NHS Trust , Hereford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.252.title: 528 QI/Audit Project on Improving FY1 Doctor's Confidence with Difficult Catheters
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.252.abstract: Abstract Introduction Catheter insertions are a common procedure that resident doctors are expected to carry out on the wards. Some catheter insertions can be particularly difficult, and many will not have the training or the exposure to help manage with these. Aim The main aim of this 2-cycle audit was to assess a group of surgical FY1s’ confidence levels with difficult catheter insertions, and how that changed following a teaching session. Method An initial survey was sent out to the group of FY1s. It looked at how confident they were with difficult catheters, how many catheters they had done so far, and if they had been taught how to insert Tiemann-Tipped and 3-way catheters. We then led a teaching session on proficient and safe technique for difficult catheters, and how to insert Tiemann-Tipped and 3-way catheters. Following this, we re-surveyed the group to see if their confidence had increased with difficult catheterisations. Results The initial survey showed a wide range of confidence levels; the average score was 5 out of 10. 82% had never been shown how to use a Tiemann Tip catheter. 90% had never been shown how to use a 3-way catheter. Following the teaching session, 100% of participants felt more confident with difficult catheters. Conclusions The intervention was successful in increasing confidence levels with difficult catheterisations in the FY1 group. To improve the audit, we would have run it over multiple rotations, with more participants, and would see how many difficult catheters they were able to manage independently.
affiliations: Altnagelvin Hospital , Londonderry ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.180.title: 979 Optimising Surgical Documentation: A Vascular Department Audit Against RCSEng Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.180.abstract: Abstract Aim Clear and detailed documentation of surgical interventions is vital for ensuring continuity of care and patient safety. The Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCSEng) provides specific guidelines for operation notes, aligned with the GMC’s Good Medical Practice. Poor operative note documentation practices were identified in the Vascular Department at University Hospitals North Midlands. This project aimed to compare the department’s documentation practices against national guidelines, address identified shortcomings and evaluate improvements after implementing changes. Method A retrospective review of 34 consecutive vascular operation notes was conducted in January 2024. The notes were evaluated against national standards, and the results were presented in a teaching session for clinicians. A second cycle, analysing 30 operation notes from September 2024, followed to assess improvement. Data were processed using Microsoft Excel. Results The initial audit revealed significant deficiencies. Only 3% of the notes recorded the operation time, 32% noted the urgency of the procedure (elective or emergency), 12% mentioned intraoperative complications, and 9% reported extra procedures carried out. None documented blood loss or included a surgeon's signature. After intervention, the second cycle showed improvement: 6.67% of notes recorded the time, 13.3% commented on complications, 23.3% on extra procedures, 6.67% on blood loss, and 13.3% included a signature. However, documentation of the procedure urgency decreased to 10%. Conclusions This audit identified deficiencies in operative note documentation practices in the Vascular Department. While improvements were noted following intervention, further steps, including clinician education and revisions to the standard operation note proforma, are necessary to meet national standards.
affiliations: University Hospitals North Midlands , Stoke-on-Trent ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.281.title: 839 An Evaluation of Drain Usage After Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: A Dual-Cycle Audit at a Tertiary Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.281.abstract: Abstract Aim To audit our practice of drain tube insertion after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, in accordance with the SAGES guideline. Method This prospective audit was conducted in three phases:Pre-intervention (August – October 2023): Data was collected on all consecutive adult patients undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.Educational intervention: The surgical team was provided the importance of the audit and educated about the SAGES guideline on drain use.Post-intervention (November - December): Data was again prospectively collected to complete the audit cycle. Results In the first cycle, there were 30 patients (mean age 45.77 years), 26 were female (86.7%). Drainage was used in all patients, despite it being clinically indicated in only 16.6% of the cases. In the second cycle, involving another 30 patients (mean age 47.03 years). The findings showed that a drain was used in 53.3% of patients, despite only 23.3% of the patients requiring it. Significantly, following the educational intervention, the rate of drain usage in inappropriate cases was reduced by a significant 60.87% (from 100% to 39.13%). Conclusions This audit, the first of its kind in a tertiary centre in a low-income country like Syria, highlights the value of evidence-based practices in enhancing patient care. It confirms that routine drain placement after uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy is unnecessary, leading to reduced hospital stays, complications, and costs, while fostering surgical team awareness of quality improvement initiatives in resource-limited settings.
affiliations: Al-Mouwasat University Hospital, Damascus University , Damascus ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.280.title: 836 Single Installation of Mitomycin C in New Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: A Clinical Re-Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.280.abstract: Abstract Aim To measure the adherence of our tertiary urology service to providing a single dose of intravesical Mitomycin C (MMC) during the first transurethral resection of a bladder tumour (TURBT) in patients with newly diagnosed bladder cancer (NICE guidelines NG2 1.2.7). Method A single centre ambidirectional re-audit was performed and included patients with newly diagnosed bladder cancer who underwent their first TURBT. Data was collected from 2022 to 2023 and during 2024. Demographic and clinical details were collected from electronic systems, where available. Local audit and ethical approval were granted. Results An initial audit carried out in 2022 and presented at a departmental meeting in 2023 showed 5-10% compliance. A re-audit collected data from March 2024 to August 2024. One hundred and thirty patients were screened, and 77 patients were included (62 male, 15 female). MMC was given in 28 patients (36% compliance). 86% of these patients were administered MMC post-operatively rather than during the operation (n=24). In 63.6% of the total cases, MMC was not given (n=49). In 76%, there was no documented reason for not giving MMC (n=37). In 7 of 49 cases (14%) MMC was not given due to bleeding-related risks. Conclusions Improvements in the adherence of providing MMC to newly diagnosed bladder cancer patients during TURBT are needed. In a planned third cycle of the audit, the impact of introducing a novel electronic prescribing system and encouraging the use of new TURBT proforma will be measured.
affiliations: Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust , Chelmsford ,
Faculty of Health, Education, Medicine, and Social Care, Anglia Ruskin University , Chelmsford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.216.title: 195 Close Loop Retrospective Audit of Acute Ureteric Stone Management: A Comparison with NICE Guidelines and GIRFT
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.216.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit evaluates adherence to the NICE guidelines and GIRFT recommendations for acute ureteric stone management, focusing on reducing stent insertions and promoting URS/ESWL for non-septic patients without clear indications for stenting. Method A retrospective audit was conducted in two cycles. The first cycle reviewed 89 patients admitted to ESH between August to November 2023, and the second cycle included 65 patients from July to September 2024. Data were collected from Powerchart notes and ward lists, analyzing the management referred from A&E to on-call team. Results Improvements were observed between cycles, including better adherence to serum calcium checks (47% to 66%) and dietary advice provision (17% to 72%). Stent insertions without clear indications or sepsis decreased from 83% to 57%. Conservative management rates declined from 65% to 46%, with reduced failure rates and more urgent treatments offered within 48 hours (35% to 53%). Efforts to improve follow-up led to a significant reduction in lost hot stone clinic follow-ups. Despite opening a hot primary URS theatre, reduced manpower and lack of CEPOD support limited its success, resulting in stent insertions for patients unlikely to pass stones due to pain, stone size, or location. Conclusion The audit demonstrates improvements in metabolic workup, patient counseling, and follow-up adherence, while highlighting gaps in theatre and manpower support for primary URS. Recommendations include developing a standardized care pathway, enhancing follow-up processes, and implementing datix or iPhase reporting for delays in primary URS and urgent stent decisions. Re-audit is planned in 6–12 months to assess progress.
affiliations: East Surrey Hospital, Surrey and Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust , Redhill ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.215.title: 180 Audit of the Ponseti Clinic & Management of Clubfoot Deformity at RHC, Glasgow
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.215.abstract: Abstract Aim BSCOS published a consensus statement on clubfoot deformity in 2021 which prompted a clinical service change in 2023 with the development of a dedicated clubfoot clinic at RHC, Glasgow. This audit looked at a 12-month period following implementation of this weekly clinic. All cases of clubfoot in this institution had their treatment begin with Ponseti casting. Method BSCOS consensus statement on clubfoot was reviewed and auditable standards were identified. The clinic was audited starting June 2023 for 12 months. Results 48 new patients were reviewed, 22 of these had clubfoot (19 idiopathic, 3 secondary) and 26 had other foot and ankle presentations or were normal. 63% of patients had their Ponseti casting started between 2 and 6 weeks of age. 91% of babies received a screening US hip scan. In the clinic records folder, the Pirani scoring system was used 100% of the time. The number of casts required per patient ranged from 3 to 6 and the mean was 4.5. Ponseti casts should be changed every 4-7 days. [1] 73% of patients met this. BSCOS expected that a tenotomy will be required in 85 to 95% of cases. [1] Achilles tenotomy was performed for 91% of patients. The post-tenotomy cast was on for 90% of cases for 3 weeks and the remaining patients were in cast for 4 weeks. Conclusions This audit has highlighted overall good clinical practice, and that the clinic meets nearly all the standards as expected for clubfoot management.
affiliations: Royal Hospital for Children , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.214.title: 123 How Useful Is Murphy’s Sign in Evaluating Acute Cholecystitis? a Clinical Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.214.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate if Murphy’s sign is being performed in line with NICE guidance for suspected cholecystitis. To evaluate the utility of Murphy’s sign for acute cholecystitis. Method 100 patients with appointments for suspected gallbladder pathology at the Surgical Same-Day Emergency Care unit were included. Data was collected on pre-ultrasound abdominal examination documentation and ultrasound findings. Results Murphy’s sign was examined for in 54% of patients: the emergency department (ED) examined for the sign in 54% of those assessed, and general surgery in 56%. When both teams examined for Murphy’s sign, the result differed in 24% of cases. For general surgery, Murphy’s sign had a sensitivity of 67%, specificity of 42%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 7% and negative predictive value (NPV) of 95%. For the ED, the sensitivity was 67%, specificity was 15%, PPV was 7% and NPV was 83%. Conclusions The completion rate was below the 100% NICE standard. An examination proforma has been developed to increase compliance, with a re-audit planned. There was high inter-rater variability between teams for the outcome of Murphy’s sign. There was a higher false positive rate in ED (85%) than general surgery (58%). Using the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve, Murphy’s sign when assessed by general surgery is marginally better than using chance alone to diagnose cholecystitis, whereas an ED assessment is marginally worse. The negative predictive value is high for both teams; a negative Murphy’s sign could be useful in assessing for the absence of cholecystitis but a positive result holds little value.
affiliations: West Suffolk Hospital , Bury Saint Edmunds ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.213.title: 100 Weightbearing Status Documentation in Orthopaedic Operation Notes – A Snapshot Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.213.abstract: Abstract Aim A snapshot audit was performed to assess current compliance with the most recent guidelines on weightbearing documentation in accordance with British Orthopaedic Association Standards (BOAST). Weight-bearing terminology has been shown to be ambiguous and is often understood variably by both healthcare professionals and patients. Standardisation of terms has been suggested to reduce confusion for patients and therapy teams during rehabilitation following surgery. Method A single-centre retrospective audit of 50 lower-limb operation notes (25 trauma; 25 elective) from electronic patient records to correct weightbearing terminology use and documentation of mobilisation limitations following surgery in accordance with BOAST guidelines. After baseline measurement and consultation with physiotherapists, educational interventions were implemented for surgeons including theatre posters, template training and reminder messages via WhatsApp groups. A target of 80% compliance was set. Results The baseline audit showed 6% compliance (for “non-weightbearing” cases only) with significant variability in terminology used. None of the cases in which patients were limited or non-weightbearing had rationale given for this. Functional and duration limitations were given for 60% and 86% of cases respectively. Conclusions It is evident that knowledge on the changes in recommended weightbearing terminology is severely lacking. Simple educational methods and use of a template can invariably improve compliance with this. This particular topic promotes interdisciplinary working among therapy colleagues who have a vested interest in the timely rehabilitation of postoperative patients, accurate to surgeon preferences. A series of rapid-cycle audits are currently underway to review the impact of these interventions.
affiliations: Sandwell and West Birmingham Hospitals NHS Trust , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.289.title: 900 A Single-Centre 2-Cycle Audit of Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumour Post-Operative Documentation
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.289.abstract: Abstract Aim TURBT procedures are carried out aiming to resect bladder tumours, and the events and findings documented in the operation note heavily influence the decision and action taken by the urology multi-disciplinary team (MDT) going forwards. However not all operation notes are completed with the information required, e.g. tumour size, number or location. We have carried out a 2-cycle audit to assess the documentation of essential information in TURBT post-operation notes, to identify and optimise any scope for improvement in recording and allow for better decision making in the MDT. Therefore, our aim is to assess operation note documentation for TURBT cases to assess whether all required information is being recorded. Method 25 patients were identified in a single centre across a 3-month period undergoing a TURBT. As an intervention, there was a teaching session at our local urology departmental teaching, as well as implementing a template operation note for staff use to ensure all information is documented. We compared our results to a standard checklist by Kikuchi et al. Results Initial results showed that 24% of the 25 cases audited record whether there was a pre-op rectal examination, whilst 40% comment on tumour number and 32% record whether there was felt to be complete tumour resection. Whilst 96% do record tumour location, even this figure was not 100%. Conclusions All staff documenting TURBT operation notes should use the template op note checklist provided to ensure there is thorough information recorded.
affiliations: George Eliot Hospital , Nuneaton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.287.title: 895 Enhancing Frailty Assessment and Geriatric Liaison in Acute Surgical Admissions at Bedford Hospital: A Quality Improvement Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.287.abstract: Abstract Aim Frailty is a key factor influencing surgical outcomes in older adults, linked to higher risks of complications, prolonged hospital stays, and increased mortality. National guidelines, including those from National Emergency Laparotomy Audit(NELA), recommend early frailty screening. This audit assessed frailty documentation in surgical admissions across general surgery, urology, and vascular specialties and evaluated the impact of introducing a frailty liaison service. Method A retrospective audit was conducted over two months (June–July 2024), reviewing emergency surgical admissions to the Surgical Assessment Unit (SAU). Data collected included demographics, operative interventions, Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) scores, and evidence of geriatrician input. Following the audit, a frailty liaison service was introduced, consisting of biweekly ward rounds. A second audit cycle (September–November 2024) was performed to assess changes in frailty documentation and geriatrician referrals. Results In Cycle 1, none of the patients aged ≥65 years had frailty scores documented, and no patients received geriatric input. After introducing the frailty liaison service, Cycle 2 showed a significant improvement, with 88% (103/117) of patients having a documented CFS. Of these, 43% (44/103) were identified as frail (CFS ≥5). However, only 18% (8/44) of frail patients received geriatric input, with delays in referral contributing to under-referral. Conclusions Introducing a frailty liaison service improved the documentation of frailty but highlighted gaps in timely geriatric input. Key recommendations include implementing a mandatory electronic referral system, improving referral workflows, and increasing ward round frequency. A re-audit within six months will measure the effectiveness of these interventions.
affiliations: Bedford Hospital , Bedford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.284.title: 864 A Clinical Audit Assessing the Accuracy of Documenting Complications When Consenting Patients for Laparoscopic +/- Open Appendicectomy in Morriston Hospital (South Wales, UK)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.284.abstract: Abstract Aim Laparoscopic Appendicectomy: Consent compared to EIDO standards. The primary aim(s) of our project were to assess the documentation of risks associated with laparoscopic +/- open appendicectomies compared to EIDO standards, to improve consenting techniques and documentation of risks associated and to compare the data between The University Hospital of Wales (UHW) and Morriston Hospital. Method Prospective data collection was carried out for 6 weeks at different times across both sites. Patients booked for appendicectomy were located on TOMS (Citrix) or TheatreMan. Once idenfitied, patient consent forms were reviewed in clinical notes. Data were extracted from consent forms regarding the documented risks of procedure for 16 patients. No patient identifiable data was recorded. A period of intervention was applied in the form of information posters and clinical audit meeting presentations to educate clinicians on the risks. Re-audit was performed through another 6-week period on 16 different patients at both sites. Results Out of 16 complications (EIDO standards), 13 complications were more likely to be included on consent forms post-intervention. The average number of risks documented on consent forms was 13 post-intervention, compared to 9 pre-intervention. At UHW, there was a 20% increase in documented complications, compared to a 40% increase in Morriston. Pre-intervention, consent conversations were rarely documented in patient notes. Post-intervention, 31% of informed consent conversations were recorded in clinical notes in Morriston, and 40% in UHW. Conclusions Departmental education demonstrated improved consent for appendicectomies. Future work should focus on understanding patient retention of consent conversations and a trial of pre-populated electronic consent forms.
affiliations: Morriston Hospital , Swansea ,
University Hospital of Wales , Cardiff ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.170.title: 372 An Audit to Assess the Efficacy of Fascia Iliaca Block Teaching Amongst Orthopaedic Junior Doctors Using Homemade Models
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.170.abstract: Abstract Aim Fascia iliaca block (FiB) provides excellent analgesia for patients with neck of femur fractures, now often performed by emergency staff to ensure prompt pain relief, resulting in a lack of FiB experience amongst orthopaedic junior doctors (OJDs). However, OJDs should be competent to administer repeated FiB if surgery is delayed to reduce discomfort and prevent pain-related complications. Anatomical models are expensive (>£1000), so models made from cardboard and sponges were used to simulate relevant anatomical structures. This audit aims to assess the efficacy of FiB teaching using homemade models. Method The one-off small group teaching session included a theory discussion and a practical session using models. A pillow and sponges were used to represent soft tissue, cardboard to mimic the fascia, and a pillowcase for the skin and to illustrate anatomical landmarks (Figure. 1). A survey was taken before and after teaching to assess students’ confidence in anatomy, equipment, technique, performing FiB. Confidence was self-rated and scored out of 10. Results Equipment to make models totalled £10. Of eight students (seven senior house officers and one physician associate), none had received formal Fib teaching previously. Mean confidence improved from 3.75-5.75 to 8.00-9.25 (Table 1 & Figure 2). Many positive comments were received about the homemade models. 87.5% rated the session as ‘excellent’, and 12.5% as ‘good’. Conclusions Homemade models provided excellent tactile feedback, demonstration of anatomy and procedural technique for FiB teaching. The teaching sessions may be beneficial to be included as part of induction to ensure competency amongst new rotating OJDs.
affiliations: University Hospitals Plymouth , Plymouth ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.706.title: 997 An Audit into Compliance with Boast Standards for Mobilisation and Weightbearing After Orthopaedic Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.706.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aimed to assess compliance within our department to the new BOAST Standards for documentation of mobilisation and weightbearing status after orthopaedic surgery. Method This audit identified all orthopaedic operations which had occurred over a two-month period from August 1st 2024 to September 30th 2024. Scanned operation notes were then obtained for each operation and compliance with the BOAST Standards was assessed. Results In total, 159 patients who underwent orthopaedic surgery during the specified time period were identified, with 11 operation notes being compliant with BOAST standards. Identified patients were further separated into three groups: upper limb surgery, lower limb surgery (excluding neck of femur fractures) and neck of femur fractures. Of these, lower limb surgeries showed highest compliance of 14% (7 of the 50), compared to 7% of upper limb surgeries (4 out of 59) and 0% of neck of femur fractures (0 out of 50). All but one of the neck of femur fractures had ticked the “full weightbearing” box on the operation note, making them technically non-compliant with the updated nomenclature of “unrestricted weightbearing”. Conclusions This audit has shown there is currently poor compliance with the BOAST standards within our department, leading to potential confusion in patients’ rehabilitation pathways. If compliance is to be improved then simple structural changes such as reformatting the operation note, which encourages incorrect documentation, should lead to a marked increase. Further education and awareness into the new standards will also likely be required.
affiliations: Bristol Royal Infirmary , Bristol ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.626.title: 725 Re-Audit: Diagnosing the Improvements Required for Enhancing the Medical Student Bedside Teaching Experience Utilising a Cohort of Surgical Teaching Fellows
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.626.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this study is to evaluate the impact of changes made to third-year students’ Surgical bedside teaching with the inclusion of surgical teaching fellows, as compared to the initial survey results. Method Post-event, retrospective, optional questionnaire formed of 5 Questions evaluated by a Likert scale and 2 open-ended Questions. First Cycle: 2022-2024 Year 3 BSMS Student, 40 responses Second cycle: September – December 2024 Year 3 BSMS students, 11 responses Results Changes: Smaller teaching groups, improved communication between the Fellows and surgical teams, improved teaching material. Most students agreed that Surgical Ward Round Bedside Teaching sessions with dedicated fellows effectively enhanced clinical knowledge and skills. Compared to an initial 48%, 60% strongly agreed that teaching fellows were engaging and approachable during Surgical Ward Round Teaching. Also, the majority agreed that they felt comfortable asking questions and seeking clarification during the Teaching sessions. However, 55% agreed that Bedside Teaching sessions were well-organized and focused on relevant surgical/clinical cases compared to an initial 35%. When asked, ‘How could the bedside/Ward Round teaching sessions be improved?’ – Responses revolved around suggesting including more teaching fellows on ward rounds, a de-brief session of the patients on the ward, and having clearer learning objectives, more structured as well as spending more time on history taking and examinations. Conclusions The introduction of surgical teaching fellows has had a positive impact on the students’ Surgical Teaching experience. However, there is still room for future refinement, and further enhancement strategies are in progress.
affiliations: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust , Brighton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.446.title: 1128 ENT Treatment Room Swabs Audit and Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.446.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this audit and quality improvement project was to: assess the frequency of ear swabs in the ent treatment room; determine if patients being swabbed had follow-up arranged and if swab results changed management. Method All treatment room visits for acute ear presentations during october and november 2023 were reviewed. Information was collected from clinical portal and collated on excel. Following review of results, quality improvement measures were implemented, including the display of a poster in the ent treatment room with indications for swabbing. Data was collected again in october and november 2024. Results In the first audit cycle, swabs were taken in 77% of acute ear presentations. There was no follow-up in 20% of patients who were swabbed and swab results changed management in 9% of cases. The recommendation following review of these results was that there should be specific indications for ear swabs which might ultimately lead to a change in management. Patients should also have follow-up arranged to ensure that swab results are actioned. In the second audit cycle, swabs were taken in 47% of cases and there were fewer patients who did not have follow-up arranged (12%). Swab results changed management in 11% of cases. Conclusions This audit has shown that swab results change management in very few acute ear presentations therefore swabbing should not be a routine part of patient assessment. Our quality improvement measures have helped to reduce the frequency of unnecessary investigations and ensure that patients are followed up appropriately.
affiliations: University Hospital Monklands , Airdrie ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.324.title: 189 Audit of Preoperative Axillary Staging and Axillary Recurrence in Early Invasive Breast Cancer at a Single Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.324.abstract: Abstract Aim This study aimed to assess our hospital's compliance with the Association of Breast Surgery guidelines for axillary management in early breast cancer. The guidelines recommend preoperative axillary ultrasound for invasive breast cancer, with ultrasound-guided biopsy for suspicious findings. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is the preferred staging procedure, and axillary node clearance (ANC) is advised for confirmed axillary node metastasis. Effective staging should ensure axillary recurrence rates remain below 5% at 5 years. Methods Data was collected for patients undergoing axillary procedures between October 2017 and October 2018. Inclusion criteria were invasive breast cancer or ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with mastectomy. Exclusions included prior breast cancer or axillary procedures for non-breast cancer reasons. Key data included preoperative imaging, biopsy findings, surgical interventions, and 5-year outcomes. Results Among 235 patients (mean age 61), 61.7% had invasive cancer, 37% had DCIS, and 1.3% had both invasive cancer and DCIS. SLNB was performed in 203 patients, ANC in 26, and axillary sampling in 2. All patients with ultrasound findings of U3 or higher underwent ultrasound-guided biopsy. Of 26 patients with suspicious (B4) biopsies, 25 underwent ANC, while 1 underwent SLNB with no recurrence at 5 years. Axillary recurrence occurred in 3 patients (1.27%), two of whom experienced local recurrence first. Conclusions Our data show high compliance with staging guidelines and a low axillary recurrence rate of 1.27%, well below the 5% benchmark at 5 years, supporting the effectiveness of current practice.
affiliations: The Dudley Group NHS Foundation Trust , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.257.title: 580 Outcomes of Skin Grafts for Skin Cancer Patients on Anticoagulation: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.257.abstract: Abstract Introduction Skin grafting is a key reconstructive technique following skin cancer excision. Many patients are on anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy, raising concerns about skin graft failure due to bleeding and impaired wound healing. This study evaluated the failure rates of full-thickness (FTSG) and split-thickness skin grafts (SSG) in patients on anticoagulants/antiplatelets versus those not on anticoagulation and assessed the impact of various factors that may affect the graft outcomes. Method A retrospective review of 88 patients who underwent FTSG or SSG from July to September 2024 was conducted. Data on demographics, social history, co-morbidities, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, graft type, donor site, cancer type, and outcomes were analysed. Results The overall graft failure rate was 26.1%, with higher but non-significant rates in patients on anticoagulants (37.5% vs. 19.6%, p=0.114). FTSG had higher failure rates than SSG (35.7% vs. 17.4%, p=0.087). Graft failure varied significantly by cancer type, with squamous cell carcinoma (30.8%) showing higher rates than basal cell carcinoma (16.2%, p=0.048). The use of chloramphenicol 1% ointment significantly reduced failure rates (7.7% vs. 33.9%, p=0.022). Conclusions Patients on anticoagulants have increased but non-significant risks of graft failure. FTSG and SCC are associated with higher failure rates, while chloramphenicol ointment significantly improves outcomes. Recommendations include optimising pre-operative assessment including maintaining perioperative anticoagulation for low-risk cases, enhance intra-operative factors such as ensuring haemostasis and using chloramphenicol ointment, and ensure follow up planning, A re-audit is planned to achieve a graft failure rate below 33%.
affiliations: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust , Leicester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.256.title: 535 A Clinical Audit of Out-of-Hours Red Cell Transfusions in a Regional Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.256.abstract: Abstract Aim It is recognised that transfusing outside of ‘routine’ hours is less safe and should be avoided unless clinically essential. This audit evaluates out-of-hours red cell concentrate (RCC) transfusions by indication. Method We identified prospectively RCC transfusions occurring out of hours in our institution over a one-month period. Indications were examined against NICE blood transfusion guidelines. Based on these guidelines and advice from our local haemovigilance officer we defined five criteria for an appropriate out of hours transfusion. Transfusions fulfilling any one of these criteria were defined as appropriate. Results Following withdrawals, data on 51 units of RCC transfused out of hours were included in the analysis of which 70.6% were defined as appropriate as per our criteria. Transfusion recipients were male in 54.9% of cases. The mean pre-transfusion haemoglobin (Hb) level was 7.6 m/dL. The mean post-transfusion Hb was 8.4 m/dL. Incidence of active haemorrhage was 31.4%. Incidence of symptomatic anaemia was 51%. The haemoglobin level was appropriately low in 29.4% of cases. 3.9% of the transfusions were given in the context of perioperative haemorrhage. A further 3.9% were given for low haemoglobin pre-operatively. There were no recorded transfusion complications. Conclusions Although the majority of transfusions were clinically indicated, 29.4% of out-of-hours RCC transfusions were not indicated under our criteria. We recommend the implementation of a verbal proforma prior to a re-audit, with a view to improving patient safety and compliance. Guidelines outlining appropriate requests should be developed and reasons for delays in the transfusion process be explored.
affiliations: Wexford General Hospital , Wexford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.243.title: 380 Re-Audit of Documentation of Closed Hand Fractures Referred to Hand Therapy Trauma Clinic at Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.243.abstract: Abstract Aim The British Society for Surgery of the Hand (BSSH) guidelines for closed hand fractures outline that there should be clear documentation of the decision for non-operative management and factors that have influenced this, particularly if the decision for non-operative management is not the expected approach. At Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust, this cohort of patients are referred to a Hand Therapy Trauma Clinic (HTTC) for triage and appropriate non-operative management. Method A retrospective review was conducted of all closed hand fractures referred to HTTC over a two-week period in November 2024. The referral forms were assessed against objective criteria and outcomes were compared to data from the initial audit in March 2024 prior to intervention. Results There were 36 closed hand fracture referrals to HTTC, of which 21 (58%) were adults and 15 (42%) were children. The number of patients with electronic documentation of the referral to HTTC was improved when compared with initial data (17% vs 8%, p=0.45). There were 34 referrals (94%) with a specific diagnosis recorded and 32 (89%) had documented senior input (speciality registrar or consultant) in the decision for non-operative management. Only 64% of referrals had a detailed description of the mechanism of injury. Conclusions The HTTC referrals for closed hand fractures have clear diagnoses and senior involvement in the decision for non-operative management The number of referrals with electronic documentation has increased compared to the initial data but there remains significant improvement to be made.
affiliations: Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust , Wakefield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.571.title: 926 “Why Radiology Requests Are Not Being Accepted”, a Quality Improvement Audit in a Surgical Department
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.571.abstract: Abstract Aim Radiology requests serve as the primary communication tool between clinical physicians and radiologists, enabling radiologists to provide accurate diagnostic support. This audit aimed to evaluate the radiology request acceptance rate, identify common reasons for request rejections, and implement measures to improve request quality. Method According to the Royal College of Radiologists, radiology requests should include comprehensive and relevant information, although specific content requirements are not defined. The audit was conducted in two cycles: the first in September-October 2023 and the second in August 2024. Patients were randomly selected from clinical handover records and SACU clinic logs. Radiology requests on the TrakCare system were reviewed to determine their acceptance status, assess the quality of information provided, and identify reasons for requests being placed on hold. Results During the first audit cycle, 73% (52/71) of radiology requests were accepted. The primary reasons for rejections included inappropriate imaging (21%, 4/19), duplicate requests (21%, 4/19), and insufficient clinical details (21%, 4/19). Following these findings, a structured request format was developed, and staff were educated on its use. In the second audit cycle, the acceptance rate improved significantly to 89% (89/101). Conclusions A high-quality radiology request should include a concise patient background, current symptoms, examination and investigation findings, relevant differential diagnoses, and the clinical situation. Radiology requests should be presented as well-informed proposals rather than directives. Implementing a structured request format can enhance communication, optimize resource utilization, and expedite patient care planning for improved outcomes.
affiliations: NHS Lanarkshire , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.562.title: 761 Closing the Loop: Evaluating and Enhancing Adherence to a Local Acute Abdomen Pathway
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.562.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute Abdomen pathways are a staple in Trust guidelines, allowing clinicians to identify deteriorating patients with surgical pathology, and manage them accordingly. We aimed to assess adherence and improve upon the local Acute Abdomen pathway. Method During the first cycle, patients who underwent emergency abdominal surgery over a 3-month period were identified using the hospital’s theatre logbook. Following this, an updated pathway was created. The cycle was closed 7 months later, where patients were identified via specific presenting complaints highlighted by post-take ward round documentation. Data was analysed using Fisher's Exact test, with a p-value of <0.05 being statistically significant. Results A total of 55 and 91 patients were audited in our first and second cycles respectively. 78% of patients had emergency imaging requested within the pathway’s timeframe, compared to 60% initially (p-value =0.03). 91% were surgically reviewed within the guideline’s time frame compared to 38.2% in the initial cycle (p-value <0.01). 50% of septic patients received antibiotics within 1 hour as opposed to 80% in the initial cycle (p-value = 0.33). 1% of patients had a NELA score documented as compared to 5.5% in the initial cycle (p-value = 0.15). Conclusions Having implemented changes, we have demonstrated statistically significant improvements in the adherence to the pathway. Positives such as surgical review and CT request time should be reinforced and continued. With limitations identified, we have suggested further changes which we hope to re-audit after incorporating them into hospital guidelines ensuring enhanced outcomes; ultimately hoping to contribute to advancing national standards.
affiliations: Southport and Formby District General Hospital NHS Trust , Liverpool ,
Royal National ENT Hospital & University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.308.title: 1097 Improving Infant Male Circumcision Practices: A Two-Cycle Clinical Audit
