DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.308.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate practices and outcomes of male baby circumcisions using Plastibell technique at the Musamedics clinic, assess compliance with WHO guidelines for early infant male circumcision, and enhance patient care through an iterative audit process. Method This two-cycle audit reviewed 209 cases in the first cycle and 120 cases in the second cycle. Data, including demographics, procedural details, and outcomes, were collected and analysed. Findings from the first cycle were presented to staff, with recommendations discussed and implemented before the second cycle. Key metrics included documentation quality, local anaesthesia administration, discharge efficiency, and complication rates. Results Documentation completeness improved markedly, with missing data on gestation reduced from 4% to 0.8%, and on Plastibell size from 10% to 5.8%. Compliance with post-operative checks increased dramatically from 0% to 98.3%. The local anaesthetic dose was optimised, with a mean reduction from 2.36 ml to 2.18 ml, and variability decreased (SD 0.72 to 0.48). Time for anaesthesia to take effect improved from a mean of 4.63 minutes (range: 3–10) to 4.36 minutes (range: 3–8). Intraoperative complications dropped from 2.5% to 0.8%, with only minor bleeding recorded. Discharge efficiency increased significantly, with 91.6% discharged within 15–30 minutes, compared to 55% in the first cycle. Conclusions The audit demonstrated significant improvements in compliance with best practices, documentation, local anaesthesia practices, and patient flow, while maintaining a low complication rate. Structured audits and collaborative staff discussions were instrumental in achieving these enhancements. Future efforts will focus on incorporating long-term patient follow-up to assess outcomes and satisfaction.
affiliations: Musamedics Ltd , Leicester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.307.title: 1091 An Audit to Evaluate the Effectiveness of the Implementation of an Enhanced Recovery Programme (ERP) Discharge Checklist for Elective Colorectal Cancer Resection Patients Is on Length of Stay in a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.307.abstract: Abstract Aim Enhanced Recovery Programs (ERPs) in colorectal surgery, popularized in the early 2000s, are associated with reduced morbidity and shorter hospital stays. However, their success depends on effective implementation by surgical teams. An audit at a District General Hospital revealed delayed discharges in over 50% of elective colorectal surgery patients. As a result, an ERP discharge checklist was introduced to improve discharge efficiency. This study evaluates its impact. Method A single-center, retrospective audit was conducted using patient data from January 5 to June 27, 2024. Compliance with the ERP discharge checklist was assessed, including outcomes such as length of stay, catheter removal, and first flatus. Results The audit included 45 patients (22 males, 23 females) who underwent elective colorectal cancer surgery without stoma formation. The median length of stay was reduced (4 vs 5 days), more patients were discharged on the day the checklist was completed (61% vs 46%), and a higher percentage had catheters removed on day 1 (80% vs 63%). The most common reasons for discharge delays were weekends (6 cases) and co-morbidities (6 cases). Conclusions This audit demonstrates that the ERP discharge checklist contributes to a reduced length of stay following elective colorectal cancer surgery. Improving weekend discharges is a focus for future work, with plans to implement junior doctor education and a weekend discharge strategy for elective colorectal patients.
affiliations: St Richard’s Hospital , Chichester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.231.title: 289 Evaluating Documentation Accuracy for K-Wire Removal Timing in Hand Surgery: An Audit Study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.231.abstract: Abstract Background Accurate documentation is crucial for patient safety and continuity of care. The Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) guidelines, published in 2014, emphasize the need for detailed postoperative care instructions, such as recording K-wire removal timing. Concerns about inconsistent documentation of K-wire removal prompted this audit. Proper documentation minimises risks such as infection, wire migration, ensures optimal healing, and prevents unnecessary delays or interventions. Inadequate records can lead to inappropriate appointment bookings, resulting in unnecessary healthcare costs and resource use. Aim To assess the baseline accuracy of K-wire removal documentation and implement interventions for improvement. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on 100 operative notes from 02/08/2023 to 12/09/2024 for hand surgery patients who underwent K-wire fixation. Key variables assessed included K-wire removal date, K-wire size, date and time, name of surgeon, operative procedure, operative findings, and closure details. Data were analysed using R 4.4.0, including Chi-Square test and Cramér’s V to evaluate associations between variables. Results 27% of patients lacked documentation for K-wire removal date, and 22% lacked documentation for K-wire size. Other variables achieved 98-100% accuracy. A significant and moderate association (p = 0.00002075, Cramér’s V = 0.464) was found between documenting K-wire removal date and size. Conclusions Gaps in documenting K-wire removal date and size highlight areas for improvement. The significant association between these variables suggests that enhancing the accuracy of one will positively influence the other. Laminated posters and educational interventions have been implemented, and a second audit cycle is planned.
affiliations: Lister Hospital , Stevenage ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.230.title: 287 Neurovascular Status Assessment and Documentation in Long Bone Fractures Admitted to Orthopaedics in a Major Trauma Centre: A Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.230.abstract: Abstract Introduction Acute fractures have the potential to disrupt neurovascular structures, which may be limb or life-threatening for patients. Recent case reviews highlighted the importance of documenting neurovascular status on admission. The current orthopaedic clerking booklet has been acknowledged to not provide suitable space for concise neurovascular documentation. Aim To improve the assessment and documentation of neurovascular status for all long bone fractures admitted to orthopaedics. The documentation was audited against BOAST (British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma) guidelines. Method Retrospective review of clerking booklets of 70 inpatients with long bone fractures for documentation of neurovascular status on admission. This was audited and results presented locally, along with colleague education. An intervention was developed, consisting of a sticker with tick boxes for the correct neurovascular documentation. The neurovascular status documentation of 70 inpatient clerking booklets after this intervention was assessed to complete the cycle. Results The complete documentation of neurovascular status (including motor and sensory for each nerve and peripheral pulses) improved almost 3-fold from 29% before the intervention to 86% after. Documentation of pulses increased 2.5-fold, from 36% to 89%. 20% of patients had no neurovascular documentation at all prior to the intervention; this improved to no patients having absence of documentation. Conclusions This study has shown that a simple and cost-effective intervention can vastly improve documentation compliance. Locally, this intervention has provided scope to alter the clerking booklet to include the tick box proforma. This has knock-on benefits for patient safety and potential avoidance of medicolegal financial penalties.
affiliations: Nottingham University Hospitals , Nottingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.234.title: 313 An Audit of Lynch Syndrome Testing Practices at Kettering General Hospital Against NICE Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.234.abstract: Abstract Aim Lynch syndrome (LS), a hereditary colorectal cancer predisposition, necessitates timely and accurate testing to facilitate early intervention and risk reduction. NICE guideline DG27 recommends comprehensive LS testing for all newly diagnosed colorectal cancer patients. This audit assesses the adherence of Kettering General Hospital (KGH) to these guidelines. Method Data were analyzed from 34 patients (aged ≥18 years) diagnosed with colorectal cancer between 1 January 2022 and 31 March 2022. The primary outcome measures were the time to IHC results and referral rates for genetic testing. Results All patients received immunohistochemistry (IHC) testing. However, only 15% received IHC results within the recommended 7–10 days. Only 50% of patients with MMR-deficient IHC results were referred for genetic testing. While 100% of patients with available tumor tissue underwent testing, the delays in IHC results and low referral rates for genetic testing highlight significant areas for improvement. Conclusions This audit reveals substantial discrepancies between KGH's LS testing practices and NICE guideline DG27 recommendations. To improve efficiency and timely diagnosis, we recommend appointing a clinical lead to optimize the LS testing pathway, enhance inter-specialty collaboration (including obstetrics and gynecology), and align local protocols with national guidelines. Targeted educational initiatives should improve awareness among healthcare professionals and patients. Further research with a larger sample size is warranted to validate these findings and inform the development of more effective LS testing pathways.
affiliations: Kettering General Hospital , Kettering ,
North Middlesex University Hospital , London ,
Royal Hobart Hospital , Hobart ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.464.title: 302 Post Traumatic Closed Rhinoplasty Approach in the Treatment of Traumatis Nasal Deformity
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.464.abstract: Abstract Background The application of rhinoplasty in the treatment of traumatic nasal deformity remains one of the most challenging problems in plastic surgery. Aim This study presents our experiences in the reconstruction of traumatic nasal deformities using the internal rhinoplasty approach. Method We conducted a retrospective study from January 2001 to December 2013. We included in this study all patients operated for nasal post-traumatic deformity using closed approach. Each patient chart was reviewed with regard to age and gender, circumstances and date of nasal trauma, timing of the rhinoplasty as well as for the functional and aesthetic outcomes. Results One hundred seventy-two of these patients, including 115 males and 57 females, underwent the internal approach. The patients were, on average, 26 years old at the time of reconstruction and were followed up for an average period of 16 months. The interval from injury to the rhinoplasty procedure was 4,5 years, on average. The outcome was assessed by (an independent investigator and the patients themselves). The overall aesthetic-improvement rate was 88%, and the patient-satisfaction rate was 95%. There was no complication. Conclusions Not only is the skeletal structure severely deformed, but the soft tissue may also be disfigured by a previous injury. The closed rhinoplasty technique provides great predictability and minimal postoperative discomfort, with no aesthetic damage.
affiliations: Tunis Medical School. Tunis-El Manar University , Tunis ,
Monastir Medical School. Monastir University Tunisia , Monastir ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.550.title: 601 Are Surgical Ward Rounds EPIC? – Audit of Ward Round Documentation Following Introduction of an Electronic Health Care System
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.550.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the impact of an Electronic Healthcare system on the safety (documentation of essential information) and accuracy of history and decision making within the daily ward round notes in a surgical unit. Method A prospective audit of general surgical ward round notes was undertaken in September 2024. These were audited against the RCS Edinburgh’s SHINE Ward Round Tool and a consensus from the unit Consultants of the “ideal” ward round note (recording of essential and accurate information). Following the initial data collection cycle, a feedback session was held with the resident doctors in the unit responsible for ward round documentation. Notes were re-audited one week following this session. ANOVA was used to compare the two audit cycles. Results 434 and 533 notes were audited in cycle 1 and cycle 2, respectively. In both cycles, essential information in several domains was missing. However, following the educational session, there was improvement in recording of names of team members present, examination findings, patient understanding and management plan (p <0.05). There was no improvement in recording of diagnosis, new issues, observations, VTE and antimicrobials (p>0.05). Conclusions Accurate documentation of the patient journey is fundamental to safe and effective patient care. The introduction of a new electronic system provides an opportunity to facilitate improved documentation. The utilisation of templates as prompts provides an opportunity to enhance patient safety.
affiliations: South Eastern Health and Social Care Trust , Belfast ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.292.title: 937 Adherence to MMR Reporting Standards in Newly Diagnosed Colorectal Cancer as Part of the Lynch Syndrome Workup Pathway: A Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.292.abstract: Abstract Aim Lynch syndrome is an inherited condition caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, which significantly increases the risk of colorectal, ovarian, endometrial, and small bowel cancers. According to NICE guidelines, individuals diagnosed with colorectal cancer (CRC) should undergo screening for Lynch syndrome through immunohistochemistry (IHC) testing for MMR proteins or microsatellite instability (MSI). Early identification of Lynch syndrome can guide personalised management strategies. This re-audit evaluates the Trust's adherence to the recommended Lynch screening pathway. Method Patients diagnosed with CRC between March and April 2024 were identified from multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting records. Data collected from electronic patient records included patient demographics, diagnosis dates, TNM staging, IHC MMR results, and additional tests for BRAF and MLH1 hypermethylation. Reporting dates for these tests were also reviewed. Results 32 cases were reviewed, with 100% undergoing MMR testing, compared to 97% in the initial audit. The average time from biopsy to histology results was 8 days (range 2-22), an improvement from 8.6 days (range 4-32) previously. MMR results were reported within an average of 4.3 days, with 97% reported within 10 days, up from 90% in the first audit. Four patients showed MMR deficiencies, with three undergoing additional BRAF and MLH1 methylation testing. The time between MMR and MLH1 results significantly improved, averaging 91 days, compared to 251 days in the previous audit. Conclusions The Trust’s adherence to Lynch syndrome screening has improved, now meeting NICE targets. Continued audits are necessary to ensure sustained compliance with national guidelines.
affiliations: Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust , Nottingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.235.title: 314 Evaluation of Anaesthetic Practice for Total Knee Replacement - an Audit at the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.235.abstract: Abstract Aim Total knee replacement is a prevalent procedure that necessitates effective management of post-operative pain to enhance recovery. This study aims to evaluate the anaesthetic techniques utilised by anaesthetists and surgeons at the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital, focusing on their impact on opioid use, physiotherapy outcomes, and hospital length of stay. Method An audit and retrospective review were conducted on 30 patients who underwent total knee replacement from May 10 to June 2, 2023. Data collected included demographics, types of anaesthesia (spinal, general, and peripheral nerve blocks), post-operative opioid consumption, and timing of physiotherapy interventions. Results The median age of patients was 71 years, with a range of 48 to 89 years. A variety of anaesthetic techniques were employed, with 16 out of 26 patients receiving spinal anaesthesia without general anaesthesia, and 10 receiving a combination of spinal and general anaesthesia. The median oral morphine equivalent daily dose for postoperative opioid use was 30mg, with a range of 0-60mg. Patients receiving peripheral nerve blocks demonstrated a trend towards reduced opioid consumption and shorter hospital stays. The mean anaesthetic time was 19 minutes, and the mean recovery time was 51 minutes. Conclusions This evaluation highlights the variability in anaesthetic practices for total knee replacement at ROH. While no single technique emerged as superior, the use of peripheral nerve blocks appeared to correlate with reduced opioid requirements and shorter hospital stays. Further research is needed to establish best practices in anaesthetic management to improve patient outcomes and reduce reliance on opioids.
affiliations: Walsall Manor Hospital , Walsall ,
Royal Orthopaedic Hospital , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.207.title: 54 An Audit of the NELA Standards in a Busy District General Hospital: 4 Years of Post-Operative Management and Outcomes in Emergency Laparotomy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.207.abstract: Abstract Aim An audit of the compliance of a busy district general hospital surgical department to the NELA Standards (2019 and 2023). Method Single-centre, retrospective audit of emergency laparotomies between April 2019 and December 2023. Patients were included if the NELA risk score was ≥5% (‘high-risk’) or if they were deemed ‘high-risk’ based on clinical judgement. Demographic, management, and outcome data were collected from the local NELA database and EPR and were analysed using Microsoft Excel. The primary outcome was the proportion of ‘high-risk’ patients directly admitted to critical care. The secondary outcome was the difference in length of stay (LOS) and 30-day observed/expected (O/E) mortality ratio between high-risk patients admitted to critical care and those admitted to the ward. This audit was approved locally. Results 709 laparotomies were performed and 161 (22.7%) were deemed ‘high-risk’ during the audit period. Of ‘high-risk’ patients, the median age was 74 (18-95), 52% were female, and the median mortality risk was 11.1% (3.1%-77.1%). 136 (84%) ‘high-risk’ patients were directly admitted to critical care with a median LOS of 22 days (4 days – 131 days) and a 30-day O/E mortality ratio of 0.98 (26 patients died). One of the twenty-five patients directly admitted to the wards was escalated to ICU care and one died. The median LOS of ward-admitted patients was 10 days (3 days – 49 days). Conclusions The parsimonious mortality risk score is a tool for post-operative management in emergency laparotomy, but appropriate clinical judgement can prevent excessive care and preserve critical care beds.
affiliations: Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust , Chelmsford ,
Bolton NHS Foundation Trust , Bolton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.305.title: 1060 Audit on Compliance with GIRFT and WM RSN Standards for Management of Cauda Equina Syndrome Patients at UHNM
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.305.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this audit was to quantify the average time taken for a patient referred with suspicion of Cauda Equina Syndrome to receive an MRI and management outcome at UHNM; and compare that duration to national guidelines. Method This closed-loop quality improvement audit evaluated 25 patients referred to the Spinal Surgery department between February 2020 - March 2020 with clinical symptoms suggestive of Cauda Equina syndrome (CES). Time intervals from initial referral to specialist team review, MRI scan, MRI report, and final management decision were assessed. A second audit cycle was conducted on a subsequent cohort of 25 patients referred between November 2023 - December 2023. Results Of cohort one, 16 patients self-presented to A&E and 9 were GP referrals; of the second cohort, 22 were GP referral, 2 self-presented and 1 was an out-of-area transfer. The average time intervals of cohort one: from presentation to Spinal surgery referral was 176 minutes; 69 minutes for GP referrals and 242 minutes for self-referred. For cohort two: 60.8 minutes, 60.7 minutes and 161 minutes, respectively. Mean wait time from arrival to MRI scan was 438 minutes for cycle 1 and 185 minutes for cycle 2. MRI reporting intervals were on average: 254 minutes for the first cycle, and 95.75 minutes for the second cycle. Conclusions This QIP demonstrated an overall improvement in the investigation of suspected CES evidenced by a decreased in A&E referral time, decreased wait time for specialist review, decreased wait time for MRI scan and reporting.
affiliations: UHNM , Stoke-on-Trent ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.304.title: 1059 Audit of Adherence to Gentamicin Guidelines in a Tertiary Hospital Surgical Unit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.304.abstract: Abstract Aim Gentamicin is frequently administered to surgical patients for both prophylaxis and treatment of infections. Proper dosing and administration are crucial to maximize its therapeutic efficacy and minimize adverse effects. Local guidelines have been established to standardize dosing and monitoring practices. This audit aims to assess the appropriateness of gentamicin prescriptions in a surgical unit. Method This audit was conducted in a tertiary care hospital surgical unit over two months. Data were collected from gentamicin charts of surgical patients. The parameters assessed include the accuracy of initial dosages and the adherence to monitoring serum levels in accordance with these guidelines. Initial dosage accuracy was determined by comparing prescribed dosages to guideline-recommended values. Results In the first cycle, a total of 48 patients were reviewed throughout a one-week period. Initial dosage accuracy was high, with 70% of prescriptions aligning with recommended weight-based dosing protocols. However, adherence to serum level monitoring guidelines was suboptimal with only 55% of patients having serum levels measured within the appropriate timeframe. After implementing targeted interventions, including poster displays and departmental teaching, a reaudit at one and two months demonstrated substantial improvements. 92% of initial gentamicin dosages were accurately prescribed while adherence to monitoring serum levels has increased, with 78% of patients receiving timely measurements. Conclusions The audit demonstrated that targeted interventions such as appropriate visual reminders and departmental teaching, significantly improved adherence to guidelines for gentamicin prescribing.
affiliations: Glasgow Royal Infirmary , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.689.title: 501 Post-Operative Pain Management in Elective Arthroplasties – Results of a Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.689.abstract: Abstract Aim Effective pain management following elective arthroplasty influences early mobilisation, patient satisfaction and reduces hospital stay length. The hospital perioperative arthroplasty protocol highlights a combination of opioid and non-opioid analgesics to achieve this goal. In this second-cycle audit, the elective arthroplasty protocol powerplan was implemented within the Surrey Safe Care electronic patient record (EPR). Primary objectives Evaluate the adherence to the new elective arthroplasty protocol powerplan. To determine if the powerplan led to improved compliance with the standardised regimen. Method EPR drug charts were reviewed in the 24 hours from the operation. The data collection period spanned between June-July 2024. A non-validated, ad-hoc, protocol-based scale was used for data analysis: 0 = no analgesia; 1 = 1 regular non-opioid analgesic (NOA) + PRN analgesics; 2 = 1 regular weak opioid + regular NOAs + PRN analgesics; 3 = Regular opioids + regular NOAs + PRN analgesics(protocol standard). Results 51 drug charts were analysed (age range of 43-84 years) - 20 knee (39%) and 31 hip arthroplasties (61%). The proportion of patients achieving a Score 3 rose from 34% to 61%. Of those that adhered to the protocol, 87% of them utilised the powerplan. Conclusions This closed loop audit demonstrates an improvement in protocol compliance with EPR implementation. However, there remains a subset of patients who did not receive the recommended analgesia. Continued monitoring and education around the use of the powerplan will help sustain and improve these results, ultimately enhancing pain management and recovery outcomes for elective arthroplasty patients.
affiliations: Orthopaedic Department, Royal Surrey County Hospital , Guildford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.552.title: 618 Improving Adherence to Antibiotic Prescribing Guidelines in Patients with Intra-Abdominal Sepsis: A Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.552.abstract: Abstract Introduction Intra-abdominal sepsis is a critical condition requiring timely and appropriate antibiotic therapy. Local guidelines recommend IV co-amoxiclav with gentamicin as first-line treatment and IV gentamicin, teicoplanin, and metronidazole for penicillin-allergic patients. Antibiotics should be discontinued 24 hours post-surgery or continued for 5-7 days if source control is not achieved. This audit assessed baseline adherence to guidelines and evaluated the impact of targeted interventions. Method A baseline audit of 50 patients admitted under the general surgical team between January and March 2023 was conducted. Data on demographics, diagnoses (20 cholecystitis, 12 appendicitis, 10 colitis, 8 cholangitis), antibiotic regimens, and duration were collected. A re-audit of 48 patients (18 cholecystitis, 10 appendicitis, 12 colitis, 8 cholangitis) was performed between August and November 2024 after two teaching sessions and guideline dissemination via posters. Results Baseline compliance with IV co-amoxiclav and gentamicin was 4.0% (2/50), improving to 33.3% (16/48) post-intervention. Penicillin-allergic regimen adherence increased from 4.0% (2/50) to 6.25% (3/48). Antibiotic duration improved from 4.59 days to 5.71 days, with fewer patients receiving under 5 days (54.0%, 27/50 vs. 39.6%, 19/48). Gentamicin was the most underprescribed antibiotic. Overuse (>7 days) occurred in 12.0% (6/48) of post-intervention cases. Conclusions Targeted education significantly improved adherence to prescribing guidelines for intra-abdominal sepsis. Further audits are necessary to sustain progress and address remaining gaps in practice.
affiliations: North Middlesex University Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.075.title: Robotic total pelvic excenteration – audit from a tertiary referral center for locally advanced pelvic cancer
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.075.abstract: Abstract Introduction The aim was to perform a retrospective review of short term outcomes of robotic total pelvic excenterations (rTPE) at a tertiary referral center. Results were compared to open total pelvic excenterations (oTPE) during the same time period. Method Data were retrieved from electronic medical records. All patients operated with rTPE or oTPE from 2014 until 2024 were included. TPE was defined as complete cystectomy combined with total or partial rectal resection. Result In total, 210 patients were operated with total pelvic excenteration and of those 23 patients underwent rTPE, the majority for pelvic malignancy and a minority due to chronic pelvic fistula. 84% were males. 32% of the patients were referred from another region. Patients in the rTPE group were older than in the oTPE group (median age 72 vs 68, P < 0.001) and had higher ASA score (III-IV 74% vs 47% P < 0.047). Operation time was similar (566 min vs 540 min, P = 0.88) but intraoperative bleeding was lower (550 ml vs 2085 ml, P < 0.001). The proportion of patients with postoperative serious adverse events was smaller in the rTPE-group (Clavien-Dindo > II: 17% vs 34%, P < 0.085). Lengt of stay was similar (11 vs 12 days). In the rTPE group R0 resection was achieved in all patients with colorectal malignancy (100%). One rTPE was converted to oTPE (4%). The proportion of rTPE increased over time (3% 2014-2020 vs 20% 2021-2024, P < 0.001). Discussion rTPE is associated with favorable short term outcomes in selected cases and has been increasingly performed over time.
affiliations: Department of Pelvic Cancer, Colorectal Surgery Unit, Karolinska University Hospital and Department of Molecular Medicine and Surgery, Karolinska Institutet , Stockholm ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf159.015.title: 3 Embedding surgical site infection surveillance data within a national clinical audit for hip fracture
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf159.015.abstract: Abstract Aims The Irish Hip Fracture Database (IHFD) is a national clinical audit established to measure care and outcomes of hip fracture patients since 2012. It is managed by the National Office of Clinical Audit and each year data is collected on almost 4000 patients. In 2022, the IHFD integrated surgical site infection surveillance (SSI) data into the audit. This was conducted in collaboration with the national Anti-Microbial Resistance Infection Control (AMRIC) in the Health Service Executive following publication of their strategy (HSE, 2021)1. In the UK surgical site surveillance is mandatory for many surgical procedures including surgery following a hip fracture since 2004. Embedding this surveillance data set is one of the first steps in achieving this in Ireland (PHE, 2022)3. Methods The dataset incorporates the required data fields as recommended by the European Centre for Disease Control (ECDC, 2017)2 and is benchmarked against other data collection tools used within Public Health England (PHE 2022)3 and Scottish/Northern Irish healthcare systems. AMRIC and the IHFD committee developed a dataset specific to the pathway of care around surgical wounds and SSI. In 2023, following a pilot study with three hospitals the dataset was activated for all hospitals. Questions added included antibiotic use, skin preparation, surgery length of time, wound closure and dressings applied. Data was inputted in the electronic portal used for data entry within the IHFD which captures data on patient’s demographics and journey through the acute hospital stay. Monthly training and education webinars were created and facilitated by the IHFD audit management team including user friendly infographics designed to ensure consistency in SSI diagnosis definitions. Results In May 2024 the first full year of data was received on 3983 patients. The overall incidence of SSI was <1%, the greatest impact from which was on length of stay (from 19 days to 34 days). Development of a national framework for capturing SSI using a standardised defined criteria was published and recommendations for the prevention of SSI are being updated currently. Challenges and facilitators across each site were discussed via monthly webinar. Analysis of the data was conducted using Excel, SPSS and Tableau. Completeness for additional variables ranges from 68 to 100%. Modifications to the dataset were reviewed using a Plan-Do- Act- Study (PDSA) cycle. Updates were presented to the AMRIC/IHFD steering committee and changes implemented within the dataset. Conclusions The use of a national clinical audit as a conduit for a national SSI surveillance programme is a very effective and efficient way of collecting data. Reducing duplication of effort within the Health Service for data collection and building on already established governance for hip fractures. Each participating hospitals have a clinical hip fracture governance committee which now include members of the infection and protection control team. The IHFD furnishes hospitals and AMRIC with quarterly SSI reports as routine outputs from the data and talks have begun about extending this work into other audits with surgical cohorts.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.490.title: eP587 Ceiling of Care and Escalation Pathway Decision Making in General Surgical Patients at JCUH – Loop Completion
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.490.abstract: Abstract Aim South Tees Trust resuscitation guidelines (on intranet) suggest that escalation plan for all the patients must be completed within 24 hours of the admission. Primary aim of this audit is to assess compliance to local trust guidelines in the general surgery department and the reaudit is to complete the loop after the recommendations from first cycle have been implemented. Inclusion – all patients admitted under the department of general surgery at James Cook University Hospital from the emergency department from 1 Jan 2025 to 22 Jan 2025. Methods Registered as an audit with the Clinical Audit team at JCHU with an id of 1835. Retrospective data collection from the colorectal and upper GI patient lists. A total of 100 patients included in the study. Variables collected include patient number, age, sex, date of admission, date of discharge, LOS, ceiling of care discussion and date, date of DNACPR, DNACPR in community, DNACPR in hospital. Intervention – email was sent to all the junior doctors and Consultants in general surgical department, highlighting the findings of first cycle and importance of ceiling of care documentation. Results All the patients placed on ward based level of care died in the hospital. 10 patients with community DNAR did not have documentation of the same in the clerking documents. Conclusion The adherence in 1st cycle was 6.18% and it has come down to 5% in second cycle. We plan to organise teaching session for all the general surgical junior doctors to adhere to the trust guidelines.
affiliations: James Cook University Hospital , Middlesbrough

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.011.title: SP1.05 Optimizing Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: A GIRFT-Based closed loop audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.011.abstract: Abstract Aim Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) is the gold standard management for symptomatic gallstone disease and is usually performed as a day case. A Getting it Right First Time (GIRFT) analysis at our institution highlighted a decline in the rate of day-case elective LC. This prompted an audit and subsequent quality improvement initiative. Methods We analysed patient data for elective LC between October 2023 and February 2024. Analysis identified areas for improvement, leading to the development of a business case and implementation of two interventions. First, the day surgery unit (DSU) recovery’s operational hours were extended to 9 PM. Second, the local anaesthetic (LA) protocol during LC was modified. In addition to port sites, LA was also infiltrated into the liver bed, thereby improving postoperative pain control and early mobilization. Following this, a re-audit was conducted between March and August 2024. Results Initial data from 86 elective LCs between October 2023 and February 2024 revealed a day-case rate of 64% (55/86), above the national median of 60%. The primary reasons for unplanned admissions were DSU closing at 6 PM, intraoperative concerns and post-operative pain. As per NHS national tariff 2024/25, the cost of unplanned admissions (median 1 day) was approximately £12,000. Our re-audit encompassing 101 elective LCs demonstrated an increase in our day-case rate to 73% (74/101). Conclusion This data suggests that extending DSU hours and optimizing LA techniques can positively impact day case rates. These findings have implications for resource utilization, reducing inpatient bed occupancy, associated costs and improved patient satisfaction through reduced hospital stays.
affiliations: Northampton General Hospital NHS Trust
University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.377.title: WTP6.04 Identifying Patients Undergoing Surgery for DCIS Suitable for Sentinel Node Biopsy – a Single Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.377.abstract: Abstract Aim Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast cancer precursor, confined to the ducts, with a very low risk of lymph node metastasis (<1%). The NICE guidelines recommend sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) for patients undergoing mastectomy for DCIS to detect occult invasive disease. For breast-conserving surgery (BCS), SLNB is considered in high-risk patients, such as those with extensive microcalcifications, a palpable mass, or mass-like lesions, due to the added morbidity and resource use of SLNB. Method Data were prospectively collected from patients undergoing BCS or mastectomy for DCIS at a single unit between 2017 and 2022. Parameters included pre-operative tumor size, histological grade, type of surgery, and postoperative tumor size and histology, with SLNB data recorded where applicable. Results Eighty-five patients underwent WLE and 17 mastectomy. Mean age was 62 years in both groups. Four high-risk BCS patients underwent upfront SLNB; one had microinvasion. Of the 81 BCS patients without upfront SLNB, three developed invasive disease and underwent SLNB as a second procedure. The odds ratio for upfront SLNB in high-risk patients was 8.66 (95% CI: 0.68–109.9, p=0.0956), indicating higher likelihood of invasive disease postoperatively, though not statistically significant, due to small sample size. Conclusions This audit supports selective SLNB for high-risk patients undergoing BCS. While the high-risk group was more likely to have invasive disease, the result was not statistically significant due to the small sample size. Further studies are needed to refine SLNB indications in DCIS.
affiliations: Wrightington, Wigan and Leigh NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.452.title: eP267 Audit of Cholecystostomy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.452.abstract: Abstract Aims Percutaneous gallbladder drainage (PGB) should be restricted to managing patients who are unfit or unable to undergo early cholecystectomy. We audited the indication for PGB in our Trust and the fate of patients who underwent PGB. Methods All patients who underwent PGB over a 13 month period were included. Data were collected on demographics, Charlson comorbidity index (CCI), CRP, NEWS and location in the hospital at the time of PGB request. Length of stay, hospital encounters, incidence of delayed cholecystectomy and any morbidity and mortality were recorded. Results 84 patients underwent PGB. The median age was 73. At the time of PGB request 55% of patients had a (CCI) of 0–4, a median NEWS of 2 and CRP of 272. 76% of patients were being managed on a regular surgical ward. Following drain insertion, 23% of patients experienced morbidities. Patients with PGB required a mean/ median of three extra visits. Delayed cholecystectomy was performed in 45% of patients. 66% of these were Nassar Grade IV difficult procedures. Mortality was observed in 9 patients. Conclusions A significant proportion of patients undergoing PGB satisfied the criteria for emergency cholecystectomy. Insertion of PGB has a considerable impact on patients and healthcare systems. Cholecystectomy following PGB is complex.
affiliations: Frimley Health Foundation NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.311.title: TTP8.03 Reaudit of Radiological Discrepancies in Emergency Laparotomies: A Comparison of Two Audit Cycles (Dec 2019–Dec 2020 vs. Jan 2021–Jan 2024)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.311.abstract: Abstract Aims/Objectives This reaudit aimed to assess changes in the frequency, classification, and factors contributing to discrepancies between radiological CT findings and operative findings in emergency laparotomies, comparing results from two audit cycles. Methods The initial audit (2019–2020) included 114 cases, while the reaudit (2021–2023) analyzed 328 cases. Both audits evaluated discrepancies (major, minor, nil), and examined factors such as age, gender, reporting type, and timeliness. Statistical analyses, including chi-square tests and p-values, were used to identify trends. Results The initial audit found a discrepancy rate of 27.2%, with 11.4% classified as major. Reporting delays were noted, with only 23% completed within 24 hours. Recommendations focused on improving pre-operative communication and radiologist expertise. The reaudit showed a reduced discrepancy rate of 5.8%, with 21.1% major and 73.7% minor discrepancies. Age, gender, and reporting type showed no significant associations (p > 0.05). Discrepancies were often linked to complex conditions, while common findings like adhesional small bowel obstruction (14.9%) and gastric perforation (5.2%) demonstrated strong radiological accuracy. Conclusion The reaudit demonstrated a significant reduction in discrepancies, reflecting improvements in radiological accuracy and processes. Efforts should focus on refining workflows, enhancing diagnostic accuracy for complex cases, and ensuring timely reporting to maintain high standards and improve outcomes.
affiliations: Department of General & GI Surgery, George Elliot NHS Trust Hospital , Nuneaton
Department of Radiology, George Elliot NHS Trust Hospital , Nuneaton
Department of General & GI Surgery, George Elliot NHS Hospital , Nuneaton

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.307.title: TTP7.14 Audit of Management of Testicular Torsion in a Rural General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.307.abstract: Abstract Aims Patients who present with suspected testicular torsion to our hospital are managed by the on-all general surgeons because of long travel time to the nearest hospital where urology service is provided. Currently there is no established guidelines/protocol locally or in the Health Board regarding management of this condition. The aim of this audit is to review the management of all patients who presented to our hospital with suspected “Testicular Torsion” over the last 5 years and compare it against the available national & international guidelines aiming to develop a local protocol. Methods A retrospective study included all the patients who underwent scrotal exploration for suspected testicular torsion in our hospital between January 2019 and January 2024. Patient were identified from emergency theatre surgical register and Information Technology department. Data were collected from the patients’ notes, Welsh Clinical Portal and Welsh Patient Administration System. Results 34 patients had exploration of the scrotum for suspected torsion during this period. 13 patients were found to have torsion testicle, the testicle was found to be non-viable in 4 out of them. 3 patients with testicular torsion with non-viable testicle on exploration presented very late after onset of symptoms (1-3 days). Conclusions Management of these cases is done in a timely manner however a local protocol is being developed includes direct referral to the on-call surgical registrar to further decrease time to theatre. It includes TWIST score to guide diagnosis. Raising awareness of children and their carers/parents is of paramount importance.
affiliations: Bronglais General Hospital , Aberystwyth, Wales

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.036.title: SP3.02 Unnecessary Preoperative Blood Tests for Patients Undergoing Abscess Incision and Drainage: A Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.036.abstract: Abstract Background + Aims According to NICE, ASA grade 1 or 2 patients should not receive preoperative blood tests for abscess incision and drainage (I&D). This audit investigated the incidence of preoperative blood tests for low-risk abscess I&D at our centre and evaluated the financial implications. Methods Data was collected retrospectively over a 4-month period (December 2023 – April 2024). Information about type of abscess drainage, ASA grade, and preoperative blood tests was recorded. The findings were disseminated to the department, and posters were hung advising not to take bloods for routine abscess I&D. The same data was collected over another 4-month period (May 2024 – September 2024). Results In the initial study period, 71 cases of abscess I&D were recorded; 55 cases were ASA 1 or 2. Of the ASA 1 and 2 cases, 50 cases (91%) had routine bloods done. These tests amounted to £2,151 spent. In the re-audited period following intervention, 63 cases of abscess I&D were recorded; 55 cases were ASA 1 or 2. Of the ASA 1 and 2 cases, 15 cases (27%) had routine bloods done. These tests amounted to £406 spent during the follow-up period. Conclusions In our General Surgery department, educating staff that ASA 1 and 2 patients do not require pre-operative blood test for abscess I&D led to a reduction of patients receiving blood tests from 91% to 27%. This intervention saved the department £1745 during the 4-month period and will save the department more than £5,000 per year.
affiliations: Victoria Hospital Kirkaldy

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.231.title: TTP1.11 An outcome of reassessment of 2740 colorectal (CRC) cancer referrals with initial qFIT<7ugHb/g, a retrospective audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.231.abstract: Abstract Colorectal cancer is one of the most common cancers in the UK. qFIT (faecal immunochemical test) was proposed as an adjunct test to prioritize urgent cancer suspected referrals (UCS). qFIT has a high negative predictive value (NPV) for significant bowel disease. A threshold of FIT <10μg Hb/g is selected for discharge to primary care without clinical assessment in most Trusts. The purpose: To determine the outcome of re-assessment of symptomatic patients with initial qFIT <7ugHb/g. Method: A survey of a prospective collected dataset on colorectal UCS referrals over 3 years was completed, (Jan2021-Dec 2023). The outcome of investigations for qFit<7ugHb/g subgroup was analysed. The focus here was on cohort of qFit<7ugHb/g who were not initially assessed and recalled after a mean period of 6 months. All patients offered a consultant phone assessment. Results: After Initial clinical phone assessment 29% underwent colonoscopy. Only 0.14% of this cohort was found to have invasive cancer (n=4).. 71% were not investigated and reassured. After a mean period of 6 months, a cohort of 225 of patients with no initial clinical assessment were re- invited. 24 patients failed to respond. 47% had a second qFIT <7ugHb/g and discharged. 49% discharged without any further investigation. 5 patients underwent colonoscopy which were normal. No cancer found on this reassessment. Conclusion: This study reaffirms reliability of qFIT <7 in excluding significant pathology even after reassessment within 6 months.
affiliations: NHS Ayrshire & Arran

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.483.title: eP514 General Surgical Inpatient Falls: An Audit of Current Practices
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.483.abstract: Abstract Aims As the surgical population is becoming older and frailer, the risk of inpatient falls is increasing. This audit aimed to assess how well we were complying with preventing and managing falls on the general surgical patients over 64 years per Royal College of Physician national guidance. Method We conducted an audit from 25/11/23 - 25/12/23 of all inpatient falls. Demographic and admission data were captured, along with falls risk assessments when completed. Further data included circumstances of the fall, the extent of harm, use of falls proforma and further medical review. Data was collected and analysed from physical and electronic notes, using Microsoft Excel. Results 14 patients had an inpatient fall of whom two had multiple falls. Median age was 80 (range 59-91) with male:female ratio 10:4 All patients were assessed for risk of falls within 24 hours of admission. None of the falls were unwitnessed. All falls were reviewed, however in only 10 cases (71%) was local protocol fully followed. 57% (8/14) were further investigated (radiology/bloods). One patient came to moderate harm. One patient who was admitted with a fall and further fell, died. Conclusions All patients were adequately assessed for risk of falls, but these still occurred, resulting in use of additional resources. Use of the standard proforma for assessing these patients is not routinely used. Raising awareness of falls risk and management is desirable.
affiliations: General Surgery, Doncaster and Bassetlaw Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Doncaster
Division of Clinical Medicine, School of Medicine and Population Health, University of Sheffield , Sheffield

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.343.title: WTP3.03 Enhancing Laparoscopic Appendicectomy documentation: A GIRFT & ASGBI based closed loop audit and quality improvement initiative
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.343.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate and comprehensive operative notes are essential for effective clinical communication and serve as valuable documentation for reviewing surgical procedures. This audit evaluates the quality of laparoscopic appendicectomy (LA) operation notes at our hospital against the best practice guidelines set by Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT), Royal College of Surgeons England (RCS), and the Association of Surgeons of Great Britain and Ireland (ASGBI). Methods A retrospective review of LA notes (n=29) between June and July 2024 was conducted. Following this, areas for improvement were identified, leading to the development of a standardised proforma and an educational poster to enhance documentation practices. This first cycle was presented at our departmental meeting. Copies of the educational poster and standardised proforma were displayed in the surgeons’ room. A second data collection cycle was undertaken between October and November 2024 (n=27) to determine the impact of these interventions. Results Out of the 31 measured variables recommended to be included in operation notes we found that 19 variables were included in less than 70% of notes in the first cycle. After our interventions, there were overall improvements in documentation across 26 out of 31 (89.7%) measurable variables. Moreover only 7 variables had an inclusion rate of less than 70%. While most domains showed progress, minor gaps remained in documenting appendix location and arterial division methods. Conclusion This audit highlights the effectiveness of the newly implemented proforma and poster in achieving better adherence to the guidelines. Accurate documentation is essential for good clinical practice and patient care.
affiliations: Northampton General Hospital NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.285.title: TTP5.12 A Trust-Wide Audit Evaluating Gallbladder and Biliary Tree Ultrasound Reporting and Compliance with The Royal College of Radiologists Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.285.abstract: Abstract Background Gallbladder and biliary tree ultrasound is the gold-standard imaging modality for diagnosing gallbladder pathology. Adherence to the Royal College of Radiologists' (RCR) standards ensures an accurate and consistent reporting system. Aim To assess adherence to the Royal College of Radiologists' gallbladder and biliary tree ultrasound standards, including gallbladder neck, bile echogenicity, wall thickness, common bile duct (CBD) assessment, and CBD lumen measurement. Method The first cycle involved a retrospective review of the ultrasound scans of 70 patients at Princess of Wales Hospital (POWH) and Neath Port Talbot Hospital (NPTH). The results were presented in the joint audit meeting. We implemented several interventions, including introducing a new local reporting protocol, educational posters, and teaching sessions on gallbladder US reporting. In the second cycle, prospective data of 45 patients at POWH and NPTH was reviewed and presented. Results In the first cycle, adherence was as follows:Gallbladder neck assessed: (7.1%)Echogenicity of bile reported: (17.1%)Wall thickness commented on: (55.7%)CBD assessed: (84.3%)CBD lumen measured: (45.7%) In the second cycle (45 patients), adherence improved:Gallbladder neck assessed: (77.8%)Echogenicity of bile reported: (33.3%)Wall thickness commented on: (75.6%)CBD assessed: (97.8%)CBD lumen measured: (44.4%) Conclusion The audit showed a remarkable improvement in adherence to RCR reporting standards for Gallbladder and biliary tree US, particularly in gallbladder neck assessment and CBD evaluation. However, further improvement is needed in documenting bile echogenicity and CBD lumen measurement. Continued monitoring and staff education are essential for sustainable improvement.
affiliations: Esophagogastric Surgery Unit, Leicester Royal Infirmary Hospital, University Hospitals of Leicester
Colorectal Surgery Unit, Chelsea and Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , London
General Surgery Department, Princess of Wales Hospital , Bridgend

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.132.title: MTP1.14 Optimising Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: An Audit of Success Rates and Influencing Factors
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.132.abstract: Abstract Background Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is a common procedure for gallstone disease, with national targets recommending a 75% day-case completion rate to improve patient care and optimize healthcare resources. This audit evaluates factors influencing day-case success at Ealing Hospital to identify opportunities for improvement. Methodology A retrospective analysis was conducted on 71 elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies performed between January and July 2024. Data, including patient demographics, surgical duration, recovery times, intraoperative findings, and surgery start and end times, were analyzed to identify predictors of day-case success. Emergency cases and incomplete records were excluded. Results Of the 71 cases, 64 (90.1%) were booked as day cases, with a success rate of 74.4%. Age was a significant predictor, with patients under 60 achieving higher success rates (82.4%) compared to those aged 60–79 (55.6%) and over 80 (33.3%) (p=0.002). Surgical duration strongly influenced success, with operations lasting ≤120 minutes significantly more likely to succeed (OR 2.1, p=0.015). Although early morning surgeries achieved slightly better outcomes (76.9%), start and end times were not statistically significant predictors. Intraoperative findings such as normal anatomy correlated with higher success rates (72.4%), while adhesions (60%) and large gallbladders (33.3%, p=0.048) reduced success. Drain placement, comorbidities, and postoperative pain were common reasons for overnight stays, with only 37% of failures anticipated preoperatively. Conclusion Achieving a day-case success rate of 74.4% aligns closely with national targets. Younger age, shorter surgical duration, and straightforward anatomy were key predictors of success. Enhanced patient selection and surgical efficiency can further optimize outcomes.
affiliations: Ealing Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.417.title: eP73 “Why Radiology Requests are not Being Accepted”, a quality improvement audit in a surgical department
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.417.abstract: Abstract Aim Radiology requests serve as the primary communication tool between clinical physicians and radiologists, enabling radiologists to provide accurate diagnostic support. This audit aimed to evaluate the radiology request acceptance rate, identify common reasons for request rejections, and implement measures to improve request quality. Method According to the Royal College of Radiologists, radiology requests should include comprehensive and relevant information, although specific content requirements are not defined. The audit was conducted in two cycles: the first in September-October 2023 and the second in August 2024. Patients were randomly selected from clinical handover records and SACU clinic logs. Radiology requests on the TrakCare system were reviewed to determine their acceptance status, assess the quality of information provided, and identify reasons for requests being placed on hold. Results During the first audit cycle, 73% (52/71) of radiology requests were accepted. The primary reasons for rejections included inappropriate imaging (21%, 4/19), duplicate requests (21%, 4/19), and insufficient clinical details (21%, 4/19). Following these findings, a structured request format was developed, and staff were educated on its use. In the second audit cycle, the acceptance rate improved significantly to 89% (89/101). Conclusions A high-quality radiology request should include a concise patient background, current symptoms, examination and investigation findings, relevant differential diagnoses, and the clinical situation. Radiology requests should be presented as well-informed proposals rather than directives. Implementing a structured request format can enhance communication, optimize resource utilization, and expedite patient care planning for improved outcomes.
affiliations: NHS Lanarkshire

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.416.title: eP60 Management of splenic trauma at Aintree University Hospital: an audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.416.abstract: Abstract Introduction Damage of the spleen can result in haemorrhage and life-threatening haemodynamic instability. This study aimed to evaluate the management of traumatic splenic injury at a major trauma centre against current international guidelines, and identify areas of good practice and areas for improvement. Methods Data was obtained from an existing data set of trauma patients presenting between 2018-2022. Patients with splenic injury confirmed on CT scan were included. Electronic and scanned notes were reviewed for data collection, and results were analysed. Standards included:80% of patients received CT/FAST scan100% of patients receiving correct grading of their splenic injury according to American Association for Surgery of Trauma (AAST) guidelines.100% of patients received correct treatment based upon the World Society of Emergency Surgery guidelines. Results All patients underwent CT scan (n=115). 73% received AAST grading, of whom 93% were graded correctly. 64% had non operative management in the form of conservative management and/or interventional radiological embolization. 37% underwent operative management. 5% failed conservative management and required surgery. 37% were managed according to WSES guidelines. Management was undetermined in 27% due to lack of AAST grading. Patients with WSES III and IV had a lower adherence to management (40% and 43% respectively) versus WSES I and II. Conclusion This audit highlights the variability in current guideline adherence and applicability for the management of splenic trauma. Intervention, education, and re-audit are required to improve patient outcomes.
affiliations: Aintree University Hospital , Liverpool

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.208.title: MTP7.17 An audit project on the completion of treatment escalation plan (TEP) for surgical patients for decisions about the ceiling of care in a tertiary care major NHS trauma
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.208.abstract: Abstract Aims The objective of this project is to evaluate the number of acute and elective surgical patients with variable frailty (Rockwood) score admitted on the surgical floor with or without documented ceiling of care in the form of a treatment escalation plan (TEP) form. Methods A closed loop audit was performed after getting approval from the local R & D department. Data was collected from the patient case notes. The results of the first loop of the audit project were discussed in the departmental clinical governance meeting in the presence of the frailty consultant. After getting recommendations, data for the second loop of the project was collected. Results The case notes of seventy-eight consecutive acute and elective surgical admissions were reviewed in the first loop of the audit. The first loop of the audit cycle yielded only 58 % (45/78) of surgical patients who had a documented ceiling of care in the form of a completed TEP form. After the implementation of the recommendations and regular reviews of patients with variable frailty scores by the frailty consultant, the documentation and decisions about the ceiling of care improved to 83 % (65 patients out of a total of 78 patients recruited in the second loop of the audit). Conclusion Decisions about the ceiling of care in the form of completed TEP proforma in surgical admissions provide greater autonomy to the patients, relatives, and help the surgical doctors to determine the ceiling of care, especially out of hours. Current audit project demonstrates improved compliance in the second cycle.
affiliations: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust General Surgery ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.338.title: WTP2.12 An Audit of anastomotic leak rate and mortality after abdominal surgery in a specialised Surgical Emergency Unit at John Radcliffe Hospital, Oxford
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.338.abstract: Abstract Aims Expected anastomotic leak rates in the context of general surgery vary depending on type of anastomosis, but generally range from 0.5-18% [1]. This audit aimed to assess anastomotic leak rate after abdominal surgery from an entirely emergency population in a specialised Surgical Unit at John Radcliffe Hospital, Oxford. Methods Anastomotic leak rates were audited based on M&M data and patient records between 25/03/2024-02/01/2025. Data including patient demographics, type of join, length of stay, rate of leak/ return to theatre, and mortality were collected. The rate of stoma formation vs anastomosis was not assessed in this audit. Results Overall 78 cases (M=33, F=45) were analysed. Median age of patients was 67.5 years, mean ASA was 2. Leak and return to theatre rates were both determined to be 4% (n=3). Of the three recorded anastomotic leak cases, two were small bowel anastomoses, and one was ileocolic anastomosis. Mortality rate was 4% (n=3); one patient passed away due to other co-morbidities unrelated to the operation. Median length of stay was 10 days. Conclusions It is possible to have an acceptable rate of anastomotic leak in an emergency setting. To further this, it may be beneficial to audit the rates of stoma formation vs anastomosis in managing surgical emergency cases. References 1. Ellis, C.T. and J.A. Maykel, Defining Anastomotic Leak and the Clinical Relevance of Leaks. Clin Colon Rectal Surg, 2021. 34(6): p. 359-365.
affiliations: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.039.title: SP3.05 Improving Fluid Resuscitation and Maintenance Prescription Practices in Surgical Admissions: Closed loops double audits
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.039.abstract: Abstract Background Intravenous fluid plays a vital role in perioperative care. Despite this, adherence to the British Consensus Guidelines on Intravenous Fluid Therapy for Adult Surgical Patients remains suboptimal. This quality improvement initiative aimed to evaluate and enhance fluid prescription practices for surgical admissions, addressing gaps in compliance. Methods Data were collected retrospectively from CERNER for both audits' cycles. The first audit cycles covered the period from April to May 2024, with resuscitation data set including 59 patients and maintenance dataset listing 53 patients. The second cycle, a re-audit, was conducted from 26 September to 1 November 2024, with resuscitation dataset including 53 patients and maintenance dataset listing 24 patients. Results Initial findings revealed only 43% of patients received optimal fluid resuscitation, with 36% receiving no fluids and 34% prescribed non-optimal fluid types. For maintenance fluids, 74% of patients were prescribed fluids, with only 66% meeting daily sodium requirements and 47% meeting free fluid requirements. Following targeted interventions, significant improvements were observed in the re-audit. Optimal fluid resuscitation increased to 83%, with non-optimal prescriptions decreasing to 17%. Fluid prescription rates improved from 64% to 94%. For maintenance fluids, prescription rates increased to 91.7%, sodium requirements to 91.7%, and free fluid targets to 75%. Additionally, the use of appropriate fluid types improved from 36% to 45.5%. Conclusions Educational interventions proved effective in improving adherence to GIFTASUP guidelines for fluid resuscitation and maintenance in surgical admissions. Sustained improvements require ongoing training for junior doctors and routine monitoring to ensure high standards of perioperative care.
affiliations: Ealing Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.304.title: TTP7.10 Compliance with NCEPOD Guidelines in the Management of Acute Pancreatitis - A Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.304.abstract: Abstract Aim The management of acute pancreatitis requires prompt identification and treatment of the underlying cause. Early antibiotics are not recommended initially, as organ dysfunction is not primarily due to bacterial infection. For gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy should ideally occur during the initial hospitalization once symptoms improve. This audit aimed to assess management practices against NCEPOD recommendations to influence future practice. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of acute pancreatitis cases diagnosed biochemically or through imaging from June to October 2023, presenting results at a local meeting. We recommended increasing “hot chole” slots and establishing dedicated waiting lists for gallstone pancreatitis. We re-evaluated these changes from June to October 2024. Results 64 patients were audited in the first cycle, compared to 66 in the second. Gallstone pancreatitis was diagnosed in 33 (51%) and 32 (48%) patients, respectively. MRCP and/ or EUS usage for unclear aetiology rose from 37% to 48%, while inappropriate antibiotic prophylaxis decreased from 42% to 28%. Previous admissions for gallstones decreased from 12 (36%) to 5 (16%). Early cholecystectomy rates improved from 18% to 31%. Conclusions There was a reduction in antibiotic prophylaxis and an increase in MRCP and/ or EUS usage for unclear aetiology. Additional “hot chole” slots and dedicated waiting lists improved early cholecystectomy rates and reduced repeat admissions with gallstone flare-ups.
affiliations: Great Western Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.317.title: TTP8.11 Audit of Compliance, Documentation, and Score validity in Emergency Laparotomy Care: An overview of NELA scoring
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.317.abstract: Abstract Background This audit evaluated compliance with (NELA) standards, analyzed mortality outcomes, and examined the predictive utility of NELA scores. Emphasis was placed on preoperative risk assessment, documentation practices, and identifying gaps in care for emergency laparotomy patients. Methods A total of 57 cases were reviewed, collecting data on patient demographics, NELA mortality scores, and documentation of preoperative and postoperative management. Multidisciplinary team input and mortality risk communication were analyzed. The sensitivity and specificity of NELA scores for predicting mortality were assessed using a 10% threshold. Results Significant gaps in documentation practices were observed. Although NELA scores were preoperatively calculated in 94.7% of cases, mortality risk discussions were documented in only 17.86% of consent forms, suggesting limited communication of risks to patients or their next of kins. Elderly care team involvement was documented for just 12.5% of older patients (≥60 years). Critical care input was noted in 66.07% of cases, leaving a third without evidence of multidisciplinary collaboration. The NELA score demonstrated limited sensitivity (33.33%) for predicting mortality. While specificity was higher (84.31%), two-thirds of deceased patients were classified as low risk, raising concerns about the score’s reliability in identifying patients at risk of mortality. The overall mortality rate was 5.26%, with deceased patients being older (mean age 72.7 years). Conclusion The audit highlights substantial gaps in documentation, particularly in communicating mortality risks and involving elderly care teams. The limited sensitivity of NELA scores suggests the need for supplementary tools to improve risk prediction and care planning for emergency laparotomy patients.
affiliations: Ealing Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.059.title: SP4.13 Use of MRCP in the Management of Patients with Symptomatic Gallstones and Low-to-Moderate Risk of CBD Stones: A Retrospective Audit guided by The SUNFLOWER Study Protocol
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.059.abstract: Abstract Aims To evaluate the role of preoperative MRCP in detecting choledocholithiasis in patients with symptomatic gallstones and compare its utility against expectant management Methods A 12-month retrospective review (January–December 2024) was conducted, focusing on patients at low-to-moderate risk of CBD stones. Exclusion criteria included known CBD stones, CBD diameter ≥7mm, bilirubin ≥50 µmol/L, or ALT/ALP >3× normal. MRCP findings, ERCP interventions, and postoperative outcomes were analysed. Results Of one hundred and seventy-two patients undergoing MRCP, seventy-two met low-to-moderate risk criteria. Mean admission values were: total bilirubin 24.2 µmol/L [5–49 µmol/L], ALT 218.4 U/L [12–1237 U/L], and ALP 129.2 U/L [34–378 U/L]. MRCP identified CBD dilation [mean 8.2mm] in twenty patients, with five showing CBD stones. Three underwent ERCP within 1–7 days, while two had repeat imaging [MRCP/EUS] showing no stones. All underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1–54 days post-admission. Postoperative complications included one retained CBD stone requiring ERCP and one gallbladder collection. Discussion MRCP identified choledocholithiasis in 6.9% of low-to-moderate-risk patients, but false positives led to unnecessary investigations. Given the low rate of retained stones, expectant management may be a viable alternative to routine MRCP. Further investigation would involve investigating the outcomes of expectant management for comparative analysis; from which cost-benefit analysis can be conducted with the aims of standardising imaging practises within the department.
affiliations: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Trust Surgical Emergency Unit ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.058.title: SP4.12 An Audit of the investigations of suspected ureteric/kidney calculus in adults in Great Western Hospital, Swindon
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.058.abstract: Abstract Aim Renal or ureteric colic secondary to urinary stones is common, with an annual incidence of 1–2 cases per 1000 people. It also has a high recurrence rate ranging from 50% to 80%. Most of these patients presenting to the A&E are initially managed by the general surgery on-call juniors and then subsequently referred to urology. NICE guidelines (NG118) recommend urgent low-dose non-contrast CT of the urinary tract for adults with suspected renal colic and ultrasound scans instead of CT if a woman is pregnant. It also recommends measuring serum calcium for adults as a part of the metabolic assessment. The audit aimed to evaluate the local practice compared to the NICE guidelines. Methods A retrospective review of 101 non-pregnant adult patients presenting to the A&E or surgical assessment unit with suspected renal or ureteric colic was conducted (58 patients for cycle 1, 43 patients for cycle 2). Patients were consecutively recruited from the general surgery on-call list (Cycle 1: March-May 2024) (Cycle 2: October - December 2024). Verbal demonstration, email reminders, and added notes to the handover sheet were completed before the completion of cycle 2. Results 100% of CT of urinary tract was performed within 24 hours of presentation in both cycles. Serum calcium was measured in 21% and 72% of patients in Cycle 1 and 2, respectively. Conclusion All patients had a CT of urinary tract performed within the timeframe recommended by NICE Guidelines. There has been a significant improvement in the measurements for calcium.
affiliations: Great Western Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.458.title: eP294 A Retrospective Audit: Evaluating the Management of Acute Pancreatitis at the Surgical Emergency Unit of a Tertiary Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.458.abstract: Abstract Aims To evaluate severity scoring, underlying causes, and management pathways in patients presenting to the Surgical Emergency Unit at a tertiary centre with acute pancreatitis. Methods Retrospective analysis of patient records over two months (September–October 2024). Data collected included demographics, aetiology, severity scoring, management and outcomes. Key metrics were admission duration, rate of operative interventions, time to surgery [TTS], and complications. Results Eighty-one patients were analysed. Formal scoring using the Glasgow-Imrie system was completed in 9 patients, with a median of 2 [range: 0-3]. Gallstones [33 cases] and alcohol excess [18 cases] were the primary aetiologies. Seventy patients were admitted, with an average length of stay of 5.73 days. Three patients developed serious complications requiring ITU admission [admission NEWS Score: 3-10], with one patient suffering cardiac arrest and multi-system organ failure, resulting in death on the day of admission. Six patients were managed via an ambulatory pathway for further investigation [MRCP/US/EUS] which confirmed 4 cases of gallstone pancreatitis. Twenty-one patients with gallstone pancreatitis underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy; 14 during index admission [TTS: 6.5 days, range: 1–18 days], with average length of stay as 8.5 days. One case was following ambulatory investigation [TTS: 31 days]. Five cases were discharged for elective day-case surgery [TTS: 9-11 days]. Conclusion Severity scoring was underutilised, limiting risk stratification and care planning. Management pathways, including timely surgical intervention within 6 weeks and ambulatory care were effective, with most patients discharged without complications. Serious cases were escalated appropriately, reflecting robust acute care management.
affiliations: Surgical Emergency Unit, Oxford University Hospitals NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.069.title: SP5.11 Reducing Female Misidentification: A Closed-loop Audit of Low Resource Interventions on FY1 Doctors in General Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.069.abstract: Abstract Aims We sought to quantify the issue of misidentification of female F1s as non-doctor roles within their general surgical rotation during the 2023-2024 year. We aimed to use this feedback to measure the effect of crowdsourced low resource interventions by re-audit. Method A survey was emailed to rotating female F1s on General Surgery to quantify those experiencing misidentification of their role by patients, and to crowdsource solutions. We implemented two interventions. Firstly, we centralised the application process so all new FY1s had “Hello my name is …” ID badges with “Dr. lastname” on them. Secondly, we encouraged senior staff to introduce FY1s as doctors during the ward round. We then surveyed the next group of female FY1s to assess the uptake and impact. Results In both cycles, we had a 100% response rate. 84% of the pre-intervention group reported being misidentified by patients. Everyone in the post-intervention group had received name badges with “Dr *lastname*” on them yet 86% reported having their role misidentified. 72% reported that role introduction by seniors was done regularly. Despite this, 100% of responders subjectively felt the name badges reduced misidentification. In both cohorts, there were 15% who never experienced role misidentification. Conclusions Name badges and role introduction by seniors did not reduce the absolute percentage of female F1s experiencing role misidentification on their surgical rotation. However, the qualitative feedback indicates that the badges helped in at least some instances.
affiliations: Royal United Hospital Bath

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.441.title: eP185 A case report and literature review of Ischaemic Meckel’s Diverticulum, Mesodiverticular Band, and Small Bowel Volvulus with Closed Loop Obstruction
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.441.abstract: Abstract Aims Meckel’s diverticulum (MD), the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, can present with rare but severe complications like obstruction and ischemia. This report aims to highlight the importance of early laparoscopic intervention in cases of small bowel obstruction (SBO) due to MD and associated mesodiverticular band (MDB). Methods A 12-year-old male presented with acute abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Clinical evaluation indicated acute appendicitis, prompting emergency diagnostic laparoscopy. Intraoperatively, an ischemic MD with an MDB causing a closed-loop SBO was identified. The MDB was divided, the small bowel untwisted, and the MD excised laparoscopically. A literature review of 16 reported cases of MDB-related SBO from the past five years was conducted for comparative analysis. Results The patient’s postoperative recovery was uneventful, with discharge on day four. Histology confirmed infarcted MD without malignancy. Compared to reviewed cases, this case had the shortest time from admission to surgery (4 hours) and no ischemic bowel or resection required. Laparoscopic management was associated with reduced postoperative stay (average 4 days) and no complications, contrasting with higher ischemia rates and longer stays in laparotomy cases. Conclusion MDB-related SBO is rare but requires urgent surgical intervention to prevent ischemia. This case underscores the diagnostic and therapeutic advantages of laparoscopy, enabling minimally invasive management with shorter recovery times and favorable outcomes compared to laparotomy. Prompt diagnosis and early surgical intervention are critical for optimal patient outcomes.
affiliations: Isle of Wight NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.266.title: TTP4.03 MRCP use in gallstone pancreatitis audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.266.abstract: Abstract Introduction The use of magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) scanning to identify common bile duct (CBD) stones in those presenting with gallstone pancreatitis is controversial. The guidance is not agreed for those with mild/moderate risk of CBD stones. This leads to significant differences in the management of this phenomenon. The aim of this two-cycle audit is to quantify consultant attitude toward MRCP scans for patients admitted with gallstone pancreatitis. Method During the year of 2022, all patients admitted with clinical and biochemical gallstone pancreatitis to a surgical unit were included. Data pertaining to MRCP scan use was assessed. An assessment of change to acute management as a result of this scan was made. This data was shared with all surgical consultants at a local meeting and then the same data parameters were measured over the following 6 months. Results The first cycle highlights that 87% of patients received an MRCP scan. 86% of scans showed no radiological evidence of CBD stone. 24% of patients had an acute surgical procedure. The second cycle shows that 59% of patients were offered an MRCP scan, 82% showed no CBD stone and 25% of patients received an emergency procedure. Conclusion A similar proportion of patients receive an emergency procedure upon their index admission for gallstone pancreatitis, despite a 28% drop in MRCP scan use following departmental education. The use of MRCP does not acutely change management in the majority of cases.
affiliations: South Tyneside and Sunderland Hospital Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.336.title: WTP2.10 Appendicitis Patient Pathway at an East Midlands Hospital - a closed loop audit
