DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.336.abstract: Abstract Background GIRFT data shows only 12.4% of patients in Leicester, Leicestershire, and Rutland (LLR) achieve the target 2-day length of stay (LOS) and place the region in the highest quartile for average LOS. An initial audit in 2023 found just 4.4% of patients met the target LOS. Since then, theatre and imaging capacities have increased. Aims This study aimed to evaluate overall LOS and time intervals between admission, imaging, operation, and discharge. Secondary aims included assessing digital consent adoption following its departmental implementation in 2022. Methods Data from 91 adult patients undergoing laparoscopic appendicectomy between 04/01/2023 and 04/03/2023 were analysed. Paediatric cases were excluded. Times for admission, imaging, operation, and discharge were retrieved from ICE, ORMIS, and Concentric Health. Data were analyzed using Excel, with weekday and weekend admissions compared via independent samples median tests. Results Mean times were: presentation to imaging (8.91 hours), imaging to operation (26.82 hours), operation to discharge (53.94 hours), and total LOS (3.74 days). LOS improved to 3.7 days (from 4.3), with 14.3% meeting the 2-day target. Imaging-to-operation time decreased significantly (29.15 vs. 26.82 hours, p=0.003). Weekend admissions had significantly shorter imaging-to-operation times (36.23 vs. 21.91 hours, p<0.01). Digital consent adoption increased to 98% from 78% last year. Conclusions LOS and time intervals have improved with enhanced imaging and weekend capacity, alongside increased digital consent uptake. However, LLR remains in the highest GIRFT quartile, necessitating further optimisation.
affiliations: Russells Hall Hospital
University of Leicester
UHL

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.055.title: SP4.09 A follow up audit of negative appendicectomy rates in a single site acute hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.055.abstract: Abstract Aims The negative appendicectomy rate (NAR) in the UK is estimated to be 20%. Negative appendicectomies (NA) carry an unnecessary risk to patients and a financial burden on the healthcare system. This study evaluated clinical practices at a single site acute hospital to identify ways to reduce NAR and compared outcomes to a study performed in the same hospital (2019), in which preoperative imaging was 69% and the NAR was 10.3%. Methods Data from appendicectomy/diagnostic laparoscopy cases for appendicitis (June–December 2024) were analysed retrospectively. Variables assessed included inflammatory markers (WCC, CRP), NEWS scores, length of stay (LOS), imaging, intraoperative findings, and histopathology. Results 100 patients underwent appendicectomies/diagnostic laparoscopy, (56% male, mean age of 38±16 years). 86 were admitted after initial assessment, while 14 had planned returns. Same-day appendectomy occurred in 37 cases. Mean LOS was 2.8±2.38 days. On admission, 22% had normal WCC(<10x109/I), 22% normal CRP(<10mg/L), and 4% both normal. 47% of patients had an initial NEWS score of 0. Preoperative imaging was performed in 88%, mostly CT (n=83), with appendicitis reported in 96% (17 complicated vs 63 uncomplicated). Imaging and intraoperative findings regarding nature of appendicitis correlated in 76%. Of available histopathology (n=84) 98% confirmed appendicitis, with an institutional NAR of 3% (all male). Conclusions Increased cross-sectional imaging has reduced our NAR, highlighting the importance of surgeon-radiologist collaboration. Appendicitis should not be excluded based on normal inflammatory markers alone. The study recommends CT imaging as an effective strategy to reduce NAR.
affiliations: Royal Alexandria Hospital , Paisley

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.054.title: SP4.08 Enhancing Pediatric Appendicitis Care in Alignment with GIRFT Guidelines: A Two-Cycle Audit at a District Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.054.abstract: Abstract Aims The audit aimed to evaluate the management of pediatric appendicitis at a District Hospital against GIRFT (Getting It Right The First Time, June 2022) guidelines. It sought to identify areas for improvement in diagnostic pathways, surgical timing, and antibiotic protocols across two audit cycles. Methods A retrospective review was conducted over two cycles: the first from May to October 2022 (27 patients) and the second from January to December 2023 (48 patients). Data included demographics, time to surgery, pre- and post-operative antibiotic use, histological outcomes, and complications. Results In the first cycle, the negative appendicectomy rate was 22%, and the median time to surgery was 23 hours. Antibiotics were inconsistently prescribed pre-operatively (81%) and post-operatively, with limited adherence to best practice. The complication rate was 18%. By the second cycle, interventions had reduced the negative appendicectomy rate to 4%, aligning below the national average of 10%. The median time to surgery improved to 19.25 hours, with 85% of patients receiving pre-operative antibiotics. However, unnecessary post-operative antibiotics were given in 35% of simple cases, and only 86% of complex cases met the 48-hour guideline. Complication rates fell to 6%. Conclusions The second cycle demonstrated significant improvements in negative appendicectomy rates, time to surgery, and complication rates, reflecting enhanced adherence to GIRFT guidelines. However, variability in antibiotic prescribing persists, necessitating protocol standardization. Continued focus on diagnostic tools, such as clinical scoring and imaging, and consistent antibiotic stewardship are crucial for sustaining and furthering these improvements.
affiliations: Yeovil District Hospital, Somerset Foundation Trust
Royal United Hospital
Musgrove Park Hospital, Somerset Foundation Trust
Severn Deanery
University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust
Bristol Children's Hospital
Walsall Manor Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.280.title: TTP5.05 Improving diagnostic endoscopy pathways: an audit of inpatient referrals and outcomes
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.280.abstract: Abstract Aims Inpatient endoscopy referrals are made for various indications; however, delays in performing these procedures can extend hospital stays, often with normal outcomes. With increasing pressure on NHS resources, inpatient endoscopy slots and hospital beds are critical assets. This audit aimed to evaluate referral patterns and diagnostic endoscopic procedures within a single health board in Wales. Methods A retrospective analysis of an electronic inpatient endoscopy database reviewed referrals within a single Welsh health board over two months (August–October 2024). The analysis included referrals from a large teaching hospital, focusing on diagnostic oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) and flexible sigmoidoscopy (FS). Results Of 297 inpatient referrals, 175 (59%) were for OGD, including 137 diagnostic and 38 therapeutic procedures. Forty-two (14%) referrals were for FS, 21 (7%) for colonoscopy, and 21 (7%) redirected to outpatient care. Thirty-eight (13%) cases were cancelled due to withdrawal, being unfit, no longer requiring the procedure, or death. The analysis included 179 cases: 137 OGDs and 42 FS. Of these, 71 (40%) of OGDs and 19 (11%) of FS referrals were priority 1 (1–24 hours). Sixty-seven (49%) OGD and 24 (57%) FS inpatients waited over one day for their procedure. Additionally, 46 (34%) of OGD and 14 (33%) of FS patients were discharged within two days post-procedure, suggesting they might have been discharged earlier if scoped sooner. Conclusion Delays in inpatient endoscopy may unnecessarily extend hospital stays. Redirecting suitable referrals to outpatient pathways could improve resource efficiency and support timely discharges.
affiliations: Centre for Healthcare Evaluation, Device Assessment and Research (CEDAR), Cardiff and Vale University Health Board
Department of Surgery, Cardiff and Vale University Health Board

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.119.title: SP9.10 Rethinking waste for a greener tomorrow in General Surgery: A two-cycle audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.119.abstract: Abstract Aims In this study, we aim to assess the current implementation of waste management strategies at an NHS district general hospital (DGH) in general surgery. We have surveyed the volume of waste produced in a variety of cases. Methods We observed elective and emergency cases. For each case, we weighed the waste produced - both recyclable and clinical. After the first cycle, we have distributed surveys and posters to raise awareness of the correct waste segregation guidelines. Thereafter, we have re-surveyed the volume of waste produced after each case. Results The average total waste produced was 5.9kg in our first sample, with majority of the waste being clinical. A significant proportion of non-infectious recyclable waste was incorrectly placed into the clinical waste bin. In our second cycle, the average waste total waste after each operation was higher; however, this may have been because our second sample included longer operations. There has been a noticeable improvement in the appropriate usage of segregated waste into smaller cases; the proportion of recyclable waste usage increased from 17% to 28%. Conclusion On average, 5.9kg of waste is produced after an operation in general surgery, which is mostly clinical. However, we have shown it is possible to improve waste segregation by raising awareness. Key statement We have demonstrated that waste segregation in our trust is not optimised. Further education of staff and raising awareness at meeting and creating posters are the next steps currently being taken for improvement.
affiliations: Princess Alexandra Hospital, NHS Trust
London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.400.title: WTP8.06 Supportive Decision-Making: An audit on consent in General Surgery at Tertiary Centre and adherence to guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.400.abstract: Abstract Aims This study audited the quality of consent forms for General Surgery patients listed for elective and CEPOD emergency theatre cases, focusing on how often patients were offered a copy of their consent forms. The Royal College of Surgeons recommends providing patients with a copy for review and retention. This is critical as inadequate consent resulted in 1,194 claims between 2014–2019, costing the NHS £202 million, primarily in surgical specialties and gynaecology. Methods A prospective study was conducted at a Major Trauma Centre and a District General Hospital. Patients were identified from elective surgical lists using the Bluespier Theatre software and from CEPOD lists during handovers. Adults with mental capacity and clinical stability were included. Post-operative feedback was also collected through a retrospective qualitative study. Results Over three months, 141 consent forms were reviewed. In the first cycle (40 patients), all forms were adequately completed, but none (0%) were offered a copy, and only 1 patient (2.5%) received one. After implementing educational interventions and poster reminders, the second audit (101 patients) showed marked improvement: 76 patients (74%) were offered a copy, and 68 patients (67%) received one (percentage differences: 74%, p<0.05; and 64.8%, p<0.05). The result of this study suggests guidelines on consent forms are not being strictly followed at a tertiary hospital site. With encouragement, poster reminders and education the rate of patients receiving a copy of their consent was improved. Our intervention has improved the quality of consenting within our hospitals and thus patient experience.
affiliations: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation
Brighton and Sussex Medical School

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.251.title: TTP3.02 A three-cycle audit reviewing compliance with Enhanced Recovery after Surgery (ERAS) protocol following colorectal resections
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.251.abstract: Abstract Aim This 3-cycle audit looks at our local compliance with the ERAS protocol to improve patient outcomes. Methods Mixed method study. Per cycle, this prospective project of 10 consecutive patients undergoing elective colorectal resections identified quantitative data for assessment of compliance levels (30 total). Qualitative response to changes were sought from the wider MDT to assess the response to the booklet and suggestions for improvements. Data collection took place over a 2-year period. Interventions included staff education and a comprehensive post-operative ERAS booklet for completion during the inpatient stay. Results Key areas of success:Average length of stay between cycles 2 and 3 reduced from 9 to 6Compliance improvements in oral nutritional supplementation, promotion of deep breathing exercises, oral fluid intake and completion of stoma care plans; all now average >90% compliance.More clear documentation regarding time out of bed and mobilisation on/off the ward. Key areas of concern:Poor documentation of discharge planning – less than 50% had this documentedMany patients are declining nutritional supplementationQuantification of mobilisation remains low (<50%) Conclusions Overall, the introduction of an ERAS protocol booklet to inpatient care has shown significant improvements in compliance with numerous aspects of the ERAS protocol. This project demonstrated the importance of multi-disciplinary team working to ensure the best outcomes. This project in on going and hopes to incorporate pre- and peri-operative aspects of ERAS soon. This local audit may demonstrate strategies that are transferrable to other centres.
affiliations: North Cumbria Integrated Care NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.197.title: MTP7.04 The Extended Surgical Team – The role of the doctor’s assistant as part of the surgical team, a closed loop audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.197.abstract: Abstract Aims As part of a larger scale project looking to improve surgical training for foundation doctors. We hope to quantify the impact of the introduction of a doctor’s assistant role as part of the extended surgical team. This project looks to quantify the quality of documentation for all surgical admissions against set national standards. Methods Assessed against the Academy of Medical and Royal Colleges – Guide to Record Keeping Standards, we reviewed documentation for all general surgical admission prior to and following the employment of a doctor’s assistant. Data collections each took place over a 1-week period. Results 40 and 35 patients were admitted respectively over the two cycles. Key areas of success Proportion of consultant reviews documented to be occurring within 14 hours of admission increased from 47% to 97%. Continued high standards in the use of a standardised proforma / MUST score completion and VTE prescriptions (>85%) Social history taking improved from 58% to 75% Key areas of concern Although some improvements in completion of dementia screening tool and oxygen prescriptions occurred, there is still room for improvement. Conclusions The valuable doctor’s assistant role provides a primarily administrative role within the team to enable foundation doctors to partake in tasks deemed to be of more educational value, as per the recent ASiT survey[1]. Increased variety of sessions are now available for foundation doctors. In further projects we hope to demonstrate any impact on individual wellbeing and satisfaction with the post for doctor's and doctor's assistants.
affiliations: North Cumbria Integrated Care NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.161.title: MTP4.04 Decarbonisation of Surgery - Making the laparoscopic cholecystectomy tray smaller, undertaken as prospective audit leading to quality improvement by reducing unjustified energy wastage and reducing cost
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.161.abstract: Abstract Aim To cut down the size of the upper GI general tray (UGIGT) used in laparoscopic cholecystectomy containing around 63 instruments to a much lesser by removing the ones that are never used in LC but sterilized and packed every time the tray is prepared. The intended effect of the project is to prevent wastage of water, carbon emissions, cost by avoiding sterilisation of instruments that are never used but packed and sterilised each time. Method Our sample size was 100 LC, in which we included 90 elective and 10 emergency cases. We recorded the type and the number of each instrument that were used from the UGIGT with the help of scrub nurses in each surgery. A survey was also done to make sure all the surgeons were happy with with the contents of the new tray. Results We found that out of 63 instruments on the tray we used maximum of 19 instruments and minimum of 7 in those 100 LC that we audited. Most of the instruments that were used were common, however, there were some rare occasions when few other instruments were used from the tray. Around 5000 liters of water and carbon emissions of 220kgs were unjustified waste in 100 surgeries in around the period of 5 months. Conclusion Created a new smaller tray called 'Lap general tray' (60% lesser instruments), to be used for LC and can also be used of appendicectomy and laparoscopic inguinal hernias as the principle remains the same.
affiliations: University NHS Foundation Trust Manchester
Royal College of Surgeons, England

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.050.title: SP4.04 A Standards-Based Audit of Elective Procedures in a Tertiary Care Vascular Surgery Department in London
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.050.abstract: Abstract Aims In accordance with the NHS Constitution, our centre mandates that if a procedure (open or endovascular) is cancelled for non-clinical reasons, it must be rescheduled within 28 days. In this paper we aim to:Evaluate the department’s compliance with NHS guidelines for rescheduling cancelled procedures within 28 days.Identify avenues for improvement in current outcomes. Methods Procedure outcomes from 1st March to 31st August 2024 were reviewed, including number of procedures listed (scheduled, completed and cancelled), reasons for cancellations, and if cancellations were rescheduled within 28 days. This was communicated to the Consultants, the Admissions and Waiting List Manager, and the Cardiovascular Service Manager. Data from 1st October–30th November 2024 was collected using the same metrics to evaluate changes in performance. Results Of 402 initially scheduled procedures, 165 were cancelled. Rescheduling rates at 28 days were 14.75% (17.5% for open and 12.0% for endovascular). Following implementation of targeted departmental collaboration, the second data cycle reported improved rates of rescheduling - 65.2% (15/23) for open and 87.7% (57/65) for endovascular procedures. However, bed unavailability remained the major reason for cancellations. Conclusion Surgical postponement and cancellations are currently a major challenge as highlighted in the nationwide project, PACE (Postpone and Cancellations in Elective care). Our study indicates that facilitating structured dialogue within a surgical department and increasing awareness of guidelines enhanced compliance with performance targets.
affiliations: King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.474.title: eP446 Optimising Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Operation Notes: A Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.474.abstract: Abstract Aim Operation notes serve as the standard documentation of intraoperative findings. The Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCS) and NHS England introduced the Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) program, outlining 32 essential components for operation notes. This study evaluates the quality of laparoscopic cholecystectomy operation notes before and after implementing GIRFT recommendations. Methods A retrospective analysis of laparoscopic cholecystectomy operation notes from two biliary surgeons over a two-year period was conducted. Following the first audit cycle, GIRFT recommendations were implemented. Operation notes were then reassessed and compared before and after adopting these recommendations. Results A total of 245 operation notes were included. There were 132 operation notes in the first cycle and 113 in second cycle. All operation notes included 19 out of 32 recommended points, such as operation indication, consent, date/time of operation, surgical checklist, skin preparation and drugs administered. Further details are specified in the table below. Cycle 1 (n=132)Cycle 2 (n=113)Median GIRFT score27 (IQR 26-29)30 (IQR 29-32)All (32) GIRFT points included037 (32.7%)Laparoscopic pressure settings095 (84.1%)Laparoscope under direct vision2 (1.5%)77 (68.1%)Reverse Trendelenburg Position4 (3.0%)79 (69.9%)Intraoperative Pictures94 (71.2%)88 (77.9%) Discussion This study demonstrates improved quality of operation notes following the implementation of GIRFT guidelines. Adopting these standards should be encouraged and integrated into surgical training to enhance consistency and patient care. Additionally, incorporating instant digital upload of intraoperative photos could further improve documentation and prevent data loss.

School of Medicine, Dentistry & Nursing, University of Glasgow , Glasgow, Scotland

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.152.title: MTP3.06 Optimizing Blood Retesting Intervals: A Surgical Audit on FBC and U&E Tests in surgical in-patients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.152.abstract: Abstract Aim Frequent Full Blood Count (FBC) and Urea & Electrolyte (U&E) testing in surgical patients can lead to unnecessary phlebotomy, increasing risks such as infections and prolonged hospital stays. This audit aims to assess compliance with recommended retesting intervals and implement improvements to enhance patient safety and optimize resource utilization. Financially, save hospital resources as per saving un-necessary blood tests we could save Millions of pounds every year, which can be used in other benefits. Methodology A retrospective analysis was conducted using hospital system data from 70 randomly selected surgical patients in two cycles first August,2024 cycle 2nd cycle is December 2024. A total of 731 blood test requests (FBCs +U&Es) were reviewed. Requests were categorized as compliant or non-compliant based on national guidelines (Royal College of Pathology, NHS England and NICE guideline), with non-compliant tests further classified as either unnecessary or missed but necessary. Ethical considerations ensured patient confidentiality. Results The second audit cycle demonstrated:A 49% improvement in appropriately requested necessary tests.A 5% reduction in unnecessary blood tests.An overall 22.8% increase in compliance with best practice guidelines. Conclusion Enhancing awareness among surgical teams and incorporating guideline-based recommendations led to improved compliance with appropriate retesting intervals. Future initiatives should involve allied healthcare professionals, expand monitoring to all blood tests, and integrate routine teaching into new doctor inductions. Regular audits remain crucial in sustaining and further optimizing blood testing practices in surgical care. This way we could save more than 100,000 £ monthly in every hospital.
affiliations: Mersey and West Lancashire NHS Trust Foundation

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.239.title: TTP2.04 Unravelling the Genetic Enigma of Lynch Syndrome: An Audit of Practice in a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.239.abstract: Abstract Aim Lynch syndrome, caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, is the most common hereditary cause of colorectal cancer (CRC) in the UK, contributing to approximately 1,100 new cases annually. This autosomal dominant condition necessitates timely genetic testing and surveillance. This study aimed to assess adherence to NICE guidelines in the Lynch syndrome testing pathway for CRC in our department. Methods A retrospective review of newly diagnosed CRC cases from January 2022 to December 2023 was conducted using the hospital’s electronic database. Focus was placed on identifying MMR deficiency in histology reports and documentation in MDT outcome proformas, followed by an analysis of genetic testing referrals for MMR-deficient cases per NICE guidelines. Results Out of 193 diagnosed CRC cases, 17 (8.8%) exhibited deficient MMR (dMMR). Genetic testing revealed 14 cases with MLH1 mutations and 3 with mutations in non-MLH1 genes. Genetic testing referrals were made for 5 dMMR cases, resulting in 2 somatic variations, 2 with no variants, and 1 missed referral. The missed referral was promptly addressed with follow-up testing. Conclusion Lynch syndrome requires lifelong surveillance and genetic counseling. This study underscores the importance of adhering to NICE guidelines to ensure timely genetic testing and appropriate referrals. An interprofessional approach, including Surgical and medical oncology, gastroenterology, genetic counselors, and specialist nurses, is essential for comprehensive patient care. Education and collaboration among healthcare professionals are key to improving Lynch syndrome management as guidelines evolve.
affiliations: Airedale General Hospital , West Yorkshire

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.374.title: WTP6.01 Audit of Preoperative Axillary Staging and Axillary Recurrence in Early Invasive Breast Cancer at a Single Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.374.abstract: Abstract Aims This study aimed to assess our hospital's compliance with the Association of Breast Surgery guidelines for axillary management in early breast cancer. The guidelines recommend preoperative axillary ultrasound for invasive breast cancer, with ultrasound-guided biopsy for suspicious findings. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is the preferred staging procedure, and axillary node clearance (ANC) is advised for confirmed axillary node metastasis. Effective staging should ensure axillary recurrence rates remain below 5% at 5 years. Methods Data was collected for patients undergoing axillary procedures between October 2017 and October 2018. Inclusion criteria were invasive breast cancer or ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with mastectomy. Exclusions included prior breast cancer or axillary procedures for non-breast cancer reasons. Key data included preoperative imaging, biopsy findings, surgical interventions, and 5-year outcomes. Results Among 235 patients (mean age 61), 61.7% had invasive cancer, 37% had DCIS, and 1.3% had both invasive cancer and DCIS. SLNB was performed in 203 patients, ANC in 26, and axillary sampling in 2. All patients with ultrasound findings of U3 or higher underwent ultrasound-guided biopsy. Of 26 patients with suspicious (B4) biopsies, 25 underwent ANC, while 1 underwent SLNB with no recurrence at 5 years. Axillary recurrence occurred in 3 patients (1.27%), two of whom experienced local recurrence first. Conclusion Our data show high compliance with staging guidelines and a low axillary recurrence rate of 1.27%, well below the 5% benchmark at 5 years, supporting the effectiveness of current practice.
affiliations: Dudley Group NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.324.title: WTP1.01 The Use of Audit and Quality Improvement for Selection to Surgical Training
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.324.abstract: Abstract Aims Audit and quality improvement (QI) are routinely used as part of shortlisting for national selection in surgical specialties. This may incentivise behaviours to maximise rewarded points, such as high volume and low quality, to improve chances of selection. This study aims to quantify how each surgical specialty uses audit & QI for selection and explore this in the context of national priorities in the area. Methods A comprehensive list of surgical specialties was gathered from NHS England webpages, along with shortlisting matrices. Proportion of points allocated for audit and QI was calculated. Further analyses were performed to investigate the number of projects required, whether it must be specialty-specific, as well as the maximum potential yield of this activity. Results 12 surgical specialties were included (5 core/ST1 level entry, 7 higher/ST3 entry), accounting for 1364 training places and 7759 applications in 2024. Mean proportion of points ringfenced for audit/QI was 12% (range 6-35). 1/12 specified audit activity must be undertaken for points, the remainder accepted either audit or QI. 2/12 required specialty-specific activity to occur. In fulfilling all audit/QI points available, post holders would generate 2098 individual projects, and applicants 11,631. The average number of complete audit/QI projects required for maximum points is 1.9 (range=1-4). Conclusions All surgical specialties use audit/QI for shortlisting. This may influence applicant behaviour with regards audit/QI practice, and generates significant data burden. Further research is needed to examine whether this activity improves patient outcomes.
affiliations: Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP)

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.217.title: MTP8.11 A Service Review and Retrospective Audit of Diagnostic Imaging and Clinical Outcomes in Acute Appendicitis: Evaluating Service and Adherence to the World Society of Emergency Surgery 2020 Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.217.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is one of the most common general surgical emergencies, requiring prompt, evidence-based care to minimise morbidity and improve outcomes. This audit aimed to evaluate diagnostic interventions and clinical outcomes in acute appendicitis at our trust, in accordance with the World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) 2020 guidelines. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on patients diagnosed with acute appendicitis. Patients undergoing appendicectomy from August 2023 to July 2024 were included. Key metrics assessed were diagnostic imaging use, time to surgery, length of stay, and complication rates. Results Among 119 patients, pre-operative diagnostic imaging was performed in 92.5% of cases. Of 97 CT scans, the positive predictive value was 96.9% when confirmed by histology. A discrepancy rate of 45.2% was observed in distinguishing uncomplicated from complicated appendicitis on CT versus intra-operative findings. CT imaging was used in 96% of patients over 40. Complicated appendicitis was reported intra-operatively in 44.5% of patients with a drain usage rate (34.4%). The negative appendicectomy rate was 4.2%, with malignancy identified in 1.7% of patients. The mean length of stay was 8.5 days (SD 4.5) for complicated cases and 1.4 days (SD 0.98) for uncomplicated cases with 89.1% of patients undergoing appendicectomy within 24 hours. Postoperative complications occurred in 10.1% of cases. Conclusion This audit demonstrates strong compliance with guidelines for timely intervention and imaging, whilst demonstrating low complication and negative appendicectomy rates. Our results suggest areas for improvement in post-op length of stay, minimising use of intra-operative drains, and imaging reporting accuracy.
affiliations: Leighton Hospital, Mid Cheshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.407.title: WTP8.15 An audit of the consent obtaining process and shared decision making in elective surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.407.abstract: Abstract Aim Consent obtaining process in surgery is a legal requirement and an important element to uphold ethical and patient-centred care. This audit examines the adherence of consent obtaining process to trust policy of a two-stage consent process, focused on the dates of generating electronic consent form, patient signature and consent confirmation against the date of surgery. Methods A retrospective audit on all patients that underwent elective operation in the general surgery department in a selected month, within a trust comprising of 2 hospitals, totalling 270 patients. Date of electronic consent form generation, patient signature and consent confirmation is audited against date of operation. EIDO forms (patient leaflet information) is also audited as linked to the e-consent form, and if documented on clinical letter of first consultation. Result Analysis identified poor adherence to the two-stage process of consent seeking, although all initial consultations comprise of the shared-decision making process, 58% of collected data suggests electronic consent forms are generated on the date of surgery rather than first consultation in outpatient clinic. Delayed consent generation compromises the consent obtaining process, leading to avoidable pressures and human error. The main error identified is consent confirmation signed but not dated, notably seen in consent forms generated on date of surgery. Conclusion Action and improvements must be made in the consent obtaining process, especially in relation to electronic consent forms to avoid legal disputes and promote satisfactory clinical communication.
affiliations: South Tyneside and Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.402.title: WTP8.08 Snapshot audit of adherence to hospital infection prevention and control policy pertaining to the monitoring of IV cannulae. A quality improvement project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.402.abstract: Abstract Aims A quality improvement project was undertaken in a small district general hospital to investigate whether Infection and prevention control policies pertaining to IV cannulation were being followed. This guidance stated that cannulae should be: correctly dressed and labelled, documented in the electronic record and assessed twice daily to ensure there are no signs of thrombophlebitis. Methods On 15th May 2024 every inpatient in the hospital with a cannula was examined to assess whether the aforementioned criteria had been met along with the duration of time the cannula had been in and examination findings. Results It was found that 38%(n=86) of inpatients had a peripheral cannula sited. Of these, over 30% were documented in the notes and only 10 cannulae had a date label attached. The time since insertion of the cannula ranged from 24 to 240 hours. There were 26 cannulae that had spoiled dressings in situ and evidence of thrombophlebitis in 18 cannulae, which, once identified were promptly removed by staff. Conclusions From this audit it was concluded that there should be more awareness of the basic standards set out by the trust on IV cannulation to help prevent pathogenic infiltration into the cannulae. These results have been presented at the hospital’s grand round and a poster detailing these recommendations has been created to highlight the areas of concern and hopefully improve clinical practice. The audit will undergo a second cycle to investigate whether these interventions have improved things.
affiliations: STDH

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf230.title: Effect of standard wound dressing versus prophylactic closed incision negative-pressure therapy on surgical-site infection after open incisional hernia repair: multicentre randomized clinical trial
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf230.abstract: Abstract Background The benefit of closed incision negative-pressure therapy (ciNPT) after open incisional hernia repair in reducing surgical-site infection (SSI) is uncertain. Methods The PROPRESS multicentre RCT was conducted from 1 March 2023 to 25 June 2024 at three Danish hospitals. Patients undergoing elective open incisional hernia repair were randomized to ciNPT or a standard wound dressing (SWD). The primary outcome was the incidence of SSI at 30 days. Secondary outcomes at 30 days included the pooled incidence of surgical-site occurrences (SSOs), patient-reported quality of life (QoL), and patient-reported scar assessment. The last follow-up date was 25 July 2024. Results A total of 110 patients were randomized (54 SWD patients and 56 ciNPT patients; median age of 63.9 (interquartile range 50.7–69.0) years; 45 (40.1%) were female) and 108 (98.2%) completed follow-up at 30 days. In total, 7 of the 110 patients (6.4%) were smokers, the mean(s.d.) BMI was 29.3(4.1) kg/m2, and the mean(s.d.) horizontal defect size was 8.7(4.7) cm. One death in each group was unrelated to the intervention, but surgery and anaesthesia may have been predisposing factors for mortality. There was no difference in SSI rates; 4 of 53 patients (8%) in the SWD group versus 7 of 55 patients (13%) in the ciNPT group (P = 0.673). With regard to SSOs, these affected 12 of 53 patients (23%) in the SWD group versus 14 of 55 patients (26%) in the ciNPT group (P = 0.907). There was no difference in scar scores (equal mean scores of 24; P = 0.892) and overall QoL improved significantly (mean score difference: −12.8 (95% c.i. −15.4 to −10.2); P < 0.001) without a difference between the groups (mean score change: SWD −12.6 versus ciNPT −13.0; P = 0.874). Conclusion ciNPT did not reduce SSI after open incisional hernia repair in this RCT, which was limited by the relatively small number of patients. Registration number NCT05050786 (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov).

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf186.title: Variation in outcomes after metabolic bariatric surgery: multilevel analysis to assess the contribution of patient, surgeon, and hospital factors
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf186.abstract: Abstract Background Metabolic bariatric surgery (MBS) quality registries monitor various outcomes, enabling the assessment of hospital performance in comparison with national benchmarks. However, if there is considerable between-surgeon outcome variation, surgeon-level feedback may be better suited. The aim of this study was to assess the extent to which patient-, surgeon-, and hospital-level factors contribute to the variation in outcomes after MBS. Methods All primary procedures registered in the Dutch MBS quality registry between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2023 were included. Outcomes included severe postoperative complications, reoperation, prolonged length of stay (LOS), readmission, textbook outcome, and achieving ≥25% total weight loss within 1 year. Multilevel logistic regression models were built for each outcome, including all available patient characteristics, operating surgeon, and hospital, to determine the variance explained by patient-, surgeon-, and hospital-level factors. Results In total, 30 610 patients were included, operated on by 144 surgeons in 19 hospitals. Hospital-level factors contributed most to the explained variance for all outcomes, ranging from 59.6% for reoperation to 90.3% for prolonged LOS. Surgeon-level factors explained less variance, ranging from 3.2% for prolonged LOS to 28.2% for reoperation. Patient characteristics explained the least, ranging from 4.4% for textbook outcome to 13.1% for severe postoperative complications. Conclusion Variation in outcomes is mostly explained by hospital factors, rather than surgeon factors, supporting hospital-based performance feedback. The results suggest that the pre- and postoperative trajectory and perioperative care may affect MBS outcomes more than patient characteristics or surgical team performance.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.006.title: 243 Timeliness of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy in Acute Cholecystitis: An Audit of Compliance and Associated Morbidity
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.006.abstract: Abstract Aim This study aimed to assess local adherence to guidelines set out by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and the British Benign Upper Gastrointestinal Surgical Society (BBUGSS): offering early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) within 1 week of an acute cholecystitis diagnosis to minimise complications (CG188), and morbidity post-LC of <10%. Method Medical records of 61 patients, who underwent LC for acute cholecystitis at a district general hospital between May 2023 and February 2025, were reviewed for admission dates, operation dates, and postoperative complications, which were graded using the Clavien-Dindo classification. Results Of the 61 LCs, none were performed within 1 week of diagnosis with acute cholecystitis, and were elective instead, many of which were day-cases. One patient underwent a percutaneous cholecystectomy, and later a LC. 26 patients experienced grade II and IIIa complications (43%) following LC. Conclusions No patients underwent a LC within 1 week of diagnosis with acute cholecystitis, failing to meet NICE CG188 guidance. Elective LC was performed instead. Delayed surgery may have been due to patients’ comorbidities, severity of inflammation, limited theatre capacity, or surgeon availability. Morbidity post-LC exceeded the <10% BBUGSS benchmark, potentially linked to delayed intervention or patients’ pre-existing comorbidities. Future work should focus on identifying and addressing such barriers to early surgery and evaluate interventions to improve compliance and patient outcomes.
affiliations: Cardiff University , Cardiff ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.101.title: 270 An Audit Looking at the Peri-Operative Management of Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Surgical Patients Under the Upper Gastrointestinal Team at Royal Liverpool University Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.101.abstract: Abstract Aim Venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains a major preventable cause of postoperative morbidity and mortality. Inadequate prophylaxis may raise thrombotic risk by up to 30%. This audit evaluates compliance with VTE prevention guidelines in the Upper Gastrointestinal (UGI) surgical team at the Royal Liverpool University Hospital, focusing on prescription accuracy, timing, and peri-operative assessment. Method A retrospective audit was conducted for patients undergoing invasive UGI procedures from 1/12/24 to 31/1/25. Data from electronic patient and prescribing records included surgical urgency, VTE risk assessments, pharmacological (enoxaparin) and mechanical (anti-embolism stockings) prophylaxis, dosing accuracy (weight/renal adjusted), administration timing, perioperative suspension, and inpatient VTE events. Results Among 96 patients, 99% had risk assessments completed. Combined prophylaxis was advised in 71%, with enoxaparin prescribed in 84%. Yet, 11% received prophylaxis when not indicated, while 6% missed it despite indications. Appropriate dosing occurred in 82%, with 40 mg once daily most common. Administration timing met guidance in 79%, and 76% began within 24 hours. Prophylaxis was suspended peri-operatively in 40%, typically with two missed doses. Anti-embolism stockings were prescribed in 87%, with 93% appropriate. In hospital VTE occurred in 6%. Conclusions Overall compliance with assessment and prescribing was high, but issues were found in peri-operative assessment accuracy, prescription errors, missed doses, and timing. Suspension decisions seemed subjective, and missing critical care data limited the analysis. Targeted education, standardised protocols, and re-auditing are recommended to enhance adherence and reduce preventable VTE complications in surgical patients.
affiliations: Royal Liverpool University Hospital , Liverpool ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.105.title: 370 Evaluating Noise and Light in Critical Care and Their Impact on Patients’ Sleep: A Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.105.abstract: Abstract Aim Sleep quality is often impaired in hospitalised patients, particularly in critical care, and is associated with worse outcomes such as increased delirium. Environmental factors, including excessive noise and bright lighting at night, contribute significantly to sleep disruption. This audit evaluated compliance with local guidelines on noise and light control and their impact on patients’ sleep. Method Compliance with the trust guideline ‘lights out and radios off by 10 pm’ was assessed in the Intensive Therapy Unit (ITU) and High Dependency Unit (HDU). Night-time noise levels were recorded at 4-hourly intervals. Patient-reported sleep quality was assessed using the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ). A second cycle was then conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions such as raising awareness of critical care staffs, offering eye masks and ear plugs to patients, and clustering nursing intervention and care overnight. Results Compliance improved in both ITU (lights: 20% to 30%; radio: 70% to 70%) and HDU (lights: 56% to 70%; radio: 56% to 80%). Average night-time noise levels fell from 46 dB to 40 dB. Reported sleep duration increased in ITU (5.1 to 5.3 hours) and HDU (4.0 to 5.5 hours). RCSQ scores improved in both units (ITU: 53.5 to 56.4; HDU: 34.8 to 60.2). Fewer patients reported being disturbed by noise and monitor alarms (ITU: 33% to 25%; HDU: 80% to 30%). Conclusions Targeted environmental changes improved both compliance with sleep-promoting guidelines and patient-reported sleep quality. Ongoing education and interventions are recommended to sustain improvement and optimise sleep conditions in critical care.
affiliations: Newcastle Upon Tyne Hospitals , Newcastle Upon Tyne ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.104.title: 304 Impact of ICU Bed Availability on Admission of High-Risk Emergency Laparotomy Patients: An Audit of NELA and P-POSSUM Correlation
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.104.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess whether ICU admission following emergency laparotomy aligns with preoperative mortality risk scores (NELA or P-POSSUM) Method A retrospective audit was conducted on emergency laparotomy cases performed between January 2019 and November 2024 at Huddersfield Royal Infirmary. Cases were identified using the hospital’s theatre electronic record system (Bluespier) by two independent reviewers. Electronic patient records were reviewed to obtain NELA or P-POSSUM scores. ICU bed data was recorded daily and obtained from ICU staff. Patients were stratified by risk category (low, medium, high) based on their predicted 30-day mortality, and analysed against ICU admission status. Statistical analysis included chi-square tests. Results Of 620 laparotomies, 241 had NELA scores and 86 had P-POSSUM scores documented. Upper GI laparotomies made up 4% of the total number of laparotomies. The mean NELA and P-POSSUM scores were 9.74% and 14.19% respectively. Among high-risk patients (NELA or P-POSSUM >10%), 31.94% and 28.12% respectively were not admitted to ICU despite the availability of ICU beds on most days. Chi-square analysis showed a significant association between risk category and ICU admission (p < 0.00001). Conclusions ICU admissions generally aligned with higher risk scores, particularly NELA. However, a notable proportion of high-risk patients were not admitted despite available beds, suggesting the need for improved documentation, risk-based triage, and escalation protocols to ensure equitable critical care access.
affiliations: Calderdale and Huddersfield NHS Foundation Trust , Huddersfield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.119.title: 48 Audit on the Management of Patients Admitted with Acute Gallstone Disease
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.119.abstract: Abstract Aim To quantify the proportion of eligible patients admitted with acute gallstone disease receiving a cholecystectomy within 8 days at our hospital, using Chole-QuIC’s methodology. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on all patients admitted with acute gallstone disease to our district general hospital between 01/08/24-31/10/24 (n=119). Hot cholecystectomy candidates were identified using Chole-QuIC’s methodology. Additional data was collected for: surgery waiting times, starvation time (nil by mouth, NBM), length of stay, investigations and interventions. Data was analysed using GraphPad Prism. Results Out of 119 patients, 71.4% and 57.1% underwent CT and ultrasound scans respectively. 77/119 (64.7%) were acute cholecystitis (AC) patients, 7 of whom had percutaneous cholecystostomies. 40 AC patients were fit surgical candidates. 25/40 had inpatient cholecystectomies whilst 15 were discharged with outpatient cholecystectomies. AC patients with inpatient cholecystectomies had lower median surgery waiting times (3 vs 31 days, p< 0.0001). 5/15 discharged AC patients were re-admitted within 30-days. Median NBM days in AC patients was slightly higher in the inpatient cholecystectomies cohort compared to those discharged with outpatient cholecystectomies (2 vs 1 day, p=0.0204). Median admission length was higher in AC patients who had inpatient cholecystectomies (5 vs 3 days, p< 0.0071). Overall, 31/53 (58.5%) eligible acute gallstone disease patients received a cholecystectomy within 8 days. Conclusions There are significant challenges to meet the 8-day surgery rate of 80% targeted by Chole-QuIC in our unit. Inpatient cholecystectomies in the AC patients reduced surgery waiting times and prevented re-admissions but had drawbacks including longer fasting and admission duration.
affiliations: East Surrey Hospital , Redhill, Surrey ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.131.title: 353 Re-Audit on the Utilization of CT Scans in Acute Pancreatitis Management Following Implementation of Local Policy in a Northwest NHS Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.131.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute pancreatitis is a frequent emergency surgical condition where CT scans play a key role in diagnosis and monitoring. However, overuse of CT imaging can lead to unnecessary radiation exposure and higher healthcare costs. A previous audit, presented at AUGIS 2023, revealed that 28% of CT scans performed for acute pancreatitis were unnecessary. Following this, hospital staff received targeted education and retraining on the local imaging policy. This audit aimed to assess adherence to the local hospital policy regarding CT scan use in acute pancreatitis after the intervention. Method A retrospective review was conducted on 32 patients admitted under the Emergency Surgical Team with acute pancreatitis between August and October 2023. The mean age was 53.2 years, with a slight female predominance (53.1%). CT scan utilization and indications were evaluated against local policy standards. Results CT scans were performed in 23 patients (71.8%). Among these, 15 (46.1%) were done in patients without diagnostic amylase levels, 3 (9.4%) after 72 hours to evaluate complications, 3 (13.0%) for co-existing abdominal pathology (such as pancreatic cancer or abdominal aortic aneurysm), and 1 (4.3%) due to suspicion of an alternative diagnosis. Only 1 CT scan (4.3%) was classified as unnecessary, reflecting a 95.6% compliance rate with the imaging policy. Conclusions This audit demonstrates a substantial improvement in adherence to imaging guidelines following targeted education and retraining. Continued staff education and periodic audits are recommended to sustain appropriate and cost-effective use of CT scans in acute pancreatitis management.
affiliations: Salford Royal Hospital , Manchester ,
Ulster Hospital , Belfast ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.127.title: 292 Outcomes of NoLap Patients in the National Emergency Laparotomy Audit at a Single Tertiary Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.127.abstract: Abstract Aim The NoLap category of the National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA), introduced in April 2024, captures outcomes for patients presenting with acute bowel ischaemia or perforation in whom emergency surgery was indicated but not performed - either due to the patient’s frailty and high surgical risk or by patient choice. This study aimed to evaluate outcomes in this cohort and identify opportunities to improve palliative and end-of-life care. Method We conducted a prospective, single-centre study between February 2024 and February 2025. Adults (≥18years) with radiological evidence of bowel perforation or ischaemia, for whom surgery was indicated but not undertaken due to significant comorbidities or patient preference, were included. Patients who underwent radiological or endoscopic therapeutic interventions were excluded. The primary outcome was overall survival. Secondary outcomes included multidisciplinary involvement and advance care planning. Results Seventeen patients met inclusion criteria. The cohort was predominantly female (94.1%) with a median age of 87 years. The overall mortality rate was 64.7%. The median Clinical Frailty Score was 8, and the mean NELA-predicted mortality was 51.8%. All patients had CT-confirmed diagnoses. On admission, only 41.1% had an advance care plan or DNACPR in place. Following the decision for conservative management, 88.2% received formal input from palliative care or geriatric medicine. Conclusions This early experience highlights a frail and high-risk patient group often underrepresented in audit and quality improvement initiatives. Despite high predicted mortality, proactive end-of-life care planning was often lacking. Early palliative services involvement and structured advance planning are essential to support patient-centred care.
affiliations: Addenbrooke's Cambridge University Hospitals , Cambridge ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.132.title: 379 Improving Documentation of Severity Scores in Acute Pancreatitis: A Two-Cycle Audit Against AUGIS Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.132.abstract: Abstract Background Severity scoring in acute pancreatitis is vital for early risk stratification, guiding escalation decisions and improving patient outcomes. The Association of Upper Gastrointestinal Surgeons (AUGIS), alongside the British Society of Gastroenterology, recommends that all patients with acute pancreatitis have a severity score documented within 48 hours of admission using a validated tool. Aim To assess adherence to AUGIS-endorsed guidelines on severity score documentation in acute pancreatitis and evaluate the impact of local quality improvement interventions. Method A retrospective audit was carried out across two cycles:Cycle 1 (1 Jan – 28 Feb 2025): 24 patients were identified. Only 4 (17%) had severity scores documented.Intervention: Local initiatives included FY/SHO teaching, staff posters summarising guidelines, and an electronic documentation template.Cycle 2 (1 Jun – 12 Jul 2025): 23 patients were reviewed. Seven (30%) had documented severity scores — all completed within the first 24 hours. One additional case was incomplete due to pending labs.Scoring systems used included Glasgow-Imrie, Modified Glasgow, and BISAP, based on clinician preference and data availability. Conclusions Following low baseline compliance, structured educational and system-level interventions improved both the rate and timeliness of severity score documentation. Embedding these practices into routine care supports adherence to AUGIS guidelines and enhances early risk stratification in acute pancreatitis.
affiliations: Ulster Hospital , Belfast ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.136.title: 186 Improving Emergency General Surgery Theatre Efficiency Through a Structured Warm List Pathway: A Closed Loop Audit at a Tertiary Hospital in London
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.136.abstract: Abstract Aim To improve Emergency General Surgery (EGS) theatre efficiency through the implementation of a structured Warm List pathway, aligned with GIRFT principles. Method A closed loop audit was conducted over two cycles. The first cycle reviewed EGS lists from January to June 2023. The second cycle, from October 2024 to March 2025, followed the implementation of a Warm List pathway. Data were collected on list usage, procedures performed, cancellations, and discharge outcomes. Results In the first cycle, 57 out of 71 scheduled lists were completed. A total of 102 procedures were performed (average 1.8 per list), with eight lists cancelled due to no suitable emergency cases. Same day discharge was achieved in 37 percent of cases. The Warm List pathway introduced defined inclusion criteria: patients ASA I or II, low anaesthetic risk, suitable for hernia repair or lymph node biopsy, able to attend on short notice, commute within one hour, aware of possible cancellation, and accompanied by an escort. Patients were reviewed, consented, and added to the Warm List for rapid scheduling. Following implementation, 12 additional patients were safely operated on using previously unused time. Conclusions The Warm List pathway improved EGS theatre utilisation and patient flow, reducing cancellations and enhancing efficiency. This approach supports better use of emergency theatre resources and improved patient experience.
affiliations: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.137.title: 319 An Audit on Calls to Surgical ACU Consultants: Frequency, Outcomes Andpathway Appropriateness in Altnagelvin Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.137.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate the referral patterns, triage outcomes, and documentation practices of consultant-led calls to the Acute Surgical Ambulatory Care Unit (ASACU), and to identify areas for improvement in service delivery and governance. Method A prospective audit was conducted between 14/04/2025 and 09/05/2025. Consultants covering ASACU logged all incoming clinical calls in real-time over a 13-day period. Data collected included the source of contact, triage outcome, and whether the call was formally documented. A total of 45 calls were captured and analysed. Results General Practitioners initiated 78% of the calls, highlighting primary care as the predominant referral source. Only 2 calls originated from the Emergency Department. Of the 45 calls, 24 (53%) resulted in ASACU referrals, 9 were redirected to the ED, and the remainder were managed via outpatient pathways or consultant advice. Despite effective triage decisions, only 40% (18/45) of calls were documented formally, raising concerns about clinical governance. Good practices included real-time data collection, high primary care engagement, and categorisation of diverse call outcomes. Conclusions This audit demonstrates effective consultant triage and strong engagement with primary care but identifies a significant gap in call documentation. Recommendations include implementing mandatory documentation, standardising referral protocols, reducing informal contact routes, and disseminating clear ASACU referral criteria. A follow-up re-audit is planned to assess the impact of these changes and ensure sustained improvement.
affiliations: Western Health and Social Care Trust, Altnagelvin Area Hospital , Londonderry ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.160.title: 183 Management of Patients with Hereditary Diffuse Gastric Cancer (HDGC) at Leeds Teaching Hospitals Trust (LTHT): A Clinical Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.160.abstract: Abstract Aim Is mainstream genetic testing for HDGC (CDH1) effective within the setting of an UGI Cancer MDT? Method A retrospective analysis from 2009-2019 identified failures to refer eligible patients for CDH1 testing, and led to a collaboration between UGI, Oncology and Clinical Genetics services to mainstream genetic testing for HDGC within the UGI Cancer service. A Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) was introduced, and outcomes re-evaluated. Results In the 10 years prior to introduction of the CDH1 SOP, 17 patients with confirmed diffuse type gastric cancer fulfilled CDH1 testing criteria. A further 7 patients did not have histological subtype recorded. 12/17 patients (70%) were referred to Clinical Genetics and 10 (58%) underwent CDH1 testing. 3 patients were diagnosed with a pathogenic CDH1 mutation. In the 2.5 years following introduction of the SOP, 25 patients with diffuse type gastric cancer fulfilled CDH1 testing criteria and had this documented in the MDT minutes. 15 patients were seen at our institution and 13/15 (87%) underwent mainstream CDH1 testing. 3 patients were diagnosed with a pathogenic CDH1 mutation. The remaining 10 patients were seen at peripheral centres where mainstream testing is not currently available, only 2 (20%) patients were referred to Clinical Genetics for consideration of CDH1 testing. Conclusions Mainstream genetic testing for HDGC (CDH1) within an UGI Cancer service is feasible and can lead to improved uptake of CDH1 testing for eligible patients. There is scope to widen access to mainstream testing and improve referral pathways in centres where this is not available.
affiliations: Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust , Leeds ,
Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust , Wakefield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.171.title: 217 An Audit on Image Documentation in Upper GI Endoscopy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.171.abstract: Abstract Aim Complete photo-documentation of eight standard oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) landmarks is a key quality indicator yet remains inconsistently achieved in routine practice. We conducted a retrospective surgical audit to quantify completeness of eight-site OGD documentation Method We reviewed 59 OGDs performed from 1st to 15th of May 2025 Patient demographics, pathology outcomes and the rate of photograph capture at eight anatomical sites were recorded. Complete eight-site documentation and individual landmark photo-rates were analysed Results Patients’ median age was 57 years (range 18–89) with a female:male ratio of 33:26. Complete eight-site photo-documentation was achieved in only 6.35% of procedures. Individual photo-rates varied widely: upper oesophagus 15.9%, GOJ 73.0%, fundus (retroflexion) 76.2%, gastric body 34.9%, incisura/angulus 27.0%, antrum 49.2%, duodenal bulb 41.3%, and second part of duodenum 79.4%. Gastroenterologists performed the majority of OGDs (n=27; 45.8%) averaging 4.15 sites documented, Surgeons performed 17 OGDs (28.8%) with an average of 3.94 landmarks documented and gastroenterology trainees performing 15 OGDs (25.4%) with an average of 4.73 landmarks documented. Conclusions This baseline audit reveals marked heterogeneity and suboptimal completeness in OGD photo-documentation, with full eight-site capture achieved in fewer than one in fifteen examinations. The findings underscore the need for targeted interventions such as structured reporting templates, operator education and regular feedback to standardise practice and improve documentation quality. We will present these results at an upcoming surgical conference and initiate a second audit cycle following implementation of improvement measures.
affiliations: Sunderland and South Tyneside NHS Trust , Sunderland ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.227.title: 29 Evaluating Adherence to NICE Guidelines for Urgent Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy in Acute Cholecystitis: A Clinical Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.227.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate adherence to NICE guidelines recommending laparoscopic cholecystectomy within seven days of acute cholecystitis diagnosis, benchmarking against the Cholecystectomy Quality Improvement Collaborative (Chole-QuIC) national standards. Method A retrospective audit reviewed 257 consecutive laparoscopic cholecystectomies from January to March 2025, with 66 indicated for acute cholecystitis. Time from symptom onset to surgery was assessed against NICE standards (Warttig et al., BMJ, 2014). Results Of 66 cases, 18.2% (12/66) underwent surgery within seven days, and 21.2%. Only five cases were documented to have utilized the dedicated hot gallbladder pathway, with 40% (2/5) meeting the seven-day target. Average time to surgery was 68 days, with delays due to waiting lists, booking issues, delayed presentation, and associated comorbidity (analysis ongoing). Conclusions Adherence to NICE guidelines (18.2%) is below Chole-QuIC benchmarks, where top sites achieve 20–60% for surgery within 8 days. We are currently further analyzing reasons for delayed surgical intervention. Recommendations include optimizing the hot gallbladder pathway and improving communication to align with NICE and Chole-QuIC standards.
affiliations: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.230.title: 43 Audit of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Operative Notes in a DGH
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.230.abstract: Abstract Introduction Operation notes are essential documents in patient care. The use of standardized guidelines, such as those endorsed by recognized organizations, is crucial to ensure consistent and detailed record-keeping. Documenting parameters specific to laparoscopic cholecystectomy provides valuable information for management in the event of complications and it also provides direction for follow-up care. Aim This audit aims to assess the quality of laparoscopic cholecystectomy operative notes in our trust by comparing them against NHS England’s GIRFT (Getting It Right Rirst-Time) recommendations. It also aims to Identify areas for improvement and implement targeted interventions. Method A retrospective audit of 78 laparoscopic cholecystectomy operative notes conducted in 2024 were selected by systematic random sampling. Data were compared against GIRFT recommendations. After intervention, a re-audit of 78 laparoscopic cholecystectomy operative notes from 2025 was done using the same methodology and compared against initial audit. Results Significant improvement was observed in the re-audit compared to the initial audit, after intervention in the form of surgeon education and use of modified operation note proforma specific to laparoscopic cholecystectomy was implemented. Documenting significant steps involved in Laparoscopic cholecystectomy for example, details of calot’s triangle dissection, details of bile/gallstone spill and its management and mention of port used to extract gallbladder increased by 13%, 42%, and 48%, respectively. Conclusions This audit demonstrates a significant improvement in operative note quality by implementing interventions from an initial audit, emphasising the importance of use of recommendations issued by GIRFT. Audits should be conducted at regular intervals to sustain improvements.
affiliations: Shrewsbury and Telford Hospital NHS Trust , Shrewsbury ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.262.title: 197 A 13-Month Retrospective Audit of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Across a Multi-Site NHS Trust
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.262.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate practice and outcomes of laparoscopic cholecystectomy across a large NHS Trust, assessing indications, imaging pathways, surgical approach, and complications. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on all patients listed for cholecystectomy between January 2024 and January 2025 across three sites. Data included demographics, imaging, surgical modality, complications, and 90-day readmission. Results 675 patients underwent cholecystectomy (73% female, mean age 53.6 years). The most common indication was symptomatic biliary colic (46%), followed by gallstone cholecystitis (28%) and gallstone pancreatitis (14%). Most cases were elective (79%), with CholeQuIC (13%) and emergency (8%) pathways. Laparoscopic surgery was performed in 89.5%, with robotic and subtotal approaches in 3.0% and 4.1%, respectively. Pre-operative ultrasound was performed in 93%, and 36% underwent MRCP. Of those, 31% proceeded to ERCP for stone retrieval. A drain was inserted intra-operatively in 14% of cases. The overall complication rate was 2.2%, including retained stones (1.3%), wound infections (1.3%), and bile leaks (0.9%), with no significant variation based on pre-operative imaging modality. Complication rates were higher in emergency presentations (5.6%) compared to elective cases (2.0%). Readmission rate was 3.9%. Elective cases achieved an 87% day-case rate, exceeding NICE targets. Conclusions Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is delivered safely and consistently across the Trust with excellent outcomes. However, MRCP was used in over one-third of cases, often without influencing complication rates, and may contribute to delays and additional costs. A more selective, evidence-based imaging strategy incorporating intraoperative ultrasound may reduce unnecessary MRCP use, streamline patient care pathways, and improve cost-effectiveness while maintaining clinical safety and outcomes.
affiliations: University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust , Bristol ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.271.title: 249 Bile Leak After Laparoscopic Subtotal Cholecystectomy with an Open Versus Closed Gallbladder Remnant
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.271.abstract: Abstract Aim Subtotal cholecystectomy (STC) is a sometimes unavoidable measure when dissection of Calot’s structures is deemed unsafe. The GB remnant is at risk of postoperative bile leak even when closed (Purzner 1a, 1b), but some advocate leaving it open (Purzner 2a, 2b, 3) to prevent recurrent cholecystitis. This study compares the rate of bile leak with an open versus closed GB remnant at subtotal cholecystectomy. Method A retrospective review was carried out on all STC performed by three Upper GI surgeons between 2018 and 2025. Outcomes were compared between Purzner Grade 1 (closed) vs Grade 2 and 3 (open). These included bile leak, postoperative ERCP requirement, postoperative length of stay (LOS), and readmission to hospital. Results 28 patients underwent laparoscopic STC during the study period, of which only one was converted to open (3.6%). The GB remnant was closed in 14 patients (50%) and left open in 14 patients (50%). Whilst no statistically significant differences were found between the two groups; the rate of bile leak was higher in the open group (100% vs 79%, p=0.07), as was LOS (8 days vs 5 days, p=0.15). However, the need for postoperative ERCP (28% vs 36%, p=0.65) and return to theatre (7% vs 7%, p=1.0) was similar. Readmissions were higher in the closed group (29% vs 7%, p=0.13). Conclusions Bile leak and the need for postoperative ERCP are common after both open and closed management of the GB remnant at STC. Consideration of long-term sequelae like recurrent cholecystitis should factor into the choice of technique.
affiliations: Stockport NHS Foundation Trust , Stockport ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.282.title: 326 Are GIRFT Standards Being Met? a Comparative Audit of Cholecystectomy Operation Notes by Biliary and Non-Biliary Surgeons
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.282.abstract: Abstract Aim High-quality operation notes are vital for safe post-operative care, effective communication, and medico-legal protection. The RCSEng and GIRFT guidelines recommend clear, comprehensive, and preferably typed documentation for all procedures (total score 32). This audit assessed the quality of cholecystectomy operation notes against these standards, comparing biliary versus non-biliary surgeons. Method This multicentre retrospective cohort study included consecutive adult patients who underwent elective or emergency cholecystectomy across three hospitals between August 2023 and July 2024. Cases were grouped based on whether the operating surgeon was classified as biliary or non-biliary specialist. Operation notes were audited against GIRFT guideline criteria, and results were compared between the two groups. Results Of 564 patients, 405 (71.8%) were female, with a median age of 53 years. Biliary surgeons performed 125 (22.2%) procedures, while non-biliary surgeons performed 439 (77.8%). Emergency cholecystectomies were more frequently performed by biliary surgeons (44.8% vs 35.1%, p=0.047), who also had a higher rate of typed operation notes (94.4% vs 59.0%, p<0.001). The median GIRFT score was significantly higher among biliary surgeons (29 [IQR 27–31]) compared to non-biliary surgeons (19 [IQR 16–21]), p<0.001. Notably, none of the non-biliary surgeons achieved a perfect score (32/32). Conclusions This audit highlights a clear and concerning gap in compliance with GIRFT standards among non-biliary surgeons. The marked disparity in operative note quality carries important implications for patient safety, medico-legal accountability, and clinical continuity. To address this, the implementation of typed, standardised operation notes should be mandated, with targeted interventions to ensure adherence to national documentation standards.
affiliations: Department of Upper GI Surgery, University Hospital Hairmyres , NHS Lanarkshire, East Kilbride ,
School of Medicine, Dentistry & Nursing, University of Glasgow , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.332.title: 237 Audit of Operative Note Quality in HPB Surgery: Adherence to RCS Good Surgical Practice Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.332.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess adherence to the RCS Good Surgical Practice (2025) standards in HPB operative note documentation and additionally evaluate documentation of intraoperative adjuncts—Pringle’s manoeuvre, ICG fluorescence, intraoperative ultrasound (IOUS), and frozen section—in liver procedures. Method A prospective audit of 75 HPB operations was conducted. Operative notes were reviewed for compliance with RCS 2025 documentation standards, including key parameters such as incision, findings, complications, closure, estimated blood loss (EBL), prophylaxis, and postoperative instructions. Intraoperative adjunct documentation was analysed for liver procedures specifically. Results High adherence was observed for core parameters including incision (93%), findings (100%), closure (100%), postoperative instructions (100%), and surgeon signature (100%). Lower compliance was noted in the documentation of EBL (20%), specimen details (71%), and extra procedures (13%). Among 9 laparoscopic liver resections, ICG usage was documented in 2 cases (22%). Pringle’s manoeuvre was recorded in all applicable liver resections. IOUS and frozen section documentation were present in 25% and 30% of relevant cases, respectively. Conclusions This preliminary audit demonstrates strong compliance with core RCS documentation standards in HPB surgery. However, documentation of intraoperative adjuncts in liver procedures remains inconsistent. Planned interventions include implementing a standardised electronic operative note template, delivering educational sessions, and placing visual reminders in theatres. A second-cycle audit will be conducted in August, with loop closure planned by September.
affiliations: King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , London ,
Madras Medical College , Chennai ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.333.title: 251 Prospective Audit of Protocol CT Scans in Asymptomatic High-Risk Patients with Postoperative Pancreatic Fistula After Pancreatoduodenectomy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf270.333.abstract: Abstract Aim Early intervention for patients with CR-POPF after pancreatoduodenectomy (PD) may improve outcomes. Our aim was to evaluate the impact of protocol CT scans in asymptomatic POPF patients. Method Since September 2022, protocol CT scans were performed in POPF patients at high-risk of progression to CR-POPF ("CR score" > 5, based on gender, POD3-drain amylase, POD3-serum albumin, POD3-serum CRP) after PD. The effect of this policy was evaluated by comparing outcomes between historical controls (Jan 2020-August 2022) and a prospective cohort (September 2022-Dec 2024): data collected included number/timing of CT scans; type/timing of interventions; complications; hospital stay. Results The study cohort included 437 consecutive patients who underwent PD (2020-24). Incidence of CR-POPF was 17.4% and 90-d mortality was 4.6%. 130 patients with POPF were diagnosed by DFA-POD3, including 44 who were high-risk of CR-POPF (historical 13, prospective 31). Positive findings were present on protocol CT scans in 17/24 (70.8%) asymptomatic POPF patients, of whom 13 (76.5%) underwent invasive intervention within 13 days (IQR 10.5-16). In CR-POPF patients, the prospective cohort were scanned earlier than historical controls (median 5 v. 8 days; p<0.001) and underwent earlier invasive intervention (10 v. 12.5 days; p=0.03). There was no difference in postoperative LOS (21 v. 17 days; p=0.57) or 90-day mortality (19.5% v. 14.3%; p=0.76) in CR-POPF patients between groups. Conclusions Implementation of protocol CT scans in high-risk POPF patients after PD was associated with earlier CT scans and invasive interventions, although this did not translate into reduced hospital stay or mortality. Larger, prospective studies are recommended.
affiliations: Queen Elizabeth Hospital , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.039.title: SRS22 - Traumatic bowel and mesenteric injury in England, wales and Ireland: a retrospective analysis of the trauma audit and research network data registry, 2012–2021
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.039.abstract: Abstract Background Traumatic bowel and mesenteric injury (TBMI) confer significant morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to characterise the epidemiology and clinical outcomes of TBMI in England, Wales and Ireland after the inception of a national major trauma network. Methods A retrospective observational analysis of the Trauma Audit and Research Network national data registry was performed. Demographics, injury descriptors, patient management and outcomes were extracted for all patients enrolled between 2012 and 2021. Results From 2012–2021, 4124 patients met the inclusion criteria. Annual case volume increased from 249 to 510 over the observation period. Median age at presentation was 34 years (IQR 23–50) and males comprised 77% of cases (n = 3175). Blunt trauma accounted for 54% of injuries (n = 2222) and almost half of the cohort had ISS > 15 (48%, n = 1983). Haemorrhagic shock occurred in 8% of cases (n = 360) and 67% (n = 2777) presented outside of normal working hours (17:00–08:00). CT imaging was performed in 77% (n = 3177). Operative management occurred in 84% of cases (n = 3469): laparotomy 74% (n = 3037) and laparoscopy 10% (n = 413). Thirty-day and 24-hour mortality were 9.1% (n = 377) and 5.3% (n = 219), respectively, with a decline in 30-day mortality from 11.4% in 2013 to 7.3% in 2021. Median hospital stay was 9 days (IQR 6–18). Conclusions Following the implementation of major trauma networks, TBMI incidence increased while mortality decreased. Rapid access to diagnostics and operative intervention seem integral to improved healthcare outcomes. Ongoing improvements to the granularity of registry data will support ongoing quality improvement efforts across the system.
affiliations: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London ,
Imperial College London , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.042.title: SRS25 - Sustainability in hand trauma surgery: an eco-audit of the flexor tendon laceration repair pathway
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.042.abstract: Abstract Background Hand trauma accounts for nearly one third of Emergency Department (ED) attendances in the United Kingdom (UK). Flexor tendon repair is one of the most commonly performed Plastic Surgery procedures requiring months of repeat contact with hand therapy for optimal outcomes, the environmental impacts of which have not previously been evaluated. Methods A retrospective study of 17 patients undergoing flexor tendon repair. Process mapping and life-cycle analyses of the patient pathway, from ED to surgery, to rehabilitation and full recovery, was performed. Estimates for carbon dioxide emissions were generated in kgCO2eq. allowing identification for specific opportunities for pathway optimization, in line with national guidelines. Race and ethnicity were not reported in this study. Results This study estimated the carbon footprint of a patient undergoing flexor tendon repair to be approximately 113.2 kgCO2eq. The rehabilitation phase made the greatest contribution to emissions (59.85 kgCO2eq., 52.9%) and patient travel was responsible for a staggering 79.42% of total emissions (89.88 kgCO2eq.), followed by the production and transport of equipment (8.52 kgCO2eq., 7.53%) needed for treatment. Conclusions To reduce carbon emissions, reducing the need for patient travel was suggested. This can be achieved by greening hand therapy through increased use of virtual consultations and encouraging the use of mobile phone applications. Adoption of circular economy principles through the use of reusable surgical gowns and drapes, creation of procedure-specific equipment packs, and increased use of wide-awake local anaesthesia, no tourniquet (WALANT) was also recommended.
affiliations: Univeristy College London , London ,
