Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust , London ,
University of Bristol Medical School , Bristol ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.064.title: SRS52 - When risk goes unspoken: an audit of consent documentation for laparoscopic appendicectomy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.064.abstract: Abstract Accurate and comprehensive documentation of risks during the consent process is essential to respect patient autonomy and meet national standards set by the General Medical Council (GMC) and Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) England. We conducted a retrospective audit of 68 consent forms for laparoscopic appendicectomy over a three-month period at our institution. Each form was reviewed for documentation of 17 key risks identified through national guidelines and consultant consensus, including common complications such as bleeding, infection, and conversion to open surgery, as well as specific organ injuries and intraoperative contingencies. Overall, only four risks were documented in more than 75% of cases: bleeding (98.5%), infection (95.6%), injury to nearby structures (83.8%), and conversion to open procedure (88.2%). Documentation of specific organ risks was variable, with bowel injury noted in 61.8% of forms, bladder injury in 36.8%, and ureter injury in only 22.1%. Among 46 female patients, documentation of gynecological risks was present in just 30.4%. Other important risks, including hernia formation (63.2%), death (13.2%), and need for reintervention (23.5%) were frequently omitted. These findings reveal poor compliance with GMC and RCS consent guidelines, highlighting a lack of procedure-specific and gender-specific risk documentation. In response, a procedure-specific consent template has been introduced, and a re-audit is planned to evaluate its impact on improving consent quality and compliance. This audit underscores the need for structured consent processes to ensure informed decision-making and medicolegal safety in laparoscopic appendicectomy.
affiliations: The Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust , Wolverhampton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.067.title: SRS55 - Improving consent form compliance in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a closed-loop audit using pre-printed risk templates
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.067.abstract: Abstract Informed consent is a fundamental component of safe surgical practice, yet we identified inconsistent documentation of risks in laparoscopic cholecystectomy consent forms at our institution. Comprehensive disclosure of all material risks is essential for patient understanding and medicolegal protection, but variability exists, especially in emergency surgery. We conducted a retrospective audit of 46 emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy consent forms over seven months, assessing documentation compliance for 15 commonly accepted risks. Pre-intervention results showed wide variability: while bleeding, infection, and conversion to open surgery were documented in 100% of cases, less frequent risks such as keloid formation (17.4%), death (2.2%), and chest infection (6.5%) were often omitted. To improve consistency, we introduced a pre-printed consent form template listing all standard risks, implemented across the surgical team. A re-audit of 23 subsequent consent forms over two months demonstrated complete compliance, with all 15 risks documented in 100% of cases. This simple, low-cost intervention significantly improved risk documentation quality, enhancing patient safety and alignment with national guidelines. Although limited by a smaller post-intervention sample and short re-audit period, the approach is scalable and easily replicable in similar settings. Standardizing consent documentation through pre-printed templates represents an effective strategy to ensure thorough risk communication and support informed surgical decision-making in laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
affiliations: The Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust , Wolverhampton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.096.title: SRS99 - An audit assessing the surgical outcomes of Major Lower Limb Amputation (MLLA) in south tyneside and Sunderland NHS foundation trust
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.096.abstract: Abstract This audit evaluates peri-operative care and outcomes for patients undergoing major lower limb amputation (MLLA) at Sunderland Royal Hospital between August 2024 and March 2025. MLLA, defined as any amputation above the ankle, is a critical intervention primarily for patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) and diabetic foot infections (DFI). The audit assessed compliance with national standards from the Vascular Society of Great Britain and Ireland (VSGBI) and the National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD), focusing on consultant review timing, operative timing, prophylaxis, multidisciplinary team involvement, and patient outcomes. Data from 45 eligible MLLA cases revealed full compliance with consultant review within 24 h, antibiotic and venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis, and physiotherapy involvement during admission. However, only 67% of amputations occurred within 48 h of decision, and just 45% of diabetic patients received specialist diabetes team input. The below-knee to above-knee amputation ratio was 2:1, meeting best practice standards. Post-operative stump complications occurred in 20% of patients, with a 30-day mortality rate of 2.2%. The average hospital stay was prolonged at 34 days, with nearly half of patients remaining hospitalized beyond 30 days, highlighting potential inefficiencies in discharge planning and rehabilitation. The audit recommends improved diabetic specialist engagement through a blanket referral policy or weekly multidisciplinary ward rounds and enhanced physiotherapy input pre- and post-operatively to optimize rehabilitation and expedite discharge. These measures may reduce post-operative complications and length of stay, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing healthcare costs.
affiliations: Sunderland Royal Hospital , Sunderland ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.098.title: SRS101 - A closed loop audit assessing the rate of surgical site infections after wound closure with sutures in Major Lower Limb Amputations
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.098.abstract: Abstract Introduction Major lower limb amputations (MLLA) are a last resort treatment for patients with peripheral arterial and diabetic foot disease. A significant number of patients subjected to MLLAs will develop a surgical site infection (SSI), which can have an impact on patient morbidity and mortality. This audit, based in a single Vascular centre, aimed to assess whether the materials that MLLA skin wounds were closed with are an associated risk factor for SSIs. Methods A closed-loop audit was carried out by retrospectively looking at the notes of all patients who had undergone MLLA between August 2022 to January 2023. The material used to close skin was identified for all patients, as was the presence of any SSI. The data was presented at a local audit meeting and a re-audit was carried out 6 months later. Results A total of 64 patients were included. In the first cycle, the SSI rate was 40% (10/25), with staples being statistically significant (Fischer exact test value: 0.0027, P < 0.05) at increasing the infection rate. Following the second cycle, the SSI was 10.2% (4/39), with sutures being statistically significant (Fischer exact test value: 0.0154, P < 0.05) at reducing the infection rate. Of the risk factors that were analysed, none were statistically significant between the two groups of patients. Discussion Closing MLLA wounds with sutures rather than staples appears to reduce the rate of SSI. Due to the low sample size, this audit cannot exclusively show that closing MLLA with staples increases the risk of infection.
affiliations: Black Country vascular network , Dudley ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.162.title: SRS169 - An audit of Global Vascular Guidelines implementation at two large teaching hospitals in differing healthcare settings
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.162.abstract: Abstract Introduction The Global Vascular Guidelines (GVG) provide a framework for assessment and management of patients with Chronic Limb Threatening Ischaemia (CLTI) as laid out by Conte et al. (2019). This audit describes compliance with GVG standards across two teaching hospitals in different healthcare settings: UK (Higher Income Country) and Sri Lanka (Lower-Middle Income Country). Aim Our aim was to identify key similarities, differences, and barriers to implementation of these guidelines. Methods All new CLTI patients admitted or seen in outpatient podiatry clinic at Guy’s and St Thomas’ Hospital (GSTT) and National Hospital of Sri Lanka (NHSL) between 1/5/2024–31/5/2024 were included. Data were collected according to recommendations set out in the GVG. Statistical significance was analysed with Fisher’s Exact Test. Results Sixty-five patients were included (GSTT: 38; NHSL: 27) and forty-nine outpatients (GSTT: 21; NHSL: 28). Among the Inpatients, GVG-compliant foot examination was poorly performed, (GSTT: 10 (26%); NHSL: 0 (0%), P = 0.004). Among the Outpatients, GVG-compliant foot examinations were performed in all 21 outpatients at GSTT but in none of the 28 outpatients at NHSL (0%, P < 0.001). Limb severity scoring systems were utilised for all outpatients seen at GSTT, whereas only 5 of 28 outpatients at NHSL (18%) had scoring systems documented (P < 0.001). Conclusions Implementation of the GVG is challenging, with even large teaching hospital centres failing to meet all the recommendations for assessment of patients with CLTI. Further work is needed to understand the barriers to implementation and address these.
affiliations: Guy's, King's and St Thomas' School of Medical Education , London ,
Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Trust , London ,
King's College London , London ,
National Hospital of Sri Lanka , Colombo ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.203.title: SRS217 - Modelling angiogenesis and tissue formation using the arteriovenous loop for vascularised tissue engineering
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.203.abstract: Abstract Introduction The clinical demand for vascularised tissues still remain unmet. Clinical case studies have utilised the arteriovenous loop (AVL) vascularise tissues. We show using histological methods and spatial transcriptomics the evolution of tissue grown with this model. Methods The surgical model used is the rodent arteriovenous loop model, where the rat femoral artery and vein is anastomosed together and placed in a chamber together with fibrin hydrogel. Tissue grown was analysed every 7 days till 28 days. Results There was a significant increase in the percentage of chamber filled with new tissue between day 7 and day 14 which was maintained till day 28 (9.44% ± 1.90 versus 43.58% ± 4.52, P = 0.01). This was accompanied by a similar increase in vessel density (16.96 ± 6.12 versus 154.6 ± 14.08, P = 0.01). Collagen deposition was later, only reaching a peak at day 28 for both red and yellow fibres. Preliminary analysis using spatial transcriptomics show the different stages of angiogenesis with a higher expression of VEGFA and ENG at day 7 and a higher expression of EPHB4 and NOTCH1 at day 28. There were also two different cell clusters representing different mechanisms of vascularisation, mesenchymal cells migrating from the AVL (intrinsic vascularisation) and macrophages through the chamber pores (extrinsic vascularisation). Conclusions We show that the AVL is a model for growing vascularised tissues and studying the mechanisms of angiogenesis and tissue formation in vivo. Further work will involve exploring the role of mesenchymal cells and macrophages in vascularisation and new tissue formation.
affiliations: University of Manchester , Manchester ,
Plastic Surgery Department, Mersey West Lancashire Foundation Trust , Liverpool ,
Plastic Surgery Department, Manchester University Foundation Trust , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.295.title: SRS326 - How accurately can carotid body tumours be distinguished from nerve neck paraganglionomas on imaging? An audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.295.abstract: Abstract Introduction Neck paragangliomas require surgical excision when they are secretory, malignant, or symptomatic. Preoperative distinction between carotid body tumours (CBTs) and nerve-associated paragangliomas (for example vagal) is essential for optimal surgical planning and informed patient consent. Vagal tumour excision may result in dysphagia, hoarseness, cardiac arrhythmias, gastrointestinal disturbance and autonomic dysfunction. Conversely, CBT excision is associated with risk of perioperative stroke, making preoperative diagnosis crucial for patient safety. Methods Ten anonymised images of neck paragangliomas (five CBTs) were reviewed by ninety healthcare professionals of varying expertise, ranging from nurses to consultant surgeons. Participants were asked to identify tumour type. Four key distinguishing imaging features were then outlined, and participants re-assessed the same images. Diagnostic accuracy was analysed by tumour type, professional role, imaging modality (CT versus MRI), and image orientation (transverse versus longitudinal planes). Results Initial diagnostic accuracy of participants was 65%. Binary logistic regression suggested a significantly higher accuracy among consultant reviewers and when using CT imaging (P < 0.01), while no significant difference was observed for tumour type. After awareness of distinguishing imaging features, overall diagnostic accuracy improved substantially to 81%, with CBTs showing significantly better identification rates (P < 0.05). MRI imaging and non-consultant reviewers were consistently associated with lower diagnostic confidence levels. Conclusions Preoperative identification of neck paraganglioma subtype remains diagnostically challenging across healthcare professionals of all experience levels. However, targeted education about key imaging features significantly improves diagnostic accuracy, particularly for carotid body tumours. These findings have immediate clinical implications for surgical planning, perioperative risk stratification, and comprehensive patient counselling.
affiliations: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.304.title: SRS339 - Zenker’s diverticulum—case closed, or case open?
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.304.abstract: Abstract Introduction Endoscopic treatments offer minimally invasive techniques for management of Zenker’s Diverticulum (ZD) or Cricopharyngeal (CP) muscle dysfunction. Selected cases, may require open surgery due to patient or pouch factors. We describe our experience of managing ZD/CPMD with surgical images to depict how we manage an open surgical approach. Methods A retrospective case series was conducted at South Infirmary Victoria University Hospital. Theatre records from 2024–2025 were reviewed. ZD were classified using the Van Overbeek staging system. Results Twelve patients were included with 7 males and 5 females with a mean age of 73. Endoscopic surgery was attempted in all cases with 8 (67%) requiring no further management. Four (33%) subsequently required external approach surgery with diverticulectomy and CP myotomy due to anatomical limitations preventing safe endoscopic management. The Van Overbeek staging score did not correlate with need for open surgery (P > 0.05). All 4 patients (100%) demonstrated clinical and radiographic improvement with a return to normal diet within 10 days. Conclusions Endoscopic surgery is an effective first-line treatment for ZD. Anatomical features may preclude endoscopic surgery and open surgery offers a safe, effective alternative management strategy.
affiliations: Department of Otolaryngology, South Infirmary Victoria University Hospital , Cork ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.341.title: SRS385 - Audit of routine pus swabbing in abscess drainage: are we following guidance?
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.341.abstract: Abstract Aims Routine pus swabbing during incision and drainage of uncomplicated cutaneous abscesses remains common despite guidance recommending selective use for recurrent, persistent, or treatment-resistant cases. This audit assessed whether routine swabbing influences clinical outcomes and evaluated adherence to current guidance in emergency general surgery practice. Methods A retrospective audit of 122 consecutive abscess I&D cases was conducted between January and April 2025. Data were extracted from electronic records and operation notes. Firth penalised logistic regression was used to analyse associations between patient and treatment factors and 30-day readmission and reoperation, adjusted for age, sex, diabetes, abscess site and discharge on antibiotics. Descriptive statistics summarised case-mix and swab utilisation patterns. Results Median age was 38 years; 57.4% were male. Pus swabs were taken in 76/122 (62.3%) cases, with results acted upon in only 5/76 (6.6%). Thirty-day recurrence was nearly similar for swabbed versus non-swabbed patients (3.9% versus 4.3%). Discharge on antibiotics was associated with higher odds of recurrence (aOR 13.76; 95% c.i. 2.11–151.91; P = 0.004). Notably, 80% of recurrences occurred in patients discharged on antibiotics. Age, sex, diabetes, and abscess site were not significant; Reoperation events were rare (3/122); adjusted estimates had very wide 95% CIs and should be interpreted cautiously. Conclusions Routine swabbing rarely altered management and showed no outcome benefit, with likely confounding by indication for antibiotics–recurrence signal. Current practice appears to over-utilise swabbing relative to guidance. A selective swab policy targeting complex, recurrent or systemically unwell patients, or where antibiotics are planned, could optimise resources.
affiliations: Calderdale and Huddersfield NHS Trust , Huddersfield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.228.title: 552 Appendix Out, Antibiotics Out: A Closed-Loop Audit of Post-Operative Use of Antibiotics After Appendicectomy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.228.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is the most common abdominal surgical emergency worldwide, with around 50,000 appendicectomies performed annually in the UK. The World Journal of Emergency Surgery and British Medical Journal have issued peri-operative antibiotic guidelines, advising against postoperative antibiotics for uncomplicated appendicitis and against extending antibiotics beyond 3–5 days postoperatively in complicated cases. We audited antibiotic use in acute appendicitis at our district general hospital against these guidelines and aimed to improve stewardship by reducing unnecessary and prolonged antibiotic courses. Method Appendicectomies were identified using electronic theatre logs, retrospectively for the first cycle (October–December 2024) and prospectively for the second (April–June 2025). Our intervention consisted of and presenting our findings at our local surgical forum and clinical governance meeting and disseminating a poster displayed in emergency theatres. Results A total of 70 and 53 appendicectomies were identified in the first and second cycles respectively. Among uncomplicated cases, 90.2% in the first cycle wrongly received postoperative antibiotics compared with 84.4% in the second, a reduction of 5.8%. Antibiotic courses for complicated appendicitis averaged 7.8 days in the first cycle compared with 6.3 days in the second, a reduction of 1.5 days. Whereas, uncomplicated appendicitis averaged 2.9 days in the first cycle, versus 2.7 days in the second, a reduction of 0.2 days. Conclusions This audit demonstrated poor adherence to international recommendations, particularly the routine use of postoperative antibiotics in uncomplicated cases and prolonged regimens in complicated appendicitis, highlighting key areas for improvement that may be relevant across surgical services nationally.
affiliations: Chelsea and Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.196.title: 773 The Environmental Cost of Printed MDT Agendas in Colorectal Surgery: A Sustainability Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.196.abstract: Abstract Aim Colorectal MDT documentation is already distributed electronically, yet printed packs remain part of routine practice. This audit aimed to determine the environmental and financial impact of printing colorectal MDT packs and assess whether transitioning to digital-only documentation could improve sustainability, reduce waste and lower costs Method A five-week prospective audit was conducted from across five colorectal MDT meetings at Northampton General Hospital. Data collected included the number of pages printed, paper type (recycled vs virgin), printing format (single- vs double-sided; colour vs black-and-white), and which staff groups performed printing. Paper emissions were calculated using the UK Government GHG Conversion Factors 2025 (Purchased Goods & Services) with an assumed A4 sheet weight of 0.005 kg. Toner emissions were estimated using published lifecycle data (4.8 kg CO₂e per 5000-page cartridge). Financial costs were taken from local procurement data. Results Across five MDTs, 8078 pages (4036 sheets) were printed, generating 21.32 kg CO₂e from paper and 7.75 kg CO₂e from toner (29.1 kg CO₂e total; mean 5.8 kg per MDT). Annualised, colorectal MDT printing at NGH produces 279 kg CO₂e/year. Nationally, assuming weekly core cancer MDTs across 175 acute hospitals (84,000 MDTs/year), printing equates to approximately 488 tonnes CO₂e/year. Printing five MDTs cost £41.31, including paper (£11.89), toner (£29.08), and waste disposal (£0.32), equating to £396 annually. Conclusions Routine MDT printing creates avoidable carbon debt and cost; switching to digital-only documentation would remove these emissions and reduce expenditure.
affiliations: Northampton General Hospital , Northampton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.775.title: 742 Improving Cardiovascular Risk Optimisation in Vascular Surgery Patients: A Two-Cycle Audit of Adherence to VSGBI Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.775.abstract: Abstract Introduction Peripheral arterial disease carries high cardiovascular morbidity, yet best medical therapy (BMT) prescribing and relevant risk assessments remain variable. The Vascular Society of Great Britain and Ireland (VSGBI) framework provides guidance on BMT, glycaemia and lipid assessments. This quality improvement project aimed to improve adherence to VSGBI cardiovascular risk reduction standards through targeted education and visual reminders. Method Cycle one (C1): Retrospective analysis of vascular inpatients over a three-month period, assessing:BMT (antithrombotic, statin) prescribing;Gastro-protection;HbA1c testing;Lipid profiles. Intervention Surgical team teaching sessions, supported by departmental posters. Cycle Two (C2): Post-intervention snapshot audit of vascular inpatients, one-month duration. Results C1 included 153 patients (mean age 68; 117, 76.5% male) and C2 included 60 patients (mean age 66; 45, 75% male). Most admissions across C1/C2 were for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and diabetic foot infections. Modest improvement occurred across prescribing domains: antiplatelet therapy (124/153, 81.1% to 50/60, 83.3%); anticoagulation (60/153, 39.2% to 30/60, 50.0%); statin (122/153, 79.7% to 48/60, 80.0%) and gastroprotection (54/153, 35.3% to 40/60, 66.7%). Metabolic evaluation increased considerably: HbA1c (17.7%, 27/153 to 30.0%, 18/60) and lipid profiles (12.4%, 19/153 to 65.0%, 39/60). Conclusions Targeted teaching and visual interventions moderately improved BMT prescribing, diabetic screening/monitoring and lipid assessment. However, substantial work is still required to optimise this fundamental cornerstone of cardiovascular medicine in this uniquely high-risk population. Developing these educational strategies with team empowerment to apply basic cardiovascular risk reduction principles and regular re-auditing may benefit long-term cardiovascular outcomes in vascular inpatients.
affiliations: Ninewells Hospital , Dundee ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.279.title: 1378 Adherence to Guidelines on Smoking Cessation and Weight Optimisation in Elective Umbilical and Epigastric Hernia Repair: A Multi-Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.279.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess compliance with European and American Hernia Society guidelines on preoperative smoking cessation and weight optimisation in patients undergoing elective umbilical and epigastric hernia repair. Method A retrospective multi-centre audit was conducted across three hospitals (FPH, WPH and HWH). All adult patients undergoing elective umbilical or epigastric hernia repair between November 2024 and January 2025 were included. Emergency cases and patients under 18 years were excluded. Data collected included age, sex, BMI, smoking status, and documentation of lifestyle modification advice or referral for patients with BMI ≥35 kg/m² or who were active smokers. Results Fifty-nine patients were included (41 males, 18 females) with a median age of 54 years (range 22–86). Nineteen patients (32.2%) had a BMI ≥35 kg/m², and 10 patients (16.9%) were active smokers. Of the obese cohort, only one patient had surgery postponed and was referred for weight loss, while 17 (89.5%) proceeded without documented intervention. Among smokers, only two received documented cessation advice, while eight had no evidence of intervention. Six patients were both smokers and had a BMI ≥35 kg/m². Conclusions This audit demonstrates poor compliance with guideline-recommended preoperative risk optimisation in elective umbilical and epigastric hernia repair. Standardised documentation, routine counselling, and structured referral pathways are required to improve modifiable risk factor management and surgical outcomes.
affiliations: Wexham Park Hospital, Frimely NHS , Slough ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.224.title: 499 Improving Patient Safety in Upper Limb Surgery: A Closed-Loop Audit of Tourniquet Use Practices Against BSSH/BOAST Guidance in a Tertiary Plastic Surgery Trauma Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.224.abstract: Abstract Introduction Upper limb tourniquet use carries recognised risks, making adherence to BOAST/BSSH safety standards vital in modern trauma surgery practice. Aim The aim of this closed-loop audit was to assess compliance with BOAST/BSSH (2021) guidelines on the safe use and documentation of intraoperative upper limb tourniquets within a single tertiary plastic surgery trauma centre, identify areas of poor compliance, implement targeted interventions, and evaluate subsequent improvement. Method A retrospective audit was undertaken reviewing operative and anaesthetic documentation from upper limb trauma cases. Data were collected using a standardised proforma. The first audit cycle analysed 50 cases performed between 5–30 March 2025, identifying documentation rates for key standards including skin condition assessment, method of exsanguination, skin isolation, tourniquet pressure, tourniquet time, and complications. Interventions introduced included departmental teaching, circulation of guideline material, placement of laminated reminders on tourniquet machines, and development of an electronic documentation template. A second cycle of 50 cases (5 September–31 October 2025) assessed compliance post-intervention. Results Significant improvements were observed across multiple parameters following intervention. Documentation of pre-operative skin condition improved from 33% to 50%, post-operative assessment from 0% to 50%, skin isolation method from 80% to 100%, and safe tourniquet pressure documentation from 94% to 100%. No tourniquet-related burns occurred in either cycle. Tourniquet time recording remained unchanged, with 4% lacking clear documentation. Conclusions Targeted interventions led to improvements in key documentation standards relating to tourniquet safety. Ongoing staff education and refinement of electronic mandatory fields are required to optimise compliance and sustain improvement.
affiliations: Sheffield Teaching Hospitals , Sheffield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.220.title: 432 Enhancing Surgical Documentation: A Clinical Audit on Operative Notes Compliance
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.220.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit, conducted at a secondary care hospital (Dr Gray's Hospital), aimed to evaluate the quality of operative note documentation in reference to the Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCS) guidelines and assess the utilisation of the online theatre-based system. Method A retrospective review of operative notes was undertaken across two audit cycles, with an intervention introduced between cycles. The intervention included facilitated online access, consultant induction, dissemination of user guides and mass communication to surgical teams. Results In the first cycle, 70 operative notes were assessed, followed by 66 in the second. Compliance with RCS documentation standards improved significantly from 69% to 96.6% post-intervention. Use of the post-operative template increased from 18.2% to 44.1% and electronic documentation remained at 60%. The absence of timely online access at staff induction was identified as a major barrier to electronic note access. The audit demonstrated that structured interventions can markedly enhance the quality and completeness of operative notes. This, in turn, will facilitate improved documentation and continuity of care, post-operative management and medico-legal standards. Key recommendations include ensuring early electronic access for new staff along with a structured induction of user guide, documentation protocols and ongoing monitoring to maintain high standards. Conclusions This quality improvement initiative highlights the critical role of electronic surgical operation notes in maintaining patient safety and clinical efficiency.
affiliations: Dr Gray's Hospital , Elgin ,
Aberdeen Royal Infirmary , Aberdeen ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.020.title: 387 Time Matters: A 2.5-Year Audit of Delays to Appendicectomy and Their Impact on Outcomes in Emergency General Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.020.abstract: Abstract Aim Appendicectomy is the gold-standard treatment for acute uncomplicated appendicitis, yet delays to surgery may increase perforation risk, operative difficulty, postoperative complications, and length of stay (LOS). This audit aimed to evaluate waiting times from ED, diagnostic confirmation to appendicectomy, and to assess their relationship with surgical outcomes, complications, and LOS. Method A retrospective audit was conducted of appendicectomy cases between September 2022 and May 2025. Electronic patient records were reviewed on the HIVE system across 23 predefined variables, including demographics, symptom duration, ED arrival time, imaging modality, operative approach, surgical duration, complications, and LOS. Of 496 cases identified, 22 were excluded, leaving 474 patients for analysis. Results Patients ranged from 5–86 years (median 31); 56% were male. Symptom duration varied from hours to 14 days. Appendicitis was confirmed via CT in 67% and USS in 10%, with 15% undergoing no imaging. Laparoscopic appendicectomy accounted for 91% of cases, with a 5.9% conversion rate. Perforation was reported on imaging in 16% and intra-operatively in 28%. Time-to-surgery ranged from 3 to 116 hours (mean/median 18 hours). Only 50.6% underwent surgery within 18 hours of ED arrival, although 75% were operated within 18 hours of diagnostic decision. Mean operative time was 92 minutes; 30% required postoperative drains. A further 9% required postoperative imaging and 12% re-presented or required follow-up for complications. Conclusions Substantial variation in time-to-surgery exists, with longer delays linked to higher perforation rates and increased postoperative intervention. Streamlined pathways are required to optimise outcomes and minimise preventable morbidity.
affiliations: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.234.title: 615 Septic Arthritis in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.234.abstract: Abstract Aim To determine the incidence of septic arthritis at a busy urban district general hospital and to assess compliance against the BOAST guidelines for management of musculoskeletal soft tissue infections. Method All referrals to the orthopaedic service for suspected soft-tissue infection between April and September 2025 were retrospectively identified. Analysis identified confirmed cases of septic arthritis. Clinical pathways, operative management and sampling were assessed against BOAST guidelines. Results Of 86 referrals, 7 cases (8.1%) were confirmed as septic arthritis. The median age was 67 years (16-89). The knee accounted for 57% of cases, the shoulder 29% and elbow 14%. Two patients had pre-antibiotic joint fluid cultures, and only 2 patients had pre-antibiotic blood cultures, indicating a key area for improvement. All cases had a sample sent for microscopy in line with guidelines. Six cases proceeded to operative management, all by arthroscopic washout. Microbiology cultures were obtained in five cases, although histological sampling was performed in only one case. Streptococcus species accounted for five infections; Staphylococcus aureus and Neisseria meningitidis were isolated in the others. Thirty-day mortality was zero; the median length of stay was 16 days (10-44). Conclusions Septic Arthritis represents an uncommon but debilitating condition which presents on the acute orthopaedic take. Our findings show strong local compliance with BOAST guidelines, while also highlighting targeted areas for improvement, notably consistent pre-antibiotic culture collection and increased intra-operative sampling. These gaps will be addressed through a teaching series and workshop with relevant healthcare professionals, pathway optimisation and re-audit to ensure sustained improvement.
affiliations: Lewisham and Greenwich NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.169.title: 1026 Non-Lump Presentations of Breast Cancer: An Audit at an NHS One-Stop Clinic
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.169.abstract: Abstract Aim To quantify non-lump initial presentations among confirmed breast cancer cases, assess documentation quality, and determine clinical detectability on examination. Method A retrospective audit of all patients attending Whipps Cross Hospital's one-stop breast clinic over a six-month period was conducted. Cases with histologically confirmed breast cancer were included. Data collected: referral source, presenting symptom, and palpation score (P1–P5). Results Over six months, 2,611 patients attended the clinic, and 98 cancers were diagnosed. Of these, 17.3% (n=17) were screen-detected, 2.0% (n=2) were known cancer patients, and 80.6% (n=79) were primary presentations. Among primary cases, 61.2% (n=60) presented with a lump, while non-lump presentations accounted for 19.4% (n=19), including 18 incidental findings (18.4%) and one patient (1.0%) with symptoms other than a lump (breast pain). Symptom documentation was complete (100%) for all encounters; however, palpation score was recorded in only 73.7% (n=14) of non-lump cases; of these, 64.3% (n=9) were clinically abnormal (P>2) and suspicious for malignancy (P≥4). Clinical examination sensitivity for detecting malignancy in this subgroup was 64.3%. Conclusions Almost one in five breast cancers presented without a palpable lump, and clinical examination identified malignancy in fewer than two-thirds of these cases. This low sensitivity challenges proposals to assess non-lump presentations clinically without full triple assessment. Incomplete documentation further undermines assessment standards. A major limitation was the absence of routinely collected data on initial presentation, which restricted interpretation. Future audits require comprehensive datasets and should explore strategies to enhance documentation quality and improve recognition of atypical presentations.
affiliations: Barts Health NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.230.title: 564 Audit of Pregnancy Testing in Girls Over 12 Years Presenting with Acute Abdominal Pain
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.230.abstract: Abstract This audit evaluates compliance with pregnancy testing guidelines for girls over 12 years presenting with acute abdominal pain. According to Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital guidance, all patients within this group should undergo pregnancy testing as part of the initial assessment. The objective of this audit was to determine whether pregnancy testing is consistently performed and appropriately documented, including confirmation of test completion and recorded results. A retrospective review was undertaken of the 150 admissions to CHED or CAU involving girls over 12 years presenting with acute abdominal pain. Data were collected from May 2024 to May 2025 using Symphony, ICE and ED clerking records. Variables extracted included age, admission date, and documentation of pregnancy testing with results. The audit standard was set at 100% compliance with pregnancy testing on admission. The audit found that only 13.3% of cases had a documented pregnancy test, while 86.7% had no evidence of testing within the records. Among documented tests, 20% recorded a negative result, 1% a positive result, and 30% indicated that a pregnancy test was performed without a documented result. In these cases, the result was presumed to be negative. Nursing staff reported that pregnancy test documentation is entered within nursing notes on Symphony and that dipstick testing is the method most frequently used. The audit demonstrates a need for improved documentation regarding whether pregnancy testing was offered, performed or declined, as well as consistent recording of results. Recommendations include ensuring completion of pregnancy testing and integrating results within the management plan and nursing documentation.
affiliations: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital , Norwich ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.734.title: 37 From Stones to Standards: A Two-Cycle Audit on Optimising Urolithiasis Management
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.734.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute ureteric colic is a common presentation, with an annual incidence of 1–2 cases per 1,000 people (1). The British Association of Urological Surgeons (BAUS) recommends urgent CT KUB in standard, non-pregnant adults to diagnose urolithiasis and guide management (2). We aimed to evaluate the positive yield of CT KUB in patients presenting with suspected ureteric colic in NHS Lanarkshire and assess whether patients with confirmed urolithiasis had appropriate metabolic tests in accordance with EAU guidelines. Method In February 2025, 136 patients with suspected ureteric colic underwent CT KUB. Data collected included age, past history of urolithiasis, CT KUB results, and calcium and uric acid blood levels. An email reminder was sent to urology middle grades and consultants after the first cycle. A second cycle assessed whether calcium levels were checked, two months post-intervention. Results CT KUB was positive in 60 patients (44.1%). Of these, 38.3% (23/60) had calcium levels checked in the first cycle, improving to 71.1% (32/45) post-intervention. Urate levels were assessed in 20.0% (12/60) of patients. 48.3% (29/60) had a previous history of urolithiasis. Abnormal calcium levels were identified in 4.3% (1/23) in the first cycle and 6.25% (2/32) in the second. Conclusions CT KUB demonstrates good diagnostic yield for urolithiasis, consistent with a study at Newham University Hospital (40.5%) (3). However, metabolic investigations remain underutilized. Targeted interventions, such as reminders, improve compliance with guideline-recommended metabolic testing. Further strategies are required to ensure all patients with confirmed urolithiasis undergo appropriate metabolic assessment.
affiliations: NHS Lanarkshire , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.382.title: 177 Modification of Skin Closure in Closed Hemorrhoidectomy: Analysis of Impact on Early Morbidity and Comparison with Classic Technique Reported in the Literature
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.382.abstract: Abstract Aim Ferguson´s closed hemorrhoidectomy is considered a safe and reliable technique; however, early postoperative morbidity-particularly bleeding and infection-remains a primary concern. This study assessed the impact of a modified skin-closure (anodermal marsupialization) on early postoperative outcomes and compared these findings with published data on the conventional Ferguson technique. Method A retrospective observational study was conducted including 155 patients who underwent a modified closed hemorrhoidectomy (marsupialization with a running anchored suture) between 2017 and 2024. Outcomes from the institutional cohort were compared with data from the literature through an exploratory meta-analysis (surgical site infection [SII] and recurrence) and a narrative synthesis (major postoperative bleeding and time to complete healing), adapting comparisons to the degree of homogeneity across studies. Key outcomes included SSI, major postoperative bleeding and average time to complete wound healing. Results Comparative analysis showed a lower SSI rate with the modified technique (0.6%) compared with the pooled proportion reported for Ferguson´s technique (2.0%). Major postoperative bleeding was absent (0.0%) in the institutional cohort. Recurrence rate were comparable (5.2% modified vs 4.0% pooled). The mean time to complete healing was 35.2 days, although direct comparison was limited by heterogeneity in reporting among published studies. Conclusion Modified closed hemorrhoidectomy with anodermal marsupialization demonstrated a clear Clinical advantage in reduce early morbidity, particularly rate of SSI. This technique appears to be a feasible and safe alternative to the classic approach, supporting the need for prospective studies with standardized outcome reporting to validate its effectiveness.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.038.title: 1392 Adherence to NICE Guidance for Endometrial Cancer Detection in Women ≥55 Years Referred With Visible Haematuria: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.038.abstract: Abstract Aim NICE guidelines recommend direct access pelvic ultrasound for women aged ≥55 years presenting with visible haematuria and/or abnormal cancer risk markers (unexplained anaemia, thrombocytosis, or hyperglycaemia) to exclude endometrial cancer. However, awareness and implementation of this guidance within urology remain variable. This audit aimed to assess local adherence to NICE guidance and its diagnostic yield for endometrial cancer in this population. Method A retrospective audit was conducted of all female patients aged ≥55 years referred to the haematuria clinic in 2023. Data collected included demographics, haematuria type, blood results, imaging, referral pathway, ultrasound utilisation, and cancer outcomes. Adherence was defined as performance of pelvic ultrasound in patients meeting NICE criteria. Results 216 patients were reviewed. Overall compliance with NICE guidance was 1/17 (5.8%). Three patients (1.3%) were diagnosed with endometrial cancer. Flexible cystoscopy was normal in all three cases. CT urography failed to identify gynaecological pathology in one patient. Trans-abdominal ultrasound detected endometrial thickening in one case, prompting urgent gynaecology referral and cancer diagnosis. The third patient had a pre-existing diagnosis as she was referred simultaneously to urology and gynaecology due to unclear bleeding source. None of the three patients met NICE haematological or biochemical trigger criteria. Conclusions This audit demonstrates poor adherence to NICE guidance due to limited awareness within the flexible cystoscopy team. Failure to perform pelvic ultrasound risks delayed cancer diagnosis, particularly as CT urography alone is insufficient to exclude endometrial pathology. Urologists should proactively apply NICE criteria and ensure early gynaecological referrals to improve diagnostic safety and pathway efficiency.
affiliations: Ashford and St Peter's Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Chertsey ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.265.title: 1029 Time to Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) in Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Two Cycle Audit at a Rural District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.265.abstract: Abstract Aim At Dumfries & Galloway Royal Infirmary, a rural district general hospital, referrals for the management of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (AUGIB) with oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) are the responsibility of the on-call general surgeons. This audit assessed local compliance with NICE guidance, which recommends OGD within 24 hours of admission. Method A retrospective cohort study of all AUGIB OGD referrals over 10 months was conducted. It was agreed that formally including the AUGIB caseload in the on-call handover could improve timely access to OGD, and this change was implemented. A second 10-month audit cycle was undertaken one month after implementation. Results In cycle one, 60 patients underwent OGD, and 32% (n=19) received it within 24 hours. In cycle two, 89 patients underwent OGD, but only 16% (n=14) met the 24-hour target. Intervention rates were similar (11.7% [n=7] vs. 11.1% [n=11]). Conclusions Implementing formal discussion of the AUGIB OGD caseload at handover did not improve compliance with NICE guidance on the timing of OGD after AUGIB. The increase in AUGIB OGD caseload during the second cycle likely had a significant impact on this outcome, and, coupled with a similar intervention rate, supports the case for a dedicated emergency OGD list to meet this clinical need.
affiliations: Department of General Surgery, Dumfries & Galloway Royal Infirmary , Dumfries ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.165.title: 134 Audit of Implant Selection for Simple Proximal Femoral Fractures at North Manchester General Hospital: Sliding Hip Screws Versus Short Intramedullary Nails
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.165.abstract: Abstract Introduction Sliding hip screws (SHS) and short intramedullary nails (IMN) achieve equivalent clinical outcomes for AO A1/A2 proximal femoral fractures. The NHFD confirms the majority of these simple fracture patterns are treated with SHS in the UK however some centres almost exclusively utilise IMN with no proven benefit. We investigated current practice at North Manchester General Hospital using a retrospective consecutive case series analysis. Method 106 patients with proximal femoral hip fractures were identified from the NHFD records treated Jan-Dec 2024. 55 patients treated with short IMN and 51 treated with SHS. Case notes, blood results and images from the electronic patient record were analysed using the consensus of parametric non-parametric tests. Results There were no statistical differences between the two techniques regarding age, gender, ASA status, preoperative hemoglobin, perioperative delay, methods of anaesthesia and post-operative mobility. 120-day mortality (12%) and revision surgery rates (0%) were the same for both groups. SHS performed statistically better (p<0.05) in relation to post-operative hemoglobin levels (101 vs 91 g/dl), surgical time (29 minutes faster) and length of hospital stay (16 vs 23 days). 28 of 55 fractures treated with short IMN could have been treated with SHS (AO A1/A2). Conclusion NICE UK recommend SHS for AO type A1/A2 hip fractures, the implant is non inferior and more cost effective than short IMN. Our study revealed that over half of patients treated with short IMN could have been treated with SHS. SHS demonstrated modest clinical and cost benefits over the IMN implants despite a small sample size.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.638.title: 828 Improving Access to Lymph Node FNA: An Audit of Diagnostic Timelines, Inconclusive Rates, and Outcomes in Cutaneous Malignancy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.638.abstract: Abstract Introduction Fine needle aspiration (FNA) under ultrasound (USS) guidance is the first-line investigation for lymphadenopathy in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) and melanoma according to Cheshire and Merseyside guidelines. The Faster Diagnosis Standard (FDS) requires diagnosis or exclusion within 28 days. This audit evaluated diagnostic delays, inconclusive rates, and inefficiencies in the pathway for melanoma and cSCC patients undergoing USS-guided FNA. Method A retrospective analysis was performed for patients referred for USS-guided lymph node assessment between 1st August 2024 and 28th August 2025. Electronic notes, histology, USS reports, and FNA outcomes were reviewed. Fifty-eight diagnostic cases were included. Primary outcomes included median times from lymph node detection to FNA, from FNA to histology, and overall time to diagnostic confirmation. Secondary outcomes included inconclusive FNA rates, repeat sampling, and subsequent management decisions, compared with GIRFT standards. Results Of the 58 diagnostic nodal scans performed on radiology consultant lists, 22 patients (38%) underwent FNA, while 36 did not require biopsy. Over half of FNAs confirmed metastatic disease requiring surgical or systemic treatment. The median time from detection to FNA result exceeded the 28-day target by 8 days. Inconclusive FNAs nearly doubled diagnostic timelines, with an average of 62.5 days to final diagnosis after repeat sampling. Conclusions The major delay occurred between lymph node detection and USS/FNA, largely due to limited radiology consultant capacity and the absence of two-week-wait prioritisation. Evidence supports surgeon-performed USS/FNA to improve access and reduce delays. Expanding surgical-led USS and integrating USS/FNA training into surgical curricula would streamline diagnostic pathways.
affiliations: Mersey West Lancashire NHS Trust , Liverpool ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.261.title: 973 Assessing the Quality of TURBT: A Comprehensive 18-Month Audit from a UK District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.261.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the quality of transurethral resection of bladder tumour at a district general hospital, focusing on detrusor muscle sampling, documentation standards, Mitomycin C instillation, adherence to EAU indications for re-resection, and early recurrence patterns. Method A retrospective review was conducted of all first TURBTs performed between January 2023 and July 2024 (n=101). Data collected included tumour stage and grade, presence of detrusor muscle, operative documentation, MMC use, operator grade, re-TURBT indications and findings, and recurrence at 3 and 12 months. Results were compared with BAUS and EAU guideline standards. Operator case volume was considered when interpreting individual performance, including procedures carried out during a period of locum consultant cover. Results Detrusor muscle was present in 55.4% of specimens, below the BAUS standard of 70%. Documentation was variable, with tumour number recorded in 86%, tumour size in 84%, and completeness of resection in 78% of cases. MMC was administered in 53.5% of all cases and 58.8% of eligible NMIBC cases. Forty-three patients underwent re-TURBT; 39 met EAU indications, while four had no clear indication. Residual tumour was identified in seven patients, and one case was upstaged from T1 to T2. Recurrences were documented in nine patients at 3 months and eight at 12 months, mainly within the high-risk cohort. Conclusions The audit demonstrates reasonable adherence to BAUS re-TURBT criteria and MMC usage, but highlights areas for improvement, particularly muscle sampling and documentation. A standardised TURBT operative template and targeted education are being introduced, with plans to re-audit following these interventions.
affiliations: East Surrey Hospital , Redhill ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.210.title: 288 Improving Operation Note Documentation Against Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) Standards: A Completed Audit Cycle in the Department of Surgery, Holy Family Hospital, Pakistan
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.210.abstract: Abstract Aim Incomplete operation notes compromise postoperative management, handover, and medicolegal accountability. We aimed to audit operation-note compliance in surgical unit 1, Holy Family Hospital, Pakistan, against the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) Good Surgical Documentation Checklist and evaluate the standardized performa with real-time theater reminders. Method A two-cycle retrospective clinical audit was performed. Cycle-1 reviewed 100 consecutive emergency and elective major general surgery notes against the 23 RCS documentation elements (2022). Interventions included the introduction of a revised RCS-based operation note template, real-time OT reminders, and staff awareness feedback in morning meetings. Cycl-2 was reaudited six weeks post-intervention. Patient data and identifiers were anonymized and confidential. Results Cycle-1 showed critical absence of 5 RCS elements in all notes (n=100): estimated blood loss, antibiotic prophylaxis, time-in, complications, and nature of surgery (0%). Other major deficiencies appeared in the operative diagnosis (30%), OT staff names (43%), anesthesiologist details (73%), incision details (70%), and DVT prophylaxis in 3/37 relevant cases (8.1%). Furthermore, a greater completion rate (>95%) was highlighted in the remaining elements, e.g., surgeon name, operative findings, postoperative care instructions, assistant name, procedure name, and time out. Following intervention, cycle-2 demonstrated significant improvement across 22/23 elements as highlighted in complications (98%), time-in (89%), estimated blood loss (96%), and antibiotic and DVT prophylaxis (83% and 80%, respectively). OT staff names were the least compliant across all elements (71%). Conclusions A standardized RCS-based template combined with low-resource OT reminders and staff feedback produced high improvement in operation-note compliance, supporting patients' postoperative care and improved medicolegal accountability.
affiliations: Holy Family Hospital , Islamabad ,
Rawalpindi Medical University, Holy Family Hospital , Islamabad ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.145.title: 727 Implementing High-Risk Criteria to Optimise Perioperative Antibiotic Use in Hernia Surgery: A Two-Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.145.abstract: Abstract Aim European Hernia Society (EHS) guidelines recommend perioperative antibiotics only for high-risk hernia repairs, yet overuse remains common in clinical practice. We conducted two audit cycles to evaluate local compliance with these guidelines and implemented a targeted intervention to reduce unnecessary antibiotic administration. Method All adult patients undergoing elective or emergency groin, umbilical, epigastric, or ventral hernia repair were included. Incisional, parastomal, and complex abdominal wall repairs were excluded. Cycle 1 findings were presented locally and nationally, after which a departmental intervention was introduced: a standardised set of “high-risk criteria” (e.g. smoking status, large umbilical hernia, immunosuppression, or recurrent hernia cases) that defined when perioperative antibiotics were indicated. Data was extracted from operative and perioperative documentation. Antibiotic use was treated as a binary variable. Descriptive statistics were calculated, and differences between cycles were analysed using a two-proportion z-test. Results Cycle 1 included 227 hernia repairs (173 elective; 54 emergency), with perioperative antibiotics administered in 89% of elective groin, 85% of elective ventral/umbilical, and 80% of emergency repairs (combined usage 87.8%, SD 0.33). After introduction of the high-risk criteria, Cycle 2 (n=262) demonstrated a reduction in antibiotic use to 48.1% (SD 0.50), representing a 39.7% absolute decrease (p < 0.0001). Postoperative complication rates remained low and did not increase between cycles. Conclusions Implementation of clearly defined high-risk criteria, coupled with departmental education, led to a substantial and statistically significant reduction in perioperative antibiotic use without compromising patient safety. This demonstrates that simple, evidence-aligned interventions can effectively improve antimicrobial stewardship in hernia surgery.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.218.title: 406 The Long Road Home: A Single-Centre Audit into Postoperative LOS After Aortic Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.218.abstract: Abstract Aim Open aortic surgery is high-stakes and high-risk for long recovery. The aim of this audit was to assess LOS after open aortic surgery, compare characteristics between patients with standard versus prolonged LOS, and identify opportunities to improve perioperative flow. Method All patients undergoing open aortic surgery from January 2024 to September 2025 were included. Of the fifty-two, two remained inpatient and were excluded. Patients were divided into Group 1 (LOS ≤7 days; n=13) and Group 2 (LOS >7 days; n=37). Demographics, ASA grade, operative complexity, level of postoperative care, ICU LOS, and ICU step-down delays were analysed. Results Only 26% of patients achieved the national benchmark LOS of ≤7 days. Group 1 had lower perioperative risk (30% ASA 2; 70% ASA 3), whereas Group 2 had greater physiological burden (24.3% ASA 2; 62.1% ASA 3; 10.9% ASA 4; 2.7% ASA 5). Median ICU LOS was shorter in Group 1 (3 days) compared to Group 2 (7 days). All Group 1 procedures were infrarenal AAA repairs, while Group 2 included complex cases such as TAAA, JRAAA, aorto-iliac repair, and ruptures. Higher levels of postoperative support were more common in Group 2, with 32.4% requiring Level 3 care versus 15.3% in Group 1. Overall, 54% of patients experienced step-down delays despite clinical readiness. Conclusions Prolonged LOS was associated with greater patient complexity, higher ASA grade, and delays in ICU step-down. In response, our unit will implement a structured ICU de-escalation protocol and explore adoption of a vascular-specific ERAS pathway to streamline recovery and reduce delays.
affiliations: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.741.title: 328 Is It Our Culture to Culture? a Second-Loop Audit of Preoperative MSU Screening Prior to Endourological Procedures
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.741.abstract: Abstract Background Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) remains a significant contributor to peri-operative delays and complications in urological surgery. Whilst EUA (2024) recommends treating ASB, GIRFT (2025) emphasises tailored urine testing prior to procedures that breach the mucosa. Local practice in the first audit loop demonstrated poor MSU uptake and suboptimal management of positive cultures. This second-loop audit evaluates the impact of implemented changes within the Pre-Operative Assessment Clinic (POAC) and Microbiology team. Method A retrospective review of 73 patients undergoing endourological procedures (TURP, TURBT, FURS, URS) between July–August 2025 was conducted, three months after new screening pathways were introduced. Data were collected from theatre lists, operation notes, discharge summaries, and microbiology results. Primary outcomes were MSU submission rates and actioning of positive cultures; secondary outcomes included postoperative infections. Results MSU uptake improved from 3.8% in the first loop to 47.9% (35/73). Of the samples submitted, 13 (37.1%) were culture-positive; however, only 3 patients received documented antibiotic treatment. No postoperative infections or infection-related admissions were recorded. Despite improvement, compliance remains below the expected 100% standard, with several positive results demonstrating no evidence of clinical action. Limitations Challenges included incomplete documentation of antibiotics issued outside hospital systems, patient compliance with sampling instructions, and capturing individuals assessed prior to policy changes. Conclusions Enhanced POAC and microbiology processes substantially improved MSU submission rates; however, management of positive cultures remains inconsistent. Further refinement of patient information, documentation practices, and microbiology processing pathways is required. A re-audit is planned following refinement of the local protocol.
affiliations: Leighton Hospital , Crewe ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.541.title: 1247 Audit of Single-Centre Timing for Acute Major Nerve Repair
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.541.abstract: Abstract Introduction Optimal timing for acute major nerve repair remains undefined. Experimental studies show irreversible deterioration from 72 hours post-injury, supporting early repair, but clinical thresholds are unclear. This study evaluates whether time to surgery influences outcomes following complete median and ulnar nerve repair. Aim To assess the impact of surgical timing on motor and sensory recovery after acute median and ulnar nerve transection. Method A retrospective cohort (December 2017–September 2025) included adults with complete median or ulnar nerve transections distal to the elbow, treated with end-to-end or graft repair. Decompressions, transfers, non-traumatic causes and cases without MRC follow-up data were excluded. Extracted variables included time to surgery, follow-up duration and final MRC and TENS scores. Outcomes were analysed by <72 h versus ≥72 h repair and via Spearman correlation. Results Seventy-two repairs had complete motor outcomes (27 median, 45 ulnar); 76.4% were male. Overall, 65.3% achieved ≥M3 and 45.8% ≥M4. 76% underwent repair <72 h, with ≥M3 recovery of 65.5% (<72 h) versus 64.7% (≥72 h). Mean time to repair was 74.2 ± 32.7 h; median 38.7 h (IQR 49.5). Median follow-up was 828.8 days (IQR 847.5). Final scores showed median MRC 4 (IQR 3.5) and TENS 5 (IQR 5). Time to surgery showed a weak negative association with motor recovery (ρ = –0.26, p = 0.19) and a moderate negative association with sensory recovery (ρ = –0.38, p = 0.043). Conclusions Earlier repair trends toward improved outcomes, but optimal timing remains uncertain. Prospective multicentre evaluation is needed.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.418.title: 1186 Outpatient Colonoscopy After Appendicectomy in Patients Over the Age of 40: Clinical Audit of Compliance in Practice
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.418.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is commonly triggered by obstruction of the appendiceal lumen or orifice. Multiple studies have highlighted increased risk of underlying colonic malignancy in older adults presenting with acute appendicitis. This audit aimed to evaluate compliance with recommending postoperative outpatient colonoscopy or CT colonography in patients aged ≥40 undergoing appendicectomy, and to assess the effectiveness of an intervention designed to improve adherence to this local guideline. Method An audit was conducted in two cycles at a district general hospital. The first cycle included patients aged ≥40 who underwent emergency appendicectomy between February and October 2024. The second cycle followed implementation of an action plan, consisting of educational email with supporting evidence sent to surgical teams, and included patients from March to July 2025. Electronic clinical records were reviewed for demographics, imaging, operative findings, histology and documentation of postoperative colonic evaluation. Exclusion criteria were primary appendiceal tumours, conversion to right hemicolectomy, recent prior colonic imaging, or other intraoperative findings. Results Cycle 1 included 67 patients. Only 25 patients (37.3%) were referred for postoperative colonic evaluation, and no malignant/premalignant lesions were identified. Cycle 2 included 45 patients. Following the intervention, referral rates improved substantially, with 28 patients (62.2%) receiving appropriate postoperative colonic evaluation—almost doubling compliance. Notably, two patients were found to have proximal ascending colon polyps, one demonstrating high-grade dysplasia. Conclusions This audit demonstrates significantly improving compliance with postoperative colonic evaluation in patients aged ≥40 following appendicectomy. Ongoing reinforcement and further re-audit are planned, aiming for early detection of caecal and colorectal pathology.
affiliations: Broomfield Hospital, Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust , Chelmsford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.245.title: 756 Junior Clinicians Can Deliver Safe ENT Emergency Care: Audit of Otitis Externa Management
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.245.abstract: Abstract Aim The Ear, Nose and Throat Emergency Clinic (E clinic) at a UK tertiary hospital is staffed by junior clinicians from F1 to ST2 level. It manages a defined set of urgent presentations including recurrent epistaxis, sudden sensorineural hearing loss, and otitis externa (OE). This first cycle of a three-part audit evaluated the ability of junior clinicians to manage OE safely and effectively, with specific focus on recognition of scope of practice and appropriate senior escalation. Method A retrospective review identified 243 true cases of OE. A random sample of 100 appointments were analysed. Data collected included documentation quality, escalation decisions, antimicrobial choice, swab use, and safety related prescribing behaviours. Errors were categorised using predefined criteria. Results 40 appointments involved suspected complication or atypical features including possible cholesteatoma, persistent otalgia, or hearing loss following infection resolution. Of these, 24 were escalated appropriately to the on-call registrar or consultant led clinic, while 16 showed no documented escalation. Antimicrobial prescribing was determined appropriate in 78% of cases, based on empirical need or prior swab results. Common errors included inadequate documentation, insufficient microbial coverage, and unnecessary steroid use. Five cases involved prescription of an ototoxic topical medication without documented visualisation of an intact tympanic membrane, and 1 case involved ototoxic prescribing despite a documented perforation. Conclusions OE can be effectively managed within a junior led clinic. However, safety and consistency could be improved ahead of the second audit cycle through supportive protocolisation and structured induction teaching.
affiliations: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.718.title: 858 Audit of Management of Warfarin Reversal for Patients With Atrial Fibrillation Undergoing Hip Fracture Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.718.abstract: Abstract Aim NICE guideline recommends that patients with hip fracture undergo surgery on the day of or the day after admission. However, patients receiving warfarin often experience delays due to the need for anticoagulation reversal, potentially worsening outcomes. This audit evaluated warfarin reversal management in patients with atrial fibrillation and its impact on time to surgery in a district general hospital. Method A retrospective review was conducted using the National Hip Fracture Database for patients admitted locally between March 2021 and March 2023. Electronic records, clinical notes, and imaging were examined. Data collected included demographics, time to surgery, warfarin reversal strategy, and postoperative outcomes. Patients taking warfarin for indications other than atrial fibrillation or with incomplete data were excluded. Results Of 568 hip fracture local admissions, five patients (0.8%) met inclusion criteria (mean age 90.2 years). Mean admission and preoperative INR values were 2.8 and 1.3, respectively. All patients received intravenous vitamin K. The median time from radiological confirmation of hip fracture to vitamin K administration was 8 hours. Mean time from emergency department arrival to surgery was 43.2 hours, with three patients meeting NICE surgical timing targets. 3 patients received general anaesthetic while 2 were done under spinal. One patient died within 30 days post-operative from hospital-acquired pneumonia. Conclusions Only three out of five patients met NICE standards for time to surgery, with delays primarily related to inconsistent preoperative warfarin management. Standardised warfarin management protocols and improved staff education are recommended to reduce variability and optimise surgical timing.
affiliations: Wrexham Maelor Hospital , Wrexham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.041.title: 853 Optimizing Supported Consent for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: An Audit of a DGH
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.041.abstract: Abstract Aim To improve patients’ preoperative understanding of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (LC) ensuring better-informed consent. To ensure the documentation of the supported consent process meets the standard of the GMC's Guidance on Informed Consent. Method A Pilot audit tested a survey tool designed on Microsoft Forms on 8 patients. The tool was refined with advice from industry experts and administered to 42 patients on the morning of their operation. Questions evaluated retention of complications of LC (eg, Bile leak) and the documentation of the consent process, including receipt of both an eConsent form via email to deliberate upon and the EIDO LC patient information leaflet (PIL). The patient was asked what a gallbladder was. Separate forms were used to capture “SHO” grades and consultant opinions. Results Despite 88% receiving the EIDO PIL, 19% of patients did not know what a Gallbladder was or described the wrong organ. 76% of patients had a day-of-surgery consent. 50% of consultants said they weren’t allocated enough time to initiate consent to this standard. SHO grades were unsure they understood the potential procedural complications, but they ‘took’ day-of-surgery consent, nevertheless. Conclusions Consent and its documentation have not kept pace with its modern expectations, for LCs done at our DGH. A department teaching session was conducted. SHOs are now being allocated to clinics with consultants. Two videos are being made: a training video for SHOs that covers initiating the consent process and an operative video of a representative LC for patients. The effect of these will be subsequently measured.
affiliations: Royal United Hospitals Bath NHS Foundation Trust , Bath ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.155.title: 577 An Audit of the Assessment and Management of Paediatric Patients Undergoing Emergency Scrotal Exploration at a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.155.abstract: Abstract Aim ‘Gold standard’ investigation and treatment of testicular torsion is emergency scrotal exploration within 4-6 hours, with delays increasing the risk of orchidectomy. The NCEPOD Twist and Shout report found use of the TWIST score and Doppler ultrasound significantly increased finding torsion at exploration without increasing orchidectomy rate. GIRFT subsequently published a national pathway responding to those findings and recommendations. Our aim was to audit practice in our DGH general surgery department against this pathway. Method Data were analysed from all paediatric emergency scrotal explorations 2020-2023, calculating percentage compliance against seven of the pathway standards. Results were presented, with teaching on the TWIST score and creation of guideline posters for display in general surgery and PED. The re-audit then analysed data 2024-2025. Results There were 23 cases initially and 15 in the re-audit.70% were seen in one or fewer healthcare settings both cycles40% improving to 50% were seen by a surgical decision maker within 60 minutes of ED arrival0% documented a TWIST score in both cycles18% improving to 50% had an USS if >48 hours of pain0% were in theatre within one hour in both cycles67% improving to 75% of those who had an orchidectomy were followed up Conclusions After the interventions, there was some improvement in meeting the GIRFT standards. Improvements can still be made, particularly in the use of the TWIST score and timing to review and theatre. Ensuring teaching as registrars rotate and adequate display of the guideline posters should help.
affiliations: Sherwood Forest Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Sutton-in-Ashfield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.751.title: 730 Are We Over-Stenting? a Single-Centre Audit of Ureteric Stent Use After Uncomplicated Ureteroscopy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.751.abstract: Abstract Aim Guidelines advise against routine ureteric stenting after uncomplicated ureteroscopy (URS) for stones, yet practice varies considerably. The aim of this audit was to evaluate local stent use following uncomplicated rigid or flexible URS and compare post-operative outcomes between stented and non-stented patients. Method All uncomplicated RURS/FURS procedures with presumed complete stone clearance performed between January and December 2024 at a single centre were reviewed. Exclusions included planned second-stage URS, PCNL/ECIRS, concomitant procedures, and non-stone indications. Outcomes assessed were stent insertion rate, day-case vs inpatient stay, 30-day emergency re-presentations, and complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥2). Results A total of 143 URS procedures met inclusion criteria: 91 stented (63.6%) and 52 non-stented (36.4%). Among stented patients, 56 (61.5%) were day cases and 35 (38.5%) required overnight admission (mean stay 1.2 days, range 1-5). In the non-stented cohort, 39 (75%) were day cases and 13 (25%) were admitted (mean stay 1.2 days, range 1-3). Emergency re-presentations occurred in 7 stented patients (7.7%; 2 pain, 5 UTI) and 2 non-stented patients (3.8%; 1 pain, 1 UTI). One stented patient developed a ureteric stricture; one non-stented patient had a calyceal perforation requiring nephrostomy. Overall complication rates were low and comparable between groups. Conclusions Routine stenting after uncomplicated URS did not reduce re-presentation or complication rates. These findings support more selective stent use and improved adherence to guideline recommendations to reduce avoidable morbidity.
affiliations: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.508.title: 792 IR-Guided Cerebral Angiograms: A Local Audit of RCR Compliance
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.508.abstract: Abstract Aim IR-guided cerebral angiography is central to the diagnosis and management of cerebrovascular disease. This audit evaluated local practice against Royal College of Radiologists (RCR) standards with particular attention to complication rates and documentation quality. Method Data collected between April and October 2025, obtained from WebICE, PACS (angiogram reports), the departmental angiogram log and collated in Excel. Practice was assessed against key RCR standards, including documented written consent (100%), accurate procedural documentation (100%), and complication benchmarks: pseudoaneurysm/AV fistula ≤1%, access-site haematoma requiring intervention ≤3%, arterial dissection ≤1%, reversible neurological deficit ≤2%, permanent neurological deficit ≤1% and major contrast reactions ≤5%. Results A total of 206 procedures were performed, comprising mainly diagnostic DSA (n=175) and embolization (n=60). Common indications included subarachnoid hemorrhage, incidental aneurysm and follow-up imaging. Complications recorded were: groin hematoma with pseudoaneurysm (n=2), pseudoaneurysm with groin hematoma (n=6; managed with 2 surgical repairs, 3 thrombin injections, and 1 conservatively), procedure-related bleeding (n=4;two required craniotomy) and procedure-related stroke (n=4). Thirteen deaths occurred within the cohort, predominantly reflecting underlying pathology rather than procedure-related harm. Conclusions Complication rates were broadly in line with RCR thresholds, although the frequency of pseudoaneurysm formation exceeded the ≤1% target, highlighting a need to strengthen ultrasound-guided access and post-procedure monitoring. Documentation standards and consent recording were consistent but further streamlining is planned. Recommendations have been implemented and a re-audit will reassess compliance.
affiliations: South Tees NHS Trust , Middlesbrough ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.251.title: 844 Evaluating the Accuracy of CT Reported Uncomplicated Appendicitis Versus Intraoperative Findings: A Single Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.251.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the accuracy of CT reports in correctly identifying and classifying complicated versus uncomplicated appendicitis through comparison with intraoperative findings. Method A single-centre retrospective audit was conducted over a 3-month period (14/08/25–15/11/25). All adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis for suspected appendicitis and proceeded to appendicectomy were included. Complicated appendicitis was defined intraoperatively as perforation, abscess, phlegmon, or gangrenous change. Data extracted included CT classification, reporting radiologist grade, timing of consultant radiologist addenda, pre-operative inflammatory markers, operative findings, histology if applicable and time from CT to theatre. Diagnostic accuracy metrics were calculated. Results A total of 33 patients were included. CT correctly identified four of 13 cases with complicated appendicitis and 16 of 18 cases with uncomplicated appendicitis. We noted two patients labelled as uncomplicated appendicitis on CT had no appendicitis at surgery and two patients with a normal appendix on CT had uncomplicated appendicitis intraoperatively. For detection of complicated appendicitis, CT yielded a sensitivity of 31%, specificity 100%, positive-predictive value of 100%, negative-predictive value of 69%, and a false-negative rate of 69%, indicating substantial under-detection of complicated disease. Conclusions A substantial proportion of complicated appendicitis was not recognised on CT interpretation, with nearly 70% of complicated cases misclassified as uncomplicated. These findings highlight the need to improve reporting precision, strengthen radiology–surgical communication, and review local pathways to reduce diagnostic delay and optimise patient outcomes.
affiliations: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.204.title: 65 Improvement of FY1 Fluid Review Quality in Urology Using a Novel Electronic Proforma: A 2-Cycle Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.204.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aimed to assess the quality of FY1 fluid reviews within a high-volume tertiary Urology centre and to implement a novel electronic proforma to improve compliance with NICE guidelines on fluid assessment. A secondary aim was to evaluate FY1 confidence in performing fluid reviews and enhance this through targeted teaching. Method All documented FY1 fluid reviews over two weeks (02/09/24–15/09/24) were prospectively collected using our electronic clinical software TrakCare, recording compliance with NICE-defined clinical parameters. FY1 confidence in fluid prescription was assessed via an anonymous questionnaire (response rate 75%, n=15) using a 5-point Likert scale. An electronic proforma, incorporating NICE-recommended review parameters as headers, was subsequently introduced into TrakCare, accompanied by Urology-specific fluid management teaching to all FYs. The audit was then repeated over three weeks (11/11/24–01/12/24), with follow-up questionnaires distributed (response rate 50%, n=10). Data were analysed using Stata-BE v19.0 for Mac. Results There were 26 reviews in the first cycle and 23 in the second. Following proforma implementation, documentation improved significantly for recording fluid balance (78% vs 38%, p<0.01), heart rate (96% vs 35%, p<0.01), and blood pressure (96% vs 38%, p<0.01) amongst other clinical features.
