Initially, 27% of FY1s reported sufficient fluid management teaching prior to starting FY1 and 27% had confidence in performing reviews, increasing to 90% post-intervention. Conclusions The introduction of an electronic proforma significantly enhanced FY1 documentation and compliance with NICE fluid assessment standards. Focused teaching and the structured electronic prompt improved FY1 confidence in fluid management.
affiliations: Western General Hospital , Edinburgh ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.304.title: 333 Rates and Outcomes of Renal Replacement Therapy in Post-Cardiac Surgery Patients: A Single-Centre Audit Against National Recommendations
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.304.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute renal failure is a recognised complication after cardiac surgery and is associated with increased mortality and prolonged length of stay (LOS). National guidance recommends benchmarking rates of renal replacement therapy (RRT). This study aims to describe the rates, preoperative factors, outcomes associated with RRT in post-cardiac surgery patients at a single institution. Method This is a retrospective audit of all adult cardiac surgery between January 2019 and October 2024 at Northern General Hospital, Sheffield. Demographics, comorbidities, operative variables, postoperative outcomes were compared between patients requiring RRT and others. Results were benchmarked against GIRFT and NICOR data. Results Of 3,261 patients, 90 required RRT (1.14%), below the GIRFT 2018 benchmark (1.56%). However, isolated CABG had a higher RRT rate (2.76%) than NICOR reports (0.98–1.45%). Mortality was significantly higher in RRT cohort (33.3% vs 2.2%, p < 0.0001). Lower pre-operative eGFR (50 vs 73 ml/min/1.73m², p < 0.0001). EuroSCORE was an independent predictor, with 16.4% increase (OR 1.164, 95% CI 1.101–1.232). Complex procedures and prolonged aortic cross-clamp time were strongly associated with RRT (p < 0.0001 and p = 0.0469, respectively). Patients requiring RRT had longer hospital stays (38.41 vs. 15.91 days, p < 0.0001) and higher reoperation rates (6.7% vs. 1.6%, p = 0.0014). Median RRT duration was 6 days; early RRT (1–3 days) was associated with the highest mortality. Conclusions RRT after cardiac surgery remains infrequent but carries increased mortality and LOS. Pre-existing renal dysfunction, CVA, higher EuroSCORE and complex surgery significantly predict postoperative RRT.
affiliations: Northern General Hospital , Sheffield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.104.title: 1080 Assessing Surgical Education and Exposure Amongst Foundation Trainees in the Yorkshire and the Humber Deanery: A Comparative Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.104.abstract: Abstract Introduction National concern persists regarding limited operative exposure and training opportunities for Foundation Doctors in surgical posts. This Yorkshire and the Humber deanery-wide audit evaluates the adequacy of surgical training opportunities and preparedness for Core Surgical Training (CST) relative to accepted standards. Method A questionnaire was distributed to Foundation Year 1 and 2 Doctors across the Yorkshire and the Humber deanery assessing hospital size, surgical specialty, theatre exposure, procedural experience and career guidance. Descriptive and comparative analyses (F1 vs F2; district general hospital (DGH) vs tertiary centres) were performed, with audit standards derived from RCS England, GMC NTS 2024, and GIRFT productivity guidance. Results 82 responses were analysed (F1 n=51, F2 n=31). 96% undertook at least one surgical post in the 2024-25 year; 54.9% expressed interest in a surgical career. Only 42% had consistent theatre access, 25.9% assisted in surgical procedures, 11% received regular feedback and 20.5% reported career guidance; further, 8% felt prepared for CST. Quality ratings clustered at 1–2 of 5 and DGH vs tertiary differences were small with both underperforming benchmarks. Identified barriers to training include: rota gaps, list cancellations, and lack of protected time. Conclusions Surgical exposure for Yorkshire and the Humber Foundation Doctors falls substantially below national expectations. Deficits in theatre access, procedural supervision, feedback, and mentorship threaten early surgical skill development and CST readiness amid rising competition ratios (2025 candidate ratio ≈8.6:1). Targeted interventions at hospital, trust, deanery, and national levels are required to restore training quality and equity.
affiliations: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Bradford ,
Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust , Hull ,
Doncaster and Bassetlaw Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Doncaster ,
York and Scarborough NHS Foundation Trust , Scarborough ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.259.title: 902 Day-of-Surgery Cancellations as a Systemic Burden in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Evidence from a Four-Month Audit at a Tertiary Care Center
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.259.abstract: Abstract Aim Elective surgery cancellations on the day of operation remain a major challenge for operating room efficiency, resource utilization, and patient experience. These issues are amplified in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where surgical capacity is limited and waiting lists are long. This study evaluated the frequency, patterns, and preventable causes of day-of-surgery cancellations over four consecutive months (April–July 2025) at a tertiary care center in Nepal, with a focus on identifying system gaps and actionable improvement pathways. Method A retrospective review of operating theatre records was performed, including all elective cases cancelled on the day of surgery. Reasons for cancellation were categorized into patient non-arrival, medical unfitness, pending investigations, surgeon/hospital factors, and financial constraint. Descriptive analysis was used to assess monthly trends and specialty-specific contributions. Results A total of 356 cancellations were recorded, rising from 77 in April to 101 in July. Patient non-arrival was the leading cause (49%), indicating significant gaps in pre-operative communication, counselling, and logistical preparedness. Medical unfitness accounted for 32% of cancellations, mostly due to poorly optimized chronic conditions. Gastrointestinal surgery contributed the highest share of cancellations (41%), followed by urology (22%) and orthopaedics (20%). A notable rise in medically related cancellations was observed in July, indicating possible gap in pre-operative checkup and optimization. Conclusions Day-of-surgery cancellations remain alarmingly high, with nearly four-fifths attributable to potentially preventable causes. Improved pre-operative communication, mandatory early pre-anesthetic checkup (PAC) completion, structured patient counselling, and robust checklist enforcement could significantly reduce avoidable cancellations and enhance operating room efficiency.
affiliations: Dhulikhel Hospital , Dhulikhel ,
Kathmandu University School of Medical Sciences , Dhulikhel ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.100.title: 1063 Audit of Acute Mesenteric Ischaemia: Presentation, Aetiology and Management, at Basildon & Thurrock University Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.100.abstract: Abstract Introduction Acute Mesenteric Ischaemia (AMI) is characterised by vascular compromise of bowel which, without resolution, results in ischaemia and is associated with significant mortality which reportedly varies from 30% to 80%. Aim To review patients with confirmed AMI, assessing their initial presentations, underlying aetiologies and subsequent management outcomes. Method Surgical admission records at Basildon hospital were retrospectively reviewed between 2010 and 2023. A total of 112 eligible patients were identified with a primary diagnosis code of AMI. Subsequently inpatient records were reviewed, and relevant data related to diagnosis and management of AMI was extracted. Results The most prevalent primary cause of AMI was arterial thrombosis, representing 38%. Followed by venous thrombosis and non-occlusive intestinal ischaemia (NOMI),15% and 13% respectively. Categorical CT scan proven AMI was demonstrated in 63% of cases, with “high index of suspicion” observed in a further 6% of cases. Where undertaken, Mesenteric angiography confirmed AMI in 12%. 46 patients (41%) underwent surgery. In cases in which CT had not shown AMI, 15 (13% of total cases) had it diagnosed intra-operatively. Total cohort mortality within 24 hours of admission was 16%, a further 39% died within 90 days and 2% within a year. Conclusions Our findings reflect that AMI arises from several underlying aetiologies and often present with a range of non-specific symptoms, making early recognition challenging. In line with World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) guidance, CT angiography is integral in rapid diagnosis and timely decision-making. Minimising delays is essential to reduce morbidity and improve patient outcomes.
affiliations: Basildon University Hospital , Basildon ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.609.title: 1431 Rectal Cancer Outcomes at a UK Tertiary Centre: A Five-Year Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.609.abstract: Abstract Introduction Rectal cancer management has evolved significantly over the years, with increasing use of minimally invasive techniques, neoadjuvant therapy, and non-operative management. Understanding local outcomes is essential for evaluating services, identifying areas for improvement, and ensuring alignment with national standards. Aim To review all rectal cancer cases managed at University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) over a five-year period (January 2020–June 2025) and evaluate operative outcomes, non-operative pathways, complication rates, and mortality. Method A retrospective audit was conducted analysing 419 patients diagnosed with rectal cancer. Data collected included demographics, operative approach, neoadjuvant therapy response, postoperative complications (Clavien–Dindo grade ≥III), mortality at 3 months and 1 year, and recurrence in operatively managed patients. Cases with incomplete documentation were excluded (n=100). Results Of the 419 cases, 214 underwent surgery with curative intent. The most common operation was low anterior resection (n=63), followed by AP resection (n=58), high anterior resection (n=38), and TAMIS (n=28). Minimally invasive approaches predominated, including 174 robotic and 28 TAMIS procedures. Postoperative Clavien–Dindo ≥III complications included anastomotic leak (n=2), bleeding (n=1), collections (n=5), iatrogenic perforation (n=1), and stoma complications (n=1). Mortality was 1.40% at 3 months and 2.34% at 1 year. The recurrence rate among operatively managed patients was 10.75%. A total of 88 patients were managed non-operatively, with 16 achieving a complete response to chemoradiotherapy. Conclusions Rectal cancer outcomes at UHCW demonstrate high utilisation of minimally invasive surgery and low perioperative mortality. This audit highlights strong curative outcomes and supports continued development of robotic and organ-preserving strategies.
affiliations: University Hospital Coventry & Warwickshire , Coventry ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.409.title: 117 Initial Severity Assessment in Patients with Acute Pancreatitis in a UK District General Hospital: A Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.409.abstract: Abstract Aim The existing Inernational Association of Pancreatology guidelines provide the standard framework for assessing the aetiology and severity of acute pancreatitis, with the Modified Atlanta Classification being the most widely adopted severity scoring system. This study aimed to audit compliance with IAP guidance regarding initial severity assessment in acute pancreatitis and to evaluate the impact of implementing a Pancreatitis Severity Scoring proforma incorporating the Modified Atlanta system. Method A retrospective audit was conducted of all acute pancreatitis admissions to a large UK district general hospital between October and December 2023 (Group 1). A Pancreatitis Severity Scoring proforma, including the Modified Atlanta criteria, was subsequently introduced, supported by education sessions during morbidity and mortality meetings, junior doctor inductions, and multidisciplinary awareness campaigns. Prospective data were then collected between February and March 2025 (Group 2). Data were obtained from hospital e-care records and discharge summaries. Results Fifty-one patients were included in Group 1 and twenty-seven in Group 2. In Group 2, 66.6% (18/27) had a proforma completed in e-care, of which 38.8% (7/18) were fully completed. In comparison, none of the Group 1 patients had a formal severity assessment recorded. Introduction of the proforma improved documentation of severity assessment by 66.6%. Conclusions Implementation of a structured Pancreatitis Severity Scoring proforma significantly improved compliance with IAP severity assessment standards. Regular reassessment facilitated monitoring of clinical progress and escalation needs. Ongoing education, re-auditing, and hospital-wide dissemination are planned to sustain and enhance adherence.
affiliations: West Suffolk NHS Foundation Trust , Bury St Edmunds ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.250.title: 804 Improving Antimicrobial Stewardship in Acute Urology: A Two-Cycle Targeted Intervention Audit Using a Composite Compliance Framework
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.250.abstract: Abstract Background Antimicrobial resistance is a growing challenge in the UK. The 2025 ESPAUR reports rising E. coli resistance to frontline UTI antibiotics. Inappropriate antimicrobial prescribing contributes significantly to this trend. We applied a multi-domain compliance framework across two audit cycles to assess antimicrobial prescribing in a tertiary urology centre. Aim To assess local guideline adherence using a multi-domain composite framework and evaluate whether interventions improved antimicrobial stewardship. Method We prospectively analysed acute urology admissions at Liverpool University Hospitals. Data included diagnosis, culture results, antibiotics, and length of stay. Prescribing was assessed across four domains: initiation, subsequent changes, discharge, and duration. Domain-level compliance and a patient-level composite score (0–4), adjusted for non-applicable domains, were calculated. Length of stay was compared across composite-score groups using the Kruskal–Wallis test. Interventions included QR-code posters, teaching sessions, and a faculty meeting. Results 84 patients were analysed: 44 in cycle 1; 40 in cycle 2. Initial antibiotic choice improved from 59% to 82%. Duration compliance also improved from 61% to 68%. Subsequent antibiotic changes were similar between cycles (86% in cycle 1; 81% in cycle 2). Discharge antibiotic choices remained at 61%. Composite compliance increased from 43% to 53%; in cycle 2, 33% were compliant, 20% had justified deviations, and 48% had unjustified deviations. Length of stay differed (p=0.002), reflecting differences in illness severity rather than compliance. Conclusions Cycle-based interventions improved antimicrobial prescribing, although discharges remained suboptimal. The multi-domain composite framework used in this audit offers a reproducible approach to quantifying antimicrobial stewardship with potential for wider implementation.
affiliations: Liverpool University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Liverpool ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.254.title: 855 Management of Frail Patients in Acute Surgical Wards: A First-Cycle Audit of Compliance With National Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.254.abstract: Abstract Introduction Frailty is associated with increased postoperative complications, mortality, and prolonged hospital stay. National guidance recommends early frailty assessment, recognition of high-risk patients, and involvement of specialist geriatric services. This audit evaluates compliance with these standards for older adults admitted under general surgery at Hull University Teaching Hospitals. Method A retrospective snapshot audit was conducted for patients aged ≥65 years admitted to acute surgical wards between April and July 2024. Frailty was assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale. Data were collected on frailty documentation, frailty team involvement, ReSPECT and DNACPR completion, length of stay, management, and 30-day outcomes. Results Eighty-three patients were included; 29 (34.9%) were frail with a Clinical Frailty Scale score ≥5. Frailty status was documented in all cases. Despite this, none were referred to or reviewed by the frailty team. Among frail patients, DNACPR status was recorded as “Not for CPR” in 51.7%, “For CPR” in 24.1%, and was undocumented in 24.1%. Mean length of stay for frail patients was 24.7 days (range 2–86). Surgical intervention was required in 55.2%. Thirty-day readmission was 24.1%, and mortality was 17.2%. Conclusions Although frailty assessment was completed for all patients, frail individuals received no specialist geriatric input and experienced high readmission, mortality, and prolonged hospital stay. These findings demonstrate the need for a structured frailty pathway within general surgery, including routine specialist referral, geriatric review, and multidisciplinary involvement. The results will guide the second audit cycle and support development of a dedicated frailty service to improve outcomes for older surgical patients.
affiliations: Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust , Hull ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.209.title: 256 Straight to the Point: Improving Nasal Fracture Care Through a Face-to-Face-First Pathway - a Closed Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.209.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess whether changing from a telemedicine-first to a face-to-face-first (F2F) pathway for suspected nasal fractures improved timeliness of care and reduced clinician consultation time, whilst maintaining compliance with ENT UK standards (≤ 21 days). A secondary aim was to evaluate whether patient age influenced the likelihood of manipulation under anaesthesia (MUA), informing potential age-based triage refinement. Method Data were collected retrospectively for two audit cycles. The pre-intervention cohort followed a telemedicine-first pathway; the post-intervention cohort was reviewed F2F initially. For each patient, age, date of injury, telemedicine and F2F appointments, and date of MUA were recorded. Time intervals from injury to each stage and total consultations were calculated. Comparisons were made using t-tests. Violin plots visualised age distribution for MUA and non-MUA patients. Results Mean time to F2F review decreased from 16.5 to 13.3 days (p=0.0068). Mean time to MUA reduced from 15.2 to 13.9 days (p=0.19), with 100% completed within 21 days. The proportion of MUAs ≤ 14 days increased from 38.9% to 57.1%. Consultations per patient fell from 1.23 to 1.04 (15% reduction), and discharge from ENT services occurred earlier (15.2 to 12.2 days, p=0.0019). MUA patients were younger (mean 31.3 vs 41.7 years, p=0.009). Conclusions The F2F-first pathway improved patient access to assessment, reduced consultation burden, and maintained compliance with national standards. The findings highlight opportunities for an age-based triage system to enhance efficiency. This audit demonstrates a sustainable service improvement model with clear implications for patient-centred care, reduced duplication of reviews, and more efficient clinic workflow.
affiliations: University of Oxford , Oxford ,
Oxford University Hospitals , Oxford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.558.title: 430 A Two Cycle Closed-Loop Audit Evaluating MSU Compliance for New Urology Admissions at Royal Bolton Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.558.abstract: Abstract Aim Mid-stream urine (MSU) sampling is used to investigate urinary tract infections (UTI). An initial audit at Royal Bolton Hospital (RBH) in November 2024 revealed a 60% compliance, with only 16.7% of patients having an MSU sample sent before antibiotics were started. The SMART aim was to improve MSU adherence for suspected UTIs in all new RBH admissions to 100% by July 2025. Interventions were implemented, followed by a second audit in July 2025 to evaluate the impact and identify improvements. Method A retrospective analysis of electronic records identified 30 patients in the first cycle and 21 in the second who met the inclusion criteria: new urology admissions via Emergency Department with indications for MSU based on national and local guidance, admission exceeding one day. Data included patient demographics, admission reason, timing and location of MSU sampling, and timing of antibiotics. PDSA cycles focused first on raising awareness amongst doctors, then nursing and HCA staff. The second cycle also included time between triage to MSU collection. Results The second cycle showed improved MSU sampling from 60% to 67%. Number of patients receiving antibiotics following MSU collection improved from 16.7% to 50% and the median time between MSU and administration of the first antibiotic dose decreased from 22.25 hours to 5. Conclusions This closed-loop audit demonstrated improvements in MSU compliance, antibiotic timing and reduction in treatment delays at RBH. Although complete adherence has not been achieved yet, further PDSA cycles-such as introducing yellow wristbands to identify patients in ED-may strengthen compliance and improve patient care.
affiliations: Royal Bolton Hospital , Bolton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.758.title: 1000 Improving Ureteric Stent Follow-Up: A Retrospective Audit of Delayed and Retained Stents in a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.758.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate documentation, follow-up planning and timeliness of ureteric stent removal in a district general hospital without an electronic stent-tracking system, and to quantify delayed or retained stents to support adoption of a registry. Method A retrospective review of all ureteric stents inserted between 1 March 2024 and 30 April 2025 was performed. Operation notes, discharge summaries and clinic letters were examined for removal plans and final outcomes. Long-term stents were excluded. Stents were classified as Not Delayed (≤6 weeks or by target), Delayed (>6 weeks without justification), Possible Retained (in situ at audit close), or Not Known (status unclear). Complications and device-related patterns were recorded. Results Ninety-three short-term stents were analysed. A documented removal plan appeared in 95.7% of cases and in 93.5% of discharge summaries. Timely removal occurred in 59.1%. Delayed removal occurred in 35.5% (33/93), including 4.3% that had remained in situ for more than six months. A further 3.2% had no evidence of removal at audit close (possible retained), and 2.1% could not be classified due to incomplete documentation. In 88% of delayed cases, no reason was recorded. The Cook UFI-600-R accounted for nearly half of insertions but 73% of delays and 93% of encrustations. The overall complication rate was 22.6%, predominantly encrustation. Conclusions Most delays lacked a recorded reason, and the Cook UFI-600-R accounted for the majority of prolonged dwell times and encrustations. These findings demonstrate significant gaps in follow-up processes and support the introduction of an electronic stent-tracking registry together with review of device choice.
affiliations: Dorset County Hospital , Dorchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.405.title: 1195 Asymmetrical Tonsils - Audit of Clinical Practice
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.405.abstract: Abstract Aim Diagnostic tonsillectomy is commonly performed to exclude malignancy. We aimed to audit local diagnostic tonsillectomy practices to determine if tonsillar asymmetry is predictive of significant weight difference of the tonsils. Method Retrospective audit of diagnostic tonsillectomy cases performed at Salford Royal Hospital between September 2022-September 2024. Clinical notes were reviewed for primary indication for procedure, Brodsky grading on clinical examination, histological results, post-tonsillectomy bleeding and detection of malignancy. Results Data from 149 tonsillectomies were reviewed, with 44 performed for histological analysis. Asymmetrical tonsils were the most common and primary indication in 29 cases. Only 16 histology reports contained the required data on tonsil weight, with 60% showing a weight difference of 0.5g or less. In 20% of cases, the clinically “enlarged” tonsil was the lighter of the two. The tonsillar asymmetry on visual inspection was not predictive of significant weight difference of the two tonsils on histology (t-test p= 0.0561 P<0.05). No malignant cases were detected, and the rate of postoperative bleeding was 10.3%. Conclusions Based on our data, pre-operative detection of tonsillar asymmetry and visual grading system do not correlate with significant weight difference on histology. The high risk of post-tonsillectomy bleeding and absence of any malignant cases suggests that asymmetrical tonsils in isolation, with no red flag symptoms, should be carefully considered for tonsillectomy. Other approaches such as a period of observation, or additional imagining may be safer, this however may increase the risk of missing neoplasia. Further studies with bigger sample size may be helpful to draw further conclusions.
affiliations: NHS Highlands , Inverness ,
NCA NHS Foundation Trust , Salford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.258.title: 895 Improving Ward Round Documentation Through Implementation of a Structured Template: An Audit Cycle
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.258.abstract: Abstract Introduction Ward round documentation is an important communication tool in healthcare. The recent implementation of electronic patient records (EPR) in our trust raised concerns regarding ward round documentation. We conducted an audit on the endocrine ward in October 2024, and the main observation was that there is great variability between ward round entries, between doctors, and between entries from the same doctor. Aim This re-audit aimed to evaluate whether the implementation of a ward round template improved the documentation of essential components. Method Data were collected by analysing ward round notes from the EPR on the endocrine ward. The data was collected as a snapshot in time. 1-3 ward round entries were analysed per patient. The data was collected using a 16-point checklist developed by the audit team based on the guidelines and standards used for this audit Results There was improvement in documentation across all categories. The average number of fields completed per ward round entry out of a 16-point checklist ranged between 43.75% fields to 100% with the average of 82.1% completeness per ward round entry. Improved from 71.38% in the initial audit. Bleep number documentation increased to 57% from 37%. Medication reviews documentation improved: VTE prophylaxis 69.5% (26.5%), Antibiotics 58.5% (30.1 %), Analgesia 58.5% (19.28%). Conclusions Using a structured ward round template helped improve ward round documentation. Given the rotational aspect of resident doctors’ training leading to working across different specialties, the use of a structured template can prompt review and documentation of essential elements during daily ward rounds and improve patient safety.
affiliations: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust , Birmingham ,
University Hospital Coventry & Warwickshire , Coventry ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.211.title: 290 Post-Orchidectomy Tumour-Marker Testing in Suspected Testicular Cancer: An Audit Against EAU and BAUS Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.211.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate compliance with guideline-recommended timing of post-orchidectomy tumour-marker testing (in 5-7 days) in patients undergoing radical inguinal orchidectomy for suspected testicular germ-cell tumours, and to identify key pathway failures contributing to delayed staging. Method A retrospective audit was performed at a single UK district general hospital, examining all adult patients who underwent radical inguinal orchidectomy for suspected testicular cancer over two years (15/11/2023–14/11/2025). Data were collected from electronic patient records, theatre systems, discharge documentation and MDT conclusions. Compliance with preoperative AFP, β-hCG, and LDH measurement and repeat testing within 5–7 days postoperatively was compared against EAU (2025) and BAUS guideline standards. Documentation of a clear post-operative marker plan was also assessed. Results 23 orchidectomy cases were identified (median age 43 years; 78% malignant germ-cell tumours). All patients had complete pre-operative tumour markers (100% standard achieved). Only 3/23 (13%) had AFP/β-hCG/LDH repeated within the guideline window of 5–7 days post-surgery, against a target of ≥90%. Although 48% eventually had markers checked, these were often delayed by weeks to months and mostly initiated at MDT review. A clear post-operative marker plan was documented in only 26%, indicating this as the key driver of non-compliance. All malignant cases were escalated to MDT review; however, the absence of timely markers risks missing Stage IS disease. Conclusions The current pathway delivers excellent pre-operative marker compliance but fails to provide guideline-compliant early post-orchidectomy tumour-marker testing. Introducing automatic post-operative blood test scheduling and pathway education is required to ensure timely staging and oncological safety.
affiliations: Kettering General Hospital NHS Trust , Kettering ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.415.title: 1008 Management of Suspected Testicular Torsion – Audit of Current Practice
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.415.abstract: Abstract Aim Recent publications from NCEPOD and GIRFT have prompted a review of the care provided to patients with suspected testicular torsion. A local audit was performed comparing our practice to these new guidelines. Method All patients who underwent emergency surgery for suspected testicular torsion between 1stJanuary and 31stDecember 2023 were included in the audit. Primary outcomes were time from arrival to review by a surgical decision maker, and time from decision to operate to surgery. Secondary outcomes included post-operative diagnosis, procedures performed, and post-operative complications. Results 32 patients were included in the audit. 53.1% of patients (n=17) were reviewed by the surgical team within 1 hour of presentation and 37.5% (n=12) of patients underwent surgical exploration within 1 hour of surgical review. 21.8% (n=7) of patients were diagnosed with testicular torsion, 3 of which (42.8%) required an orchidectomy. A further 3 patients (9.3%) were suspected to have had testicular torsion which had de-torted by the time of surgery. Other post-operative diagnoses included hydrocoele (15.6%), epididymo-orchitis (21.9%) and torted hydatid of Morgagni (12.5%). 7 patients (21.8%) re-presented post-operatively: 3 were discharged with reassurance, 3 required antibiotics, and 1 required contralateral scrotal exploration following trauma. Conclusions Improvement is required to meet the standards recommended by GIRFT and NCEPOD. The data has been presented at a local governance meeting and a new clinical pathway has been created to facilitate prompt assessment and treatment of these patients. Data following its distribution has been collected and analysed.
affiliations: Ninewells , Dundee ,
NDDH , Barnstaple ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.248.title: 790 Management of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding in a District General Hospital- Clinical Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.248.abstract: Abstract Aim Lower Gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB) is a common indication for hospital admission, accounting for 20% of all GI bleeding cases and 3% of annual surgical referral in the UK. Reported inpatient mortality rate of 3.4% to 17.8%, highlighting the need for timely assessment and management. The aim was to assess adherence to British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidelines on LGIB and identify areas of improvement. Specific objectives include assessment of initial management, risk stratification, diagnostic and therapeutic intervention. Method Retrospective analysis of patients admitted with LGIB for >24 hours over two 3-month audit cycles. Data collected includes anticoagulant use, Digital rectal examination (DRE), shock index (SI), Tranexamic acid (TXA) and CT-angiography (CT-A). Action plan implemented after the first cycle involved distributing educational posters and email summarising BSG guidelines and key audit recommendations- DRE for all patients, risk stratification with SI and Oakland score, avoiding TXA (HALT-IT trial) and CT-A use in haemodynamically unstable patients (SI >1) or active bleeding. Result 32 patients (M:F 1:1.3) were reviewed in the second cycle, compared with 34 in the first. DRE compliance improved from 79% to 91%, Oakland score documentation was unchanged, TXA use decreased from 44% to 38% and CT-A reduced from 29% to 19%. Conclusions LGIB is a potentially life-threatening condition requiring prompt and effective management. This audit demonstrated improved compliance in current practice, highlighting that ongoing education and continuous improvement in clinical practice, reinforced by adherence to established guidelines are essential to further optimise patient outcomes.
affiliations: Medway NHS Foundation Trust , Gillingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.040.title: 422 Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy in Gallstone Pancreatitis – Audit and Improvement of Trust Performance
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.040.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute pancreatitis (AP) is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Gallstones account for up to 40% of cases, and up to 20% of patients who retain their gallbladder may experience recurrence. British Society of Gastroenterology guidance recommends index or early (within 2 weeks) cholecystectomy for mild gallstone pancreatitis, with delayed surgery in moderate/severe cases. We assessed our guideline adherence and evaluated service improvements following interventions. Method A retrospective review was conducted of adults admitted with AP in two cycles: 01/06/2024–30/09/2024 and 01/02/2025–31/07/2025. Data collected included aetiology, length of stay (LOS) and timing of cholecystectomy. Severity graded using the Modified Atlanta criteria. Post-baseline intervention included listing gallstone pancreatitis patients as P2 when booking, cancelling other elective activity when required, and encouraging inpatient cholecystectomy. Patients were excluded if unfit, declining surgery, out of area, or with clearly documented justified delays. Mann-Whitney U and Chi-Squared tests for non-parametric and categorical data, respectively, in STATA. Results Gallstones were the most common cause of AP in both cycles. Adherence to BSG guidance improved to 86% from 71% following intervention (p=0.71). Patients undergoing index cholecystectomy displayed increased median LOS from 3 to 6 days (p<0.05). Non-compliance to guidelines due to inadequate documentation and slow outpatient processing. Conclusions Guideline adherence improved following intervention, driven by prioritisation of inpatient cholecystectomy. Increased LOS due to difficulty accessing CEPOD theatre. Lack of statistical significance likely reflects small sample sizes. Further gains may be achieved through improved documentation and clearer pathways for outpatient management of gallstone pancreatitis.
affiliations: Dorset County Hospital , Dorchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.244.title: 752 Use of Percutaneous Cholecystostomy in the Management of Acute Cholecystitis: A Retrospective Audit on Its Indications
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.244.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute cholecystitis (AC) represents a major contributor to emergency general surgery admissions, accounting for approximately 30% of cases. While laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) remains the gold standard treatment, its safety is reduced in patients with significant comorbidities or physiological compromise. For individuals deemed unfit for general anaesthesia, percutaneous cholecystostomy (PC) is recommended by the Tokyo Guidelines (TG) as an alternative. This audit evaluates local adherence to TG indications for PC and examines associated patient outcomes. Method A retrospective audit was conducted at Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary, reviewing all patients undergoing PC between October 2019 and January 2024. Data collected included demographics, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), ASA grade, ECOG status, inflammatory markers, imaging modality, time to drain placement, drain duration, complications, and incidence of interval cholecystectomy. Adherence to TG indications—CCI ≥6 and/or ASA ≥3, or septic shock with organ dysfunction—was assessed. Results 60 patients underwent PC during the study period, with complete data available for 58. The adherence rate to TG indications was 76%. Interval cholecystectomy occurred in 32% of patients meeting TG criteria compared with 43% of those who did not. Outcomes were consistent with published evidence, including the CHOCOLATE trial, which demonstrates poorer outcomes in lower-risk patients managed with PC rather than LC. Conclusions PC use at our centre largely aligns with TG recommendations. The higher interval cholecystectomy rate and inferior outcomes among patients not meeting TG criteria underscore the importance of appropriate patient selection. Clinically fit patients with lower comorbidity should preferentially undergo early LC to optimise outcomes.
affiliations: Royal Free London , London ,
Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary , Dumfries ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.740.title: 327 Improving Compliance with a Ureteric Stent Database: A Two-Year Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.740.abstract: Abstract Introduction Timely removal of ureteric stents is essential to prevent complications such as infection, encrustation, blockage, and complex removals. Our trust maintains a stent database to track insertion and removal dates; however, concerns were raised about incomplete documentation and overdue stents. This audit assessed compliance with the existing database and identified patients requiring further action. Method A retrospective review of the stent database was performed for all entries between June 2023 and June 2025. Data were cross-referenced with clinical systems to establish insertion dates, expected removal dates, documented outcomes, and reasons for delays. A total of 407 patients were analysed. Results A total of 407 patients were recorded on the database. 173 patients (42.5%) had no documented stent outcome, largely related to removals performed in flexible cystoscopy lists or outpatient clinics without subsequent database updates. Of 16 patients with overdue stents, 12 were already listed for removal or exchange; 4 required further follow-up due to DNAs, pending investigations, or difficulty contacting the patient. Among 5 additional patients, stents were removed privately, at other centres, or fell out spontaneously. Importantly, only two patients were found to have been missed completely by the service. Conclusions Compliance with documenting stent insertions was good; however, outcome documentation after stent removal was inconsistent, leading to risk of overdue or missed stents. Most overdue cases were already actioned once identified. Improving accountability—such as allocating responsibility to a designated SHO or healthcare professional for routine database maintenance—may enhance completeness, reduce overdue stents, and improve patient safety.
affiliations: Leighton Hospital , Crewe ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.219.title: 428 An Audit of Inappropriate Referrals to the Virtual Fracture Clinic at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.219.abstract: Abstract Aim The virtual fracture clinic (VFC) at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital works with the accident and emergency department (A&E) to streamline patients and reduce face-to-face appointments. Patients meeting criteria can be discharged and reviewed remotely by an orthopaedic consultant. However, referrals are often varied and inconsistent with guidelines. This work analysed VFC referrals to identify safety issues and resolve problems within the referral system. First round Inappropriate referrals over a four-month period (4/9/23-4/1/24) were identified by VFC nursing staff and reviewed. Referrals were categorised based on the reason for the inappropriate referral, and data on fracture type, referral origin, and VFC outcomes were collected. 80 inappropriate referrals were identified: 52.5% presented with injuries not requiring follow-up after discharge, and 30% had no identifiable fracture. 3 patients required urgent inpatient orthopaedic assessment and were admitted after VFC review. Second round Assessment of guidance showed a discrepancy between A&E and orthopaedic protocols. Updated guidelines were therefore developed jointly with A&E and a second data collection (4/10/24–4/2/25) was carried out three months after the implementation of the new guidelines. 24 inappropriate referrals were identified: 70.8% involved injuries normally discharged from A&E, 8.3% had no fracture, and none required inpatient assessment. Conclusions This closed-loop audit demonstrates a clear reduction in inappropriate referrals and improved patient safety, with no patients requiring inpatient assessment being mis-referred. Remaining inappropriate referrals may reflect a need for additional reassurance for clinicians or patients, or a delay in the full uptake of the updated guidelines.
affiliations: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, NHS GGC , Glasgow , . , Glasgow ,
University of Glasgow , Glasgow , . , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.235.title: 622 Compliance With ABS 2023 Phyllodes Guidelines in the Buckinghamshire Breast Unit: An Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.235.abstract: Abstract Introduction Phyllodes are rare breast tumours. Surgical excision remans the mainstay but a recent international survey demonstrated wide variation in practice. Emerging data suggests that narrower excision margins can be safely accepted; reflected in new ABS guidelines. This audit aimed to assess unit practice against latest national guidance for excision margins. Method Hospital records were searched using operative codes to identify phyllodes excised during the last 5 years. A retrospective case-note review was conducted by trainee surgeons using a pre-determined proforma. Results 34 women underwent excision of phyllodes between May 2018- Oct 2023. 18 (53%) were benign, 8 (24%) borderline and 4 (12%) were malignant. One was upgraded to sarcoma and 3 (9%) downgraded to fibroadenoma. 29 women (85%) were treated with breast conservation, 5 (15%) underwent mastectomy. Most underwent one operation (59%, n= 20) but 29% (n=10) required two and 12% (n=4) three to obtain clear margins. 11 patients underwent repeat surgeries for either incomplete excision (benign) or tumour at margin i.e. 0mm margin (borderline). One mastectomy was indicated for malignant phyllodes when 11mm margin was not accepted after WLE. This case may have avoided mastectomy under new guidelines. Conclusions Our unit is not yet fully compliant with latest ABS Phyllodes guidance but the audit did not identify excess mastectomies to obtain wide-clear margins. However, 41% (n=14) required >1 operation to obtain clear margins and patients require counselling about this prior to surgery. Performance will be re-audited in due course after disseminating new guidance within departmental and regional networks.
affiliations: Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust , High Wycombe ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.268.title: 1221 Evaluating Initial Management and Referral Pathways for Traumatic Open Hand Injuries Using BSSH Hand Triage Standards: A Single Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.268.abstract: Abstract Aim Hand injuries account for 5–10% of UK emergency attendances, and 20–30% are inadequately assessed or misdiagnosed. The British Society for Surgery of the Hand (BSSH) provides standards for assessment, initial management, and referral. This audit evaluates assessment quality and compliance with BSSH standards in a district general hospital emergency department. Method All patients presenting with hand injuries between 1 January and 31 December 2024 were identified. Forty patients meeting inclusion criteria were selected. Data were retrospectively extracted from electronic records, including demographics, mechanism and site of injury, neurovascular and tendon findings, imaging, medications, and referral outcomes. Analysis was performed using Microsoft Excel. Results A total of 137 patients attended with hand injuries; 40 were included. No patients demonstrated poor distal perfusion. Three had associated fractures and were appropriately referred. Tendon injury was suspected in 13 patients and all were referred to a tertiary centre; nine underwent repair. Nerve injury was suspected in five patients, none requiring repair. Wound photography occurred in 52%, and 73% received X-ray imaging. Tetanus status was considered in 58%. Wound washout occurred in 65% and dressing in 73%. Antibiotics were given to 60% overall and to all high-risk lacerations. Conclusions Documentation of neurovascular and tendon examinations limited the audit. Concerns identified clinically or radiologically were appropriately referred. Standardisation of initial investigation and management requires improvement. Planned next steps include service improvement through BSSH hand triage guideline implementation and a second audit cycle.
affiliations: West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals , Watford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.260.title: 927 Cholecystostomy Audit of Practice in a District General Hospital: Time for a Standardised Pathway
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.260.abstract: Abstract Aim Percutaneous cholecystostomy is a recognised option for high-risk patients with acute cholecystitis who are unsuitable for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Our Trust currently lacks a standardised clinical pathway for its use, which has contributed to variation in decision-making and post-procedure management. This audit’s aim was to evaluate adherence to best-practice standards and identify areas for improvement. Method A retrospective review was undertaken of all patients undergoing cholecystostomy between January 2022 and August 2025. Data extracted from electronic records included indication, timing of decision and intervention, procedural details, post-procedure management, tubogram completion, and documentation of definitive plans. Fifty cases met inclusion criteria. Results Only 56% of procedures were performed in patients with Tokyo Grade II/III cholecystitis (standard >90%). Decision-making within 48 hours of admission was achieved in 52% of cases (standard >80%). Antibiotic administration met standards (100%), and immediate post-procedure documentation was completed in 96% of patients. Tubogram completion was low at 40% (standard >80%). A definitive management plan within 8 weeks was documented in 80% of cases, with many patients managed with long-term drains. Only 22% ultimately underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Conclusions There is significant variability in the indications, timing, and follow-up of cholecystostomy within our Trust. Key deficiencies include non-adherence to severity criteria, low tubogram utilisation, and inconsistent definitive planning. These findings highlight the need for a unified, evidence-based pathway to improve patient selection, ensure consistent practice, and reduce prolonged dependence on cholecystostomy drains. The pathway we have devised will be introduced in early 2026, with plan for re-audit one year after establishment.
affiliations: Sandwell and West Birmingham Hospitals NHS Trust , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.183.title: 1058 Evaluating Comprehensive Best Medical Therapy and Lifestyle Optimisation in Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischaemia: An Integrated Audit of Adherence to ESVS 2023 Cardiovascular Standards and Global Vascular Guideline Recommendations
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.183.abstract: Abstract Background Comprehensive best medical therapy (BMT) remains fundamental to the management of Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischaemia (CLTI). The 2023 European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) guidelines advocate consistent provision of antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statins, lipid profiling, blood pressure optimisation, and structured smoking cessation counselling. The Global Vascular Guidelines complement these recommendations by emphasising lifestyle modification and robust glycaemic assessment, including HbA1c testing within three months for diabetic or high-risk patients. This audit examined how closely current inpatient practice aligns with these combined guideline standards. Method A retrospective audit was undertaken over a 2-month period, reviewing consecutive inpatients with confirmed CLTI. Key measures included antiplatelet and statin prescription, completion of a lipid profile during admission, discharge blood pressure <140/90 mmHg, documentation of smoking cessation advice for active smokers, and availability of HbA1c within the previous three months. Results Of 35 CLTI inpatients, 80% received statin therapy and 60% received antiplatelet treatment. A lipid profile was completed in only 1 of 34 patients (2.9%). Blood pressure targets were achieved at discharge in 29 of 35 patients (82.9%). Smoking cessation counselling was documented in 5 of 36 active smokers (13.9%). HbA1c within three months was available in 14 of 49 diabetic patients (28.6%). Conclusions Adherence to evidence-based BMT and lifestyle optimisation in CLTI remains inconsistent, with notable gaps in lipid assessment, smoking cessation support, and glycaemic monitoring. Implementing structured clinical pathways, automated prompts, and routine lifestyle documentation may enhance delivery of guideline-directed care.
affiliations: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust , Leicester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.239.title: 711 A Retrospective Audit on the Management and Follow Up Practices of Acute Diverticulitis
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.239.abstract: Abstract Aim The ACPGBI guidelines in emergency colorectal surgery lays out a framework for the management of acute diverticulitis and for indications for endoscopic follow up after recovery from diverticulitis. The aim of this audit was to evaluate the management practices of acute diverticulitis at the University Hospital North Durham. Method A retrospective cross-sectional study covering a period of 1 year, which included all patients presenting with acute diverticulitis. Results Study population included 161 patients of which 67% had uncomplicated diverticulitis. In the uncomplicated group, antibiotics were prescribed in all but 2 patients and 85% of this group were managed as inpatients with an average hospital stay of 3.5 days. Although 106 patients had an indication for follow up endoscopy as per guidelines, 41 of them didn’t have an endoscopy. From the 55 patients for whom endoscopy was not indicated, 42 had an endoscopy (11 colonoscopies and 31 flexible sigmoidoscopies). The excess cost incurred by doing endoscopies for whom it was not indicated was £35,202. Four malignancy/high grade dysplasia lesions were detected in the group for whom endoscopy was indicated while none were found in the group who had endoscopies without an indication. Conclusions Most patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis were managed as inpatients and had antibiotics although the guidelines recommend otherwise. The lack of clear departmental protocol meant that many inappropriate endoscopy referrals were made resulting in significant cost to the hospital. Many patients for whom endoscopy was indicated did not have it done (39%) which may result in pathologies being possibly missed.
affiliations: University Hospital of North Durham , Durham ,
The James Cook University Hospital , Middlesbrough ,
Diana, Princess of Wales Hospital , Grimsby ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.460.title: 473 Primary Care Perspectives on Bariatric Surgery: An Audit of Outcomes and Monitoring of Patients Discharged to Primary Care
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.460.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate long-term outcomes of bariatric surgery in primary care by determining (1) changes in BMI, comparing pre-operative, post-discharge and current values, and (2) the GP practice’s compliance with BOMSS recommended nutritional monitoring following bariatric surgery, which was not commissioned or resourced. Method A retrospective audit was conducted, identifying adults who had undergone gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy more than 2 years before the search date, indicating discharge from specialist care. 91 patients met the inclusion criteria: correct procedure type, and sufficient BMI data documented. Mean percentage BMI reduction was calculated using pre-operative, 2-years post-operative and latest BMI values. Compliance with monitoring was assessed by identifying whether patients had received all five recommended blood tests (FBC, ferritin, B12 and folate, bone profile, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D) within the past 12 months. Results Mean BMI reduction from pre-operative to current measurement was 23.07%, exceeding the audit standard of 20%. Further analysis of a 10-patient sub-sample revealed mean BMI reduction of 32.85% within the 2-year post-operative period. 14.29% of patients had received all five recommended annual blood tests; adherence varied by test, with FBC highest (63.74%) and 25-hydroxyvitamin D lowest (25.27%). Conclusions Bariatric surgery produced sustained BMI reduction, meeting expected long-term efficacy, although BMI increased after discharge from Tier 4 Weight Management. Annual nutritional monitoring in primary care fell below the 80% standard, highlighting the need for dedicated commissioning, improved systems in GP practices, such as proactive follow-up for non-responders and dedicated post-bariatric monitoring clinics, and suggesting benefit in extending specialist hospital follow-up beyond two years.
affiliations: Newcastle University , Newcastle upon Tyne ,
Bridge View Medical Group , Sunderland ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.487.title: 1088 Evaluating the Impact of an Advanced Nurse Practitioner on Surgical Referral-to-Review Times in General Surgery: A Closed-Loop Quality Improvement Cycle
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.487.abstract: Abstract Background East Suffolk & North Essex Foundation Trust (ESNEFT) intends to achieve the four-hour emergency department (ED) standard, by reviewing surgical referrals within 30 minutes. Cycle One revealed that 33% of referrals were reviewed within this guideline, with administrative burden identified as a major barrier. Aim Evaluate the impact of an Advanced Nurse Practitioner (ANP) on referral-to-review times (RTR) within General Surgery. Method Direct observation of on-call resident surgeons took place during 8am-8pm shifts and referral times, and activity data were recorded using pro-formas. Cycle one included General Surgery, Vascular and Urology. The ANP was introduced in Cycle Two to General Surgery only, as the poorest performing department. Results There was an improvement in RTR performance following the intervention. The mean RTR decreased from 1h 52m (Cycle One) to 1h 2m (Cycle Two) and median RTR dropped from 1h 8m to 40m. The proportion of patients reviewed within 30 minutes increased from 27% to 34%. Time spent on administrative tasks decreased from 33.2% to 24.4% (p = 0.045), and medical scan waiting times also decreased (p = 0.026). Addtionally, SHOs saw fewer patients within the trust guideline in Cycle Two (100% to 25%) . Conclusions The introduction of the ANP within General Surgery was associated with improved RTR performance and reduced administrative burden. While the 30-minute target was still not consistently met, the intervention showed promise improving patient triage and senior clinical review. Further audits with a longer data collection period and direct observation of the ANP are recommended.
affiliations: Anglia Ruskin University Medical School , Chelmsford ,
East Suffolk and North Essex Foundation Trust , Colchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.760.title: 1068 Identifying gaps in the transition to benign LUTS Care Following Negative 2WW Prostate Cancer Referral: A NICE and EAU Guideline-Based Outpatient Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.760.abstract: Abstract Background Men referred via the two-week-wait (2WW) suspected prostate cancer (PCa) pathway frequently report lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), the majority of which are benign rather than malignant. NICE CG97 and EAU 2024 guidelines emphasize structured LUTS assessment, lifestyle advice, and appropriate transition into benign LUTS pathways once malignancy has been excluded. Failures in this transition can contribute to persistent symptoms and avoidable pressure on outpatient services. This audit assessed local adherence to guideline-recommended LUTS care following a negative cancer work-up. Method A retrospective audit was conducted in a district general hospital urology service. All men referred via the 2WW suspected PCa pathway between January–June 2024 who were subsequently confirmed cancer-negative were included (N = 268). Standards assessed were: (1) documentation of LUTS assessment at the initial 2ww appointment, and (2) evidence of lifestyle counselling, structured follow-up, or activation of a formal LUTS pathway. Data were analysed descriptively. Results LUTS assessment was documented in 203/268 patients (76%). LUTS were present in 143 men (53%). Of these, 54 (38%) had formal LUTS pathway activated, 4 (3%) received general lifestyle advice and 1 (1%) declined referral. Consequently, 84 symptomatic men (59% of those with LUTS; 31% of the total cohort) had no documented lifestyle advice, pathway activation, or follow-up plan, representing a gap in benign symptom management. Conclusions Significant deficiencies exist in both LUTS assessment and onward transition into benign LUTS care following negative PCa investigation. Embedding routine LUTS evaluation and automatic pathway referral are required to deliver guideline-aligned, continuous care.
affiliations: Barts Health NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.270.title: 1237 Clinical Predictors of Diagnostic Muscle Biopsies in Inflammatory Myopathies: A 10-Year Retrospective Single Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.270.abstract: Abstract Aim Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies present with varied clinical and biochemical features, often making early diagnosis challenging. Muscle biopsy remains an important investigation, but yield varies, and interpretation differs between centres. This study aimed to assess the diagnostic yield of muscle biopsies performed, characterise symptoms patterns, and identify which clinical features predict a positive diagnostic biopsy. By integrating biopsy findings with clinical parameters, we explored developing a predictive model to guide referrals and reduce unnecessary invasive procedures. Method A retrospective analysis of all muscle biopsies was performed from 2015 to 2025 at Luton and Dunstable Hospital. Data included demographics, biopsy site, presenting symptoms, histopathological findings and treatment. Biopsies were classified as diagnostic (inflammatory, necrotising, metabolic, granulomatous, infectious, or inclusion-body myositis) or non-diagnostic (normal or non-specific). Symptoms were grouped into standard categories, and diagnostic yield was analysed by symptom pattern and biopsy location. Results Thirty-six patients were included (mean age 57.7 years; 72% male). Overall diagnostic yield was 50% (18/36). The most frequent symptoms were muscle weakness (81%), pain/myalgia (47%), and raised CK (28%). Raised CK showed the highest diagnostic yield (89%), followed by muscle wasting (83%) and weakness (51%). Quadriceps was the most common biopsy site (21/36; yield 62%). Calf biopsies showed the highest yield (80%). Most patients with diagnostic biopsies proceeded to receive corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy. Conclusions Raised CK, wasting and weakness, strongly predicted diagnostic biopsy outcomes. These findings support development of a predictive referral model to improve biopsy selection and reduce unnecessary procedures, ultimately allowing more consistent therapeutic decision-making across centres.
affiliations: Luton and Dunstable Hospital , Luton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.593.title: 896 The Length of Stay Benefit of Robotic Lobectomy Is Driven Entirely by Low-Risk Patients: A Thoracoscore-Stratified Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.593.abstract: Abstract Aim The VIOLET trial demonstrated the benefit of thoracoscopic (VATS) access for lung resection over thoracotomy in lung cancer patients. Ongoing trials explore whether robotic-assisted (RATS) lung resection offers similar advantages. The aim was to determine whether RATS reduces Length of Stay (LOS) and 30-day Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE) compared to VATS and open approaches, stratified by preoperative risk (Thoracoscore). Method A retrospective audit of standard lobectomies (n=346) performed in 2024. From a total of 495 patients, exclusions included: sublobar resections (n=94), procedure conversions (n=29), complex resections (n=13, e.g. chest wall) and pneumonectomies (n=11). Cohorts: RATS (n=205), VATS (n=108), and Open (n=35). In sub-analysis, RATS and Open were stratified by Thoracoscore (low-risk <3.0, higher-risk >3.0). LOS was analysed using non-parametric tests (Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn's, Mann-Whitney U), and 30-day CV events with Fisher's Exact test. Results An initial Kruskal-Wallis test revealed significant overall difference in LOS (P=0.0323), primarily driven by RATS vs. Open (Dunn's test, P=0.0273). Sub-analysis isolated benefit to low-risk RATS patients, with a 2-day reduction in median LOS (4.0 vs 6.0 days, P=0.0445). 30-day CV event rates were not significantly different across all three approaches (P=0.6423). Conclusions RATS demonstrates a 2-day LOS reduction for low-risk patients without compromising cardiovascular status. Low-risk patients represent 57% of total volume (178/346); for units establishing programs, prioritising these patients for RATS offers a high-value scheduling strategy. High-risk patients showed no LOS benefit (5.5d both groups, P=0.2407). Recommendations endorsed at unit CME (Nov 2025); implementation via scheduling, with re-audit planned using 2026 data to quantify potential resource savings.
affiliations: University of Dundee , Dundee ,
Golden Jubilee National Hospital , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.229.title: 560 Stop the Bleed: Audit of the Management of Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding at Cavan General Hospital, Republic of Ireland
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.229.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) is a common emergency with mortality rates of 5–10%. NICE (CG141, QS38) and BSG guidelines emphasise early resuscitation, risk stratification using the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS), timely endoscopy, and evidence-based pharmacological therapy. This audit assessed local practice against these standards. Method A retrospective review of 40 adult patients admitted with suspected UGIB from January–December 2024 was conducted. Data were extracted from clinical notes, laboratory results, transfusion records and endoscopy reports. Compliance was benchmarked against NICE/BSG standards and UK AUGIB audit results. Results Initial assessment was strong: 100% had complete vital signs documented, 100% received IV access, and 97% received fluid resuscitation. However, GBS was not documented in most cases, representing a major variance from recommended practice. Pre-endoscopy PPI use was high (∼98%). Among suspected variceal bleeds (13%), compliance with guideline therapy was suboptimal: 50% received terlipressin and 83% received prophylactic antibiotics. Endoscopy occurred in 85% of patients, but only 63% were scoped within 24 hours (mean delay 42.8 h). Only 1/5 variceal cases met the <12-hour target. Transfusion practice was appropriately restrictive (mean Hb 7.5 g/dL pre-transfusion; documentation 94%). No rebleeding or endoscopy-related complications were reported; 9% required repeat endoscopy. Conclusions Strengths included effective initial resuscitation, high PPI compliance, and appropriate transfusion thresholds. Key deficiencies were absence of GBS scoring, delayed endoscopy, and incomplete variceal bundle adherence. Implementation of a UGIB proforma, anticoagulation/variceal checklists, and improved endoscopy access is underway. Re-audit is planned within 12 months.
affiliations: Cavan General Hospital , Cavan ,
Beaumont Hospital , Dublin ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.393.title: 1090 "Follow-Up Colonoscopy in Acute Diverticulitis: A Retrospective Audit of Guideline Adherence"
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.393.abstract: Abstract Aim This retrospective audit evaluated compliance with follow-up colonoscopy guidelines in patients with acute diverticulitis, specifically adherence to the recommended 6-8 week follow-up for complicated cases. Current guidelines from the World Society of Emergency Surgery and European Society of Coloproctology advise colonoscopy 6-8 weeks after resolution of complicated diverticulitis to rule out malignancy. Colonoscopy is not routinely recommended for uncomplicated cases unless malignancy is suspected. Method The audit was conducted in two cycles. The first cycle (September 2023–March 2024) included 51 patients: 23 with complicated and 28 with uncomplicated diverticulitis. The second cycle (September 2024–March 2025) included 46 patients: 24 complicated and 22 uncomplicated cases. Colonoscopy rates, timing, and findings were recorded and compared. Malignancy rates and the need for emergency surgery were also assessed. Results In the first cycle, only 1 of 21 colonoscopies was performed within the 6-8 week period, and 1 malignancy was detected. After staff training and awareness initiatives, 6 of 18 complicated cases in the second cycle received timely colonoscopy, representing a significant improvement. No malignancies were detected in the second cycle. Overall, 46% of complicated cases had timely colonoscopy, compared to 5% in the first cycle. Conclusions The audit shows significant improvement in colonoscopy compliance for complicated diverticulitis. Given the low malignancy risk, routine colonoscopy for uncomplicated cases should be reconsidered. Future recommendations include enhancing discharge procedures and prioritizing colonoscopy for complicated cases.
affiliations: NHS Lanarkshire , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.221.title: 433 From Scan to Scalpel: A Retrospective Audit of Imaging and Surgical Timeliness in Acute Abdomen Following Digitalisation of CT Vetting
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.221.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate whether digitalising the CT vetting workflow improved imaging timeliness, adherence to Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) guideline standards and surgical pathway efficiency in adults presenting with acute abdominal pain. Method A retrospective audit was conducted of adults referred to general surgery with acute abdominal pain at Ealing Hospital. Outcomes were compared before and after implementation of digital CT vetting. Measures included radiology process intervals, compliance with RCS targets, surgical pathway intervals and clinical outcomes. Continuous variables were analysed using Mann–Whitney U tests and categorical variables using Fisher’s exact test. Results Time from admission to imaging improved significantly following implementation of the digital vetting process. Median time decreased from 6 hours 8 minutes pre-intervention to 4 hours 35 minutes post-intervention (p=0.0488). Radiology process mapping showed descriptive improvement in several intervals, although the interval from scan completion to first report increased significantly from 13 minutes to 27 minutes (p=0.0404). Compliance with RCS imaging standards increased from 28 percent to 38.5 percent, but the change was not statistically significant (p=0.68). No significant differences were found in time to first surgical review (p=0.904) or time to surgery (p=0.1138). Clinical outcomes also remained similar. Conclusions Digitalising CT vetting improved overall imaging timeliness but did not accelerate surgical review or operation. Broader workflow optimisation is required to translate imaging gains into improvements in surgical timelines and outcomes for high-risk patients.

London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust Northwick Park Hospital , London ,
London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust Ealing Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.278.title: 1374 Theatre Turn-Around Times in Northern Ireland (NI) – a Baseline Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.278.abstract: Abstract Aim To establish a contemporary baseline for theatre turn-around times across Northern Ireland (NI) and identify areas to improve efficiency within gynaecological and general surgery theatres. Method A prospective multicentre audit was conducted across nine NI hospital sites. Only general surgery and gynaecology lists were included. Data collection was carried out over six consecutive weeks. Forty-six variables were collected for each case, capturing key components of the turn-around process. Descriptive statistics were generated, normality was confirmed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, and t-tests were performed for inter-trust comparisons. Results A total of 116 cases were analysed (Belfast n=17, Northern n=56, Southern n=20, Western n=23). Mean component times included: scrub time 4.7 mins (SD 2.2), induction of anaesthesia 4.59 mins (SD 4.19), transfer onto table 1.27 mins (SD 1.18), operation duration 70.59 mins (SD 47.85), transfer back to bed 3.03 mins (SD 3.17), extubation 5.11 mins (SD 4.87), cleaning 8.11 mins (SD 5.51), and ready time 3.3 mins (SD 9.33). The mean overall theatre turn-around time was 37.7 mins (SD 15.4), exceeding the accepted gold standard. Median turn-around times were longer in general surgery than in gynaecology. No significant differences were observed between trusts in relation to delayed list starts (p=0.2703). Specific causes of delay could not be determined. Conclusions This audit provides the first contemporary baseline of theatre turn-around times in NI, demonstrating times well above the national benchmarking targets(15 minutes). Targeted local reviews are required to identify actionable areas for improvement.

Student Healthcare Audit Society , Belfast ,
Belfast HSC Trust , Belfast ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.562.title: 542 Assessment of Inflammatory Markers and Antibiotic Prescribing Practices in Acute Diverticulitis: Insights from a District General Hospital Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.562.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute diverticulitis accounts for a substantial proportion of emergency presentations in the UK. Current national guidelines recommend selective antibiotic use in uncomplicated diverticulitis and emphasize the role of inflammatory markers and CT findings in stratifying severity. We evaluated real-world practice and explored clinical factors associated with complicated diverticulitis in a district general hospital. Method A retrospective analysis of 143 patients with CT-confirmed acute diverticulitis over 6 months was performed. Data collected included demographics, inflammatory markers (CRP, WCC), CT severity, modified Hinchey classification, antibiotic use, immunocompetence and 30-day reattendance. Associations between inflammatory markers, age, time-to-presentation and complicated disease were analysed using t-tests and chi-square tests. Results are reported using descriptive statistics following analysis. Results Uncomplicated diverticulitis accounted for 74.9% of cases. Among immunocompetent patients with CT-confirmed uncomplicated diverticulitis (modified Hinchey </=1A), antibiotic prescribing remained almost universal at 95.3%, rising to 97% in the entire cohort. CRP was significantly higher in complicated cases (148.1 vs 71.2 mg/L, p=0.0035), as was WCC (12.55 vs 10.70×10⁹/L, p=0.049). Complicated patients were older (66.2 vs 60.0 years, p=0.035) and less often immunocompetent (30.6% vs 59.8%, p=0.0044). Time-to-presentation was not significantly different. The 30-day reattendance rate was 8.4%, primarily due to recurrent symptoms. Conclusions CRP, WCC, age and immunocompetence are significantly associated with disease severity. However, antibiotic prescribing was almost widespread, irrespective of clinical risk indicators. These results highlight importance of consideration of these factors in patient assessment and support the adoption of severity-guided prescribing pathways in line with NICE NG147, ACPGBI and GIRFT recommendations.
affiliations: Frimley Health NHS Foundation Trust , Surrey ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.481.title: 863 Renal Transplant Survival at Belfast City Hospital: A Five-Year Retrospective Audit of Predictors and Performance
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.481.abstract: Abstract Aim Belfast City Hospital has maintained a historically strong record in renal transplantation; however, outcome variability continues to reflect donor, recipient, and perioperative factors. This study aimed to evaluate graft and patient survival over a five-year period and identify key determinants influencing post-transplant outcomes. Method A retrospective review was conducted of all renal transplants performed from 2014–2019. Data on donor demographics, cold ischaemic time, pre-transplant dialysis, rejection episodes, and discharge renal function were analysed. Graft and patient survival were calculated using Kaplan–Meier methodology, with subgroup comparisons by univariate methods. Results Despite historically favourable outcomes, overall five-year survival during this period was below national benchmarks. Increased donor age and prolonged cold ischaemic time were significantly associated with inferior graft and patient survival. Pre-transplant dialysis and biopsy-proven rejection also independently predicted poor outcomes. Conversely, lower discharge serum creatinine correlated with improved long-term function. Donor gender had no significant impact. Data consistency limited multivariate modelling; incomplete records precluded robust assessment of recipient comorbidities such as BMI and diabetes in some cases. Conclusions Between 2014 and 2019, Belfast City Hospital’s renal transplant survival outcomes were below average compared with previous years. Key modifiable risk factors included donor selection, cold ischaemic duration, and early graft function. Enhancing perioperative optimisation will be critical to improving future survival rates.
affiliations: Queen's University Belfast School of Medicine, Dentistry and Biomedical Sciences , Belfast ,
Department of Transplant Surgery, Belfast City Hospital , Belfast ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.466.title: 558 The Cost of Primary Hip and Knee Arthroplasty Components in BCUHB: An Audit of National Practice
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.466.abstract: Abstract Aim This retrospective audit aims to compare each Welsh health board’s average cost for a fully cemented hip, fully uncemented hip, hybrid hip and knee arthroplasty against the NWSSP standard of £800. Method Using Q1 & Q2 2024’s total spends, the average cost was calculated, per health board, for each hip and knee component. These figures were used to calculate the cost for each prosthesis type and the number of each performed. Results The standard of £800 was met by all health boards for fully cemented hips (average of £508.30) (excluding those not using fully cemented hips). From Welsh averages, hybrid hips were also under the national standard at £717.70. When compared to uncemented hips, fully cemented hips would save £41,109 per 100 primary hip arthroplasties. No health board met the national standard for knee arthroplasty costs. Conclusions We recommend an all-Wales plan to standardise the supply of hip and knee arthroplasty components or rationalisation from each health board independently. Alternatively, fully cemented hips could be stated as the preferred prosthesis for hip arthroplasty in Wales. Results from this audit have been used to make recommendations for the new orthopaedic centre in Llandudno.
affiliations: Cardiff University , Cardiff ,
Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board , Bangor ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.766.title: 1421 Epididymitis and Orchitis Management: An Audit of Compliance With GIRFT and Local Antimicrobial Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.766.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess local performance in the management of epididymitis and orchitis against GIRFT guidelines and local antimicrobial guidelines. Method A retrospective audit of patients presenting with testicular pain to the Surgical Same Day Emergency Centre (SSDEC) and Surgical Assessment Unit (SAU) was conducted. The first cycle of the audit reviewed compliance with age-based antimicrobial prescribing, sexual health assessment and compliance with the GIRFT pathway. Following this, an intervention was implemented consisting of QR code links to GIRFT pathways and antimicrobial guidelines. These were in poster format throughout SSDEC and SAU. A second audit with the same parameters was conducted after intervention. Results Across both cycles, 88 patients were included in the audit: 58 in cycle 1 and 30 in cycle 2. Antibiotics compliance improved from 50% to 70% following the intervention. Uptake of sexual health history and assessment increased by 34%. However, the main barrier for compliance was the non-compliance of IM ceftriaxone due to a lack of familiarity with reconstituting with 1% lidocaine. Conclusions Following 2 audit cycles, there was demonstrable improved adherence to GIRFT and antimicrobial guidelines and sexual health assessment as part of epididymitis/orchitis management. Patients with LUTS and symptomatic hydroceles were given outpatient follow-up. The above findings were discussed in a local meeting which yielded a collaboration with the antimicrobial team and prompted a change from IM to IV administration for ceftriaxone to increase compliance. This will be further re-audited to ensure the achieved improvements are sustained.
affiliations: Royal Stoke University Hospital , Stoke-on-Trent ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.137.title: 1358 The Price of Precision: A Financial Audit of Organ Transport Logistics and Cost-Benefit Analysis of Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV) Integration
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.137.abstract: Abstract Aim Organ transplantation relies on time-critical logistics, yet rising costs threaten sustainability. This study audited transport expenditure at a major Scottish transplant centre to model the financial viability of integrating Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to replace high-cost conventional transport legs. Method A retrospective financial audit of all organ transport invoices was conducted (2024-2025). Transport modes were categorised into road and air (commercial/charter). Efficiencies were evaluated by identifying high-cost "first-mile/last-mile" transfers and regional charters. A cost-benefit analysis modelled the acquisition of a long-range VTOL UAV (SkyLane-480; CAPEX £115,570; Range 1,000km) against current outsourcing costs. Results Total annual expenditure was £177,260. Air transport consumed 65.5% (£116,056) of the budget despite representing a minority of journeys. Single charter flights cost up to £18,905.
