Significant inefficiencies were identified in "last-mile" logistics, where short hospital-to-airport transfers (<15 miles) utilized private ambulances costing up to £1,951 per leg. Comparative modelling demonstrates that replacing regional charters (e.g., Newcastle - Edinburgh) with a UAV achieves break-even after just 10-12 missions. Additionally, UAV ownership eliminates the financial loss of non-refundable deposits (∼£10,000) when charters are cancelled due to donor unsuitability - a sunk cost in current charter models. Conclusions Current logistics are characterised by disproportionate costs for short-range transfers and expensive ad-hoc charters. Integrating long-range UAVs is a financially prudent strategy. Our model suggests capital investment in drone infrastructure yields a return on investment within a single financial year by displacing inefficient legacy spending.
affiliations: University of Edinburgh , Edinburgh ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.233.title: 614 Necrotising Fasciitis in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.233.abstract: Abstract Aim To determine the incidence of necrotising fasciitis at a busy urban district general hospital and to assess departmental compliance against recently published BOAST guidelines for management of musculoskeletal soft tissue infections. Method All referrals to the orthopaedic service for suspected soft-tissue infection between April and September 2025 were retrospectively identified. Analysis identified confirmed cases of necrotising fasciitis. Clinical timelines, operative intervention and microbiological investigations were assessed for compliance with BOAST guidelines. Results Of 20 referrals, 3 (15%) were confirmed as necrotising fasciitis, all affecting the lower limb. All patients were clinically septic on admission and received the sepsis six within one hour, meeting BOAST guidelines. All cases underwent emergency operative management, with a mean decision-to-incision time of 2 hours (range 1-3), meeting the BOAST guidance for prompt surgical debridement. Intra-operative sampling was performed in all cases, median 1 specimen per procedure (range 1-3), and histology was obtained in 2/3. Polymicrobial growth (Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus species) was seen in two cases; Serratia Marcesecens was isolated in the third. One patient died within 72 hours; the remaining two required multiple returns to theatre (3 and 7 respectively) with a mean hospital stay of 50 days (34-66). Conclusions Necrotising Fasciitis remains an uncommon but rapidly fatal and costly condition presenting to the acute orthopaedic take. We demonstrate high local compliance with BOAST guidelines, particularly regarding early recognition, sepsis management and urgent debridement. Improvements will be driven through focussed teaching and workshops with relevant healthcare professionals, structured pathway reinforcement and planned re-audit to ensure sustained, measurable progress.
affiliations: Lewisham and Greenwich NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.033.title: 398 Artificial Intelligence vs. Clinical Interpretation in the Detection of Hip Fractures: A Comparative Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.033.abstract: Abstract Aim To compare the diagnostic accuracy of a specialised medical artificial intelligence system (RBfracture) and a general-purpose Large Multimodal Model (Gemini) with standard clinician interpretation in detecting occult neck of femur (NOF) fractures on pelvic radiographs, using computed tomography (CT) as the gold standard. Method This retrospective audit involved 63 trauma patients presenting with hip pain and inconclusive initial pelvic radiographs. Each case was independently evaluated by RBfracture (versions 1.8–2.1), Gemini, and routine clinical interpretation. Diagnostic performance metrics, including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), were calculated for each modality against final CT findings to assess their effectiveness in detecting radiographically subtle NOF fractures. Results The specialised RBfracture AI demonstrated the highest sensitivity (94.1%) and NPV (94.4%), significantly outperforming clinicians, whose sensitivity was 39.1%, leading to most occult fractures being missed. Clinicians, however, achieved the greatest specificity (63.8%), indicating a superior ability to correctly identify normal anatomy and reduce false positives compared with RBfracture (37.0%). Gemini showed intermediate performance (sensitivity 47.1%, specificity 58.7%), similar to clinicians but below the threshold deemed necessary for reliable triage. Notably, Gemini successfully detected the single fracture missed by RBfracture. Conclusions Specialised fracture-detection AI provides a highly sensitive safety net for occult NOF fractures, significantly reducing missed injuries compared with clinician interpretation alone. Although general-purpose multimodal models show emerging usefulness, they currently lack adequate sensitivity for frontline triage. Integrating specialised AI into a tiered diagnostic pathway could enhance early detection and clinical decision-making.
affiliations: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.227.title: 549 ‘Group and Save’ Practice in Emergency and Elective Surgery: An Audit of Adherence in a Surgical Unit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.227.abstract: Abstract Aim Surgical centres around the UK have their own protocols regarding routine collection of ‘group and save’ (G&S) samples prior to emergency and elective surgeries, due to lack of guidance provided by governing bodies. A single G&S sample costs £29. Our aim was to establish the indication for, and adherence to, G&S sampling in emergency and elective procedures in our unit. Method A retrospective audit was conducted within a surgical department at a tertiary centre over one month. Data was collected for all emergency and elective procedures; number of G&S samples collected, indication for the procedure and intra-operative transfusion received. Following intervention targeted to pre-operative clinics via posters and email communication, the audit cycle was repeated. Results 391 procedures were performed in cycle 1 (153 emergency, 238 elective) and 450 in cycle 2 (171 emergency, 279 elective). In cycle 1, 203 G&S samples were collected, 52 (26%) of which were not indicated - 25/82 (30%) emergency, 27/121 (22%) elective. In cycle 2, 73 of 260 samples taken were not indicated: 44/114 (28%) emergency, 29/146 (20%) elective. This represented an avoidable monthly cost of £1508 in cycle 1 and £2177 in cycle 2, corresponding, respectively, to £18,096 and £25,404 per annum. Conclusions This audit highlights gaps in adherence to local G&S sample protocols; despite a small decrease in unnecessary samples taken for elective procedures, emergency procedures remain a problem. Given the significant cost burden to the NHS, review of current guidelines and further reinforcement of compliance to guidance is important.
affiliations: NHS Mersey and West Lancashire , Liverpool ,
University of Edinburgh , Edinburgh ,
The Dudley Group NHS Trust , Dudley ,
NHS Lothian , Edinburgh ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.399.title: 468 Post-Thyroidectomy Voice and Vocal Cord Function Outcomes and Management: A Two-Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.399.abstract: Abstract Aim Voice changes and recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) injury remain key complications following thyroid surgery. Although national guidelines (BAETS/ENT UK) recommended; structured documentation, early flexible nasendoscopy (FNE), timely SLT referrals, practice varies. This audit assessed adherence to these standard in a high-volume tertiary centre and identified opportunities to optimised postoperative voice outcomes. Method A retrospective audit of adult thyroidectomies performed between September 2024 and June 2025 evaluated compliance with BAETS/ENT UK postoperative standards: (1)voice documentation within 24 hours, (2)FNE for symptomatic/asymptomatic patients, (3)SLT/Laryngology referral when indicated, (4)use of validated PROMs. Secondary measures included incidence of VC dysfunction and comparing outcomes between benign and malignant disease. Minimum follow-up being three months. Results 100 patients were included (mean age 50; 75% female). Malignancy confirmed in 66%. Postoperative voice changes occurred in 20%, with 18% resolving and 2% persisting at three months. RLN injury occurred in 4%; two patients were referred to SLT and two developed bilateral vocal cord palsy. Among symptomatic patients, 35% underwent FNE within 24 hours, 55% confirmed malignancy. PROMs (VHI-10, EAT-10) were not routinely used. Voice documentation within 24 hours was achieved in 89%, but longer-term monitoring was inconsistent. Following implementation of targeted interventions (structured proforma, SLT referral, PROM integration), early second-cycle data indicated improved documentation and referral rates. Conclusions This audit highlights variability in adherence to national voice-care standards post-thyroidectomy. Implementing structured documentation, mandatory SLT referral pathways and routine PROM use can enhance MDT care, support early detection of complications and improve patient-reported outcomes.
affiliations: Kings College London , London ,
Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.299.title: 1108 Improving Patient Flow in a 2 Week Wait One-Stop Breast Clinic: A Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.299.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate the time patients spend in the Breast Outpatient Clinic during triple assessment, identify factors contributing to prolonged total clinic duration, and assess the impact of introducing a new breast clinic proforma on reducing waiting times and improving patient experience. This quality-improvement project was guided by the Royal College of Surgeons’ Outpatient Clinics: A Guide to Good Practice and the GIRFT Clinically-Led Specialty Outpatient Guidance (2023), both of which promote efficient one-stop outpatient pathways. Method A prospective audit (n=38) was conducted analysing key time intervals: patient arrival-to-clinical review, clinical review-to-imaging, imaging-to-results, and total clinic duration. A new breast clinic proforma was developed to improve documentation, optimise workflow, and facilitate earlier discharge for patients with normal clinical and radiological findings. A prospective re-audit was performed following implementation (n=56). Results The initial audit demonstrated prolonged waits, with a mean 2 hours 20 minutes from imaging to results. Only 20% required core biopsy, additional imaging or further assessment, indicating potential to reduce unnecessary waiting by over one hour for the majority of patients. Following introduction of the proforma, the re-audit showed a 36-minute reduction in total clinic duration. Time saved was redirected to patients requiring more complex assessment, while overall clinic flow and patient experience improved. Conclusions A standardised breast clinic proforma and pathway redesign significantly reduced patient waiting times and improved efficiency and patient experience within the one-stop 2 Week Wait breast clinic.
affiliations: Blackpool Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Blackpool ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.595.title: 1481 Oesophageal Perforation Following Heller’s Cardiomyotomy: A Single Centre Audit of Outcomes Following Laparoscopic Versus Robotic Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.595.abstract: Abstract Aim To compare the incidence of oesophageal perforation following robotic Heller’s cardiomyotomy (HC) to laparoscopic HC in a single centre in the United Kingdom. Method We performed a retrospective review of outcomes comparing robotic HC (2023-2025) to laparoscopic HC (2018-2023). Demographic and perioperative data were collected. The primary outcome was rate of oesophageal perforation detected post-operatively. Secondary outcomes were 30-day morbidity and mortality. Results There were 21 patients in each group. The median age in the robotic group was 37 years compared to 52 years in the laparoscopic group. 14/21 (66.7%) in each group were male. There was a history of abdominal surgery in 3/21 (14.3%) of the robotic group compared to 4/21 (19.0%) in the laparoscopic group. Pre-operative endoscopic intervention was performed in 8/21 (38.1%) of the robotic group compared to 15/21 (71.4%) of the laparoscopic group. Median length of myotomy was 8cm in both groups. There were zero conversions to open surgery in either group. There were zero oesophageal perforations identified post-operatively in the robotic group compared to 3/21 (14.3%) in the laparoscopic group. All perforations were associated with ITU admission, return to theatre and a mean post-operative length of stay of 46 days. Other morbidity included intervention for upper gastrointestinal bleed and gastric outlet obstruction in 2/21 (9.5%) cases in the laparoscopic group. There were no mortalities. Conclusions There was a lower rate of oesophageal perforation and other morbidity in robotic HC compared to laparoscopic HC. Our findings support the continued use of the robotic approach to HC in our centre.
affiliations: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust , Bristol ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.272.title: 1264 Audit: Compliance With ESTS and BTS Guidelines for Intraoperative Lymph Node Staging in NSCLC Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.272.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit assesses variations in surgical practice and evaluates compliance with European Society of Thoracic Surgeons (ESTS) and British Thoracic Society (BTS) intraoperative lymph node (LN) staging guidelines in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) surgery, aiming to improve staging accuracy and optimise oncological treatment pathways. Method A retrospective closed-loop audit of NSCLC resections (lobectomy and wedge with LN dissection) was undertaken at a tertiary thoracic centre. Cycle 1 included 92 cases (10/2024–02/2025), followed by 76 re-audited cases after presentation of results and dissemination of guideline summaries (03/2025–07/2025). LN yield was stratified, and “potential compliance” was assessed where N1 nodes may have been incorporated within the specimen. Operative notes and histopathology were reviewed for N1/N2 involvement. Percentage compliance was compared across thoracotomy, VATS and RATS. Results Across both audit cycles, modest improvement in guideline compliance was observed. Overall compliance rose from 16.3% to 17.1%, with slight increases in thoracotomy (8.7% to 12.5%) and VATS (6.5% to 8.0%), while RATS remained the highest-performing approach. The average LN stations dissected were similar across cycles, with a cohort median of 5 stations (range 1-9; IQR 4-6). RATS consistently yielded the greatest nodal clearance and highest compliance. Although station 7 was consistently dissected, overall clearance remained below ESTS standards, partly due to hilar nodes being included within the specimen. Conclusions This closed-loop audit showed persistent variability and overall low compliance, highlighting a continued gap in nodal staging that may risk under-staging. Continued education and regular audit cycles are needed to standardise practice and improve staging accuracy.
affiliations: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust , London ,
University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust , West Sussex ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.252.title: 848 Improving Compliance With Indwelling Catheter Securement in an Orthopedic Unit: A Two-Cycle Audit Against Best-Practice Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.252.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess compliance with evidence-based guidelines on securing indwelling urinary catheters in an orthopedic ward and evaluate the necessity of a targeted educational intervention. Major CAUTI-prevention guidelines (CDC and AHRQ) recommend applying a securement device during insertion and maintaining it throughout the catheter use. Based on these standards, a benchmark target of ≥90% appropriate catheter securement was expected. Method A two-cycle retrospective audit was conducted in a tertiary care orthopedic unit over four months per cycle. Data were collected on all catheterized inpatients, focusing on securement presence, site, and documentation. After the first cycle, a multifaceted intervention was implemented: structured teaching for nursing and junior medical staff on guideline-based securement practice, and introduction of a catheter care checklist incorporating securement as a mandatory item. A re-audit measured post-intervention compliance. Results 86 patients were included in the initial cycle. Only 10.4% had appropriately secured catheters while 6.9 % of them were done intraoperatively and the rest in ICU setting. The majority of ward-inserted catheters had no securement, demonstrating major deviation from best-practice standards. After the intervention, 76 patients were reviewed in the re-audit, with appropriate securement improving to 40.7%, representing a near 4-fold increase but remaining below the ≥90% benchmark. Conclusions Lack of awareness of the importance of securing a catheter among the staff was identified as the main reason for suboptimal practice. A simple, low-cost intervention comprising staff education and checklist implementation produced substantial improvement. Sustained reinforcement and further cycles are required to achieve guideline-compliant practice and optimize patient comfort and safety.
affiliations: Post Graduate Institute of Medicine, University of Colombo , Colombo ,
National Hospital of Sri Lanka , Colombo ,
University Hospital of Derby and Burton , Derby ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.556.title: 403 Audit of Time Efficiency in Creating Clinical Discharge Documents (CDDs) Using Copilot Agent in General Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.556.abstract: Abstract Background Timely completion of Clinical Discharge Documents (CDDs) is critical for patient flow and bed availability in surgical wards. Administrative burden on junior doctors often leads to delays, impacting service efficiency. AI-assisted tools such as Copilot may streamline documentation and reduce cognitive load. Aim To evaluate the time-saving potential and usability of the Copilot agent in generating CDDs compared to manual completion. Method A prospective audit was conducted in the general surgery department at NHS Grampian. Five patient cases were selected. Resident doctors recorded time taken to complete CDDs manually and then using Copilot for the same patient. Efficiency gains were calculated, and qualitative feedback on accuracy and usability was collected. Results Copilot reduced documentation time by an average of 4 minutes 32 seconds per case (35.6%), with the greatest saving of 7 minutes 45 seconds (81.6%). One case showed negative time saving, likely due to a learning curve. Accuracy was generally acceptable; most errors stemmed from incomplete inpatient records and medication discrepancies. Conclusions Copilot demonstrates strong potential to improve discharge efficiency in surgical settings. Integration with Electronic Patient Record systems and enhanced data handling are essential for reliability. Wider implementation could reduce administrative burden and improve patient flow.
affiliations: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary , Aberdeen ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.246.title: 770 Audit of Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) Negative Referrals to Urgent Suspected Cancer Pathway in Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust (MSE)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.246.abstract: Abstract Introduction National Guidance stipulates that Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) should be used in primary care to guide referrals to the Colorectal Urgent Suspected Cancer Pathway (USCP). With normal blood count and normal examination, there is 0.1% chance of finding a colorectal cancer if a patient is FIT-negative. These patients should be managed on a non-USCP. In MSE, the Rapid Diagnostic Centre (RDC) still receive up to 20% FIT-negative patients on the USCP. As no FIT-negative internal pathway exists in MSE, patients are still being offered endoscopy at index referral. Aim To review how many confirmed cancers were FIT-positive and how many were FIT-negative. Method MSE and shared GP records were searched between December 2023 and October 2025. 20752 patients were referred on the USCP, 1037 were confirmed cancer. Results 925 (89.2%) patients were FIT-positive, 9 (0.87%) were FIT-negative. Of these nine FIT-negative, five had iron deficiency anaemia (IDA), two had significant weight loss and two had anal mass. 103 had no FIT test, of these 37 were emergency admissions or incidental findings; 13 were from surveillance; 37 had other red-flag symptoms; 16 were IDA. Conclusions FIT-negative cancer is rare (0.87%), and these patients all had other symptoms/clinical indications which warranted investigations on the USC pathway. Local data supports the national guidance that FIT-negative patients with normal blood count and normal examination, can be safely reassured and/or managed on a non-USC pathway. This audit has supported the proposed change that FIT-negative referrals to the USCP should be discharged and managed on other pathways.
affiliations: Basildon University Hospital , Basildon ,
Southend University Hospital , Southend-on-Sea ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.217.title: 380 Where We Stand Against the National Standards: A Multi-Centre Audit of Post-Operative Appendectomy Documentation in Adult and Paediatric Populations
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.217.abstract: Abstract Aim High-quality post-operative documentation is essential for correct care and reducing complications. National recommendations from Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) and the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) emphasize the need for clear, standardized post-operative records that reliably communicate post-operative plans. This audit evaluates local post-operative appendectomy documentation against GIRFT and RCS standards to identify compliance and improvement opportunities. Method A retrospective review of appendectomy cases undertaken between March and April 2025 at Frimley Park Hospital (FPH) and Wexham Park Hospital (WPH) was performed. Patients were identified through the trusts’ electronic records, and post-operative notes were reviewed. Documentation was assessed for completeness in key domains: antibiotics, blood tests (if indicated), recovery location, observation frequency, drain removal (if applicable), VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis, diet instructions, discharge planning, suture removal, and follow-up arrangements, the presence of signatures and photo attachments. Compliance was calculated as the proportion of cases meeting each standard. Results Eighty-three patients were identified (45 FPH, 38 WPH). Compliance varied by domain and site. High-compliance areas included antibiotic documentation (87% FPH, 68% WPH), VTE documentation (80% FPH, 55% WPH), and diet instructions (94% FPH, 90% WPH). Poor compliance was noted for recovery location (7% FPH, 10% WPH), observation frequency (4% FPH, 7% WPH), and suture removal (22% FPH, 16% WPH), with details often vague or incomplete. Conclusions Post-operative appendectomy documentation only partially meets standards. Key shortfalls relate to post operative monitoring and removal of sutures. Introducing a standardized post-operative proforma and education for trainees may improve documentation consistency.
affiliations: Frimley Park Hospital , Camberley ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.243.title: 750 Audit of the Timing of Cholecystectomy in Gallstone-Induced Pancreatitis: Adherence to Guidelines and Impact on Patient Outcomes
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.243.abstract: Abstract Aim Gallstone-induced pancreatitis (GIP) is a major cause of surgical admissions in theUK. Early cholecystectomy, ideally during index admission or two weeks following discharge, is recommended by national guidelines to prevent recurrent biliary events. To assess adherence to these guidelines at University Hospital Monklands (UHM) and evaluate the clinical impact of delays in cholecystectomy Method Retrospective data collection was conducted for patients admitted with gallstone-induced pancreatitis between September 2023 and September 2024. Data were retrieved under Caldicott approval (CG Ref No: 2568, LanQIP registry 25855). Exclusion criteria included severe pancreatitis, frailty, and refusal. Outcomes measured: timing of cholecystectomy, readmission rate, and time to intervention. A re-audit (Jan–Jun 2025) followed pathway implementation. Results First Cycle: Of 69 total cases, 8 excluded; 2 deaths; 59 eligible. Procedures performed: 30(50.8%), timely procedures: 9 (15.2%), mean delay 11.2 weeks. Nineteen (32%) readmitted, 10 with recurrent GIP.Second Cycle: 41 admissions, 11 excluded; 30 eligible. 15 operated (50%), 13 (43%) timely—12 during index admission, 1 within 2 weeks post-discharge. Compliance improved following expedited cholecystectomy pathway and live tracker introduction. The audit identified poor adherence to guidelines in the first cycle, with significant readmission and recurrence rates. Root causes included lack of structured follow-up, delays in anaesthetic clearance, and limited theatre availability. Implementation of the expedited pathway and live tracker improved outcomes. Further gains depend on multidisciplinary cooperation and sustained monitoring. Conclusions Performing cholecystectomy during index admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis reduces readmission and complications. Structured pathways and real-time tracking enhance adherence to standards. Continued re-audit is recommended.
affiliations: NHS Lanarkshire Monklands Hospital , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.213.title: 311 Improving Surgical Site Infection Surveillance in Vascular Surgery: Findings from a Single-Centre Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.213.abstract: Abstract Aim Surgical site infections (SSIs) are a major source of postoperative morbidity, unplanned readmissions, and healthcare costs. Vascular surgery carries a higher risk due to patient comorbidities and complex surgeries. This audit aimed to evaluate SSI rates within a single vascular surgery department and establish sustainable prospective SSI data collection. Method A retrospective review was undertaken of 145 predominantly arterial procedures (125 patients) between March–April 2025. SSIs were defined using UKHSA criteria, as surgical wound infections within 30 days of surgery. Exclusion criteria included previously infected wounds in the context of osteomyelitis, DM and revision surgeries for non-healing wounds due to poor vascularisation. Results Case mix comprised 69.7% elective procedures. 13.6% of patients needed more than 1 procedure. Seven SSIs were identified (4.8%). Five cases required antibiotics, one surgical re-intervention, and one was managed conservatively. There were no unplanned ITU admissions and only one readmission within 30 days. Documentation was frequently incomplete, with skin preparation absent in 36% of operative records and dressing type unspecified in 28.9%. Conclusions The observed SSI rate appears higher than national pooled vascular figures, reflecting the arterial inpatient case mix studied. Prospective surveillance will be conducted via a departmental spreadsheet, with SSIs systematically coded from electronic records and reviewed weekly at the vascular MDT. A dedicated induction poster has been developed and incorporated into staff induction to ensure sustainability across rotations. These measures support compliance with national quality improvement initiatives, including GIRFT, and provide a framework for accurate prospective surveillance.
affiliations: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London ,
Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.247.title: 776 Quality of Long-Term Follow-Up After Bariatric Surgery in Primary Care: A Quality Improvement Audit Comparing UK and Overseas Surgery Patients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.247.abstract: Abstract Aims To assess whether bariatric surgery patients registered at a UK general practice are receiving long-term follow-up in accordance with national recommendations, including NICE CG189/NG246 and BOMSS 2020 guidance, mandating specialist follow-up for at least a year post-surgery and lifelong annual monitoring in primary care. A secondary aim was to compare follow-up outcomes between patients who underwent surgery in the NHS, privately in the UK, and abroad. Method A retrospective review of electronic records identified 29 eligible bariatric patients (April 2009–September 2025). Data extracted included evidence of specialist follow-up, discharge communication, annual review(s), biochemistry monitoring, supplementation, and weight documentation. Outcomes were compared between UK versus abroad-operated patients using Chi-square testing. Results Continued involvement of a bariatric service was documented in 100% of NHS patients, 87.5% of private UK patients, and 0% abroad. Discharge letters into shared care were received in 81.8% (NHS), 100% (private), and 30% (abroad). Evidence of 1 annual review was 45.5% (NHS), 62.5% (private), and 40% (abroad), while ≥2 reviews occurred in 0%, 25%, and 10%. Annual biochemical monitoring occurred in 54.5% (NHS), 62.5% (private), and 50% (abroad). Evidence of lifelong multivitamin supplementation was lowest abroad (20% vs 81.8% NHS). Weight review was also poorest abroad (10% vs 45.5% NHS). Patients treated abroad demonstrated significantly reduced communication into primary care and lower adherence to supplementation. Conclusions Compliance with national standards is suboptimal, particularly among patients receiving surgery overseas. Service improvements include recall alerts, a structured bariatric review template, and strengthened communication pathways. Re-audit in 12 months is planned.
affiliations: University of Leicester , Leicester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.212.title: 297 Early Pain Control and Phyfsiotherapy Engagement Drive Recovery After Rotator Cuff Repair: A Two-Year Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.212.abstract: Abstract Aim Rotator cuff repair is a common orthopaedic procedure, and optimal recovery depends heavily on structured rehabilitation and adequate early pain management. National guidelines highlight the importance of consistent physiotherapy engagement; however, variability in follow-up and documentation may impact long-term outcomes. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on patients undergoing rotator cuff repair between 31/10/2023 and 31/10/2025. Data were extracted from ORMIS records and clinical notes, including demographics, perioperative factors, analgesia regimes, physiotherapy engagement, and six-month outcomes. Patients with incomplete documentation or not yet at the six-month postoperative point were excluded. Results Of 83 cases, 66 met inclusion criteria (mean age 61.1). No associations were found between demographics, ASA grade, operation side, or analgesia regime and six-month recovery. However, early engagement was strongly predictive of outcome: only 3% of patients with documented physiotherapy and pain improvement at two weeks required further follow-up, compared with 19.7% of those with unresolved pain or absent engagement. Of those requiring extended care, 92.31% required additional physiotherapy, clinic appointments, or imaging. Conclusions Early physiotherapy engagement and effective pain management are strongly associated with improved recovery and reduced postoperative burden on services. To improve consistency and guideline alignment, a quality improvement objective will be set to increase documented physiotherapy engagement and pain review at two weeks from 27.3% to ≥70% within six months, through standardised documentation and earlier patient education and engagement.
affiliations: Whittington Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.457.title: 450 Evaluating the Implementation and Awareness of the 'SipTilSend' Protocol: A Clinical Quality Improvement Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.457.abstract: Abstract Aims This Quality Improvement Audit assessed: (1) patient awareness and understanding of preoperative clear-fluid intake; (2) staff knowledge, confidence and perceived challenges in implementing the ‘SipTilSend’ (STS) programme; and (3) barriers and opportunities to improve communication and adherence. Method Surveys were administered via Microsoft Forms to 40 surgical patients pre- and post-anaesthetic assessment, evaluating understanding of clear fluids, fasting instructions and perceived comfort. 20 nurses caring for these patients completed parallel surveys assessing STS knowledge, contraindications and barriers. Each survey included validated MCQs, binary items and free-text responses. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively; qualitative responses underwent thematic analysis. Independent reviewers collected all data with explicit consent. Results Before assessment, 20% of patients reported receiving no fasting instructions, and 80% believed only water qualified as a clear fluid. Post-assessment understanding improved, yet >50% remained unsure whether they were permitted to drink clear fluids, though most correctly excluded milk-containing drinks. Themes included dehydration-related headaches, anxiety and uncertainty regarding safety; only 2 patients reported no perceived difference when allowed to sip. Among nurses, 70% had only “maybe” heard of STS. While all recognised unsuitable fluids, thematic analysis showed misconceptions (“STS = sips of water only”), inconsistent perceived barriers (“aspiration risk,” “easier to keep NBM”), and low programme awareness (21% rating education 1/10). Conclusions Gaps in patient and staff understanding continue to limit effective STS implementation. Inconsistent communication, limited awareness and workflow pressures contribute to poor adherence. Targeted education and clearer visual aids represent key opportunities for improvement.
affiliations: Imperial College London, School of Medicine , London ,
London North West University NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.253.title: 854 An Audit of Perioperative Diabetes Management Against GIRFT Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.253.abstract: Abstract Aim GIRFT guidance for perioperative diabetes management was developed to reduce perioperative infection, length of stay and readmission for surgical patients with diabetes. In this double-cycle audit, we evaluate perioperative diabetes care at a tertiary centre against GIRFT guidance, aiming to identify safety-critical gaps and inform targeted improvements before cycle-2 re-audit. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on 145 National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD) Category 3 surgical inpatients in August 2025 at University Hospital Southampton. 19 patients had diabetes. Data were extracted from anaesthetic charts, perioperative documentation, inpatient paper records, and biochemical results. Standards were defined using GIRFT guidance. Domains assessed included pre-operative investigations, withholding SGLT-2 on admission, intra-operative and recovery glucose monitoring, variable rate insulin (VRI) initiation and transition, anaesthetic-to-ward handover, and postoperative glycaemic outcomes. Results Among the 19 patients, metabolic optimisation before surgery was incomplete, with only 53% receiving HbA1c and ketones checks. Intra-operative and recovery CBG monitoring were 59% and 63% respectively. VRI management showed variability, with only 45% receiving the appropriate long-acting insulin dose while on VRI. Anaesthetic to ward handover occurred in only 42% cases. Glycaemic outcomes showed clinically significant dysglycaemia, with 42% of patients experiencing hyperglycaemia and 21% with hypoglycaemia. Conclusions Cycle-1 demonstrates important shortfalls in perioperative diabetes documentation, monitoring, and handover. Findings highlight the need for multidisciplinary interventions, including targeted education for surgical and anaesthetic teams and clearer handover processes. These actions will be implemented before cycle-2 re-audit to improve compliance with GIRFT standards.
affiliations: University Hospital Southampton , Southampton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.257.title: 887 Enhancing Frailty Assessment in Emergency Surgical Admissions: Two-Cycle Audit of Screening Practices
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.257.abstract: Abstract Aim Frailty is a strong predictor of adverse outcomes in emergency general surgery (EGS), yet assessment remains inconsistently documented. Guidance from GIRFT and the British Geriatrics Society’s “Six Steps to Better Care for Older People in Acute Hospitals”, recommend frailty screening at admission for all ≥65 year old patients. This closed-loop audit evaluated frailty screening using four measures - Clinical Frailty Score (CFS), baseline mobility, 4AT delirium screening, and Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), aiming to develop a frailty assessment bundle for routine clerking. Method Two retrospective audit cycles were undertaken. The first reviewed 50 consecutive EGS admissions ≥65 years between 27/08/2025–08/09/2025. Following this, a targeted intervention was introduced, including - raising awareness, education of clerking teams, and promoting a frailty screening bundle comprising CFS, baseline mobility, 4AT and MUST. The second cycle reviewed 52 EGS admissions between 03/11/2025–17/11/2025. Documentation rates were compared across cycles and benchmarked against GIRFT and BGS standards. Results Documentation improved across several domains. CFS completion increased from 8% to 28%, baseline mobility from 44% to 48%, and 4AT remained high (100% → 92.3%). Nutritional screening showed a modest decline (82% → 67.3%). The intervention improved awareness and uptake of CFS, though variation persisted across supporting assessments. Conclusions Targeted intervention improved compliance with frailty assessment, though it still remains below recommended levels. Continued reinforcement of the frailty assessment bundle is likely to sustain progress. Improved CFS documentation will help identify patients with CFS >6, providing essential data to support a business case for dedicated comprehensive geriatric assessment within the surgical pathway.
affiliations: Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust , Leeds ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.226.title: 538 Audit of Abdominal Pain Pathway for Paediatric Surgery Patients in Compliance with Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.226.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute abdominal pain is a high-risk paediatric presentation, with appendicitis being the most common surgical emergency. Variation in management can lead to delayed diagnosis or unnecessary surgery. This audit assessed Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital’s (NNUH) compliance with Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) best-practice standards for acute appendicitis. Method A six-month retrospective audit was undertaken of children aged 0–16 years presenting with acute abdominal pain to the emergency department. Data were collected across 17 GIRFT-derived standards including analgesia, diagnostic assessment, MDT review, imaging access, surgery <24 hours of admission, antibiotic stewardship, intraoperative sampling, and post-operative outcomes including negative appendicectomy and readmission rates. Outcomes were compared with GIRFT recommendations and national benchmarks. Results Fifty-three appendicectomy cases were reviewed. Readmission rates were 0% at 6 months (0/53) and 2.9% at 3 years (8/275), both significantly lower than the national benchmark of 9.7% (p<0.05). The negative appendicectomy rate was 1.9% (1/53), lower than the national average of 6.1% (p>0.05). Full compliance was achieved across 15/17 audited standards. Identified areas of improvement related to peritoneal swab sampling and surgery being performed within 24 hours of admission. Conclusions NNUH demonstrates high compliance with GIRFT paediatric appendicectomy guidance; our audit suggesting this is associated with improved outcomes. Structured assessment and targeted investigations likely contribute to low negative appendicectomy rates, while low readmission rates reflect effective antibiotic stewardship, pain management and MDT involvement. Following departmental education, a re-audit to assess compliance with all 17 GIRFT standards should be undertaken.
affiliations: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital , Norwich ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.622.title: 112 Empowering Surgical Trainees in ENT Emergencies: Lessons From a Dual-Cycle ED Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.622.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate and strengthen clinicians’ competence in managing ENT emergencies (epistaxis and vertigo) within the emergency-general-surgical (EGS) framework, using structured teaching, simulation, and pathway-based quality improvement in a district general hospital. Method Two sequential audits assessed emergency clinicians’ knowledge and management of epistaxis and vertigo against NICE and RCEM standards. Domains included anatomy, first aid, procedural skills (nasal cautery, packing, Dix-Hallpike, Epley, HINTS), escalation, and documentation. Interventions comprised:Joint ED–EGS teaching sessions with simulation and practical workshops.Introduction of ENT management proformas and algorithmic flowcharts accessible via the intranet.Visual learning resources and QR-linked videos for procedural refreshers. Cycle-2 data captured post-intervention improvement and qualitative feedback on applicability to surgical training. Results Knowledge and confidence improved across both domains: first-aid and procedural steps (Epistaxis: 33 → 84 %; Vertigo: 69 → 80 %) and recognition of central-cause red flags (Vertigo: 32 → 85 %). Respondents reported better procedural confidence, more consistent escalation, and reduced inappropriate ENT referrals. Simulation sessions were rated highly useful for embedding skills transferable to other surgical emergencies such as airway and bleeding control. Conclusion Integrating ENT emergency management into surgical education through structured teaching, visual tools, and re-audit enhances diagnostic accuracy, procedural skill, and interdepartmental collaboration. The project demonstrates a reproducible, low-cost model linking quality improvement with surgical-training objectives. Sustained incorporation into induction and re-audit cycles can improve workforce readiness, promote safer patient care, and help develop confident, adaptable surgeons prepared for cross-specialty acute scenarios.
affiliations: Hereford County Hospital , Hereford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.126.title: 535 A Retrospective Audit on Assessing Orbital Fracture in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery in a Teaching Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.126.abstract: Abstract Aim Orbital fracture is a common presentation in oral and maxillofacial surgery. Management often involves inputs from multi-disciplinary teams. The aim of the audit is to evaluate the assessment pathways on the appropriateness of imaging modalities and referral to ophthalmic and/or orthoptic assessment against the Get It Right First Time (GIRFT) pathway. Method A retrospective audit study was conducted between January and December 2024. Patient lists were reviewed to identify patients presenting with orbital fracture. Patients aged 18 or above were included in this study. Electronic case note review was subsequently performed. Results 27 patients were included in this study. All 27 patients underwent CT scan for diagnosis with 3 patients who initially had a plain film X ray prior to CT. 15 patients attended ophthalmic assessment with 13 attended orthoptic assessment. Among the 12 patients who received neither ophthalmic nor orthoptic assessments, none of them demonstrated positive findings on physical examination aside from mild bruising or swelling. Conclusions 12 patients met the criteria for plain radiographs on initial assessment. However, only three (25%) had plain radiographs initially and all subsequently underwent CT imaging. The findings showed the inconsistency on the choices of imaging and indicated the need for a local protocol. Standardised guidelines on imaging choices with a checklist of physical signs should be adopted to reduce the use of CT. Referral pathways for ophthalmic and orthoptic assessment would enhance the consistency of patient care.
affiliations: University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust , Derby ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.777.title: 780 Assessment of Alignment with National ReSPECT and Cardiac Arrest Decision-Making Standards: A Quality Improvement Audit of Escalation of Care Planning for Frail and Older Vascular Inpatients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.777.abstract: Abstract Background Timely escalation-of-care planning is critical to delivering safe, patient-centred care for frail and elderly inpatients. National guidance from the British Medical Association (BMA), Royal College of Nursing (RCN), and Resuscitation Council (UK) recommends early senior-led discussions, shared decision-making, and structured documentation using the ReSPECT (Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment) form. This audit evaluated adherence to these standards in a vascular inpatient cohort. Method A retrospective audit was conducted over 2 months, including vascular inpatients aged ≥75 or clinically frail. The audit standard, based on national recommendations, was 100% completion of a ReSPECT form for eligible patients. Documentation rates were assessed using electronic health records and analysed descriptively. Results A total of 47 patients met inclusion criteria. ReSPECT forms were completed in 11 cases (23.4%), significantly below the expected standard. Most missing documentation occurred in patients with urgent admissions—contexts where early escalation planning would be most valuable. Timing of form completion was inconsistently recorded, and no additional escalation-related domains met guideline expectations. Conclusions Compliance with national standards for escalation-of-care planning was low, highlighting systemic gaps in the application of ReSPECT and CPR decision-making frameworks in frail vascular patients. Integrating ReSPECT initiation into admission workflows, incorporating escalation discussions into multidisciplinary team (MDT) rounds, and introducing electronic prompts may improve uptake. Targeted education for junior clinicians could further strengthen documentation. Re-audit following implementation of these interventions is warranted.
affiliations: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust , Leicester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.077.title: 556 The Value of ‘check XRs’ Post Hemiarthroplasty- Challenging Whether Routine Post-Operative Pelvic Radiographs Are Clinically Important Following Hemiarthroplasties for Neck of Femur Fractures- a Retrospective Audit from a UK Major Trauma Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.077.abstract: Abstract Aim Currently, there is no national guideline regarding routine pelvic X-rays in the post-operative period following hemiarthroplasties for NOF fractures. Practice varies locally, and increasing evidence suggests that routine imaging may be unnecessary unless clinically indicated. This audit assessed the current practice at our Major Trauma Centre- University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW)- and evaluated the value of routine post-operative radiography. Method A retrospective review was conducted of all hemiarthroplasties performed for NOF fractures between May and October 2025 (n = 100). Data collected included whether a check pelvic x-ray was performed post-operatively, timing, documented clinical indication, mobilisation status before imaging, radiological findings, imaging reviewer documentation, and resultant intervention. Results Post-operative pelvic radiographs were performed in 98% of patients, with a mean timing of 2.71 days post-surgery. 90.8% of patients mobilised successfully with physiotherapy before imaging. Only 8.2% had a documented clinical indication (pain, fall, failure to mobilise, or suspected dislocation). Positive findings were identified in 3.1%: one dislocation and two leg-length discrepancies. The only clinically significant finding (dislocation) occurred in a patient unable to mobilise, appropriately prompting imaging and subsequent revision to THR. 32% of documentation lacked reviewer attribution. Conclusions Routine post-operative pelvic radiographs following hemiarthroplasty demonstrate a low diagnostic yield and limited impact on management. The only clinically significant case was associated with clear clinical indications. We recommend reserving post-operative imaging for clinically indicated cases. Implementation of an electronic proforma may support targeted imaging, enhance documentation, reduce radiation exposure, provide cost savings, improve patient comfort, and potentially shorten hospital stay.
affiliations: UHCW NHS Trust , Coventry ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.284.title: 1475 Advancing Rib Fracture Care: Two-Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.284.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate departmental compliance with local Trust guidelines for the management of multiple rib fractures, and to assess improvement following implementation of recommendations from the first audit cycle. Method A two-cycle retrospective audit was undertaken at Peterborough City Hospital. The first cycle reviewed patients admitted with multiple rib fractures between March 2023 and February 2024. The re-audit assessed practice between November 2024 and April 2025 after targeted interventions. Data were obtained from eTrack, ICE, EVOLVE, Symphony and Xero Viewer. Compliance with analgesia standards, imaging, chest injury scoring, pain team and regional anaesthesia referral, ABG performance, CCU referral and complication rates were evaluated. Length of stay (LOS) and patient comorbidities were also analysed. Results The first cycle included 101 patients and the second 62 patients. Across both cycles, elderly patients formed a substantial proportion and showed higher complication rates. Improvements observed in appropriate analgesia prescription and documentation of chest injury scoring. In the second cycle, regional analgesia was associated with reduced LOS (9.8 vs 12.6 days). However, persistent deficiencies remained: over 75% of patients meeting criteria were not referred to Critical Care, and compliance with ABG performance in hypoxic patients deteriorated. Pneumonia continued to significantly prolong LOS, increasing mean stay from 10.4 to 18.3 days. Patients with ≥16 fractures had markedly higher complication rates (27% vs 9%). Conclusions Despite targeted interventions, compliance with rib fracture management guidelines remains suboptimal. Key safety issues include inadequate CCU referral and inconsistent use of ABGs. Standardised pathways, mandatory proformas and improved education are required to enhance patient outcomes.
affiliations: Peterborough City Hospital , Peterborough ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.263.title: 1016 A 2 Cycle Audit Evaluating the Impact of an RCS-Aligned Proforma on Surgical Handover Compliance in a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.263.abstract: Abstract Aim Effective surgical handovers are essential for patient safety, continuity of care and minimising clinical errors. The Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) outline core criteria for safe handover. This audit evaluated local compliance with RCS standards in a district general hospital and assessed whether a structured proforma could improve handover quality. Method A two-cycle audit was conducted. In Cycle 1, a questionnaire based on 13 RCS criteria was distributed to surgical staff (n=27). Data were collected on the quality of information handed over, handover structure, and staff perception of safety. A structured RCS-aligned proforma was subsequently introduced. Cycle 2 repeated the questionnaire to assess its impact (n=20). Following cycle 2, the proforma was incorporated into the electronic system to enhance compliance. Mean adherence scores were compared using Student’s t-test. Results Cycle 1 compliance revealed shortcomings in key areas including operational issues and resuscitation status. Following intervention, adherence improved across all criteria, with notable gains in the documentation of admission date, existing management plans and outstanding tasks. The mean total compliance score improved significantly from 44.6% to 70.2% between cycle 1 and cycle 2 (p<0.001). Staff rated the proforma positively as a guide for safe handover. Conclusions This audit demonstrated the value of a structured proforma in enhancing the quality and consistency of surgical handovers with minimal resource investment. Following cycle 2, an electronic proforma was developed to improve adherence. Further re-audit is recommended to evaluate long-term uptake and patient-centred outcomes as well as embedding staff induction training.
affiliations: West Suffolk Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.480.title: 856 Gallbladder Polyp Surveillance at MFT Hospitals: Audit of Current Practice Against Latest Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.480.abstract: Abstract Aim Gallbladder polyps are a common incidental finding on ultrasound imaging. The majority are benign; however, studies report 4% are neoplastic with malignant potential. Appropriate surveillance is warranted to optimise early detection of these high-risk lesions. Although local guidelines direct surveillance to primary care, recent service pressures have redirected responsibilities to secondary settings. The latest guidelines provide updated evidence-based surveillance pathways. This study aims to evaluate the adherence of current gallbladder polyp surveillance against the latest 2021 joint European guidelines across Manchester NHS Foundation Trust (MFT) hospitals and identify factors influencing adherence. Method A retrospective audit across 8 MFT hospitals reviewed 448 ultrasound reports between 2023-2025. 100 patients with gallbladder polyps meeting the inclusion criteria were audited against the 2021 joint European guidelines. Data on demographics, polyp characteristics, radiological reports, clinician acknowledgement, follow-up intervals and outcomes were retrieved from electronic records. Results Adherence for polyps sized 5.1-5.9mm and 9.1-9.9mm was not assessable due to a lack of guideline acknowledgement. Only 17% of patient pathways adhered to the 2021 guidelines. 58 unnecessary scans were performed, and 35 referrals for cholecystectomy were missed. For patients with risk factors, only 14% of surveillance plans were adherent. 63% of ultrasound reports had no documentation of gallstones, 35% had no documentation of gallbladder wall thickness, and 0% documented polyp sessility. Conclusions Adherence to the guidelines was suboptimal. Poor clinician awareness of risk factors and inconsistent radiological reporting may have contributed to poor adherence. Revisions to include unacknowledged size thresholds, single guideline distribution, and standardised radiological reporting template are recommended.
affiliations: University of Manchester , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.563.title: 550 A Closed Loop Audit of Ultrasound Use in Paediatric Patients Presenting with Abdominal Pain in a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.563.abstract: Abstract Aim Ultrasound is the gold standard imaging modality recommended in paediatric patients presenting with suspected acute appendicitis. Ultrasound is highly specific and moderately sensitive for assessment of appendicitis in children. An audit of paediatric appendicectomy outcomes from 2022 showed that ultrasound use was limited to 30% of patients diagnosed with appendicitis. MRI was the most common index modality in 42% of patients. Subsequent interventions included increasing slot availability and access to sonographer training and providing a standardised ultrasound reporting format for suspected appendicitis to aid surgical decision making. Cycle two aims were to evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention. Method Retrospective case study analysis of 220 patients up to age 16 admitted to general surgery with abdominal pain from 01/10/2023-30/09/2024. Results Ultrasound was used as an index imaging modality in 77% patients presenting with suspected appendicitis. Specificity of appendicitis was 93% (n=80) and sensitivity 27% (n=11). Clinical suspicion was the most sensitive indictor for appendicitis. Analysis of ultrasound reports compared to the standardised format found only 5% commented on all markers of inflammation. 25% of patients initially imaged with ultrasound required re-imaging. Outcome was changed in 25%. Conclusions Ultrasound is highly valuable tool in assessing children presenting with suspected appendicitis. A standardised reporting format can prove extremely helpful in guiding the need for further imaging or clinical intervention by describing the presence of inflammatory changes in cases where the appendix was not identified. Integrating this model into practice can help improve communication between the surgical and radiology department and ultimately reduce time to diagnosis.
affiliations: Mid Cheshire Hospital Trust , Crewe ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.280.title: 1386 Are We Recording What We Should? a Closed-Loop Audit of Surgical Operation Notes
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.280.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the quality of general surgery operation note documentation at our hospital against RCSEng Good Surgical Practice standards, evaluate the impact of targeted interventions introduced after the first audit cycle, and identify areas requiring further improvement. Method A closed-loop, retrospective audit was completed over two cycles. 50 randomly selected elective and emergency cases were reviewed in Cycle 1 (August-September 2025). Following this, interventions were introduced, including presenting findings at the departmental audit meeting and displaying posters in the theatre office. Cycle 2 reviewed a further 50 cases from November 2025. Documentation was assessed against the 2025 RCSEng Good Surgical Practice standards. Results Cycle 1 demonstrated high compliance for surgeon details, procedure, date, and operative findings (>98%), but several key fields were poorly documented, including time of operation, elective/emergency status, complications, prosthesis details, estimated blood loss (EBL) and antibiotic/DVT prophylaxis. Following interventions, Cycle 2 demonstrated improvement in: time of operation (2% to 28%), elective/emergency status (10% to 28%), complications (22% to 40%), prosthesis documentation (18% to 55%), EBL (2% to 20%), antibiotic prophylaxis (50% to 66%) and DVT prophylaxis (48% to 56%). Core elements remained consistently well recorded. However, several fields continued to fall below expected standards. Conclusions Operation notes are essential medico-legal documents that contribute to the safe continuity of care of surgical patients post-operatively. Targeted interventions improved overall documentation quality, though many remain below the expected standard. Continued reinforcement of documentation requirements, ongoing availability of guideline reminders, and repeat audit within 6-12 months are recommended for sustained improvement.
affiliations: Blackpool Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Blackpool ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.267.title: 1206 Surgical Site Infection Trends After Hip and Knee Surgery: A 2022-2024 Audit ofAntibiotic Prophylaxis Compliance and Modifiable Risk Factors
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.267.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate current surgical site infection (SSl) rates following hip and knee surgery between 2022 and 2024, assess compliance with updated perioperative prophylaxis guidelines, and identify modifiable risk factors, with emphasis on antibiotic dosing accuracy and skin preparation. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on all patients undergoing primary hip or knee surgery at a UK trauma centre from January 2022 to June 2024. SI diagnosis followed CDC criteria. Compliance with the perioperative antibiotic bundle (agent, dose, timing) and preparation method was recorded. Associations between risk factors and SSI were analysed using chi-squared testing with a 95% confidence interval. Results A total of 586 cases were reviewed. The SSI rate was 5.4% (n=32). Significant predictors included current smoking (p=0.018), suboptimal diabetic control (HbA1c ≥58 mmol/mol; p=0.029), operative duration >120 minutes (p=0.041), and incorrect dosing of guideline-recommended prophylactic antibiotics (p=0.022). Incorrect antibiotic choice alone was not associated with SSI (p=0.31). Alcohol-based chlorhexidine (2% CHG in 70% IPA) demonstrated a lower SI rate compared with povidone-iodine preparations (p=0.037). Full compliance with the antibiotic bundle was achieved in 74.1% of cases. Conclusions SI rates have improved compared with historical data but remain influenced by modifiable perioperative variables. Accurate antibiotic dosing, minimising operative time, optimising diabetic control, and encouraging smoking cessation are key. Alcohol-based chlorhexidine should remain the standard skin preparation. Strengthening perioperative bundle compliance and introducing real-time monitoring may further reduce SSl rates.
affiliations: Birmingham, Birmingham, United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.388.title: 751 A Retrospective Audit Analysing Clinical Outcomes in Adult Patients Having Reversal of Loop Ileostomy at Bristol Royal Infirmary (BRI)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.388.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit assesses the clinical outcomes of patients undergoing Loop Ileostomy Reversal at BRI in 2024. Background Reversal of Loop Ileostomy is a common procedure carrying significant post-operative risk, with morbidity reported at 13.1% (Peltrini et al., 2023). The CLOSE-IT study highlighted that frequent delays in bowel closure and restoration of bowel continuity, driven by service-related factors, increase the risk of Low Anterior Resection Syndrome (LARS) (Duke’s Club Research Collaborative, 2021). Method This retrospective audit was performed at BRI. Patient data was extracted from electronic theatre Lists and the Colorectal register. The parameters were set to include patients having a Reversal/Closure of Loop of Ileostomy in 2024. Exclusion criteria were set to exclude Reversal/Closure of Loop of Ileostomy before or after 2024. We got a sample population consisting of 31 patients. Results Of 31 patients, 20 underwent reversal for underlying malignancy. Post-operative complications occurred in 45.2% of patients, including 2 patients who experienced anastomotic leak. The mean interval to reversal was 10 months. Of the 5 patients who underwent ileostomy reversal within 6 months, only 1 had a complication. Among patients with a reversal interval of 7 months or more, the postoperative complication rate increased to 50%. Median length of stay (LOS) was 6 days. Mean LOS was 10.8 days with complications, compared to 3.7 days without complications. Conclusions The most common post-op complication was wound infection/SSI in 4 patients. The post-operative complication rate was higher with delayed closure as documented in the literature, although acknowledging our reduced sample size.
affiliations: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust , Bristol ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.232.title: 601 Compliance With Perioperative Antibiotic Guidelines in Patients Undergoing Emergency Appendicectomy: A Three-Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.232.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is the leading acute surgical emergency worldwide, with variable use of perioperative antibiotics. This audit completed the third cycle reviewing compliance with the World Society of Emergency Surgery acute appendicitis 2020 and local guidelines. Method Our third audit cycle retrospectively identified 59 adult patients undergoing an emergency appendicectomy between 1st September 2025 - 1st November 2025 in one NHS trust. Two previous audit cycles in 2022 and 2023 led to interventions of local presentation with informative posters displayed in clinical areas, and an operative note proforma for appendicectomy. Data were collected on demographics, severity of appendicitis, perioperative antibiotic use and any post-operative complications. Compliance to audit standards was then reviewed. Results Reporting our three audit cycles, compliance with preoperative antibiotic usage was improved, from 85% initially to 87% and within this audit cycle 95% of patients received preoperative antibiotics in line with local and international guidelines. Omission of postoperative antibiotics for patients with simple appendicitis was compliant in 79%, 100% and 97% of patients respectively. Patients with complicated appendicitis had postoperative antibiotics appropriately for 3-5 days in 12.1%, 20% and 61% of patients. Conclusions Over three audit cycles, interventions including departmental educational resources, creation of local guidelines and an operative note proforma have shown significant improvement in compliance with guidelines for perioperative antibiotics use. However, the postoperative antibiotic use in patients with complicated appendicitis has ongoing disparity, requiring further clinician education and targeted initiatives to ensure safe patient care and antibiotic stewardship.
affiliations: Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust , Newcastle Upon Tyne ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.636.title: 676 So What Is NEWS? an Audit of Near to Peer Surgical Teaching With Qualitative and Quantitative Analyses
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.636.abstract: Abstract Aim To analyse and improve the effectiveness of an existent surgical teaching programme by incorporating formal assessment. Method Southport Hospital (MWL Teaching Hospitals) operates a teaching programme for Y5 medical students from the University of Liverpool, which includes a hybrid session on NEWS2 utilising didactic and bedside teaching techniques. Advancing the feedback process used in a previous cycle, the authors developed a compound questionnaire to assess confidence and formatively test knowledge before and after each session, allowing qualitative and quantitative analysis. Results Previous analysis found that following the session, confidence responding to NEWS rose 62.2%, confidence taking histories rose 7.09%, and confidence examining a patient rose 25.3%. This repeat cycle demonstrated consistency with confidence responding to NEWS rising 87%, using ABCDE rising 51%, and new tenets of the teaching -escalating concerns (38%), and delivering emergency treatments (86%). The authors demonstrated efficacy in addressing students’ self-reported pre-session aims with feedback highlighting the benefits of exposure to a real patient scoring high NEWS and the hybrid approach built confidence and forced critical thinking. Students improved in formative assessment from scoring initially 61% to 72% (after the session) on average – underperforming mainly on questions about septic screening. Conclusions This project demonstrated that the teaching methods are effective in addressing students’ aims, concerns, and built confidence. The addition of formative assessment revealed gaps in the teaching that were not covered by text-based feedback. Further adaptation to the didactic component would cover the gap in knowledge of septic screening and be amenable to re-audit.
affiliations: Mersey and West Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust , Southport ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.488.title: 1101 Impact of a Targeted Educational Campaign on Smoking Status Documentation and Cessation Support in Fracture Patients: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.488.abstract: Abstract Aim Smoking is a major risk factor for fracture non-union and deep surgical site infection. NICE guidance recommends that all patients admitted to secondary care receive smoking cessation advice. This single-centre retrospective audit assessed the documentation of smoking status, delivery of cessation interventions, and the impact of a targeted educational campaign on clinical practice. Method Electronic patient records were reviewed for documentation of smoking status, formal offers of cessation services, evidence of clinical discussions, nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) prescriptions, and completion of an electronic Smoking Assessment Form. Data were collected from adult fracture patients admitted during two periods: pre-intervention (30th December 2024 - 3rd February 2025) and post-intervention (30th July - 3rd September 2025). Interventions comprised educational posters, a teaching session delivered by the smoking cessation team, and presentation of first-cycle audit findings at a local meeting. Proportions were compared using Chi-squared analysis. Results The pre- and post-intervention cohorts included 214 and 140 patients, with 33 (15.4%) and 30 (21.4%) smokers respectively. Following the intervention, undocumented smoking status decreased significantly from 19.6% (n=42) to 7.8% (n=11) (p=0.002). Among smokers, no statistically significant improvements were observed in formal cessation service offers (45.5% vs 30.0%; p=0.21), documented clinical discussions (57.6% vs 43.3%; p=0.26), NRT prescriptions (33.3% vs 16.7%; p=0.13), or Smoking Assessment Form completion (39.4% vs 23.3%; p=0.17). Conclusions Targeted educational measures significantly improved documentation of smoking status in fracture patients. Although cessation support delivery was not improved, this work highlights key gaps and provides a foundation for ongoing quality improvement.
affiliations: Imperial College School of Medicine , London ,
Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.236.title: 637 Audit of Time to Fracture Clinic Review for Distal Radius Fractures
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.236.abstract: Abstract Aim Timely consultant review of distal radius fractures is essential for appropriate management. BOAST guidelines state that all acute fractures should receive consultant’s review—virtual or face-to-face—within 72 hours of Emergency Department presentation. This audit assessed local compliance with national standards and evaluated the effectiveness of the Virtual Fracture Clinic (VFC) pathway. Method A retrospective analysis was conducted over a two-week period, reviewing all adults (≥16 years) presenting to the ED with confirmed distal radius fractures. Exclusions included pathological, open, high-energy or unstable injuries requiring admission, polytrauma, paediatric cases, and patients incorrectly referred. Data were extracted from electronic records, including date of ED presentation and date of specialist review. Compliance was defined as review ≤72 hours. Results Fifty patients met inclusion criteria. Overall, 46/50 patients (92%) received review within 72 hours. The VFC pathway accounted for 49 reviews, achieving 93.8% compliance (46/49). Only one patient was initially reviewed face-to-face, outside the 72-hour target. Most patients were reviewed within 1–2 days ; four cases (8%) breached the standard due to delayed referral or weekend presentation. Conclusions The VFC model delivers high compliance with BOAST standards, supporting its effectiveness in providing timely specialist assessment. Delayed cases highlight areas for improvement, particularly weekend referral pathways and administrative processes. A longer re-audit period and inclusion of on-call fracture referrals are recommended.
affiliations: Royal Victoria Hospital , Belfast ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.632.title: 462 Closing the Loop: A Circuit-Based Model for Preclinical-to-Clinical Surgical Skills
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.632.abstract: Abstract Aim Medical students often experience a steep transition between the preclinical years and clinical clerkships. Limited exposure to procedural skills can create anxiety and diminish preparedness, particularly for the core surgical rotation. To address this gap, we developed ‘Surgical Circuits,’ a peer-led programme designed to enhance procedural confidence and clinical rationale among preclinical students. Method Preclinical students rotated through simulation-based stations (20-30 minutes each) contextualized to a presentation of acute cholecystitis. Skills included venepuncture, cannulation, prescribing, nasogastric tube insertion, scrubbing and suturing, alongside an ultrasound demonstration. The session concluded with a group reflection exploring clinical reasoning and differentials. Pre- and post-session surveys captured self-reported confidence on a Likert scale from 1-5, with 1 representing no confidence, and 5 representing absolute confidence. Results Twenty-four students participated (Year 1: n=16; Year 2: n= 8). Across all procedures, mean confidence scores increased following the session (p<0.005 as a paired t-test). The largest gains were observed in nasogastric tube insertion (from 2 to 4.1, 104% improvement) and prescribing (from 2 to 3.8, 94% improvement). Participants valued the fun, fast-paced format, framed within a clinical scenario. Most students were able to sequence the patient journey correctly and articulated the contribution of each skill to patient management. Conclusions : 'Surgical Circuits’ improved preclinical students’ procedural confidence by enhancing their understanding of workflow within surgical practice. Future developments may include incorporating interdisciplinary roles and expanding complexity. This model offers a scalable, customisable approach to early surgical education that supports a supportive transition into clinical clerkships.
affiliations: American University of the Caribbean School of Medicine , Cupecoy, Sint Maarten (Dutch part)
Frimley Health NHS Foundation Trust , Slough ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag080.005.title: 12 Post-ERCP Pancreatitis in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit of Incidence, Peri-Procedural Practice, and Clinical Outcomes in 157 Consecutive Procedures
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag080.005.abstract: Abstract Introduction Post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) is the most clinically significant complication of ERCP, with a reported incidence of 3–8%. Evidence from district general hospital (DGH) settings, where operator volume and resources differ from tertiary centres, remains limited. This audit evaluated PEP incidence, peri-procedural management compliance, and outcomes at a single DGH endoscopy unit. Method This was a retrospective audit of all ERCPs performed between September 2024 and August 2025. Variables included demographics, procedural indication, operator, cannulation technique, pharmacological prophylaxis, intravenous fluid administration, amylase documentation, and clinical outcomes. PEP was defined according to consensus criteria as abdominal pain with serum amylase ≥3× the upper limit of normal at 24 hours, requiring unplanned admission or prolonged stay. Results A total of 157 procedures were analysed (58% female; mean age 70 years). The commonest indication for ERCP was choledocholithiasis (120/157; 76%). PEP occurred in 9/157 cases (5.7%). All 9 PEP cases arose at the index procedure. Rectal diclofenac compliance was ≈99%, meeting BSG standards. Significant deficiencies identified included pre-ERCP amylase documentation in only 6.3% of cases, pre-operative IV fluids in 29%, and post-operative IV fluids in 41.4%. Younger age and female sex were identified as risk factors. Severe PEP occurred in 1/9 cases (11%), including one ITU admission leading to one procedure-related death. Conclusions PEP incidence is within published benchmarks; however, remediable deficiencies in pre-procedural amylase documentation, hydration protocols, and pancreatic duct cannulation management were identified. Implementation of a standardised ERCP peri-procedural pathway aligned with current guidelines is recommended to optimise patient safety.
affiliations: UHMBT , Lancaster ,
University of Lancashire , Preston ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag080.002.title: 4 Prospective Audit and Observational Study of GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use in a Surgical Patient Cohort
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag080.002.abstract: Abstract Background GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are prescribed for patients with type 2 diabetes or obesity. In the UK there has been a recent rise in use of GLP-1RAs, which are often issued privately. Known complications from GLP-1RAs include gallstone disease,1 however clear guidance does not exist for patients using GLP-1RAs who experience biliary symptoms. Method We audited patients on GLP-1RAs attending the Surgical Observation Unit at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh from March to October 2025. Follow-up was performed atleast six weeks after initial presentation via telephone. Patients with confirmed pathology unrelated to GLP-1RAs (eg. appendicitis) were excluded from follow-up. Results Ninety-one patients were identified, 87 of whom (95.6%) presented with abdominal pain. The most common diagnosis was biliary colic (23/91, 25.3%). Most patients were taking Mounjaro (tirzepatide) (82/91, 90.1%) frequently issues by online pharmacies (65/91, 71.4%). Six patients (6.59%) had diabetes and 22 (25.3%) had a BMI under 30. Mean reported weight loss on GLP-1RA was 17.3+/-12.0 kg. Follow-up was completed for 57 patients, of which 35/57 (61.4%) stopped their GLP-1RA after initial presentation. Of these, 17/35 (48.6%) reported subsequent weight gain. Only 28/57 (49.1%) reported their symptoms completely resolved but only 19/57 (33.3%) received support or safety netting from their drug provider. Conclusions This data highlights the growing use of GLP-1RAs amongst non-diabetic populations. The high proportion of patients experiencing persistent symptoms, combined with limited support from drug providers and variability in advice given to patients, indicates a potential gap in patient education and safe follow-up care.
affiliations: NHS Lothian , Edinburgh ,
University of Edinburgh , Edinburgh ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag080.012.title: 13 Routine Intraoperative Cholangiography (IOC) in Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: A Single-Centre Audit of 279 Consecutive Cases
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag080.012.abstract: Abstract Background Bile duct injury (BDI) remains a serious complication of laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC), with reported rates of 0.3–0.6%. Intraoperative cholangiography (IOC) offers real-time biliary anatomy delineation reducing the rate of BDI and allowing common bile duct (CBD) stone detection. Despite endorsement in SAGES 2025 guidelines, NICE CG188, and EAES consensus statements, IOC uptake remains inconsistent across UK surgical centres. Aim To evaluate IOC performance rates, diagnostic yield, and impact on post-operative biliary imaging and clinical outcomes in a consecutive LC + routine IOC cohort. Method A retrospective single-centre audit of 279 patients undergoing LC with routine IOC. Successful IOC performance rate, mutually agreed quality metrics (12-point checklist) by three independent surgeons for reading IOC in a standard manner, BDI rates, CBD filling defect detection, post-operative imaging requirements, and length of stay (LOS) were assessed. Guideline compliance against SAGES 2025 standards was evaluated. Results IOC was successful in 93.2% of cases.
