CBD filling defects indicating choledocholithiasis were identified in 6.2% of IOC patients. Only 4/279 (1.5%) required further imaging. Zero patients had pancreatitis after routine cholangiography. Demographic and comorbidity profiles were consistent across subgroups. Conclusions Routine IOC in LC is achievable, diagnostically valuable, and associated with reduced post-operative imaging, shorter LOS, and less costly. These findings support routine IOC as standard practice. Sustained implementation requires IOC training and theatre infrastructure. However, for validation in the UK a multicenter study is recommended.
affiliations: Ipswich Hospital , Ipswich ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag080.007.title: 11 A Closed-Loop Audit of Operative Note Quality in HPB Surgery: Adherence to RCS Good Surgical Practice 2025 Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag080.007.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess and improve operative note quality in HPB surgery through a closed-loop audit of compliance with RCS Good Surgical Practice 2025 standards. Method Elective HPB procedures at a tertiary centre were audited across two cycles: Cycle 1 (May–June 2025, n=71) and Cycle 2 (August–September 2025, n=75). Emergency cases were excluded. Parameters included RCS core fields and HPB-specific adjuncts: Pringle’s time, intraoperative ultrasound (IOUS), indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence, and frozen section. Following Cycle 1, interventions included integration of a structured EPIC SmartPhrase template (hpbopnote), departmental presentations, theatre visual reminders, and targeted education. Results Overall compliance improved from 67% to 94%. The greatest gains were observed in operative diagnosis (18.3%→93.9%), estimated blood loss (23.9%→95.5%), and intraoperative complications (1.4%→69.7%). HPB-specific adjunct documentation improved markedly: IOUS (40.9%→100%), Pringle’s time (88.2%→100%), frozen section (21.4%→69.2%), and ICG usage (28.6%→58.3%). Improvements were observed across all remaining audited parameters. Conclusions Structured, prompt-driven documentation tools significantly improved operative note quality and adherence to RCS standards in HPB surgery. Embedding a SmartPhrase template within the electronic health record standardised documentation of both RCS-mandated fields and HPB-specific adjuncts. Well-documented operative notes are fundamental to continuity of care, trainee education, and medico-legal protection. This project demonstrates that closed-loop audits drive sustainable, meaningful improvements and provide a transferable model for documentation quality initiatives across surgical specialties.
affiliations: King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.612.title: EP 523 Minimally Invasive Transanal Excision Techniques for Rectal Neoplasms: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.612.abstract: Abstract Aim Minimally invasive techniques for local excision of rectal neoplasms, such as transanal minimally invasive surgery (TAMIS) and transanal resection of tumour (TART), have become increasingly common for treating benign polyps and early-stage (T1) lesions in the mid and lower rectum. This audit reviews the outcomes of these procedures at our institution. Methods This retrospective audit included all patients aged 16 years and older, who underwent transanal excision of rectal neoplasms at our institution from January 2019 to December 2022. Results Thirty-eight patients were included (TART 24 - 63.1%; TAMIS 14 - 36.8%), with a female predominance (55%). Neoplasms were primarily detected via colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy (94.7%), with CT colonography and rectal MRI in 26.3% and 21%, respectively. Most lesions (81.5%) were in the lower rectum; the remainder were in the anal canal. Histology showed tubulovillous adenoma with low-grade dysplasia in 60.5%, TVA with LGD and focal HGD in 7.9%, TVA with HGD in 5.2%, serrated adenoma with LGD in 10.5%, malignancy in 2.6%, and anal intraepithelial neoplasia in 5.2%. Conclusions The transanal approach to rectal neoplasms, including TAMIS, provides significant benefits such as organ preservation and reduced morbidity. With the rising incidence of early rectal cancers and the risks associated with total mesorectal excision, minimally invasive transanal techniques represent a safe and effective alternative. Ongoing clinical trials continue to evaluate their long-term oncological outcomes.
affiliations: Airedale General Hospital , West Yorkshire

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.416.title: TPW 9.18 Prospective Audit of Reducing Carbon Footprint in A District Hospital by Changing Internal Paper Referral into an Electronic System
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.416.abstract: Abstract Background Paper-based systems contribute to carbon emissions through production, printing, and disposal The NHS Net Zero Plan health service aims to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2040. Within our trust, several specialties continue to use paper referral slips that often get misplaced or discarded, leading to poor traceability, delays in patient care, and unnecessary waste. In addition, referrals submitted after 4 pm may not be actioned same day leading to risk of missed patients if paper referrals are lost. Aim To reduce the carbon footprint, improve referral traceability, and enhance timeliness of patient review by changing into an electronic system. Methods Data was collected over 6 weeks for 60 consecutive yellow referral sheets by different specialities. Each sheet 15×12 cm weighing 1.5 g equating to 5 g CO2e when production, printing, and disposal are included. Results The 60 sheets collated equated to 43g of CO2e with annual usage estimated at 520 sheets representing 2.6 kg CO2e per year. This is equivalent to driving 6.5 miles or producing 33 plastic bottles. Conclusion Replacing paper referral sheets with electronic referrals is a no cost, easily implemented change with measurable environmental and clinical benefits. Scaling this intervention across additional specialties could produce greater carbon savings and standardise referral processes hospital-wide. Action plan The planned intervention is to replace paper with an electronic form already embedded in the hospital IT Lorenzo system. Limitations True usage was approximated as some referral sheets were retained by consultants which couldn’t be analysed.
affiliations: University Hospitals of Morecambe Bay Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.047.title: SP 3.16 “After the MDT Decision”: An Audit of Management and Survival in Colorectal Cancer Patients Allocated to Best Supportive Care
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.047.abstract: Abstract Background Prognosis in advanced colorectal cancer is influenced by primary tumour site, metastatic burden, comorbidities and frailty. However, little is known about the clinical course of patients once the decision has been made that their care goals are palliative. This project aimed to evaluate the survival time of colorectal cancer patients managed palliatively and establish what care these patients received. Method A retrospective audit of patients deemed for palliative care after discussion at MDT at the Royal Derby Hospital July 2022- April 2023 was carried out. Data collected included TNM staging, primary tumour site, details of palliative treatment, and date of death. Results Seventy-six patients were included, with a mean age at diagnosis of 79.5 years. Colonic primaries accounted for 62% (n=47) of diagnoses, with rectal primaries accounting for 38% (n=29). Twenty percent of patients (n=15) had metastatic disease at the time of decision to palliate. Twenty-nine patients were referred to palliative oncology: 14 (48%) had palliative radiotherapy and none had chemotherapy. The overall median survival was 16 months [IQR 7-25.5]. Patients with a colonic primary had a median survival of 14 months compared to 21 months for rectal primaries (p= 0.35). The median survival time of patients with liver metastases at presentation was 7 months [IQR 4-12] compared to 2 months [IQR 1-15] in those with lung metastases (p=0.41). Conclusion Colorectal cancer patients managed palliatively had expectedly poor survival, with worse survival in the context of colonic rather than rectal primaries and in metastatic lung disease.
affiliations: Royal Derby Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.447.title: TPTh 3.09 Audit of Diagnosis and Management of Acute Lower Gastrointestinal Tract Bleeding (LGIB) in a Rural General Hospital, can we reduce hospital admissions?
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.447.abstract: Abstract Aims This audit was conducted to compare our practice of management of LGIB to British Society of Gastroenterology 2019 guidelines, and to evaluate the benefits of applying Oakland Score in assessing safe discharges. Methods Adult patients who presented with acute LGIB were included. Data were collected from hospital information systems and physical notes. An excel sheet was developed to collect: patient demographics, data to calculate shock index and Oakland score on admission, investigations, blood transfusion, length of stay (LOS), cause of LGIB and in-hospital mortality. Analysis of the data was undertaken using excel. Results Between February 2019 and September 2023, 73 patients fit the criteria to be included (39 females, 34 males) with median age of 76 years (19-102 years). Using Oakland Score, 13 patients were deemed minor and 60 patients major. Out of 73 patients, 4 were discharged same day, 2 with Oakland score of 9 & 10 while the other two scored below 8. The median LOS was 3 days (1-38 days) 3 patients required surgery and 18 patients required blood transfusion, all other patients were treated conservatively (72%) with observations. Commonest cause of LGIB was diverticular disease (45%), followed by haemorrhoids (17%). Conclusions Oakland score appears insufficiently accurate for identifying patients who can be discharged. As 72% patients were managed by observations only, admission decisions may be better guided by other criteria as shock index, blood transfusion or surgical requirement. Patients not meeting these criteria could be safely managed outside hospital, for example through outreach or ambulatory service.
affiliations: Bronglais General Hospital , Aberystwyth, Wales
Cardiff University

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.547.title: EP 116 Audit of Perioperative Prescription of LMWH In Spinal Surgery at The Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.547.abstract: Abstract Aims Spinal surgery patients are at increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) due to prolonged operative times and reduced postoperative mobility. Conversely, early administration of low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) increases the risk of spinal or epidural haematoma with potentially devastating neurological consequences. Appropriate timing of LMWH is therefore critical. This audit aimed to evaluate compliance with local guidelines for postoperative LMWH timing in spinal surgery patients at a tertiary orthopaedic centre. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted using electronic patient records over a four-month period (August–November 2025). Postoperative surgical plans and medication charts were reviewed to assess whether LMWH was administered within the locally recommended postoperative timing window. All adult patients undergoing spinal surgery during the study period were included. Compliance was defined as LMWH administration within the prescribed timeframe documented in the postoperative plan. Results Twenty-seven patients were included. LMWH was administered within the correct postoperative timeframe in 22 patients (81.5%), demonstrating good overall compliance with local guidelines. Five patients (18.5%) experienced delays in LMWH administration. Timely administration was consistently associated with clear documentation of LMWH timing and effective nursing handover. Delays were mostly linked to inconsistent documentation and communication gaps during handover. Conclusions While compliance with LMWH timing guidelines was high overall, nearly one in five patients experienced delays, representing a clinically significant safety risk. Targeted interventions including standardised postoperative documentation, strengthened handover processes, staff education, and electronic prompts are planned. A re-audit will assess the impact of these measures on guideline adherence and patient safety.
affiliations: Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.553.title: EP 183 Quality Improvement in Surgical Discharge Summaries: An Audit of the Performance of a London Tertiary Colorectal Surgery Department
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.553.abstract: Abstract Discharge summaries are critical to continuity of care. The Professional Records Standard Body and Royal College of Physicians have published national guidelines on hospital discharge summaries. The aim of this audit was to assess the adherence of discharge summaries from a London tertiary centre colorectal surgery department to national guidelines and implement changes to improve discharge summary quality. A scoring system based on national standards was created to assess 100 consecutive discharge summaries from March 2024 to April 2024 in the first cycle. These results were presented locally, with dissemination of a discharge summary proforma based on national standards. The second cycle involved assessing 100 consecutive discharge summaries from December 2024 to January 2025 using the same criteria to assess improvement. The median and modal scores based on the criteria in the first cycle were 5.00/7.00. The mean score was 4.15/7.00. 4 patients did not have discharge summaries recorded on the system. The events/procedures during admission was the criterion with the highest adherence (89%), while safety netting advice had the lowest (14%). In the second cycle, the median and modal scores were 6.00/7.00, the mean was 6.06/7.00. Both median and mean score showed a statistically significant improvement. Reason for admission, events/procedures during admission and post-op plan had the highest adherence (100%), while safety netting advice had the lowest adherence (32%). All individual criteria showed a statistically significant increase in adherence. The audit demonstrated successful quality improvement in surgical discharge summaries through the successful implementation of a proforma.
affiliations: Guy's & St Thomas's NHS Foundation Trust
St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.194.title: TPT 3.11 Evaluating Emergency Appendicectomy Practice in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.194.abstract: Abstract Aims Emergency appendicectomy is a common urgent surgical procedure, with national guidance emphasising timely surgery, appropriate use of diagnostic imaging, and rational postoperative antibiotic prescribing. This audit evaluated emergency appendicectomy practice in a district general hospital reviewing these principles. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted of emergency appendicectomies performed between January and June 2025. Data was collected from theatre logbooks and electronic records, including time from decision to operate to surgery, documented reasons for delay, use and findings of preoperative imaging, histopathology results, postoperative antibiotic prescribing, and 30-day readmission rates. Results 186 emergency appendicectomies were included. Surgery was performed within 24 hours of decision to operate in 73.4% of cases. Of delayed procedures, 45.0% had documented justification, with lack of emergency theatre capacity accounting for 41.0% of recorded delays. Histopathology confirmed acute appendiceal pathology in 79.0% of cases. Preoperative imaging was performed in 61.3% of patients. Of CT scans reported as acute appendicitis, 27.3% showed no histological evidence of appendicitis, while 25.0% of ultrasound-diagnosed cases were histologically negative, contributing to a notable negative appendicectomy rate. Postoperative antibiotics were prescribed in 67.2% of cases, with substantial variation in choice and duration. No clear association was identified between antibiotic prescribing and postoperative recovery or 30-day readmission. Conclusion This audit identified delays to surgery primarily related to theatre capacity, inconsistencies in diagnostic pathways, and variation in postoperative antimicrobial prescribing. Standardised imaging protocols, improved theatre prioritisation and evidence-based antibiotic guidelines may reduce negative appendicectomy rates and improve patient care. Re-audit following implementation is planned.
affiliations: Dudley Group NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.273.title: TPT 8.16 Is Routine Pre-Operative Group and Save Necessary for Cholecystectomy? A Single Centre Retrospective Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.273.abstract: Abstract Aims Cholecystectomy is one of the most commonly performed general surgical procedures in UK. Despite a low risk of peri-operative haemorrhage and no specific recommendations, routine pre-operative group and save (G&S) testing remains widely practiced in cholecystectomy. This audit aimed to determine the incidence of peri-operative blood transfusion, compare current practice with previous departmental audit and evaluate cost-effectiveness of routine pre-operative G&S testing. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted of all cholecystectomies performed at a single tertiary centre between 1 January and 31 December 2024. Laboratory records, operative notes and discharge summaries were reviewed. Patients undergoing concurrent intra-operative procedures involving other organs were excluded. Results Of 844 cholecystectomies identified, 776 met the inclusion criteria. The median age was 49 years (interquartile range 35–62) and 94% of procedures were performed laparoscopically. Routine pre-operative G&S testing was performed in over 92% of cases. Only one patient (0.12%) required a postoperative blood transfusion, following coffee-ground vomiting and blood observed in the surgical drain. No intraoperative transfusions occurred. Two bleeding-related complications were recorded: one required same-day return to theatre for washout and another patient developed a subcapsular haematoma; neither required blood transfusion. These findings were consistent with a previous audit conducted in 2020 (n=448) where no patients required peri-operative blood transfusion. Conclusion Routine pre-operative G&S testing was not supported by the observed transfusion requirements in this cohort. A selective, risk-based approach to pre-operative G&S testing appears safe and may optimise transfusion service utilisation while offering potential cost savings.
affiliations: Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.477.title: TPTh 5.09 Evaluating Adherence to ATLS Protocols in the Assessment of Trauma Patients: A Full-Cycle Audit in a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.477.abstract: Abstract Aims Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) provides an internationally standardised framework for trauma assessment and management. This full-cycle audit aimed to evaluate adherence to ATLS protocols in the assessment and management of trauma patients presenting to the General Surgery department at a District General Hospital. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted in two cycles. The first cycle reviewed trauma cases assessed and/or admitted under General Surgery between 01/06/25 and 11/08/25. After the first cycle, interventions were implemented, including resident doctor education emphasising ATLS principles, promotion of ATLS certification, and introduction of a structured ATLS trauma clerk in template. The second cycle evaluated cases between 14/11/25 and 10/12/25 using identical audit standards. Data was extracted from electronic patient records, focusing on documentation of primary and secondary surveys and incidence of missed injuries. Results In the first cycle (n=45), a primary survey was done in only 9% of trauma cases, and a secondary survey was done in only 7% of patients; the missed injury rate was somewhat high at 4.5%. Following interventions, the second cycle (n=23) demonstrated marked improvement, where 78% of patients had primary surveys and 69.5% underwent secondary surveys and there were no missed injuries. Conclusions This audit emphasises that a structured and standardised approach in trauma is crucial for the provision of best quality of care for trauma patients. Targeted education and standardised documentation significantly improve adherence to ATLS protocols. Sustained emphasis on ATLS training, particularly for Resident doctors, remains essential to ensure consistent, high-quality trauma assessment.
affiliations: Altnagelvin Area Hospital
Western Health and Social Care Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.373.title: TPW 7.03 Shared Decision-Making and Documentation before ERCP for Choledocholithiasis: A GMC-Aligned Audit Using Prespecified Operative-Risk Strata
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.373.abstract: Abstract Background ERCP is widely used for duct clearance in choledocholithiasis but carries material risks (including pancreatitis, bleeding, and perforation); alternatives include single-stage LCBDE and intraoperative (“rendezvous”) ERCP. UK legal and professional standards require discussion and documentation of material risks and reasonable alternatives. We aimed to quantify documented options-based discussions before ERCP and benchmark against contemporaneous LCBDE practice. Methods Retrospective documentation audit of prospectively maintained biliary stone pathway database across two acute hospitals in one UK health board. Included index ERCP for choledocholithiasis and contemporaneous LCBDE cases (January 2023–December 2024). Non-stone indications and repeat ERCPs were excluded; each patient counted once. The primary outcome was explicit pre-procedure documentation of an options-based shared decision-making (SDM). Risk strata were prespecified as low/medium/high (ASA grade and Charlson comorbidity index); variation assessed by calendar quarter. Results 394 index duct-clearance procedures were analysed: 356 ERCP and 38 LCBDE. ERCP SDM was auditable in 356/356 and documented in 73/356 (20.5%). Rates by risk were: low 19/78 (24.4%), medium 21/141 (14.9%), high 33/137 (24.1%) (p=0.105). Documentation increased from 12.5% (2023Q4) to 31.8% (2024Q4) (OR 1.09 per quarter, 95% CI 0.96–1.24; p=0.160). Among ERCP episodes with a recorded procedure date (355/356), 30- and 90-day all-cause mortality were 1.4% (5/355) and 2.5% (9/355). LCBDE: no deaths; SDM 38/38 (100%). Conclusion Only one in five ERCP episodes had contemporaneous documentation of options and alternatives. Complete documentation in LCBDE indicates feasibility; an options-led consent template prompting locally available alternatives and patient priorities could standardise recording and strengthen governance.
affiliations: Department of Upper GI Surgery, University Hospital Hairmyres , East Kilbride, NHS Lanarkshire, Scotland
Department of Gastroenterology, University Hospital Hairmyres , East Kilbride, NHS Lanarkshire, Scotland
School of Medicine, Dentistry & Nursing, University of Glasgow , Scotland

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.026.title: SP 2.07 A National Prospective Audit of Acute Pancreatitis in the era of GLP-1 agonists (PANDORA): Breaking Results
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.026.abstract: Abstract Background Acute pancreatitis (AP) occurs in 56 per 100,000 people each year in the UK. The use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) is increasing and may be linked to the development of AP. The PANDORA audit aimed to describe the diagnosis, management, and outcomes of patients presenting with AP with concurrent use of GLP-1RA. Methods A national, observational, snapshot audit of practice was undertaken between Sept-Dec 2025. Consecutive patients presenting with proven AP and concurrent GLP-1RA were included. Endpoints of interest comprised diagnostic (biochemical & radiological) modality, incidence of ICU admission and complications, and compliance to MHRA Yellow Card reporting. The data presented are early breaking results based on an interim analysis. Results The audit took place across 105 UK hospitals. A small majority of patients were female (53.4%) with median age 45-55. The most common aetiology of AP was gall stones (54%). Some 8% of patients with proven AP were taking a GLP-1RA, most commonly for the indication of weight loss (90%) and mostly sourced from private pharmacies (42%). Few instances of AP with GLP-1RA were reported to the MHRA (<5%). Admission to critical care occurred in 4.8% (GLP-1RA) and 4.2% (non-GLP-1RA) patients in this interim analysis. Conclusion Early breaking results of the national PANDORA audit are presented. Almost 1-in-10 patients presenting to UK hospitals with AP are taking a GLP-1RA. The full data will inform our understanding of diagnosis, management, and outcomes of this important group.
affiliations: White Rose Surgical Collaborative
North West Research Collaborative

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.422.title: TPTh 1.09 Improving Prescribing of Regular Medications in Nil-by-Mouth Surgical Patients: A Closed-Loop Audit at a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.422.abstract: Abstract Aims Omission of essential regular medications in ‘nil by mouth’ (NBM) surgical patients is a recognised patient safety issue despite national guidance advising continuation of most regular medications. This audit assessed adherence to national standards and the impact of an intervention at a district general hospital in London. Methods A retrospective audit of electronic healthcare records was conducted across two audit cycles. Adult general surgical inpatients prescribed at least one regular medication were included. Day-case procedures, patients on no regular medications, and medications withheld for documented clinical reasons were excluded. Outcomes measured were prescribing of regular medications while NBM on the day of surgery, duration of omission, and documented reasons for withholding. Following the first cycle, graphical reminders were placed in clinical workspaces and a departmental audit presentation delivered. Pre- and post-intervention outcomes were compared using Fisher’s exact test. Results Regular medication prescribing while NBM on the day of surgery increased from 13.7% pre-intervention (n=51) to 28.6% post-intervention (n=42), p=0.12. In emergency surgery patients, prescription rates improved from 15.0% (n=20) to 43.5% (n=23), p=0.054. Failure to prescribe was the most common reason for medication omission in both cycles. The proportion of patients with medications omitted for four or more days did not differ significantly between groups (19.6% vs 11.9%, p=0.40). Conclusions Prescribing of regular medications for NBM surgical inpatients improved following low-cost interventions but remained suboptimal. Planned electronic prescribing prompts to document reasons for withholding may support further improvement.
affiliations: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust
London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.326.title: TPW 3.12 Limitations of Expert-Based Assessment in Laparoscopic Skills Training: An Inter-Rater Reliability Analysis of Pattern Cutting and Ligation Loop Tasks
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.326.abstract: Abstract Expert-based laparoscopic assessment is inherently subjective, giving rise to the hypothesis that inter-rater reliability would be low to moderate. This uncertainty motivated the exploration of objective assessment measures, such as neurophysiological techniques including EEG and fNIRS. Novice participants completed a structured laparoscopic training programme, under EEG-fNIRS recording, involving Pattern Cutting (PC) and Ligation Loop (LL) tasks using an INOVUS laparoscopic box. Performance videos from Day 5 and Day 10 were independently scored by four experienced laparoscopic surgeons using a standardised rubric derived from the Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills and Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery score sheets. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using two-way random effects intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), with absolute agreement analysed separately for each task and training day. Inter-rater reliability was consistently limited, particularly for single-rater assessments. At Day 5, agreement was poor for both PC (ICC (2,1) =0.11) and LL (ICC (2,1) =0.16), indicating substantial variability between expert judgements during early skill acquisition. Although averaging ratings improved agreement (PC ICC (2,k) =0.32; LL ICC (2,k) =0.43), reliability remained suboptimal. By Day 10, single-rater reliability increased only to low-moderate levels (PC ICC (2,1)= 0.41; LL ICC (2,1) =0.26), while averaged ratings reached moderate-to-good agreement (PC ICC (2,k) =0.73; LL ICC (2,k) =0.58).Greater agreement was observed for high-performing trainees, with persistent variability among lower performers. These findings demonstrate the limitations of expert-based assessment in laparoscopic training and support the integration of objective neurophysiological and behavioural metrics to enable more reliable and unbiased evaluation of surgical skill acquisition.

Clinic of Surgical Oncology, Samsun Training and Research Hospital , Samsun, Türkiye

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.526.title: TPTh 9.11 Acute Pancreatitis in Surgical Admissions: A Closed- Loop Audit of Compliance Against the British Society of Gastroenterology Guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.526.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the compliance with the British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines for the diagnosis, aetiology assessment and risk stratification of Acute Pancreatitis in a District General Hospital. Methods Data was collected retrospectively for the 1st of August- 30th of September 2025. All adult patients admitted with acute pancreatitis by the general surgery team were included. Patients referred more than 48 hours post-admission were excluded. 29 patients were included in the first cycle. The first cycle was presented at the local audit meeting, and an action plan was implemented to improve compliance with the guidelines. After implementation of change we re-audited from the 14th of November- 31st of December 2025. 20 patients were included in the second cycle. Results 97% of cases were correctly diagnosed within 48 hours in the first cycle, improving to 100% in the second cycle. Compliance with risk stratification in 48 hours improved from 38% to 65%. Aetiology assessment improved from 62% to 100% with 5% of cases deemed as idiopathic. Conclusions In the first cycle, compliance with diagnosis in accordance with the Atlanta criteria was high however, risk stratification and aetiology assessment did not meet the BSG Standard. After introduction of measures such as presenting the results, MDT posters and teaching sessions we noted a significant improvement in all three parameters. Compliance with diagnosis and aetiology assessment now meet the Standard. There was substantial improvement in risk stratification within 48 hours. We will continue working with the general surgery department to further improve our compliance.
affiliations: Wye Valley NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.232.title: TPT 6.09 Enhancing Patient Safety through Standardised Operative Note Documentation- A Closed-Loop Audit on Laparoscopic Appendicectomy Operative Note
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.232.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate operative note documentation is essential for patient safety, effective postoperative care, and medico-legal protection. National guidance from GIRFT and the Royal College of Surgeons of England emphasises the importance of comprehensive operative documentation. This closed-loop audit aims to evaluate the impact of a procedure-specific operative note for laparoscopic appendicectomy and education following the first-cycle audit, which identified significant deficiencies in the documentation. Methods A retrospective closed-loop audit was conducted at a District General Hospital. In first cycle, laparoscopic appendicectomy operative notes (n=56; February–April 2025) were assessed against GIRFT standards. Interventions included distribution of a standardised procedure-specific operative note template, targeted teaching, and workflow reinforcement. A re-audit was performed (n=46; July–October 2025) to compare compliance across standardised templates, handwritten/self-designed notes, and first-cycle results. Results Following the intervention, significant improvement was noted in the documentation of laparoscopic appendicectomy operative notes. 27 criteria were assessed in operative notes, and comprehensive documentation of all 27 measured criteria (100% in 22 and >95% in 5 criteria) was achieved using a standard operative note template. In second cycle, 85% (n=23/27) of standardised template operative notes achieved 100% compliance, compared with 7% (4/56) of operative notes in the first cycle. None of handwritten or self-made operative notes in the second cycle achieved full compliance. Conclusion This study demonstrated that implementing a standardised, procedure-specific operative note template with targeted teaching significantly improved documentation quality, enhancing patient safety. These interventions, grounded in human factors principles, are easily reproducible and applicable to other surgical procedures.
affiliations: The Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.467.title: TPTh 4.15 Negative Appendicectomy Rate Audit in our Local Trust
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.467.abstract: Abstract Background Acute appendicitis (AA) is a common surgical emergency, usually managed by laparoscopic appendicectomy. Negative appendicectomy rate (NAR) is defined as the removal of a histologically normal appendix in suspected appendicitis. The main clinical feature of appendicitis, right iliac fossa pain, has a broad differential diagnosis which can contribute to increased NAR. Therefore, in our trust, pre-operative imaging is required. The UK NAR was reported as 20% in the Right Iliac Fossa Pain Treatment (RIFT) study in 2020. Furthermore, a systematic review estimated a global NAR of 13% in 2023. An audit in 2021 in our Trust demonstrated a NAR of 3.05%, improving to 2.04% on re-audit. The aim is to evaluate our Trust’s current NAR comparing it with national, global and previous Trust data. Methods A retrospective review of histopathology reports was conducted for all emergency appendicectomies performed over a six-month period. Patients aged ≥16 years who underwent an appendicectomy with pre-operative diagnosis of AA were included. The NAR was calculated as a proportion of appendicectomies with normal histopathology. Results 150 patients (77 male, 73 female) underwent emergency appendicectomy. 7 patients (6 female, 1 male) had normal histopathology, resulting in a NAR of 4.67%, all had pre-operative imaging. Compared with our previous audit, the overall NAR increased (p=0.21). In patients aged 16-25, NAR increased to 11.54% but remained below the reported national rate. Conclusion Our Trust continues to demonstrate a lower NAR than national standards, though an increase from previous audits. This highlights the importance of ongoing clinical education.
affiliations: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Norwich Medical School, University of East Anglia

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.389.title: TPW 7.20 Closed Loop Audit: Assessing Parenteral Nutrition in General Surgical Patients in A Busy Teaching Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.389.abstract: Abstract Aims Early consideration for Parenteral Nutrition (PN) in general surgical patients can reduce poor surgical outcomes and hospital length of stay (HLOS). This quality improvement project and audit assessed the quality of referrals for PN and the on impact timely delivery. The first cycle was presented at ASGBI 2025 (EP513). Methods A retrospective review was undertaken of patients referred for PN from General Surgery wards between 01/11/23–01/12/23 and re-audited in 2024. Data were compared against local nutrition standards and analysed using Microsoft Excel. Results Fourteen patients were referred in 2023 and eighteen in 2024. 20232024Median Age (range)75 years (28-89)67.5 years (24-80)Median BMI (range)20.1 (13.7-31.2)31.4 (17.3-54.3)Median HLOS (range)30 days (6-44)17 days (7-38) All cases across both cycles had a documented reason for gut failure (nil by mouth, poor intake, or vomiting) and appropriate baseline blood tests. Documentation improved by 4% in recorded height and weight (from 11/14 to 15/18) and by 30% in documented MUST scores (from 9/14 to 17/18). Median time from referral to venous access was 1 day, and all patients were reviewed by the PN nurse within 1 day, compared to a median of 1 day (0–2) previously. Rejected referrals decreased by 53%, PN commencement improved by 19% (from 9/14 to 15/18) and median duration increasing from 4 to 6 days. Conclusions Referral quality has significantly improved, allowing earlier and more appropriate nutrition, with an associated reduction in hospital length of stay.
affiliations: Surgery, Royal Victoria Infirmary, Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
General Surgery, Doncaster and Bassetlaw Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Doncaster ,
Division of Clinical Medicine, School of Medicine and Population Health, University of Sheffield , Sheffield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.437.title: TPTh 2.12 Regional Adherence to National GIRFT Surgical Guidelines on Post-Operative Antibiotic Prescribing in Paediatric Appendicitis: Multi-Centre Multi-Cycle Audit of Clinical Practice
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.437.abstract: Abstract Introduction National guidelines for paediatric appendicitis stipulate a pathway for post-operative antibiotic management based intraoperative findings. Despite this, significant variation in practice persists between surgeons and departments. Unnecessary post-operative antibiotics contribute to antimicrobial resistance, C. difficile infection and prolonged inpatient stay. We assessed compliance with GIRFT guidelines on post-operative antibiotic prescribing in uncomplicated and complicated paediatric appendicitis and aimed to standardise practice in line with GIRFT guidelines. Methods We conducted a retrospective review of paediatric appendicectomies performed at four central London hospitals over a 3-month period. Findings were presented at department and site-wide governance events. This was followed by a second prospective cycle after targeted education-based interventions at each site, focusing on junior doctors most commonly responsible for prescribing. Results The average number of cases across four sites was 20.5 (range=13-34) and compliance with GIRFT guidelines ranged from 46-75% between hospitals. Compliance did not significantly vary between sites (p=0.08). Non-compliant practice seen was the continuation of antibiotics following an uncomplicated appendicectomy, with a median duration of 4.5 days antibiotics post-op. Following education-based interventions, rates of compliance improved in subsequent cycles to 53-73%. (p=0.045). Conclusions Post-operative antibiotic prescribing for uncomplicated appendicitis were grossly discordant with national guidance. Clear documentation of antibiotic plans in operation notes and empowering junior doctors to challenge prescriptions with seniors helped improve compliance. Ongoing education supports appropriate cessation of antibiotics, reducing harm and healthcare costs.
affiliations: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust
Whittington Health Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.337.title: TPW 4.11 Audit of Knowledge and Utilization of Oakland Scores for Lower GI Bleeds in Ulster Hospital Dundonald (UHD)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.337.abstract: Abstract Aims Lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB) is a common reason for emergency surgical referral. The British Society of Gastroenterology 2019 guidelines recommend use of the Oakland score to risk-stratify patients and identify those suitable for discharge. This audit aimed to assess knowledge and utilisation of the Oakland score among Emergency Department (ED) and surgical residents and to improve adherence to guideline-based management. Methods A pre-intervention survey assessed knowledge and self-reported use of the Oakland score among ED and general surgical trainees. Surgical handover lists were reviewed to identify patients referred from ED with LGIB between July–August 2025, and clinical notes were assessed for Oakland score documentation. Interventions included posters in ED and seminar rooms, and a departmental teaching session. Re-audit was conducted over October–November 2025. Inpatients with per-rectal bleeding were excluded. Results Thirty-four clinicians completed the baseline survey – 61.8% of respondents were unaware of the Oakland score. In cycle 1, 21 patients were identified; only one patient (4.8%) had an Oakland score documented. Following intervention, 43 patients were identified in cycle 2, with Oakland scores documented in 48.8% of cases. Seven patients (33.3%) had scores ≤8; five were appropriately discharged and two admitted for alternative medical diagnoses. Fourteen patients (66.7%) had scores >8; ten were admitted and four discharged following senior review, all with appropriate follow-up or recent endoscopic assessment. Conclusions Targeted education significantly improved use of the Oakland score in LGIB assessment. Routine incorporation of the Oakland score may further enhance patient safety and optimise resource utilisation.
affiliations: The Ulster Hospital , Dundonald, Belfast

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.385.title: TPW 7.16 Improving Compliance with Severity Scoring in Acute Pancreatitis: A Two-Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.385.abstract: Abstract Aims The British Society of Gastroenterology recommends that all patients admitted with acute pancreatitis undergo severity scoring within 48 hours, as this facilitates early risk stratification, guides management, and improves prognostication. Failure to implement this standard may contribute to avoidable morbidity and mortality. Methods Medical records of patients admitted with acute pancreatitis at a District General Hospital were audited. The first cycle reviewed admissions between 23/11/2024 and 09/12/2024 for documentation of severity scoring using the Glasgow Imrie score. Following targeted teaching for resident doctors and the introduction of a process whereby the on-call team ensured scoring for all new admissions, a second cycle was conducted between 23/12/2024 and 10/01/2025. Results In the first cycle, only 2 of 12 patients (16.7%) had a Glasgow Imrie score recorded. Retrospective scoring revealed two patients had a score of ≥3 within 48 hours; one was not escalated until day five, requiring ICU admission for ARDS. After interventions, compliance improved markedly: 9 of 11 patients (81.8%) in the second cycle received severity scoring, and no ICU admissions occurred. Conclusions This audit demonstrates that simple, targeted educational and procedural interventions can substantially improve compliance with national guidelines on severity scoring in acute pancreatitis. Improved adherence ensures earlier identification of severe cases and timely escalation of care, with the potential to reduce complications and improve patient outcomes.
affiliations: Altnagelvin Area Hospital
Western Health and Social Care Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.366.title: TPW 6.13 Timing of Cholecystectomy for Gallstone Disease in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit of Guideline Compliance, Readmissions and Service Burden
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.366.abstract: Abstract Aims To assess compliance with guideline-recommended timing of cholecystectomy for patients admitted with acute cholecystitis and gallstone pancreatitis, and to evaluate the associated burden of gallstone disease, including readmissions, length of stay, and operative outcomes. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted of adult patients admitted with gallstone-related disease between January and April 2025. Patients with acute cholecystitis or gallstone pancreatitis were included. An initial cohort was identified via a data extract, with individual case review performed using electronic patient records. Data collected included admission diagnosis, timing and type of cholecystectomy (emergency or elective), drain usage, length of stay, and readmissions. Time to surgery was calculated from admission to cholecystectomy. Results A total of 136 patients were included. Although 73 patients were deemed fit for surgery, only 11% underwent cholecystectomy within 10 days. Among patients awaiting elective surgery beyond 10 days, 13 of 28 (46%) experienced at least one readmission. Emergency surgery was associated with higher drain usage (approximately 75%) but favourable recovery, with a mean length of stay of 3 days (median 2 days) which is in line with the benchmark average for the trust of 3 days. Elective surgery had lower drain usage (approximately 25%) but was frequently preceded by recurrent admissions. Conclusions Compliance with guideline-recommended early cholecystectomy was low. This led to preventable readmissions and increased healthcare utilisation. Emergency cholecystectomy appears safe and resource-efficient. Optimising acute gallbladder pathways and access to early surgery may improve outcomes and reduce service burden.
affiliations: Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.576.title: EP 349 Audit of Updated ERAS Guidelines Followed in Elective Colorectal Surgery in a Teaching Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.576.abstract: Abstract Aims To look into current practices for elective colorectal surgery and compare with the updated ERAS guidelines published in June 2025.To look for areas of improvement that are feasible and as learning points for the department. Methods 4 months of data between June to September 2025 was collected retrospectively and all elective colo-rectal surgeries with the exception of day case benign proctology was included. 10 out of the 23 recommendations from ERAS 2025 guidelines with high grade of evidence and high strength of recommendation with relevance to surgical practise was identified and data collected. Results There was a total of 56 surgeries performed electively of which right hemicolectomies were most common (30%) followed by Anterior resections (23%). More than 90% compliance was noted in the 6 categories of Post op nausea and vomiting prophylaxis, Removing NG tube post op, multimodal analgesia, post op enteral nutrition, IV antibiotics and VTE prophylaxis was noted. Mechanical bowel prep was being routinely prescribed for more than 85% of resections which is not recommended by the updated guidelines. All the patients receiving MBP had oral antibiotic compliance. More than 78% of patients had minimally invasive laparoscopic or robotic surgery and 73% of patients had no drain placed post operatively. Conclusion There is fair adherence to the ERAS guidelines in our teaching hospital. Recommendations with good evidence should be taken into consideration for good medical practice.
affiliations: Sandwell and West Birmingham Hospitals NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.172.title: TPT 2.02 The Right Tool for the Job: A Completed Audit Cycle of Trainee Surgical Equipment Knowledge with A Novel Educational Intervention
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.172.abstract: Abstract Introduction Early career introduction to the operating theatre can be an intimidating prospect. Resident doctors (RDs) at our institution reported low confidence and anxiety using surgical instrumentation and drapes. We hypothesised this reflected a lack of practical teaching and sought to audit competence and knowledge in this area with a view to addressing these concerns. Methods Junior surgical RDs underwent a 14-item multiple choice questionnaire (MCQ) on surgical equipment, adapted from the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons (RACS) membership examinations. A digital survey captured demographics, experience, prior teaching, and subjective confidence using Likert scales. The audit standard was the RACS MCQ pass grade of 60%. Following first-cycle results, a practical multidisciplinary teaching session was delivered in collaboration with scrub nurse educators, incorporating demonstration of a general surgical set and patient draping. Re-audit was conducted four weeks post-intervention using the same MCQ and survey. Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare pre- and post-intervention MCQ scores. Results Sixteen surgical RDs participated. 81% felt the topic was overlooked. First-cycle MCQ results did not meet the audit standard (mean 46.4%, median 35.7%, range 28.6–85.7%). Following the intervention, second-cycle MCQ results reached the standard (mean 80.4%, median 71.4%, range 71.4–100%), with a highly significant improvement in scores (p < 0.001). Conclusion This completed audit cycle identified a gap in education and demonstrated that a focused multidisciplinary intervention can improve both objective knowledge and subjective confidence. Our novel intervention has been incorporated biannually into the RD teaching programme and expanded to other hospital sites.
affiliations: Department of Surgery, St John of God Subiaco Hospital , Subiaco, WA ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.091.title: SP 7.04 Retrospective Audit of Cardiovascular Risk in Patients Undergoing Pancreaticoduodenectomy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.091.abstract: Abstract Introduction Pancreatic cancer is a highly metabolic disease with high-risk of major adverse cardio-vascular events (MACE). Those undergoing surgery who take statins have longer survival. QRISK3 scoring estimates the risk of acute myocardial infarction or stroke within 10 years in the UK population, and NICE recommends its validated use to guide optimal metabolic therapy (OMT). In patients undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy the relationship between QRISK3 score and OMT, MACE, or survival is unknown. Methods QRISK3 was retrospectively calculated in patients undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy for invasive malignancy (2022-2024). Rates of OMT and MACE (+/- all cause mortality [ACM]) were determined. The relationship between QRISK3 and survival was explored using Cox regression. Results Data from 114 patients were reviewed; male 50 (44%), median (IQR) age 67 (59-73) years. At 1-year: in high-risk (QRISK3≥20%) patients OMT 4/46 (8.7%), MACE+ACM 7/46 (15.2%); moderate-risk (QRISK3≥10%) OMT 6/38 (15.8%), MACE+ACM 3/38 (7.9%); low-risk (QRISK3<10%) OMT 29/30 (96.7%), MACE+ACM 2/30 (6.7%). QRISK3 score independently predicted survival (median 24 months) in all cancer types (HR [95%CI] 1.033 [1.002-1.065] p=0.037). In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (n=46), QRISK3 score remained a predictor of survival (HR [95%CI] 1.056 [1.001-1.140] p=0.047) after accounting for T stage, N stage, R0 resection and chemotherapy status. Conclusion Patients undergoing pancreatic surgery are at high-risk of MACE and mortality and receive sub-optimal prevention. Pre-operative cardiovascular risk assessment and mitigation with OMT could improve outcomes. QRISK3 score may predict overall survival but further work is required to validate and fully understand this relationship.
affiliations: Department of Pancreatic Surgery, Leeds Teaching Hospital NHS Trust ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.495.title: TPTh 7.05 Urgent MRCP Pathway Performance: A Baseline Audit of Delays and Service Impact
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.495.abstract: Abstract Aims To evaluate the efficiency of an urgent MRCP pathway at a District General Hospital by quantifying time from request to imaging and definitive treatment, identifying modifiable contributors to delay, and the associated service impact to guide targeted quality improvement intervention and re-audit. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted between 1st June and 22th September 2025 of all MRCP requests for suspected biliary pathology. Cases where MRCP was not performed or where key data fields missing were excluded. Outcomes were MRCP request to scan time (overall, inpatient, outpatient), documented reasons for delay, readmissions while awaiting MRCP, and inpatient bed-days attributable to waiting. Results 123 requests were identified; 4 were excluded due to MRCP not performed, leaving 119 requests. Overall, the median time from request to scan was 3 days (IQR 2-6 days), and mean of 7.99 days. Inpatients (n=85) waited median 2 days (IQR 1–4) and mean 2.96 days. For outpatients (n=34), the waited median time was 13 days (IQR 3–31), with mean 18.56 days. Key contributors to delay were scheduling delays (64/119, 54%), and weekend delays (33/119, 28%). While awaiting MRCP, 4 patients were readmitted. Inpatients awaiting MRCP accounted for 252 bed-days. Conclusions Turnaround times within the urgent MRCP pathway were prolonged, and were associated with avoidable bed occupancy and readmissions, delaying definitive management. Awaiting MRCP inpatient days equated to £86,940, suggesting a scope for pathway optimisation. Protected MRCP slots, a prioritisation list, and escalation triggers for inpatient waits >48hrs will be implemented, with a re-audit.
affiliations: Croydon University Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.076.title: SP 6.03 Improving Surgical Handover Report Documentation: A Three-Cycle Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.076.abstract: Abstract Aims To evaluate the completeness and timeliness of general surgery handover report documentation used for weekend on-call cover. To assess whether an induction-embedded intervention improved compliance with national handover standards. Methods A prospective three-cycle audit assessed handover reports for all general surgery inpatients across three wards prior to weekend on-call cover. Variables assessed included patient inclusion on the handover list, whether entries were updated prior to handover, and documentation completeness in line with Royal College of Surgeons of England guidance on safe handover. Following the initial audit cycle, results were disseminated departmentally, after which a structured handover tutorial was embedded into resident doctor induction. Compliance with audit standards was then compared across cycles. Results Across 304 patients, patient inclusion in the handover list rose from 42% at baseline to 89%, and the proportion of entries updated prior to handover rose from 27% to 77%. Documentation completeness in line with guidance increased from 23% to 50%; however, omissions in patient status and outstanding investigations persisted. These gains were most marked in the acute admission ward and among on-call teams and were sustained despite resident doctor turnover. Conclusions Embedding handover expectations into resident doctor induction was associated with sustained improvements in handover list inclusion and update frequency, despite staff turnover. Documentation completeness plateaued at 50%, indicating that while human-factor interventions improve consistency of handover report updates, further gains are likely to require system-level solutions such as electronic handover templates.
affiliations: South Tyneside and Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.427.title: TPTh 1.14 Healing Outcomes Following 2-Minute Versus 3-Minute Phenol Application in Onychocryptosis: A Retrospective Comparative Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.427.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate whether reducing phenol application time from three minutes to two minutes improves postoperative healing time following phenol chemical matrixectomy for onychocryptosis. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted of patients who underwent partial nail avulsion with phenolisation for onychocryptosis. Patients were divided into two groups based on phenol application time: two minutes (n = 26) and three minutes (n = 20). Healing time was defined by the absence of wound exudate, formation of a protective scab, ability to remain uncovered, and absence of infection, erythema, inflammation, or hypergranulation tissue at the nail folds. Healing time data were non-normally distributed and are presented as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR). Groups were compared using a two-tailed Mann–Whitney U test, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results Median healing time was 14 days (IQR 14–28) in the two-minute phenol group compared with 28 days (IQR 28–42) in the three-minute phenol group. This difference was statistically significant (Mann–Whitney U = 152.5, z = −2.37, p = 0.018). No postoperative infections were recorded in either group. Conclusion Reducing phenol application time to two minutes was associated with a significantly shorter healing time following surgical treatment of onychocryptosis. These findings suggest that shorter phenol exposure may reduce postoperative morbidity without compromising treatment effectiveness.
affiliations: Foot & Ankle Centre

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.256.title: TPT 7.17 Standardising Docking Time in Robotic General Surgery: A Closed-Loop Audit Using Phase-Based Workflow Analysis
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.256.abstract: Abstract Aims To standardise docking time in robotic general surgery by implementing a structured, phase-based workflow analysis, enabling reproducible benchmarking and identification of workflow inefficiencies. Methods A closed-loop audit was conducted across two cycles in a robotic general surgery programme. Cycle 1 (n=43) measured docking time from knife-to-skin until the surgeon sat at the console. Procedures included cholecystectomies (n=9), inguinal hernia repairs (n=14), and major colorectal resections (n=17). Cycle 2 (n=30) introduced a phase-based approach, dividing docking into five sequential steps: (1) knife-to-port placement, (2) drive-in, (3) drive-in to dock, (4) dock-to-target, and (5) target-to-console. Times were prospectively recorded and analysed to identify workflow delays, procedure-specific variation, and learning curve effects. Results Mean docking time decreased from 34 minutes in Cycle 1 to 32 minutes in Cycle 2. Inguinal hernia docking improved from ∼28 to 20 minutes, and major resections from 58 to 42 minutes. Cholecystectomy times increased slightly due to a small sample size and the inclusion of a new surgeon. Phase-based timing allowed precise identification of workflow bottlenecks and facilitated targeted optimisation. The structured approach enabled consistent benchmarking and assessment of team performance across different procedures. Conclusions Breaking‍‌‍‍‌‍‌‍‍‌ down robotic docking into discrete, quantifiable stages provides a consistent way to standardise docking time and pinpoint inefficiencies in the workflow. The use of phase-based docking as a tool to understand the surgical team’s workflow is thus a strong, widely applicable method to not only enhance operative workflows but also to set up significant performance metrics in robotic general ‍‌‍‍‌‍‌‍‍‌surgery.
affiliations: James Paget University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.552.title: EP 182 A Rare Cause of Closed-Loop Obstruction: Caecal Volvulus within a Petersen’s Hernia following Gastric Bypass
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.552.abstract: Abstract Keywords Caecal volvulus, Petersen’s hernia, Gastric bypass, Closed-loop obstruction, Internal hernia, Acute abdomen Background Internal herniation through Petersen’s defect is a recognised late complication of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, usually involving small bowel loops. Caecal volvulus within a Petersen’s hernia is extremely rare, with few cases reported. Such presentations pose diagnostic and operative challenges due to altered post-bypass anatomy and atypical imaging features. Case Presentation A 41-year-old woman presented with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and absolute constipation. She had a history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and cholecystectomy. Examination revealed a distended, rigid abdomen with peritonism and elevated inflammatory markers. CT imaging demonstrated a markedly dilated, gas- and fluid-filled ahaustral caecum (maximum diameter 9.4 cm) displaced into the left upper quadrant with twisting of the mesentery, engorged vessels, and features of closed-loop obstruction. Emergency laparotomy revealed a grossly distended caecum twisted clockwise on its mesentery within a large Petersen’s defect. The terminal ileum was uninvolved. Moderate pelvic pus was present without perforation. The remaining colon was viable. A right hemicolectomy with stapled ileocolic anastomosis and closure of the Petersen’s defect was performed. Discussion and Conclusion Caecal volvulus within a Petersen’s hernia is an exceptionally rare but life-threatening cause of intestinal obstruction. Post-bariatric anatomical distortion may obscure diagnosis. Awareness of this entity, detailed CT interpretation, and prompt operative management with mesenteric defect closure are critical to prevent ischemia and improve outcomes in post-gastric bypass patients presenting with acute abdomen.
affiliations: Department of General & GI Surgery, George Elliot NHS Hospital , Nuneaton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.407.title: TPW 9.08 Establishing and Evaluating a Laparoscopic Peritoneal Dialysis Catheter Insertion Service in NHS Lanarkshire: A Two-Cohort Comparative Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.407.abstract: Abstract Aims Renal transplantation remains the gold-standard treatment for end-stage renal disease, but peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a valuable alternative. A laparoscopic PD catheter insertion service was reintroduced in NHS Lanarkshire and has matured. This audit retrospectively compares outcomes from the initial reimplementation phase with a recent cohort to assess ongoing performance against International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis (ISPD) guidelines. Methods Two cohorts were compared: - Cohort 1 (initial reintroduction): 19 consecutive patients undergoing laparoscopic PD catheter insertion from 17/12/2019 to 06/01/2021, followed up for 6 months. - Cohort 2 (recent audit): 34 patients from 24/04/2023 to 13/11/2024, followed up for up to 6 months. Demographics, complications, day-case success rates, and catheter survival were evaluated. ISPD guidelines were followed in both groups. Results Both cohorts had 0% 30-day peritonitis and surgical site infection rates. At 6 months, PD peritonitis was 22% (4/18) in Cohort 1, improving to 5.8% (2/34) in Cohort 2. Postoperative urinary retention fell from 11% (2/18) to 2.9% (1/34). Day-case feasibility improved, with overnight stays required for 83% (15/18) initially versus 44.1% (15/34) recently. Only one case of PD peritonitis had a positive PD fluid culture (Stenotrophomonas maltophilia). Conclusion The laparoscopic PD catheter insertion service in NHS Lanarkshire has matured, with reduced early complication rates in the recent cohort. Day-case procedures are feasible, supporting the long-term safety and viability of the service.
affiliations: University Hospital Monklands

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.007.title: Learning from Regional Excellence: Geographic Analysis of the National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) Mortality Improvement
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.007.abstract: Abstract Background NELA demonstrates mortality improvement from 11.36% (2016) to 8.15% (2025), representing a 28% relative reduction across 145,163 verified patients. Understanding the geographic distribution of this improvement offers opportunities for knowledge transfer and targeted quality enhancement. Methods Longitudinal analysis of NELA data (2016-2025) examined mortality trends across 15 geographic regions. Cross-sectional 2018 analysis of 23,929 patients across 190 hospitals characterised regional variation. Subsequent datasets confirmed patterns: 2022 (65,561 patients, 193 hospitals), 2025 (55,673 patients, 167 hospitals). Process standards, including critical care admission, CT imaging, data completeness, and elderly assessment, were analysed alongside outcomes. Results Geographic analysis revealed substantial regional variation, ranging from 5.4% (London-South-West) to 11.3% (Yorkshire & Humber). Excellence concentrated geographically: 60% of London-South-East hospitals achieved <8% mortality, compared with 13.3% in Yorkshire. In 2018, 6,439 patients (26.9%) received care in consistently low-mortality regions, whilst 7,700 patients (32.2%) underwent surgery in higher-mortality regions. North West (3,362 patients, 27 hospitals) achieved 8.4%, demonstrating scalable excellence at volume. Within-region variation suggested individual hospital practices merit investigation. Critical care admissions remained stable (78% to 77.5%), reflecting capacity constraints. CT imaging declined (65% to 54%) before standard redefinition. Data capture decreased (91% to 83%). These patterns suggest mortality improvement mechanisms differ from traditionally measured processes. Conclusions Analysis identifies high-performing regions: North-West demonstrates low mortality at scale (8.4%), London South West achieves exceptional outcomes (5.4%). Future initiatives should establish peer-learning networks, conduct site visits to identify transferable practices in surgical technique and perioperative management, and address infrastructure constraints, particularly in critical care capacity.
affiliations: Royal Liverpool University Hospital , Liverpool ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.403.title: TPW 9.02 Routine Preoperative Investigations in Low-Risk Elective Inguinal Hernia Patients: A Closed-Loop Audit
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.403.abstract: Abstract Background NICE recommends specific preoperative investigations which should or should not be performed routinely in adult patients undergoing elective inguinal hernia repair, depending on their ASA grades and comorbidities. This two-cycle audit aimed to evaluate the routine investigations performed in ASA 1 and 2 adult patients prior to their elective inguinal hernia repair at a large tertiary centre. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 200 elective inguinal hernia patients between September 2023 and March 2024. The results were presented at a local meeting, and interventions were subsequently implemented including updated trust guidance and a digital decision-aid tool. To evaluate the impact of these changes, 96 patients were retrospectively analysed between December 2024 and June 2025. This was limited to one of the two hospitals within the trust, where interventions were first implemented. Results The first cycle showed poor overall compliance with NICE guidelines, but the second cycle demonstrated a marked improvement. Among ASA 1 patients, unnecessary preoperative tests decreased by 20.5% for FBC, 21.4% for haemostasis, 22.6% for U&E and 33.0% for ECG. In ASA 2, reductions were 75.0% for FBC, 16.7% for haemostasis, 11.9% for U&E and 9.4% for ECG. No lung function tests or ABG were performed in either cycle. Conclusion The updated trust guidance and digital decision-aid tool were effective in improving compliance with national standards. Further improvements can be achieved by wider implementation across the trust and continued re-auditing. Additionally, the audit can be expanded to assess financial and environmental impact.
affiliations: The Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Newcastle ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.307.title: TPW 2.08 Post-Colonoscopy Colorectal Cancer (PCCRC): Two-Year Audit Using the WEO Framework to Target Preventable Harm
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.307.abstract: Abstract Aims Post-colonoscopy colorectal cancer (PCCRC) is a key quality marker reflecting missed lesions, incomplete therapy, or pathway delays. We audited PCCRC rates across two annual cohorts and applied the World Endoscopy Organization (WEO) framework to identify avoidable factors and improvement actions. Methods All colorectal cancers diagnosed between March 2023 and March 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Cases preceded by lower GI-endoscopy within 36 months were classified as PCCRC using WEO criteria. Index endoscopy records were assessed for bowel preparation, lesion recognition, completeness, resection planning, coding, and time to definitive-therapy. Results Two PCCRC cases were identified across two cycles with low rates. Cycle 1 (03/2023–03/2024) recorded one PCCRC (0.6%), WEO Category C (detected but not resected), following poor bowel-preparation and delayed-definitive management. Learning themes included missed appointments, missed surveillance, cancers after flexible sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy >3 years prior, and cancers diagnosed within 6 months. Improvements strengthened bowel prep/rebooking, surveillance tracking, and pathway awareness. Cycle 2 (03/2024–03/2025) recorded one PCCRC (0.7%) in an 81-year-old male with distal sigmoid cancer diagnosed 28 months after an index colonoscopy reporting small-benign-polyps and diverticulosis; further learning points related to investigation choice and referral delays. Conclusions The incidence of PCCRC at DGH remains below the threshold of 5%, suggested by JAG. Contributing factors included structured follow-up for patients ensuring optimal surveillance in tune with ACPGBI guidelines, improved awareness of PCCRC, enhanced techniques such as double walk on the right colon with white light and Narrow Band Imaging, standardised withdrawal times and regular emphasis on Key performance indicators.
affiliations: George Eliot Hospital
University of East Anglia

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.413.title: TPW 9.15 National Emergency Laparotomy (NELA) Deaths Within 90 Days: A Cohort Study with INARC Scores (Intensive Care National Audit Research Centre)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.413.abstract: Abstract Aims There has-been a-reduction in 30-day-mortality: 11% to 8.1 % (NELA report 2025). NELA has-set care-pathways-in-management-of-emergency-laparotomies. Aim of study is to assess-outcomes of emergency-laparotomy amongst-the-90-day-deaths. Methods Cohort-study of NELA-deaths within-90-days, from Jan’2014 to Jan’2026 at single institution. Descriptive-demography & surgical-outcomes were analysed. NELA survivors beyond >90 days were controls. Results < 90-day(n=130) >90-day(n=930) Mann-Whitney-U(p-value) Age (yrs) 74.5±1.1 66.8±0.5 <0.0001 Sex(M:F) 64:66 423:507 NS ASA 3±1 3±1 <0.0001 BMI(kg/m2) 26.7±0.7 25.7 ± 0.2 NS RCS-category(n) 2 2 NS Lap(n) 22 312 0.0112 30-D-deaths 86 60-D-deaths 119 90-D-deaths 130 ITU(n) 89 398 <0.0001 Direct 73 374 <0.0001 Indirect 16 24 <0.0001 APCHES-II 16.1±0.7 12.8±0.3 <0.0001 INARC-mortality(%) 22.5±1.9 12.0±0.5 <0.0001 Hosp Mortality(%) 23.6±1.9 13.7±0.5 <0.0001 Con-surg(n) 129 899 NS Con-anae(n) 118 716 NS Op-time(mins) 124.8±5.5 124.3±2.2 NS LOS(days)(med±IQR) 17±5.5 12±7.5 NS Lactate(mmol/L) 2.9± .3 1.9±0.1 <0.0001 WCC(x109/L) 13.1±0.6 12.2±0.2 NS CRP(mg/L) 101.8±10.5 74.4±3.4 0.0011 Physiological-score 28.2±0.8 21.7±0.3 <0.0001 Operative-severity-score 19.9±0.5 16.4±0.2 <0.0001 Pre-possum score 29.4±3.3 11.9±0.8 <0.0001 PP-mortality-score 25.9±1.9 8.1±0.4 <0.0001 PP-morbidity-score 82.4±2.1 63.5±1.3 <0.0001 Survival-Rate(%) 1st year 82.0 5th year 63.2 10th year 49.9 Conclusion At our-centre, crude-NELA 30-day & 90-day mortality-rates-were 8.1 % & 12.3 % respectively.
