DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.485.title: 667 Enhanced Recovery in Cranial Surgery (ERACraS) – a Single-Centre Qualitative Improvement Study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.485.abstract: Abstract Aim To establish an Enhanced Recovery After Cranial Surgery (ERACraS) protocol for patients as part of a quality improvement project (QIP) with the intention of reducing hospital length of stay (HLOS), similar to the evidence-based Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol. Method This QIP was carried out in the Department of Neurosciences (DCN), Edinburgh, over two four-month periods. A total of 40 patients over 18 years of age undergoing elective craniotomy surgery under a sole neurosurgeon were invited to take part in this QIP. Subsequently, data was retrospectively collected through our institution’s online documentation system. Results 19 patients received conventional perioperative care (pre-ERACraS group) during December 2021-March 2022, and 21 received care according to the novel ERACraS (ERACraS group) during June-September 2022. Regarding supra-tentorial surgery, there was a reduction of 73% in HLOS in the ERACraS group. No change was observed in infra-tentorial surgery. Overall, the ERACraS protocol reduced HLOS by 50% in cranial surgery. Conclusions The QIP data from ERACraS in our unit has shown that implementing ERAS protocols is feasible. A reduction in HLOS has implications for patient morbidity, mortality, and quality of care. We endeavour to collect long-term data by collaborating with neurosurgical units across the UK and Ireland to validate its feasibility and sustainability as part of a major QIP in neurosurgical practice. This can be potentially adopted by neurosurgical centres across the globe in a safe and sustained manner.
affiliations: Al Amiri Hospital , Kuwait , Kuwait
University of Aberdeen , Aberdeen , United Kingdom
Department of Clinical Neurosciences , Edinburgh , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.489.title: 174 The Histopathological Assessment of Gastro-Oesophageal Carcinoma Resection Specimens: A Quality Improvement project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.489.abstract: Abstract Aim HERO consensus and Royal College of Pathologists provide guidance for the minimum dataset pathological evaluation of gastro-oesophageal cancer resection specimens. The project aimed to assess and improve adherence. Method A retrospective study of the pathological evaluation of gastro-oesophageal cancer specimens resected surgically at a tertiary cancer unit (October 2021-March 2022), and re-audit (July-December 2022) following presentation of first cycle results. Results 26 and 23 specimens in rounds 1 and 2 respectively met inclusion criteria. Adherence was good in both rounds for reporting lymphovascular invasion status (92.3% vs 100%), correct reporting as R1 if tumour cells are found within 1mm of the margin (100% vs 100%), lesser curvature fat-blocking (100% vs 100%), and reporting of lymph node response following neoadjuvant chemotherapy (100% vs 100%). Improvement was seen in testing a minimum of 15 lymph nodes (88.5% vs 91.3%) and recording of resection margins in millimetres (CRM 77.8% vs 100%; LRM 80.8% vs 82.6%). One of the three specimens with <15 node yield was retested in round 1, compared with both specimens in round 2. Reporting of peri-oesophageal fat blocking showed no improvement (88.9% vs 77.8%). Conclusions Adherence was good during cycle 1, and there was improvement in most domains following presentation of results. Of note, both specimens in the second cycle with lymph node yield <15 were re-examined. Lymph node yield is determined by both surgical technique and avid pathology node search. The project proved to be an incentive for the MDT group as a whole to seek and adhere to good reporting practice.
affiliations: University College Hospital , London , United Kingdom
Royal London Hospital , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.535.title: 83 Quality Improvement Project on the Adherence to Hot Gallbladder Pathway Clinical Guidelines: An Improvement of the Hot Gallbladder Referral Pathway
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.535.abstract: Abstract Aim The quality improvement project’s main aim is to improve utilization of the Hot-Gallbladder(HGB) list. Although the guidelines are clear, a large number of referrals did not meet the criteria and were deemed inappropriate. We designed a self-explanatory proforma and added educational posters/aids that helped increase orientation and clarified the process and criteria. Method A set period of referrals was examined and audited and compared to the data collected post introduction of the proforma. The first audit cycle looked at patients referred for emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy during April-May 2023 which determined the need for interventions to improve utilization of the HGB list and adherence to guidelines. A well designed self-explanatory pro-forma was introduced along with informative posters. A second audit cycle was done during the months of June-July 2023 showing significant improvement. Results April-May 2023: 38 referrals, 4/34 accepted (10.5% successful). June-July 2023: 24 referrals, 7/24 accepted (29.2% successful). Average stay in hospital: April-May 2023: 6.45 days, June-July 2023: 3.88 days. Conclusions The introduction of the well-designed self-explanatory proforma has improved the quality of referrals and raised the awareness of the presence of the pathway. This has in turn improved utilization of HGB lists, decreased the load on elective lists and improved outcomes.
affiliations: Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust , Tunbridge Wells , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.542.title: 321 Improvement of Nasal Spray Technique in Patients in an ENT Outpatient Clinic: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.542.abstract: Abstract Background anagement of allergic rhinitis involves administration of intranasal corticosteroid sprays and efficacy relies on correct technique. Treatment failures result in poor disease control, non-compliance, increased ENT appointments and unnecessary surgeries. The correct technique involves applying the spray to the turbinates (side wall), to reduce inflammation that leads to obstructive symptoms. Aim To improve Nasal spray technique amongst patients in an ENT outpatient clinic, using a patient education tool. Method PDSA 1: Designed a survey to assess current technique and identify areas for improvement. PDSA 2: First cycle identified 4 key steps for improvement. A leaflet was designed highlighting these steps and handed out to patients who were prescribed the spray. Patients were called 2 weeks later to assess technique. PDSA 3: Leaflet and teach-back method was used to demonstrate correct technique and patients were called back in 2 weeks. Results PDSA 1: Only 2% (1/53) of patients used spray correctly and 86.8% of patients administered the spray in the centre of the nose. PDSA 2: 60% (7/11) of patients used spray correctly. PDSA 3- 100% (6/6) of patients used correct technique. Aim of spray to the side of nose was only 5.7% in PDSA 1 which increased to 100% in PDSA 3. Conclusions This QIP identified poor nasal spray technique amongst 98% of ENT patients, which may cause treatment failure. Introducing simple and cost-effective interventions, increased the number of people using the spray correctly. These interventions could easily be implemented in ENT and GP clinics, to improve technique reducing repeat appointments and unnecessary referrals.
affiliations: Queens Hospital Romford , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.541.title: 269 Quality Improvement: Implementing a General Surgery Ward Round Proforma at Stoke Mandeville Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.541.abstract: Abstract Aim In keeping with Good Medical Practice endorsed by the Royal College of Surgeons, a specialised surgical ward round proforma was launched to ensure accurate, clear and comprehensive daily clinical records.1 This is to ensure professional practice and delivery of best medical care. Method The specialised surgical ward round proforma was designed and implemented for general surgery inpatients in May 2023. Data was collected at regular intervals to include compliance and aspects of proforma filled. In parallel, feedback forms were collected to improve subsequent versions of the proforma. Two cycles have been completed by October 2023. Results Compliance of use of the newly launched surgical proforma over the study period was >85% (n=159). Essential items such as date, patient identity, ward name, NEWS score and presenting issue had high recording rates >95%. Spaces dedicated to details such as analgesia and VTE were removed when transiting from version one to version two having noted reduced rates of completion <30%. Supported by individual feedback, sections with similarly low documentation rates such as antibiotic regime and imaging results were retained due to their value on a patient-by-patient basis. Conclusions The introduction of a general surgery ward round proforma has proved useful in ensuring multiple aspects of a patient’s management are considered and documented. Our team looks to implement this proforma at a trust-wide level and aim to analyse improvements in multiple aspects of patient care including informed decision making in patient management, antibiotic stewardship, collaboration amongst the multidisciplinary team and continuity of care.
affiliations: Oxford University Hospitals NHS , Oxford , United Kingdom
University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire NHS , Coventry , United Kingdom
Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS , Aylesbury , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.547.title: 423 Implementation of Standardised Consent Forms for Hip Fracture Surgery: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.547.abstract: Abstract Aim Informed consent is pivotal for patient care. We assessed the quality of written consenting for surgical management of neck of femur fractures (NOFF) at a UK District General Hospital. This resulted in the development of standardised consent forms to promote best clinical practice. Method A retrospective review of consent forms for 50 consecutive patients admitted with NOFF from July 2023 evaluated legibility, documentation of procedure name, benefits, risks, and consenter details. Standardised consent forms endorsed by the British Orthopaedic Association were used as a standard and a guide for our standardised consent forms, introduced in September 2023. We reviewed the compliance with the new forms for inpatients with NOFF in October 2023 (n=21). Results On consent 1 forms (n = 37), nearly 60% lacked documentation of benefits (pain relief and mobility), and 78% missed more than 5 risks. All forms were legible and 98% completed by speciality registrars or consultants. Venous thromboembolism was documented on all forms. Chronic pain, stiffness and death were missed on most forms. Procedure name was the only documentation found on consent 4 forms. The new standardised forms included both consent 1 and 4 forms and were utilised in 86% of cases. Users of the new form also included foundation year 2 doctors who clerked the patients on admission. Conclusions Standardised forms prevent oversight of crucial procedure risks, facilitate time efficiency, and instil confidence in junior team members to consent. Future steps aim to extend this standardised approach to other common orthopaedic procedures, like wrist and ankle fracture fixations.
affiliations: James Paget University Hospital , Great Yarmouth , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.551.title: 478 Improving the Prescription of Key Medications for Inpatients Admitted to the Royal Cornwall Hospital with an Acute Sore Throat: A Quality-Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.551.abstract: Abstract Introduction The regular administration of intravenous antibiotics, analgesia, steroids, and adequate venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis is important when managing patients with an acute sore throat. Therefore, a quality-improvement project, aiming to improve the prescription of these medications within the Royal Cornwall Hospital (RCHT) Ear Nose and Throat (ENT) department, was undertaken to enhance patient recovery and reduce length of stay (LOS). Method Electronic drug charts of adult patients admitted under ENT with an acute sore throat from March to May 2023 were consulted. Information on whether patients had been prescribed regular analgesia, antibiotics, steroids (if indicated), adequate VTE prophylaxis and their LOS was sought. Results A total of 58 patients were included. The majority (59%) were male, and the mean age was 29. The most common diagnoses were Tonsillitis (43%), followed by Quinsy (30%) and Supraglottitis (10%). The mean LOS was 1.2 days. Regular analgesia was prescribed for 52% of patients on admission, and 78% during their inpatient stay. Regular antibiotics were prescribed for 73% of patients on admission, and all patients during their inpatient stay. Regular steroids were only prescribed to 42% of patients that needed them, and 69% of patients were prescribed VTE prophylaxis. Conclusions These findings indicate a need to improve the prescription of regular analgesia, antibiotics on admission, VTE prophylaxis and steroids if indicated. An Acute ENT Sore Throat electronic prescribing protocol has subsequently been developed and disseminated amongst RCHT junior doctors. A second cycle of data-collection will be undertaken to examine the subsequent effects on patient care and LOS.
affiliations: Royal Cornwall Hospital , Truro , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.555.title: 535 Improving the Quality of Consent Forms and Operation Notes for Laparoscopic Appendectomies Using the Best Practice Standards Outlined in Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.555.abstract: Abstract Aim This study aimed to enhance compliance with the Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) best practice initiative to standardise documentation of consent process and operation notes for laparoscopic appendicectomies. Method The documentation of laparoscopic appendicectomy was reviewed to assess compliance with GIRFT's 32 standards (n=15). The initial overall compliance rate was found to be 42%. Haemostasis and estimated blood loss was not documented (n=0). In response, templates were developed based on GIRFT standards, incorporating pre-filled consent form stickers and a digital operation note for electronic upload to patient records. The templates aimed to enhance accessibility and security of patient information by reducing reliance on handwritten notes. Results Following the intervention, the overall compliance rate increased to 63% (n=15). Notably, when the GIRFT template was utilised, compliance increased to 98% and haemostasis and EBL was documented in 100% of cases (n=5). However, the incorporation of pre-filled consent form stickers showed limited impact, with only 2 out of 15 cases utilizing them. Despite this, discussions regarding blood transfusion increased from 27% to 36% (n=15). Conclusions The implementation of standardised templates significantly improved compliance with GIRFT best practice standards for laparoscopic appendicectomies, particularly when utilizing the provided template. Challenges remain regarding the adoption of pre-filled consent form stickers. Future directions will explore the development of a patient information leaflet to enhance risk communication and promote the consistent use of template-based documentation. The study highlights the importance of tailored interventions to address specific components of GIRFT standards for optimal impact on patient care and outcomes.
affiliations: Walsall Manor Hospital , Walsall , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.557.title: 543 Improving Outcomes in Patients with Fragility Femur Fractures: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.557.abstract: Abstract Aim To improve compliance with measurable variables of the Best Practice Tariff (BPT) for fragility femur fractures. These include Abbreviated Mental Test Score (AMTS), 4AT delirium screen, Malnutrition Screening Tool (MUST) and Falls Assessment. Method Utilising the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) methodology, a quality improvement project was designed in a UK district general hospital to enhance compliance with four BPT measurable variables. Retrospective baseline data collection commenced in November 2022. The first PDSA cycle, in April 2023, resulted in the introduction of daily fractured femur reports, identifying patients admitted with a fragility femur fracture and tracking completion of the BPT parameters. The second PDSA cycle, in August 2023, involved teaching sessions at the junior doctor induction and the creation of a fragility femur fracture handbook for junior doctors facilitating accurate completion of BPT parameters on the patient electronic records. Prospective identification of post-intervention patients allowed for comparison of pre-intervention and post-intervention compliance. Results From November 2022 to October 2023, 331 patients over 60 were admitted with a fragility femur fracture. Following the PDSA cycles, completion rates for AMTS and 4AT assessments rose from 54.5% to 100% and 16.6% to 97.8%, respectively. MUST assessment completion improved from 82.7% to 100%, while falls assessment consistently exceeded 95%. Conclusions The project demonstrated the need to enhance best practices in fragility femur fracture care. Targeted junior doctor education and addressing assessment completion gaps significantly improved BPT compliance, leading to overall elevated care standards. Moreover, meeting BPT criteria contributed to increased revenue, allowing the trust to receive up to £100,000 annually.
affiliations: Royal Free Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.566.title: 673 Is There a Need for Patient Education and Empowerment Through Information Leaflets? – a Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.566.abstract: Abstract Aim Patient information leaflets, which are supplied by NHS trusts, represent an underutilized resource within our surgical department. Despite patients expressing a keen interest in accessing these informational materials, there is currently no automatic provision. This study seeks to measure the existing usage and knowledge levels concerning these leaflets among healthcare workers, while also evaluating patients' attitudes towards receiving them. Method Employing the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle methodology, we executed a Quality Improvement Project through the administration of questionnaires. In the initial PDSA cycle (PDSA-1), we evaluated clinicians' awareness of the accessibility and current utilization of information leaflets. Subsequently, in the second PDSA cycle (PDSA-2), our focus shifted to comprehending the patient's perspective and attitude towards these informational materials. Results In PDSA-1, involving doctors in the general surgical department, 54.2% were aware of trust information leaflets, with only 8.2% routinely providing them to patients. A concerning 87.5% didn't know how to access these leaflets. PDSA-2 revealed that 80% of inpatients didn't receive leaflets, while 73.33% desired them. Of those, 83.3% (23.3% extremely important, 40% very important, 20% somewhat important) believed leaflets were crucial for informed treatment decisions. Conclusions The study underscores the underutilization of NHS trust-supplied patient information leaflets in our surgical department. Clinician awareness and patient accessibility gaps were evident in PDSA-1 and PDSA-2. The disconnect between patient interest and leaflet provision highlights an opportunity for improvement. We recommend implementing an automatic provision of information leaflets and enhancing clinician awareness to bridge the gap, fostering better patient engagement and informed decision-making in our department.
affiliations: Department of General Surgery, QEQM Hospital, East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust , Margate , United Kingdom
Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother Hospital , Margate , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.563.title: 650 Standardised Management of Ureteric Colic: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.563.abstract: Abstract Aim Ureteric colic is a condition that contributes a significant amount to the workload of both emergency and urological services. The standards of its management are outlined by the British Association of Urological Surgeons (BAUS). We therefore endeavoured to evaluate the effectiveness of our treatment centre in achieving these standards with the aim to develops a new diagnostic pathway to improve the efficiency of managing ureteric colic. Method A pre-post intervention study design was used. The first cycle evaluated all ureteric colic cases referred to our department between September-October 2022. Data was extracted using local clinical and radiological software in line with local clinical governance guidelines. We subsequently developed a treatment pathway in conjunction with our emergency department to guide both diagnosis and initial management of acute presentations. The second cycle was performed during September 2023 to assess the efficacy of our pathway. Results Of the 37 new acute ureteric colic referrals reviewed during our second cycle, (Mean age: 48 years, Male: Female 2.4:1), 100% received their CT scan within the target window of 14 hours (Mean time: 02:12). 80% had correct Xray imaging performed which demonstrated a relative increase of 30% from the previous cycle (80% vs 50%). Furthermore 75% of patients had non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) prescribed and 70% had the correct blood tests done (Calcium and Urate). Conclusions Our pathway has demonstrated a significant improvement in the efficiency and accuracy of our department’s management of acute ureteric colic.
affiliations: University Hospital of Wales , Cardiff , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.583.title: 938 Prospective Interviews to Comprehend Patient Perspectives on the Digitisation of Ophthalmology Clinics: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.583.abstract: Abstract Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized medicine, enhancing efficiency and patient care. Moorfields, in collaboration with Google Health and DeepMind, employs AI algorithms to swiftly and accurately diagnose retinal diseases from scans and photographs. This improves treatment timelines and optimizes NHS resource allocation. While widespread AI integration is a few years away, it's crucial to gauge patient awareness, trust, and acceptance. This quality improvement project aims to assess patients' understanding of AI and their attitudes towards it. Method We surveyed 30 patients at Moorfields Eye Hospital's Medical Retina clinic between December 2022 and January 2023. The questionnaire included ten questions covering demographics, prior AI knowledge, trust in future AI implementation, and factors enhancing confidence and patient experience. Results In the cohort, 83.7% were aged 50-79, 60% female, and 40% male. White ethnicity dominated (50%), followed by Black or Black British (20%) and Asian or Asian British (16.7%). While 53.3% felt not confident about AI understanding, 26.7% were very likely to trust AI in treatment. Income correlated significantly with trust (p = 0.015; r = 0.605), showing lower trust in AI among those from deprived backgrounds. Over 80% preferred pre-appointment AI explanations through leaflets/videos for an improved patient experience. Conclusions Patients generally lack confidence in understanding AI, yet they express trust in its use in their treatment. Educating patients about AI is crucial for building trust, and this can be achieved through explanatory leaflets and videos.
affiliations: Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, London, United Kingdom. Chelsea and Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.578.title: 824 Assessing the Quality of Surgical Operation Notes in the General Surgery Department at a District General Hospital (QI Project)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.578.abstract: Abstract Aim assessing the current adherence to Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) guidance on the standards of documenting operation notes. There are 18 elements that must be present on operation notes including date and time of operation, name of surgeon and anaesthetist, type of anaesthesia, findings of operation, potential complications, closure technique, information on implants and signature of the surgeon. Method The present audit was a retrospective study of patients' notes to review their operation notes. 93 operation notes that were recorded August-September 2022 were reviewed in the first cycle. The second cycle reviewed 46 operation notes in May 2023. Results The outcome of the audit showed satisfactory adherence to majority of the RCS recommendations. Time of the operation was only recorded in 9% of operation notes in the first cycle which improved to 76% in the second cycle. Only 46% of operation notes in the first cycle were signed by a surgeon which improved to 67% in the second cycle. Conclusions Areas that mainly required improvement were identified to be recording time of the operation and signature of the surgeon in the first cycle. The result of the first cycle of audit was communicated to surgeons. The electronic operation note templates were also updated. The second cycle showed a significant improvement in the quality of operation note documentation in May 2023. A continuous cycle of audit should be implemented to ensure the documentation standards are maintained.
affiliations: Kettering General Hospital , Kettering , United Kingdom
College of Life Sciences, University of Leicester , Leicester , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.594.title: 1185 Improving the Time Between TURP and TWOC: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.594.abstract: Abstract Aim To achieve time between TURP to TWOC of four days or less. Background Most trans-urethral resection of prostate (TURP) operations is now done as day case procedures. Catheterisation is standard post TURP, to avoid clot retention and allow bladder irrigation if required. Currently, as patients are being discharged the same day, they are discharged with their catheter in situ. The catheter can be in-situ for longer than necessary, due to long waiting lists of the TWOC clinic. Method I performed a quality improvement project with the aim to achieve mean time between TURP and TWOC of four days or less. I reviewed the records 100 patients who underwent TURP between 21/07/2022 and 2/11/2022 in a district general hospital. For each patient, I calculated the time between TURP and TWOC. Results The average elapsed time was 9.49 days. The method of organising a TWOC post TURP is to email the urology nurses on the day of the TURP, stating that the patient requires a TWOC. My intervention was to therefore ask the bookings team that when they book in a TURP procedure, they also email the urology nurses to tell them in advance of the patients’ TURP date, that this patient will need a TWOC. Post intervention data was collected: the medical notes of 45 patients post intervention were reviewed. Conclusions The average time between TURP and TWOC had decreased to 6.61 days. This is an improvement but has not met the aim of less than or equal to 4 days.
affiliations: Bristol Royal Infirmary , Bristol , United Kingdom
Cheltenham General Hospital , Cheltenham , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.591.title: 1102 Maximising Safety on Surgical Ward Rounds with a Concise Ward-Round Template: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.591.abstract: Abstract Aim Concerns raised at clinical governance meetings highlighted incomplete ward round documentation and near miss events in prescribing. Checklists have demonstrated improved patient safety and ensure standards of care are maintained. We evaluated documentation and prescribing accuracy in a baseline audit and sought to improve these with the implementation of a concise ward-round template. Method We identified essential patient safety orientated criteria for ward round documentation from trust and departmental guidelines. Compliance with criteria was assessed by audit before and after the introduction of a standardised ward-round template. A root cause analysis was performed to identify reasons for errors between cycles and to optimise the design of the ward-round template. A poster promoting the template was circulated to junior doctors and the results presented in clinical governance. Each cycle included fifty consecutive patients. Results The baseline audit identified no ward-round documentation in 8% of inpatient days. Prescribing errors with near misses were identified in two cases. Poor documentation and communication were the most significant contributing factors in root cause analysis. After implementation of a ward-round template all inpatient days had a ward round entry, 96% using the template. Documentation of essential criteria improved from 32% to 93% (p<0.05) and there were no prescribing errors. Compliance with VTE guidelines improved from 70% to 98% (p<0.05). Conclusions This quality improvement project implementing a ward-round template improved documentation of essential patient safety orientated criteria and compliance with trust guidelines. Adherence to the ward round template was high several months after implementation, suggesting that ongoing use is viable.
affiliations: Oxford University Hospitals , Oxford , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.592.title: 1128 A Quality Improvement Project on the Understanding of Patients Undergoing Urological Procedures
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.592.abstract: Abstract Aim In this Quality Improvement project, we aimed to enhance patient understanding of urological procedures. Our approach involved designing a BAUS QR code poster and integrating paperless leaflets into consultations, with the future goal of sustainability. Method Initial data collection from 30 patients, through a questionnaire during urology consultations, guided the project. The introduction of QR code posters linked to BAUS leaflets was assessed through a re-audit involving 25 patients. Results Results showed that all 55 participants used smartphones, with 71% utilizing them for medical searches. While 56% were initially familiar with QR codes, patient satisfaction remained consistently high before and after the QR code poster implementation. Among pre-operative patients, 85% received patient information leaflets initially, increasing to 100% patients receiving patient information leaflet post QR code poster implementation. Post-operative patients receiving patient information leaflets was only 40% but incremented to 72% after the QR code poster implementation. Conclusions The project demonstrated that QR codes, complementing verbal consultations and paper leaflets, effectively provided information on urological procedures and lifestyle advice. Importantly, this innovation supports the transition to a paperless approach, contributing to long-term sustainability.
affiliations: Northampton General Hospital , Northampton , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.599.title: 859 RoboticFoundations: A Quality Improvement Programme Developing Robotic Surgical Skills in Foundation Doctors
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.599.abstract: Abstract Aim Although many surgical specialties have adopted robotic surgical techniques as standard, basic surgical skills training amongst early-career doctors neglects this paradigm shift. Our tertiary centre has pioneered a longitudinal quality improvement programme focused on integrating Foundation Doctors into robotic surgical teams, such that they are exposed to these skills early rather than during their registrar years. This approach is particularly relevant in preparing Foundation Doctors for a future that is increasingly reliant on robotic surgery, thus addressing immediate and long-term demands in surgical education, as well as leading the extended surgical workforce in this domain. Method The programme commenced with an Intuitive platform-based course, which introduced newcomers to being a robotic-bedside assistant. Foundation Doctors progressed from supervised sessions to independent simple tasks, under the guidance of both registrars and consultants. This programme is currently in its data collection phase, focusing on both quantitative and qualitative aspects, such as skill progression, number of procedures performed, and feedback from participants of all stages. Results We identified three primary benefits: Foundation Doctors gain hands-on, future-oriented experience, and feel more empowered; senior registrars accrue more console time; and consultants engage in meaningful mentorship — shaping future surgeons of every stage. Preliminary results indicate increased procedural involvement and more motivated trainees. Conclusions This novel and structured educational programme offers a beginner-friendly approach to training in robotic surgery, addressing key gaps in the current NHS climate. This model offers a viable and scalable solution for other institutions to further surgical training, aligning with the evolving demands of a robotic future.
affiliations: Royal Surrey Hospital NHS Foundation Trust , Guildford , United Kingdom
University College London , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.607.title: 826 Does Prehabilitation Improve Quality of Life After Gastrointestinal Cancer Resection?
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.607.abstract: Abstract Aim This study aims to evaluate the effects of prehabilitation on the quality of life (QoL) of patients undergoing gastrointestinal cancer resection, addressing the existing gap in knowledge regarding this specific population. Method A systematic search of relevant terms was independently conducted by two authors across multiple databases. Selection criteria were applied rigorously, with conflicts resolved through consultation with senior researchers. From the initial pool of 33 articles, 6 studies were chosen for inclusion. Data extraction and analysis were performed to assess the significance of prehabilitation interventions on post-resection QoL. Result The selected 6 studies, despite displaying noticeable heterogeneity in methodologies and outcomes, consistently indicated a positive impact of prehabilitation on the role functioning aspect of QoL, as measured by the C30 QoL survey. The studies collectively involved a substantial number of patients. Conclusions The evidence from the reviewed studies suggests a favourable influence of prehabilitation on the post-resection QoL of gastrointestinal cancer patients, particularly in the domain of role functioning. However, limitations such as heterogeneity in Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs) and a lack of long-term follow-up data, should be acknowledged. To provide more definitive conclusions, future RCTs should employ standardised QoL questionnaires like the C30 QoL and extend follow-up periods. This would enhance our understanding of the role of prehabilitation in improving patient outcomes following gastrointestinal cancer resection.
affiliations: Luton and Dunstable University Hospital , Luton , United Kingdom
Lincolnshire Hospitals NHS Trust , Boston , United Kingdom
Mid Essex University Hospitals , Broomfield , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.630.title: 421 Surgical Bedside Teaching at St Helier Hospital – a Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.630.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the impact of bedside sessions on medical students’ confidence in clinical assessment. It aims to assess strengths and weaknesses and guide further interventions. Method It employed a mixed-methods approach using both quantitative and qualitative measures in anonymised surveys. The intervention that was introduced was a ‘learning objective ticket’, whereby learning objectives were distributed and discussed prior to the session. Results There were 22 responses in the first cycle of the evaluation. Quantitative data revealed that the mean confidence in history taking was 3.55(+/- 0.59) before the session, and 4.32(+/-0.56) after the session (P<0.001).There was also a significantly significant difference in mean confidence levels in examination skills (p<0.001) with confidence going from 3.14(+/-0.56), to 4.45(+/-0.51). Qualitative data highlighted areas of improvement such as clearer learning objectives, greater alignment with assessments and better adherence to time constraints. There were 18 responses to the survey in the second cycle of this evaluation. Quantitative results showed that 88% of students ‘strongly agreed’ that the learning objectives were clear, 88% of students ’strongly agreed’ learning objectives were relevant, and 72.2% ‘strongly agreed’ that they had met their learning objectives. 12 out of 18 responders (66.7%) ‘strongly agreed’ that the timings of the session were adhered to. Conclusions Overall bedside teaching sessions are a valuable tool in undergraduate surgical education. Their impact can be further advanced by linking with learning objective as per constructivist alignment theory. Applying closer alignment with formal assessment could further improve these sessions.
affiliations: Epsom and St Helier Trust , London , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.659.title: 1023 Implementation of NHS Net Zero: An Analysis of Clinician Engagement and Quality Improvement
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.659.abstract: Abstract Aim Since the NHS Net zero report in 2020, UK hospital trusts have been working to achieve net zero carbon emissions by 2040. Henceforth, sustainability leads and working groups have been appointed to formulate and implement “Green Plans”. Clinician involvement and quality improvement (QI) are crucial to achieving net zero emissions. 133 Hospital Trusts in England were surveyed, to establish the extent to which sustainability has been embedded into clinical governance and quality improvement. Method 130 NHS Trusts in England were contacted during two time periods between 2021 and 2023 using Freedom of Information (FOI) requests. Each trust received a standardised sustainability questionnaire involving induction programmes, clinical governance, audits, QI and research projects. Trusts were required to respond within 20 working days upon receiving an FOI request. Follow-up emails were sent to trusts which did not respond within the timeframe. Requests for further clarification were answered. Data collection and extraction were undertaken using an Excel spreadsheet. Results In 2023 sustainability was identified as the theme of 38.8% of audits, QI, or research projects. Most trusts had a sustainability working group (70.7%), the majority of trusts had 0-5 clinicians in their sustainability working group (44.4%). 73.2% of respondents had a sustainability lead, 22.4% included sustainability in clinical governance meetings, and 18.1% included sustainability in junior doctor inductions. Conclusions Clinicians remain poorly engaged in matters relating to healthcare sustainability and carbon impact. This may represent a glaring omission in Trusts’ Net Zero plans and a missed opportunity to maximise progress.
affiliations: Department of Intensive Care, Charing Cross Hospital , London , United Kingdom
GKT School of Medical Education, King's College London , London , United Kingdom
Department of General Surgery, Aneurin Bevan University Health Board , Newport , United Kingdom
Department Of Plastic Surgery, East and North Hertfordshire NHS Foundation Trust , Stevenage , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.665.title: 210 Assessing the Quality of Guidelines for the Management of Gastro-Intestinal Stromal Tumour
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.665.abstract: Abstract Introduction Gastro Intestinal Stromal Tumours (GISTs) are tumours of the gastro-intestinal tract that arise from connective tissue and they have potential for malignancy. A number of guidelines exist in their management. The aim of this study is to assess the quality of these guidelines. Method A search of the literature was undertaken for appropriate guidelines pertaining to the diagnosis and management of GISTs. The AGREE II checklist was used to assess the current GIST guidelines. Results A total of nine guidelines were included in this study. The overall median score across all guidelines was 68% (lowest; 50%, highest 89%). Guidelines tended to score highly in Domain IV (Clarity of Presentation, median score 76%) as well as Domain VI (Editorial Independence, 67%) and Domain I (Scope and Purpose, 61%). However, lower scores were noted in the Domain V (Applicability, 39%), Domain III (Rigor of Development, 52%) and Domain II (Stakeholder Involvement, 56%). None of the guidelines scored a unanimous ‘Yes’ vote for clinical usage, and all needed some level of modifying. Conclusions Whilst some of the current guidelines for the management of GISTs is of a high quality, there is a need for improvement with regards to the quality of the methodology used to formulate the guidelines and how they can be implemented in daily clinical use.
affiliations: Luton and Dunstable University Hospital NHS Trust , Luton , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.381.title: 773 Quality of Life in Patients with Colostomy: A Comparative Analysis of Surgical Settings and Procedure Types
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.381.abstract: Abstract Aim Quality of Life (QoL) is a crucial metric for evaluating the success of clinical interventions. This study aims to assess and compare the QoL of patients with a stoma based on surgical settings, types of procedures undergone, and the amount of support received before discharge. Method The methodology involved the identification of patients and the administration of a structured QoL questionnaire (ASCN UK). The sample population included individuals who underwent five different surgeries which were Hartman’s, sigmoid colectomy, anterior resection, low anterior resection, and abdominal perineal excision of the rectum in the past three years, encompassing both elective and emergency settings. Results Results revealed the mean QoL score for elective procedures was notably higher at 78.6%, compared to 62.6% for emergency settings. Among elective surgeries, sigmoid colectomy demonstrated the highest mean QoL score (90.4%), while Hartman’s procedure showed the lowest (72.4%). In emergency settings, Hartman’s procedure had the highest mean QoL score (75%), contrasting with anterior resection's lowest score (46%). The study emphasized the multifactorial nature of QoL, highlighting the positive impact of pre-surgery information and support. Gender and age were significant contributors, with males and older individuals exhibiting higher QoL scores. Conclusions In conclusion, QoL in patients undergoing elective settings was significantly higher than in emergency settings. This trend was consistent across different procedures, as elective settings consistently yielded higher mean QoL scores compared to their emergency counterparts where applicable. This study highlights the pivotal role of support in enhancing QoL for colostomy patients, providing valuable insights for healthcare decision-making and management planning.
affiliations: Diana, Princess of Wales Hospital , Grimsby , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.388.title: 19 An Evaluation of the Quality and Readability of Online Information Regarding Foreign Bodies of the Ear, Nose and Throat
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.388.abstract: Abstract Aim Foreign body (FB) inhalation, ingestion and insertion account for 11% of ENT emergency hospital admissions. Children are disproportionately affected, and urgent intervention may be needed to maintain open airways. High-quality, readable online information could help reduce poor outcomes from foreign bodies. The aim is to determine the quality and readability of online health information relating to FB. Method Google was used to conduct searches using 6 search phrases. For each search phrase, the first 30 results were captured for inclusion in the study. Eligibility criteria were applied to select only health information. The EQIP tool was used to assess information quality. Readability was assessed using the Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES) and the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Results Of the information websites included (n=73), most (63%) were from the USA. The median EQIP score was 21 (IQR18-25, max29), suggesting moderate information quality. Precautionary measures were not mentioned on 40% of websites and 30% did not identify disc batteries as a risky FB. Red flags for urgent care were identified on 95% of websites, 89% advised patients to seek medical attention and only 38.4% of websites advised patients on safe foreign body removal. Readability scores (FRES:12.4 years; FKGL:6.2) showed most websites (56%) were below the recommended 6th-grade level. Conclusions The EQIP score suggests that information quality should be improved to provide patients and parents with clear information to help identify high-risk foreign bodies such as disc batteries and magnets, while providing guidance for removal of low-risk foreign bodies.
affiliations: New Cross Hospital , Wolverhampton , United Kingdom
Royal Surrey County Hospital , Guildford , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.391.title: 188 Assessing the Quality and Readability of Online Patient Information: ENT UK Patient E-Leaflets Versus ChatGPT Responses
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae163.391.abstract: Abstract Introduction The evolution of artificial intelligence has introduced new ways to disseminate health information, including natural language processing models like ChatGPT. However, the quality and readability of such digitally generated information remains understudied. This study is the first to compare the quality and readability of digitally generated health information against leaflets produced by professionals. Method Patient information leaflets for five ENT UK leaflets, and their corresponding ChatGPT responses, were evaluated using the Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP) tool and readability tools including the Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES) and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Statistical analysis was performed to identify differences between leaflets, assessors, and sources of information. Results ENT UK leaflets were of moderate quality, scoring a median EQIP of 23. Statistically significant differences in overall EQIP score were identified between ENT UK leaflets but ChatGPT responses were of uniform quality. Non-specialist doctors rated the highest EQIP scores while medical students scored the lowest. The mean readability of ENT UK leaflets was higher than ChatGPT responses. The overall EQIP scores negatively correlated with readability metrics of ChatGPT responses. In short, the information quality of ENT UK leaflets was moderate and varied between topics. Equivalent ChatGPT information provided comparable content quality but with reduced readability. Conclusions ChatGPT patient information leaflets had comparable content, but were less readable, and required a higher reading age than ENT UK leaflets. With the increasing use of online health resources, this study underscores the need for a balanced approach that optimises both the quality and readability of patient education material.
affiliations: Royal Stoke Hospital , Stoke , United Kingdom

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.155.title: WP4.6 - Reducing Unnecessary Transfusion of Blood Products – A Quality Improvement Project in a General Surgical Department in a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.155.abstract: Abstract Aims To audit adherence of transfusion of blood products against NICE guideline thresholds. To reduce unnecessary blood transfusions following departmental teaching sessions and installation of posters on surgical wards. Methods We retrospectively audited all patients receiving packed red cells transfusions consecutively across two consecutive four-month periods in a general surgery department. Departmental teaching sessions were held after the first audit cycle, supplemented by installation of posters including NICE guideline thresholds on surgical wards. The medical notes for each patient were assessed for pre-transfusion haemoglobin, indication for transfusion, and whether each transfusion was prescribed according to NICE guidelines. Results A total of 112 units of packed red blood cells in 42 patients and 133 units in 43 patients were transfused, respectively, before and after intervention. 45 units (40.2%) were prescribed according to NICE guidelines on first audit, improving to 67 units (50.4%) following intervention. 23 units of blood (20.5% of total) were transfused back-to-back inappropriately on first audit, reducing to 6 units (4.51% of total) after intervention. There were 2 self-limiting transfusion-related reactions (1.79%) on first audit, both in patients transfused above guidance thresholds, and no reactions following intervention. At a raw cost of approximately £135 per unit of donated blood, savings of £1830 were made over a four-month period (£5493pa), not including nursing and administration costs Conclusions Through simple local interventions and stricter adherence to transfusion thresholds, we reduced inappropriate above-threshold blood product transfusions in our hospital. This corresponded to a reduction in unnecessary blood-transfusion reactions and significant hospital savings.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.352.title: FP2.6 - Opportunities for Improvement in Venous Thromboprophylaxis (VTE) of High-Risk Patients Hospitalized for Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) Related Bowel Resection
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.352.abstract: Abstract Background IBD had a relative risk of 2.2 for VTE compared to the normal population. In May 2020, an international consensus created a statement on VTE prevention in IBD patients. 28days of extended thromboprophylaxis was recommended after discharge only in high risk patients. We aimed to identify high-risk patients for VTE post-IBD-related bowel resection. Methods Retrospective review of 131 patients over 5 years of surgical admissions for IBD-related resection at DGH. Examined factors included patients’ demographics, risk factors for VTE, disease history, and compliance with extended thromboprophylaxis. SPSS22 and Chi-square test were used for analysis. Results The median age was37years.76(58%) were female,74(56.5%) were white-British, Chron’s disease (CD) was98(74.8%), median disease duration was65 months, 101(77.1%) were done laparoscopically, 87(66.4%) were elective, and the median LOS was7days. 5 patients (3.7%) had VTE events. No postoperative stroke happened. DVT and PE were associated with failure of extended thromboprophylaxis prescription (P=0.004,0.000). All VTE events were seen in the 1st 10 days post-discharge. Occurrence of DVT was associated with white-British ethnicity(P=0.000), CD> ulcerative colitis (P=0.001), emergency > elective surgery (P=0.026), bowel anastomosis >stoma formation (P=0.029), ITU admission (P=0.000), Post-operative leak (0.0001), postoperative wound complications(P=0.000). Surgical approach, previous VTE event, and site of diseases weren’t associated with VTE occurrence (P=0.8,0.97,0.94). Conclusion IBD patients are vulnerable to VTE events more than the normal population. Bowel resection in this group of people needs attention for extended VTE prophylaxis, particularly in patients with CD, ITU admission, postoperative leak, and wound complications. These data outline opportunities for improvement, particularly in regard to the extended VTE prophylaxis for 28 days in the before-mentioned high-risk patients.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.501.title: EP474 - Recycling Theatre Waste: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.501.abstract: Abstract Background Theatre waste recycling is a crucial aspect of sustainable theatre production. Staff are usually under time pressure to empty and clean the theatre. This quality improvement project (QIP) aims to assess and reduce waste-related cost and carbon footprint by improving the proportion of waste recycled. Methods A retrospective review of the waste data and related cost for main theatres in Nottingham City Hospital (NCH) in 2022 was audited. A quick guide for waste disposal and recycling was made with the help of environmental department and was disseminated to the theatre staff electronically and physically. Data was reaudited for February to March 2023 post intervention. Results 86.6 tons of waste was generated from the main theatres in NCH in 2022 and 18.4% of the waste was recycled. Monthly proportion of waste recycled ranged from 9.3% (January 2022) to 35.0% (December 2022). The proportion of waste recycled for February and March was 36.7% and 26.4% respectively. Conclusion The findings of this QIP demonstrate the potential for significant improvements in theatre waste recycling rates, which can lead to reduced cost and carbon footprint. The use of a quick guide for waste disposal and recycling proved to be an effective intervention in improving recycling rates among theatre staff. This QIP highlights the importance of promoting sustainable practices in the theatre industry, and the necessity to sustain the effort to maintain the impact.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.399.title: FP6.13 - A Quality improvement project to reduce the number of readmissions to surgical assessment unit (SAU) in East Sussex hospitals (ESHT) following laparoscopic cholecystectomy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.399.abstract: Abstract Aim This is a QI project aiming to reduce the number of readmissions following laparoscopic cholecystectomy in ESHT from the current rate of 8.1% to the UK national average rate of 5%. This proposal followed an audit I conducted previously. About two-thirds of those readmissions occurred on day one following discharge, half of them due to pain, and almost 90% of them discharged without any intervention needing only reassurance, pain control, and analgesia. Methods Problem identified, SMART objectives followed, which means our intervention is: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time specified. Set up a process map showing areas where intervention is desirable/beneficial. These include time allowed for consent, preoperative assessment clinic, and postoperative discharge information. Then a driver diagram is drawn to indicate the primary and secondary drivers we need to tackle in order to achieve our goal. In summary, the proposed changes include allowing more time in clinic for patients to explain procedure and consent, junior doctors and nurses’ education, resources, and provision of leaflets and websites for information. Identification of stakeholders including managers, anaesthetists’ nurses, and patients, and dealing with them according to their influence and interest. PDSA (plan do study and act) cycle, TQM (total quality management), SPC (statistical process control), and lean methodology were implemented. Conclusion This project is aimed primarily at reducing readmissions numbers to SAU following laparoscopic cholecystectomy from 8.1% to 5% within a year. Areas in the process map were identified to achieve this objective, and since about 90% of patients were discharged without any intervention, we believe this should be achievable.
affiliations: East Sussex Healthcare NHS trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.220.title: WP8.10 - Ultrasound Cannulation Training Programme: Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.220.abstract: Abstract Aim Familiarisation with ultrasound skills can be very useful. This reduces stress for patients from multiple access attempts and preserves venous access. In our District General Hospital (DGH), no teaching on ultrasound-guided venous access was available. Our aim was to create a formal training programme on ultrasound-guided venous access for junior doctors. Methods Discussions were held with the medical education team at our DGH to understand how to organise a formal teaching programme. The interest of junior doctors was gathered through informal discussion. Those interested were then asked to complete course evaluation forms. Data was gathered on experience using ultrasound, confidence (out of 5) in performing ultrasound cannulation, and usefulness of the session (out of 5). Results Of the 49 participants, only 65% (n=32) filled in the course forms. Data was only analysed from these individuals. 47% (n=15) had previous experience using an ultrasound machine. Of the 32 participants analysed, 87.5% (n=28) felt the session was very useful and the other 12.5% (n=4) found the session to be useful. 100% (n=32) felt more confident performing ultrasound-guided access after the session. The average confidence score pre vs post-session was 1.59/5 vs 3.88/5, respectively. Conclusions This programme can improve confidence in procedural skills amongst junior doctors, whilst also minimising stress for patients of multiple access attempts. Though the sample obtained was small, it is clear to see increased confidence in participants, regardless of prior experience. The results obtained will be critical in continuing this programme in our hospital and hopefully roll out to a wider audience.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.091.title: SP8.5 - Enhancing the confidence of FY1 Doctors in managing General Surgical Patients through the introduction of an online handbook– A quality improvement project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.091.abstract: Abstract Background Emerging as a Foundation Year 1 (FY1) doctor from undergraduate training can be daunting. Furthermore, working in Colorectal Surgery can pose challenges: managing both elective and acute surgical patients with complex needs. We designed a General Surgery and Colorectal Surgery handbook to help FY1 doctors navigate training. This Quality Improvement Project aimed to assess the impact of and alleviate some of the uncertainty experienced by FY1 doctors during this transitional phase. Methods An electronic handbook was compiled with contributions from across the Multidisciplinary Team which was reviewed and approved for distribution within our Trust. An online questionnaire was distributed to assess pre-placement confidence in key domains on a 10-point Likert scale. This was sent to FY1 doctors who had previously completed a rotation within colorectal surgery without the handbook. The handbook was distributed to new cohort of FY1 doctors a week prior to the start of their rotation in Colorectal Surgery. An identical questionnaire was sent to the new cohort of FY1s within a month of their rotation and results were compared with previous cohort. Results In all surveyed areas, there was an improvement in confidence in the post-intervention group compared to that shown in the pre-intervention group. The average improvement in median score across all areas was 3.8 points. Conclusion This project demonstrated an overwhelmingly positive response to a formalised handbook by FY1 doctors in training. This intervention has helped FY1 doctors manage colorectal and general surgery patients with enhanced confidence thus paving way for safer patient care.
affiliations: West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.393.title: FP6.1 - Core Surgical Training in Northern Ireland: Regional Compliance with Quality Indicators
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.393.abstract: Abstract Aims Standards for training programmes are set by the GMC, with the Joint Committee for Surgical Training developing a curriculum and quality indicators (QIs) specific to Core Surgical Training. To ensure local training fits within these guidelines, placement quality is evaluated by NIMDTA, using specialty specific surveys sent to all Core Trainees in the region. Methods A survey, related to their current post, was sent to all Core Trainees in Northern Ireland. The responses were collated and cross-referenced against the 14 generic QIs for Core Surgery in order to assess compliance with published standards. Results Response rate from trainees was 70%. Compliance with the quality indicators was generally poor; 24% of trainees reported receiving the recommended 2 hours per week of formal teaching, 59% were able to complete a quality improvement project, 83% of trainees completed a learning agreement within the recommended 6 weeks from post commencement, 21% reported adequate exposure to simulation training and only 11% reported attending the expected one or more MDT meetings per week. Conclusions The level of adherence to the QIs for core surgery in Northern Ireland could be significantly improved. Despite some themes achieving a majority response in line with the QIs, overall alignment is poor. Subsequently we have developed key recommendations for focused improvement in the local Core Training programme in NI in an effort to better align our training with the JCST QI framework. A further survey will be conducted to assess the effect of these recommendations on compliance with JCST QIs.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.343.title: FP1.10 - Functional Outcomes of a Standard vs Modified Brooke Ileostomy – A Quality of Life Study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.343.abstract: Abstract Aim Previous studies have shown that IBD patients with a modified Brooke ileostomy, where there is retention of the ileocolic sphincter, may have improved stoma function by preserving a functional high pressure zone. This study aims to review functional outcomes through a patient-reported quality of life survey. Methods This cohort study was conducted across two sites, one performing Standard Brooke Ileostomy (SBI), and the other Modified Brooke Ileostomy (MBI), as standard practice. Patients with diagnosis of colitis were identified from a prospectively collected database. A stoma activity log and a validated stoma Quality of Life survey (PRATO) was sent, with 23 responses obtained (14 MBI, 9 SBI). Activity log included bag emptying, hours of interrupted sleep, and number of visits to stoma nurse. Results For QoL survey (minimum score 20, max 80), patients with MBI scored higher (mean 55.36), compared to SBI (mean 48.22), (p=0.037). Bag emptying over 24 hours was similar (MBI mean 5.71, SBI mean 5.86), as was bag emptying overnight (MBI mean 1 (range 0-3), SBO mean 1 (range 1-2). MBI patients reported longer mean uninterrupted sleep (7.07 hours vs 5.43 hours (p=0.005)). MBI patients required fewer stoma nurse visits in the first year (mean 5.3, median 5, range 0-13). SBI (mean 10.7, median 10, range 2-33). Conclusion A practice of Modified Brooke Ileostomy has comparable patient reported quality of life outcomes to a standard Brooke Ileostomy and performs better overall in terms of less interruption to sleep and lower disruption of daily life through hospital visits.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.059.title: SP5.6 - Sleep Quality and Barriers to Sleep on a Postoperative Surgical Ward
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.059.abstract: Abstract Aim Sleep is an essential part of recovery post-operatively and poor sleep quality has been linked to increased patient pain, increased rates of post-operative complications such as delirium and to longer hospital stays. It is widely accepted that adults need at least seven hours of sleep at night. Surgery can induce a degree of insomnia and thus we sought to identify quality of sleep on a postoperative general surgical ward and to identify common barriers to sleep and reasons patients experience interruptions to sleep. Methods Using patient questionnaires, we investigated quality of sleep and explored factors, both intrinsic and extrinsic, which influenced patients both falling asleep and being woken throughout the night. Results Average age of participants was 73yrs. Average length of sleep was only 5.4 hours. 89% patients reported having sleep interrupted throughout the night and on average patients were awoken 2.4 times throughout the night. Only 11% reported feeling refreshed in the morning after sleep. Noise and pain were the most common barriers identified to falling asleep affecting 73% of patients. The predominant reasons for being awoken from sleep were noise (94%), interruptions for observations/bloods (67%) and thirst (33%). Conclusions This study has identified a high prevalence of poor sleep quality in postoperative surgical patients. Common factors influencing this are noise, pain and interruptions by medical staff. Many of these can be addressed through simple interventions to promote better recovery of patients by recognising and supporting the need for high quality sleep.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.199.title: WP7.3 - FAMiSH: FAsting prior to eMergency general Surgery in Hospital – Quality improvement project protocol
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.199.abstract: Abstract This study was conducted to evaluate adherence to preoperative fasting guidelines at the RD&E hospital, focusing on safety and reducing prolonged fasting complications particularly in patients with extremes of age, diabetic or co-morbid. Data were gathered anonymously over 2 cycles for 4 weeks through patient records and questionnaire to access patient given instructions for fasting. All patients with planned procedures were included, excluding emergency operations (NCEPOD) 1 or 2a/2b classification. Issues such as inadequate communication, excessive fasting, insufficient monitoring, and medication mismanagement were addressed. Cycle one revealed 25% of patients fasted for more than 6 hours, 56.25% did not consume liquids for more than 12 hours, and 25% abstained from drinking for more than 8 hours preoperatively. It was noted that guidelines were not thoroughly adhered to. Some patients have missed their medications, as well as diabetic patients with prolonged hours of fasting. We have provided a session for junior doctors and nurses aiming education on ASA guidelines and encouraging individualised fasting plans for patients. Information leaflets were created to be distributed to patients planned for surgery. In the second cycle only 20% and 24% of patients didn’t follow fasting guidelines for solids and liquids respectively as compared to 68.75% of the patients receiving inappropriate instructions in 1st cycle, showing significant improvement in patient care. In our study at the RD&E we have noted an improvement in departmental focus on adherence to fasting guidelines, which focus on abstaining from solid foods up to 6 hours and drinks up to 2 hours prior to surgery, aiding patient safety and improvement of quality of care.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.061.title: SP5.8 - A survey of the actual incidence of Low Anterior Resection Syndrome in our patients and its effect on their quality of life
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.061.abstract: Abstract Aim Following rectal surgery, bowel function is often affected and leads to a constellations of symptoms called Low Anterior Resection syndrome (LARS). Whilst several risk factors have been identified from previous studies, the most important question is how these symptoms impact the quality of life (QOL) of our patients. The aim of our study was to gain an overview of LARS among our patients, identify risk factors, quantify how it affects their daily lives and recommend preventive and management options. Method We contacted all patients who had undergone anterior resections 01/10/2020-01/10/2023 via a telephone consultation carried out by a single doctor. Using the LARS questionnaire which has been internationally validated, we quantified the severity of LARS symptoms and effects on QOL in our patients. Results A total 36 patients were included in the study. We found 75% patients had no LARS, 25% had minor LARS; no patients had major LARS. 15 patients experienced tenesmus, 11 urgency, 11 accidental leakage of stool, 10 inability to control flatus and 8 frequency. Only 8.33% reported their symptoms affecting their QOL; in this group, accidental leakage of stool was the common symptom. We found no correlation between the incidence of LARS and post-operative time period. None of our LARS patients had had pre-op radiotherapy; only 10% patients who had post- op chemo developed LARS. Conclusion In our cohort of Anterior resection patients, most had no LARS; none had major LARS. Though some patients had some symptoms, QOL was affected in only 8.33%. Those who had symptoms were directed to our LARS clinic in Lower GI physiology for further management.
affiliations: Scunthorpe General Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.180.title: WP5.18 - Quality Improvement Project – Assessing current practice of percutaneous cholecystostomy tube (PCT) management in a DGH and proposal of local guidelines
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.180.abstract: Abstract Rationale The absence of evidence-based guidelines for Percutaneous Cholecystostomy Tube (PCT) management has led to a lack of standardization in its care across NHS Trusts. Existing literature provides varied recommendations. Davis et al.(1999) suggested allowing 7-10 days for tract maturation, although they did not describe how this was evaluated. Other authors recommended proposals based on their local practice. Aim To establish standardized care following PCT insertion at our DGH, focusing on improving efficiency and ensuring uniformity in performance. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted, reviewing the period between January 2021 to December 2022. 68 patients were identified to have PCT insertions. Results Findings revealed 24% (16/68) had no documented discharge plan. 57% (39/68) of patients had a planned Surgical Assessment Unit review within a wide timeframe (4-49 days). A tubogram was arranged for 47 of 68 patients (69%) meaning the rest had no fluoroscopic examination before PCT removal. This was performed on average at 4.8 weeks and (range 1-10 weeks). 31% (21/68) had no UGI clinic review. The mean PCT removal time was 9.4 weeks with some outliers ranging between 0.5 to upto 40.5 weeks. Conclusion While some patients had PCT in-situ for longer than necessary, in two cases PCTs were removed prematurely, though no complications were recorded. The observed practice variability prompted the introduction of a local pathway, with recommendations from UGI consultants. This initiative should help prevent delays in patient care, particularly considering that the rotating junior doctors usually will lack familiarity with the management of such cases.
affiliations: Royal Berkshire Hospital NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.106.title: SP9.8 - Assessing the quality of guidelines for the management of Gastro-Intestinal Stromal Tumour
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.106.abstract: Abstract Introduction Gastro Intestinal Stromal Tumours (GISTs) are tumours of the gastro-intestinal tract that arise from connective tissue and they have potential for malignancy. A number of guidelines exist in their management. The aim of this study is to assess the quality of these guidelines. Methods A search of the literature was undertaken for appropriate guidelines pertaining to the diagnosis and management of GISTs. The AGREE II checklist was used to assess the current GIST guidelines. Results A total of nine guidelines were included in this study. The overall median score across all guidelines was 68% (lowest; 50%, highest 89%). Guidelines tended to score highly in Domain IV (Clarity of Presentation, median score 76%) as well as Domain VI (Editorial Independence, 67%) and Domain I (Scope and Purpose, 61%). However, lower scores were noted in the Domain V (Applicability, 39%), Domain III (Rigor of Development, 52%) and Domain II (Stakeholder Involvement, 56%). None of the guidelines scored a unanimous ‘Yes’ vote for clinical usage, and all needed some level of modifying. Conclusion Whilst some of the current guidelines for the management of GISTs is of a high quality, there is a need for improvement with regards to the quality of the methodology used to formulate the guidelines and how they can be implemented in daily clinical use.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.522.title: EP588 - Review of the need for Immediate Nasogastric Tube Insertion in patients with Small Bowel Obstruction: Single Centre Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.522.abstract: Abstract Aim This QIP was conducted in a busy UK hospital. It aims to review, improve, and stress the importance of early insertion of an NG tube in patients who have clinically suspected or radiologically confirmed small bowel obstruction. Method Retrospective data collection involving 72 patients, in a period from Jan to April 2023 (50 patients) and from May to July 2023 (22 patients)Inclusion criteria: adult patients with SBO (clinically suspected or radiologically confirmed) and NGT insertion advised by the surgical teamExclusion criteria: paediatric patients, LBO, and patients not advised NGT in ED Results In the first cycle, we found that NG insertion is delayed 84% > 7 hrs. With associated morbidity of pneumonia, including aspiration in 20% of patients, ileus and sepsis in 8%, and re-admission and mortality in 6%, respectively. The following interventions were carried out. Broad communication with the ED team to highlight the importance of NG insertion for suspected patients. Provide NGT training for ED nursing staff The surgical team and admission nurses should inquire about NGT insertion before accepting patients' admission to surgical emergency wards. Circulating the QIPS recommendation Trust-wide as sharing learning point Post-intervention, we noticed a 50% delay in NGT insertion, which is a huge improvement compared to the 84% delay Conclusion Early insertion of NG for decompression in both pre and post-op periods is known to decrease associated complications, including bowel oedema, perforation, aspiration pneumonia, and post-ileus, leading to better outcomes and a significant decrease in hospital stay length.

The Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae228.title: Longitudinal health-related quality of life in people with thoracic aortic aneurysms
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae228.abstract: Abstract Background Surgical intervention for thoracic aortic aneurysms is high risk. Understanding changes in health-related quality of life before and after endovascular stent grafting and open surgical repair can aid treatment decision-making. Methods The Effective Treatments for Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (‘ETTAA’) study (ISRCTN04044627) was a longitudinal, observational study. Adults with new/existing arch or descending thoracic aortic aneurysms greater than or equal to 4 cm in diameter were followed from 2014 to 2022. Five domains of health-related quality of life (Mobility, Self-Care, Usual Activities, Pain/Discomfort, and Anxiety/Depression) were recorded using the EuroQoL, five dimensions, five levels (‘EQ-5D-5L’) questionnaire and analysed using a range of longitudinal mixed models. Results Of 886 thoracic aortic aneurysm participants, 824 completed at least 2 questionnaires. Patients had slightly worse health-related quality of life than age-matched norms. Without surgery, deterioration occurred over time in Mobility (0.072/year (95% c.i. 0.042 to 0.101), P < 0.001) and Self-Care (0.039/year (95% c.i. 0.018 to 0.061), P < 0.001) in both sexes and Pain/Discomfort in women (0.069/year (95% c.i. 0.020 to 0.118), P = 0.005). For 6 weeks after endovascular stent grafting, there was a significant impairment in Self-Care (0.214 (95% c.i. 0.112 to 0.316), P < 0.001) and (for women only) in Usual Activities (0.625 (95% c.i. 0.338 to 0.911), P < 0.001), which then returned to pre-endovascular stent grafting levels. Six weeks after open surgical repair, the impairment in health-related quality of life was greater (Mobility 0.492 (95% c.i. 0.314 to 0.669), Self-Care 0.474 (95% c.i. 0.364 to 0.583), Usual Activities 1.469 (95% c.i. 1.042 to 1.896), and Pain/Discomfort 0.561 (95% c.i. 0.363 to 0.760), all P < 0.001) and took longer to return to pre-open surgical repair levels, partly due to increased complications and longer hospitalization. Anxiety/Depression decreased after open surgical repair (−0.214 (95% c.i. −0.326 to −0.101), P < 0.001). Age, sex, frailty, smoking, New York Heart Association class, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease were significantly associated with health-related quality of life. Conclusion Without intervention, health-related quality of life declines as age increases. Changes in health-related quality of life should contribute to surgical treatment decision-making.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae223.title: Association of Upper Gastrointestinal Surgery of Great Britain and Ireland (AUGIS)/perioperative quality initiative (POQI) consensus statement on prehabilitation in oesophagogastric surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae223.abstract: Abstract Background Prehabilitation is safe, feasible and may improve a range of outcomes in patients with oesophago-gastric cancer (OGC). Recent studies have suggested the potential of prehabilitation to improve body composition, sarcopenia and physical fitness, reduce surgical complications and improve quality of life. Despite this, prehabilitation services are not offered throughout all OGC centres in the UK. Where prehabilitation is offered, delivery and definitions vary significantly, as do funding sources and access. Methods A professional association endorsed series of consensus meetings were conducted using a modified Delphi process developed by the Peri-Operative Quality Initiative (POQI) to identify and refine consensus statements relating to the development and delivery of prehabilitation services for OGC patients. Participants from a variety of disciplines were identified based on a track record of published studies in the field of prehabilitation and/or practice experience encompassing prehabilitation of OGC patients. Approval from the POQI board was obtained and independent supervision provided by POQI. Results A total of 20 statements were developed and agreed by 26 participants over a preliminary meeting and 2 semi-structured formal POQI meetings. Ten research themes were identified. In the case of one statement, consensus was not reached and the statement was recorded and developed into a research theme. A strong recommendation was made for the majority of the consensus statements (17 of 20). Discussion Consensus statements encompassing the interventions and outcomes of prehabilitation services in oesophago-gastric cancer surgery have been developed to inform the implementation of programmes.
