DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf092.081.title: Outcomes of Minimally Invasive Median Arcuate Ligament Release: Symptom Improvement and Quality of Life Assessment
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf092.081.abstract: Abstract Background Median arcuate ligament syndrome (MALS) is a rare and complex condition with both vascular and neurologic components. Surgical repair is the treatment of choice; however, the proximity of the surgical field to the aorta and celiac trunk presents significant challenges. Aims This study aims to evaluate symptom improvement and postoperative quality of life (QoL) in patients undergoing minimally-invasive median arcuate ligament release (MALR) at our institution. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on patients undergoing minimally invasive MALR between 2017 and 2021. Patient characteristics, postoperative morbidity, symptoms before and after surgery, and postoperative quality of life using the 2-Item Short-Form Health Survey were assessed. Results Thirty patients underwent laparoscopic MALR, with 80% (n=24) being female. The median age was 32 years (range: 18–63), and the median BMI was 20.3 kg/m² (range: 14.4–32.4). The predominant symptom at presentation was abdominal pain (29 of 30 patients). The median time from symptom onset to diagnosis was 12 months (range: 3–59 months). Laparoscopic MALR was performed without conversion, and no major postoperative morbidity was observed. Median follow-up was 24 months (range 6- 48 months). Symptom resolution or significant improvement was reported in 80% of patients (n=24). Postprandial symptoms showed a trend of reduction but were not statistically significant: nausea (50% to 33%), vomiting (17% to 7%), and diarrhea (30% to 13%). Bloating symptoms remained unchanged. Postoperative quality of life, assessed with the 2-Item Short-Form Health Survey, revealed generally positive outcomes across all domains (health change: 80(+/-18), pain:78(+/-20), emotional:82.7 (+/-24) and physical limitations:78(+/-32), and social functioning: 77(+/-24)). Conclusion Minimally invasive MALR is a safe procedure that results in symptom improvement in most patients. However, some gastrointestinal symptoms might persist at follow-up underscoring the importance of managing patient expectations and thoroughly excluding other gastrointestinal conditions.
affiliations: Department of Visceral Surgery and Medicine, Inselspital, Bern University Hospital , Bern

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf096.035.title: Quality of life after Pancreatic Surgery for Neuroendocrine Tumors of the Pancreas: Long-term outcomes of 100 patients evaluated with new EORTC questionnaires
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf096.035.abstract: Abstract Background Patients with Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors (PanNETs) often have a good prognosis with long overall survival. We evaluated Quality of Life (QoL) after surgery for PanNETs, using the new EORTC specific questionnaires. Methods PanNETs operated in our Unit (1990–2023) received three EORTC QoL questionnaires (QLQ-C30, and new P.NET15 and P.NET19). We evaluated: 1) QLQ-C30 outcomes; 2) mixed domains from QLQ-C30 and the new P.NET15/19 questionnaries; 3) domains from P.NET19 or P.NET15 only. Both functional and symptomatic scales were investigated in relationship with clinical variables. Gamma regression and multivariate analysis were used for statistic with R software. Results 100 subjects enrolled (median 133 mo. after surgery), showing a good global QoL (median 83.3/100). Older age was related with worse global QoL and physical functioning (p=0.007 and<0.001). Diabetes negatively influenced QoL (p<0.001), physical functioning (p=0.005) and fatigue (p=0.03). Who had parenchyma-sparing surgery showed less fatigue (p=0.047), while diagnosis of non-insulinoma PanNET was related to worse QoL (p=0.039). The presence of multiple comorbidities was negatively related with physical functioning (p=0.01), fatigue (p=0.001) and pain (p=0.021). Analysing only the new questionnaires, the most affected outcome was muscle-energy, depending on age (p=0.043), diabetes (p=0.014), type of surgery (p=0.019) and non-insulinoma diagnosis (p=0.007). Conclusion A good QoL evaluated with the new EORTC questionnaires, is reported in PanNET after surgery; older age, standard resective surgery, diabetes mellitus and those investigated with P.NET15 questionnaire (gastrinomas and non-functioning PanNETs) showed significative worsening of QoL outcomes.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf123.title: Long-term survival and quality of life in patients more than 10 years after pelvic exenteration
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf123.abstract: Abstract Background Pelvic exenteration is a curative treatment option for selected patients with advanced primary or recurrent pelvic cancer. This study aimed to evaluate survival and quality-of-life outcomes beyond 10 and up to 17 years following pelvic exenteration. Method This longitudinal study included patients who underwent pelvic exenteration between 2008 and 2014. Quality of life was assessed using Short-Form Survey (SF-36v2) and Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy—Colorectal Cancer (FACT-C) questionnaires at 10 different time points from baseline up to 17 years following pelvic exenteration. Survival data were obtained through registry linkage, with outcomes analysed using Kaplan–Meier methods. Results Of the 273 patients included (median age 61.0 years, 59.3% male), 91 (33%) survived beyond 10 years. Median overall survival was 4.8 years (95% c.i. = 3.6 to 6.0), with survival rates of 48.4%, 35.1%, and 31.5% at 5, 10, and 15 years respectively. In the 216/273 (79.1%) patients who consented to participate in quality-of-life surveys, 32 (15%) completed surveys beyond 10 years. FACT-C scores showed steady improvement over the first 18 months, maintaining thereafter. Mental Component Summary scores approached population norms after initial improvement, while Physical Component Summary scores stayed within the population norm and remained stable throughout the follow-up period. Conclusion In a specialized setting, pelvic exenteration shows promising long-term outcomes with one-third of patients surviving beyond 10 years. Quality-of-life measures demonstrate sustained improvement and are comparable to population norms in several domains, supporting its use as a curative treatment for selected patients with advanced and recurrent pelvic malignancies.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.489.title: 667 Assessment of the Quality of Acute Post-Operative Pain Management in Orthopaedic Department in Sudan 2022
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.489.abstract: Abstract Aim The study aimed to evaluate post-operative pain levels and the quality of care in orthopaedic surgery patients in Sudan. Method A cross-sectional hospital-based study was conducted at Ibrahim Malik Teaching Hospital and Sharg Alneel private Hospital from October 11th to November 23rd, 2022. Participants were interviewed on their first post-operative day using a pre-tested questionnaire. Pain levels were assessed using a numerical pain scale, and quality of care was evaluated with the SCQIPP scale. Data were analyzed using SPSS software version 26.0, with a P-value < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Results A total of 114 adult patients (mean age 43.9, 68.4% male) participated in the study. Most surgeries (53.5%) were performed under spinal anesthesia. 70.2% of participants received counseling before their surgeries. Despite this, 84.2% of patients believed pain was an inherent part of surgery, with 22.8% withholding their pain and 19.3% stating it should be tolerated. The mean highest pain intensity reported was 7.39 (SD=2.73), and the lowest was 2.84 (SD=2.68). NSAIDs, paracetamol, and opioids were the most commonly used analgesics. The overall quality of care was poor, scoring 47.65 out of 70 on the SCQIPP scale, with low scores in communication (3.34), trust (3.75), actions (3.00), and environment (3.33). Significant differences were observed between hospitals (P<0.001) and among patients who reported pain (P=0.024). Pain levels negatively correlated with both care quality (P=0.043) and communication scores (P=0.013). Conclusions Post-operative pain management remains inadequate in Sudan, highlighting the need for effective protocols and improved access to essential analgesics like opioids.
affiliations: Faculty of Medicine, University of Khartoum , Khartoum, Sudan, Khartoum ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.572.title: 985 Smartpage: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.572.abstract: Abstract At James Cook University Hospital, the Surgical Foundation Year 1 (FY1) doctor provides medical cover for four general surgery wards, including medical outliers. Task management is facilitated by the Hospital at Night's Smartpage system, which communicates tasks with urgency codes. This study aimed to review and assess the relevance of tasks assigned to Surgical FY1s during night shifts to improve quality of care and prevent patient delays. We conducted a retrospective analysis of Smartpage tasks sent to the Surgical FY1 over a 7-day period. We categorised the tasks into distinct themes and reviewed patient data to interpret their level of appropriateness. Analysis revealed a significant number of tasks were more appropriate for the day team to complete. We also identified a lack of categorisation with Smartpage tasks. Key areas for development were found with post-operative analgesia and IVT for NBM patients. Targeted teaching and informational interventions were implemented for relevant teams. A repeat analysis one-month post-intervention demonstrated a substantial reduction in inappropriate night shift tasks. This improvement highlights the effectiveness of focused interventions in enhancing task relevance and optimising the workflow of Surgical FY1 doctors during demanding night shifts whilst also maintaining a delivery of high-quality care.
affiliations: General Surgery James Cook University , Middlesbrough ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.222.title: 213 Quality of Primary Care Referrals to the Breast Clinic for Patients with Gynaecomastia
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.222.abstract: Abstract Aim Gynaecomastia, the benign proliferation of male breast tissue, is a common condition with a variety of etiologies. Appropriate primary care referrals are critical for timely and effective management. This audit evaluates the quality of referrals to the breast clinic for gynaecomastia, focusing on adherence to referral guidelines and the inclusion of clinical details. Method A two-cycle retrospective audit was conducted at West Middlesex University Hospital (WMUH) in 2024. In the first cycle, primary care referral letters for patients with gynaecomastia were reviewed over a 6-month period. Data were analyzed to assess the completeness of referral information, including clinical history, physical examination, potential contributing factors. Interventions included GP education on referral guidelines, the introduction of a structured referral template, and distribution of educational materials. A second audit cycle was conducted after 3 months to evaluate the impact of these interventions. Results A total of 120 referral letters were reviewed. Only 58% (n=69) included a thorough clinical history, while 43% (n=52) documented findings from a physical examination. Evaluation of potential contributing factors, such as medication history or hormonal disorders, was included in 36% (n=43) of referrals. Imaging or blood test results were provided in 28% (n=34) of cases. Overall adherence to referral guidelines was 45% (n=54). Following interventions, referral letters were reviewed and analysed in the second cycle. Conclusions This two-cycle audit highlights substantial improvements in the quality of primary care referrals for gynaecomastia following targeted interventions. Structured referral templates and GP education proved effective in enhancing adherence to guidelines and ensuring comprehensive clinical information.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.351.title: 540 Optimising Follow-Up Guidelines for Patients Who Underwent the Arterial Switch Operation for Transposition of the Great Arteries: A North-West Quality Improvement Initiative
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.351.abstract: Abstract Aim Transposition of the great arteries is a rare congenital-cardiac-malformation (∼1 in 5,000 births) characterised by ventriculoarterial-discordance and atrioventricular-concordance, resulting in isolated pulmonary and systemic circulations. The arterial switch operation (ASO) involves translocation of the aorta and pulmonary trunk to facilitate physiological circulation; with excellent early outcomes, we focus on optimising long-term results. Long-term follow-up reveals several complications, including pulmonary stenosis, neo-aortic dilatation/insufficiency, coronary artery occlusion, and arrhythmia, which warrant targeted investigations. Currently, our centre has no formal follow-up guidance, therefore we evaluated current practices, and propose recommendations for alignment with optimal care. Method We conducted a comprehensive literature review and integrated findings with current guidelines to create a standard of practice. Given the rarity of the condition, six patients who underwent ASO within the past 15 years were included. Clinical follow-ups were analysed to assess care components and timing against these proposed standards. Results Follow-up frequency, history taking, physical examination, and echocardiography aligned with the recommended standards. However, Holter-monitoring was performed in 0% of patients <5-years, 16% biennially for ages 1–9, and 12.75% for ages 10–18. Exercise-testing, cardiac-MRI, and coronary patency assessments were not utilised in the 1–9 and 10–18-year categories, although cardiac-MRI was appropriately used in patients aged 10–18. Conclusions Significant disparities were identified between current follow-up practices and evidence-based standards. However, the proposed recommendations have the potential to improve the consistency and quality of care. Further evaluation is necessary to assess the feasibility of implementing these changes and their impact on long-term outcomes.
affiliations: University of Manchester , Manchester ,
Royal Preston Hospital , Preston ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.031.title: 907 Quality of Life After Robotic Distal Pancreatectomy: A Systematic Scoping Review
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.031.abstract: Abstract Aim Pancreatectomy is associated with a risk of major complications, death, and reduced quality of life, particularly in the first six months after surgery. Laparoscopic surgery can negate some of the impact on quality of life, allowing for shorter hospital stays, earlier return of gastrointestinal function and normal functional activity. Robotic surgical approaches to distal pancreatectomy have become increasingly widespread, with reports of good clinical outcomes compared to laparoscopic or open surgery. However, the impact of robotic distal pancreatectomy (RDP) on quality of life remains unclear. This systematic scoping review aims to evaluate the existing literature on quality of life after RDP and compare this to laparoscopic or open surgery. Method PubMed, Medline, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases were searched through September 2024. Inclusion criteria were all studies reporting quality of life outcomes after RDP and published in English/French. Results Of 149 articles identified, four met the inclusion criteria (n=736 patients). All studies showed improved quality of life in robotic cohorts compared to laparoscopic or open cohorts. This was significant in two studies: one at 3 months and the other at 12 months post-operatively. Data on clinical outcomes suggest favourable outcomes for patients undergoing RDP. Conclusions This scoping review suggests robotic surgery may improve quality of life for patients undergoing distal pancreatectomy. Current evidence is limited due to the heterogeneity of published data. The findings of this report suggest further high-quality studies are needed to properly assess quality of life as a primary outcome after RDP when compared to laparoscopic and open surgery.
affiliations: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.025.title: 952 Reducing Length of Stay After Appendectomy for Acute Appendicitis: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.025.abstract: Abstract Introduction The Royal Wolverhampton Trust was an outlier in the length of stay (LOS) for emergency appendectomies, with only 4.1% of patients discharged within 2 days. This project aimed to reduce LOS to under 2 days by implementing a standardized care-pathway. Method Baseline data from June 2022-May 2023 revealed 142 cases of acute appendicitis (out of 169 total), with 32% of patients staying more than 2 days. The median LOS was 5 days, despite 92% being treated laparoscopically. Key factors contributing to prolonged stays included excessive imaging, prolonged intravenous (IV) antibiotic use, and surgical drains. A standardized care-pathway was developed with the primary goal of reducing LOS. Key interventions included reducing the use of CT scans, limiting the duration of IV antibiotics, and avoiding the use of surgical drains. This pathway was presented to stakeholders, implemented in clinical areas, and supported by the Surgical Same Day Emergency Care (SSDEC). Results Post-intervention data (January-March 2024) showed significant improvement, with 40% of patients discharged within 2 days (41% in January, 42% in February, 37% in March) compared to an average of 22% pre-intervention. Further analysis is currently ongoing. Conclusions By addressing key drivers of prolonged LOS, this project is successfully standardizing care, reducing unnecessary variation and improving patient outcomes. The new pathway, supported by SSDEC and virtual ward services, significantly increased early discharges. Continued refinement of the pathway is expected to further reduce LOS variability, benefiting the NHS by optimizing resource use and enhancing patient-care through faster recovery and reduced hospital-acquired risks.
affiliations: Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust , Wolverhampton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.560.title: 736 Diagnostic and Documentation Quality in First-Time TURBT Performed in North Devon District Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.560.abstract: Abstract Aim Audit our TURBT operation note and documentation quality practice against NICE guidelines for diagnosing bladder cancer (1.2.6 and 1.2.7 i.e tumour size and number, and mitomycin instillation) Assess the requirements in the documentation related to NICE recommendations. Implement the action plan to meet the NICE recommendations Re-audit after 6months Assess the quality improvement after-action planning Method Retrospective data collection of consecutive patients who underwent transurethral resection of bladder tumour for a new bladder tumour diagnosis from August 1st, 2022, to February 28th, 2023, with the help of a spreadsheet. Re-audit; Data collection from August 1st, 2023, to February 28th, 2024 (6 months after the action plan) compared to results before the action plan with the help of a spreadsheet. Results 78.20% of operation notes didn't include the instillation of mitomycin and its justification for not giving. 98.71% of operation notes mentioned tumour number and 88.46% of operation notes mentioned tumour size. After the implementation of action plans, the quality of documentation of operation notes is improved doubly. Conclusions Bladder cancer is the seventh most common cancer in the UK. Most bladder cancers (75 to 80%) are non-muscular invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). They are usually treated by telescopic removal of cancer (TURBT) followed by the instillation of chemotherapy into the bladder which is proven to decrease relative risks of occurrence by 39%. Our NDDH is one of the most remote acute hospitals in mainland England and will decrease the burden on NHS and the public with just exact documentation of operation notes.
affiliations: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust , Barnstaple ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.004.title: 42 Evaluation of Microvascular Free Flap Reconstruction for Large-Scale Perineal Defects Post-Pelvic Exenteration: A Long-Term Multicenter Study on Functional Outcomes, Infection Rates, and Quality of Life
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.004.abstract: Abstract Aim This study aims to evaluate the long-term outcomes and complications of microvascular free flap reconstruction for perineal defects following pelvic exenteration, with a focus on functional recovery, infection rates, and quality of life. Method The study included 120 patients who underwent pelvic exenteration with microvascular free flap reconstruction for perineal defects, followed for 24 months. Functional outcomes, infection rates, and quality of life were assessed at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months using standardized measures: Modified Braden Scale and FIM for functional recovery, surgical site surveillance for infections, and EQ-5D and WHOQOL-BREF for quality of life. Results At 24 months, 75% (90/120) of patients achieved full functional recovery, with a mean FIM score of 95 (range: 70-100). 25% (30/120) experienced partial functional recovery, with a mean score of 55 (range: 40-69). Postoperative complications included infection rates of 18% (22/120), with 15 cases of wound infection requiring surgical debridement. There was a 9% (11/120) incidence of flap failure, primarily due to vascular compromise within the first 6 weeks. Patients with flap failure had significantly lower quality of life scores, with an average EQ-5D score of 0.42 compared to 0.75 in patients with successful flap reconstructions (p < 0.01). At 24 months, 60% of patients reported an overall improvement in quality of life based on the WHOQOL-BREF, with no significant differences based on flap type (p = 0.13). Conclusions Microvascular free flap reconstruction provides high functional recovery and acceptable complication rates in perineal reconstruction after pelvic exenteration.
affiliations: October 6th University , October City, Cairo ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.569.title: 878 Quality Improvement Project: Completion of Treatment Escalation Plan (TEP) in Surgical Patients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.569.abstract: Abstract Aim To ensure that surgical patients at King’s College Hospital have a documented TEP,detailing their level of escalation and DNACPR status,within 48 hours of admission. TEPs ensure patient- centred care by aligning treatment decisions with individual patient values.Studies show that well-documented DNACPR and TEPs help in preventing inappropriate resuscitation attempts and promoting dignity in end-of-life care(Pitcher.et.al,2017). Method Setting:KCH assessing surgical patients from the following departments:General Surgery,Trauma,Colorectal,Upper GI,Urology,Vascular. Design:Cross-sectional study using Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) methodology. PDSA1Intervention Focus:The initial hypothesis suggested low TEP completion rates were due to insufficient priority given to TEP documentation.Interventions:Educational Sessions PDSA2Intervention Focus:Clerking doctors play a critical role in completing TEPs for elective patients,but this task was often forgotten during the clerking process.Interventions:Handout for Junior Doctors, guide and pre-made proforma templates on EPIC Results Cycle1(Sept 2024):51% of surgical patients had a TEP documented.40% of TEPs were completed within 48 hours of admission. Cycle2(Oct 2024):72% of surgical patients had a TEP documented.58% of TEPs were completed within 48 hours of admission. The time to TEP completion reduced from 7 to 3 days Overall TEP completion rates improved by 157% from 28%to 72%. Conclusions Targeted interventions,including educational sessions and the introduction of proforma templates, effectively increased TEP completion rates Ongoing education and integration of TEP completion into daily workflows are essential for continued improvement Full TEP documentation remains a key objective for ensuring that surgical patients receive appropriate,patient-centered care.
affiliations: Kings College Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.542.title: 274 Job-Sharing Efficiency: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.542.abstract: Abstract Aim This quality improvement project aimed to evaluate and improve the sharing of jobs between resident doctors in the orthopaedic department through implementation of an online jobs sharing system. Method Baseline Data Collection: A questionnaire was sent to medical staff asking them to report on average how often they felt ward-based jobs were missed and how efficient they found current job-sharing strategies. Intervention: Based on baseline data results, a comprehensive online job-sharing system was created, allowing staff to update in real time. Jobs were separated by category and staff could easily assign themselves to different tasks. A colour coded system was used to demonstrate the status of a job and indicate what was yet to be done. Post intervention data collection: The same questionnaire was re-administered to evaluate improvement in jobs sharing. Additional questions were included to assess for any further feedback. Results The post intervention results demonstrated significant improvements in the sharing and completion of ward jobs:Staff went from reporting jobs were missed 1-4 daily to 1-2 times a weekThe percentage of staff reporting “very efficient” or “efficient” handover increased from 38% to 93%.100% of staff answered that they preferred using the new online job-sharing system Conclusions This quality improvement highlights the importance of the systems we use and how to adapt them to best suit staff needs so we can better support our patients. The improvements observed reinforce the value of evaluating current methods of work organisation and working to optimise efficiency.
affiliations: NHS Grampian , Aberdeen ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.541.title: 266 Improving Consent with Pre-Filled Consent Forms in Emergency General Surgery: A Quality Improvement Study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.541.abstract: Abstract Aim Informed consent is a critical component of surgical practice, ensuring that patients understand the risks and benefits of procedures. However, handwritten consent forms are often incomplete, illegible, and inconsistent. This quality improvement project aimed to review the informed consent process for laparoscopic cholecystectomy and appendicectomy at a District General Hospital in the United Kingdom and subsequently introduced pre-filled, procedure-specific consent forms. Method A retrospective review of 20 handwritten consent forms compared the documented risks to a standardised set of risks developed from multiple resources. This demonstrated suboptimal documentation on the handwritten consent forms. In response, two pre-filled consent forms were developed, incorporating a standardised set of risks, layman’s explanations and provided space for additional risks to be added depending on the patient’s needs. These new forms aimed to enhance patient-surgeon communication and facilitate patient understanding and improve documentation. A second retrospective analysis of 74 consent forms post-intervention was then performed. Results Pre-intervention only 68.57% of risks mentioned for appendicectomy and 58.89% for cholecystectomy. The most commonly documented risks were bleeding, bruising, and infection, while less frequent risks such as infertility were often omitted. Post-intervention demonstrated an improvement in documentation of risks, with the mean percentage increasing to 81.82% and 79.69% for appendicectomy and cholecystectomy respectively. Conclusions The consent forms created facilitate patient surgeon discussions, by being customisable they allow for thorough documentation. This project demonstrates that pre-filled consent forms improve documentation of risks, increase legibility, as such act as a valuable aid in the consenting process reducing chances of human error and omission.
affiliations: Whiston Hospital , Prescot ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.539.title: 217 Quality Assessment of Post-Take Ward Round Documentation in General Surgery Patients at a Single Centre Hospital: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.539.abstract: Abstract Aim Clinical records require accuracy, legibility and pertinent findings as outlined in Good Medical and Surgical Practice. This is for patient safety, multi-disciplinary team (MDT) and medico-legal standpoints. Our aim was to assess various parameters of ward round documentation in post-take general surgical patients. Method This was the first cycle of a quality improvement project. Prospective data collection commenced from 9th to 30th September 2024 of paper notes for patients admitted during this time. Parameters assessed included patient labels, date, time, designation, bleep, signature, diagnosis, history of presenting complaint (HPC), examination findings, observations, fluid monitoring, current medications, allergies, radiology, impression and plan. Analysis of discrete data was with percentages. Results Of 143 potential records, 93 records were eligible. 52% of patients were male and 48% female. Age range was 10-99 years with mean age being 53 years old. 51% of cases could not identify the doctor who documented. A HPC was not documented in 45.2% of cases, and of those with HPC, 74.5% of cases were not in enough detail. Ward round noting mostly lacked detail in HPC, past surgical history, past medical history, drugs, social history, radiology, observations, recent bloods, allergy status, fluid monitoring and impression. Conclusions This project identified ward documentation majorly lacked detail in areas of history taking and clinical observations such as fluid monitoring. While doctors may check such parameters, these were not documented. To improve ease, quality and support MDT integration, we are introducing a pro-forma for documentation to target these poorer areas with plans to re-assess after implementation.
affiliations: Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , Bedford ,
Department of Surgery, Specialised Foundation Programme, University of Cambridge , Cambridge ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.534.title: 137 Antibiotic Provision in Adult Acute Appendicectomy: A Quality Improvement Initiative at a London Tertiary Centre
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.534.abstract: Abstract Aim Appendicitis is a common surgical emergency, yet variations exist in the prescription of antibiotics. Recent evidence suggests postoperative antibiotics should be reserved for cases with infectious complications, with no routine need for long-term prescriptions. This study evaluates local practices for antibiotic use in acute appendicitis and their impact on complication rates. Method A 6-month retrospective analysis of adult patients undergoing appendicectomy for acute appendicitis at a Tertiary Centre was conducted. Medical records were reviewed to assess appendicitis severity, antibiotic type, route, and duration used. Complications and causes for readmission were evaluated. Results Forty-five patients (27 males, mean age 36.5) were included. The mean length of stay was 3.95 days. Preoperatively, 96% received IV antibiotics, with 48% having complicated appendicitis (perforation, gangrene, or abscess). All complicated cases received post-operative antibiotics (mean duration 9.6 days)- 73% received IV with oral stepdown, with course length mean 9.6 days- while 30% of uncomplicated cases received post-op antibiotics (mean 5.1 days). Only 4% received no post-operative antibiotics. Six patients experienced infection-related complications or readmissions, with differing antibiotic regimens before and after surgery. Conclusions Significant variability exists in antibiotic prescribing practices for acute appendicitis. Unnecessary postoperative antibiotics in uncomplicated cases and prolonged courses in complicated appendicitis may contribute to antibiotic overuse. Standardising antibiotic protocols based on current evidence is crucial to improve care and reduce inappropriate use.
affiliations: St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.735.title: 813 Improving Discharge Medication Compliance for Secondary Prevention in Peripheral Arterial Disease: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.735.abstract: Abstract Aim Adherence to discharge medications is critical in preventing recurrent cardiovascular events in patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD). This quality improvement project evaluated and aimed to improve compliance with discharge medications—Atorvastatin 80mg, Rivaroxaban 2.5mg, and Aspirin 100mg—following COMPASS trial recommendations. Method A four-week data collection period was followed by sequential interventions to address medication errors. Week 1 served as the baseline with no intervention. In Week 2, a poster detailing correct medication dosages was displayed on the ward. Week 3 involved an email reminder to junior doctors emphasizing proper dosing. In Week 4, a consultant-led discussion reinforced discharge medication protocol. Compliance was assessed through review of discharge prescriptions. Results Baseline compliance (Week 1) was low: Atorvastatin 16.67%, Rivaroxaban 0%, and Aspirin 0%. By Week 2, compliance improved slightly: Atorvastatin 20%, Rivaroxaban 0%, and Aspirin 20%. The email intervention in Week 3 resulted in a significant improvement: Atorvastatin 75%, Rivaroxaban 25%, and Aspirin 50%. In Week 4, compliance stabilized: Atorvastatin 50%, Rivaroxaban 25%, and Aspirin 50%. Conclusions The email intervention proved most effective for improving atorvastatin compliance, but Rivaroxaban adherence remained suboptimal. Future efforts should include targeted education, clearer dosing guidelines, and continuous staff reinforcement. Additionally, involving specialist pharmacists as part of the vascular MDT within vascular hubs could enhance medication management for this high-risk group, ensuring more tailored and consistent care.
affiliations: NHS Grampian , Aberdeen ,
NHS , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.734.title: 739 Assessing the Quality of Life of Patients Undergoing Endovascular Treatment of Pelvic Congestion Syndrome
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.734.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the credibility of the Visual analog scale pain score and specific quality-of-life questionnaires in women who underwent ovarian vein coil embolization to reduce chronic pelvic pain. Method A retrospective, observational single-center study was conducted to examine the quality of life including pain in 30 women diagnosed with pelvic congestion syndrome between 2019 and 2024 in Jordan. Clinical information was retrieved from Cerner’s electronic health record platform. Patients’ demographics, symptomology, procedure details, and follow-up variables including PVVQ and PVCSS scores were collected. Patients were contacted by telephone to assess pain perception using a visual analog scale pre-and post-intervention. Data analysis was performed using R Studio. Results The results revealed a statistically significant, high positive monotonic correlation between PVVQ and PVCSS (τ= 0.60, p<0.00). A statistically significant difference between pre-and post-operative VAS scores existed (V=406, p < 0.00) with post-operative VAS being found lower than pre-operative VAS scores. There was a substantial, medium positive correlation between PVCSS and Post-op VAS (τ = 0.31, p = 0.03). Likewise, a significant, low positive correlation between PVVQ score and Post-op VAS was detected(τ = 0.33, p = 0.02). Conclusions PVVQ, PVCSS, and the VAS pain score could be credible tools to evaluate the quality-of-life outcomes of ovarian vein coil embolization for women with pelvic congestion syndrome. Further effort with larger samples of prospective studies would be recommended to measure the validity and reliability of these scores.
affiliations: Abdali Medical Centre , Amman ,
Irbid Specialty Hospital , Irbid ,
Trinity Centre for Global Health, Trinity College Dublin , Dublin ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.087.title: 371 Lights, Camera, Surgery: A Quality Improvement Project Enhancing Medical Education with Surgical Cameras in Thyroid and Parathyroid Operations
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.087.abstract: Abstract Aim Thyroid and parathyroid surgeries often prove challenging for medical students to observe due to overcrowding within the sterile field and a restricted operative view when not scrubbed in. This ultimately leads to an inability to access meaningful learning opportunities. This Quality Improvement Project (QIP) addresses these barriers using surgical cameras to enhance education while maintaining sterility. Method Using the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle, this problem was identified through pre-intervention surveys involving 9 medical students, revealing limited visibility and consequently poor engagement during thyroid and parathyroid surgeries. In response, cameras, projecting real-time magnified surgical views onto external monitors, were introduced at Hammersmith Hospital, allowing students to observe procedures in theatres when unable to scrub in. A post-intervention survey then assessed learning engagement, visual accessibility, and educational impact, comparing responses to those pre-intervention. Results Quantitative analysis revealed an improvement in the learning environment, with the mean ‘effectiveness’ score rising from 2.1 to 4.0 (‘the environment supports learning most of the time’) on a 5-point scale. Post-intervention, 75% of students also reported enhanced visibility of the thyroid gland. Students further highlighted better comprehension of anatomy, enhanced ability to follow surgical techniques, and increased engagement. Conclusions This QIP harnesses the ability of surgical cameras to transform thyroid and parathyroid surgical education by addressing barriers to learning. Given these promising outcomes, further iterations of the QIP will be undertaken on a wider scale with superior camera technologies to improve educational outcomes further and increase external validity. Implementing these changes should provide a scalable, sustainable approach to enhancing surgical education.
affiliations: Imperial College London , London ,
Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.043.title: 281 The Role of Vascularized Lymph Node Transfer in Reducing Infection and Enhancing Quality of Life After Microvascular Free Flap Reconstruction for Perineal Defects
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.043.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate the impact of vascularized lymph node transfer (VLNT) on infection rates and quality of life in patients undergoing microvascular free flap reconstruction for perineal defects following pelvic exenteration. Methods This prospective study will enroll 100 patients undergoing microvascular free flap reconstruction for perineal defects post pelvic exenteration. Fifty will receive vascularized lymph node transfer, and fifty will have standard reconstruction. Primary outcomes include infection, wound healing, and quality of life (EQ-5D, WHOQOL-BREF). Secondary outcomes include flap survival, wound dehiscence, etc. Follow up at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months. Results At 24 months, 80% of the VLNT group achieved full functional recovery (FIM ≥90) vs. 65% in the control group (p = 0.01). Infection rates were lower in the VLNT group (12%) vs. 22% in the control group (p = 0.045), with fewer requiring debridement. Flap failure occurred in 6% of the VLNT group and 12% of the control group (p = 0.22). Quality of life (EQ-5D) was higher in the VLNT group (0.78 vs. 0.65, p = 0.02), with improvements in physical health and psychological well-being (p = 0.03, p = 0.04). Wound dehiscence was lower in the VLNT group (2% vs. 5%, p = 0.28). VLNT improved functional recovery, reduced infections, and enhanced quality of life without affecting flap survival. Conclusions VLNT in microvascular free flap reconstruction for perineal defects post-pelvic exenteration improved functional recovery, reduced infection rates, and enhanced quality of life compared to standard reconstruction, without affecting flap survival.
affiliations: October 6th University , October City ,
Alexandria University , Alexandria ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.028.title: 1015 Improving the Management of Buckle Fractures at a District General Hospital: A Quality Improvement Project Based on Evidence from the FORCE Trial
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.028.abstract: Abstract Buckle fractures (BF) are common paediatric injuries, and the FORCE (Fracture Observational Research in Children Evaluation) trial demonstrated that BF can be safely and effectively managed with a soft bandage (SB) or nothing, and discharged without follow up. This quality improvement project audited BF management at a District General Hospital and implemented interventions to align with these findings and de-escalate treatment. The study aimed to reduce plaster casts (PC) in BF management. Patients were identified during separate 3-month cycles (aged 1-15 years) pre and post interventions; 41 patients in cycle one versus 42 patients in cycle two. Interventions included revising paediatric wrist fracture guidelines, updating virtual fracture clinic leaflets, and staff education. Pre versus post-intervention findings showed: PC 34% versus 10%; removable splints 66% versus 68%; SB or nothing 0% versus 22%. Fracture clinic follow up reduced from 43% to 17%. Interventions resulted in a 24% reduction in treatment with PC and a 26% reduction in fracture clinic follow up. The EQ-5D-Y questionnaire collected patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) 6 weeks post-injury. No complications were reported, and the average health outcome score was 96/100 (100 being the best health imaginable). These findings highlight the effectiveness of targeted educational and guideline-driven interventions in improving adherence to evidence-based BF management. Adoption of FORCE trial recommendations significantly reduced the use of restrictive PC treatment without compromising patient outcomes, promoting comfort and convenience for children and families while saving time and money for both the patients and the trust.
affiliations: Musgrove Park Hospital , Taunton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.565.title: 823 Implementing a Secure, Remote Electronic Platform for Structured, Dynamic Handover Practices in a UK ENT Department; a Quality Improvement project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.565.abstract: Abstract Background Clinical handover is the effective transfer of communication and responsibility in patient care. Structured handover has been shown to reduce errors and improve patient outcomes. Exploration of electronic information-sharing for handover is encouraged by Royal College of Surgeons e.g. ‘live lists’ of patients. Aim Explore the role and implementation of a live electronic information-sharing platform for enhanced handover in a DGH ENT department. Method Baseline local process=direct clinician-clinician email handovers. Intervention=live patient lists hosted on NHS SharePoint, accessible only to relevant clinical personnel via NHS email. Pre/post-intervention questionnaires explored clinician ratings of perceived efficiency, accuracy, transparency, and patient safety in handover. Outcome measures= Likert scale 1-5 ratings (5=best outcome). Results Mean (N=5) clinicians’ ratings on perceived handover efficiency increased from 2.0 (/5) to 4.8. Paired student t-test p=0.0016 (significance <0.05); perceived accuracy increased 2.6 to 4.8 (p=0.0029); perceived transparency (data auditing capability) increased 2.0 to 4.8 (p=0.0060), transparency (tracking updates within the team throughout the day) increased 1.8 to 4.8 (p=0.001); perceived patient safety showed no significant difference (Mean 3.4 to 4.3). Free-text responses highlighted dynamic editing capabilities from phone/laptop, removing need for printed lists, confidentiality and ease of use as attractive features. Conclusions NHS SharePoint lists may be effectively employed in small clinical teams for enhanced surgical handover. No perceived benefits to patient safety were identified. Direct patient safety exploration in larger study cohorts is warranted.
affiliations: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust , Brighton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.250.title: 525 Reducing Cross-Sectional Imaging Delays from a Virtual Fracture Clinic: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.250.abstract: Abstract Background A virtual fracture clinic (VFC) provides a safety net for orthopaedic injuries coming through a hospital. Cross-sectional imaging is sometimes necessary to guide surgical decision-making. The BOA Standards for Trauma (BOAST) Fracture Clinic Services recommend timely imaging to avoid undue delays to surgery. Aim To assess and improve VFC compliance to the BOAST guidelines. This was done by identifying and evaluating sources of delays between the date of VFC review and date of surgery before and after implementation of an interdepartmental imaging pathway. Method An initial retrospective audit was undertaken from January to June 2024. An imaging pathway between the T&O and radiology departments was introduced following this, which implemented priority slots for VFC patients. A prospective re-audit was performed from July to October 2024 post-pathway introduction. Data collected included demographics, timestamps of imaging, and details of surgical intervention. Results The pre-intervention period had 86 imaging requests (41 CT, 45 MRI). The mean time between imaging request and performance was 4.51 days (range 0-30 days). 9 patients required surgical management, with imaging delays accounting for 29.5% of the total time between VFC review and surgery. The post-intervention period had 86 imaging requests (36 CT, 50 MRI). The mean time between imaging request and performance was 3.56 days (range 0-24 days). 10 patients required surgical management, with imaging delays accounting for 21.0% of the total time between VFC review and surgery. Conclusions The introduction of an interdepartmental pathway has successfully reduced the imaging delay between request and performance by 21.1%.
affiliations: Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.575.title: 1025 Optimising Emergency Surgical Workflows in a Shared Theatre During COVID-19 in Sri Lanka: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.575.abstract: Abstract Aim This study addressed delays and inefficiencies in managing surgical casualties in a shared operating theatre at Base Hospital, Horana, Sri Lanka, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Observations revealed operational bottlenecks, including reduced staff availability, prolonged procedural times due to PPE use, and restricted access to theatre beds, which delayed and extended casualty lists into late evening hours, compromising post-casualty care management. Method Conducted in May 2020, the project involved a retrospective analysis of theatre caseloads for surgical and Obstetrics & Gynaecology units pre- and post-COVID-19 lockdown from January 2020 to April 2020. The data was collected through a comprehensive review of entries in the theatre logbook. This study used comparative period sampling to include all theatre cases and times of surgical casualty theatre closures during the pre- and post-COVID lockdown. Results Data revealed no significant reduction in caseload despite the cancellation of elective surgeries and the assumption of reduced admissions during lockdown. Before the lockdown (Jan-Feb 2020), 1,532 theatre cases were recorded, with an average casualty closure time of 7:15 PM. Post-lockdown (March-April 2020), case numbers remained relatively stable at 1,344, though the average closure time extended to 10:45 PM. Interventions proposed included performing minor procedures under local anaesthesia in an alternative space, optimising admissions to prioritise essential cases, and delegating simpler procedures to trained primary care unit staff, which resulted in the expected outcome. Conclusions This study highlights the challenges of managing emergency workflows in resource-limited settings, like during crises. Data-driven interventions can improve theatre efficiency and ensure timely, equitable patient care.
affiliations: University Hospital of Wales , Cardiff ,
Royal Cornwall Hospital , Cornwall ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.447.title: 160 Awareness of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding Guidelines Among Surgical Doctors and Efforts to Improve Them. a Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.447.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess education levels of lower GI bleeding guidelines among surgical doctors and measures to improve them. Method The BSG guidelines for lower GI bleeding were taken as the gold standard format. A questionnaire(10 questions in a google survey document) was made to assess the knowledge of the finer points of the guideline. The survey was taken up predominantly by registrars and all participant responses were documented electronically and anonymized. An informal teaching session was held subsequently along with uploading of the guidelines onto the trust software, which allowed for easy referral by all staff members. The same survey was conducted again to note the improvement in knowledge levels. Results In both cycles of the audit 18 members took part including 14 registrars and 4 SHOs. Following the measures undertaken the awareness levels of the BSG guideline increased from 7 to 12(38% to 66%). The awareness of using the shock index to determine the need for a CT angiogram increased from 5 to 14(27% to 78%).The knowledge of the Oakland score for safe discharge of patients increased from 9 to 13(50% to 72.2%). Improvement of patients being scored for safe discharge from 7 to 11(38% to 61%). Conclusions Our initiatives have resulted in better knowledge levels among surgical doctors regarding lower GI bleeding guidelines used in the emergency setting resulting in better compliance and a safer patient environment.
affiliations: Aneurin Bevan University Health Board , Newport ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.440.title: 265 An Improvement in Paediatric Post-Tonsillectomy Discharge Information
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.440.abstract: Abstract Aim Tonsillectomy is a common paediatric surgical procedure. Post-tonsillectomy bleeding is a significant risk (2-5%.) In extremes, bleeding can be fatal. Prompt presentation to emergency department is crucial. ENT UK have constructed guidelines for paediatric tonsillectomy discharge information- highlighting where to present with certain complications and how to prevent them. This project aimed to audit local compliance with guidelines and subsequently improve discharge information. Method A retrospective audit was performed analysing paediatric post-tonsillectomy discharge summaries over two 4 -week cycles 9/9/24-7/10/24 (baseline) 21/10/24-18/11/24 (post-intervention). Patients were identified through hospital admission records and data recorded in a standardized excel spreadsheet. A survey was distributed to the local department to formulate the intervention (one-click inserts of pre-defined discharge summary information- “snippets”). Results There were 28 patients identified in the first cycle. Only 21% of discharge summaries stated to go to ED if they had a significant bleed (6). 7% stated to see the GP if they had a persistent fever (2). 78% stated to take regular analgesia (22) and 46% stated the importance of a regular diet (13). 15 patients were identified in the second cycle. 93% of discharge summaries stated to go to ED if they had a significant bleed (14). 73% stated to see the GP if they had a persistent fever (11). 100% stated to take regular analgesia (15) and 73% stated the importance of a regular diet (11). Conclusions There was an improvement with all discharge information post snippet. Further cycles are warranted looking at parent understanding and satisfaction of the information.
affiliations: Musgrove Park Hospital , Taunton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.559.title: 732 Appendicectomy: Swift Surgery and Quick Recovery Through Quality Improvement
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.559.abstract: Abstract Introductions The national average length of stay (LOS) following appendicectomy is 3.5 days. According to Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT), a national programme aimed at improving NHS care, discharging all patients with acute appendicitis within 2 days could free 30,000 bed days and save 8.5 million nationally. Aim This two-cycle quality improvement project aimed to determine and reduce LOS for emergency appendicectomy at a single centre. Method The first cycle comprised a retrospective analysis of 100 patients admitted for emergency appendicectomy from 21 July to 20 November 2023. Data collected from electronic records included demographics, imaging, and admission events. The primary outcome was LOS from admission to discharge. Recommendations for improvement were communicated through departmental presentation and posters. Data collection is ongoing for the second cycle, which will prospectively analyse 100 patients admitted for appendicectomy from 13 October 2024. Results Of the 90 patients included in the first cycle, 42 were male, with a median age of 37 years (range 18 to 82 years). The median LOS was 4.40 days (range 0.97 to 17.1 days), with only 6.67% meeting the GIRFT standard of 2 days. Pre-operative imaging was used in 91.1% of patients, with 73.3% and 14.4% undergoing CT and US, respectively. The median time from operation to discharge was 3.26 days, prolonged by complications including collections. Conclusions While appendicectomy is common and typically has a short LOS, complications can prolong recovery. The first cycle identified significant opportunities for improvement, with the ongoing second cycle anticipated to demonstrate progress.
affiliations: North Middlesex University Hospital NHS Trust , London ,
University College Hospital, University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.556.title: 700 Surviving to Thriving in Medical School – a Quality Improvement Endeavour
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf128.556.abstract: Abstract Aim Transitioning from medical school to clinical practice as a junior doctor poses significant challenges. This quality improvement project aimed to address gaps in preparedness and core training application success through a structured teaching series. Method Over two months, a teaching series of five one-hour sessions was conducted in a hybrid format. Topics covered:Introduction to Medical School—focusing on early orientation and skills for academic success.Foundation Training & Core Training Applications—detailing the application process and strategies for portfolio development.Maximising Clinical Placements—emphasising practical skills, communication, and making the most of learning opportunities.Prescribing for Beginners—introducing safe prescribing practices and common pitfalls.Day in the Life of an FY1—providing insights into ward rounds, task prioritization, and escalation protocols.Sessions were designed to be interactive, featuring case discussions, Q&A segments, and practical scenarios. A total of 125 students, including international participants, attended. Feedback was gathered via pre- and post-session surveys to assess confidence, knowledge, and satisfaction. Results Quantitative survey results demonstrated a significant increase in confidence and knowledge of subject being taught. Qualitative results demonstrated students appreciated interactive scenarios, practical insights, and detailed application guidance. They expressed a preference for in-person sessions, particularly for skills-based topics like prescribing and clinical task management. Conclusions The teaching series significantly improved students’ confidence in readiness for clinical practice and applications. Targeted, practical, and interactive interventions address critical gaps in medical education. Future iterations will emphasise in-person teaching for hands-on skills while maintaining virtual accessibility for broader participation.
affiliations: Barts and the London School of Medicine and Dentistry , London ,
Barts Health , London ,
Oxford University Hospital , Oxford ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.072.title: Effects on delayed surgery in inflammatory bowel disease – health related quality of life
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.072.abstract: Abstract Introduction Timing in surgery for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is important considering risk of complications, such as fistulizing disease, severe proctitis and high stoma output. This study aimed to address Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) when waiting for surgery. Method This study was a cross-sectional register-based study combined with individual-level collected data on the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire assessing the effects of delayed elective surgery on HRQoL amongst patients with IBD. Patients either waiting for, or who had undergone surgery at Sahlgrenska University Hospital during 2017-2023 with an IBD-diagnosis were identified. Result Of the 214 patients included in the study (33.64% women, mean age 44.3+16.9 years), 60% of the patients had undergone surgery, while the remainder were still awaiting surgery. The mean EQ VAS for the entire sample was 64.9, with the lowest scores observed when waiting for surgery for more than one year, compared to previous age matched population norms in Sweden, with a mean score of 87.0. The mean EQ-5D-5L index for patients waiting less than 3 months differed from those who waited 12-24 months (p=0.017) and >24months (p=0.012) respectively. Likewise, the mean EQ-5D index for those who waited 3-6 months differed from those waiting >12-24 months (p=0.036) and >24 months (p=0.032), using the Swedish value set. Discussion There were significant differences in HRQoL between patients who had undergone surgery within the Swedish health care guarantee (<3 months) and those who had been waiting for at least one year. This indicates that waiting time for surgery may impact HRQoL among patients with IBD.

Department of Surgery, Sahlgrenska University Hospital/Östra , Gothenburg ,
Gothia Forum for Clinical Trials, Region Västra Götaland, Sahlgrenska University Hospital , Gothenburg ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.005.title: Validation of postoperative period of care and Textbook Outcome as quality measures for gallstone surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.005.abstract: Abstract Introduction A universally accepted quality measure for gallstone surgery is lacking. We performed a retrospective study where we evaluated the duration of postoperative care, completion with laparoscopic approach, absence of procedure-related complications, and no readmission as criteria for Textbook Outcome (TO). Method We collected data from the Swedish National Register for Gallstone Surgery (GallRiks) during the period 2007-2022. We analyzed postoperative stay as exposure and postoperative complications as outcome using Receiver Operation Characteristic (ROC). The definition of TO was laparoscopically completed operations, discharge within three days after surgery, no postoperative complication > Clavien-Dindo 2, no contact with the care provider or new readmission/intervention within 30 days post-surgery. The outcome of TO was further validated based on patients 6 months postoperatively answering SF-36. Result A total of 193 201 cholecystectomies were analyzed. The sensitivity was 50% and the specificity 87% for predicting a surgery-related complication using discharge within three days postoperatively as threshold. The rate of TO in the entire cohort was 79,4%. Patients who met the TO criteria rated notably higher on physical and mental scoring 6 months postoperatively (both p<0.05) compared to those that did not. Discussion For evaluating results after gallstone surgery, the postoperative period of care and TO can be considered robust outcome measures.
affiliations: Department of Acute and Trauma Surgery, Karolinska University Hospital , Stockholm ,
Department of Surgery , Södersjukhuset, Stockholm ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.057.title: Minor impact of anastomotic leakage on long-term quality of life after anterior resection: a population-based cohort study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.057.abstract: Abstract Introduction Anastomotic leakage (AL) following anterior resection (AR) for rectal cancer impacts morbidity and bowel dysfunction. The aim of this study was to evaluate the impact of leakage on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) three years after surgery, as the evidence regarding long-term effects is limited. Method This population-based observational study included patients who underwent AR in Sweden between 2015 and 2017, retrieved from the Swedish Colorectal Cancer Registry. The main outcome measure was the summary score of EORTC QLQ–C30, a validated questionnaire developed to assess the quality of life of cancer patients, three years after surgery; secondary outcomes were from the colorectal-cancer specific EORTC QLQ–CR29. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation was used to assess the influence of leakage on HRQoL, accounting for confounders. Result Of 1,778 eligible patients, 1,178 (66.3%) responded, including 104 (8.8%) with AL. Patients with leakage reported a significantly lower summary score, considered a small difference (80 vs. 86, p < 0.001); this effect was estimated at -4 (p = 0.002) after adjustment. These patients also had worse body image, more sore skin around the anus and more leakage of stool from the stoma bag (if present), considered medium differences. Discussion AL following AR seems to have a minor negative impact on HRQoL three years postoperatively, while these patients have a worse reported body image, sore skin around the anus and leakage of stool from the stoma bag. These findings highlight the importance of patient counselling and long-term follow-up for patients with AL.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.020.title: The impact of antibiotic prophylaxis on postoperative infections in breast cancer surgery – a retrospective quality assessment
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.020.abstract: Abstract Introduction Breast cancer is the most frequent cancer among women, with surgery playing a central role in the treatment. Various surgical approaches exist, including a growing field of oncoplastic techniques. Despite classified as a clean surgery, breast surgery has higher rates of postoperative infections compared to other clean surgeries. The role of prophylactic antibiotics in preventing infections remains indecisive. Method This study aimed to investigate the correlation between prophylactic antibiotics and postoperative infections in breast cancer surgery. Secondary objectives included assessing the impact of surgical complexity and demographic factors on infection risk. This study included 578 patients with an invasive breast cancer diagnosis undergoing surgery at Skåne University Hospital during year 2022. Patient records were reviewed in Melior to gather information on demographics, surgical type, prophylactic antibiotic administration and postoperative infections. Result The overall postoperative infection rate after breast cancer surgery was 14% and 72% received prophylactic antibiotics. Mastectomy had the highest postoperative infection rate. No significant difference regarding postoperative infection could be observed between the patients who received prophylactic antibiotic treatment and those who did not (p = 0.88). An increased body mass index was significantly correlated with an increased risk of postoperative infection (p = 0.01). Discussion Prophylactic antibiotics were not associated with a decreased risk of developing postoperative infection. The complexity of the procedure may correlate to the risk of developing a postoperative infection but overall no significance was shown in this study. However, demographic factors as higher body mass index was significantly correlated with an increased risk for postoperative infection.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.112.title: Impact of minimal incision repair of Rectus Abdominis Diastasis (MIRRAD) on quality of life and stress incontinence: a prospective study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf149.112.abstract: Abstract Introduction Rectus Abdominis Diastasis (RAD) is a common condition where separation of the rectus abdominis muscles results in a widening of the linea alba. This separation is often due to increased intra-abdominal pressure most notably during pregnancy. This study evaluates the impact of the minimal incision repair of rectus abdominis diastasis (MIRRAD) procedure on physical activity, muscle strength, quality of life, and overall satisfaction in women with postpartum rectus abdominis diastasis (PP-RAD). Method A cohort of 31 female patients, aged 20-50 years, diagnosed with PP-RAD unresponsive to conservative treatment, underwent the MIRRAD procedure. Assessments were conducted preoperatively and one year postoperatively, these included the Modified Abdominal Trunk Function Protocol (MATFP), Disability Rating Index (DRI), and Urinary Disability Index (UDI) questionnaires. Physical activity intensity was monitored using accelerometers. Result Significant improvements were observed in vigorous physical activities (Z = -2.352, p = .019), vector magnitude counts per minute (Z = -2.163, p = .031), and steps per minute (Z = -3.131, p = .002). DRI showed significant improvements in physical tasks like dressing, walking, and strenuous work (Z ranging from -2.705 to -4.603, p < .001). UDI indicated significant improvements in urinary symptoms, including reduced frequency (Z = -2.984, p = .003) and less urinary leakage (Z = -2.357, p = .018). MATFP demonstrated gains in back and abdominal muscle strength (Z = -4.321, p < .001) and trunk stability (Z = -3.991, p < .001). Discussion The MIRRAD procedure significantly improves physical strength, trunk stability, and urinary function, enhancing daily activities and overall physical health in women with PP-RAD. Further research is recommended to evaluate long-term outcomes.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.065.title: SP5.05 Learning From Medical Errors in Invasive Procedures: Current Situation and Perspectives of Improvement: A Semi-Structured Interview
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.065.abstract: Abstract Background Learning from medical errors helps prevent their recurrence. Learning takes formal and informal forms. This study explored the management of safety incidents and medical errors, as well as the learning process involved. Methods A semi-structured interview with NHS practitioners involved in invasive procedures was conducted, featuring 14 questions. An inductive thematic analysis identified descriptive and analytical themes. Results The interviews involved 15 participants (11 consultants, 2 senior trainees, and 2 senior nurses) and lasted 445 minutes. Many were unfamiliar with textbook definitions and the WHO classification of medical errors. Concerns include under-reporting key incidents and over-reporting futile ones, with little learning. Near-miss reporting is divided. Most organizations have error management pathways, but the main issue is lack of feedback. Most believe M&M meetings offer the best platform for discussing medical errors, though concerns exist about meeting length, case selection, and the lack of anonymised discussions. While central reporting could drive change, the absence of widespread lesson-sharing is a major issue. Confidentiality, fear of public backlash, and media influence prevent the publication of errors and lessons. There is also a lack of formal support for second victims and a tendency toward defensive medicine. Conclusions Concerns focus on incident reporting processes and purpose. M&M meetings are preferred for clinicians to discuss errors. Main issues include lack of feedback and horizontal knowledge sharing. Publishing medical errors is sensitive, influenced by multiple factors. A formal NHS program is needed to support the second victim. Defensive medicine has become the norm.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.200.title: MTP7.07 Quality improvement project on introduction of basic simulation-based laparoscopic skill teaching for third year medical students during surgical placement and students’ satisfaction and confidence after the course
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.200.abstract: Abstract Background Simulation-based training plays a vital role in medical education. There are proven studies regarding the surgical simulation training for laparoscopic skill increase the confidence of the surgical trainees. The aim of this project is early introduction of laparoscopic skills to medical students to gain better understanding and confidence in operating theatre. Materials and methods Optional half day small group laparoscopic simulation teaching sessions for third year medical students were introduced during their surgical placements. Grasping and manipulation task (Task 1) and cutting the accurate disc (Task 2), which were reference from ALSGBI LapPass course, were taught and practiced. Minimal 1: 3 of faculty members and candidates were arranged to focus on skill development. Feedback from the candidates was taken regarding comparison of surgical ability and confidence in own skill at the start and end of the course, the clarity of the learning points, the overall timing and the usefulness of the course. tania Results Of 12 candidates, 50% thought the skill at the end of the course improved from none to low and 50% improved from none to intermediate. 91.67% of candidates had confidence improved from no confidence to intermediate after the course. 100% agreement on the overall usefulness and overall timing of the course were achieved. Conclusions All the candidates expressed a high satisfaction level after the course. Most candidates suggested to organize the course regularly and agreed that the level of the course is suitable for the medical students.
affiliations: Royal Devon University Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.253.title: TTP3.04 Revisiting Enhanced Recovery (ERAS) in the Post-Operative Phase – A Quality Improvement Project at A District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.253.abstract: Abstract Aim To re-assess our current practice of enhanced recovery (ERAS) pathway based on the 2018 ERAS Society recommendations Method First cycle of the audit included patients who underwent elective colorectal resections between January – March 2024. Post-operative elements of the ERAS pathway were assessed including analgesia, nutrition, mobilisation, venous thromboemboli (VTE) prophylaxis, and prophylaxis for post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Data was analysed by descriptive statistics. Educational and nutritional interventions were introduced, and second cycle of the audit was completed between September – October 2024. Results A total of 46 patients and 20 patients were included in the first and second cycle of audit respectively. ERAS recommendationsCycle 1 (n=46)Cycle 2 (n=20)Early mobilisation – referral to physiotherapy100%85%Resumption of oral intake from day of surgery100%100%Oral nutritional supplements (ONS) from day of surgery0%75%VTE prophylaxis for 28 days98%100%Prescription of PONV prophylaxis70%85% Conclusion There was good compliance in most aspects of ERAS with successful introduction of ONS to improve post-operative nutrition. Continued re-assessment of ERAS pathway is recommended with the development of interventions, such as e-prescription bundle, to improve outcomes.
affiliations: University Hospital of North Tees

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.128.title: MTP1.09 Quality of Life Changes in Lipectomy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.128.abstract: Abstract Introduction Abdominal liposuction and abdominoplasty are widely performed body-contouring procedures that provide aesthetic and functional benefits. These procedures are also associated with improvements in quality of life (QoL), including physical, psychological, and psychosocial domains. This study aims to evaluate and synthesise evidence on the QoL changes following these interventions. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. From a total of 3030 screened records, eight studies were included. Data from these studies were pooled using the DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model to estimate the standardised mean difference (SMD) for QoL changes pre- and post-lipectomy procedures. Included studies utilised validated QoL measurement tools, such as SF-36, BODY-Q, and FACIT-SP. Results The meta-analysis revealed a significant improvement in QoL with an SMD of -1.65 (95% CI: -1.21, -0.08; p < 0.001). Key findings from the individual studies demonstrated improvements in general health, self-esteem, and emotional stability following abdominoplasty and liposuction. There was a reduction in depressive symptoms and psychological distress. Enhanced physical function and decreased discomfort associated with excess skin were also reported. Conclusion Lipectomy procedures, including liposuction and abdominoplasty, lead to substantial improvements in QoL, spanning physical, psychological, and social well-being. These findings underscore the importance of integrating QoL assessments in clinical decision-making and patient counselling. Future studies should aim to standardise QoL measurement tools to enhance comparability and guide clinical practice.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.067.title: SP5.08 Optimising Staff Identification and Communication in a Surgical Emergency Unit Through Grade-Denoting Lanyards: A Quality Improvement Initiative
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.067.abstract: Abstract Aims Escalating unwell patients requires effective communication within medical and surgical teams. This study aimed to optimise staff identification and communication on a busy Surgical Emergency Unit (SEU) by introducing colour-coded, training grade-denoting lanyards for Foundation and Core-Training Doctors. Methods Surveys of SEU staff, including doctors and MDT (nurses, HCAs, and ANPs), gathered quantitative data using a ten-point scale alongside qualitative feedback. Customised lanyards were introduced for F1 and CT doctors, followed by a post-implementation survey a month later to assess effectiveness. Results From the pre-implementation survey, 96% of 46 SEU doctors valued knowing colleagues’ training grades, and 93.5% consider it when seeking advice, despite 37% feeling uncomfortable enquiring. Pre-implementation difficulty identifying training grades averaged 5.48/10, compared to 4.60/10 after implementation, based on 15 responses. All doctors believed the lanyards improved staff identification. Pre-implementation surveys of 21 MDT members revealed 100% value knowing doctors' training grades, and 85.7% consider it when escalating care. Only 52.4% were familiar with doctors' grades, and an equal proportion feeling uncomfortable enquiring. 71.4% of 14 MDT members surveyed post-implementation identified care escalation as the prominent improvement from lanyard implementation. 100% of doctors and the MDT stated that the new lanyards would be beneficial to all training grades. Conclusions Lanyards denoting grade improved staff identification on the SEU, enhancing workflow during handovers and care escalation. Staff fully supported the lanyards, with all agreeing they would benefit all training grades. Expanding this initiative to include all doctors and MDTs across departments could optimise communication and patient care.
affiliations: OUH (Oxford University Hospitals)

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.398.title: WTP8.04 Title: “Meet the Team” – A personalised approach to quality improvement in the DIEP flap service
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf166.398.abstract: Abstract Introduction Deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) reconstruction is a complex surgery that requires cohesive multidisciplinary teamwork. It is well evidenced in its benefits to patients’ physical and psychological wellbeing. However, limited research has been performed into the patients’ perspective and lived experience. Aim To improve our local DIEP service by hosting an interdisciplinary patient feedback event to produce patient guided goals to guide our development. Methods Sixteen randomly selected patients attended a face-to-face event sponsored by our local Breast Cancer Charity. Patients were given a questionnaire pre-event and divided into groups to discuss various themes following the patients’ journey from pre-op to post op. Cross-specialty focus groups of staff then discussed the patients’ concerns and created ‘SMART’ goals to address them. Results Concerns and action plans generated from the discussions are outlined in Table 1. Conclusions This event allowed us to highlight patient directed areas of improvement across all aspects of their journey. By bringing all stakeholders together this has also had a secondary benefit of improved interdisciplinary links and co-ordination of quality improvement in a highly specialist service, something that is difficult to achieve in complex hospitals systems. We believe this model is beneficial and replicable to other services. Table 1.Patient concernsAction planDelayed dischargePost operative pathways with discharge medication bundles.Lack of experienced ward staffRegular ‘Turbo Teaching’Intimidation in anaesthetic room5-minute pauseLimited preparation for comorbid patientsPrehabilitation for high-risk patientsLack of peer support from other patientsSignposting + patients
