Royal Free Hospital , London ,
St Mary's Host=pital, Long ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.057.title: SRS43 - Assessing patient-reported quality of life outcomes after meningioma surgery using a condition-specific measure: a single centre study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.057.abstract: Abstract Introduction Meningiomas are the most common primary intracranial tumour, yet evidence on long-term functional outcomes of surgical resection remains limited. Postoperative evaluations focus on radiological and oncological outcomes, often overlooking cognitive, emotional, and psychosocial sequelae. Many patients experience persistent deficits, including visual impairment, fatigue, sleep disruption and anxiety, despite clinical remission. As healthcare shifts towards patient-centred care, integrating the assessment of health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in the postoperative functional outcome is essential to improve surgical management of meningioma. The aim of this study was to characterise the postoperative HRQOL of patients who have undergone surgical resection of skull base meningiomas in a reference centre, intending to influence the National Anterior Skull Base Audit dataset. Methods The Meningioma Quality of Life (MQOL) questionnaire, a validated, condition-specific patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) was delivered via semi-structured telephone interviews. HRQOL, neurological deficits, and impairment patterns were assessed. Results 48 patients were included. MQOL scores were obtained for the week prior to surgery and the current time point. On average 8 of 9 domains deteriorated postoperatively, with 53% of patients reporting a net reduction in QOL. The mean change across domains was –0.29 (P = 0.036, d = 0.44) Conclusions To our knowledge, this marks the first use of disease-specific PROMs in the UK to evaluate postoperative HRQOL in meningioma. Early findings suggest that significant QOL impairments persist despite favourable surgical outcomes. Integration of PROMs like the MQOL into the anterior skull base audit dataset may help improve postoperative care and enhance preoperative counselling.
affiliations: King's College London , London ,
King's College Hospital , London ,
Barts and the London School of Medicine and Dentistry , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.070.title: SRS59 - Assessment of the quality and reliability of social media videos for patient information on common general surgical procedures
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.070.abstract: Abstract Introduction Social media is a significant platform for health information. However, the quality and reliability of patient facing surgical content is uncertain. We evaluated the quality and reliability of TikTok and Instagram videos about three common general surgical procedures: laparoscopic appendicectomy; laparoscopic cholecystectomy; and inguinal hernia repair, and compared performance by platform, procedure, and creator type. Methods We conducted a crosssectional study of the top fifty results per procedure per platform. Videos were classified as useful, misleading, personal experience, or irrelevant and quality and reliability assessed with the Global Quality Score (GQS) and modified DISCERN (mDISCERN) score respectively. Results 300 videos, accruing 592 975 likes and 11 489 comments, were analysed. Videos were low in both quality and reliability across both platforms although higher on Instagram (GQS 1.95; mDISCERN 1.65) than TikTok (GQS 1.27; mDISCERN0.33; both P < 0.0001). 53/300 (17.7%) videos were judged to be misleading. Useful content was less frequent on TikTok than Instagram (14/150, 9.3% versus 82/150, 54.7%; P < 0.0001). Professional content was deemed more useful than that of non professionals (54/117, 46.2% versus 42/183, 23.0%; P < 0.0001) with higher quality and reliability scores (GQS 1.80 vs 1.49; mDISCERN 1.36 vs 0.76; both P < 0.0001). Conclusions Surgical educational videos across popular social media platforms are low in quality and reliability. Patients should be wary of the risk of possible health misinformation. Clinicians and professional bodies should be aware of the growing popularity of social media and consider the production of evidence-based content on these platforms to disseminatecredible information and counter misinformation.
affiliations: Croydon University Hospital , London ,
Imperial College London , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.080.title: SRS70 - Evaluating quality of colorectal cancer surgery across elective and emergency health systems: a secondary analysis of prospective cohort studies in 95 countries
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.080.abstract: Abstract Background Colorectal cancer is the world’s third most common malignancy and second leading cause of cancer death, yet 30% of patients still present as a surgical emergency. We aimed to determine whether surgical quality differs between potentially curative emergency and elective colorectal resections. Methods This pre-planned secondary analysis included patients undergoing curative-intent colorectal cancer surgery from three global prospective cohort studies (GlobalSurg-3, n = 5506; CovidSurg-Cancer, n = 6719; APOLLO, n = 876). Surgical quality was measured by margin-positive resection. Hierarchical multilevel logistic regression adjusted for patient-, disease- and health-system factors. Bootstrap simulations assessed modification by country income, cancer stage, and tumour site. Results Among 13 101 patients from 95 countries, 678 (5.4%) had margin-positive resections, with higher rates in emergency versus elective surgery (13.7 versus 4.5%, P < 0.0001). Emergency surgery independently increased odds of margin positivity (adjusted OR 2.45, 95% c.i. 1.86–3.22), consistent across all income groups. Bootstrap-derived absolute risk differences were greatest in stage III–IV rectal cancer: 12.6% (95% c.i. 10.2–15.7) in high-income countries, 19.0% (95% c.i. 13.6–23.9) in upper-middle, and 14.1% (95% c.i. 10.9–16.5) in lower-middle/low-income countries. Hospital- and country-level factors explained 76% of observed variation versus 23% at the patient level. Conclusions Emergency surgery conferred a two- to three-fold higher risk of margin positivity globally, independent of resources. These findings challenge the assumption that poor outcomes are solely due to advanced disease and highlight the urgent need for enhanced resectability assessment, specialist availability, and bridge-to-surgery pathways.
affiliations: NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery, School of Health Sciences, University of Birmingham , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.104.title: SRS107 - Predictive accuracy of the american college of surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (NSQIP) surgical risk calculator for patients undergoing infra-inguinal bypass for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.104.abstract: Abstract Background Patients with chronic limb threatening ischaemia (CLTI) are often at high peri-operative risk from associated co-morbidities yet require expedient revascularisation. Several risk-prediction models exist, with the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (NSQIP) Surgical Risk Calculator widely used. However, it lacks external validation specific to CLTI, questioning its reliability for this population. Methods A retrospective review consecutive patients undergoing infra-inguinal bypass for CLTI between December 2023 and September 2024 at a single institution. NSQIP calculated risk scores were evaluated using Receiver Operating Characteristic curves, Brier scores, and correlation coefficients to assess predictive accuracy and discriminative ability. Results A total of 120 infra-inguinal bypass procedures were analysed. The NSQIP calculator demonstrated strong discriminative ability for predicting cardiac complications (Area Under the Curve [AUC] = 0.92; Brier score = 0.02) and moderate performance for sepsis prediction (AUC = 0.73; Brier score = 0.05). However, the tool showed poor predictive accuracy for 11 out of the 13 operation-specific outcomes assessed. For predicted length of hospital stay, the mean absolute error was 10.4 days, and the Pearson correlation coefficient was low (R = 0.213), indicating a weak association between predicted and actual durations. Discussion While the NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator demonstrated value in predicting cardiac and sepsis complications in CLTI patients, its limited performance across most outcome domains raises concerns about its broader applicability. Caution is advised when using this tool for informed consent and shared decision-making in this patient population. Alternative or supplementary risk assessment tools should be considered.
affiliations: Manchester Academic Vascular Research and Innovation Centre (MAVRIC) , Manchester ,
University of Manchester , Manchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.131.title: SRS135 - Assessing the impact of advancements in human epidermal growth factor receptor-2-positive breast cancer therapeutics on quality of life: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.131.abstract: Abstract Background Targeted molecular therapy has transformed the management of human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2+) breast cancer. Alongside survival outcomes, randomised controlled trials (RCTs) are increasingly incorporating quality of life (QoL) and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). Aim To systematically evaluate how RCTs of targeted therapies in breast cancer have assessed PROMs and QoL, and to investigate whether treatment effects on overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) align with preservation of QoL. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Statistical analyses were performed using R. Results Twenty-five RCTs involving 24 234 HER2+ breast cancer patients (mean age 55.6 years, range 20–91) were included. CONSORT-PRO scores ranged from 5–9 (median 8.0). Meta-analysis demonstrated that antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) significantly prolonged time to deterioration compared with non-ADC therapies in the metastatic setting (HR 0.64, 95% c.i. 0.49–0.83; P < 0.0001) and were associated with an improvement in QoL change from baseline (MD = 2.0 points, 95% c.i. 0.4–3.6; P = 0.015). Dual HER2 blockade significantly prolonged time to deterioration (TTD) (HR 0.81, 95% c.i. 0.69–0.94; P = 0.006). Trial-level associations between TTD and OS (P = 0.73) and between TTD and PFS (P = 0.91) were not significant. Conclusions Breast cancer RCTs increasingly integrate PROMs, reflecting a shift towards patient-centred evaluation. While treatments significantly prolonged TTD, there was no consistent evidence that survival gains translated into better QoL preservation. These findings highlight the need for future trials to balance efficacy with sustained quality of life.
affiliations: Department of Surgery, The Lambe Institute for Translational Research, University of Galway , Galway ,
Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland , Dublin ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.147.title: SRS151 - Healing beyond the wound: diabetic foot reconstruction—evaluating quality of life and patient satisfaction
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.147.abstract: Abstract Aims To measure the impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and patient satisfaction following diabetic foot reconstruction utilising plastic surgery techniques. Methods A retrospective single-centre study assessed patient reported outcome measures in diabetic patients who have had plastic surgical reconstruction. HRQoL was calculated using the Euroqol EQ-5D-5L questionnaire at two time points, pre- and post-surgery, comparing both pain and perceived quality of life. Digital records were analysed and telephone interviews were conducted for all patients since the involvement of plastic surgery in the diabetic foot reconstruction service in 2021. To explore satisfaction, patients were asked whether they would undergo the procedures again and recommend the procedures to others. Results A total of 23 patients completed the evaluation. Mean post-operative EQ-5D scores showed an improvement from [11.5 ± 4.9] to [9.8 ± 4.9]. Mean EQ-VAS scores improved significantly from 52 pre-operatively to 65 post-operatively (P = 0.03). Additionally, 96% of patients reported that they would recommend diabetic foot reconstruction to others, and 87% stated they would undergo the procedure again, reflecting high levels of patient satisfaction and perceived value. Conclusions Reconstructive surgery for diabetic foot wounds improved patient reported HRQoL and had high levels of patient satisfaction. This data highlights the need for a fundamental change to pathways with which patients with diabetic feet are managed.
affiliations: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust , London ,
University College London , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.171.title: SRS180 - Addressing delays in post-operative X-rays in hip replacement surgery: a quality improvement project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.171.abstract: Abstract Background Post-operative X-rays are essential for assessing outcomes after hip replacement surgery, but compliance with timely imaging protocols varies. This quality improvement project sought to facilitate the prompt acquisition of post-operative X-rays for trauma patients undergoing hip replacement surgery. Methods We conducted a quality improvement project using Plan-Do-Study-Act methodology over three iterative cycles between April 2024 and March 2025. Cycle 1 established baseline performance through retrospective review of 100 consecutive patients. Cycle 2 prospectively evaluated implementation of targeted interventions across all 55 eligible patients over a six-week period. Cycle 3 assessed sustainability through retrospective analysis of all 150 eligible patients without staff awareness of monitoring. Data collected included time from surgery to X-ray request, request quality, and time to X-ray acquisition. Results Baseline assessment showed 74 % of X-rays were requested on surgery day, however only 50% performed within one day post-operatively. After implementing interventions, Cycle 3 demonstrated significant improvements: 73% of requests submitted within one hour of surgery, average request time decreased from 12.3 to 5.8 h, and time from surgery to X-ray reduced from 44 to 35.6 h. The percentage of X-rays performed within one day increased from 50 to 65%. Conclusions A structured quality improvement approach successfully improved the timeliness of post-operative X-rays despite external constraints such as staffing variability and seasonal pressures. Sustainability requires robust protocols, educational tools and addressing resource limitations, particularly patient transport equipment.
affiliations: ESNEFT , Colchester ,
NNUH , Norwich ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.192.title: SRS206 - BAHA in practice: a retrospective review of 490 patients assessed for a BAHA device over a 10 year period: patient eligibility and quality of life analysis
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.192.abstract: Abstract Background Bone anchored hearing devices have been utilised in clinical practice in SIVUH since 2013. These devices are beneficial for patients with conductive hearing loss who are not suitable candidates for conventional hearing aids. This study aims to evaluate all patients referred for assessment to the BAHA unit for eligibility and quality-of-life outcomes following BAHA implantation. Methods A retrospective review was conducted at the South Infirmary Victoria University Hospital, examining patient charts and theatre records from 2014 to 2025. Data for BAHA eligibility was recorded including audiological and patient centred criteria. Patient-reported outcomes were assessed between 2023 and 2025 using the Glasgow Benefit Inventory (GBI) to evaluate functional benefit and quality-of-life changes following BAHA implantation. Results 490 patients were assessed for BAHA eligibility. Of these, 238 proceeded to implantation, and 252 were deemed unsuitable for the procedure. Quality of life outcomes were measured for patients implanted from 2023 onwards, 30 patients completed the GBI. Analysis demonstrated improvements in quality of life among recipients in the post operative period. Conclusions BAHA implantation can provide significant quality-of-life benefits for appropriately selected patients. However, more than half of those assessed were unsuitable. Careful preoperative selection ensures BAHA implantation delivers meaningful quality-of-life benefits.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.233.title: SRS249 - To swab or not to swab? The utility of pus swabs in surgically drained cutaneous abscesses: a quality improvement project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.233.abstract: Abstract Introduction A pus swab specimen can determine the microbiological characteristics of infections and therefore help guide antimicrobial management. The current evidence in their utlity in superfical cutaneous abscesses is limited. Aims Primary AIms: Assess current practice in the use of pus swabs for general surgery patients undergoing incision and drainage of cutaneous abscesses. Methods A retrospective analysis of clinical coded data between 1 January 2023 and 1 January 2024 was performed. Data included location, pus swab use, and if so, were the results reviewed and did they change clinical pratice. A cost analysis was also performed. Results A total of 338 patients were identfied of these, 231 patients were including in the analysis: exclusion was due to lack of data, other speciality, duplication, and coding errors. The most common site of abscesses were: trunk (79), perianal/ischiorectal (58), axilla (28), groin (28), gluteal (11), pilonidal (12) and other (15). A pus swab was sent in 85% (196/231) of cases. 36% (70/196) of results were chased. 4% (3/70) wer used to guide antimicrobial therapy. Of these 4%, two patients had necrotising fasciitis and one had a mesh infection. Out of the 197 swabs taken, over 209 micro-organisms were isolated with an estimated cost of £1733 for the culture and sensitivity testing of these organisms. Conclusions The use of pus swabs generates a significant use of resources and cost with minimal clinical benefit in the use of simple cutaneous abscess in the general surgical patient.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.269.title: SRS297 - Decellularisation barotrauma in rat liver scaffolds compromises scaffold quality and recellularisation capacity
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.269.abstract: Abstract Liver transplantation remains the only life-saving treatment for end-stage liver failure, but is limited by organ shortage, and transplanted patients face significant immunosuppression-related pathologies. Bioengineering neo-organs by repopulation of decellularised scaffolds with candidate cells offers the possibility of recipient-specific, immunosuppression-free transplantation. Scaffold preparation requires cell removal whilst minimising damage to extra-cellular-matrix (ECM), which provides biophysical/biochemical cellular fate-defining instructions. Portal vein perfusion with decellularisation solution is an established method of generating liver scaffolds, but flowrate effects on scaffold characteristics are poorly defined. We therefore studied effects of decellularisation flowrates on scaffold properties by light-microscopy, immunofluorescence, residual DNA, glycosaminoglycan and hepatocyte growth factor content, structural ECM proteins, and scaffold recellularisation quality with vascular progenitor stem cells. We show that decellularisation solution flowrate is a determining factor of scaffold physical and biochemical quality and report the appearance of previously undescribed disruptions within scaffold ECM with 3D-structure consistent with false passages distinct from vascular lumina. Compared to sub-physiological flowrates (5 mL/min), disruptions were 20-fold more frequent (P = 0.0022) at physiological and higher flowrates (15 and 30 mL/min). Disruptions resulted in poor decellularisation with 5-fold higher levels of remnant DNA (P = 0.0045), out-with established quality criteria. Disruptions were also associated with poor scaffold recellularisation, with 2-fold reduction in sinusoidal repopulation (P = 0.0066), 7-fold imbalance in peripheral to central scaffold cellular engraftment (P = 0.0049), 3-fold and 4-fold reduction in portal and hepatic venous recellularisation efficiency (P = 0.0001). These results demonstrate previously undescribed effects of perfusion decellularisation and contribute to the evolving definition of optimal parameters for the generation of decellularised tissue scaffolds.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.347.title: SRS391 - Global outcomes after robotic left pancreatectomy: learning curve, morbidity, and oncological quality
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.347.abstract: Abstract Background Robotic left pancreatectomy (RLP) is increasingly adopted worldwide. Current guidelines suggest a learning curve of 21 cases, yet its impact on major morbidity and oncological quality remains uncertain. Methods A retrospective multicentre international study was undertaken across 10 centres in the UK, Spain, Germany, the USA, and Australia (2014–2025). Consecutive patients undergoing RLP were categorised into competency (first 21 cases per centre) or proficiency phase (>21). The primary outcome was major morbidity (Clavien–Dindo grade ≥ IIIa), and secondary outcome was the R1-margin rate. Mixed-effects logistic regression and risk-adjusted cumulative sum (RA-CUSUM) analyses were performed. Results 521 patients underwent RLP, including 200 (38.4%) in the competency phase and 321 (61.6%) in the proficiency phase. Median age was 63 years (IQR 54–73), and 56.4% were female. Rates of major morbidity were similar between phases (14.5% versus 14.0%, P = 0.981), as were R1 margin rates (21.6% versus 19.7%, P = 0.092). Independent predictors of major morbidity included male sex (OR 1.76, P = 0.037), preoperative pancreatitis (OR 2.23, P = 0.031), and multivisceral resection (OR 2.29, P = 0.034). Among patients with adenocarcinoma (n = 110), prolonged operative time (OR 1.39 per hour, P = 0.004) and nodal positivity (OR 2.62, P = 0.047) predicted R1 resection, while learning phase was not associated with margin status. RA-CUSUM demonstrated no excess morbidity over time in any centre. Conclusions In this first multicentre international analysis, the learning phase of RLP did not increase the risk of major morbidity or compromise oncological quality. These findings support the safe global adoption of RLP with appropriate training and case selection.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.350.title: SRS394 - Defining quality in robotic pancreas surgery: predictors of textbook outcomes in a multicentre UK series
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag018.350.abstract: Abstract Background Textbook outcome (TO) is an objective benchmark of surgical quality. Current Brescia guidelines suggest proficiency in robotic left pancreatectomy (RLP) after 21 cases for morbidity risk, but the influence of learning phase on TO has not been validated in multicentre series. Methods All RLPs performed across six UK centres (July 2014–August 2024) were analysed. TO was defined as absence of major morbidity (complication ≥Clavien-Dindo 3a), in-hospital mortality, 90-day readmission, prolonged length of stay, and clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF). Predictors of TO were assessed using multivariable logistic regression. Results A total of 281 patients underwent RLP, of whom 143 (50.9%) achieved TO. Major morbidity occurred in 13.5%, CR-POPF in 20.3%, and 90-day readmission in 24.2%. There was no difference in TO between competency (n = 109) and proficiency (n = 172) phases (52.3% versus 50.0%, P = 0.801). The proficiency phase was characterised by longer operative time (315 versus 230 min, P < 0.001), lower splenic preservation (13.4% versus 24.8%, P = 0.023), and fewer resections for vascular involvement (7.0% versus 20.2%, P = 0.002). On multivariable analysis, prolonged operative duration independently reduced the likelihood of TO (OR 0.82 per additional hour, P = 0.010), with a non-linear association observed. Conclusions In this first multicentre UK series, half of patients achieved TO after RLP. Contrary to guideline assumptions, TO rates were unaffected by learning phase, likely reflecting prior laparoscopic expertise. Operative duration emerged as the strongest predictor of TO, serving as a surrogate for case complexity and highlighting the importance of patient selection and procedural standardisation as robotic pancreas surgery evolves.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag055.007.title: Automating the Comprehensive Complication Index With Artificial Intelligence: Evaluation of Quality and Clinical Potential
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag055.007.abstract: Abstract Background The Comprehensive Complication Index (CCI) is a validated, clinically established, and sensitive measure of postoperative morbidity but is underutilised due to the labor-intensive and error-prone nature of manual complication extraction and grading. Large language models (LLMs) can analyse free-text surgical discharge summaries and accurately apply the Clavien-Dindo Classification (CDC). However, their ability to reliably compute the more complex CCI – requiring identification of multiple events, correct severity grading and weighted aggregation – remains unclear. Aims To evaluate the feasibility and accuracy of contemporary LLMs in extracting postoperative complications and computing the CCI from unstructured surgical discharge summaries. Methods Six LLMs (ChatGPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek-V3.2, Mistral AI (2024), Gemini 3 Flash and Llama 4) were assessed using a tiered validation framework. After conceptual testing, each model analysed 20 de-identified real-world surgical discharge summaries. A three-layered prompting framework (preprocessing, complication extraction and computation, and consistency checking) was compared with naïve end-to-end analysis. Agreement with expert reference CCI values was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Bland-Altman analysis. Results All models correctly defined the CCI concept. Naïve analysis showed moderate agreement with reference CCI values (ICC(3,2) = 0.87), with the observed disagreement being driven by missed complications and incorrect aggregation. Structured prompting improved agreement to excellent (ICC(3,1)=0.93) with minimal systematic bias. ChatGPT and Claude achieved full agreement with reference CCI values across all cases. Discrepancies in other LLMs were attributable to ambiguity in clinical documentation or inherent interpretive boundaries of the CCI framework, rather than computational errors. Conclusion LLMs can accurately extract complications, assign CDC grades, and compute CCI from unstructured free-text surgical discharge summaries when guided by structured prompting. This demonstrates that AI can reliably perform complex morbidity aggregation and may reduce clinical workload while improving standardization of surgical outcome reporting. Further large-scale validation is warranted.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.696.title: 82 Improvement in Patella Resection Angle with Next-Generation Total Knee Replacement Instruments
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.696.abstract: Abstract Aim To compare the accuracy of patellar resection between legacy and next-generation total knee replacement (TKR) instrumentation from two major orthopaedic manufacturers, using the patellar resection angle (PRA) as an objective radiographic measure of resection alignment. Method A retrospective observational study was conducted on 400 primary TKRs performed for osteoarthritis at a single centre. Patients were divided into four groups (n=100 each): Company A legacy, Company A next-generation, Company B legacy, and Company B next-generation systems. Standardised postoperative skyline radiographs were assessed to measure PRA, defined as the angular deviation of the resected patellar surface from the native coronal plane. Positive values represented lateral angulation, negative values medial. Mean PRA and range were calculated for each group, and comparisons between legacy and next-generation systems were made using a two-tailed Student’s t-test (p<0.05). Box-and-whisker plots were generated to visually compare the distribution, variability, and skewness of PRA across all groups. Results For Company A, mean PRA improved from 6.9° (range −8.2° to 22.0°) with the legacy system to 5.0° (range −9.3° to 14.1°; p=0.005). For Company B, mean PRA improved from 6.4° (range −17.8° to 22.4°) to 2.2° (range −4.4° to 11.3°; p=0.00001). Box-and-whisker analysis demonstrated reduced variability and narrower interquartile ranges for next-generation systems. Conclusions Next-generation TKR instrumentation significantly improves the accuracy and consistency of patellar resection compared with legacy systems. Enhanced precision, demonstrated by reduced mean PRA, variability, and skewness, supports the role of improved instrument design in achieving reproducible surgical outcomes and potentially better patellofemoral function.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.571.title: 809 Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) for Emergency Colorectal Patients - a Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.571.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess referral rates of the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol for patients undergoing emergency colorectal surgery. Method A two-cycle project was conducted at a single centre on referral rates of ERAS for patients aged ≥18 years old undergoing emergency colorectal surgery. During the first cycle, data was collected on the total number of patients suitable for ERAS post-emergency colorectal surgery, and the number of these patients who were referred to the ERAS team. Data was also collected on the method of referral. Our interventions to increase referral rates included delivering a session with the ERAS team for clinical staff highlighting the ERAS service and referral criteria whilst also displaying this in clinical areas. A second cycle of data collection was completed on the same points as well as assessing post-operative outcomes of ERAS implementation. Results First cycle results showed a referral rate of 9.1% through multiple routes of referral. Post-intervention, this referral rate increased to 23.3%. Early referral and implementation of ERAS resulted in a reduced length of hospital stay of 1.5 - 3 days when compared to literature studying traditional post-operative care. This QIP showed return to mobilisation by a median of two days post-operatively, and a median of four days to return to first diet. The early implementation of ERAS also decreased the risk of post-operative complications. Conclusions There was an increase in referral rates to ERAS post-intervention. Further implementations finalising referral route and documentation are being trialed to ensure easier and early referral of emergency colorectal patients for ERAS.
affiliations: The Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust , Wolverhampton ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.575.title: 1022 Compliance With BSSH Flexor Tendon Repair Standards and Documentation Quality in a UK Regional Hand Unit: A 2023–2025 Service Evaluation
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.575.abstract: Abstract Aim High-quality flexor tendon repair relies on adherence to BSSH operative standards and clear documentation to guide rehabilitation and optimise patient outcomes. This three-cycle audit assessed local compliance with BSSH standards and reviewed year-on-year improvements in operative documentation following implementation of SmartText, an EPR function supporting consistent data entry. Method A retrospective review was undertaken for 42 consecutive operations involving flexor tendon or multistructural hand trauma (Jan–Apr 2025). Variables evaluated included technique used, level of laceration, pulley preservation, neurovascular injury/repair documentation, and intra-operative tendon testing (IOTT). Documentation quality was assessed against an 11-point audit repeated in 2023, 2024 and in 2025 following SmartText introduction. Results Sixty-three flexor tendons were repaired, predominantly within zones 1–2 (83.8%). Compliance with BSSH standards was high: digit documented (92.8%), zone of laceration (71.4%), repair technique (88%), and pulley preservation/venting documentation (90.4%). Neurovascular injury and repair were consistently documented. IOTT occurred in 34.9% of cases, with satisfactory glide in all tested tendons. Findings showed ≥80% compliance in six standards, including site, digit, repair technique and pulley management. Neurovascular documentation improved from 87% (2023) to 100% (2025). The main persistent deficit was strand-number documentation (44% in 2024; 45% in 2025). Conclusions The unit shows strong adherence to BSSH operative standards with continued documentation improvements. Increasing IOTT use and improving strand-number recording remain key goals. Ongoing optimisation and induction-level training should support full compliance to improve postoperative management and patient outcomes. This audit demonstrates how SmartText tools could enhance operative documentation across all surgical specialties.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.171.title: 411 Implementation of a Patient-Initiated Follow-Up Pathway Following Paediatric Grommet Insertion: A Quality Improvement Study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.171.abstract: Abstract Aim National guidelines recommend a 6-week post-operative audiometry following grommet insertion, with discharge and safety-netting if hearing has normalised. Despite this, many children continue to receive routine follow-up appointments. This quality improvement project aimed to quantify unnecessary post-operative follow-ups after normal audiometry and evaluate the potential role of Patient-Initiated Follow-Up (PIFU) in optimising clinic efficiency. Method A retrospective review of paediatric grommet insertions performed between 2020–2025 was undertaken. Data collected included the number of patients undergoing post-operative audiometry, audiometric outcomes, follow-up appointments arranged, reasons for follow-up (routine vs symptomatic), and clinical outcomes. Patients were assessed for eligibility for PIFU based on normal audiometry, absence of complications, and no documented clinical indication for ongoing review. Results Forty-three patients were reviewed. Sixteen demonstrated normal audiometry at six weeks post-operatively. Of these, nine patients (21% of the total cohort) were followed up despite having no documented indication, representing over 50% of the normal-audiometry group. . Key barriers identified were inconsistent documentation, lack of standardised criteria, and concerns around symptom reporting in younger children. Conclusions Routine follow-up after normal audiometry following grommet insertion represents an inefficiency in service provision. Implementation of a structured PIFU pathway for low-risk children over five years old is a safe, guideline-aligned, and sustainable intervention that significantly reduces unnecessary clinic appointments, while maintaining patient safety.A PIFU proforma has been established, and the effectiveness will be assess in a second cycle.
affiliations: Chelsea and Westminster Hospital , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.271.title: 1250 Improving Documentation of the Clinical Frailty Scale and Social History in ICU Admissions: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.271.abstract: Abstract Introduction Accurate documentation of social history and the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) is vital for holistic assessment, care escalation decisions, and discharge planning. Incomplete information can overlook key psychosocial and frailty factors. This audit assessed the completeness of social history and CFS documentation in ICU clerking proformas and evaluated the impact of targeted educational interventions. Method A prospective review of clerking proformas was conducted for 30 ICU admissions (≥18 years) between 13–27 January 2025. Two PDSA cycles were completed. Data collection focused on CFS and social history subsections. A pre-audit survey was distributed to resident doctors and consultants. Following analysis, Interventions included educational posters and daily reminders during the morning handover. Results were shared at the monthly audit meeting. The second cycle, using the same methodology, reviewed 19 ICU admissions between 24 October and 7 November, 2025. Results Survey results showed that 67% of resident doctors recognised the importance of the CFS, while 87% of consultants felt CFS and social histories were often 'incomplete' despite being 'heavily relied upon' for decision-making. After the intervention, CFS completion improved from 52% to 68%, and social history completion from 54% to 84%, reflecting improvement across family history, mobility, carer status, alcohol use, and smoking. Mental health history (11%) and recreational drug use (42%) remained poorly documented. Conclusions The QIP improved completion of both the CFS and social history documentation. Although CFS documentation increased, further work is needed to raise completion rates above 80%. Regular audits, targeted teaching, and consistent reminders appear key to sustaining good documentation.

Morriston Hospital, Swansea Bay University Health Board , Swansea ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.586.title: 1354 Introduction of a Collaborative and Modernised ERCP Referral Pathway in a District General Hospital: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.586.abstract: Abstract Aim ERCP is a lifesaving procedure that is not always available locally for many biliary sepsis patients. Organising procedures between hospitals often creates logistical difficulties at multiple levels. This QI project aimed to streamline an analogue inpatient ERCP referral pathway, improving communication gaps between teams from two DGH hospitals to reduce avoidable procedural delays and minimise workload. Method A baseline questionnaire was distributed to resident doctors (May-June 2025) exploring the quality of communication, frequency of lost or incomplete referrals, and additional workload caused by poor handover. An online Excel Live database was then introduced to allow both hospitals to view and update referral data in real time. No changes were made to the original ERCP referral form. Training sessions supported its implementation. Re-auditing (August-September 2025) was completed using the same questionnaire. All ordinal data was collected and analysed using Excel. Results The initial phase showed 50% response rate; 90% expressed dissatisfaction, and 45% of ERCPs were delayed due to poor communication. Implementation of the database resulted in a remarkable improvement in standards of patient care. Communication between two sites became more robust. Second cycle had 90% feedback with 100 % satisfaction. Only 2 patients had delayed ERCP. Missed coagulation screens, cross-site phone calls and lost referrals decreased markedly, with 95% reduction in logistical disruptions. Conclusions Introduction of a shared dynamic referral database greatly improved communication across two hospital sites. It created a robust inpatient ERCP pathway supporting an efficient and reliable referral process, markedly improving patient care outcomes.
affiliations: NHS Lanarkshire , Glasgow ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.551.title: 224 Inclusion of Diagnostic Imaging in Orthopaedic Discharge Summaries: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.551.abstract: Abstract Aim To improve inclusion of diagnostic imaging results on discharge summaries for elective and trauma orthopaedic inpatients. Method A retrospective clinical audit with re-audit cycle was conducted on elective and trauma orthopaedic wards at University College London Hospitals. The first cycle (1–31 July 2025) reviewed discharge summaries of adult elective orthopaedic inpatients with radiological investigations. Exclusion criteria were trauma admissions and patients without imaging. Data were extracted from the electronic patient record and radiology reporting system, recording whether admission imaging was referenced in the discharge summary. An educational poster on findings and national standards was disseminated, and a structured template with a mandatory “diagnostic imaging” section was introduced. A re-audit (1–30 September 2025) assessed intervention impact. A parallel audit reviewed trauma inpatients with radiological investigations during the same period. Exclusion criteria were elective patients and those without imaging. A trauma poster was created. A mandatory “diagnostic imaging” section is being introduced for trauma discharge summaries to ensure consistency with elective practice. Re-audit of this is underway. Results In the first cycle of elective discharge summaries, none of 114 eligible summaries (0%) documented imaging results. Following education and template introduction, compliance rose to 93%. In trauma, 16 of 80 eligible summaries (20%) documented imaging results; post-intervention data are pending. Conclusions Embedding a diagnostic imaging section within discharge summaries eliminated omissions and ensured radiological findings were consistently communicated. This specialty-specific intervention strengthens handover, enhances continuity of care, and improves patient safety.

Division of Surgery and Interventional Sciences, University College London , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.555.title: 347 Implementing SINBAD Classification for Improved Documentation of Diabetic Foot Ulcers: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.555.abstract: Abstract Background Proper documentation of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) is essential for assessing severity, planning treatment, and tracking outcomes. NICE guidelines recommend using a standardised system like SINBAD or the University of Texas classification. In our unit, structured documentation was rarely used. Aim To improve DFU documentation by introducing the SINBAD classification in line with NICE recommendations. Method We conducted a retrospective audit of all patients with DFUs admitted under the General Surgery team at Prince Digna Hospital, Port Sudan, Sudan. Baseline records were checked for the six SINBAD components: Site, Ischaemia, Neuropathy, Bacterial infection, Area, and Depth. Staff were then trained, and a SINBAD-based documentation template was introduced. Records were re-audited after the intervention. Results Before the intervention, compliance was low: Site 65%, Ischaemia 41%, Neuropathy 0%, Bacterial infection 35%, Area 58%, Depth 35%. None of the notes used a standardised system. After the intervention, all criteria were documented at 100% except neuropathy, which was documented in 62%. Assessment of neuropathy was limited by the lack of monofilament testing in Port Sudan, and clinical examination findings were not consistently reliable. Conclusions Using a structured SINBAD-based template significantly improved the completeness and consistency of DFU documentation, supporting adherence to NICE guidelines. Limited resources affected neuropathy assessment, highlighting the need for proper diagnostic tools. Routine use of the template and ongoing staff training are key to maintaining these improvements.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.559.title: 469 Improving the Documentation of Wound Reviews for Diabetic Foot Wounds by Foundation Doctors on Vascular Surgery Ward Rounds Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.559.abstract: Abstract Aim Diabetic foot wounds carry substantial risks of infection, deterioration and amputation. High quality documentation is essential for safe care. Baseline review on a vascular surgery ward demonstrated inconsistent junior documentation, including missing procedure details; absent post-operative day; variable wound descriptions and poorly labelled photographs. This project aimed to ensure that ≥80% of post-debridement diabetic foot wound reviews are documented: 1) a structured wound assessment aligned with the senior clinician's view; 2) procedure type and post-operative day; and 3) a correctly labelled, clearly visible wound photograph. Method Baseline data was collected on 32 wound reviews. Interventions included a 30-minute teaching session for the ward foundation doctors and ACPs, supervised by senior clinicians, covering structured wound assessments and examples of good practice. Second intervention included visual reminder posters that were placed in the doctor’s office to reinforce standards. Post-intervention data was collected after the teaching session (n=16) and after poster implementation (n=21). Senior clinician agreement was assessed as soon as practical after documentation. Results Documented wound reviews were stable at 84% (27/32); 88% (14/16) and 86% (18/21). Appropriate wound photographs increased from 50% (16/32) to 63% (10/16) and 76% (16/21). Senior clinician agreement rose from 28% (9/32) to 69% (11/16) and 81% (17/21). Conclusions Targeted education and visual prompts improved the clarity and accuracy of junior-led diabetic foot wound documentation. For ongoing sustainability, the learnings have been embedded into the 'Health Toolbox' app and foundation doctor induction. Future evaluation with a larger cohort is required, and this model should be translated to all wound reviews.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.205.title: 121 Assessment and Management of Suspected Testicular Torsion in Children and Adolescents: Impact of Local Quality Improvement and Compliance with Contemporary National Standards
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.205.abstract: Abstract Aim Testicular torsion is a time-critical paediatric emergency. Recent national recommendations (NCEPOD and GIRFT, 2024) emphasise senior review and urgent operative intervention to optimise testicular salvage. This second-cycle audit assessed current performance against these standards and evaluated the effect of sustained local quality improvement (QI) measures. Method A retrospective audit was performed of patients <18 years undergoing scrotal exploration for suspected torsion between January 2023 and June 2024. Time to senior review, time to theatre, use of pre-operative ultrasound, and operative outcomes were collected and compared with a historical cohort (2011–2015) following earlier pathway and education interventions. Results Eighty patients were included. Torsion was confirmed in 14 cases (17.5%), with one orchidectomy (1.3%). Median time to senior review was 101 minutes (IQR 65–147), with 19% reviewed within one hour. Median time from decision to operate to theatre start was 77 minutes (55–96), with 13% meeting the target of surgery within one hour. Compared with the historical cohort, orchidectomy rates improved significantly (8.5% to 1.3%, p=0.045), while ultrasound use and torsion detection rates remained similar. Conclusions Local QI interventions have contributed to improved testicular salvage; however, timely senior review and theatre prioritisation remain ongoing challenges in achieving full compliance with national standards.

Lister Hospital , Stevenage ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.548.title: 144 Renal Colic Management Improvement Through Bitesize Teaching in Emergency Department
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.548.abstract: Abstract Aim Ensure all patients who have renal colic pain has a CT KUB within 14 hours as per BAUS guidelines. Ensure appropriate analgesia given to renal colic patient either in the form of an NSAID or IV paracetamol. Ensure metabolic screening bloods are performed particularly calcium and urate levels Method Plan, Do, Study, Act model was used in this quality improvement project. Patients with renal colic pain between 2nd September 2024 and 26th October 2024 were collected retrospectively. The following parameters were collected: CT KUB performed, data and time of CT KUB request, date and time of CT KUB performed, analgesia given, calcium and urate bloods collected. Bite-sized teaching was held on the 25th March and 1st September, primarily for junior doctors. The data of the first cycle was presented at a local research and development forum presented to many hospital physicians, including ED consultants. Data was then collected from 1st September to 1st November 2025 to compare for any improvements Results CT KUB performed within 14 hours, improved from 75.96% to 88%. NSAID prescriptions rose from 44% to 62% and patients obtaining no analgesia fell from 33% to 26%. Serum calcium measurement showed a slight decrease from 61% to 57% but urate level measurements went up from 5% to 11%. Conclusions Bitesize teaching to ED junior doctors and seniors has been shown to improve compliance with BAUS guidelines for renal colic management.

City, University of London and St George's, University of London , London ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.735.title: 154 Recovering From Multiple Missed Torsions: A Service Improvement in a District General Hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.735.abstract: Abstract Aim Testicular torsion (TT) is a time-critical urological emergency in which delayed recognition can lead to testicular loss and medicolegal risk. Following five cases of ‘missed torsion’ at Wexham Park Hospital (2021-2022), this project aimed to evaluate a dedicated TT pathway designed to reduce diagnostic delay, standardise risk assessment and improve patient safety. Method Serious incidents were thematically analysed to identify contributory factors. Patient journey was audited for delays; TWIST scores were calculated retrospectively and compared with operative findings. A new TT pathway was implemented in 2023, incorporating: (1) expedited referral from triage, (2) an electronic TWIST-based risk stratification tool, and (3) targeted education for ED and urology teams. Outcomes were re-audited in 2025. Results Before pathway implementation, mean times from ED presentation and decision-to-operate to theatre were 276 and 200 minutes respectively, with TWIST scores calculated in just 3.6% of cases. Retrospective calculation showed a correlation between TWIST score and confirmed TT. From implementation to re-audit no missed torsions were reported. Re-audit (June - September 2025) demonstrated reduced mean times to theatre (162 minutes from presentation; 100 minutes from decision-to-operate) and TWIST score documentation in 75% of patients. High-risk TWIST scores (≥5) accurately predicted TT in all cases. Conclusion This QIP demonstrates how serious incident analysis can drive system-level change. A structured pathway, incorporating risk stratification and staff education, has reduced ‘missed torsions’ locally and reduced delays to theatre. Our findings support the role of TWIST scoring as a valuable adjunct to clinical assessment in safeguarding patients and providing high quality urological care.
affiliations: Wexham Park Hospital , Slough ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.583.title: 1268 Ensuring Accurate and Consistent Lesion Tattooing in Colonoscopy: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.583.abstract: Abstract Aim Surgical localisation of colorectal lesions relies on accurate colonoscopic tattooing. This project aimed to evaluate the baseline adherence to national tattooing standards within our endoscopy unit to quantify both under and over tattooing, assess documentation when tattoos were omitted and identify variation between endoscopists. Improvement targets will inform subsequent interventions. Method All colonoscopy reports between March 2021 and January 2025 were reviewed. Lesions were categorised as tattoo indicated or tattoo not indicated based on the JAG, St Mark's and Rex' criteria. Reports were analysed for tattoo placement, anatomical location, documentation of lesion distance from the anal verge, and any recorded reason for omitting tattoos. Individual endoscopist compliance was calculated Results A total of 147 lesions were located in areas where tattooing was indicated. Of these, 60.05% were tattooed and 39.45% were not. Compliance varied by location, with higher tattooing rates in the transverse (87.5%) and descending colon (70.6%), and lower rates in the sigmoid colon and lesions >20 cm from the anal verge (both 50%). Among 121 lesions where tattoos were not recommended, 8.26% were tattooed unnecessarily. Endoscopist performance showed wide variability: 12 achieved 100% compliance, while 14 demonstrated <50% compliance. Conclusions Baseline results demonstrate suboptimal adherence to tattooing standards, unnecessary tattooing in some cases, and significant practitioner variation. Cycle 1 interventions include guideline posters, mandatory documentation prompts and improved reporting of lesion distance with an aim to improve compliance, with re-measurement planned for cycle 2.
affiliations: Walsall Manor Hospital , Walsall ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.629.title: 377 From Uncertainty to Mastery: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Enhance Resident Doctor Confidence in Surgical Topics
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.629.abstract: Abstract Aim Developing surgical knowledge is key to foundation and surgical training, yet variable clinical exposure and limited teaching can leave knowledge lacking. Down trending local teaching scores from the 2025 GMC Survey (from 58.75 in 2024 to 45.66 in 2025) highlighted this challenge within the general surgery department. A quality improvement initiative using structured sessions, feedback, and evaluation aimed to aimed to transform uncertainty into mastery, improving both confidence and competence across surgical domains. Method Twenty surgical residents listed topics they lacked confidence in via survey. Teaching leads grouped topics, shared the list and scheduled weekly one-hour resident-led sessions. Feedback were collected before and after assessing change in confidence levels, knowledge gained, engagement, and facilitator effectiveness, with qualitative responses detailing specific knowledge gained. Results Twenty doctors attended six teaching sessions (Sept–Oct 2025). Average confidence on surgical topics rose from 4.35 pre-session to 7.5 afterwards. All participants rated sessions as useful, reported learning new material, and found facilitators engaging. Qualitative feedback detailed specific knowledge and skills gained, highlighting improved competence across an array of surgical topics. Conclusions This resident-led QI initiative improved confidence and knowledge of surgical topics. Increased self-reported confidence and unanimously positive feedback demonstrated empowering trainees to identify and deliver teaching on areas of uncertainty is an effective strategy for bridging knowledge gaps. Continued implementation of this model is currently being undertaken with future cohorts and has the potential to strengthen surgical training quality.
affiliations: Frimley Park Hospital , Camberley ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.570.title: 772 Improving Drug Safety in Major Amputation Patients: Outcomes of a Quality-Improvement Initiative
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.570.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate postoperative weight measurement is crucial for safe prescribing following major lower-limb amputation. This audit assessed the quality of postoperative weight-recording practices, the impact on dosing of weight-dependent medications, and the effectiveness of a targeted quality-improvement intervention. Method 66 patients who underwent major lower-limb amputation in 2024, at a Tertiary Vascular Centre, were identified. Data collected retrospectively included timing of pre- and post-operative weights, theoretical and actual need for dose adjustments for medications (DOACs, Low Molecular Weight Heparin, paracetamol, teicoplanin, local anaesthetic infusions) and whether these adjustments were made. Theoretical estimates assumed a 5% weight loss after Below-Knee Amputations and 7.5% after Above-Knee Amputations. A subsequent intervention, intraoperative weighing of amputated limbs to calculate postoperative weights, was introduced. A re-audit of five patients assessed the impact. Results In Cycle 1, 74.2% of patients were reweighed postoperatively, but only 36.4% within one week. 27% of patients were never reweighed. Only 54.5% of patients had both pre- and post-operative weights documented. 12 postoperative weights were inaccurate and were excluded. 11 patients (30.6%) required dose adjustments based on true weight change, yet 6 of them received incorrect doses. Theoretically, at least 23 patients (35%) required medication-dose changes. After the intervention, all Cycle 2 patients had accurate postoperative weights, 60% were reweighed within one week, and all required dose changes were correctly implemented. Conclusions Poor availability of accurate postoperative weights after major amputation poses a significant medication-safety risk. Intraoperative limb weighing is a simple intervention that could improve weight documentation and enhance patient safety.
affiliations: Aintree University Hospital , Liverpool ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.770.title: 83 From Decision to Discharge: Enhancing Quality of Care in Major Lower Limb Amputation
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.770.abstract: Abstract Aim Major lower limb amputation (MLLA) is a critical intervention most often performed for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) or diabetic foot infection (DFI). Over 5,000 MLLAs are performed annually in the UK and are associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Optimising peri-operative care is vital to improving survival, rehabilitation and quality of life. Method A retrospective audit evaluated peri-operative care and outcomes for patients undergoing MLLA at Sunderland Royal Hospital between August 2024 and March 2025. Practice was assessed against national standards from VSGBI and NECPOD. Key domains included consultant review, operative timing, prophylaxis, MDT involvement, patient education and outcomes. Results 45 eligible cases were identified. Compliance was 100% for consultant review <24h, antibiotic/VTE prophylaxis and the below: above-knee ratio was 2:1, meeting standards. 100% received physio input, though only 29% were reviewed pre-operatively. Only 67% of cases were performed <48h of decision and just 45% of diabetic patients were seen by the diabetic specialist team. Stump complications occurred in 20% of patients; 83% of those with infection had poor glycaemic control. Length of stay exceeded 30 days for 44% of patients and 6-month mortality was 22%. 0% of patients received formal information about MLLA. Conclusion Compliance was largely achieved but diabetes specialist involvement, early physiotherapy, discharge planning and patient education require improvement. A patient information leaflet and enhanced MDT pathways have been implemented, with re-audit underway against the 2024 SVS-ERAS consensus statement. We have liaised with the other vascular centres in the North East to drive regional quality improvement.
affiliations: Sunderland Royal Hospital , Sunderland ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.625.title: 301 Casting Techniques Teaching at Colchester Hospital: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.625.abstract: Abstract Aim Orthopaedic casting is used to immobilise limb fractures. When applied correctly, casts reduce pain and swelling and can avoid the need for fixation. When applied poorly however, casts can cause pressure sores and rarely, compartment syndrome. Casts are applied regularly by SHOs in our department, yet currently they receive no formal training. This project aimed to improve patient outcomes by providing training in casting techniques through a practical course. Method A pre-course survey assessing clinical knowledge and confidence in applying below-elbow and below-knee backslabs was distributed among Orthopaedic SHOs at Colchester Hospital. A face-to-face practical course was delivered by plaster room practitioners and an orthopaedic registrar focusing on expert demonstrations, supervised hands-on practice with concurrent feedback, and interactive discussion around manipulation techniques. A post-course survey was circulated evaluate the session and measure any qualitative or quantitative improvement. Results Nine Senior House Officers completed the pre-course assessment form. Eight of them had no prior formal practical training in orthopaedic casting. All eight attendees rated the session’s quality at 5 out of 5 and found the content useful for their daily practice. Their reported confidence levels increased from 60 to 86.67% The average clinical knowledge score significantly improved from 60% to 82.5%. Conclusions The project identified a significant gap in casting technique training among resident doctors. To address this, we organised a structured practical session that substantially enhanced participants’ confidence and knowledge. Consequently, we strongly recommend casting training be made an integral part of the trauma and orthopaedics departmental induction, along with quarterly refresher workshops.
affiliations: Chesterfield Royal Hospital , Chesterfield ,
ESNEFT - Ipswich Hospital , Ipswich ,
ESNEFT - Colchester Hospital , Colchester ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.578.title: 1075 Local Prostate Cancer Guidelines: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.578.abstract: Abstract Aim Clinicians reported uncertainty in managing patients with localized prostate cancer (PCa), leading to inconsistent care, inefficient use of senior time, and variation in management pathways. This project aimed to develop and implement a unified local PCa guideline to improve clinicians’ confidence, standardise care, and optimise patient outcomes. Method A quality improvement project was conducted using a baseline questionnaire distributed to all members of the urology department. The nine-item survey assessed professional role, familiarity with existing PCa guidelines (NICE, EAU, Northern Cancer Network), confidence in explaining care pathways, and ability to request appropriate investigations or oncology referrals. Baseline results informed the development of a comprehensive local guideline. This guideline was disseminated via email, digital folders, and printed copies placed in clinical and on-call areas. Planned evaluation includes repeat questionnaires, structured feedback, and short interviews. Results Fifteen staff members responded: 5 consultants, 5 registrars, 1 specialist nurse, 1 SHO, and 3 FY1s. Overall, 60% reported limited or no understanding of PCa guidelines. Despite good awareness of NICE (9/15) and EAU (11/15) guidance, fewer clinicians reported routinely using them. Confidence gaps were notable: 53% were not confident discussing PCa care pathways, 33% were uncertain when requesting investigations, and 53% did not know how to refer patients to oncology. Most respondents (93%) agreed that a local guideline would be beneficial. Conclusions Marked variability in clinicians’ knowledge and confidence demonstrated the need for a streamlined local PCa guideline. The implemented guideline aims to improve consistency, efficiency, and quality of care, with ongoing evaluation planned to assess its impact.
affiliations: James Cook University Hospital , Middlesbrough ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.785.title: 1414 Improving the Detection and Initial Management of Phantom Limb Pain Post-Amputation: A Close-Looped Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.785.abstract: Abstract Background Phantom Limb Pain (PLP) is a common, distressing neuropathic syndrome affecting up to 80% of post-amputation patients. If untreated, PLP often rapidly progresses into debilitating chronic pain syndrome that severely impedes rehabilitation, prosthesis use, and overall quality of life. Despite NICE guidelines advocating for early neuropathic treatment, acute surgical care frequently fails to meet this standard, contributing to significant patient morbidity and increased healthcare costs. Method A two-cycle closed loop audit was performed at a major trauma centre, on all major limb amputation patients (Pre: N=48, Post: N=27). The initial intervention included targeted educational sessions and informational posters for junior ward doctors. We measured PLP assessment, Pain Team referral, neuropathic medication initiation within 48 hours, and discharge documentation. Results The intervention successfully improved referral of PLP to the pain team, which increased by 15 percentage points (from 52% to 67%. Conversely, documentation of PLP assessment within 48 hours post-operatively paradoxically reduced from 44% to 33% The initiation of new neuropathic medication within 48 hours also dropped slightly from 42% to 37%, while discharge plan documentation saw a minimal rise from 21% to 22%. Conclusions Junior doctor education was insufficient to overcome entrenched systemic barriers to care. The failure to improve assessment and prescribing highlights a need to error-proof the clinical process rather than just improving awareness. The next QI cycle will address this by implementing an Electronic Prescribing System (EPS) Amputation Order Set and a Standardised Discharge Documentation Template to compel immediate and correct treatment initiation and ensure a comprehensive, patient-centred discharge plan.
affiliations: Royal Preston Hospital , Preston ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.572.title: 893 A Quality Improvement Webinar Series: Enhancing Resident Doctors’ Confidence in Specialty Training Applications
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.572.abstract: Abstract Aim UK resident doctors need to apply for specialty training during their second year of foundation training. This leads to resident doctors reporting feeling rushed into making this decision and lacking confidence in the application process. Mind the Bleep (MTB) is a free medical education platform that produces medical education resources. We organised a quality improvement (QI) webinar series that provides insights into UK specialty training pathways aimed at improving the accessibility of accurate career-related information and demonstrate an increase in participants’ confidence from baseline to post-webinar evaluation. Method A webinar series on specialty training pathways structured to include application process, insight into the daily life of doctors in that specialty, question and answer (Q&A) section. The effectiveness of the webinar was evaluated by mixed methods feedback that included both a five-point Likert scale and free-text answers. Free-text answers were used to guide further webinar content. Results Delivered eight webinars on topics such as core surgical training, obstetrics and gynaecology, and urology. This series had 216 (range 12-47) live attendees and 1938 (range 122-641) asynchronous views on the MTB YouTube channel 1 year (range 8-15 months) post-upload. The level of confidence was significantly improved across the webinars (p<0.05), and 198 (91.6%) attendees reported the content as helpful, with 139(64%) reporting it as “very helpful”. The Q&A section was mentioned as a positive component across all webinars. Conclusions This QI project was successful in delivering helpful information that increased the participants’ confidence in the application process for specialty training in the UK.

Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust , Kent ,
United Lincolnshire Hospitals NHS Trust , Lincoln ,
Calderdale and Huddersfield NHS Foundation Trust , Huddersfield ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.476.title: 832 Quality of Life Outcomes After Septoplasty
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.476.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate current evidence on postoperative quality of life following septoplasty and identify interventions shown to reduce healing time and optimise patient recovery. Method A structured literature review was conducted using PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Library databases. Search terms included “septoplasty”, “quality of life”, “NOSE score”, “SNOT-22”, “postoperative recovery”, and “healing time”. Studies published in English between 2010 and 2025 were included. Evidence was synthesised narratively, with particular focus on patient-reported outcome measures and strategies reported to enhance recovery. Results Across the literature, septoplasty consistently demonstrated significant improvement in nasal obstruction and disease-specific quality of life, with mean NOSE score reductions of 40–60% in most cohorts. Factors associated with delayed recovery included smoking, allergic rhinitis, untreated turbinate hypertrophy and poor adherence to postoperative advice. Several interventions were associated with faster healing and improved early outcomes, including regular saline irrigation, intranasal corticosteroids, avoidance of nasal packing, and structured postoperative education. Enhanced patient instructions and early follow-up were associated with better symptom control and fewer unplanned reviews. Evidence for novel interventions such as biodegradable splints and absorbable materials also suggested reduced discomfort and quicker return to baseline activity. Conclusions The literature indicates that septoplasty significantly improves quality of life and that recovery can be optimised through targeted postoperative strategies. Consistent use of saline irrigation, appropriate pharmacological therapy, avoiding unnecessary packing and high-quality patient education appear effective in reducing healing time. Standardised postoperative pathways may further improve outcomes and overall patient experience.
affiliations: University College Dublin , Dublin ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.242.title: 746 Optimising Delivery of Postoperative ERAS Pathways in Colorectal Surgery: A Multidisciplinary Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.242.abstract: Abstract Aim Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) guidelines are used internationally, aiming to minimise perioperative stress, maintain physiological function and support patient recovery through pre-, intra- and post-operative interventions. The audit aimed to assess adherence to the post-operative ERAS guidelines in the local colorectal department. Method A retrospective audit was undertaken of patients undergoing elective colorectal procedures via the ERAS pathway over a 9-month period. Local standards based on international ERAS guidelines were used to audit prescribing of regular medications and analgesia, nutrition, mobilisation and duration of catheter and patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) use. Multidisciplinary feedback was obtained on findings and an admissions protocol was developed. A flowchart depicting the protocol was placed at workstations. New ERAS patients were specifically highlighted on handover documents and templates developed for ward-round use. A re-audit was initiated following introduction of the protocol. Results The initial audit included 68 patients, 51 of whom were on regular medications, however only 37% had these prescribed on the day of surgery. Preliminary re-audit findings over 3 months demonstrate improvement in prescribing rates to 62%. Documentation of the reasoning for extended use of catheters and PCAs was initially missing in 45% and 74% of cases respectively making analysis difficult. Early post-intervention results indicate improvement in documentation, although a comprehensive analysis is ongoing and will be completed over the coming months. Conclusions A multidisciplinary protocol improved adherence to colorectal ERAS guidelines. Sustained improvement will require ongoing engagement from the MDT and education of doctors rotating into the department.
affiliations: Newcastle-Upon-Tyne Hospitals , Newcastle-Upon-Tyne ,
Newcastle University , Newcastle-Upon-Tyne ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.546.title: 96 Enhancing Referrals to Our Surgical Ambulatory Unit: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.546.abstract: Abstract Aim The surgical ambulatory unit (SAU) is a vital aspect of our general surgical department within the Southern Health & Social Care Trust. It reduces unnecessary admissions and facilitates early discharge. It is imperative that accurate clinical information is available for the ambulatory team to perform effective and efficient reviews. The aim of this quality improvement project is to enhance referrals to our SAU in line with National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) QS174 and Royal College of Surgeons England (RCSEng) safe handover guidelines. Method A standard was set with regards to adequate referral information (diagnosis, background & plan) with referral data collected retrospectively in the first cycle through our electronic health record and SAU calendar. Departmental intervention was made through team education and reminder prompts across the department. Post-intervention re-audit was then undertaken. Statistical analysis was performed using chi-square using graph pad, a p value <0.05 was deemed significant. Results 57 appointments were analysed in the first audit cycle and 67 appointments post-intervention in the second cycle. Improvement was seen across all referral information domains including diagnosis (p<0.0001), background (p<0.0001) and plan (p=0.0007). Referrals with no information was significantly reduced (p=0.0063). Conclusions Enhancing SAU referrals by including diagnosis, background and plan is a straightforward and easy means to provide adequate referral information to the SAU team. This can improve efficiency, effective patient reviews as well as adherence to NICE and RCSEng guidelines re clinical handover and governance.
affiliations: Southern Health & Social Care Trust , Craigavon ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.013.title: 787 Improving the Quality of Salivary Gland Cancer Care Through Research Methodology: Systematic Review of Outcome Reporting in Salivary Gland Cancer Trials
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.013.abstract: Abstract Background Salivary Gland Cancers (SGC) are a rare and diverse group of cancers, that present diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. A barrier to improved patient care is the lack of standardisation in outcome reporting, preventing comparison across SGC studies. The aim of this review is to categorise the outcomes that are currently reported amongst the salivary gland academic literature, with future direction of informing the development of a Core Outcome Set (COS) and improving research methodology. Method A systematic review following PRISMA methodology was conducted. PubMed and Scopus databases were reviewed. Inclusion criteria allowed for all primary research focussing on patient groups with diagnosed SGC, where outcomes were reported following intervention. 95 papers were included in the study following removal of duplicates and application of inclusion/exclusion criteria. Outcomes were categorised in several domains including mortality, radiological outcomes, clinical outcomes, adverse events and patient reported outcomes, as per COMET taxonomy. Results The majority of studies included were retrospective cohort studies. The most common outcomes reported included survival and radiological markers of loco-regional recurrence. There is heterogeneity of reporting other clinical outcomes and adverse events. Patient reported outcomes and treatment burden were strikingly underreported domains. Conclusions This review highlights the significant gaps that currently exist in outcome reporting for SGC. This is particularly striking with regards to patient reported outcomes along with minimal standardisation in reporting of clinical outcomes and adverse events. These findings highlight the need for a COS for SGC trials, to improve comparability and quality of studies, thus positively impacting patient-centred care.
