Wrightington, Wigan and Leigh NHS Foundation Trust , Wigan ,
Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust , Manchester ,
University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust , Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.277.title: 1340 Evaluating the Quality of Oral Care on Surgical Wards: A Cross-Sectional Survey
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.277.abstract: Abstract Aim Oral care is frequently under-prioritised in hospital, particularly for those reliant on support from others, with hospitalisation being strongly associated with a rapid decline in oral health. This audit aims to evaluate the quality of oral care provided on surgical wards, identify any gaps in practice and align care with national guidance for oral health in care homes and hospitals. Method A cross-sectional audit was conducted across 3 surgical wards at a single institution over a 4-week period. Structured surveys were distributed to inpatients and staff members. The audit was registered with the local governance team (GSACT2025409). Results Fifty-nine inpatients and 12 staff members participated. Among staff, 38% reported never receiving training in assessing or providing oral care, with 83% expressing a desire for additional training. The main barriers to provision were patient compliance (31%) and lack of time (15%). Regarding patients, almost 75% of patients were not asked about oral care needs on admission resulting in teeth and dentures being cleaned nearly half as frequently in hospital than home (7 vs 13 times per week; P>0.05). Conclusions This audit is the first study reporting on the unmet needs in provision of oral care on surgical wards in the UK and identified several key barriers. The findings suggest that oral hygiene is not routinely prioritised, despite its recognised impact on infection prevention, nutrition and prolonging admission. Addressing gaps in staff confidence and knowledge and ensuring consistent access to oral care tools will be key priorities in improving oral care on surgical wards.
affiliations: St Peters Hospital , Surrey ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.580.title: 1187 Improving Documentation and Provision of Smoking Cessation Advice in Vascular Surgery Inpatients: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.580.abstract: Abstract Aim Smoking cessation is a key modifiable risk factor in vascular disease and reduces postoperative complications, yet inpatient documentation of smoking status and provision of cessation advice is often suboptimal. This project aimed to improve these processes using a low-cost intervention. Method A prospective quality improvement project was conducted on vascular surgery inpatients in a tertiary centre. Data included age, gender, Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation (SIMD), smoking status, and whether cessation advice or nicotine replacement therapy was provided during admission. A before-and-after study was conducted with data collected at baseline and after the first intervention, on independent cohorts. The intervention consisted of eye-catching posters on wards with digital dissemination to staff. Statistical analysis was performed using R. Results Baseline (n=39) and Cycle 1 (n=33) cohorts were comparable in age (p=0.83), gender (p=0.56), SIMD decile (p=0.33), and proportion of current smokers (26% vs 21%, p=0.87). Documentation of smoking status during admission increased from 82% to 88% (p=0.72). Provision of smoking cessation advice on admission rose from 10% to 43% (p=0.25), and at any point during admission from 30% to 57% (p=0.35). While not statistically significant, these improvements demonstrate a positive trend. Conclusions Simple, low-cost and sustainable interventions, such as posters, can enhance improved smoking cessation practices in vascular surgery inpatients. Early trends are encouraging, and further PDSA cycles with active strategies, such as staff training, may achieve sustained improvement.
affiliations: NHS Tayside , Dundee ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.567.title: 675 Improving Efficiency and Access to ENT Biopsy Services, a Quality Improvement Project on the OPLA Clinic
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.567.abstract: Abstract The use of outpatient local anaesthetic (OPLA) procedures to reduce operating theatre burden is well-established, but its application to complex ENT diagnostic interventions, such as endoscopy- or ultrasound-guided biopsies, remains fairly novel. This Quality Improvement Project (QIP) evaluated the performance of an OPLA clinic in collecting biopsies and determined the resulting time to diagnosis for malignant and non-malignant conditions. The QIP aimed to assess biopsy adequacy, determine the need for subsequent biopsy under general anaesthetic (GA), calculate median time to diagnosis (MTTD), and gather staff feedback. All OPLA procedures performed at Ninewells Hospital, Dundee, from April 2024 to April 2025 were reviewed. Data focused on procedure type, biopsy adequacy, time to diagnosis, and necessity for further diagnostic steps. Out of 89 biopsies reviewed, 82 (92%) were adequate, with 79 (89%) requiring no further procedures. The MTTD for adequate samples was 12 days. The clinic successfully diagnosed 83 lesions, including 65 benign (MTTD 12 days) and 15 malignant biopsies (MTTD 9 days). For the small subset of inadequate samples requiring subsequent procedures, the MTTD significantly increased to 27.5 days. Staff feedback indicated high role clarity and adequate training, though communication and equipment availability were challenges. The OPLA clinic effectively delivered timely, convenient, and accurate biopsy diagnoses for the majority of patients, thus significantly reducing operating theatre demand. Furthermore, delivering these high-volume procedures in an outpatient setting is highly cost-effective compared to the expenses associated with utilising theatre time and general anaesthesia. This framework supports the expansion of OPLA ENT services.
affiliations: University of Dundee , Dundee ,
NHS Tayside , Dundee ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.584.title: 1349 Adapting Systems to Improve Imaging Adequacy in Patients With Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.584.abstract: Abstract Background Preoperative imaging is essential for planning abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) intervention. Variability in imaging protocols, particularly the omission of the thoracic aorta, can lead to missed pathology, delays in planning for complex endovascular repairs, repeat imaging, and increased exposure to contrast, radiation, and increased financial burden to the trust and the NHS ultimately. Aim To assess the adequacy of AAA imaging across the South Devon Vascular Network, identify the frequency and causes of repeat scans, and evaluate the impact of radiology request wording on scan quality. Method We retrospectively reviewed imaging for patients assessed for AAA intervention. We reviewed if imaging included aortic arch, wording of request and need for repeat imaging. Following first cycle, clinicians were asked to include ‘thoracic aorta’ in CT requests, and a new order entry (‘CT Whole Aorta’) was introduced on the EPIC system protocoled to include the aortic arch. Results Complete imaging of the aorta significantly improved from 45% in cycle 1 (n=80), to 80% in cycle 2 (n=60, p<0.0005). Repeat imaging decreased between cycles from 18% to 13% although not significantly (p=0.23) Requests specifically included thoracic aorta in 15% and 17% respectively. Conclusions Imaging completeness improved between cycles with a new protocol despite no significant improvement in wording of request. These findings suggest that sustainable improvements in imaging quality are best achieved through system-level changes rather than reliance on individual request detail. Embedding standardized protocols into referral workflows is essential to ensure consistently adequate imaging for AAA planning, reduce delays, and improve patient safety.
affiliations: Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust , Exeter ,
Royal Devon University Hospital , Exeter ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.588.title: 245 Quality of Life and Functional Outcomes Following Three Methods of Oesophagectomy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag063.588.abstract: Abstract Aim Functional outcomes and Health Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) scores were compared following three surgical methods of oesophagectomy - open oesophagectomy (OE); laparoscopically-assisted hybrid minimally invasive oesophagectomy (HMIE) or robot-assisted minimally-invasive oesophagectomy (RAMIE). Method Oesophagectomies conducted at Royal Preston Hospital were evaluated between August 2017 - March 2023. An in-depth questionnaire was sent to patients according to their type of oesophagectomy (OE/HMIE/RAMIE) and followed up by telephone. Four main functional domains were assessed: mobility, functional wellbeing, physical wellbeing and emotional wellbeing. Answers were translated into numerical values, which formed the HRQoL total. The analysis between surgical modalities (OE, HMIE and RAMIE) was conducted through a one-way ANOVA test and analysed using SPSS to determine whether there were any statistically significant differences between the method of surgery and HRQoL. Results Fifty patients participated in a telephone questionnaire (OE:29; HMIE:10; RAMIE:11) . The total HRQoL scores showed no statistically significant difference in functional outcomes between all three surgical modalities (p=0.619). There was equal reporting of symptoms severity across all three surgical modalities, such as pain (p=0.768), dysphagia requiring endoscopic intervention (p=0.964), dumping syndrome (p=0.849), ability to return to normal activities (p=0.307) and return to work (p=0.729). Conclusions Despite variations in technique and the physical trauma associated with open surgery, this study found no difference in patient outcomes or satisfaction. Therefore, a more in-depth study is required to assess HRQoL and other perceived benefits of robotic surgery over open surgery, determining which is truly the best modality for the patient.
affiliations: Royal Preston Hospital , Preston ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.090.title: SP 7.03 Patients’ Perceptions of a Rehabilitation Intervention to Restore Quality of Life Following Oesophageal Cancer Surgery: A Qualitative Study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.090.abstract: Abstract Aims Participation in a structured post-oesophagectomy rehabilitation programme improves vital health-related quality of life (HR-QOL) domains in survivorship. To achieve optimal HR-QOL improvements, patient engagement is important. This qualitative study assessed patients’ perceptions of participating in a home-based, post-oesophagectomy rehabilitation programme comprising exercises and multidisciplinary input. Methods This qualitative study was conducted as part of the Fitness AfteR Oesophagectomy (FARO) trial, which assessed the impact of a 12-week post-oesophagectomy rehabilitation programme upon HR-QOL and cardiorespiratory fitness. Focus groups with patients randomised to each group (REHAB-intervention; NO-REHAB-control) were individually conducted. Focus group discussions were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. A thematic content analysis approach was utilised to understand patients’ perceptions, facilitators and barriers to engagement. Results Thirteen patients (median age 64, range 48-77) attended the REHAB (n=7) and NO-REHAB (n=6) focus groups, respectively. Five themes were identified: (1) individual variation in recovery and impact on physical activity (2) changes in physical strength and body composition (3) digestive dysfunction (4) challenges with oral intake (5) long-term impact of oesophageal cancer surgery on physical strength and regular activities. Structured guidance and regular clinical contact were recognised as facilitators to participation. Barriers included side effects associated with adjuvant treatment (fatigue, nausea) and ongoing digestive issues. Participants highlighted the need for psychological support, structured post-oesophagectomy physical activity guidance and greater dietary counselling as factors that may aid swifter recovery. Conclusion Post-oesophagectomy rehabilitation can help address key patient concerns and restore key HR-QOL domains in the post-operative recovery phase and into survivorship.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.536.title: EP 031 Quality Improvement Project: The Use of Routine Blood Testing in General Surgery; Are we Testing too Much and is it of Clinical Significance?
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.536.abstract: Abstract Aim Each year, the National Health Service (NHS) spends approximately £2.2 billion on blood tests and evidence suggests that 25% are unnecessary repeats placing a burden on a financially stretched organisation. This paves the way to analyse patterns, outcomes and cost effectiveness of routine blood testing with the aim to improve current practices and enhance resource utilisation in the NHS. Method Collected initial data over 3 weeks to assess baseline frequency of bloods tests for 6 conditions: gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, colorectal resection with anastomosis, post laparoscopic appendicectomy, complex hernia repair. After analysis a poster was generated highlighting a call for reduction of blood tests in the department. The second intervention included a condition specific guideline poster using feedback from departmental consultant surgeons. Data was collected again to assess for improvement. Results Overall, there was a majority decrease of blood tests performed and the average cost of blood tests per patient decreased by 24% by the end of Cycle 2. There was no statistically significant difference between the mean blood test numbers of the cycles (p = 0.12). Furthermore, there was a discrepancy between the frequency of blood tests performed and suggested from expert opinion across all conditions. Conclusion There was an initial reduction in the frequency of blood tests thus reducing cost and highlighting the issue. Whilst the project had limited statistical power and a small sample size, it paves the way for further investigation beyond a single centre study to improve and enhance resource utilisation in the NHS.
affiliations: NHS East Kent Hospitals University Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.088.title: SP 6.15 Evaluating Quality of Colorectal Cancer Surgery Across Elective and Emergency Health Systems: A Secondary Analysis of Prospective Cohort Studies in 95 Countries
authors: NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.088.abstract: Abstract Background We aimed to understand differences in surgical quality between patients with potentially curative colorectal cancer undergoing emergency or elective resection. Methods This pre-planned secondary analysis included patients undergoing only curative-intent surgery for colorectal cancer from three contemporary global prospective cohort studies (GlobalSurg-3, n=5506; CovidSurg-Cancer, n=6719; APOLLO, n=876). Hierarchical multilevel logistic regression models quantified associations between urgency of surgery (elective vs emergency) and surgical quality, measured by margin-positive resection, adjusting for patient-, disease- and health-system factors. Bootstrap multivariable simulations evaluated effect modification by country income, cancer stage and location. Results We included 13,101 patients across 95 countries. Overall, 678 (5.4%) had margin-positive resections, with higher rates in emergency than elective surgery (13.7% vs 4.5%; p<0.0001). In adjusted models, emergency surgery was associated with increased odds of margin-positive resections (adjusted odds ratio 2.45, 95% CI 1.86-3.22), consistent across all country income groups and robust to alternate health-system indicators. Bootstrap-derived absolute risk differences revealed the greatest disparities in patients with stage III-IV rectal cancers; absolute differences of 12.6% (95% CI 10.2-15.7) in high-income countries, 19.0% (95% CI 13.6-23.9) in upper-middle-income countries, and 14.1% (95% CI 10.9-16.5) in lower-middle- and low-income countries. Conclusion Emergency surgery conferred a two-to-three-fold increased risk of margin-positive resections globally, independent of resource availability, exposing a neglected area of global surgical practice. For patients presenting as an emergency with potentially curative disease, enhanced decision-making around resectability, ensuring specialist surgeon availability, and developing bridge-to-surgery pathways represent immediate, low-cost strategies to improve global cancer outcomes.
affiliations: NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery, School of Health Sciences, University of Birmingham ,

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.237.title: TPT 6.15 Leadership in Acute Pancreatitis Care: An A3 Thinking Process for Service and Financial Improvement
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.237.abstract: Abstract Aims This study aimed to identify and address critical clinical and operational gaps in the management of acute pancreatitis. By applying the A3 Thinking Process, the project sought to align local practice with BSG, NICE, and IAP standards to improve patient outcomes and service efficiency. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted over a nine-month period involving 57 eligible surgical patients diagnosed with AP using the modified Atlanta criteria. Current performance was measured against established quality standards, including diagnostic timing, ultrasound imaging within 24 hours, severity scoring, and definitive management within two weeks. A Root Cause Analysis was performed to identify systematic barriers to care. Results While diagnostic (100%) and aetiological (91.3%) standards were met, significant gaps were identified in other areas: USS imaging within 24 hours was 43% (Standard: 95%), severity scoring was 26.31% (Standard: 100%), and definitive management within two weeks was 9% (Standard: 100%). The observed mortality rate was 12%, exceeding the <10% threshold. Operationally, delays led to an average extended length of stay of 2.7 days per patient and an 18% 30-day readmission rate, resulting in an estimated annual avoidable cost of £152,000. Conclusions The A3 analysis revealed that inconsistent pathways and resource constraints significantly impact AP care. To bridge these gaps, a strategic action plan has been developed, including the implementation of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP), expedited imaging pathways, MDT weekly ward rounds and dedicated surgical slots for definitive management. These interventions aim to reduce mortality, decrease length of stay, and achieve substantial financial savings.
affiliations: Medway Maritime Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.262.title: TPT 8.04 Assessing the Impact of Rehabilitation on Quality of Life Following Oesophageal Cancer Surgery: The FARO Randomised Controlled Trial
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.262.abstract: Abstract Aims Health-related quality of life (HR-QOL) is adversely impacted following oesophageal cancer surgery. This trial investigated whether a structured post-oesophagectomy rehabilitation programme improves HR-QOL and cardiorespiratory fitness in the first 6 months following an oesophagectomy. Methods The Fitness AfteR Oesophagectomy (FARO) trial randomly assigned patients to either receive routine clinical care alone (NO-REHAB) or participate in a rehabilitation programme alongside routine clinical care (REHAB). The REHAB group completed a 12-week rehabilitation programme comprising moderate-intensity aerobic and resistance exercises with weekly telephone follow-up and multidisciplinary care input. HR-QOL (primary outcome) was assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and OG25 questionnaires. Cardiorespiratory fitness (secondary outcome) was measured with the 6-minute walk test (6MWT). Outcomes were measured at baseline(T0), 6 weeks post-hospital discharge(T1) and 6 months post-oesophagectomy(T2). Results Sixty patients (median age 64 years, range 41–82) were randomised to REHAB (n=31) or NO-REHAB (n=29). At T1, REHAB was associated with significantly greater improvements in physical functioning (median change 23.00 vs 6.67; p=0.007; ES=0.40) and social functioning (33.33 vs 33.33; p=0.014; ES=0.37). Symptom scores favoured REHAB for fatigue (−33.33 vs −22.23; p=0.156; ES=0.21), and reflux (0.00 vs 16.67; p=0.032; ES=0.32). 6MWT distance did not differ between groups (390 m vs 400 m; p=0.302). Benefits associated with rehabilitation were attenuated by T2. Conclusion A monitored rehabilitation programme improved key HR-QOL domains in the early recovery phase following an oesophagectomy.
affiliations: Translational and Clinical Research Institute, Newcastle University ,

Sir Bobby Robson Cancer Trials Research Centre, Northern Centre for Cancer Care, The Newcastle Upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.081.title: SP 6.08 A Quality Improvement Project to Improve Compliance with Follow-Up Chest X-Ray Guidance for Pneumonia on a General Surgery Ward
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.081.abstract: Abstract Objectives National guidance recommends consideration of a follow-up chest X-ray (CXR) 6–8 weeks after inpatient treatment for pneumonia in patients at higher risk of underlying malignancy. This quality improvement project aimed to assess compliance with follow-up CXR guidance for patients admitted with pneumonia under general surgery and identify areas for improvement in discharge documentation. Methods A retrospective review was conducted of patients admitted under general surgery with either community-acquired or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Inclusion criteria were: admission under general surgery, CXR reported as infective changes, and risk factors warranting consideration of follow-up imaging (age >50 years and smoking history). Data were collected for 25 patients. Discharge summaries were reviewed to determine whether follow-up CXR was documented or arranged. Clinical context was considered when assessing appropriateness, including frailty, respiratory history, and normal admission imaging. Results Of 25 patients identified, 24 met criteria for consideration of follow-up CXR. Only 2 patients (8%) had follow-up imaging documented or arranged. One patient was discharged to hospice care, where follow-up imaging was inappropriate. Of the remaining cohort, 10 patients met NICE criteria for follow-up imaging, while a further 12 could reasonably have been considered depending on clinical context and patient preference. Overall, compliance with guidance was low, with follow-up imaging frequently omitted from discharge summaries. Conclusions Follow-up CXR documentation for pneumonia patients under general surgery was poor despite clear guidance. Simple interventions, such as discharge summary prompts or junior doctor education, may improve compliance and reduce missed diagnoses.
affiliations: Department of General Surgery
RSCH Brighton

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.191.title: TPT 3.08 Impact of Frailty on Quality of Life At 30 and 90 Days Post Emergency Laparotomy
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.191.abstract: Abstract Aims Emergency laparotomy (EmLap) is associated with high mortality and morbidity. However, its impact on post-EmLap quality of life (QoL), particularly among frail patients, remains poorly defined. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of frailty on QoL at 30 and 90 days post-EmLap. Methods Prospectively collected data from EmLap patients age ≥40 years between May'22 and July'23 at a district general hospital were analysed. Frailty was assessed using Clinical Frailty Scale, with scores >4 as frail. QoL was measured at 30 and 90 days post-EmLap using EQ-5D-5L, including utility and EQ-VAS scores. Changes across EQ-5D-5L domains were examined. Wilcoxon signed-rank test compared utility scores between timepoints, and Mann-Whitney U test assessed differences by frailty status. Statistical significant was set at p <0.05. Results 115 EmLap patients completed the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire. 10% were frail. From 30 to 90 days post-EmLap, there was a significant improvement in median EQ-VAS scores (70 to 80) and functional recovery, particularly in usual activities. Median utility scores improved significantly over time (0.850 to 0.916, p<0.001). Although frail patients had lower utility scores at both timepoints (0.717 and 0.922 at days 30 and 90) compared with non-frail patients (0.872 and 0.916), they demonstrated a significantly greater improvement in QoL between both timepoints (p=0.041). Conclusion QoL improves between 30 and 90 days post-EmLap. Despite poorer early post-operative QoL, frail patients experience clinically meaningful recovery by 90 days. These findings support a shift toward frailty-focused EmLap pathways, embedding geriatric expertise and targeted rehabilitation to optimise patient-centred outcomes.

University of Glasgow
University of Strathclyde

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.199.title: TPT 3.16 Evaluating Suitability of Harmless Acute Pancreatitis Scoring (HAPS) and Glasgow-Imrie Scoring in Early Risk Stratification of Acute Pancreatitis: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.199.abstract: Abstract Background Acute Pancreatitis is a common presentation to the Surgical Emergency Unit (SEU), with approximately 20% of cases being severe, which carry a 13-35% mortality rate. Scoring systems exist to stratify disease severity. The Harmless Acute Pancreatitis Score (HAPS) is used to rule out severe cases. The Glasgow-Imrie score is used to identify patients at risk of severe pancreatitis. Aims This study aims to evaluate the utility and safety of using these systems to risk-stratify patients with acute pancreatitis and identify risks of uncomplicated courses and clinical deterioration. Methods A retrospective review was conducted of patients admitted to the SEU with acute pancreatitis over a six-month period. HAPS and Glasgow-Imrie scores were retrospectively calculated where existing data permitted. Outcomes assessed included disease severity indicators such as length of stay, deterioration and intensive care (ICU) admissions. Results 205 patients were analysed. HAPS scoring was completed in 201 patients. Glasgow-Imrie scoring was limited to six patients due to unavailable parameters. 15 patients (7.3%) had a complicated course, including two deaths and seven ICU admissions. A HAPS score of 0 demonstrated a negative predictive value of 98.7%. Median HAPS scores for patients who deteriorated and those admitted to ICU were 0.85 and 0.71, respectively. Glasgow-Imrie scoring could not be evaluated due to insufficient data. Conclusions HAPS may help identify patients at low risk of complications; however, low scores do not fully exclude deterioration, and higher scores do not reliably predict worse outcomes. These findings emphasise the need for clinical vigilance alongside scoring systems.
affiliations: University of Oxford
Oxford University Hospitals Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.327.title: TPW 3.15 Information Booklet to Enhance Understanding of Foundation Doctors in Managing Post-Operative Patients: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.327.abstract: Abstract Aims This quality improvement project aimed to achieve a ≥10% improvement in foundation doctors’ understanding of post-operative patient management on surgical wards. We hypothesised that a written information booklet would improve understanding more effectively than verbal explanations alone. Foundation doctors are often responsible for the initial assessment and management of post-operative surgical patients, particularly out of hours. Limited understanding of common post-operative issues may result in delayed escalation, inappropriate investigations, and suboptimal patient care. This project aimed to assess and improve foundation doctor knowledge and confidence in managing post-operative patients. Methods Foundation doctors (n=20) completed a baseline questionnaire to identify high priority topics for inclusion in the information booklet. Participants rated how informed they felt across key domains of post-operative management (including analgesia, fluid prescribing, monitoring observations, recognition of complications, and escalation) using a 0-5 Likert scale. An information booklet was co-designed, distributed, and the foundation doctor questionnaire repeated. Results Prior to booklet distribution, mean self-rated understanding of post-operative management was 3.5/5. Following distribution, this increased to 4.7/5 exceeding the project aim of ≥10% improvement. Conclusion This Project demonstrates that an evidence-based booklet is an effective and sustainable intervention for improving understanding and confidence around managing post-operative patients. By providing clear guidance aligned with local protocols, the booklet supports safer clinical decision-making and potential for wider adoption across surgical specialties and training programmes. The booklet is due to receive further feedback and final modifications.
affiliations: Guy's and St Thomas' Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.423.title: TPTh 1.10 Can Evidence-Based Prompting Enable AI to Generate UKMLA-Quality MCQs? A Blinded Evaluation
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.423.abstract: Abstract Aims Developing high-quality multiple-choice questions (MCQs) is a time-consuming process that places additional pressure on already stretched clinician-educators. Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have demonstrated promise in streamlining MCQ development and optimising the question creation workflow. While emerging evidence suggests that LLM-generated MCQs are comparable to those written by human experts, their suitability for UK Medical Licensing Assessment (UKMLA)–aligned learning has not been established. Furthermore, concerns remain regarding factual accuracy and cognitive depth. This study evaluates whether embedding an evidence-based framework into question generation enables LLMs to produce high-quality MCQs suitable for UKMLA-aligned learning and revision. Methods This is an ongoing, blinded, cross-sectional comparative evaluation study. Twenty UKMLA-mapped MCQs generated using ChatGPT and guided by the five A’s of evidence-based medicine will be compared with twenty educator-authored MCQs. Independent consultant experts, blinded to question origin, will evaluate all items. Outcomes will include perceived origin, content validity, educational value and item performance metrics, alongside time taken for question generation. Results We predict that ChatGPT-generated MCQs will be comparable to human-authored questions in quality, educational value and item performance, while being produced significantly faster. Experts are expected to be unable to distinguish question origin. Conclusion This study will provide evidence on the feasibility of using evidence-informed LLMs to support UKMLA-aligned MCQ development. Findings will help inform the role of AI in medical education, with potential to reduce educator workload while maintaining assessment quality.
affiliations: Doncaster and Bassetlaw Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Department of Clinical Medicine, School of Medicine and Population Health, The University of Sheffield

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.152.title: SP 11.12 A Systematic Review of the Methodological Quality of Randomised Trials in IBD Surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.152.abstract: Abstract Aims To examine contemporary surgical randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and appraise methodological quality, statistical robustness, and real-world applicability. Methods A systematic review of RCTs including adults with IBD undergoing surgical interventions was undertaken. Electronic databases (CENTRAL, Embase, MEDLINE) and clinical trial registries were searched (2005–2025). Dual screening, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment were performed. Trials were evaluated using PRECIS-2 and the Fragility/Reverse Fragility Index. Registered but unpublished trials were also analysed. The review was prospectively registered (CRD420251058758). Results From 5,803 identified records, 18 published RCTs and 26 registered but unpublished trials were included. Median planned sample size of published RCTs was 102 (IQR 80–143), with a median of 89 (IQR 55–114) recruited. Under-recruitment occurred in 39% (7/18) and early termination in 28% (5/18). Most studies (67%) raised some concerns about bias on RoB-2, and PRECIS-2 demonstrated predominantly pragmatic designs. Ten trials were eligible for fragility analysis; the median Fragility Index for statistically significant outcomes was 3 (IQR 1–6), and the Reverse Fragility Index was 4 (IQR 3–8). Registered, unpublished trials had a higher median intended sample size (155; IQR 93–196), with Crohn’s disease studies predominating (22/26). Conclusions Surgical RCTs in IBD are predominantly pragmatic but frequently limited by modest sample size, under-recruitment, early termination, and statistical fragility. Future trials should be larger, multicentre and collaboratively delivered to enhance power, external validity, and the evidence base for surgical management in IBD.

Yeovil District Hospital, Somerset NHS Foundation Trust , Higher Kingston, Yeovil
Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Leeds Institute of Medical Research, University of Leeds
Department of Applied Health Sciences, College of Medicine & Health, University of Birmingham

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.101.title: SP 7.17 Postoperative Outcomes and Quality of Life After Post-Cholecystectomy Bile Duct Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.101.abstract: Abstract Aim To compare quality of life (QoL) outcomes among patients who sustained bile duct injury (BDI) during laparoscopic cholecystectomy in addition to those who had an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Methods A systematic search and screening of literature was conducted resulting in 19 studies that reported QoL outcomes following BDI were. 13 studies assessed QoL using Short form 36 (SF-36), of which 5 incorporated uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy control groups and used for meta-analysis. Analysis was performed using random-effects models, calculating mean differences (MD) with 95% CI. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic. Results The 19 studies Individual study sample sizes ranged from 19 to 800 patients, with a consistent female predominance (65-70%) and mean ages ranging from 40-57 years. Meta-analysis demonstrated significantly poorer QoL in BDI patients across all 8 SF-36 domains compared with controls. Compared to physical outcomes, there were significant impairments reported in mental health domains including emotional health (MD -29.48 95% Cl -49.06, -9.91) and social functioning (MD -16.82, 95% CI -27.92, -5.71). Physical limitations, vitality, general health perception and bodily pain were also reduced. Substantial heterogeneity was present across domains (I2 72-92%), reflecting the clinical and methodological variability. Conclusion BDI following laparoscopic cholecystectomy is associated with impairments to quality of life which extend beyond physical morbidity. Significant reductions to social and emotional functioning were reported following BDI. These findings show the need for mental health support, improved patient counselling, and greater emphasis on QoL as a key outcome in BDI management and research.
affiliations: University of   Birmingham
Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.119.title: SP 9.03 MANagement of Gallstone Disease in the Older Patient (MANGO): Results & Quality of Life Outcomes from a Prospective Multicentre Cohort Study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.119.abstract: Abstract Background Gallstones are a common cause of acute surgical admission in older adults and are often associated with complications. While surgery is recommended in the general population, greater comorbidity makes decision-making more complex in older patients. This study provides prospective evidence on management strategies and quality-of-life (QoL) outcomes in this cohort. Method Trainee-led multicentre prospective cohort from nine hospitals in Southwest England. Emergency admissions in patients over 70 with symptomatic gallstone disease from 25/11/2022 to 31/03/2024. Data collected at baseline, 30-day and 1-year. Results Of 194 patients, majority received non-operative management (81.4%). They had higher co-morbidities and frailty, with a comparable age to the emergency cholecystectomy group. Thirty-six laparoscopic emergency cholecystectomies were performed, with one conversion to open and no major complications. Median length of stay was similar (7 vs 5 days, p=0.105). Gallstone-related readmission at 1-year was significantly higher following non-operative management (23.0% vs 2.9%, p=0.024), while non-biliary re-admissions were similar. One-year mortality was 12.4% in the non-operative group and 0% in the operative group. Fourteen patients underwent interval cholecystectomy. Baseline QoL was similar. At 30 days, emergency cholecystectomy produced better QoL across all GIQLI domains (p≤0.007). At 1 year, QoL remained higher after emergency cholecystectomy (123.8 vs 115.6, p=0.039), but was comparable when interval cholecystectomy patients were included. Conclusion Emergency cholecystectomy in older patients deemed suitable for surgery is associated with improved QoL scores and reduced gallstone-related re-admissions at 1-year. Interval surgery also achieved comparable outcomes, and these findings support offering surgery to appropriately selected older patients.

Stoke Mandeville Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.344.title: TPW 5.02 Improving Outcomes in No-Lap Reporting: A NELA Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.344.abstract: Abstract Aim The National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) captures outcomes for patients undergoing emergency laparotomy; however, patients in whom surgery is indicated but not performed (NoLap) are frequently under-reported. These patients tend to be HIGH-RISK: older, frailer, and have more co-morbidities which is essential in identifying Care Gaps, Understanding variations in decision-making and improving future patient management. Method A quality improvement project using two PDSA cycles was undertaken between March 2024 and October 2025. Baseline review demonstrated no recorded NoLap cases and limited awareness of the criteria amongst surgeons. Initial interventions included education at M&M meetings, monthly reminders to surgical colleagues and retrospective review of previous cases. A second PDSA cycle introduced more structured measures, including involvement of junior doctors in data collection, creation of a shared NELA folder, regular review of M&M cases and on-call lists, and engagement with anaesthetic colleagues to improve case identification. Results Prior to intervention, no NoLap cases were captured. Following the first cycle, three cases were identified retrospectively. After implementation of the second cycle, ten additional NoLap patients were identified over a seven-month period. Awareness of NoLap criteria improved across the multidisciplinary teams and reporting became more consistent and reliable. Conclusion This project demonstrates that simple, low-cost interventions significantly improved recognition and reporting of NoLap patients. Regular education, shared responsibility, and clear systems for data capture were key to success. Furthermore, ongoing engagement and designated ownership are fundamental in sustaining improvements and ensuring accurate national reporting.
affiliations: Dartford and Gravesham NHS Trust

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.487.title: TPTh 6.07 A Multi-disciplinary Approach to Improving Paediatric Major Trauma Tertiary Survey Compliance, a Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.487.abstract: Abstract Aims Tertiary surveys are a key component of paediatric trauma management, designed to identify injuries missed during initial primary and secondary assessments. The South-East Scotland Major Trauma Guidelines recommend tertiary survey completion within 24 hours of admission. This study aimed to assess compliance to this standard and evaluate the impact of targeted interventions, including our multi-disciplinary approach to improve compliance. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted using electronic health record data for paediatric trauma admissions between 01/01/2024 and 30/09/2024 (“2024 audit”). Following this, an educational package was delivered, and major trauma coordinators were empowered to actively enforce completion of tertiary surveys as a discharge pre-requisite and through weekly check-ins. A re-audit was subsequently performed for admissions from 01/01/2025 to 30/11/2025 (“2025 audit”). Data collected included rates of tertiary survey completion, time to completion and identification of evolving injuries. Results 44 patients were identified in 2024 and 172 in 2025. Tertiary survey completion rates improved from 34% (15 of 44) in 2024 to 72% (124 of 172) in 2025. Completion rates within 24 hours also improved, from 20% (3 of 15) to 56% (70 of 124). Median time to completion decreased from 44.5 hours in 2024 (IQR 79; range 15.6–330.9) to 15.9 hours in 2025 (IQR 26; range 1.2-285.7). Identification of patients with evolving injuries remained similar across both cycles (13%). Conclusions Empowerment of major trauma coordinators within the multidisciplinary team significantly improved compliance with tertiary survey completion. However, there remains scope for improvement in timeliness of their completion.
affiliations: Royal Hospital for Children and Young People , Edinburgh

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.268.title: TPT 8.11 One-Stop ERCP-to-Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy for Choledocholithiasis: A District General Hospital Quality Improvement Pathway Delivering Better Flow, Better Experience, and Lower Cost
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.268.abstract: Abstract Aims Choledocholithiasis admissions experience fragmented inpatient care, prolonged length of stay, delayed cholecystectomy, and emergency readmissions. We introduced a “one-stop” pathway providing ERCP followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the same day or within 24 hours via the emergency (CEPOD) list. We evaluated feasibility, patient experience, and cost impact. Methods A service evaluation was conducted over 6 months in a district general hospital. Patients underwent ERCP followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the following day. Outcomes included pathway deliverability within existing emergency theatre scheduling and patient feedback. Cost modelling used local fully absorbed reference costs: bed day £367/day, MRCP £177, elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy £5,969, emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy £8,976. Emergency readmission £1000 and ERCP were estimated at £1,000–£2,000 per procedure. Results Twenty patients completed the one-stop ERCP-to-cholecystectomy pathway. The pathway was deliverable within existing emergency theatre capacity without additional elective resources and was well received by patients, who valued definitive treatment in a single admission and reduced uncertainty regarding waiting timing. Cost modelling demonstrated gross savings of £2,367–£4,367 per patient, driven by avoiding extra bed days and reducing preventable interval events (readmission, repeat ERCP and MRCP). Emergency cholecystectomy incurs additional cost compared with elective surgery (£8,976 vs £5,969). After accounting for this, the pathway remained cost-saving at £1,360 per patient (£27,200 across 20 patients) at the minimum. Conclusions A one-stop ERCP-to-laparoscopic cholecystectomy pathway is feasible and patient-centred in a district general hospital. Despite CEPOD cholecystectomy, it is cost-saving by reducing bed days, readmissions and repeat procedures, with patient satisfaction.
affiliations: George Eliot Hospital

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.235.title: TPT 6.12 From Procedure Metrics to Pathway Governance: Construct Validity of “Documented Discussion of Management Options Prior to Index ERCP” As a Quality Indicator in Bile Duct Stone Disease
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.235.abstract: Abstract Background ERCP quality assurance is moving from procedure metrics to pathway governance. For choledocholithiasis, ERCP and single-stage laparoscopic common bile duct exploration (LCBDE) are both accepted duct-clearance strategies where expertise exists; governance depends on a retrievable record that options were considered before the index procedure. We aimed to develop and evaluate the construct validity of a pragmatic indicator for documented discussion of duct-clearance options before index ERCP and to benchmark performance against contemporaneous LCBDE. Methods Retrospective cohort of all index ERCPs for choledocholithiasis (2023–2024) across two acute hospitals in a UK health board, plus contemporaneous LCBDEs. Indicator: explicit pre-procedure documentation that management options were discussed. Construct validity was assessed using a prespecified argument with hypothesis tests for feasibility, response process, convergent comparator association, and negative controls. Results 356 ERCPs and 38 LCBDEs were included; the indicator was auditable in 100%. ERCP attainment was 20.5% (73/356; 95% CI 16.6% to 25.0). Documentation co-occurred with a specific recorded rationale for not offering LCBDE (100% vs 11.3%; p<0.001) and differed in known-groups comparison (LCBDE 100% vs ERCP 20.5%; p<0.001). Negative controls showed no material associations, supporting bounded interpretation as documentation reliability. Conclusion A feasible indicator with construct validity signals consistent with an auditable documentation bundle at the ERCP decision point. Low attainment for index ERCPs identifies a target for measurement-for-improvement and supports quarterly run-chart monitoring, without conflating documentation with consent quality or clinical outcomes.
affiliations: Department of Upper GI Surgery, University Hospital Hairmyres , East Kilbride, NHS Lanarkshire, Scotland

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.129.title: SP 9.13 Use of National and Local NELA Data for Quality Improvement of EGS Pathways Allows Calculation of Required Provision of CT Capacity for A “Straight to Test” (STT) CT Pathway for Potential Emergency Laparotomy (EL) Patients Presenting in The Emergency Department (ED)
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.129.abstract: Abstract Aims We previously shown failure to identify patients requiring EL triples predicted mortality from first presentation and that an STT CT protocol is possible. National guidelines suggest assessment of EL patients by senior surgeons. NELA annual reports have shown that 1 in 5 EL patients are not referred to EGS from ED. We aimed to estimate the required number of abdominal CT scans needed per day to pick up all the potential adult patients requiring EL by STT CT. Methods Audit 1-week EGS admissions from ED (establish practice and which patients required EGS admission and which did not). Audit 2-weeks ED patients with GI code (assess number of potential STT CT pts). Using those characteristics with NELA data, drew up a pathway and audited two separate 7-day periods to assess pathway validity and utility. Results GS audit: 23 CTs, 50% needed GS admission, 25% another specialty & 25% did not need admission. ED audit 147 pts with GI code, 34 potential EL, 20 had CT, but only 15 referred from ED to GS. STT CT Audit: 139 CT, no discrepancies, 7 EL patients (5%), 134 (96%) changed management, 66 (54%) admissions avoided, 11% new cancers diagnosed. 10 - 12 STT CTs per day needed (1/30,000 population/day), 66 EGS admissions (132 bed days) avoided Conclusions Calculation of STT CT requirement is possible for EL patients & leads to fewer admissions and “missed” EL patients. For those patients not requiring EL diagnosis is confirmed and management changed.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.074.title: SP 6.01 A Human-Factor Intervention Bundle to Improve Rescue Efforts for Post Operative Deteriorating Emergency Surgery Patients – A Pilot Study Using Quality Improvement Approach
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.074.abstract: Abstract Introduction The mortality of emergency laparotomy is decreasing, but remains high. The rescue process for patients deteriorating after emergency surgery is a complex team activity highly prone to error and delay. Human factors interventions are a rational approach to improving the speed and quality of rescue. We used a Human Factors/Quality Improvement approach to design a bundle of HF interventions and embed them in local practice in emergency general surgery units. Methods In a three-hospital study, we tested 4 human factors interventions (patient involvement, team strengthening, standardized communication protocols, and emergency process algorithms for all staff) designed to reduce response times for acutely deteriorating postoperative emergency abdominal surgery patients. We used quality improvement methodology to iteratively enhance the interventions during this pilot study for a proposed randomized trial (RESPOND). We measured response times before, during, and after a 8-month implementation period Results Our preliminary results showed a 40% significant reduction of median response time from 259 minutes (n=83) pre-intervention to 155 minutes (n=70) during intervention to 154 minutes (n=77) post intervention across three sites combined (p=0.014). Each of the 4 strands was modified several times in response to QI feedback. Each of the 4 strands was modified several times in response to QI feedback. Conclusion A bundled human factor-based intervention substantially improved response times for emergency surgery patients with serious postoperative complications. A QI approach to iterative optimization of interventions promotes higher uptake. These results justify a randomized trial of the intervention to determine whether it can reduce mortality.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.197.title: TPT 3.14 Improving the Emergency Surgery Hot Clinic Patient Journey Using a Digital Booking and AI-Supported Patient Education Platform: A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.197.abstract: Abstract Background Emergency Surgery Hot Clinics provide ambulatory follow-up for patients with conditions such as cholecystitis, biliary colic, and unresolved abdominal pain. In our unit, appointment tracking relied on a ward-based register and informal spreadsheets, limiting accessibility and posing confidentiality risks. Patients frequently attended clinic with unresolved informational queries. Aim To improve patient journey, clinician workflow, and confidentiality within the Emergency Surgery Hot Clinic. Methods A clinician-led digital booking and patient-support application was developed and deployed via hotclinicdiary.co.uk. The platform includes a secure clinician login with a live booking calendar for eight daily Hot Clinic slots, replacing paper-based systems. A patient-facing interface provides condition-specific resources and an AI chatbot trained using NICE and WSES guidance. Access is via QR code. Results The digital system improved visibility of clinic capacity, simplified booking, and enhanced confidentiality. The patient-support component addressed common informational queries, reducing clinician workload. The project received Clinical Governance approval and is awaiting Trust Information Governance approval. Conclusion This QIP demonstrates the feasibility of a low-cost digital solution to improve Emergency Surgery Hot Clinic workflows and patient experience.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.128.title: SP 9.12 Assessing Malnutrition Risk and CT-Defined Muscle Quality in Older Emergency Laparotomy Patients
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.128.abstract: Abstract Aims Older patients undergoing emergency colorectal surgery are at high risk of adverse outcomes, yet nutritional screening tools may not capture vulnerability. This study evaluated whether malnutrition risk identified using the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) and muscle quality, assessed by CT-defined psoas muscle density, were associated with 60-day postoperative mortality. Methods A retrospective observational study was conducted at a UK hospital. Patients aged ≥65 years who underwent emergency laparotomy in a 12-month period were included. MUST scores were extracted from clinical records and psoas muscle density (Hounsfield Units, HU) was measured at L3 preoperatively. Associations between muscle quality, MUST category (low vs medium/high) and 60-day mortality were assessed using χ2 and logistic regression with age and sex as covariates. Results In 141 patients (mean age 76.6 years; 46.1% male), 64.5% were classified as medium/high MUST risk with 60-day mortality of 20.6%. In adjusted models, both MUST and psoas muscle density were independently associated with 60-day mortality (p=0.037 for MUST; p=0.003 for muscle density). Patients with medium/high risk MUST scores had higher odds of mortality compared with low-risk patients (adjusted OR 1.85, 95% CI 1.04-3.29). Lower psoas muscle density was associated with increased mortality (adjusted OR 0.911 per 1- unit HU), where each unit increase in muscle density was associated with an 8.9% reduction in mortality odds. Conclusion Older patients presenting for surgery with higher MUST or low muscle quality are at significant risk of mortality at 60 days, demonstrating the importance of early perioperative risk identification.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.238.title: TPT 6.16 Evaluating patient experience of nasogastric tube insertion in acutely admitted surgical patients: Phase 1 of a quality improvement project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.238.abstract: Abstract Objective To assess baseline patient experience of nasogastric tube (NGT) insertion and to justify the use of oral and nasal local anaesthetic in phase II of this project. Methods Phase 1 of this quality improvement project (QIP) was conducted on acute surgical patients needing NGT insertion admitted within an urban tertiary care hospital for four consecutive weeks. A patient questionnaire incorporating Likert-scale items and a numerical rating scale was developed to allow quantitative interpretation of patient-reported experience. Data were collected retrospectively following insertion and summarised descriptively using frequencies, percentages, and median or mean scores to establish baseline experience. Results All 12 patients in study cohort reported the procedure as uncomfortable: 33% somewhat uncomfortable and 67% very uncomfortable. The mean pain score was 6.5/10, corresponding to severe discomfort. Procedural difficulties and adverse effects were common: four required multiple attempts at insertion, seven experienced gagging or vomiting, and five reported coughing. Eight patients (67%) indicated that being offered a topical local anaesthetic spray would have improved tolerability. Conclusion Phase 1 of this QIP successfully demonstrates that NGT insertion without local anaesthetic is associated with universally reported discomfort, high pain scores, and frequent gagging, vomiting, or multiple insertion attempts. Most patients expected that topical local anaesthetic spray would have improved the experience. Given the low risk profile of Lidocaine spray in the throat and nose, Phase 2 of this QIP will replicate the survey with patients that have accepted Lidocaine prior to insertion to evaluate whether routine use improves patient experiences.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.065.title: SP 5.06 Digital Consent Transformation and its Effect on Documentation Quality and Clinical Process: The Largest Multi-Specialty NHS Cohort Study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.065.abstract: Abstract Aims The use of digital consent has been increasing in preference to paper-based consent. Previous studies evaluating digital consent have been small, representing only a few surgical specialties. We aimed to perform the largest study to date evaluating the transformation from paper-based to digital consent forms at an NHS teaching hospital across multiple specialties. Methods An SBRI project (SBRIH19P3055) evaluating consent forms from all specialities was conducted across two phases over a 14-month period. Phase 1 (02/2022-06/2022) assessed the current state of using paper-based consent forms, and Phase 2 (08/2022-08/2023) assessed digital consent forms (Concentric). Forms were assessed for errors, unexplained abbreviations, and whether the consent form or additional information was provided. Results A total of 2866 consent forms were analysed across 16 specialities (Paper-based: 403, Digital: 2463). In the paper-based cohort 95.8% (n=386) of forms had at least one error, compared 0.1% (n=2) in the digital cohort. Unexplained abbreviations accounted in 44.9% (n=163) of paper-based consent forms, in contrast to 2.6% (n=65) in digital. Digital consent increased the practice of providing a copy of the consent form to the patient by 62.2% (Paper: 20.8%, Digital: 83.4%), with additional information provided such as a leaflet increasing by 35.2% (Paper: 18.1%, Digital: 53.3%). Conclusion Digital consent significantly decreased form errors and improved information shared to the patient about their surgery, with those consent forms shared having more patient educational content than paper-based handwritten forms. This should benefit patients by enhancing informed consent and surgeons by providing better medicolegal documentation.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.151.title: SP 11.10 Transanal Irrigation for Low Anterior Resection Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Bowel Function, Quality of Life, and Patient Satisfaction Outcomes
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.151.abstract: Abstract Background Low Anterior Resection Syndrome (LARS) is a frequent complication after rectal cancer surgery, causing bowel dysfunction that significantly affects quality of life. Transanal irrigation (TAI) has been proposed as a management option, but existing evidence is scattered. Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted from inception to October 2025. RCTs were assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool and observational studies with the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. Extracted outcomes included LARS and Wexner scores, bowel symptom severity, fecal incontinence, SF-36 quality-of-life measures, and patient satisfaction using a visual analog scale (VAS). Results Ten studies (483 patients) were included, comprising four RCTs and six observational studies. TAI significantly improved bowel function compared with control. LARS scores were reduced at 3 months (MD = −11.15; 95% CI −15.67 to −6.62) and remained lower up to ≥12 months. Wexner scores improved at 3, 6, and 12 months (MD = −2.18, −2.30, and −2.66). TAI also lessened bowel symptom severity and fecal incontinence at all reported intervals. SF-36 scores improved across key domains, including Physical Functioning (MD = 15.61), General Health (MD = 16.24), and Mental Health (MD = 11.12). Patient satisfaction increased over time, with VAS improvements of 2.0 at 3 months, 4.96 at 6 months, and 5.20 at 12 months. Conclusion TAI provides significant and sustained improvements in bowel function, quality of life, and patient satisfaction in patients with LARS, supporting its use as an effective therapeutic strategy.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.308.title: TPW 2.10 Evaluation of Hospital Menu for Post-Operative Colorectal Patients Against the ESPEN Guideline; A Quality Improvement Project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag087.308.abstract: Abstract Aims Inadequate nutrition in the post-operative period can lead to poor healing, prolonged hospital stay and contribute to sarcopenia. The first stage of this quality improvement project (QIP) compared our institution's patient menu against the energy and protein requirements for post-operative patients recommended in the European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) Guideline. Methods A menu capacity analysis was conducted in collaboration with catering and nutritionist teams. Nutritional analysis of plated and lighter menu options was undertaken to determine minimum and maximum potential daily energy and protein provision. Menu provision was compared with estimated requirements for an average 75 kg patient (energy target 2250 kcal/day and protein target ≥90 g/day). Results Minimum plated and lighter menu options provided 1710–1832 kcal/day and 70.6–81 g protein/day, failing to meet estimated energy and protein requirements. Maximum plated menu options provided 3058 kcal/day and 89.9 g protein/day, meeting energy requirements but remaining borderline for protein, while maximum lighter menu options provided 2748 kcal/day and 78.7 g protein/day, meeting energy but not protein requirements. Snack options particularly contributed minimally to nutritional adequacy. Conclusions Our institution's patient menu can meet an average patient's energy need, if the correct items are chosen, but often falls short of protein recommendations. Encouraging selection of higher-protein plated meals, alongside targeted nutritional interventions such as a protein supplements, may help optimise post-operative protein intake and support recovery. This will be explored in the next phase of this QIP.
affiliations: University Hospital of Derby and Burton NHS

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.063.title: The impact of inhalational versus total intravenous anesthesia on health related quality of life after colon cancer surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.063.abstract: Abstract Introduction Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is a vital endpoint after colorectal cancer surgery. While surgical techniques evolve, the impact of anesthesia—specifically inhalational versus total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA)—on long-term recovery remains unclear. This study evaluated if anesthesia choice independently affects HRQoL at 6 months and identified patient-specific predictors of HRQoL changes for patients with colon cancer. Methods This retrospective study analyzed 339 patients (2012–2016) receiving inhalational (n = 207) or intravenous (n = 132) anesthesia. HRQoL was assessed using EORTC QLQ-C30 at baseline and at 6 months. Group comparisons used Mann-Whitney U tests. Multivariable linear regression, adjusting for age, sex, BMI, ASA, and TNM stage, identified independent predictors for HRQoL changes. Results Univariable analysis using Mann-Whitney U tests showed a trend toward greater cognitive decline in the inhalational group (P = 0.060), and in the multivariable analysis (P = 0.069). Anesthetic technique was not a significant predictor for other domains, including global health (P = 0.888). Higher ASA grade predicted greater decline in physical function (P = 0.003) and role function (P = 0.041). Higher BMI correlated with decreased physical (P = 0.044) and role function (P = 0.005), plus increased pain (P = 0.005). Increased age was associated with higher pain (P = 0.002) but predicted more favorable outcomes for fatigue (P = 0.014) and appetite loss (P = 0.0048). Discussion Anesthetic technique does not broadly influence long-term HRQoL. Outcomes are primarily driven by patient characteristics, specifically BMI and ASA status.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.053.title: Quality of life after conservative versus surgical treatment of acute complicated diverticulitis. Preliminary results from SCANDIV II
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.053.abstract: Abstract Introduction Patient-reported outcomes after acute complicated diverticulitis is poorly described. We evaluated quality of life (QoL) at 30 days and 1-year after conservative versus surgical treatment in the prospective multicenter SCANDIV II cohort. Methods This substudy included patients with acute complicated diverticulitis who completed QoL questionnaires at 30 days and/or 1 year. Disease severity was classified by CT-verified Hinchey stage. Treatment was conservative (antibiotics +/− drainage) or surgical (surgery +/− drainage). QoL was assessed using EQ-5D, GIQLI, and Short Health Scale. Results At 30 days, 363 (70.9%) responded, including 284 (72.1%) of conservatively- and 79 (66.9%) of surgically treated patients. At 1 year, 354 (69.1%) responded, including 284 (72.1%) of conservatively- and 70 (59.3%) of surgically treated patients. Hinchey 3 was more common in the surgical group (48 versus 16%) and Hinchey 2 in the conservative group (54 versus 22%). Conservative treatment was associated with better early QoL. More patients reported no problems with mobility (87 versus 72%, P = 0.003), self-care (98 versus 89%, P < 0.001) and usual activities (83 versus 59%, P < 0.001). GIQLI total score was higher after conservative treatment (99 versus 91, P = 0.010), and SHS showed worse recovery after surgery for activities (P < 0.001) and total score (P = 0.002). At 1-year, most differences had resolved, although GIQLI physical score remained lower after surgery (13 versus 16, P = 0.001). Discussion In acute complicated diverticulitis, surgery was associated with worse early patient-reported recovery than conservative treatment, but most differences had resolved by 1 year. Interpretation should consider greater baseline CT severity in surgically treated patients.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.016.title: Relocating blood sampling for fast-track genetic testing reduces time to surgery in breast cancer: a quality improvement study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.016.abstract: Abstract Introduction Timely completion of preoperative genetic testing is essential for selected breast cancer patients, as results may influence surgical planning and time to definitive treatment. At Stockholm South General Hospital, Stockholm, blood sampling for fast-track genetic testing was previously performed at the oncology clinic several days after the initial surgical consultation, introducing an avoidable delay. In November 2024, blood sampling was relocated to the breast surgery clinic and performed during the first surgical visit. This study aimed to examine whether relocating blood sampling affected genetic turnaround time and time to surgery. Methods This quality improvement study included patients undergoing primary breast cancer surgery with preoperative fast-track genetic testing. The pre-implementation cohort (March 2023–January 2024) followed the oncology-based pathway, and the post-implementation cohort (November 2024–October 2025) followed the updated surgery-based pathway. Primary outcomes were time from test initiation to genetic result and time from initial surgical consultation to surgery. Results Ninety-five patients were included, 37 pre-change and 58 post-change. Pathogenic variants were identified in 12.6% of patients. Following implementation, median time to genetic result decreased from 19 days (IQR 16–21) to 15 days (IQR 14–16). Median time to surgery decreased from 36 days (IQR 28–45) to 25 days (IQR 22–29). Discussion Relocating blood sampling to the surgical clinic eliminated a process-related delay in the preoperative pathway. This single workflow adjustment yielded faster genetic turnaround and a clinically meaningful reduction in time to surgery, highlighting how small structural changes can enhance efficiency in breast cancer care.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.142.title: Longitudinal study on quality of life after pancreaticoduodenectomy—a single centre cohort study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.142.abstract: Abstract Introduction Pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) is associated with substantial morbidity. As survival improves, quality of life (QoL) has become an increasingly important outcome. However, long-term QoL outcomes remains poorly characterized, particularly in longitudinal studies. The aim was to evaluate longitudinal trajectories of QoL in patients undergoing PD. Methods Patients undergoing PD at Skåne University Hospital between 2012–2019, regardless of diagnosis, were identified. Patient-reported outcomes were prospectively collected using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and PAN26 questionnaires preoperatively, one month postoperatively, and more than 5 years after surgery. Patients alive more than 5 years after PD who responded to the 2024 questionnaire were included. Results A total of 70 patients were included, of whom 58 had malignant disease. Among patients with malignancy, approximately half had advanced tumour stage, pT3-pT4 and/or node-positive disease, and adenocarcinoma was the most common diagnosis (n = 54). Clinically relevant deteriorations were observed 1 month after surgery in physical and role functioning, fatigue, appetite loss, digestive symptoms, and taste alterations among some other disease-specific symptoms. Moderate deteriorations were also observed in pain, insomnia, and social functioning, whereas cognitive and emotional functioning remained largely unchanged. At long-term follow-up, most QoL domains had returned to baseline levels or had slightly improved, but satisfaction with healthcare had notably worsened. Discussion QoL after PD decreased considerably in the early postoperative period across both general and disease-specific domains. However, these impairments appeared largely reversible over time, even in this cohort with a high proportion of patients with advanced tumour stages.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.119.title: Generic and gastrointestinal health-related quality of life in children and adolescents with hirschsprung disease: a national cross-sectional study
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.119.abstract: Abstract Introduction Persistent bowel dysfunction in Hirschsprung disease (HSCR) may impair health-related quality of life (HRQoL), yet data on the effects of disease burden on generic and disease-specific HRQoL are limited. This study evaluated generic and gastrointestinal HRQoL in children and adolescents with HSCR and explored risk factors for reduced HRQoL. Methods This national cross-sectional study recruited children and adolescents aged 8–18 years surgically treated for HSCR at pediatric surgery departments in Sweden between 2004 and 2018. Patients and parents completed the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory Generic Core Scales version 4.0 (PedsQLv4.0), the PedsQL Gastrointestinal Symptoms Module (PedsQL GI), and the Rintala Bowel Function Score (BFS). Demographic and clinical data were obtained from medical records. Results Seventy patients were included; 31 were aged 8–12 years and 39 were aged 13–18 years (median age 13 years, IQR 11–16), and 16 had associated malformations or syndromes. Children with normal bowel function (BFS ≥17) reported higher PedsQLv4.0 and PedsQL GI scores than those with impaired bowel function in both child- and parent-reported outcomes (PedsQLv4.0: 93 versus 85, P = 0.010; 90 versus 80, P = 0.014; PedsQL GI: 90 versus 83, P = 0.002; 89 versus 79, P = 0.004). Parent- and child-reported scores showed strong correlations for PedsQLv4.0 (ρ = 0.79) and PedsQL GI (ρ = 0.86). Discussion Despite generally high HRQoL in patients with HSCR, impaired bowel function was associated with reduced generic and gastrointestinal HRQoL, highlighting the importance of long-term bowel function management and psychosocial support.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.005.title: Genetic testing for breast cancer—adherence, outcomes and impact on surgical management: a quality review
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.005.abstract: Abstract Introduction Hereditary breast cancer accounts for approximately 10% of all breast cancer cases. Swedish national breast cancer guidelines specify criteria for germline genetic testing. This quality review aimed to investigate the adherence to these criteria at diagnosis of breast cancer, the prevalence of pathogenic variants and the impact on surgical management. Methods All patients diagnosed with primary breast cancer between July 2023 and June 2024 at Karolinska University Hospital were identified through the Swedish National Quality Register for Breast Cancer. Clinical data was collected from medical records for four groups fulfilling testing criteria: age £40 years, age ≤50 years with bilateral breast cancer or strong family history, patients with triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) and male patients. Results Among 630 identified patients, 138 (22%) met at least one testing criterion. Gene panel testing was completed for 114 patients (87%), and pathogenic variants were detected for 13/114 (11%). Variants were most frequently detected in patients with TNBC (15%), followed by those aged ≤50 years with bilateral disease or strong family history (11%) and those aged ≤40 years (7%), while no variants were found in the male patient. CanRisk risk prediction was performed for 47/114 tested patients (41%). Genetic findings and risk assessment by CanRisk led to modified primary surgical management for 15 patients, with bilateral mastectomy performed in 14 of these cases. Discussion Adherence to national guidelines for genetic testing was high. Pathogenic variants were identified in 11% of the patients, and the results had a substantial impact on surgical decision-making.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.114.title: Structured follow-up of endocrine therapy in breast cancer three months after treatment initiation: a clinical quality improvement project
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znag093.114.abstract: Abstract Introduction Women treated with endocrine therapy (ET) after breast cancer often experience side effects that negatively impact quality of life and daily functioning. It is well known that these side effects contribute to many patients discontinuing treatment prematurely, potentially affecting prognosis. Structured support and clear information regarding side effects, self-care, and available interventions are therefore essential. Before the quality improvement project, patients were called by phone approximately three months after starting ET to evaluate side effects, but without a scheduled appointment. This resulted in irregular contact and insufficient preparation on the part of the patients. Methods In collaboration between contact nurses, medical secretaries, and the unit manager, work schedules were reorganized to enable scheduled telephone appointments for follow-up of side effects. Procedures were established to ensure that patients receive a booked telephone appointment and complete the Assessment of Rehabilitation Needs Checklist prior to the phone call. A conversation structure was developed to systematically assess side effects, rehabilitation needs, and return to daily life. Results All patients prescribed ET are now offered a scheduled telephone appointment. This has enabled more consistent and structured follow-up of the treatment, as well as identification of rehabilitation needs. Individual needs can be identified and person-centered interventions initiated and followed up. The work environment for contact nurses has improved through scheduled calls and continuity is strengthened. Discussion Through team collaboration and structural changes, contact nurses stress has been reduced, ET follow-up has improved, and the ability to identify and address rehabilitation needs has increased.
affiliations: Department of Breast Surgery, Skane University Hospital , Malmö ,

DOI:10.1302/1358-992x.2023.3.046.title: HIP FRACTURES IN THE OLDER ADULT: ORTHOPAEDIC AND GERIATRIC SHARED CARE MODEL IN SOUTHLAND: A FIVE-YEAR FOLLOW-UP AUDIT
DOI:10.1302/1358-992x.2023.3.046.abstract: Fractures of the neck of femur are common in the older adult with significant morbidity and mortality rates. This patient cohort is associated with frailty and multiple complex medical and social needs requiring a multidisciplinary team to provide optimal care. The aim of this study was to assess the outcomes at 5 years following implementation of a collaborative service between the Orthopaedic and Geriatric departments of Southland Hospital in 2012. Retrospective data was collected for patients aged 65 years and older who were admitted with a fragility hip fracture. Data was collated for 2011 (pre-implementation) and 2017 (post-implementation). Demographics and ASA scores were recorded. We assessed 30-day and 1-year mortality, surgical data, length of stay and complications. There were 74 patient admissions in 2011 and 107 in 2017. Mean age at surgery was 84.2 years in 2011 and 82.6 years in 2017 (p>0.05). Between the 2011 and 2017 groups there has been a non-significant reduction in length of stay on the orthopaedic ward (9.8 days vs 7.5 days, p=0.138) but a significant reduction in length of stay on the rehabilitation ward (19.9 vs 9 days, p<0.001). There was a significant decrease in frequency of patients with a complication (71.6% vs 57%, p=0.045) and a marginal reduction in number of complications (p=0.057). Through logistic regression controlling for age, sex and ASA score, there was a reduction in the odds of having a complication by 12% between 2011 and 2017 (p<0.001). There was no difference in mortality between the groups. The orthogeriatric model of care at Southland Hospital appears to have reduced both the frequency of complications and length of stay on the rehabilitation ward 5 years after its implementation. This is the first study in New Zealand demonstrating medium-term post-implementation follow-up of what is currently a nationally accepted standard model of care.

DOI:10.1302/1358-992x.2023.4.006.title: A VIRTUAL FRACTURE CLINIC AUDIT: ARE WALES MATCHING THE OUTCOMES IN ENGLAND?
DOI:10.1302/1358-992x.2023.4.006.abstract: Introduction Virtual fracture clinics (VFC's) aim to reduce the number of outpatient appointments while improving the clinical effectiveness and patients experience through standardisation of treatment pathways. With 4.6% of ED admissions due to trauma the VFC prevents unnecessary face to face appointments providing a cost savings benefit to the NHS. Methods This project demonstrates the importance of efficient VFC process in reducing the burden on the fracture clinics. We completed preformed a retrospective cross-sectional study, analysing two cycles in May (n=305) and September (n=332) 2021. We reviewed all VFC referrals during this time assessing the quality of the referral, if they went on to require a face to face follow up and who the referring health care professional was. Following the cycle in May we provided ongoing education to A&E staff before re-auditing in September. Results Between the two cycles there was an average 19% improvement in quality of the referrals, significant reduction in number of inappropriate referrals for soft tissue knee and shoulder injuries from 15.1% (n=50) to 4.5% (n=15) following our intervention. There was an 8% increase in number of fracture clinic appointments to 74.4% (n=247), primarily due to an increase number of referrals from nurse practitioners. Radial head fractures were targeted as one group that were able to be successfully managed in VFC, despite this 64% (n=27) of patients were still seen in the outpatient department following VFC referral. Conclusion Despite the decrease in the number of inappropriate referrals, and the increase in quality of referrals following our intervention. The percentage of VFC referrals in CAVUHB is still higher than other centres in with established VFCs in England. This possibly highlights the need for further education to emergency staff around describing what injuries are appropriate for referral, specifically soft tissue injuries and radial head fractures. In order to optimise the VFC process and provide further cost savings benefits while reducing the strain on fracture clinics.
